This study proposes a rare double-ray scenario involving light resonant scattering by a periodic metasurface designed to generate robust non-specular reflection. The metasurface consists of an array of silicon nanodisks situated on a thin silica-on-metal substrate. Numerical simulations of light scattering demonstrate low-loss, non-specular resonant reflection for incident waves of any direction and polarization. The requirements for implementing an autocollimation scattering scheme and observing a non-specular reflected ray outside the plane of incidence have been established. Furthermore, adjusting the thickness of the dielectric substrate allows for tuning the bandwidth of non-specular reflection. Finally, the intensity of both specular and non-specular reflected rays can be regulated by varying the angle of incidence or the polarization of the incoming wave.

We introduce novel differential privacy frameworks designed for scenarios where data products must simultaneously satisfy external \emph{invariants} and \emph{integer} constraints. Such requirements are critical in real-world private data curation tasks, exemplified by the public release of the 2020 U.S. Decennial Census, yet they present significant obstacles to generating data products that are both provably private and statistically useful. To rigorously define privacy guarantees under these dual conditions, we propose \emph{integer subspace differential privacy} and establish its composition and post-processing properties. To overcome the difficulty of sampling from highly restricted discrete spaces, we develop two unbiased additive mechanisms—generalized Laplace and generalized Gaussian mechanisms—by solving the Diophantine equations imposed by the constraints. These mechanisms offer high accuracy, characterized by error distributions with sub-exponential and sub-Gaussian tail probabilities, respectively. For implementation, we design an MCMC algorithm and provide empirical convergence validation using estimated upper bounds on total variation distance derived from $L$-lag coupling. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through applications to a synthetic problem involving intersecting invariants, a sensitive contingency table with fixed margins, and 2010 Census county-level data subject to mandatory fixed state population totals.

Basic categories like animals and furniture are typically learned early in life and are essential for processing, organizing, and sharing knowledge about the world. These categories are universal across cultures, enabling efficient representation of worldly complexity while reflecting a strong communal consensus on their nature, indicative of shared mental models. However, existing models of category learning and representation are often validated using small-scale experiments with limited concepts and artificial features, predominantly involving participants from specific cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds, frequently Western English speakers such as U.S. college students. This study examines whether categorization models generalize to (a) rich, noisy data that mirrors real-world human environments and (b) across different languages and cultures. We introduce a Bayesian cognitive model capable of jointly learning categories and their structured representations from natural language text, which facilitates (a) large-scale performance evaluation and (b) application across a diverse linguistic spectrum. Our findings demonstrate that meaningful categories encompassing hundreds of concepts and richly structured feature representations emerge consistently across languages. This work highlights the potential of recent advancements in computational modeling and large-scale naturalistic datasets for advancing cognitive science research.

Electronic Mott insulators have driven significant research in condensed-matter physics because of their complex connection to high-temperature superconductivity. While Mott phases have recently been demonstrated in atomic systems for both fermions and bosons, a solid-state signature of a Mott insulator composed of bosons has remained elusive. In this study, we reveal such a signature by investigating the Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonian through semiconductor excitons trapped within two-dimensional lattices. We focus on the regime where on-site interactions are similar to the energy spacing between confined lattice states. Our observations confirm that Mott phases are achievable, featuring uniform filling of lattice sites with up to two excitons. Furthermore, our methodology enables the on-demand programming of the exciton-confining lattice geometry. This adaptability, coupled with the long-range dipolar interactions inherent to excitons, opens a new pathway to investigate many-body phases that spontaneously break lattice symmetry.

This study examines the exclusive electroproduction of $\pi^-\Delta^{++}$ using the handbag framework, where helicity amplitudes decompose into hard partonic interactions and generalized parton distributions (GPDs). We introduce the $p-\Delta$ transversity GPDs, adopting helicity non-flip GPDs from existing literature. To estimate observables numerically, we apply large-$N_C$ results to connect specific $p-\Delta$ GPDs with proton-proton counterparts, while disregarding others. In computing twist-2 and twist-3 subprocess amplitudes, we incorporate quark transverse momenta alongside Sudakov suppressions. Finally, we predict the partial cross sections for $\gamma^*p\to \pi^-\Delta^{++}$ within the large-$N_C$ limit.

Quantum walks serve as potent instruments for developing quantum search and sampling algorithms, specifically those designed to construct quantum stationary states. However, the success probabilities of these algorithms are significantly distant from unity. While amplitude amplification is typically employed to boost success rates, it introduces the "soufflé" problem. Achieving maximum probability requires stopping at the precise moment; otherwise, increasing the step count can cause the success probability to decline, creating practical challenges when the optimal step count is unknown. In this study, we introduce generalized interpolated quantum walks, capable of enhancing the success probability of search algorithms while circumventing the soufflé problem. By integrating generalized interpolated quantum walks with quantum fast-forwarding, we reduce the number of walk operator calls for search algorithms from $\Theta((\varepsilon^{-1})\sqrt{\Heg})$ to $\Theta(\log(\varepsilon^{-1})\sqrt{\Heg})$ and decrease the required ancilla qubits from $\Theta(\log(\varepsilon^{-1})+\log\sqrt{\Heg})$ to $\Theta(\log\log(\varepsilon^{-1})+\log\sqrt{\Heg})$. This combination improves success probability and eliminates the soufflé problem, where $\varepsilon$ represents precision and $\Heg$ denotes the classical hitting time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that generalized interpolated quantum walks can enhance the construction of quantum states corresponding to stationary distributions. Finally, we present an application utilizing generalized interpolated quantum walks to build a slowly evolving Markov chain sequence, a prerequisite for adiabatic stationary state preparation.

This study utilizes the functional renormalization group method to analyze a $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric gauge theory featuring a quiral superfield interacting with a vector $U(1)$ superfield. Our results confirm that the nonrenormalization theorem remains valid at the leading order of the supercovariant derivative expansion. Additionally, we derive the beta functions and examine the fixed point behavior under a local potential approximation, with a discussion on the employed regulators.

The lattice size $\operatorname{ls_\Delta}(P)$ of a lattice polytope $P$ serves as a crucial invariant; although it was formally defined in the context of bounding the total and bi-degrees of algebraic curve equations, it has appeared implicitly in geometric combinatorics prior to that. This paper demonstrates that for any empty lattice polytope $P\subset\mathbb{R}^3$, there exists a reduced basis of $\mathbb{Z}^3$ capable of calculating its lattice size $\operatorname{ls_\Delta}(P)$. This finding enables a rapid algorithm for determining $\operatorname{ls_\Delta}(P)$ in such cases. Furthermore, the result is extended to another category of lattice width one polytopes $P\subset\mathbb{R}^3$. Finally, a counterexample is presented to show that this property does not apply to arbitrary lattice width one lattice polytopes $P\subset\mathbb{R}^3$.

In 2017, Colorado implemented risk-limiting tabulation audits (RLAs) statewide, utilizing both ballot-level comparison and ballot-polling techniques. However, these audits were limited to contests contained within a single county, as methods for efficiently auditing multi-county contests that integrate both polling and comparison strategies were unavailable. Consequently, Colorado's existing audit software (RLATool) requires enhancement to handle cross-county contests and to process small contests more efficiently. This paper addresses those gaps by introducing extremely simple yet inefficient methods, more efficient hybrid approaches combining ballot polling and ballot-level comparisons via stratified sampling, and alternative methods that merge ballot-level comparison with variable-size batch comparisons without relying on stratified sampling. The study concludes with recommendations and illustrates the proposed method through examples comparing it to current practices. Additionally, open-source code and interactive Jupyter notebooks are provided to implement these methods and facilitate further investigation.

Recent self-supervised approaches have achieved feature representations comparable to those from full supervision, offering benefits such as enhanced robustness and out-of-distribution detection. This paper presents an empirical investigation into how self-supervision, when used as a pre-training strategy or integrated into adversarial training, influences a model's resilience against $l_2$ and $l_{\infty}$ adversarial attacks as well as natural image corruptions. While self-supervision can boost robustness, the nuances are critical. Merely combining self-supervision loss with adversarial training improves accuracy only for perturbations smaller than or equal to the training budget ($\epsilon_{train}$); however, accuracy declines when evaluated at test perturbations ($\epsilon_{test}$) greater than $\epsilon_{train}$. Notably, increasing the weight of the self-supervision loss exacerbates this performance drop, ultimately harming robustness. We examine various methods for integrating self-supervision into adversarial training and find that optimizing both network parameters and adversarial examples simultaneously using self-supervised loss yields the most significant robustness gains, effectively acting as ensemble adversarial training. Although self-supervised pre-training outperforms random initialization in aiding adversarial training, incorporating self-supervision directly into the adversarial training process offers no advantage for model robustness or accuracy.

This note serves as a follow-up to Shu-Xue-Yao's work \cite{BYY}, which examined enhanced groups and associated dualities within type $A$. Here, we extend the investigation of enhanced dualities to classical groups of types $B$, $C$, and $D$. To achieve this, we first define an enhanced Brauer algebra. Leveraging Proposition \ref{B dual}, we readily derive restricted and Levi dualities, thereby naturally characterizing parabolic duality. Furthermore, Section \S\ref{3} presents a specific instance through explicit computations.

Bayesian optimization typically requires an "inner optimization" step over a non-convex, highly multi-modal, and potentially non-differentiable acquisition function, which often hinders local numerical optimizers. In these scenarios, it is standard practice to substitute continuous search with a discrete approach using randomly generated candidates. This work introduces the use of candidates derived from a Delaunay triangulation of the current input design. We outline the methodology for constructing these "tricands" and provide empirical evidence demonstrating that they surpass both numerically optimized acquisitions and random candidate alternatives. Furthermore, we show their suitability for hybrid schemes through benchmark synthetic and real-world simulation experiments.

Quantum control techniques for three-level systems have recently emerged as a pivotal area of inquiry within quantum information science and technology. This study presents numerical simulations employing realistic experimental parameters to investigate quantum process tomography in both STIRAP (stimulated Raman adiabatic passage) and saSTIRAP (superadiabatic STIRAP). We determine an appropriate basis within operator space, consisting of the identity operator and the eight Gell-Mann operators, to compute the associated process matrices, which contain 81 elements ($9 \times 9$). Furthermore, we analyze these findings under two conditions: an ideal decoherence-free scenario and a more practical case that incorporates decoherence.

This document summarizes the most recent ATLAS experiment findings regarding top-quark pair production accompanied by a photon, utilizing proton-proton collision data from the LHC at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy. The report covers measurements of both inclusive and differential cross-sections within a fiducial volume aligned with experimental acceptance, specifically for single-lepton and dilepton final states.

We have discovered a novel cosmological signal, the Doppler-boosted Cosmic Infrared Background (DB-CIB), which originates from the peculiar motions of galaxies emitting thermal dust that constitutes the cosmic infrared background (CIB). This new observable serves as an independent probe of the cosmic velocity field and is closely analogous to the established kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) effect. Notably, DB-CIB avoids the 'kSZ optical depth degeneracy,' rendering it immune to the intricate astrophysics of galaxy formation. We predict that the DB-CIB effect will be detectable through cross-correlations between CCAT-Prime and DESI-like experiments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that DB-CIB functions as a new CMB foreground that could bias future kSZ cross-correlations if not adequately addressed.

Multi-agent Markov Decision Processes (MMDPs) serve as a robust framework for modeling sequential decision-making in cooperative multi-agent settings, with numerous centralized and decentralized planning algorithms developed to address them. However, the exponential growth of state and joint action spaces, combined with dynamic environmental changes, often hinders these methods from achieving both efficiency and scalability. While recent algorithms like the centralized FV-MCTS-MP and the decentralized *Alternate maximization with Behavioural Cloning* (ABC) have demonstrated strong performance, they fail to adapt to dynamic environments and lack mechanisms for agent communication, respectively. To address these limitations, we propose SiCLOP, a simulation-based online planning algorithm designed for cooperative multi-agent environments. SiCLOP integrates Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with Coordination Graphs (CG) and Graph Neural Networks (GCN) to learn cooperation strategies and deliver real-time solutions. Furthermore, it enhances scalability via effective action space pruning. Unlike its predecessors, SiCLOP incorporates transfer learning, allowing agents to operate effectively across different environments. We also present a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's convergence within multi-agent contexts. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that SiCLOP significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art online planning algorithms.

We introduce the 1-100 GeV spectral energy distribution (SED) for 148 recently identified high-synchrotron-peaked blazars (HSPs) from the First Brazil-ICRANet Gamma-ray Blazar catalogue (1BIGB). The majority of these 1BIGB sources are absent from prior Fermi-LAT catalogues, marking their gamma-ray spectral characteristics as a novel contribution and a substantial expansion of the known gamma-ray blazar population. Given that the sample was initially selected based on excess signals within the 0.3-500 GeV range, these objects are promising candidates for very-high-energy (VHE) emission, potentially observable by the upcoming CTA observatory. Our flux estimates utilize PASS8 data, integrating over more than nine years of Fermi-LAT observations. Additionally, we revisit the full broadband fit between 0.3-500 GeV originally presented in the 1BIGB study, updating the power-law parameters with the latest Fermi-LAT dataset. We evaluate the significance of these sources for VHE population studies involving both current instruments and the future CTA. To assess their detectability, we extrapolate the gamma-ray SEDs of a selected subsample to the highest energies, accounting for extragalactic background light absorption, and compare these extrapolations against published CTA sensitivity curves. Two specific sources, 1BIGB J224910.6-130002 and 1BIGB J194356.2+211821, are examined in detail. All gamma-ray SEDs, presented here for the first time, are made publicly accessible through the Brazilian Science Data Center (BSDC) service at CBPF in Rio de Janeiro.

This report outlines the findings of the Computational Frontier topical group regarding end-user analysis for Snowmass 2021. End-user analysis involves deriving physics results from reconstructed and simulated experimental data. High-energy physics experiments generate systems capable of performing shared reconstruction, calibration, and simulation tasks, which produce common data samples. These detailed samples are subsequently reduced into various analysis samples, often optimized for specific physics topics through trigger or data object selection. Analyzers (end users) then process these samples to generate physics results. Community consensus categorized the end-user analysis ensemble into five key areas: Analysis Ecosystems, Analysis Models, Dataset Bookkeeping and Formats, Collaborative Software, and Training. The following findings and recommendations address how these critical areas influence end-user analysis.

We establish that for smooth projective families of varieties with a good minimal model, the variation provides a lower bound for the base's Kodaira dimension when the base dimension is five or less and its Kodaira dimension is non-negative. This result confirms the Kebekus–Kovács conjecture for base spaces of dimension at most five.

The Xacro XML macro language expands upon the Universal Robot Description Format (URDF) and serves as a vital component of the toolchain that transforms geometric models into simulations, visualizations, and operational systems. Nevertheless, robotics community members, particularly those new to the field, often find it difficult to grasp the interaction between various systems and the Xacro preprocessing workflow. To investigate the specific challenges developers face with Xacro, we conducted a manual analysis of 712 related queries from http://answers.ros.org. Using a systematic qualitative method known as Open Coding, we categorized these misunderstandings into 10 primary groups. Furthermore, by analyzing the tags associated with these questions, we discovered that Xacro issues arise across an unexpectedly wide array of contexts. This diversity obstructs the onboarding process and complicates developers' comprehension of representations and tools within the Robot Operating System. Our objective is to establish an empirical foundation that identifies and ranks the barriers faced by users of open robotics systems, thereby enabling tool designers, educators, and practitioners to develop strategies for enhancing robot software tooling and education.

RGB-infrared person re-identification represents a challenging cross-modality task primarily due to the substantial differences between visible and infrared imagery. To address this, we introduce a novel method called Modality-Invariant Decomposition (MID), which combines modality-adaptive mixup with invariant decomposition to learn representations that are both discriminative and invariant across modalities. The proposed mixup strategy generates appropriate blended images between RGB and infrared data to reduce pixel-level discrepancies by formulating the mixing process as a Markov decision process. Within a deep reinforcement learning framework, an actor-critic agent learns a dynamic and locally linear interpolation policy for different image regions, ensuring continuous latent space invariance and preventing manifold corruption from mixed samples. Additionally, to further bridge the modality gap and maintain consistent visual semantics at the feature level, MID utilizes modality-adaptive convolution decomposition, which splits standard convolution layers into modality-specific basis layers and a shared coefficient layer. Comprehensive experiments on two difficult benchmarks confirm that MID outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

We classify complete orientable hypersurfaces with constant isotropic curvature within space forms. Our results demonstrate that such a hypersurface possesses constant mean curvature exclusively when it is isoparametric. Furthermore, we establish that minimality occurs if and only if the hypersurface is either totally geodesic or corresponds to the Clifford minimal hypersurface ${\mathbb S}^{3}(\frac{4c}{3})\times {\mathbb S}^{1}(4c)$ embedded in ${\mathbb S}^{5}(c)$.

This paper investigates algebraic invariants associated with the Stanley-Reisner rings of Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes of dimension $d-1$. We establish that for any $(d-1)$-dimensional Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complex $\Delta$ where $\Delta=\mathrm{core}(\Delta)$, the inequality $d \leq \mathrm{reg}(\Delta) \cdot \mathrm{type}(\Delta)$ is valid, with $\mathrm{reg}(\Delta)$ and $\mathrm{type}(\Delta)$ representing the Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity and Cohen-Macaulay type of the Stanley-Reisner ring $\Bbbk[\Delta]$, respectively. Furthermore, given any integers $d, r, t$ such that $r, t \geq 2$ and $r \leq d \leq rt$, we construct a Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complex $\Delta(G)$, defined as an independent complex of a graph $G$, satisfying $\dim(\Delta(G))=d-1$, $\mathrm{reg}(\Delta(G))=r$, and $\mathrm{type}(\Delta(G))=t$.

We introduce a new framework known as cone holography, which establishes a codimension-n duality between a gravitational theory in a $(d+1)$-dimensional conical spacetime and a Conformal Field Theory (CFT) residing on $(d+1-n)$-dimensional defects. Much like wedge holography, this construction emerges as the zero-volume limit of a holographic defect CFT. Notably, cone holography serves as the dual description of edge modes located on these defects. For a specific class of solutions, we demonstrate the equivalence between cone holography and AdS/CFT by proving that the classical gravitational action—and consequently the CFT partition function in the large $N$ limit—remains identical for both theories. However, in general, the two frameworks differ due to the presence of infinite towers of massive Kaluza-Klein modes on the branes. To validate our proposal, we examine the Weyl anomaly, entanglement and Rényi entropies, and correlation functions, observing strong agreement between the holographic predictions and CFT calculations. Specifically, the cone holography satisfies the $c$-theorem, providing robust support for the model. We further investigate two boundary conditions, namely the mixed and Neumann conditions, showing that both yield a consistent theory. Additionally, our analysis of the brane mass spectrum reveals that higher tension results in a more continuous mass distribution. As a generalization of wedge holography and a concept closely tied to defect CFTs, entanglement entropy, and AdS/BCFT, cone holography is anticipated to have broad applicability.

This study examines measurements within Rindler's frame, yielding a geometric and gravitational understanding of light speed, mass, and the uncertainty principle. These findings can be viewed as readings from a universal black hole clock, which facilitates a mathematically consistent emergence of a timeless gravitational state. Essentially, this suggests that space may constitute frozen time.

Pansharpening is a critical challenge in remote sensing. This study introduces a side information partially guided convolutional sparse coding (SCSC) model designed for pansharpening. The core concept involves decomposing a low-resolution multispectral image into two feature maps: one related to the panchromatic image and another unrelated to it, with the former being regularized using panchromatic side information. By applying algorithm unrolling principles, this model is extended into a deep neural network termed the SCSC pansharpening neural network (SCSC-PNN). Numerical experiments conducted on three satellites against 13 classic and state-of-the-art methods demonstrate that SCSC-PNN outperforms the other approaches. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/xsxjtu/SCSC-PNN.

To effectively leverage machine learning for better patient outcomes, understanding decision-making within clinical settings is critical. However, challenges such as limited public data, the offline nature of the problem, and the intricacy of human choices have led mainstream algorithm development to prioritize tasks that do not translate well to healthcare, often neglecting specific niche issues. To address this, we introduce Medkit-Learn(ing) Environment, a new, publicly available Python benchmarking suite tailored for medical sequential decision making. This package offers high-fidelity synthetic data through a straightforward interface, providing a standardized framework for evaluating algorithms in realistic medical scenarios. Furthermore, our generation process disentangles policy and environment dynamics, allowing for extensive customization and enabling a systematic assessment of an algorithm's robustness against distinct healthcare challenges.

Image registration presents an inherently ill-posed challenge due to the absence of constraints required for a unique voxel-to-voxel mapping, necessitating regularization to ensure physically meaningful transformations. This regularization penalty typically relies on derivatives of the displacement-vector field and can be computed either analytically or numerically. While the numerical method is computationally intensive relative to image size, a more efficient analytical framework has been devised. By employing cubic B-splines as the registration transform, we established a generalized mathematical framework supporting five distinct regularizers: diffusion, curvature, linear elastic, third-order, and total displacement. We validated this approach by comparing the accuracy of each method against its numerical equivalent. Furthermore, benchmarking results demonstrate that the proposed analytical solutions execute significantly faster—up to two orders of magnitude—compared to finite-differencing-based numerical implementations.

Word sense disambiguation (WSD) techniques determine the most appropriate meaning of a word based on its specific context. Unlike neural network-based WSD methods, which depend on sense-annotated corpora rather than lexical resources, this study leverages both contextual data and related gloss information to model the semantic connection between a target word and a set of glosses. We introduce SensPick, a stacked bidirectional Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) network designed for WSD. Experimental results indicate that SensPick surpasses both traditional and state-of-the-art models on most benchmark datasets, achieving a 3.5% relative improvement in F-1 score. Although the gain is modest, integrating semantic relationships positions SensPick as a leading approach compared to existing alternatives.

This study implements matching time estimators to calculate both entropy rate and entropy production rate for symbolic sequences. These estimators rely on recurrence properties, which are particularly effective for testing irreversibility in sequences exhibiting strong correlations or memory. By applying limit theorems for matching times, we develop a maximum likelihood estimator for entropy rate suitable for sets of moderately short, finite-duration symbolic time series. We demonstrate that this estimator is well-suited for assessing entropy rate and production (or testing irreversibility) across sample sequences of varying lengths, such as DNA coding sequences. The method is validated using controlled Markov chain examples and applied to genomic data, revealing that the irreversibility in human DNA coding sequences is significantly higher than in non-coding sequences.

Memristors have demonstrated significant potential for advancing neuromorphic computing and AI hardware accelerators. This paper introduces a user-friendly software infrastructure designed to emulate various neuromorphic architectures using memristor models. The tool facilitates research into online learning and classification tasks by simulating resistive state changes during training. Its versatility is highlighted by the ability to customize parameters within memristor and neuronal models, as well as learning rules, enabling users to validate concepts and assess their sensitivity across diverse settings. We illustrate the tool's application through an MNIST classification task. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the tool can emulate studied concepts in silico by interfacing with commercially available characterization tools to represent practical memristive devices.

We introduce a straightforward mathematical framework to model the progression of violent offenses. This approach utilizes a system of ordinary differential equations that incorporate the counts of violent crimes alongside both legal and illicit firearms. The system's behavior is driven by probabilistic factors, such as law enforcement activities and the risk perceptions that encourage civilians to acquire legal weapons. Our analytical and numerical findings indicate that while illegal guns contribute to rising criminality, an increase in legally owned firearms accelerates the surge in violent crimes. This suggests that allowing civilians access to guns is an ineffective strategy for crime control.

The charge properties of Andreev bound states (ABSs) within a three-terminal semiconductor-superconductor hybrid nanowire were investigated via local and nonlocal tunneling spectroscopy. This device was constructed from an epitaxial InAs/Al two-dimensional heterostructure incorporating multiple gate-defined side probes. Measurements revealed that ABSs oscillate near zero as a function of gate voltage, with charge variations aligning with theoretical predictions for the total Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) charge of these states.

The practical applications of braids are extensive, stemming from their deep relationship with dynamics established by the Nielsen-Thurston classification theorem. These applications include identifying coherent structures and mixing zones in ocean currents, optimizing industrial mixing equipment, analyzing the mechanics of taffy pullers, and describing chaotic movements in active nematics. In all these cases, mixing is fundamental, and the associated braids provide a metric for efficiency known as topological entropy per operation (TEPO). This leads to the inquiry of what the maximum mixing efficiency is and which braids achieve it; the answer relies on the specific definition of braids used. While standard Artin presentations have identified maximal braids with efficiencies tied to the golden and silver ratios, surface braids offer a valuable generalization using Artin-like generators on embedded graphs. This study presents a streamlined algorithm for calculating TEPO and topological entropy for surface braids on any pairing of orientable surfaces and planar graphs. Focusing on planar lattice graphs due to their symmetry and ability to naturally model planar point motion, we conduct a thorough search for a braid with maximal mixing efficiency, proposing a novel candidate that we conjecture holds this property.

Smart weight scales enhance basic weight tracking by offering bioimpedance-based body composition analysis, a feature promoted by companies like Withings and Fitbit as a means to foster self-knowledge and informed decision-making. However, these optimistic claims overlook the fact that the resulting data relies on proprietary regression equations that necessitate a binary sex/gender input. This paper integrates personal narratives informed by transgender studies with an examination of the scientific underpinnings of the bioimpedance technology used in Withings scales. We demonstrate that attempting to accommodate nonbinary individuals exposes the inherently physiologically unstable foundations of bioelectrical impedance analysis. While White nonbinary people represent only a small fraction of those who may discover their smart scales fail to accurately reflect their bodies, the issue of including trans and nonbinary individuals in personal health technology extends far beyond simply adding a third gender option or displaying a rainbow flag. Furthermore, we offer recommendations for developing more inclusive technologies, even when constrained by exclusionary datasets.

The study establishes that for elliptic pseudo-differential operators with symbols defined on $\Z^n\times \mathbb{T}^n$, the minimal and maximal operators are identical, with their domain characterized by a Sobolev space. Furthermore, for pseudo-differential operators on $\Z^n$, ellipticity and Fredholmness are demonstrated to be equivalent conditions, and the index of such an elliptic operator is calculated.

We propose a specific theoretical framework for identifying topological phase transitions in double-kicked atom-optics rotors possessing an internal spin-1/2 degree of freedom. This approach employs a one-dimensional momentum-space evolution of a kicked Bose-Einstein condensate. To mitigate the effects of atom loss and phase decoherence, we prioritize short experimental durations within a resonant protocol. Furthermore, we account for experimental constraints arising from phase noise, quasimomentum distributions, symmetries, and the AC-Stark shift. Consequently, our findings indicate a viable and optimized method for detecting topological phase transitions in quantum kicked rotors.

This master's thesis provides an overview of $A_\infty$-algebras and homological perturbation theory. It further examines the formality of compact K\"ahler manifolds and offers a direct proof of the homotopy transfer principle for $A_\infty$-algebras, commonly referred to as Kadeishvili's Theorem.

Weyl's conformal gravity extends Einstein's general relativity by linking metrics to 1-forms. When these 1-forms are locally integrable yet closed but not exact, the resulting spacetime manifolds lose simple connectivity. The associated Weyl connections produce curvature tensors that adhere to the fundamental characteristics of Riemann curvature tensors. These Ricci tensors are symmetric and conformally invariant, while the Einstein tensors derived from Weyl connections introduce a cosmological term that substitutes the standard constant with a spacetime-dependent function and a shear stress tensor. A toy model utilizing the Schwarzschild metric is introduced, where the corresponding 1-form is proportional to $d\varphi$ in Schwarzschild coordinates. This configuration results in a singularity along the entire z-axis and induces a torque effect on geodesics. Under specific initial conditions, planar geodesics maintain nearly constant velocities regardless of the radial distance $r$. In the absence of external forces, spin effects manifest near the singularity, aligning with recent observations regarding cosmic filaments.

Active learning has become a standard approach for domains like medicine, where labeled training data is scarce. Similarly, language models have become the preferred solution for many natural language tasks due to their performance improvements. However, these models often struggle in fields with limited labeled data and face challenges when class imbalance is present. In such scenarios, active learning can significantly enhance performance within a constrained label budget. To address this, we introduce ALLWAS, a novel method that combines submodular optimization and optimal transport for active learning in language models. Our approach constructs a sampling strategy by optimizing a specific objective in the gradient domain using submodular principles. Additionally, to facilitate learning from few samples, we develop a new strategy for sampling from Wasserstein barycenters. Empirical evaluations on standard text classification benchmarks demonstrate that our method outperforms existing active learning approaches for language models, achieving a relative performance increase of over 20% in some instances.

(Abridged) Blue compact galaxies (BCGs) represent low-luminosity, metal-poor, gas-rich systems undergoing rapid star formation, serving as ideal analogs for high-redshift star-forming galaxies. As low-mass starbursts, they provide excellent laboratories for studying star formation and massive stellar feedback. This study utilizes Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE) integral field spectroscopy to analyze the BCG Haro 14. The instrument's extensive field of view allows for simultaneous observation of both the starburst region and the host galaxy. We constructed galaxy maps using continuum data and emission lines, derived synthetic VRI images, and generated corresponding color index maps and surface brightness profiles. Our analysis revealed numerous clumps distributed throughout the galaxy in both continuum and emission line data, leading to a catalog detailing their positions, sizes, and photometry. This investigation enabled a detailed examination of Haro 14's morphology and stellar populations. The stellar distribution exhibits significant asymmetry, with the continuum intensity peak displaced approximately 500 parsecs southwest of the stellar host center. At this peak location, a bright stellar cluster with an absolute magnitude of M$_{V}=-12.18$ suggests a strong super star cluster candidate. Additionally, we identified a highly asymmetric, blue, non-ionizing stellar component occupying nearly the entire eastern portion of the galaxy. We conclude that Haro 14 contains at least three distinct stellar populations: a current starburst roughly 6 million years old; an intermediate-age component ranging from 10 million to several hundred million years; and an older, red, regular host several gigayears old. The marked lopsidedness observed in both continuum and color maps, along with the abundance of stellar clusters, supports a scenario involving mergers or interactions within Haro 14.

This study presents the discovery of TOI-220 $b$, a newly identified sub-Neptune found via TESS transit photometry and confirmed through radial velocity follow-up using the HARPS spectrograph. Combining high-precision radial velocity data with TESS transit observations, we derive a planetary mass of $13.8 \pm 1.0$ M$_{\text{Earth}}$ and a radius of $3.03 \pm 0.15$ R$_{\text{Earth}}$, yielding a bulk density of $2.73 \pm 0.47$ g cm$^{-3}$. The planet orbits a relatively bright (V=10.4) and ancient (10.1$\pm$1.4 Gyr) K dwarf star every $\sim$10.69 days. Consequently, TOI-220 $b$ represents a warm sub-Neptune with highly precise mass and radius measurements. A Bayesian internal structure analysis suggests that the planet's low density, driven by intense irradiation, can be explained by a steam atmosphere in radiative-convective equilibrium capping a supercritical water layer above a differentiated interior consisting of a silicate mantle and a small iron core.

Dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) amplifies NMR signals by transferring polarization from electron spins to nuclear spins through on-resonance microwave (MW) irradiation. While monochromatic continuous-wave (MCW) MW irradiation is standard, recent studies indicate that frequency modulating the MW signal can yield further DNP enhancement beyond what MCW achieves. Previous research examined this modulation effect on the solid effect (SE) and cross effect (CE) using 4-hydroxy TEMPO (TEMPOL) at temperatures below 20 K. This study extends the analysis to the room-temperature $^{13}$C-DNP of diamond powders, investigating the modulation impact on the Overhauser effect (OE) and truncated cross effect (tCE), in addition to SE and CE. Due to the heterogeneity of P1 (substitutional nitrogen) environments within diamond crystallites, diamond powders can exhibit multiple DNP mechanisms simultaneously. We analyze how the two critical frequency modulation parameters—modulation frequency ($f_{m}$) and modulation amplitude ($\Delta\omega$)—influence the enhancement provided by each mechanism. Beyond simply boosting DNP enhancement, frequency modulation offers a means to control the dominant mechanism. By selecting specific modulation parameters, it is possible to selectively amplify certain mechanisms while suppressing others.

As living standards improve and communication technologies advance, residential settings are becoming increasingly smart and interconnected, leading to a significant rise in total energy usage. Since household appliances are the main drivers of this consumption, identifying them accurately is essential to prevent wasteful, unattended operation, thereby enhancing energy conservation and sustainability. Traditionally, appliance recognition models are trained centrally by aggregating electricity data from smart plugs installed at clients, which raises privacy concerns. Furthermore, this data is prone to noise, particularly when appliances are connected to unintended smart plugs. To address these challenges simultaneously, we introduce FedAR+, a novel federated learning framework for appliance recognition. This approach enables decentralized, privacy-preserving model training across clients, even in the presence of mislabeled data. FedAR+ incorporates an adaptive noise-handling mechanism through a joint loss function that accounts for label weights and distribution, strengthening the model's resilience to noisy labels. We evaluated FedAR+ using a newly collected labeled dataset from an apartment complex, alongside two existing datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively manages up to 30% noisy labels and significantly outperforms prior solutions in terms of accuracy.

Open-domain question answering and other natural language understanding tasks frequently demand the retrieval and integration of facts from diverse sources. To tackle this, we introduce a method that embeds a semi-parametric representation of a massive text corpus into a Transformer architecture to serve as a factual knowledge base. Our approach utilizes "mention memory," defined as a table containing dense vector embeddings for every entity mention within the corpus. The resulting model, named TOME, functions as a Transformer equipped with internal memory layers where entity mentions in the input passage query this mention memory. This design allows for the synthesis and reasoning across numerous disparate information sources within a unified Transformer framework. Empirical results using a memory comprising 150 million Wikipedia mentions demonstrate that TOME excels in various open-domain, knowledge-intensive tasks, including the HoVer and FEVER claim verification benchmarks and multiple entity-based QA challenges. Furthermore, the model successfully learns to prioritize informative mentions without direct supervision. Finally, we show that TOME can generalize to novel, unseen entities by updating the memory without requiring retraining.

From an environmental perspective, several critical elements of neural network training significantly influence carbon output, including the server's geographic location and its energy source, the duration of the training process, and the specific hardware make and model employed. To estimate these emissions, we introduce the Machine Learning Emissions Calculator, a resource designed to help the community grasp the ecological footprint of training ML models. Alongside this tool, we provide detailed explanations of the aforementioned factors and offer practical steps that both individual practitioners and organizations can implement to reduce their carbon emissions.

Creating antiviral medications is an urgent challenge because viruses frequently mutate to evade treatment, rendering most drugs effective only for short durations. To account for this, we adapt the Neumann and Dahari model by incorporating time-varying drug efficacy into the differential equations to examine the relationship between viral load and medication. We investigate scenarios where the drug either blocks infection or halts viral production. First, we analyze a scenario where drug efficacy declines monotonically over time; our findings indicate that low efficacy results in a transient reduction in viral load, which subsequently rebounds, demonstrating the drug's limited duration. Conversely, high-efficacy drugs lead to a continuous decrease in both viral load and infected cell counts, while uninfected cell numbers rise. We also examine the time-dependent nature of critical drug efficacy and explore the interplay among viral load, drug efficacy, and CTL (Cytotoxic T Lymphocyte) responses. In this context, we assess how basic reproduction ratios depend on model parameters and determine critical efficacy thresholds as a function of time. Our results show that the term associated with the basic reproduction ratio increases with a stronger CTL response. Additionally, we present a simple, analytically solvable mathematical model to further analyze the correlation between viral load and antiviral interventions.

As a prime candidate for chiral p-wave superconductivity and the potential host of exotic Majorana fermion quasiparticles, UTe$_2$ has motivated recent STM investigations. Guided by these findings, we examine particle-hole symmetry breaking within chiral p-wave superconductors. By calculating the local density of states arising from Majorana surface states in the presence of significant Rashba surface spin-orbit coupling—anticipated in heavy-fermion systems like UTe$_2$—we demonstrate that the breaking of time-reversal and surface reflection symmetries induces a natural propensity for a triplet pair density wave state. This state inherently explains the observed violation of particle-hole symmetry.

This paper presents a theoretical study on the propagation of spatio-temporal solitons, known as light bullets, within nonlinear metamaterial waveguides. Our analysis employs a Lagrangian variational approach with a specific ansatz, which is then validated numerically using the split-step Fourier method. A primary focus is placed on identifying system parameter conditions that ensure stable dynamics in both negative and positive index regimes of these waveguides. Similar to conventional media, 3D light bullets are inherently unstable in metamaterials relying solely on Kerr-type nonlinearity. However, stable propagation is achievable in the negative index regime when normal dispersion balances defocusing cubic and focusing quintic nonlinearities. Likewise, in the positive index regime, stability occurs under anomalous dispersion with focusing cubic and defocusing quintic nonlinearities. To verify the solitonic nature of these 3D light bullets, we numerically examined the collision dynamics between two bullets. The results indicate that in competing cubic and quintic nonlinear metamaterials, spatio-temporal solitons propagate unchanged after collision, aside from a potential phase shift. Conversely, an improper balance between linear and nonlinear effects leads to the formation of distorted bullet molecules with significant energy following interaction. Over time, oscillations intensify, causing the bullets to filament. These collision dynamics were observed to be consistent across both negative and positive refractive index regimes of the metamaterials.

This study presents branching fraction ratios for the decays $H_b \to H_c\pi^-\pi^+\pi^-$ normalized to $H_b \to H_c\pi^-$, where the symbols $H_b$ and $H_c$ denote the particle pairs B^0-bar($D^+$), B^-$ ($D^0$), B_s^0-bar ($D_s^+$), and $\Lambda_b^0$ ($\Lambda_c^+$). Utilizing the LHCb detector and an integrated luminosity of 35${\rm pb^{-1}}$ gathered at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV, the following ratios were determined:
$B(B^0-bar \to D^+\pi^-\pi^+\pi^-) / B(B^0-bar \to D^+\pi^-) = 2.38\pm0.11\pm0.21$
$B(B^- \to D^0\pi^-\pi^+\pi^-) / B(B^- \to D^0\pi^-) = 1.27\pm0.06\pm0.11$
$B(B_s^0-bar \to D_s^+\pi^-\pi^+\pi^-) / B(B_s^0-bar \to D_s^+\pi^-) = 2.01\pm0.37\pm0.20$
$B(\Lambda_b^0 \to \Lambda_c^+\pi^-\pi^+\pi^-) / B(\Lambda_b^0 \to \Lambda_c^+\pi^-) = 1.43\pm0.16\pm0.13$.
Additionally, partial decay rates into excited charm hadrons for these processes are reported. The precision of these findings is comparable to or exceeds that of previously available measurements.

Interacting dark matter-dark energy (IDMDE) models represent a significant challenge regarding cosmic structure formation, and this study investigates the integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect within such frameworks. We begin by establishing a theoretical basis for IDMDE, briefly addressing stability conditions and deriving perturbation equations using a specific functional form for the energy density transfer rate. Subsequently, we compute the matter power spectrum amplitude for IDMDE and compare it with $\Lambda$CDM predictions. Additionally, we determine the ISW auto-power spectrum amplitude as a function of multipole order $l$. Our findings reveal that for phantom dark energy equations of state, the IDMDE ISW auto-power spectrum resembles that of $\Lambda$CDM, whereas for quintessence states, the IDMDE amplitude exceeds the $\Lambda$CDM result. Furthermore, variations in the coupling parameter $\xi$ demonstrate an inverse proportionality to the ISW auto-power spectrum amplitude in IDMDE models. Finally, utilizing four distinct surveys, we calculate the ISW-cross power spectrum amplitude for IDMDE across different multipole orders. The results show that the IDMDE cross-power spectrum amplitude surpasses $\Lambda$CDM values for all dark energy equation of state parameters ($\omega_{\rm x}$), and this amplitude also decreases inversely with increasing coupling parameter $\xi$.

Ultrastrong coupling between optical fields and material excitations represents a unique regime of electromagnetic interaction that facilitates diverse and fascinating physical phenomena. Conventional methods for achieving ultrastrong light-matter coupling typically rely on quantum emitters like organic dyes, quantum wells, superconducting artificial atoms, or two-dimensional electron gas transitions. Achieving this regime often demands stringent conditions, such as high vacuum, intense magnetic fields, and cryogenic temperatures. However, recent reports suggest that a high degree of light-matter coupling can be achieved under ambient conditions using plasmonic meta-atoms—artificial metallic nanostructures that substitute traditional quantum emitters. Despite this, the fundamental limits on coupling strength for these systems remain unidentified. This study employs a Hamiltonian approach to theoretically investigate the formation of polaritonic states and determine the upper bounds of collective plasmon-photon coupling within dense assemblies of plasmonic meta-atoms. Beginning with spherical geometries, we establish universal upper limits for the normalized collective coupling strength ($g/\omega_0$) between ensembles of meta-atoms and free-space photons. Furthermore, by analyzing spheroidal metallic meta-atoms, we demonstrate that a strongly elongated shape constitutes the optimal geometry for maximizing collective coupling strength in an array. These findings hold significant value for polaritonics research, quantum technology, and the engineering of material properties.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become leading models for various machine learning tasks, including the analysis of social networks, molecular structures, and protein interactions. Many of these datasets involve privacy-sensitive information, making differentially private machine learning a promising approach to extract insights while providing formal privacy guarantees. However, applying differential privacy to train GNNs has been under-explored due to the inherent structural complexities of graphs. This work introduces a framework for differential privacy in graph-level classification, a fundamental application of graph machine learning. Our approach, which supports deep learning on multi-graph datasets, utilizes differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD). We present results across multiple synthetic and public datasets, evaluating how different GNN architectures and hyperparameters affect performance in differentially private settings. Furthermore, we employ explainability techniques to compare representations learned in private versus non-private contexts, thereby establishing robust baselines for future research in this domain.

Robotic guide dogs offer significant benefits over animal counterparts, including lower costs, scalability through mass production, and reduced maintenance requirements. Nevertheless, despite extensive prior research, previous studies largely overlooked the critical dynamic of the handler and guide dog operating as a cohesive team for navigation. To create a truly beneficial robotic guiding system for visually impaired individuals, we conducted qualitative research comprising interviews with handlers and trainers, alongside firsthand blindfolded walking experiences with various guide dogs. Leveraging insights from these interviews and experiential data, we developed a collaborative indoor navigation scheme for a guide dog robot featuring preferred capabilities such as speed and directional control. For this collaborative navigation, we introduced a semantic-aware local path planner that ensures safe and efficient guiding by integrating environmental semantic data with the handler's position and directional cues to generate collision-free paths. We validated our integrated robotic system through indoor blindfolded walking tests, demonstrating guide-dog-like navigation behavior by successfully avoiding obstacles at a typical gait speed of 0.7 m/s.

Incorporating all relativistic effects, we have established a fully nonlinear, gauge-invariant framework to describe cosmological observables, presenting second-order perturbative formulas for light propagation and observations that require no specific gauge choice. For the first time, we have rigorously verified the validity of these second-order expressions by cross-checking their gauge-transformation properties using two independent approaches: one derived directly from metric perturbation expressions and another inferred from their nonlinear relationships. The resulting formulas for key cosmological observables, including galaxy clustering and luminosity distance, remain invariant under diffeomorphisms and are gauge-invariant at the observation point. We compare our findings with prior research, highlighting distinctions in the perturbative expressions. This second-order gauge-invariant formalism represents a significant advancement for the era of precision cosmology, with future applications poised to play a pivotal role in extending beyond the power spectrum and investigating the early universe.

Multilevel linear models provide a flexible framework for statistically analyzing complex data characterized by hierarchical stratification. However, selecting the optimal model from a vast array of candidates remains a significant challenge. In Bayesian analysis, the conventional strategy involves comparing models via model evidence or Bayes factors; while explicit formulas exist for basic linear models with simplistic priors, direct calculation is typically infeasible for most scenarios. Although Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques, including sequential Monte Carlo, are commonly employed in practice, their efficacy is not always transparent. This paper introduces a method for estimating log model evidence by performing an intermediate marginalization over non-variance parameters. This approach lowers the dimensionality required for any Monte Carlo sampling algorithm, thereby producing more reliable estimates. The study demonstrates how this framework integrates and functions in practical applications, especially with hierarchically structured data. We validate the method using both simulated multilevel data and a well-known dataset concerning radon levels in Minnesota households.
We provide a description of $S^3$ and $S^2$ up to homeomorphism as classifying spaces of small categories, such that the Hopf map $S^3\to{}S^2$ arises as the realization of a functor.

Future dark matter (DM) experiments targeting weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) must contend with sensitivity to coherent solar neutrino scattering, necessitating robust methods to distinguish signal from background. Directional detectors enhance WIMP detection capabilities even in the presence of this unavoidable neutrino floor. Wide-bandgap semiconductors provide a viable route to achieving directional detection within high-density targets. These detectors function in a hybrid manner: while the nuclear recoil induced by WIMPs or neutrinos is captured via real-time collection of charge, phonons, or photons, the directional information is permanently encoded as sub-micron damage tracks within the crystal lattice. These tracks can subsequently be analyzed using diverse atomic physics methods, ranging from point defect quantum sensing to x-ray microscopy. This white paper outlines the underlying detector principles and evaluates the current state of experimental techniques needed for reading these nuclear recoil tracks. We specifically highlight diamond as the target material, given its status as a premier platform for emerging quantum technologies and a key component in next-generation semiconductor electronics. Over the coming decade, developing and demonstrating directional readout in diamond will drive progress across multiple disciplines, ultimately enabling future WIMP detectors to advance precision dark matter and neutrino physics.

This study focuses on weakly-supervised image semantic segmentation utilizing only image-level class labels. A prevalent method involves propagating Class Activation Map (CAM) activation scores via a random-walk mechanism to generate complete pseudo labels, which are then used to train a segmentation network in a fully-supervised fashion. However, because the random walk operates in a feed-forward manner, it fails to impose regularization on the quality of these generated pseudo labels. To address this limitation, we introduce a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN)-based feature propagation framework. We model the creation of complete pseudo labels as a semi-supervised learning problem, training a distinct 2-layer GCN for each image in the dataset by back-propagating both Laplacian and entropy regularization losses. Experiments conducted on the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/Xavier-Pan/WSGCN.

Research on repeated geometric patterns within finite point sets in Euclidean space is a significant area of combinatorial and computational geometry, rooted in Erdős's foundational work. This paper examines the specific challenge of efficiently enumerating all scaled copies of a given pattern within a set of $n$ points. We first address the case of axis-parallel squares, proposing an algorithm that achieves $O(n\sqrt{n})$ time complexity and $O(n)$ space using bucket-based and sweep-line methods. This approach is worst-case optimal because it aligns with the established lower bound of $\Omega(n\sqrt{n})$ for the maximum number of axis-parallel squares determined by $n$ points, resolving a thirty-year-old open problem regarding this bound. Furthermore, we generalize this result to an algorithm that enumerates all scaled copies of any full-dimensional fixed point set in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space, operating in $O(n^{1+1/d})$ time with $O(n)$ space, which also matches the corresponding lower bound attributed to Elekes and Erdős.

Fonts appear frequently in documents and exist in diverse styles, typically existing either as native vector graphics or as rasterized, fixed-resolution images. The vector approach suffers from non-standard representations that hinder the application of modern neural network architectures, whereas rasterization leads to data fidelity loss when encoded by networks, as neural models struggle to capture font-specific discontinuities like edges and corners. Observing that complex fonts can be decomposed into a superposition of simpler occupancy functions, we introduce \textit{multi-implicits}, a permutation-invariant set of learned implicit functions that represent fonts without losing critical features. Although this method locally preserves font characteristics, acquiring ground truth multi-channel signals for supervision remains challenging. Consequently, we propose a training strategy using only local supervision, where the neural architecture directly learns globally consistent multi-implicits for font families. Extensive evaluations across reconstruction, interpolation, and synthesis tasks demonstrate the superiority of this representation over existing alternatives. Furthermore, this framework naturally facilitates glyph completion, allowing a single characteristic font to generate an entire font family in a target style.

We introduce a framework for theoretically analyzing ensembles of low-complexity empirical risk minimizers trained on independent random compressions of high-dimensional data. First, we establish a general, distribution-dependent upper bound on excess risk defined by a natural measure of compressibility. This bound remains independent of the original data's dimensionality and elucidates the inherent regularization benefits of compression. Next, we apply this general bound to classification and regression problems, utilizing Johnson-Lindenstrauss mappings as the compression mechanism. For each task, we derive tight upper bounds on the compressibility function, thereby identifying geometric distributional conditions under which the compressive algorithm achieves minimax-optimal rates, up to poly-logarithmic factors. Specifically, compressive classification attains these rates under a mild geometric margin condition and a flexible moment condition that generalizes the assumption of bounded domains. Furthermore, for regression with strongly convex smooth loss functions, we demonstrate that compressive regression can exploit spectral decay with near-optimal guarantees. Additionally, a crucial component of our central upper bound is a high-probability uniform upper bound on the integrated deviation of dependent empirical processes, a result that may hold independent interest.

The emergence of various wireless services has necessitated that sixth-generation (6G) networks deliver sensing, intelligent computing, and communication capabilities within the same radio spectrum. This paper presents a unified framework that integrates these three functions to optimize scarce system resources in 6G networks. Specifically, we derive two joint beamforming design algorithms based on multi-objective optimization problems (MOOP), targeting either the maximization of weighted overall performance or the minimization of total transmit power. Extensive simulations confirm the efficacy of the proposed algorithms. Furthermore, the analysis reveals the impact of key system parameters, offering valuable insights for designing integrated sensing, computing, and communication (ISCC) systems.

Deep learning-driven computer-aided diagnosis is increasingly utilized for reviewing and analyzing medical imagery; however, its practical clinical deployment is hindered by limited robustness and generalization capabilities, a problem exacerbated by scarce training data. This study tackles this challenge through a transfer learning perspective, diverging from the conventional approach of transferring knowledge from natural to medical images. Instead, we demonstrate that leveraging knowledge within the same domain significantly enhances model robustness and generalization. Consequently, we introduce a novel two-stage framework designed for robust and generalized medical image segmentation. Initially, an unsupervised tile-wise autoencoder is employed for pretraining to acquire both local and global knowledge. Subsequently, a downstream segmentation model is integrated with an auxiliary reconstruction network, where the reconstruction branch fosters the capture of broader semantic features. Experiments conducted on lung segmentation across multiple chest X-ray datasets yield comprehensive results, confirming the framework's superior resilience to data corruption and high generalization on unseen datasets, particularly when training data is limited.

The traveling tournament problem serves as a prominent benchmark in sports scheduling. We introduce an approximation algorithm for TTP(2), a variant constrained to limit both consecutive home and away games to a maximum of two. For a tournament involving $n$ teams, this algorithm achieves an approximation ratio of $1 + 24/n$, marking the first $1 + O(1/n)$ approximation solution for TTP(2).

For primes $p$ in the set $\{3,5,7\}$, we consider $\Delta$, the weight-twelve modular form associated with Ramanujan's tau function. We demonstrate that $\Delta$ is congruent modulo $p$ to an Eisenstein series $E_{k,\chi, \psi}$ for specific values of $k$ and Dirichlet characters $\chi$ and $\psi$. Furthermore, we establish a formula for the Iwasawa $\lambda$-invariants of the $p$-adic Mazur--Tate elements linked to $\Delta$, thereby verifying numerical findings from our earlier research.

Constraint Handling Rules (CHR) is a committed-choice declarative language initially created for constraint solvers but now serving as a general-purpose tool. CHR programs utilize multi-headed guarded rules to rewrite constraints into simpler forms until a solved state is achieved. While empirical data suggests that multiple heads enhance the language's expressive power, a formal proof for this claim has been absent until now.

The first section of this paper examines the Turing completeness of CHR relative to its underlying constraint theory. We demonstrate that if the constraint theory is sufficiently robust, limiting the language to single-headed rules does not diminish its Turing completeness. Conversely, unlike the multi-headed variant, a single-headed CHR language lacks Turing power when the underlying constraint signature lacks function symbols.

In the second section, we establish that, regardless of the constraint theory used, it is impossible to encode a multi-headed CHR language into a single-headed one while maintaining program semantics, provided reasonable assumptions hold. Furthermore, under stronger assumptions, we show that increasing the number of atoms in a rule's head amplifies the language's expressive power. These findings offer a formal validation of the assertion that multiple heads increase the expressive capabilities of CHR.

In recent times, question answering has dramatically expanded to encompass a wide array of tasks and datasets, ranging from reading comprehension, semantic role labeling, and machine translation to image and video understanding. This growth has sparked varied perspectives on the definition and utility of "question answering," with some contending that its scope is either too narrow or too broad, or that it is excessively prevalent in current datasets. In this opinion piece, we posit that question answering should be viewed as a format occasionally useful for investigating specific phenomena, rather than as a distinct phenomenon or task in its own right. We examine the criteria for when a task is accurately described as question answering versus when it is beneficially framed as such instead of utilizing an alternative format.

Although nanostructures enhance the light outcoupling of diamond color centers, their fiber coupling capabilities remain largely unexplored. This study employs the finite element method to calculate emission from color centers within inverted nanocones and assesses the overlap with single-mode fiber propagation modes. By optimizing inverted nanocone parameters against various figures of merit, we maximize fiber coupling efficiency, free-space collection, or emission rate enhancement. The resulting designs demonstrate promising performance, achieving 66% fiber coupling and 83% free-space coupling efficiency at the 619 nm zero-phonon line of the tin-vacancy center. In broadband evaluations for room-temperature collection of the full tin-vacancy spectrum, efficiencies of 55% and 76% were attained for fiber and free-space coupling, respectively. Furthermore, fabrication insensitivity analysis reveals that these nanostructures are robust against imperfections. A specific design yielding a Purcell factor of 2.34 was identified for maximizing emission rates into fiber modes. Finally, investigating a hybrid inverted nanocone created by patterning two distinct materials shows potential for improving fiber coupling efficiency to 71%.

This work introduces a framework for characterizing binary cellular automata (CA) through behavioral metrics applied to the minimal Boolean representation of their transition functions. These metrics are designed to align with heuristic principles observed in elementary CA, specifically capturing behaviors such as growth, decay, chaos, and stability. Based on these metrics, two global behavior indicators are derived: a static measure that evaluates the frequency of these behaviors across all input patterns in the minimal Boolean truth table, and a dynamic measure that calculates the average behavioral metrics over $n$ runs initiated from random states. These indicators are employed to characterize CAs and direct a genetic algorithm in selecting automata resembling Conway's Game of Life. Applying this approach yielded a broad collection of complex binary CAs with notable properties, including self-replication.

This study examines the discretization of a stochastic parabolic optimal control problem featuring a control variable within the diffusion term. Under conditions of rough data, convergence for this discretization is established, and a Monte-Carlo approach is also introduced.

Few-shot image classification aims to identify novel categories using a small amount of labeled data. While metric learning methods are common, they typically classify a query by locating the nearest prototype in a support set based on feature similarity. However, neural networks exhibit varying levels of uncertainty when calculating these similarities across different pairs. Modeling this uncertainty can enhance the effective use of limited samples during few-shot optimization. This paper introduces an Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot framework that models the uncertainty of similarities between query and support pairs to drive uncertainty-aware optimization. Specifically, we transform observed similarities into probabilistic representations and integrate them into the loss function to improve optimization efficiency. To simultaneously evaluate the relationships between a query and all prototypes in a support set, we employ a graph-based model to estimate pair-wise uncertainty. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms a strong baseline and achieves state-of-the-art results.

We suggest simulating the dynamical phases of a BCS superconductor by utilizing an ensemble of cold atoms confined within an optical cavity. Effective Cooper pairs are represented through the atoms' internal states, while attractive interactions are achieved via the exchange of virtual photons among atoms coupled to a shared cavity mode. By regulating the interaction strength alongside a tunable dispersion relation for these effective Cooper pairs, we can investigate the complete dynamical phase diagram of the BCS model across various system parameters and initial states. This proposal opens new avenues for exploring non-equilibrium characteristics of quantum magnetism and superconductivity by leveraging atom-light interactions in cold atomic gases.

This study introduces a straightforward mathematical model that offers a quantitative strategy to resolve the persistent championship struggles faced by Canadian Hockey Teams. Utilizing Competitive Intransitivity as a predictive framework, the analysis demonstrates how three teams—employing distinct salary priorities under a uniform cap while investing in three independent variables (Offence, Defence, and Goaltending)—can generate complex, often surprising results akin to rolling intransitive dice in head-to-head matchups. A key insight from this analysis is that for any given team strategy, a counter-strategy exists within the same salary constraints that a playoff opponent could adopt to secure a long-series victory, thereby providing a viable path to end prolonged championship futility.

Ultrawide bandgap semiconductor technologies promise transformative breakthroughs in fast-evolving fields such as quantum communication, short-wavelength optics, smart energy conversion, and biomedical interfaces. While these advanced technologies can partially rely on conventional devices, achieving superior performance and expanded functionality requires new hybrid architectures. This study introduces a novel concept leveraging the unique properties of a diamond pn junction, utilizing both electrical and optical control over the depletion region. By employing this junction as a gate within a junction field-effect transistor, we demonstrate a proof-of-concept non-volatile diamond photo-switch. Specifically, a diamond pn junction featuring nitrogen deep donors on the n-side exhibits optical activation via visible light. In the dark, the n-type diamond gate lacks free carriers, rendering it insulating; however, illumination restores efficient standard electrical gate control. Without light, the device remains in a "frozen" state, retaining a permanent record of its current condition. This operational mode unlocks significant potential for storing and transferring information or energy, with applications spanning aerospace and electrical aircraft electronics, power electronics, bio-electronics, and quantum communication.

This study aims to enhance recent crowd counting methods that utilize the plug-and-play patch rescaling module (PRM). To fully leverage the PRM's capabilities and achieve more reliable, accurate results on challenging images characterized by crowd variations, large perspectives, extreme occlusions, and cluttered backgrounds, we introduce a novel multi-resolution, multi-task crowd counting network. This architecture employs three deep-layered branches, each producing feature maps at distinct resolutions, which undergo feature-level fusion to construct essential collective knowledge for the final count. Furthermore, visual attention mechanisms are applied to early-stage feature maps to bolster the later-stage channels' comprehension of foreground regions. Extensive numerical and visual evaluations across four benchmark datasets demonstrate that integrating these deep branches with the PRM module and early-attended blocks significantly outperforms original PRM-based schemes. The proposed approach achieves a notable 12.6% reduction in RMSE and surpasses state-of-the-art methods in cross-dataset assessments.

Simulating diverse robot controllers has allowed for online adaptation to locomotion damage, yet discovering high-performing, varied controllers demands specialized hardware and extensive hyperparameter tuning. Conversely, the Covariance Matrix Adaptation MAP-Annealing (CMA-MAE) algorithm, an evolution strategies-based quality diversity method, avoids these constraints and achieves state-of-the-art results in standard benchmarks; however, its quadratic complexity prevents scaling to modern neural network controllers. By employing efficient approximation techniques within evolution strategies, we introduce three CMA-MAE variants capable of scaling to very high dimensions. Experimental results indicate that these variants surpass ES-based baselines in robotic locomotion benchmarks and perform comparably to leading deep reinforcement learning quality diversity algorithms. Source code and videos can be found at https://scalingcmamae.github.io.

Classifier robustness serves as a cornerstone of Machine Learning (ML), heavily influencing system reliability; consequently, methods to evaluate this robustness are vital. This study tackles the challenge of assessing corruption robustness to ensure both comparability and interpretability within specific datasets. We introduce a data augmentation technique that utilizes a robustness distance ($\epsilon$), calculated based on the dataset's minimal class separation distance. This approach yields the MSCR (mean statistical corruption robustness) metric, which enables dataset-specific comparisons of classifier performance regarding their resilience to corruption. The MSCR value is interpretable, quantifying the avoidable drop in accuracy caused by statistical corruptions. Experiments on both 2D and image data demonstrate that the metric effectively captures varying degrees of robustness. Additionally, we observed unexpected optima in robust accuracy when training and testing classifiers with different noise levels. Although a significant accuracy tradeoff is commonly cited when training robust models, our findings reinforce the perspective that such a tradeoff between accuracy and corruption robustness is not inherent. Instead, our results suggest that robustness training via simple data augmentation can even marginally enhance accuracy.

This paper introduces a technique for inferring lighting conditions from a single indoor photograph. While prior approaches typically rely on either simplistic, non-realistic parametric models or complex representations that are hard to interpret and adjust post-prediction, our proposed pipeline offers a balanced solution. It estimates an editable parametric light source capable of generating strong shadows, paired with a non-parametric texture containing high-frequency details essential for realistic specular reflections. The resulting predictions are fully interpretable and allow artists or users to make modifications with just a few mouse clicks. Both quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that our method simplifies indoor lighting estimation for non-experts while maintaining competitive performance.
