We demonstrate a theoretical link to classical image alignment, proving that coarse-to-fine registration strategies are also effective for NeRF. Additionally, we reveal that naively applying positional encoding within NeRF can hinder registration when using a synthesis-based objective. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets indicate that BARF successfully optimizes neural scene representations and corrects substantial camera pose misalignments simultaneously. This capability facilitates view synthesis and video sequence localization from unknown poses, creating new opportunities for visual localization systems (such as SLAM) and enabling applications in dense 3D mapping and reconstruction.

Software development involves information-rich collaborative work that demands awareness of artifacts like files, pull requests, and work items. As development speeds increase, information overload poses a significant challenge for developers, making it difficult to locate both people and information, particularly within large systems or for new team members. To address this, we introduce the Nalanda platform, a large-scale data ecosystem comprising two subsystems: the Nalanda graph system, a socio-technical graph, and the Nalanda index system, a recommendation engine designed to meet developers' information needs. The Nalanda graph, an enterprise-scale network, aggregates data from 6,500 repositories, containing 37,410,706 nodes and 128,745,590 edges. Leveraging this graph, we developed analytics applications, including the "MyNalanda" newsfeed, which has organically grown to 290 Daily Active Users (DAU) and 590 Monthly Active Users (MAU). A preliminary user study indicates that 74% of surveyed developers and engineering managers favor continuing to use the platform for information discovery. The Nalanda index system consists of two indices—an artifact index and an expert index—which utilize the socio-technical graph to rank results and deliver improved recommendations. A large-scale quantitative evaluation demonstrates that the Nalanda index system achieves a 78% accuracy rate for its top three recommendations.

Recent research has extensively explored the Galois module structure of local field extensions, notably utilizing Galois scaffolds. For a totally ramified $p$-extension $L/K$, a Galois scaffold provides a $K$-basis for $K[G]$ with straightforward implications for the valuations of elements within $L$. Building on the 2013 sufficient conditions established by N.P. Byott and G.G. Elder regarding the existence of such scaffolds for cyclic extensions of degree $p^2$ in characteristic $p$, this work adapts those results to the case of cyclic extensions of degree $p^2$ in characteristic $0$.

Achieving consensus amidst arbitrary faults is a foundational challenge in distributed computing, proven to be impossible if up to one-third of processes fail unless message signing is employed. This paper introduces a solution to a variant of Byzantine Agreement known as Detectable Byzantine Agreement (DBA), which operates without signed messages. The proposed algorithm leverages $Q$-correlated lists produced by a quantum source; once distributed, processes utilize these lists to achieve agreement through classical methods. While the general protocol requires $m+1$ rounds (where $m$ represents the number of faulty processes), the system converges in a single round provided that fewer than one-third of the processes fail.

Building on our prior work published in Ann. Phys. 437, 168741 (2022), we investigate infinite nuclear matter by summing ladder diagrams. The master equation for energy density is analytically solved for contact interactions using a pionless framework for nucleon-nucleon forces. Our renormalized results are formulated directly in terms of nucleon-nucleon phase shifts and mixing angles, covering partial-wave amplitudes up to G-waves, with convergence achieved by incorporating higher partial waves. We present the energy per particle, density, and sound velocity derived from this ladder series for both symmetric and neutron matter. This rigorous resummation of ladder diagrams serves as a reliable low-density reference point for other parameterizations of $\bar{\cal{E}}$ at higher densities.

Unitarity of the lepton mixing matrix is a foundational pillar of the standard neutrino-mixing framework, yet numerous theories proposing the origin of neutrino masses anticipate deviations from this unitarity within the active neutrino sector. Driven by the potential for future experiments to achieve precise measurements of the lepton mixing matrix, we re-examine existing constraints on unitarity violations derived from oscillation data and project the enhancements expected from next-generation facilities. These upcoming experiments will constrain the normalizations of all rows and columns of the matrix to within approximately 10% precision; specifically, the electron row will be measured with better than 1% accuracy, while the tau row will have the lowest precision at around 10%. Furthermore, the precision of the mixing matrix elements themselves is expected to improve by a factor of three on average. We emphasize the complementary roles of DUNE, T2HK, JUNO, and the IceCube Upgrade in driving these advancements, as well as the significance of $\nu_\tau$ appearance studies and sterile neutrino searches for testing leptonic unitarity.

This work examines the centers of universal enveloping algebras and the invariant rings associated with standard filiform Lie algebras, considering both fields of characteristic zero and sufficiently large prime characteristics. We identify explicit generators for the corresponding quotient fields and provide a concise formulation for the generators of the invariant rings. Furthermore, we establish several combinatorial properties regarding the Hilbert series of these algebras.

Evaluating the mechanical characteristics of cells and tissues frequently utilizes methods such as spherical indentation or compression between two plates. While various theoretical frameworks have previously been established to extract material parameters (such as elastic modulus) or state variables (such as pressure) from these tests, this study expands prior work on the indentation of a pressurized spherical shell by a point force to include scenarios involving both spherical probes and flat plates. We present formulas that allow for the deduction of modulus or pressure from experimental data utilizing realistic contact geometries, yielding distinct outcomes based on the pressure magnitude. We anticipate these findings to be widely applicable in the study of cell and tissue biomechanics and mechanobiology.

Metamaterials are composite structures that derive their unique characteristics from a mesoscale arrangement of their components. When this organization occurs at scales smaller than the characteristic lengths governing their response, it enables the design of properties unattainable by conventional materials, such as negative refractive indices, perfect electromagnetic absorption, and negative Poisson ratios. In this work, we present and demonstrate a novel class of materials: viscosity metamaterials. Specifically, we show that acoustic perturbations at kHz to MHz frequencies can rapidly induce large oscillations in the viscosity of a shear-thickened fluid. Since these oscillation timescales are orders of magnitude shorter than those associated with global material flow, we can engineer metamaterials with an effective viscosity that is a composite of both thickened (high-viscosity) and dethickened (low-viscosity) states. These viscosity metamaterials allow for the engineering of remarkable properties, including negative viscosity—a phenomenon impossible in standard fluids. The precise control over viscosity, the ease of access to these states, and the range of exotic properties achievable make viscosity metamaterials highly promising for technologies where managing fluid flow and instabilities is critical, spanning applications from coatings and cloaking to 3D printing.

Humans excel at interpreting emotions in others by analyzing multimodal cues like spoken words, vocal tones, and facial expressions. Conversely, machines often struggle to discern various emotions because decoding the intricate interplay between these complex signals is challenging. To address this, we introduce InterMulti, a multimodal emotion analysis framework designed to capture complex interactions from multiple perspectives and identify emotions from these signals. Our approach decomposes signals across different modalities into three distinct interaction representations: a modality-full representation, a modality-shared representation, and three modality-specific representations. Furthermore, to balance modality contributions and learn a more informative latent interaction representation, we developed a novel Text-dominated Hierarchical High-order Fusion (THHF) module. This module effectively integrates the aforementioned representations into a comprehensive multimodal interaction profile. Extensive experiments on prominent datasets—MOSEI, MOSI, and IEMOCAP—demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art performance.

Constructing robust arguments is fundamental to effective decision-making. Although automatically assessing argument quality has recently garnered significant interest within argument mining, the process demands an exceptionally high annotation burden. Consequently, we investigated uncertainty-based active learning (AL) approaches on two widely used argument-strength datasets to determine if sample-efficient learning is feasible. Our comprehensive empirical analysis reveals that uncertainty-based acquisition functions fail to outperform random sampling in terms of accuracy on these datasets.

Vorticity plays a fundamental role in the dynamics and nature of turbulence, particularly within astrophysical fluids. Consequently, findings by \cite{Raymond20a,Raymond20b} regarding vorticity in the post-shock region of the Cygnus Loop supernova remnant are highly significant. This study examines how reliably spectroscopic measurements of optically thin lines—the most prevalent method for astronomical velocity tracking—can determine unambiguous vorticity values in a fluid. We analyze an idealized scenario observing a flow within a single plane, considering two distinct cases: one where vorticity exists perpendicular to the observation plane, and another where the flow is explicitly irrotational (possessing zero vorticity). In both instances, what we term {\em pseudovorticity} is derived from spatial variations in the line-of-sight velocity component, combined with symmetry assumptions. The primary finding is that for vortical flows, the calculated pseudovorticity closely approximates the true vorticity. However, and critically, pseudovorticity is also detected in the irrotational case, reaching magnitudes comparable to those in the vortical scenario. Ultimately, this paper concludes that while astronomical spectroscopy can provide a reasonable estimate of vorticity in distant fluids, the reliability of such an inference cannot be guaranteed.

Multivariable Mendelian randomization (MVMR) typically leverages summary statistics of genetic variants to estimate the causal impact of multiple exposures on a specific outcome. However, in many MVMR applications, the exposures are subject to measurement error, meaning the available summary statistics reflect associations with the error-prone measurements rather than the true exposures. While classical measurement error inflates standard errors for genetic associations without introducing bias in single-exposure models, it induces bias toward the null in two-sample frameworks. This pattern does not always hold when dealing with multiple correlated exposures. This paper investigates how measurement error influences the direction and magnitude of bias, as well as coverage, power, and type I error rates within MVMR studies. We demonstrate a method to adjust for measurement error using a maximum likelihood framework and apply it to two case studies. The first example reveals that measurement error causes the estimated effect of body mass index on coronary heart disease risk to be overestimated and the effect of waist-to-hip ratio to be underestimated. The second example indicates that failing to account for measurement error may lead to an underestimation of the proportion of the effect of education on coronary heart disease risk that is mediated by body mass index, smoking, and blood pressure.

Research in computing education often leverages data generated within Integrated Development Environments (IDEs), such as student actions, code snapshots, and compilation logs, to deeply understand programming processes. This paper introduces a toolkit designed to collect and process student activity data during problem-solving. The first component is a plugin compatible with IntelliJ-based IDEs (including PyCharm, IntelliJ IDEA, and CLion) that captures code snapshots and interaction events to facilitate analysis across Python, Java, Kotlin, and C++. The second component handles the post-processing of this data, offering capabilities for basic analysis and visualization. To demonstrate and validate the toolkit, we present a dataset comprising activity and interaction records from 148 participants of varying ages and programming experience levels as they solved programming tasks. Finally, we outline several potential avenues for further research using this dataset.

As temperatures rise, Schwinger pair production transitions from a quantum tunneling mechanism to a classical, thermal process governed by a worldline sphaleron. This paper demonstrates this transition and calculates the corresponding pair production rates for both spinor and scalar quantum electrodynamics, incorporating the semiclassical prefactor. Specifically, for electron-positron pairs generated from a thermal photon bath under an electric field, the derived rate exceeds both perturbative photon fusion and the zero-temperature Schwinger process. By working to all orders in the coupling constant, our findings also apply to the pair production of strongly coupled magnetic monopoles during heavy ion collisions.

We numerically investigate the squeezing behavior of multiple deformable capsules passing through a constriction, a scenario common in microfluidic chips used to manipulate soft living cells. Our approach employs fully three-dimensional simulations utilizing the lattice Boltzmann method for fluid flow, the immersed boundary method for two-way fluid-structure interaction, and the finite element method to calculate capsule membrane elasticity. The results reveal two primary outcomes: continuous particle passage or blockage resulting in clogging. The transition between these states depends on the ratio of capsule size to constriction width and the membrane's deformability. Notably, increased deformability facilitates passage through narrow constrictions where rigid particles of similar diameter would otherwise be blocked and cause clogging.

This paper introduces a new technique for forecasting distances within real-world social networks. Given the complexity of predicting missing distances, we employ a two-stage strategy: first, structural parameters for families of synthetic networks are derived from limited measurements of a real network; second, these synthetic networks are utilized to pre-train predictive neural networks. Because our method identifies the optimal synthetic graph parameters to serve as an "oracle" for generating extensive training datasets, we term this approach "Oracle Search Pre-training" (OSP). For instance, since many real-world networks follow a Power law distribution in node degrees, a Power law model can act as the foundation for an oracle that generates synthetic pre-training networks, provided the relevant parameters are estimated correctly. We conducted experiments on Facebook, Email, and Train Bombing networks, demonstrating that OSP surpasses models lacking pre-training, those using inaccurate parameters, and alternative schemes like Low-rank Matrix Completion. Notably, OSP achieves a prediction error of fewer than one hop using only 1% of sampled distances from the social network. Furthermore, OSP is easily adaptable to other domains, such as random networks, by selecting an appropriate model for synthetic data generation, offering significant potential for various network learning challenges.

We investigate global quantum quenches within strongly-coupled, hyperscaling-violating-Lifshitz quantum field theories by employing a straightforward holographic toy model and utilizing entanglement entropy as our diagnostic tool. Building upon our findings in arxiv:1705.10324, we demonstrate that the holographic entanglement entropy of small subsystems adheres to a simple linear response relation. Leveraging this relation, we formulate a time-dependent first law of entanglement entropy. Typically, this law contains a time-dependent component akin to relative entropy, which we suggest serves as an effective order parameter for characterizing out-of-equilibrium states during post-quench evolution. Finally, we apply these methodologies to conduct a detailed analysis of a wide range of quantum quenches, including instantaneous, power-law, and periodic scenarios.

In their work "A Functional Abstraction of Typed Contexts," Danvy and Filinski demonstrated the derivation of a monomorphic type system for the shift and reset operators using CPS semantics. This paper extends that approach to Felleisen's control and prompt operators. Unlike shift and reset, control and prompt display more dynamic behavior by allowing manipulation of a sequence of contexts around previously captured continuations. Our primary insight is that by utilizing a functional representation of these context trails within the CPS semantics, we can derive a type system that precisely encodes every constraint imposed by that semantics.

Currently, the research domain of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has generated an extensive array of terminologies, motivations, approaches, and evaluation metrics. Given the rapid expansion of XAI methods, there is a pressing need for a comprehensive taxonomy to assist both researchers and practitioners in understanding the field's scope, comparing techniques, and selecting the most appropriate method for specific use-case requirements. Although numerous existing taxonomies vary in detail and focus, they share significant commonalities. This paper aims to consolidate these efforts by presenting a unified, complete taxonomy of XAI methods aligned with current research concepts. Through a structured literature review and meta-study, we analyzed and evaluated over 50 highly cited and recent surveys covering XAI methods, metrics, and characteristics. Following a synthesis of these "surveys of surveys," we integrated the terminologies and concepts from the articles into a cohesive, structured taxonomy. This framework is illustrated by more than 50 diverse example methods categorized accordingly. Designed as a reference and broad overview for beginners, researchers, and practitioners, this taxonomy provides the foundational basis for future research that is targeted, use-case oriented, and context-sensitive.

In computational science and engineering, workflows frequently involve integrating diverse software tools for tasks such as simulation, pre-processing, and post-processing. These components are often combined into arbitrarily complex pipelines to tackle specific research questions. To enable peer researchers to comprehend, replicate, and reuse scientific findings, several hurdles must be overcome. Key among these are the need to automate workflows, ensure full documentation of all utilized software for reproducibility, maintain result traceability, and provide a clear, readable workflow record to facilitate external verification and foster trust. This paper evaluates existing Workflow Management Systems (WfMSs) based on their capability to describe, reproduce, and reuse scientific workflows. General requirements for WfMSs were derived from user stories relevant to the computational science and engineering domain. Using an exemplary workflow implementation hosted on GitHub (https://github.com/BAMresearch/NFDI4IngScientificWorkflowRequirements), we compare various WfMSs against these criteria. This analysis aims to assist fellow scientists in selecting the most appropriate WfMS for their specific needs.

This study applies Noether symmetry analysis to field equations within an anisotropic background of $f(T,B)$-gravity. We examine the specific form $f(T,B) = T + F(B)$, which represents a minor deviation from TEGR induced by the boundary scalar $B$. For Bianchi I, Bianchi III, and Kantowski-Sachs geometries, a minisuperspace formulation is established, allowing the application of Noether's theorems to investigate invariant point transformations. Our results indicate that for Bianchi I spacetime, the gravitational field equations become Liouville integrable under the theory defined by $F(B) = -\frac{B}{\lambda}\ln B$. Consequently, an analytic solution is obtained, and the relevance of these Noether symmetries to the Wheeler-DeWitt equation in quantum cosmology is explored.

Audio denoising has been investigated for decades through both conventional and deep learning approaches, yet these techniques remain constrained by reliance on artificially generated noise or inferior audio quality outcomes. To address these limitations, we have assembled a large-scale dataset featuring natural bird sounds. We introduce a novel framework that transforms audio denoising into an image segmentation task via our Deep Visual Audio Denoising (DVAD) model. Utilizing a collection of 14,120 audio images, we created the audio ImageMask tool and implemented a few-shot generalization strategy to annotate them. Comprehensive experiments confirm that our model achieves state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach can be readily adapted for speech denoising, audio separation, enhancement, and noise estimation.

Thin, high-permeability FINEMET foils wrapped in thin plastic layers have been employed to protect photomultiplier tubes with a 20-cm diameter from ambient magnetic fields. Under the influence of Earth's magnetic field, this shielding method has been demonstrated to enhance photoelectron collection efficiency and improve the uniformity of the photomultiplier tubes' response.

This study evaluates smaller BLOOM model variants (350m/560m and 1b3/1b7) across a range of natural language processing tasks, including GLUE language understanding, prompt-based zero-shot and few-shot text classification and extraction, question answering, text generation, and multi-lingual classification. These evaluations aim to assess model strengths, weaknesses, and behavioral patterns. Empirical findings indicate that BLOOM variants underperform on all GLUE tasks (excluding WNLI), question answering, and text generation. However, they achieve an accuracy of 56.3% on the WNLI task and demonstrate competence in prompt-based few-shot text extraction for the MIT Movies and ATIS datasets. On average, BLOOM variants outperform GPT-2 and GPT-Neo models by 7% in extracting Director and Airline Names from the MIT Movies and ATIS datasets, respectively.

Certain repeating fast radio burst (FRB) sources display intricate polarization characteristics, such as frequency-dependent depolarization, rotation measure (RM) variations, and oscillating spectral structures in polarized components. Recently, Feng et al. (2022) highlighted that active repeaters show significant frequency-dependent depolarization and a robust correlation between RM scatter ($\sigma_{\rm RM}$) and temporal scattering time ($\tau_{\rm s}$), expressed as $\sigma_{\rm RM}\propto\tau_{\rm s}^{1.0\pm0.2}$. These phenomena are well explained by multi-path propagation through a magnetized, inhomogeneous plasma screen, suggesting that both temporal scattering and RM scatter arise from the same region. Notably, Feng et al. (2022) also observed that FRBs with compact persistent radio sources (PRS) often exhibit extreme $\sigma_{\rm RM}$ values. This study focuses on theoretical predictions regarding the relationships among temporal scattering, depolarization caused by RM scatter, and PRS within the magnetized plasma environment near repeating FRB sources. The observed RM scatter behaviors imply that the surrounding magnetized plasma resembles a supernova remnant or a pulsar wind nebula, with predicted $\sigma_{\rm RM}$-$\tau_{\rm s}$ relations ranging from $\sigma_{\rm RM}\propto\tau_{\rm s}^{(0.54-0.83)}$ across various astrophysical scenarios. Additionally, we provide a scenario-independent general discussion on PRS, demonstrating that the specific luminosity of a PRS correlates positively with the RM contribution from the plasma screen. This theoretical finding aligns with observations of FRB 121102 and FRB 190520B.

A word $u$ is defined as a scattered factor of $w$ if $u$ results from $w$ by removing certain letters. Specifically, there exist potentially empty words $u_1, \dots, u_n$ and $v_0, \dots, v_n$ such that $u = u_1u_2\cdots u_n$ and $w = v_0u_1v_1u_2v_2\cdots u_nv_n$. We examine the collection of length-$k$ scattered factors of a word $w$, termed the $k$-spectrum and denoted $\ScatFact_k(w)$. We establish several properties of these sets for binary strictly balanced and $c$-balanced words, where "balanced" indicates an equal count of each letter in a two-letter alphabet, and "$c$-balanced" indicates one letter appears $c$ times more frequently than the other. Specifically, we investigate which cardinalities $n = |\ScatFact_k(w)|$ are achievable for a positive integer $k$ when $w$ is either a strictly balanced binary word of length $2k$ or a $c$-balanced binary word of length $2k-c$. Furthermore, we address the problem of reconstructing words based on their $k$-spectra.

We examine the cohomology of moduli spaces of plane quartics equipped with different structures, including Cayley octads, Aronhold heptads, Steiner complexes, and G\"opel subsets, thereby addressing several inquiries posed by Jesse Wolfson. Additionally, we investigate potential arithmetic applications within the context of finite fields.

Many practical applications, such as coordinating self-driving vehicles, stand to gain from multiagent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithms. However, real-world environments pose significant challenges for these systems due to their nonstationary and partially observable characteristics. Furthermore, when agents compete for scarce resources like network bandwidth, they must learn to coordinate their usage effectively. This paper presents R-MADDPG, a deep recurrent multiagent actor-critic framework designed to manage coordination in settings with limited communication and partial observability. The study examines how recurrency influences both performance and communication efficiency within a team of agents. Results demonstrate that the proposed framework successfully learns temporal dependencies for sharing missing observations, managing resource constraints, and establishing diverse communication patterns among agents.

This document introduces a catalog compiling gamma-ray observation results from the VERITAS observatory, spanning publications from 2008 to 2020. Located at the Fred Lawrence Whipple Observatory (FLWO) in southern Arizona, VERITAS is a ground-based imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescope capable of detecting gamma-ray photons within the ~100 GeV to 30 TeV energy range. Its targets encompass galactic sources such as binary star systems, pulsar wind nebulae, and supernova remnants, as well as extragalactic objects including active galactic nuclei, star-forming galaxies, gamma-ray bursts, and various unidentified entities. The catalog provides digital access to high-level scientific findings from 112 papers utilizing VERITAS data and currently encompasses 57 sources. It is publicly available through GitHub and NASA's HEASARC.

We conducted a spectral analysis of two XMM-Newton observations of the narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy UGC 11763, which exhibited markedly different soft X-ray spectra separated by 12 years. To account for this multi-epoch variability, we evaluated three spectral models: a relativistic disc reflection model, a scenario involving multiple partially-covering absorbers paired with a warm corona, and a hybrid approach. In the first model, variability stems from a compact, size-fluctuating coronal region, which modulates the disc reflection component, while also requiring a warm absorber with moderate column density. The partially-covering absorption model attributes variability to changing covering factors of two absorbers located within $r<\approx100r_{\rm g}$, necessitating significant variations in both the warm corona's temperature and strength to match the underlying soft X-ray emission. The third hybrid model explores variable intrinsic power-law emission from the hot corona combined with variable absorption, maintaining a fixed coronal geometry. This hybrid model offers a marginally superior fit compared to the partially-covering absorption model, particularly in reproducing the iron emission band. However, current CCD-resolution data cannot distinguish between these models; future high-resolution missions like Athena and XRISM will be required to resolve the distinct spectral components and validate them.

We derive a nontrivial bound for the number of solutions to the equation $A^{x_1} + A^{x_2} = A^{x_3} + A^{x_4}$, where $1 \le x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4 \le \tau$ and $A$ is a fixed $n \times n$ matrix over a finite field ${\mathbb F}_q$ with multiplicative order $\tau$. The case $n=2$ was previously examined by Kurlberg and Rudnick (2001) regarding quantum ergodicity in linear maps over ${\mathbb F}_q$, and its multivariate counterpart (also for $n=2$) was analyzed by Bourgain (2005). Our findings provide applications that yield a novel bound for additive character sums involving matrix exponential functions, surpassing the square-root threshold, as well as addressing a specific additive problem concerning matrices. These results are particularly robust for matrices in ${\rm SL}(n,q)$ possessing an irreducible characteristic polynomial.

This study investigates the internal architecture of the proton and introduces a shell structure model. By analyzing experimental data across various energy scales in light of the proton's mass distribution and radius, we conclude that the proton contains shell structures where quark and gluon shells vary depending on the energy scale. Furthermore, we successfully account for the dip-like pattern observed in the proton-proton elastic scattering cross-section from the TOTEM Collaboration by utilizing proton mass decomposition and its energy-scale-dependent shell structure.

Although Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have achieved significant improvements in visual quality recently, they continue to struggle with degraded high-frequency content due to spectrally biased architectures and suboptimal loss functions. To mitigate this, we introduce SWAGAN, a versatile Style and WAvelet based GAN that employs progressive generation within the frequency domain. By integrating wavelets into both the generator and discriminator, SWAGAN ensures a frequency-aware latent representation throughout the entire process. This methodology not only enhances the visual fidelity of generated images but also substantially boosts computational efficiency. We validate our approach by embedding it into the StyleGAN2 framework, confirming that wavelet-domain generation produces higher-quality images with more realistic high-frequency details. Additionally, we demonstrate that the model's latent space preserves the properties necessary for diverse editing tasks inherent to StyleGAN, while our frequency-conscious strategy further improves downstream visual outcomes.

Artificial Intelligence techniques, including Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL), are increasingly employed to solve previously intractable ill-posed problems in medical imaging. A particularly significant and difficult challenge within this domain involves reducing gradient directions while utilizing High Angular Resolution (HAR) diffusion data in MR imaging that preserves essential clinical features. Although DL/ML methods show great promise, it is crucial to integrate relevant contextual data to ensure the AI model receives sufficient prior information for accurate posterior inference. This paper presents HemiHex (HH) subsampling, a method designed to optimize training data sampling across q-space geometry. This is followed by nearest neighbor regression training on HH-derived samples to upsample diffusion-weighted imaging (dMRI) data. While previous studies have attempted up-sampling dMRI via regression, they often suffer from performance deficits because they fail to generate structured geometrical measures necessary for inference. In contrast, our proposed approach employs a geometrically optimized regression technique that infers the unknown q-space, thereby overcoming the limitations identified in earlier research.

In recent years, the research community has utilized attention-based models to address vehicle re-identification (re-id), concentrating on vehicle regions that contain discriminative details. These existing methods depend heavily on costly key-point labels, part annotations, and supplementary attributes such as make, model, and color. Due to the wide variety of vehicle re-id datasets featuring diverse annotation levels, strongly-supervised approaches fail to scale effectively across different domains. This paper introduces Self-supervised Attention for Vehicle Re-identification (SAVER), a new method designed to efficiently learn vehicle-specific discriminative features. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAVER outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on challenging benchmarks, including VeRi, VehicleID, Vehicle-1M, and VERI-Wild.

This study highlights a compelling correlation between the CDF collaboration's recent high-precision measurement of the $W$-boson mass and the muon $(g-2)$ anomaly within the framework of the two Higgs doublet model. One-loop diagrams featuring neutral scalar boson exchanges can account for the muon $(g-2)$ anomaly, provided there are substantial mass differences among the members of the second Higgs doublet. These same mass splittings induce a positive shift in the $W$-boson mass, aligning with the latest CDF results. For both anomalies to be explained simultaneously, the charged and neutral scalars in the model must not exceed approximately 600 GeV in mass. The complete parameter space of this model is accessible at the LHC through a combination of same-sign dimuon signatures from $pp \rightarrow (\mu^+ \mu^+ jj + {E\!\!\!\!/}_{T})$ and $pp \rightarrow (\mu^+\mu^-\tau^+\tau^-+X)$ processes.

In spring 2021, a new instrumented baffle was installed around the suspended end mirror within the input mode cleaner cavity of the Virgo interferometer. Since its deployment, the device has been used regularly in experiments, with results showing strong alignment with simulations of stray light within the optical cavity. This baffle will be utilized during the upcoming O4 observation run, acting as a prototype for the technology intended to equip baffles ahead of the main mirrors by the time of O5. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the baffle's design, covering its mechanics, front-end electronics, data acquisition systems, as well as optical and vacuum testing, calibration, installation protocols, and performance outcomes.

Achieving equitable predictions across protected demographics is a critical requirement for numerous federated learning applications. Nevertheless, existing research on group-fair federated learning has not established formal guarantees regarding either convergence or fairness. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework designed to ensure provably fair federated learning. Specifically, we investigate and expand the concept of Bounded Group Loss as a theoretically robust mechanism for enforcing group fairness. Leveraging this framework, we develop a scalable optimization approach that minimizes empirical risk while adhering to multiple group fairness constraints. We demonstrate both convergence and fairness guarantees for our proposed method. Furthermore, empirical evaluations across standard benchmarks from fair machine learning and federated learning reveal that our approach yields predictions that are both more accurate and fairer than those of baseline techniques.

This study determines the mass spectrum and decay constants for ground and excited heavy-light $P$-wave mesons, including $1^{++}$ and $1^{+-}$ states with quark compositions $c\overline{u}, c\overline{s}, b\overline{u}, b\overline{s}$, and $b\overline{c}$. The calculations are performed within a QCD-inspired Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) framework that employs an exact treatment of the spin structure $(\gamma_{\mu}\bigotimes\gamma_{\mu})$ in the interaction kernel. Within this $4\times 4$ BSE approach, coupled Salpeter equations for $Q\overline{q}$ systems are first solved using the confining interaction, demonstrating decoupling under the heavy-quark approximation. Subsequently, the one-gluon-exchange interaction is incorporated perturbatively to derive mass spectral equations. Finally, the analytic wave functions resulting from these equations are utilized to compute leptonic decay constants for the ground and excited $1^{++}$ and $1^{+-}$ states, serving as a validation of both the wave functions and the overall framework.

Contemporary deep learning approaches have attained significant success in machine learning and computer vision by training on pre-defined datasets. However, these methods often underperform in real-world scenarios due to catastrophic forgetting, where acquiring new tasks causes the model to rapidly lose knowledge of previous ones. While current state-of-the-art incremental learning techniques address this issue in traditional classification networks, they overlook the problem within embedding networks, which are foundational for applications like image retrieval, face recognition, and zero-shot learning. Unlike traditional incremental classification, embedding networks face a primary challenge in the semantic gap between the spaces of adjacent tasks. To address this, we introduce ZSTCI, a novel class-incremental method for embedding networks that utilizes zero-shot translation to estimate and compensate for semantic gaps without requiring exemplars. Furthermore, ZSTCI aims to learn a unified representation for sequential tasks, accurately capturing the relationships between prior and current classes. Additionally, ZSTCI can be seamlessly integrated with existing regularization-based incremental learning methods to further enhance performance. Extensive experiments on CUB-200-2011 and CIFAR100 demonstrate the method's effectiveness, and the code is publicly available.

Autonomous racing has become an increasingly popular research area, serving as a rigorous testbed for autonomous driving algorithms and driving innovation. However, in scaled racing platforms, computational constraints and complexity often restrict the application of Model Predictive Control (MPC). Consequently, geometric controllers are the most commonly implemented solutions due to their performance, operational simplicity, and ease of deployment. Despite these advantages, geometric controllers do not account for vehicle dynamics, confining their effectiveness to velocity ranges where tire slip is negligible. This paper introduces Model- and Acceleration-based Pursuit (MAP), a high-performance, model-based trajectory tracking algorithm that combines the simplicity of geometric methods with the benefits of incorporating tire dynamics. The MAP algorithm enables precise trajectory tracking at significantly higher speeds than current state-of-the-art geometric controllers. Experimental validation demonstrates that the MAP controller outperforms reference geometric controllers by a factor of four in lateral tracking error, achieving an error of only 0.055 meters at speeds up to 11 m/s.

As the emphasis on large-scale analytics intensifies, there is an increasing necessity to consolidate data from diverse sources. However, these datasets are rarely ready for immediate reuse. This challenge leads to elevated costs and creates a cycle where the integrated data remains difficult to repurpose without further modification. iTelos is a versatile methodology designed to mitigate these issues. Its core principle is that data usage frequency should dictate treatment: datasets that are reused more frequently tend to remain more stable across subsequent uses, thereby reducing overall preprocessing expenses while enhancing backward compatibility and facilitating future sharing.

This study employs hyperbolic wavelet regression to rapidly reconstruct high-dimensional functions characterized by interactions limited to a few variables. We utilize compactly supported periodic Chui-Wang wavelets to construct a tensorized hyperbolic wavelet basis. Initially, we provide a self-contained characterization of tensor product Sobolev-Besov spaces on the $d$-torus, defined by arbitrary smoothness levels, based on the decay rates of these wavelet coefficients. Subsequently, we conduct and analyze scattered-data approximation using a hyperbolic cross truncation of the basis expansion within an associated least squares framework. The resulting system matrix exhibits sparsity owing to the wavelets' compact support, significantly accelerating matrix-vector operations. For independently and identically distributed samples, we can bound the approximation error with high probability, incurring only logarithmic terms independent of the dimension $d$ relative to the optimal approximation. Furthermore, when a function possesses low effective dimension, we qualitatively identify variable interactions and eliminate ANOVA terms with low variance in a subsequent step to enhance accuracy, thereby proposing an adapted approximation model. Numerical experiments confirm the efficiency of this approach.

This paper investigates the effective integration of curvature data produced via SIMD-parallel forward-mode Algorithmic Differentiation (AD) into unconstrained Quasi-Newton (QN) minimization for smooth objectives, $f$. By evaluating the gradient, forward-mode AD yields block Hessian samples $Y=\nabla^2 f(x)\,S$. These samples update approximate inverse Hessians, $H_k \approx \nabla^2 f(x_k)$, within block QN frameworks. Unlike standard line-search BFGS methods that filter and correct secant-based curvature to enforce positive definiteness, our approach directly utilizes Hessian samples to refine indefinite inverse Hessian approximations without filtering. These sampled directions augment the conventional QN two-dimensional trust-region subproblem, forming a moderate-dimensional problem capable of leveraging negative curvature. The resulting quadratically-constrained quadratic program is solved precisely using a generalized eigenvalue algorithm, with steps accepted and trust region radii adjusted via standard procedures. The study aims to circumvent serial bottlenecks, harness both accurate positive and negative curvature, and perform an initial assessment of strategies for selecting $S$.

This study investigates the electroweak production of supersymmetric particles through recursive jigsaw reconstruction, focusing on final states with two or three leptons. Utilizing 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of data from the ATLAS experiment collected in 2015 and 2016 during $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV proton-proton collisions at the CERN Large Hadron Collider, the analysis examines chargino-neutralino pair production decaying via W or Z bosons. The search targets scenarios featuring large, intermediate, and Z-boson-mass-scale mass splittings between the parent particles and the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP). While results in regions corresponding to large and intermediate mass splittings align with Standard Model predictions, excluding chargino-neutralino masses up to 600 GeV for a massless LSP at 95% confidence, the region with low mass splitting presents a challenge due to kinematic similarities with Standard Model processes. In this low mass-splitting scenario, data exhibit excesses above the expected background, with the most significant local excess reaching 3.0 standard deviations.

Particle number fluctuations during nuclear collisions at intermediate energies ($E_{\rm lab} = 1.23-10A$ GeV) are investigated using the UrQMD-3.5 transport model. This framework integrates baryonic interactions via a density-dependent potential, enabling a consistent description of a first-order phase transition that includes a mechanically unstable region at high baryon densities. The scaled variance of baryon and proton distributions is computed within the central cubic volume of the collision system at various time steps. A notable increase in fluctuations linked to this unstable region is detected, which endures into later times, indicating a memory effect for these fluctuations. In contrast, the phase transition exerts a considerably weaker influence on the event-by-event momentum-space fluctuations of protons.

This paper investigates the count of integer pair solutions to the equation $|F(x,y)| = 1$, where $F(x,y)$ is an irreducible binary form over $\mathbb{Z}$ with degree $n \geqslant 3$ and exactly three nonzero terms. Specifically, we refine the explicit upper bounds on the number of solutions established by Emery Thomas. For example, when $n \geqslant 219$, we demonstrate that the equation admits at most 32 integer pair solutions if $n$ is odd and at most 40 if $n$ is even. This represents an improvement over Thomas's findings, which indicated a maximum of 38 solutions for odd $n$ and 48 for even $n$.

We present experimental data and theoretical analysis regarding the position response function of a cold atomic cloud situated within the viscous environment of an optical molasses and confined by a magneto-optical trap (MOT). By applying a transient, homogeneous magnetic field as a perturbation, we measured this response function. Our results reveal a shift from damped oscillatory motion to over-damped relaxation, driven by the interplay between the viscous drag of the molasses and the MOT's restoring force. These findings align qualitatively and quantitatively with a theoretical framework based on the Langevin equation. Furthermore, serving as a consistency check and a model for future studies, we examined the free diffusive expansion of the cloud when the MOT's confining field was disabled. The measured diffusion coefficient matched the value predicted by our Langevin model, utilizing the damping coefficient derived from the position response function measurements at the same temperature.

This study establishes a theoretical framework for nonequilibrium ultrafast photonics within monolayer quantum spin-Hall insulators, which host numerous topological states. In these materials, intense light-matter interactions occurring on femtosecond timescales induce non-adiabatic quantum dynamics, giving rise to nonlinear optoelectronic transport phenomena that depend on topology. We examine the mechanisms governing the interaction between topological Dirac fermions and intense ultrashort light pulses, revealing specific physical quantities in the high-harmonic spectrum that serve as fingerprints of the material's topological electronic state. This work lays the theoretical foundation for leveraging time-resolved harmonic spectroscopy to detect topological invariants in two-dimensional quantum spin-Hall solid-state systems.

Estimating policy gradients (PG) is difficult when the target policy cannot be sampled directly, limiting access only to data from an unknown behavior policy. Traditional off-policy PG methods often struggle with either substantial bias or variance that grows exponentially. This paper introduces the double Fitted PG (FPG) algorithm, which accommodates arbitrary policy parameterizations provided a Bellman-complete value function class is available. Specifically, under linear value function approximation, we derive a tight finite-sample upper bound for the PG estimation error, determined by the distribution mismatch in feature space. Furthermore, we demonstrate the asymptotic normality of the FPG estimation error with a precise covariance analysis, proving its statistical optimality against the Cramér-Rao lower bound. Empirical evaluations on both policy estimation and optimization tasks—using softmax tabular policies and ReLU networks—show that FPG significantly surpasses existing off-policy PG methods relying on importance sampling and variance reduction techniques across various metrics.

We introduce a novel method for investigating a specific class of non-Hermitian (1+1)-dimensional Dirac Hamiltonians featuring local Fermi velocity. By utilizing the established Nikiforov-Uvarov technique, we resolve this system and analyze the solvability of both $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric and non-$\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric potential classes. Specifically, within the $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric framework, we derive solutions for a harmonic oscillator subjected to a linear vector potential, whereas in the non-$\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric scenario, we address the shifted harmonic oscillator problem.

The Aharonov-Bohm (AB) effect represents a purely quantum phenomenon where a charged particle encircling a confined magnetic flux experiences a measurable phase shift, despite the flux residing in a region inaccessible to the particle. Classically, this non-local behavior seems impossible because the Lorentz force relies solely on the local magnetic field. However, in quantum mechanics, the Hamiltonian and Schrödinger equation establish a local coupling between the particle's current and the electromagnetic vector potential $\mathbf{A}$, which extends throughout space beyond the area containing the finite magnetic field. This has led some to argue that $\mathbf{A}$ is more "fundamental" than the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, even though $\mathbf{A}$ is gauge-dependent and unobservable. In this work, we provide a general proof, supported by examples, showing that the AB effect can be entirely explained by considering only the gauge-invariant $\mathbf{B}$ field, provided it is included within the quantum action of the complete isolated system. The cost of this gauge-invariant approach is the abandonment of locality: the AB phase emerges from the change in the $\mathbf{B}$ field's action within the region where the particle cannot access.

Traffic congestion, social media echo chambers, pedestrian flows, and electoral opinion shifts all represent intricate social systems. Although these scenarios appear distinct, they share common mathematical inquiries regarding how individual agents—ranging from drivers and social media users to pedestrians and voters—interact. By deciphering these interactions, modelers can forecast emergent group-level behaviors resulting from changes in individual actions. This tutorial, adapted from a lecture delivered at the 2021 American Mathematical Society Short Course, outlines key terminology, methodologies, and decision-making processes involved in constructing data-driven models. It examines distinctions between statistical versus mathematical, static versus dynamic, spatial versus non-spatial, discrete versus continuous, and phenomenological versus mechanistic approaches. To provide concrete examples, the tutorial details models for election dynamics and pedestrian crowd movement. Adopting a conceptual framework, it also emphasizes the challenges associated with model construction, calibration, complexity selection, and the integration of both quantitative and qualitative data.

Emojis introduce a visual dimension to often private text-based interactions, yet predicting them poses significant challenges for machine learning due to the skewed distribution between common and rare emojis. Existing research has largely concentrated on high-resource languages and relied on traditional server-side methods. However, these conventional approaches raise privacy issues by necessitating the transmission of all data to a central server. This paper addresses the dual challenges of focusing on high-resource languages for emoji prediction and safeguarding user data privacy. We present a new dataset comprising 118k tweets (expanded from 25k unique tweets) for Hindi emoji prediction and propose an adaptation of the federated learning algorithm, CausalFedGSD, designed to balance model efficacy with privacy protection. Our results demonstrate that this approach achieves performance comparable to more complex centralized models while requiring less data for optimization and significantly reducing privacy risks.

Defant and Kravitz recently introduced the friends-and-strangers graph $\mathsf{FS}(X,Y)$ for graphs $X$ and $Y$ sharing the same vertex count $n$. The vertices of $\mathsf{FS}(X,Y)$ represent bijections between $V(X)$ and $V(Y)$, with adjacency defined between $\sigma$ and $\tau$ if they differ only at two vertices $a, b \in V(X)$ where both $a \sim b$ in $X$ and $\sigma(a) \sim \sigma(b)$ in $Y$. This work investigates generalized versions of problems posed by Alon, Defant, and Kravitz. First, we prove that $\mathsf{FS}(X,Y)$ is connected if the minimum degrees $\delta(X)$ and $\delta(Y)$ satisfy $\delta(X) > n/2$, $\delta(Y) > n/2$, and $2\min(\delta(X), \delta(Y)) + 3\max(\delta(X), \delta(Y)) \ge 3n$. This result confirms a recent conjecture by Alon, Defant, and Kravitz, which posits a threshold $d_n = 3n/5 + O(1)$ such that $\mathsf{FS}(X,Y)$ remains connected whenever both graphs have minimum degrees at least $d_n$. In the case where $X$ and $Y$ are bipartite, a parity barrier ensures $\mathsf{FS}(X,Y)$ is disconnected. Specifically, if $X$ and $Y$ are edge-subgraphs of $K_{r,r}$ satisfying $\delta(X) + \delta(Y) \ge 3r/2 + 1$, then $\mathsf{FS}(X,Y)$ consists of exactly two connected components. Consequently, we offer a nearly complete resolution to another query by Alon, Defant, and Kravitz regarding the minimum degree $d^*_{r,r}$ required for any edge-subgraph $X$ of $K_{r,r}$ to yield a two-component $\mathsf{FS}(X,K_{r,r})$. We establish that $d^*_{r,r} = r/2 + 1$ for even $r$, while for odd $r$, $d^*_{r,r}$ lies within the set $\{\lceil r/2\rceil, \lceil r/2\rceil+1\}$.

**Introduction:** Clinical practice data offers a valuable source for generating real-world evidence (RWE) regarding COVID-19 treatments, serving to corroborate findings from randomized clinical trials (RCTs). As promising instruments for precision medicine, machine learning (ML) techniques are increasingly applied within RWE frameworks. This study utilizes ML to evaluate the effectiveness of various therapies on hospital admissions for COVID-19 within the Valencian Region of Spain.

**Methods:** Data from 5,244 and 1,312 hospital admissions (recorded between January 2020 and January 2021 across 10 health departments) were utilized to train and validate distinct treatment-effect models (TE-ML) for remdesivir, corticosteroids, tocilizumab, lopinavir-ritonavir, azithromycin, and chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine. An independent test set comprising 2,390 admissions from two additional health departments was reserved to retrospectively assess survival benefits using Cox proportional hazard models, based on the population selected by the TE-ML. To mitigate pre-treatment confounding variables linked to outcomes, the TE-ML models were adjusted using treatment propensity scores and subsequently evaluated for futility. The ML architecture employed boosted decision trees.

**Results:** Within the populations identified by the TE-ML models, only Remdesivir and Tocilizumab showed a statistically significant association with increased survival time, yielding hazard ratios of 0.41 (P = 0.04) and 0.21 (P = 0.001), respectively. No survival advantages were observed for chloroquine derivatives, lopinavir-ritonavir, or azithromycin. Furthermore, tools designed to interpret TE-ML predictions were examined at the patient level as potential aids for personalized decision-making and precision medicine.

**Conclusion:** ML methods prove to be appropriate instruments for analyzing RWE related to COVID-19 pharmacotherapies. The study's findings align with published RWE results and successfully validate outcomes derived from RCTs.
This paper investigates the geometry of solutions to the radial and chordal Loewner PDEs, focusing on a specific selection of time-dependent driving measures characterized by multiple point masses.

Technical support queries are frequently lengthy and intricate, typically comprising user problem descriptions, system configurations, and attempted troubleshooting steps. These queries often include non-natural language components such as command outputs, code snippets, error messages, and stack traces, which hold vital information for resolving issues but cannot be effectively processed by standard natural language tools. This paper tackles the challenge of segmenting technical support questions by framing it as a sequence labeling task and evaluating leading approaches. We contrast these results with an intuitive baseline involving contextual sentence-level classification and a state-of-the-art supervised text segmentation method. Additionally, we present a novel approach that integrates contextual embeddings from multiple language models pre-trained on diverse datasets, yielding significant performance gains over using a single model's embeddings. Finally, we demonstrate the practical value of this segmentation technique through improved outcomes in the downstream task of answer retrieval.

This study introduces an integrated neuromorphic controller designed for a robotic arm, aiming to minimize latency and power usage. Drawing inspiration from biological muscle mechanics, which rely on spike-driven signals from motor neurons connected to central pattern generators, the system mimics nature's ability to react swiftly and efficiently to various stimuli. Unlike traditional human-engineered encoding, neural processes utilize neurons and spikes for information processing, facilitating weighted decisions through continuous learning. The Event-Driven Scorbot (ED-Scorbot) platform, featuring a 6 Degrees of Freedom robotic arm, employs a Spiking Proportional-Integrative-Derivative algorithm to emulate these biological principles. This paper details an infrastructure enhancement for the ED-Scorbot, where the original controller hardware—comprising two Spartan Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) and a basic computer—is replaced by an edge computing device, the Xilinx Zynq-7000 SoC. This upgrade significantly lowers response times, energy consumption, and system complexity.

Accurately diagnosing COVID-19 is essential for disease prevention and control, for which deep learning offers a rapid and precise solution. This study proposes a model that integrates three established pre-trained networks in parallel to differentiate between healthy and coronavirus-infected samples. Trained using a negative log-likelihood loss function on the SARS-CoV-2 dataset of lung CT scans, the model achieved nearly 97% accuracy. The dataset comprises 2,482 images, including 1,252 samples confirmed to be infected with COVID-19.

The complexity of an Ising model is typically assessed by the computational difficulty of determining its ground state energy. However, this metric merely differentiates between planar and non-planar interaction graphs, overlooking other critical attributes like average node degree, the extent of long-range interactions, and lattice dimensionality. In this work, we propose a novel complexity measure for Ising models and provide a comprehensive classification based on it. Specifically, we analyze the decision problem associated with the function graph of the model's Hamiltonian, categorizing it within the Chomsky hierarchy. We demonstrate that the language of this decision problem is (i) regular if and only if the Ising model is finite; (ii) constructive context-free if and only if the model is linear with a regular edge language; (iii) constructive context-sensitive if and only if the edge language is context-sensitive; and (iv) decidable if and only if the edge language is decidable. Applying these results, we classify the 1D Ising model, models on generalized ladder graphs, and those on layerwise complete graphs as constructive context-free, while identifying the 2D Ising model, all-to-all models, and those on perfect binary trees as constructive context-sensitive. Furthermore, we present grammars for both 1D and 2D Ising models, marking this effort as an initial step toward characterizing physical interactions through grammatical frameworks.

Robot-Assisted Therapy (RAT) has proven effective in enhancing social skills among children with autism spectrum disorders (ASD). The DREAM project investigates the delivery of efficient RAT interventions to these children within a supervised autonomy framework for robotic control, aiming to reduce the workload on clinicians. This paper outlines the application of experimental protocols developed and rigorously tested in the DREAM Project within real-world settings, detailing their deployment and validation through a new ecological study led by clinicians.

We investigate pion and kaon condensation within three-flavor chiral perturbation theory at finite isospin ($\mu_I$) and strangeness ($\mu_S$) quark chemical potentials. The resulting phase diagram includes a vacuum state and three unique Bose-condensed phases featuring charged pion condensates, as well as condensates of both charged and neutral kaons. Upon incorporating electromagnetic interactions, the phase with a charged condensate transitions into a Higgs phase, altering the phase diagram due to electromagnetic mass splittings among mesons. These findings regarding the pion-condensed phase are utilized to derive the mass-radius relationship for pion stars, with local electric charge neutrality maintained by including electrons, muons, and their corresponding neutrinos. Finally, we compare our calculated mass-radius relations with recent lattice simulation data, observing excellent agreement.

The rise of distributed energy resources and smart grid technologies has transformed passive power consumers into active participants in energy trading. Acknowledging that traditional centralized markets yield low profitability for these users, recent studies have pivoted toward decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) trading, which offers superior benefits compared to grid transactions. However, existing P2P research often neglects user perception by assuming constant availability, participation, and compliance, potentially leading to negative sentiments and diminished engagement over time. This paper presents an automated P2P energy market that incorporates user perception. We utilize prospect theory to model user attitudes and develop an optimization framework that maximizes buyer perception while aligning demand and supply. Addressing the non-linear and non-convex nature of this problem, we propose DEbATE, a Differential Evolution-based Algorithm for Trading Energy. Furthermore, we introduce PQR, a risk-sensitive Q-learning algorithm that determines optimal seller prices based on perceived utility. Experimental results using real-world energy traces and realistic prospect theory functions demonstrate that our approach delivers a 26% increase in perceived value for buyers and generates 7% additional rewards for sellers compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

Because treatments for complex conditions often benefit only a subset of patients, accurately forecasting therapeutic outcomes for new individuals is both critical and difficult. This study introduces a predictive approach that leverages patient characteristics to estimate the impact of Riluzole, the sole FDA-approved medication for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS). Our technique utilizes model-based random forests to identify similarities in treatment responses across patients, thereby generating personalized models for new cases. The process centers on a base model—typically featuring a treatment indicator as a covariate and survival time, health status, or treatment success as the primary outcome—which serves two functions: guiding the splitting variables in the forest's trees based on interactions between patient traits and treatment, and calculating personalized models by using similarity metrics as weights. We validated this approach using data from multiple ALS clinical trials sourced from the PRO-ACT database. Our findings reveal that the efficacy of Riluzole varies significantly among ALS patients. Furthermore, this method facilitates the transition from stratified to personalized medicine and holds potential for evaluating treatment effects in other diseases investigated within clinical trials.

This study introduces Bayesian frameworks for various multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) tasks, grounded in a probabilistic interpretation of MCDM methodologies and issues. Leveraging the adaptability of Bayesian models, these frameworks tackle persistent and core MCDM challenges, such as group decision-making and criteria correlation, with statistical elegance. Additionally, the models handle diverse uncertainty types within decision-makers' preferences, including normal and triangular distributions, as well as interval preferences. A probabilistic mixture model is further developed to categorize decision-makers into comprehensive groups. A probabilistic ranking scheme is also established for both criteria and alternatives, quantifying the relative importance of one over another based on decision-maker preferences. Experimental results on multiple numerical examples validate the proposed frameworks and underscore their distinct advantages compared to other approaches.

The recent emergence of nonreciprocal electromagnetic systems, including invisibility cloaks, nonreciprocal-beam antennas, and nonreciprocal metasurfaces, has significantly increased interest in nonreciprocal phase shifters. To address the constraints of traditional technologies used for creating gyrators and phase shifters, we introduce a linear, low-profile, lightweight, and low-noise nonreciprocal phase shifter that requires no magnets and is constructed from two temporal loops. This temporal device functions by generating time-harmonic signals, utilizing constructive interference for desired harmonics and destructive interference for undesired ones at various points within the structure. An external time-harmonic modulation signal provides effective electronic angular momentum to regulate the phase and frequency of both loops. The resulting temporal nonreciprocal phase shifter demonstrates low insertion loss and a substantial return loss (input matching) exceeding 28.1 dB. Furthermore, its reconfigurable design allows for direct integration into IC technology, enabling the development of high-power handling, linear nonreciprocal phase shifters based on integrated circuits.

Consider $q$-uniform hypergraphs ($q$-graphs) $F$, $G$, and $H$, where $G$ is a spanning subgraph of $F$. We say $G$ is weakly $H$-saturated within $F$ if the edges in $E(F) \setminus E(G)$ can be ordered as $e_1, \dots, e_k$ such that for every $i \in [k]$, the hypergraph $G \cup \{e_1, \dots, e_i\}$ contains an isomorphic copy of $H$ that includes the edge $e_i$. The weak saturation number of $H$ in $F$ is defined as the minimum number of edges in an $H$-weakly saturated subgraph of $F$. Although Bollobás introduced the concept of weak saturation in 1968, our comprehension of it remains constrained after decades of research. The primary challenge involves establishing lower bounds on these numbers, which often resist standard combinatorial techniques and necessitate algebraic or geometric arguments.

In this paper, we precisely determine the weak saturation number of complete multipartite $q$-graphs within a directed framework for all parameter choices, thereby extending a 1985 theorem by Alon. Our proof synthesizes Kalai's exterior algebra methodology with the colorful exterior algebra approach inspired by recent work from Bulavka, Goodarzi, and Tancer on the colorful fractional Helly theorem. Furthermore, addressing a question posed by Kronenberg, Martins, and Morrison, we demonstrate a connection between the weak saturation numbers of bipartite graphs in cliques versus complete bipartite host graphs. Similarly, we asymptotically determine the weak saturation number of any complete $q$-partite $q$-graph in a clique, generalizing another finding by Kronenberg et al.

Following the discovery of the long-range superconducting proximity effect, the interplay between spin-triplet Cooper pairs and magnetic structures like domain walls and vortices has sparked extensive theoretical debate, yet experimental verification remains limited. We have engineered nanostructured Josephson junctions featuring precisely tunable spin textures using a disk-shaped Nb/Co bilayer. In this system, the vortex magnetization of the Co layer and the Cooper pairs of the Nb layer synergistically generate long-range triplet (LRT) superconductivity within the ferromagnet. Remarkably, LRT correlations manifest in highly confined channels (under 80 nm) along the ferromagnet's edge, despite its simple band structure. We demonstrate that these resilient rim currents originate from the magnetization texture functioning as an effective spin-orbit coupling, leading to spin accumulation at the bilayer-vacuum interface. Finally, we show that modifying the spin texture of a single ferromagnet enables the realization of both $0$ and $\pi$-channels within the same device.

A satisfactory explanation for dark energy and dark matter remains elusive. Recent studies have identified a renormalization group (RG)-enhanced Swiss-cheese cosmology, featuring an evolving cosmological constant tied to the Schwarzschild radius, as a viable framework for cosmic acceleration. This paper extends that approach by incorporating the joint scaling of the Newton constant $G$ and the cosmological constant $\Lambda$ under the IR-fixed point hypothesis. We demonstrate that this model naturally accounts for the transition from deceleration to acceleration without relying on additional energy scales, exotic fields, or fine-tuning. To test the robustness of the theory, we analyzed two distinct scaling relations and confirmed that both align closely with $\Lambda$CDM cosmology. Furthermore, we show that the model adheres to local observational constraints regarding the time variation of $G$.

Assessing video captioning systems is complex due to numerous factors, including caption fluency, simultaneous actions within a scene, and subjective human preferences regarding importance. Existing metrics typically measure the similarity between generated captions and a reference set of human annotations. This paper introduces a novel evaluation method utilizing a deep learning model based on BERT, a language model proven effective across various NLP tasks. The objective is to enable the model to mimic human evaluation capabilities by training on a dataset comprising human judgments of captions generated by systems in previous years of the TRECVid video-to-text challenge. These annotations will be released publicly. Experimental results indicate that BERTHA achieves favorable outcomes, surpassing standard metrics in certain configurations.

Quantum Annealing (QA) represents a computational paradigm that leverages the continuous evolution of a quantum system to identify the global minimum of an objective function within an unstructured search space. Functioning as a broad metaheuristic for optimization, including NP-hard challenges, QA offers potential solutions if one accepts an exponentially long runtime. Although extensively analyzed heuristically, the theoretical assurances regarding solution quality achievable within polynomial time remain largely unexplored. This paper introduces novel tools derived from the Lieb-Robinson (LR) bound, a concept from theoretical physics, to demonstrate that short, constant-time quantum annealing can yield constant-factor approximation ratios for specific optimization problems on bounded degree graphs. Informally, the LR bound facilitates a locality argument on these graphs, enabling the deduction of approximation ratios by analyzing subgraphs with limited radii. We apply these methods to the MaxCut and Maximum Independent Set problems on cubic graphs, delivering explicit approximation ratios and the associated runtimes. Our findings share characteristics with established results from the related Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) framework. Finally, we explore both theoretical and experimental avenues for potential enhancements.

With user privacy becoming increasingly prominent and influencing the dynamic between service providers and users, blockchain solutions are evolving to allow for data modification without compromising consistency. This study addresses that challenge by introducing the first redactable execute-order-validate blockchain architecture, which empowers users with the "right to be forgotten." The proposed design is straightforward to integrate, as demonstrated by its implementation on Hyperledger Fabric. It alters the block structure to remove user data from the hash chain while maintaining all correctness and liveness guarantees. Evaluation results indicate that the design ensures regulatory compliance with negligible performance costs, proving it is a viable enhancement for any execute-order-validate blockchain system.

The study examined the perceived arbitrariness of the zero-point constant for $V$-band bolometric corrections ($BC_V$) and its connection to the notions that a star's bolometric magnitude should exceed its visual magnitude and that bolometric corrections are invariably negative. Following IAU 2015 General Assembly Resolution B2, which established a definitive value for the bolometric magnitude scale's zero-point constant, $C_{Bol}(W) \approx 71.197425$, the validity of the claim that bolometric corrections must always be negative was disproven. Since the $BC_V$ scale's zero-point constant, $C_2$, is derived as $C_{Bol} - C_V$ (where $C_V$ is the visual magnitude zero point and $BC_V = m_{bol} - m_V$), and given that $C_{Bol} > C_V$, $C_2$ is necessarily a definite positive number rather than an arbitrary one. Consequently, the conditions $C_2 > 0$ and $0 < BC_V < C_2$ ensure $L_V < L$, mirroring scenarios with negative $BC_V$ values and demonstrating that bolometric corrections are not always negative. Ultimately, the initial assertion is misleading, as it incorrectly implies that bolometric corrections must always be negative, a condition that is not universally true.

**Context:** Magnetic null points are linked to high-energy solar phenomena like flares and frequently serve as locations for reconnection and particle acceleration. When these null points undergo dynamic twisting, they can trigger a Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (KHI) within their fan plane; sustained twisting may further induce spine-fan reconnection and the subsequent collapse of the null point.

**Aim:** This study seeks to contrast the impacts of isotropic versus anisotropic viscosity in simulations modeling the KHI and collapse within a dynamically twisted magnetic null point.

**Methods:** Using the 3D magnetohydrodynamics code Lare3d, a custom module for anisotropic viscosity was developed. Two high-resolution simulations were conducted with identical parameters except for the viscosity type: one employing isotropic viscosity and the other anisotropic viscosity. Additionally, a parameter sweep was executed across various values for viscosity and resistivity.

**Results:** Both viscosity models facilitate the development of the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability and the eventual null point collapse. Across the tested parameters, anisotropic viscosity promotes faster instability growth, whereas isotropic viscosity can dampen the instability to the point of stabilization in certain scenarios. Although viscous heating is typically lower with anisotropic viscosity, ohmic heating dominates and is amplified by current sheets formed during the instability, resulting in a higher total heating rate. Consequently, the null point collapse occurs significantly more rapidly when anisotropic viscosity is applied.

This paper explores quaternion applications in physics, focusing on elementary particle symmetry and interactions. It demonstrates that quark colors and Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) can be derived directly from the invariance of fundamental equations under quaternion phase transformations (quaternion gauge invariance). Generalized quaternions adhere to SU(3) symmetry, establishing QCD as essentially quantum quaternion dynamics. The study further extends SU(3) quaternions to G2 octonions, showing that the G2 octonion comprises seven SU(2) symmetry tri-generator sets, three of which constitute an SU(3) subgroup. Based on this, a model utilizing octonion gauge theory is proposed to classify and describe elementary particle interactions. This model unifies color and flavor across all particles, offering a unified framework for the four categories of elementary particles—quarks, leptons, gauge fields, and Higgs bosons—along with their interactions.

This paper examines Brownian motion's local times through the lens of algorithmic randomness. We define the concept of effective local time and demonstrate that every path which is Martin-Löf random relative to the Wiener measure possesses continuous effective local times at all computable points. Furthermore, we derive a novel, computationally formulated representation of classical Brownian local times.

Routing is essential for network applications but poses significant challenges in Delay Tolerant Networks (DTNs), a subset of mobile ad hoc networks involving humans and vehicles that operate without continuous connectivity. Due to node mobility, routing in these environments is NP-hard, typically addressed via heuristic "store and forward" replication strategies that duplicate messages across nodes to increase the chance of delivery; however, current protocols often yield low success rates. This study enhances two prevalent DTN protocols, Epidemic and PRoPHET, using Genetic Improvement (GI) to optimize their delivery probabilities. The process involves decomposing the protocols into functional components—such as data transfer checks and connection broadcasting—and treating them as terminal nodes within evolving trees for manipulation. Applied in silico to six urban network scenarios involving hundreds of nodes, GI demonstrated consistent delivery probability improvements in four instances.
