Adhering to established best practices for zero-shot text classification, we approach the task using a sentence pair modeling strategy. We achieve state-of-the-art F1 scores, improving results by up to 16% for unseen intents by utilizing intent labels and user utterances without relying on external knowledge sources. Performance is further enhanced by up to 7% through the lexicalization of intent labels. Additionally, leveraging task transfer from other sentence pair tasks, such as Natural Language Inference, yields further gains.

The $S=1$ Haldane state consists of local singlet dimers within the bulk and topological edge states in a chain, serving as a primary example of topological quantum matter. Its well-known quasi-one-dimensional manifestation, SrNi$_2$V$_2$O$_8$, exhibits both conventional and unconventional magnetic Raman scattering. The conventional component appears as one- and two-triplet excitations characterized by narrow linewidths and energies linked to the Haldane gap $\Delta_H$ and the intrachain exchange coupling $J_c$, respectively. It is hypothesized that well-defined magnetic quasiparticles are stabilized by interchain interactions and uniaxial single-ion anisotropy. In contrast, unconventional scattering manifests as broad continua with an intensity $I(T)$ displaying mixed bosonic and fermionic statistics. This mixed statistic, also found in Kitaev spin liquids, may indicate non-Abelian symmetry. Since the bulk ground state of SrNi$_2$V$_2$O$_8$ is topologically trivial, we propose that fractionalization arises from light-induced interchain exchange processes, which are likely enhanced near an Ising ordered state with a quantum critical point. These claims are further supported by a comparison with SrCo$_2$V$_2$O$_8$, the $S=1/2$ analogue of the material in question.

Advanced modeling is essential for tackling challenges in bioscience, synthetic biology, and precision medicine. To foster the collaboration required for these models, the community created the Simulation Experiment Description Markup Language (SED-ML), a standardized format for documenting simulations. However, SED-ML's effectiveness has been constrained by sparse support across modeling software and inconsistent interpretations among compatible tools. To assist modelers in debugging simulations and to encourage consistent SED-ML usage, we developed a validation tool. We have already utilized this validator to rectify errors in official SED-ML example files and intend to apply it to files within the BioModels database to ensure they are simuable. We expect the validator to be instrumental in creating more predictive simulations and in boosting both the adoption and interoperability of SED-ML.

**Availability:** The validator is freely accessible as a webform, HTTP API, command-line utility, and Python package via https://run.biosimulations.org/utils/validate and https://pypi.org/project/biosimulators-utils. It is also integrated into the interfaces of 11 simulation tools, with source code provided openly in the Supplementary data.

**Contact:** karr@mssm.edu

Iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) is a widely used method for tackling sparsity-enforcing regression tasks in machine learning. While current state-of-the-art techniques offer greater efficiency, they often depend on specific coordinate pruning strategies. This study demonstrates that a remarkably straightforward reparameterization of IRLS, combined with a bilevel resolution strategy rather than an alternating one, can achieve top-tier performance across diverse sparsity types (including Lasso, group Lasso, and trace norm regularizations), various regularization strengths (even hard constraints), and design matrices (spanning from correlated designs to differential operators). Although our method, like IRLS, relies solely on solving linear systems, it differs significantly by minimizing a smooth function. Despite the non-convex nature of the problem, we prove that spurious minima do not exist and that saddle points are navigable, ensuring a descent direction is always available. Consequently, we recommend employing a BFGS quasi-Newton solver, rendering our approach simple, robust, and efficient. We conducted a numerical benchmark comparing our algorithm's convergence speed against leading solvers for Lasso, group Lasso, trace norm, and linearly constrained problems. These findings underscore the versatility of our method, eliminating the necessity to switch solvers based on the specific characteristics of the machine learning problem at hand.

This study reports a search for generic, short-duration gravitational-wave (GW) bursts within data collected during the third observing run of Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo. We employed the coherent WaveBurst (cWB) pipeline, augmented by a decision-tree classification algorithm to more effectively distinguish GW signals from noise transients. This machine-learning (ML) algorithm was trained using a representative dataset of noise events and simulated stochastic signals uncorrelated with any known signal models, thereby maintaining the search's model-independent character. Our results demonstrate that the ML-enhanced cWB pipeline achieves greater detection distances for GW signals compared to prior model-independent searches. Sensitivity gains were observed across a broad spectrum of simulated signals to validate the robustness of this model-agnostic approach. At a false-alarm rate of one event per century, detectable signal amplitudes decreased by nearly an order of magnitude, particularly for single-cycle morphologies. Furthermore, this enhanced pipeline improved the detection efficiency of compact binary mergers across a wide mass range, from stellar to intermediate-mass black holes, encompassing both circular and elliptical orbits. After excluding previously identified compact binaries, no new GW signals were detected using the two-fold Hanford-Livingston or three-fold Hanford-Livingston-Virgo networks. Leveraging the improved sensitivity of this all-sky search, we have established the most stringent constraints to date on the isotropic emission of gravitational-wave energy from short-duration burst sources.

Multi-hop Question Answering (QA) necessitates reasoning across several supporting facts to derive an answer. Nevertheless, current QA models often depend on shortcuts, such as relying on a single fact to provide the correct answer, a phenomenon known as the *disconnected reasoning* problem. To address this, we introduce a novel counterfactual multi-hop QA framework based on a causal-effect approach designed to mitigate disconnected reasoning. This method relies on explicitly modeling two types of causality: the direct causal effects of disconnected reasoning and the causal contribution of genuine multi-hop reasoning within the total causal effect. Utilizing a causal graph, we propose a counterfactual inference mechanism that disentangles disconnected reasoning from the total causal effect, offering a new perspective and technological advancement for developing QA models that prioritize true multi-hop reasoning over shortcuts. Comprehensive experiments conducted on the HotpotQA benchmark dataset demonstrate significant improvements in reducing disconnected reasoning. For instance, our approach yields a 5.8% increase in the Supp$_s$ score on HotpotQA by leveraging authentic multi-hop reasoning. The source code is accessible in the supplementary materials.

Let $H$ and $D$ be measurable spaces equipped with countably generated $\sigma$-algebras, where $P_H$ is a perfect prior probability measure on $H$ and $S: H \rightarrow D$ represents a sampling distribution. Under these conditions, a unique inference map $I: D \rightarrow H$ exists, defined up to a set of measure zero. Consequently, for any data measurement $\mu: 1 \rightarrow D$, the posterior probability $\widehat{P_H} = I \circ \mu$ can be determined. This approach is iterative: each updated $P_H$ generates a new joint distribution, which in turn produces a new inference map $I$, allowing the cycle to repeat with every new measurement. The core result relies on an existence theorem for regular conditional probabilities established by Faden, which extends beyond the limitations of Polish spaces. This broader framework facilitates non-trivial decision rules (specifically Eilenberg--Moore algebras) on both finite and non-finite spaces and unifies decision theory with Bayesian probability.

Leveraging the algebraic and order-theoretic foundations of Sahlqvist correspondence, unified correspondence theory offers robust tools for establishing correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantics and signatures, encompassing all logics defined by normal (distributive) lattice expansions ((D)LEs). Specifically, the ALBA algorithm, which is parametric for each (D)LE, efficiently determines the first-order correspondents of (D)LE-inductive formulas. We introduce an algorithm that utilizes ALBA's rules and algebraic framework to reverse its steps within the DLE context, thereby effectively deriving an inductive formula from its given first-order correspondent.

This research addresses the challenge of maximizing monotone non-submodular functions under partition matroid constraints. While related generalizations have been explored previously, our study specifically exploits the unique characteristics of partition matroids to (1) develop algorithms featuring provable theoretical bounds and efficient query complexity, and (2) offer refined analyses of the theoretical performance guarantees for existing methods. Additionally, we evaluate these algorithms in the contexts of Boosting Influence Spread and Video Summarization. Experimental results demonstrate that our approaches achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art solutions while requiring significantly fewer queries.

We present findings on the coherent, layer-by-layer enhancement of high-order harmonic generation (HHG) in artificially stacked transition metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) crystals across various stacking configurations. Using the gold foil-exfoliation technique, we synthesized millimeter-sized single-crystal monolayers and assembled them into stacks on transparent substrates. Interaction with an ultrafast mid-infrared (MIR) driving laser produced high-order harmonics up to the 19th order. Our results demonstrate that harmonic generation depends on both the number of layers and their relative orientation. In the AAAA stacking configuration, both odd and even orders show a quadratic intensity increase with layer count, indicating constructive interference from successive layers. Notably, deviations from this scaling occur at photon energies exceeding the bandgap, attributed to self-absorption. Conversely, AB and ABAB stacking configurations yield even-order harmonics below the detection limit, consistent with inversion symmetry. This study validates the ability to generate non-perturbative high-order harmonics from stacked layered materials under intense MIR fields without causing sample damage. These findings offer implications for optimizing nano-scale solid-state HHG sources and utilizing high harmonics as an ultrafast probe for artificially stacked materials. Given that HHG is a strong-field-driven process, it holds promise for probing high-momentum and energy states within band structures with atomic-scale spatial resolution, making it a valuable tool for investigating novel structures like Moiré patterns.

Invasive Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) are widely utilized in medical contexts to record, stimulate, or suppress neural activity for various therapeutic goals, such as alleviating Parkinson's disease symptoms through targeted brain stimulation. Despite recent technological advancements, securing BCIs against cyber threats remains a critical challenge, as attackers can exploit system vulnerabilities to inflict malicious stimulation or disrupt treatments, thereby altering neuronal function. This study introduces and implements a novel cyberattack termed Neuronal Jamming (JAM), designed to inhibit neuronal spiking. To evaluate and quantify the impact of JAM, we established a use case involving a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) trained to guide a mouse out of a specific maze, given the scarcity of realistic mammalian neuronal topologies. This model was mapped to a simulated neural architecture representing a segment of the mouse's visual cortex. We assessed JAM's effects on both biological and artificial networks, analyzing its ability to disrupt spontaneous neural signaling and impair the mouse's maze-solving capabilities. Furthermore, we compared JAM with an existing attack method, FLO, demonstrating that JAM results in a more significant reduction in neuronal spike rates. Finally, we discuss the potential for JAM and FLO attacks to mimic neurodegenerative disease symptoms if an implanted BCI provides comprehensive electrode coverage over targeted brain regions.

This paper aims to derive the precise formula and analyze the constant sign of the Green's function associated with a second-order perturbed periodic problem subject to integral boundary conditions at the interval's endpoints. We employ the theory outlined in \cite{CLY} for general non-local perturbed boundary value problems to determine the Green's function expression. Furthermore, we seek to identify the set of parameters for which this Green's function maintains a constant sign. This requires first examining a related second-order problem devoid of integral boundary conditions, establishing the properties of its Green's function, and subsequently applying these findings to ascertain the sign of the Green's function for the primary problem.

Democratizing artificial intelligence entails training and deploying machine learning models across diverse and often massive environments. While data diversity offers significant opportunities to enhance AI systems, it simultaneously raises critical issues regarding privacy, security, and equity that demand focused attention. This study demonstrates that it is theoretically unfeasible to construct a rational learning algorithm capable of effectively learning across heterogeneous settings, a concept we term collective intelligence (CI). By modeling learning algorithms as choice correspondences within a hypothesis space, we derive a set of essential axioms. Regrettably, the sole algorithm that satisfies all these axioms is standard empirical risk minimization (ERM), which is inherently limited to learning from a single environment. Our impossibility result identifies informational incomparability between environments as a primary barrier for researchers developing novel multi-environment learning algorithms. This insight clarifies the necessary conditions for success in pivotal machine learning domains, including out-of-distribution generalization, federated learning, algorithmic fairness, and multi-modal learning.

This study establishes the effectiveness of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in solving the non-relativistic, time-dependent Schrödinger equation. We evaluate the performance and generalizability of these PINN-based solvers regarding the temporal evolution of a quantum harmonic oscillator, examining variations in system parameters, domains, and energy states.

This research investigates two-dimensional lattice systems containing bosons and fermions subjected to nonequilibrium states characterized by a steep temperature gradient created by two thermal reservoirs. Specifically, we analyze a lattice model featuring broken time-reversal symmetry that displays both topologically trivial and nontrivial phases. By employing a nonperturbative Green function method, we map out the nonequilibrium current distribution across various parameter regimes. Our findings reveal chiral edge currents in both bosonic and fermionic systems that remain robust against reservoir coupling and the presence of defects, whether located at the boundaries or within the bulk. This resilience stems not only from topological mechanisms at zero temperature but also, notably, from dissipative symmetries that sustain it even when band topology is irrelevant. The chirality of these edge currents indicates that energy flows locally against the temperature gradient without requiring external work. Additionally, in the fermionic scenario, we identify a regime of topologically protected boundary currents that, however, do not form a complete circulation around all system edges.

We examine the three-dimensional kinematics of approximately 82,000 red giant clump (RGC) stars from the Tycho-2 catalog. Initially, utilizing all existing data, we calculated the most probable components of the residual rotation vector for the optical realization of the ICRS/HIPPARCOS system relative to an inertial frame: ($\omega_x, \omega_y, \omega_z$) = $(-0.11, 0.24, -0.52) \pm (0.14, 0.10, 0.16)$ mas/yr. Consequently, stellar proper motions in right ascension were adjusted by applying the correction $\omega_z = -0.52$ mas/yr. Our analysis reveals that, beyond participating in the general Galactic rotation characterized by Oort constants $A = 15.82 \pm 0.21$ km/s/kpc and $B = -10.87 \pm 0.15$ km/s/kpc, RGC stars exhibit kinematic peculiarities within the Galactic yz plane linked to the warped structure of the stellar-gaseous disk. Furthermore, the parameters of the linear Ogorodnikov-Milne model describing RGC star kinematics in the zx plane are not significantly different from zero. In contrast, the yz plane shows distinct behavior; for instance, the component of the solid-body rotation vector around the Galactic x-axis is $M_{32-} = -2.6 \pm 0.2$ km/s/kpc. Additionally, two deformation tensor parameters in this plane, $M_{23}^+ = 1.0 \pm 0.2$ km/s/kpc and $(M_{33} - M_{22}) = -1.3 \pm 0.4$ km/s/kpc, also deviate significantly from zero. Overall, the kinematics of the warped disk in the local solar neighborhood can be characterized as a rotation around the Galactic X-axis (near the line of nodes) with an angular velocity ranging from $(-3.1 \pm 0.5)$ to $(-4.4 \pm 0.5)$ km/s/kpc.

We introduce straightforward models in which lepton flavor-violating interactions produce the observed dark matter density via the freeze-in mechanism of an axion-like particle with a mass of a few keV. Unlike conventional flavor-diagonal freeze-in, this approach strengthens dark matter stability, relaxes constraints from stellar cooling, and boosts the sensitivity of accelerator-based experiments. These scenarios are testable using upcoming X-ray observatories, and in certain instances, they will be almost fully explored by new high-intensity searches for lepton flavor violation, such as those conducted by Mu3e and MEG II.

This study presents a method for evaluating text classification techniques by examining the inclusion or exclusion of task-specific terms and their synonyms within the text. We utilized this framework to assess six distinct transfer-learning and unsupervised approaches designed to identify articles pertinent to COVID-19 vaccines and therapeutics. The results indicated that although a search-engine-trained BERT model achieved strong overall performance, it failed to correctly classify relevant abstracts lacking specific task-related terminology. Leveraging this finding, we developed a more robust unsupervised ensemble method.

We describe a system of hard spheres governed by a straightforward collision rule that conserves energy yet breaks time-reversal symmetry. These interactions result in a stationary state that is achiral, isotropic, and homogeneous; its characteristics are established through simulations and contrasted with an approximate theory initially formulated for elastic hard spheres. Within this nonequilibrium fluid regime, velocity correlations emerge—a feature recognized in other nonequilibrium stationary states. These correlations extend over long ranges, diminishing as $1/r^d$ in $d$ dimensions. Such long-range correlations are anticipated based on general principles far from equilibrium and have been previously documented in driven or non-stationary systems.

This study addresses the challenge of reducing information leakage between communication and sensing within systems that execute both functions simultaneously. It examines a discrete memoryless state-dependent broadcast channel where (i) feedback allows a transmitter to convey data while estimating the channel state, and (ii) one receiver acts as an eavesdropper whose state must be estimated but who must remain unaware of specific portions of the transmitted information. This model captures the security complexities inherent in joint communication and sensing when the channel state represents a sensitive attribute, such as location. For scenarios involving independent and identically distributed states, perfect output feedback, and requirements to keep part of the message secret, a partial characterization of the secrecy-distortion region is established. This characterization becomes exact if the broadcast channel is either physically-degraded or reversely-physically-degraded. Furthermore, the partial characterization is extended to cases where the entire message must remain confidential. Finally, the advantages of a joint approach over separation-based secure communication and state-sensing techniques are demonstrated using a binary joint communication and sensing model.

Recent encoder-decoder models for Hawkes processes employ transformer-like architectures that utilize embeddings and self-attention to encode event histories, offering superior prediction and fit compared to RNN-based methods. However, these models often suffer from high computational and memory demands and may struggle to accurately capture the underlying triggering function. To address these issues, we propose an efficient and general encoding method that substitutes complex multi-layered attention structures with triggering kernels derived from observed data. Leveraging the similarity between point process triggering kernels and attention scores, we use these kernels to replace weights in history representation construction. Our estimated triggering function incorporates a sigmoid gating mechanism to effectively capture local-in-time triggering effects that standard decaying-over-time kernels often miss. Additionally, by accepting both event type representations and temporal embeddings, the model learns type-time kernel parameters for the underlying process based on event type pairs. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets—including a widely used COVID-19 set featuring longitudinal covariates—demonstrate that our model outperforms existing approaches with reduced computational complexity and provides interpretable results through the direct application of the new kernel.

In extensive dynamic wireless networks, channel estimation (CE) overhead has emerged as a critical performance limitation. This issue stems from the high volume of users requiring estimation, user mobility, and rapid channel fluctuations inherent to high-frequency spectrum usage, such as millimeter wave. This study introduces a novel hybrid channel estimation and prediction (CEP) framework designed to mitigate overhead in time-division duplex (TDD) cell-free massive multiple-input-multiple-output (mMIMO) systems. The approach requires each user to transmit a pilot signal only once within a specific window of coherence intervals (CIs). Subsequently, minimum mean-square error (MMSE) estimation calculates the channel for the initial CI, while a deep neural network (DNN) forecasts the channels for the remaining intervals in that window. Leveraging the temporal correlation between successive CIs and pilot signals, the DNN enhances prediction accuracy. This method reduces CE overhead by a minimum of 50% while maintaining negligible CE error under practical mobility conditions. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed CEP scheme significantly improves spectral efficiency compared to traditional MMSE CE methods, particularly in scenarios with a large number of users.

Rational Krylov subspaces have emerged as a standard reference for dimensionality reduction across various application domains. For symmetric data matrices, an associated orthonormal basis can be generated via a short-term recurrence relation. Previously, this approach was discarded because it necessitated twice as many linear system solves per iteration as the traditional long-term method. We present an implementation that achieves rational subspace reduced matrices at a lower total computational cost than previously reported by efficiently combining the two system solves. Furthermore, we discuss several applications where the short-term recurrence capability enables the avoidance of storing the complete orthonormal basis. Finally, multiple examples demonstrate the benefits of the proposed procedure.

Cavity magnomechanics has emerged as a premier system for investigating macroscopic quantum phenomena. By integrating magnons, phonons, and photons within a single physical framework, it presents numerous prospects for quantum technologies. Traditionally, this field relies on yttrium iron garnet, which demonstrates a linear magnon-phonon coupling described by $\hat{m}^\dag\hat{m}(\hat{b}^\dag+\hat{b})$, where $\hat{m}$ and $\hat{b}$ represent the magnon and phonon modes, respectively. Drawing inspiration from recent advancements in two-dimensional (2D) magnets, we introduce a novel cavity magnomechanical setup where one cavity mirror is constructed from a 2D magnetic material. The anisotropic magnetostrictive interaction in this configuration generates a distinctive nonlinear phonon-magnon coupling, $\hat{m}^\dag\hat{m}(\hat{b}^\dag+\hat{b})^2$. Our analysis reveals that stable phonon squeezing and bi- and tri-partite entanglement among the three modes can be achieved under conditions of suppressed phonon numbers. Unlike prior approaches, this scheme eliminates the need for additional nonlinear interactions or reservoir engineering and demonstrates robustness against thermal fluctuations. By expanding the landscape of cavity magnomechanics, our system offers superior capabilities in quantum-state engineering, leveraging the versatile interactions inherent to its 2D characteristics.

Although multi-view 3D human mesh estimation holds significant real-world potential for applications like motion capture and sports analysis, and offers robustness against single-view ambiguities, it has received minimal research focus. Current methods often struggle with generalization to new environments, primarily because multi-view training datasets lack sufficient diversity in image-mesh pairs. While researchers have turned to synthetic images to mitigate this, these approaches face two main hurdles: the visual discrepancy between rendered and real data, and overfitting to specific camera viewpoint distributions during training that do not match real-world scenarios. To overcome these issues, we introduce a new simulation-based training pipeline for multi-view human mesh recovery. This approach (a) utilizes intermediate 2D representations that are more resilient to the synthetic-to-real domain gap; (b) employs learnable calibration and triangulation to accommodate a wider variety of camera configurations; and (c) progressively fuses multi-view information within a canonical 3D space to eliminate ambiguities inherent in 2D data. Comprehensive benchmarking confirms that our method outperforms existing solutions, particularly in unseen, real-world scenarios.

This work examines investigations into heavy sterile neutrinos, with a focus on direct experimental searches and neutrinoless double beta decay. Utilizing a phenomenological framework, we underscore the critical role of sterile neutrino characteristics in interpreting results from neutrinoless double beta decay experiments. Although existing limits on active-sterile neutrino mixing are already tight, we draw attention to upcoming initiatives designed to explore regions motivated by the small mass of active neutrinos.

In a multi-source setting, every source possesses a distinct level of credibility. In the absence of external credibility data, the information supplied by these sources can be leveraged to evaluate their trustworthiness. This paper introduces a method for quantifying conflict within a multi-source environment as a standard metric. We validate our algorithm through three simulated scenarios featuring escalating conflict levels and one experimental case. The findings indicate that the proposed measure captures conflict in a meaningful manner consistent with human expectations, thereby enabling the identification of conflicts among the sources.

This study elucidates the connection between network topology and functional behavior, such as information transmission and synchronization, within active systems like neural networks. Specifically, we demonstrate a method for identifying an optimal network structure for data transfer. Optimality is defined by the network's capacity to convey substantial information, its abundance of communication channels, and its resilience against significant fluctuations in coupling configurations. This theoretical framework is broadly applicable and independent of the specific dynamics of the network's constituent elements; instead, the topology is derived by identifying a Laplacian matrix whose eigenvalues meet particular criteria. To validate these concepts, we apply them to neural networks composed of electrically coupled chaotic Hindmarsh-Rose neurons.

We derive leading-twist valence quark transverse-momentum-dependent parton distribution functions (TMD PDFs) for the proton using the basis light-front quantization (BLFQ) framework. These findings align with lattice QCD calculations and our prior results for the collinear limit, as well as Soffer-type bounds. Within this approach, we observe that the six leading-twist T-even TMDs are mutually independent, indicating that previously identified model-dependent relations are invalid. This independence suggests our results may represent a more robust treatment of QCD in future studies. Additionally, we find a non-trivial $ x $-dependence for $\left<(p^\perp)^2\right>$ and partial consistency with the Gaussian ansatz, though only at small $(p^\perp)^2$. These characteristics indicate that our results could serve as a valuable alternative for future experimental extractions.

We will outline several groundbreaking initiatives focused on electromagnetic radiative corrections within semileptonic decay processes, highlighting the pivotal role of lattice QCD. These investigations are vital for accurately determining the matrix element $V_{ud}$ from beta decays involving pions, free neutrons, and $J^P=0^+$ nuclei, and they are instrumental in resolving recent anomalies concerning $V_{ud}$ and $V_{us}$ that could signal physics extending beyond the Standard Model.

Optically levitated dielectric particles function as highly sensitive detectors for minute forces and torques, serve as instruments in quantum information science, and act as platforms for testing quantum coherence in macroscopic systems. Understanding the structural and optical characteristics of these particles is crucial for calibrating experimental sensitivity. This study presents nanomechanical testing results for silica nanospheres and examines an annealing method that yields samples with elastic moduli closer to bulk-like behavior. By combining these findings with experimental data on optical trap lifetimes under high vacuum and high-intensity trapping lasers for both annealed and as-grown nanospheres, we conducted a theoretical analysis of how porosity and non-sphericity affect the samples. This analysis identified potential mechanisms for trapping instabilities in nanospheres that deviate from bulk-silica properties.

In robotics, ergodic control broadens the concept of tracking by defining a probability distribution across a target area rather than following a specific trajectory. The initial formulation treats this as a spectral multiscale coverage challenge, usually involving the decomposition of spatial distributions into Fourier series; however, this method struggles to scale effectively for exploration tasks in search spaces exceeding two dimensions. To overcome this limitation, we introduce tensor trains, a modern low-rank tensor decomposition method from multilinear algebra. This solution offers significant efficiency in both computation and storage, rendering it ideal for real-time implementation within robotic systems. We validated the approach on a peg-in-hole insertion task that demands complete 6D end-effector poses using a 7-axis Franka Emika Panda robot. The results demonstrate that ergodic exploration successfully completes the task without the need for force/torque sensors.

In computer vision, fine-tuning remains the standard method for adapting pre-trained models to specific downstream tasks, yet its practical implementation is often difficult due to the need for parameter-efficient global updates and dependence on high-quality data. Recently, prompt-based learning has significantly enhanced performance in natural language tasks by introducing task-specific prompts to adapt frozen models. This work extends that success to vision models as an alternative to traditional fine-tuning by introducing Pro-tuning, a parameter-efficient approach. Pro-tuning operates by learning task-specific prompts for input images while keeping the pre-trained vision model frozen. By training only a small set of additional parameters, this method is compatible with various architectures, including CNNs and Transformers. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Pro-tuning surpasses fine-tuning across a wide spectrum of vision tasks and scenarios. These include image classification challenges such as generic object recognition, class imbalance, image corruption, adversarial robustness, and out-of-distribution generalization, as well as dense prediction tasks like object detection and semantic segmentation.

The COVID-19 pandemic continues to exert significant pressure on healthcare systems, economies, and agriculture. Existing computational and mathematical models have often proven unreliable because of the intricate nature of infection spread, a problem compounded by insufficient data collection and reporting. Consequently, there is an urgent need to re-evaluate the situation using robust data sources and novel forecasting techniques. Deep learning architectures, particularly recurrent neural networks (RNNs), are highly effective for modeling spatiotemporal sequences. This study employs various RNN variants, including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), bidirectional LSTM, and encoder-decoder LSTM models, to forecast multi-step (short-term) COVID-19 infections. We focused on Indian states identified as hotspots, analyzing both the first wave (2020) and the second wave (2021) to generate two-month-ahead predictions. Our results indicate a low probability of a new infection surge in October and November 2021, though authorities must remain vigilant due to emerging viral variants. The model's predictive accuracy suggests its applicability to other regions; however, modeling challenges persist due to data reliability issues and the difficulty of accounting for complex factors like population density, logistics, and socio-cultural aspects.

Canonical quantization has provided significant insights, such as the harmonic oscillator, which models a ball swinging back and forth on a string. In contrast, the half-harmonic oscillator restricts the ball at the bottom, causing it to bounce back immediately; this system cannot be accurately solved using standard canonical quantization. However, affine quantization, an extension of the quantization framework, successfully resolves the half-harmonic oscillator and provides correct solutions for numerous other challenges, including those in field theory and gravity. This paper aims to introduce affine quantization, explaining its nature and capabilities.

Classifying ECG heartbeats is essential for diagnosing cardiac arrhythmias. The Physionet/CinC 2021 challenge aimed to accurately determine clinical diagnoses using 12, 6, 4, 3, or 2-lead ECG recordings to assist physicians in identifying various heart conditions. While Transformers have recently achieved significant success in natural language processing, our team, CinCSEM, proposed adapting them for periodic time series by treating repeated cycles as "words" and the entire signal as a sequence of these words, thereby enabling the application of attention mechanisms. Our implementation utilized the Transformer Encoder architecture, which stacks multiple encoder layers followed by a dense layer equipped with either linear or sigmoid activation functions for generative pre-training or classification, respectively. This project focused on multi-label classification of heartbeat abnormalities within the ECG dataset provided by the challenge. Our top-performing entry, which adhered to the challenge's hardware constraints, attained scores of 0.12, 0.07, 0.10, 0.10, and 0.07 on the test sets for 12-lead, 6-lead, 4-lead, 3-lead, and 2-lead configurations, respectively. Regrettably, our team was excluded from the final rankings due to the absence of a pre-print.

This study presents thermal neutron flux measurements taken at various positions within the STAR experimental hall during the $\sqrt s$ = 510 GeV Run 13 at RHIC. These data were compared against simulations utilizing \textsc{PYTHIA} for minimum bias events, a detailed GEANT3 model of the detector and hall, and the GCALOR neutron transport code. Results showed good agreement (within approximately 30%) at locations roughly 1 meter and 10 meters from the beam pipe. However, at intermediate distances of about 5 meters, the simulation overestimated the neutron flux by a factor of approximately 3.

This study investigates local music recommendation, a task focused on generating personalized playlists of tracks from artists who predominantly perform live events within a specific geographic region. Since most local artists are obscure, long-tail performers with minimal associated user preference data, traditional collaborative filtering methods face significant cold-start challenges due to their reliance on extensive information for accurate predictions. We evaluate three standard recommender system algorithms—Item-Item Neighborhood (IIN), Alternating Least Squares for Implicit Feedback (ALS), and Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR)—on the local music recommendation task using the Million Playlist Dataset. To ensure relevance, we adapted the standard evaluation protocol to restrict rankings to tracks by local artists across eight distinct cities. Although matrix factorization techniques (ALS and BPR) typically excel in large-scale recommendation scenarios, our results indicate that the neighborhood-based approach (IIN) outperforms them specifically for long-tail local music recommendation.

Research on Ca$_{1-x}$RE$_x$FeAs$_2$ (where RE represents a rare earth element) has documented both structural transitions and antiferromagnetic (AFM) phases, even within the electron-overdoped regime. This study examines the temperature-dependent in-plane optical spectroscopy of the overdoped compound Ca$_{0.77}$Nd$_{0.23}$FeAs$_2$. Upon transitioning into the AFM state, we observed a sudden decrease in spectral weight within the low-frequency optical conductivity range (500–2,000 cm$^{-1}$). Unlike the parent compounds of the 122 family, which exhibit clear spin-density-wave gaps in their AFM states, no such gap signature appears in Ca$_{0.77}$Nd$_{0.23}$FeAs$_2$, possibly due to ineffective nesting between hole and electron pockets. Nevertheless, spectral weight analysis reveals that the lost low-frequency weight shifts to the high-frequency range (>4,000 cm$^{-1}$), indicating a localization mechanism. These findings imply that the AFM order in Ca$_{0.77}$Nd$_{0.23}$FeAs$_2$ likely arises from electron localization rather than Fermi surface nesting.

Algorithmic randomness examines the definition of randomness for infinite binary sequences within specific uncertainty frameworks. Traditionally, martingale-theoretic approaches rely on precise models, though the integration of imprecision into this domain is a recent development. Consequently, research into how imprecision reshapes our understanding of martingale-theoretic random sequences is in its infancy. In this work, which permits non-computable uncertainty models, we reveal a striking and intimate link between precise and imprecise models within this context. Specifically, we demonstrate that stationary imprecise models and non-computable, non-stationary precise models can yield identical sets of random sequences. Furthermore, we offer an initial exploration of the potential consequences of these findings for statistics grounded in imprecise probabilities, while also illuminating the practical (ir)relevance of both imprecise and non-computable precise uncertainty models in that setting.

Image reconstruction methods, such as denoising, frequently require processing the RGB data from cameras and mobile devices. However, standard additive white noise (AWN) models fail to accurately replicate the specific noise and degradation patterns found in these inputs. This discrepancy is critical for learning-based approaches, as the gap between training data and real-world conditions impairs generalization. This paper introduces a method to precisely simulate the noise and degradation transformations inherent in camera pipelines, enabling the creation of realistic RGB image distortions for training machine learning models. Using this simulation, we investigate the necessity of accurate noise modeling for learning-based denoising. Our findings indicate that realistic noise models are essential for effectively denoising real JPEG images; specifically, a neural network trained on realistic noise outperforms one trained with AWGN by 3 dB. Furthermore, an ablation study reveals that simulating both denoising and demosaicking is vital to this performance gain, highlighting the need for realistic demosaicking algorithms which have previously been overlooked. We anticipate this simulation will benefit other image reconstruction tasks and will make the code publicly available.

To facilitate spectrum sharing, dual-function radar communication (DFRC) systems have been introduced to unify radar and communication on a single platform, utilizing various signaling strategies to embed data into radar waveforms. Specifically, complex beampattern modulation (CBM) conveys information by adjusting the amplitude and phase of transmit beampatterns directed at the communication receiver. However, embedding random data induces clutter modulation and elevates range-Doppler sidelobes. Furthermore, pulse-to-pulse waveform variations impair radar target detection performance when traditional sequential pulse compression (SPC) and moving-target detection (MTD) are employed. This paper proposes a minimum mean square error (MMSE) filter termed joint range and Doppler adaptive processing (JRDAP). This approach adaptively estimates target impulse response coefficients within each range-Doppler cell to mitigate high range-Doppler sidelobes and clutter modulation. The proposed method achieves performance comparable to full-dimension adaptive multiple pulses compression (AMPC) while significantly reducing computational complexity.

As networks advance toward the sixth generation (6G), Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite communication systems have emerged as promising solutions due to their distinctive and comprehensive capabilities. However, these benefits are counterbalanced by significant challenges, including security vulnerabilities, the complexities of managing hybrid systems, and high mobility. This paper first identifies a physical-layer security deficiency within a conceptual framework that accounts for the cyber-physical nature of satellite systems, while highlighting potential attack vectors. Secondly, a learning-driven detection scheme is introduced, featuring a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN). The performance of this CNN architecture is evaluated against a common machine learning algorithm, the support vector machine (SVM). The findings demonstrate that the proposed scheme effectively detects deficiency attacks targeting satellite systems.

We present an analytical approach to determining optimal driving strategies that minimize total tractive energy usage for a train fleet traveling in the same direction on a shared track, adhering to clearance-time equality constraints that guarantee safe separation and optimize line occupancy. The track is segmented by fixed trackside signals, where each intermediate signal defines a segment comprising its two adjacent sections. Safe separation is achieved when the leading train exits each signal-location segment before the following train enters, a condition satisfied by a complete set of clearance times and associated inequality constraints. While optimal scheduling for two trains has been previously resolved, the problem becomes computationally intractable for larger fleets due to the exponential increase in trains and signals. The primary challenge lies in identifying which equality constraints are active versus which inequality constraints are inactive. The curse of dimensionality renders it impractical to evaluate every possible combination of active constraints, optimize the resulting times, and compute the associated costs. Consequently, we formulate and solve an alternative problem by enforcing active clearance-time equality constraints for successive trains on every segment. We demonstrate that this can be modeled as an unconstrained convex optimization problem and propose a viable algorithm to derive the optimal schedule and driving strategies for each train. Finally, we apply this solution to generate optimal schedules for a busy inter-city shuttle service.

This paper investigates the scattering theory for cubic inhomogeneous Schrödinger equations featuring an inverse square potential, defined as $iu_t+\Delta u-\frac{a}{|x|^2}u=\lambda |x|^{-b}|u|^2u$ in three dimensions, where $a>-\frac14$ and $0<b<1$. In the defocusing scenario ($\lambda=1$), we prove global well-posedness and scattering for arbitrary initial data within the energy space $H^1_a(\mathbb R^3)$. Conversely, for the focusing case ($\lambda=-1$), we demonstrate scattering for initial data situated below the ground state threshold. This result is achieved by employing virial and Morawetz arguments, following the approaches of Dodson-Murphy and Campos-Cardoso, which circumvent the need for an interaction Morawetz estimate.

This paper investigates the convergence of the dynamical discrete web (DyDW) to the dynamical Brownian web (DyBW) within the path space topology. We demonstrate that, almost surely, the DyBW possesses right-continuous paths with left limits (RCLL) in a suitable metric space, and as a sequence of such RCLL paths, the scaled DyDW converges to the DyBW. Consequently, this establishes the weak convergence of the DyDW process to the DyBW process.

Forest fires result from a complex interplay of environmental conditions, topography, and socioeconomic elements (Bedia et al., 2014). Consequently, comprehending the causal mechanisms and enabling early prediction are vital for managing these events and protecting human lives. This study aims to construct a spatio-temporal model to analyze the causality of forest fires across Europe at the NUTS2 level between 2012 and 2016, incorporating both environmental and socioeconomic variables. We employed a disease mapping approach, frequently utilized in small-area studies to evaluate spatial patterns and pinpoint regions with abnormally high or low relative risks.

A polynomial $P \in \mathbb{C}[z_1, \ldots, z_d]$ is defined as strongly $\mathbb{D}^d$-stable when it possesses no zeros within the closed unit polydisc $\overline{\mathbb{D}}^d$. For such a polynomial, the spectral density function is defined by $\mathcal{S}_P(\mathbf{z}) = \left(P(\mathbf{z})\overline{P(1/\overline{\mathbf{z}})}\right)^{-1}$. An abelian square refers to a finite string $ww'$ where $w'$ is a permutation of $w$. This study investigates a polynomial-valued operator whose spectral density function's Fourier coefficients serve as generating functions for combinatorial classes of constrained finite strings on a $d$-character alphabet. These classes extend the concept of abelian squares, and their corresponding generating functions constitute the Fourier coefficients of a unique (up to equivalence) operator valued in $L^2(\mathbb{T}^d)$. The analysis yields integral representations, divisibility characteristics, and recurrent and asymptotic behaviors for the coefficients of these generating functions. Key tools employed in deriving the asymptotic formulas include a lattice-point translation summation variant of Laplace's method by Greenhill, Janson, and Ruci\'{n}ski; a complex-phase stationary phase method for oscillatory integrals by Pemantle and Wilson; and polynomial identities concerning powers of modified Bessel functions of the first kind, attributed to Moll and Vignat.

This study examines a continuous-time Ehrenfest model situated on an extended star graph, conceptualized as a lattice comprising the integer points of $d$ semiaxes meeting at the origin. While linear transition rates govern the dynamics along each ray, the switching between rays at the origin follows a general stochastic matrix. We conduct a thorough analysis of both the transient and asymptotic behaviors of this system. Furthermore, we derive a diffusive approximation yielding an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process defined over a "spider" domain formed by semiaxes joined at the origin. Our results demonstrate that this approximating process exhibits a truncated Gaussian stationary density. Finally, we evaluate the quality of this approximation by comparing stationary distributions, as well as means and variances.

The deployment of recent deep reinforcement learning advancements in real-world scenarios is impeded by excessive data requirements, resulting in poor efficiency and scalability. Although independent enhancements to components like replay buffers or learning algorithms, alongside massively distributed systems, can reduce training times for standard benchmarks from days to hours, reward evaluation remains a critical bottleneck in many practical settings. In tasks such as molecular optimization, where state evaluation necessitates computationally intensive simulations or physical experiments, the cost of obtaining ground-truth rewards can make training prohibitively expensive without vast computational resources. To address this, we propose substituting costly ground-truth rewards with those predicted by neural networks, while mitigating non-stationarity in state and reward distributions through an active learning module. Our proposed ACRL framework (Actively learning Costly rewards for Reinforcement Learning) demonstrates the ability to train agents in complex real-world environments orders of magnitude faster. By facilitating the application of reinforcement learning to new domains, we illustrate the discovery of meaningful and non-trivial solutions to optimization challenges in chemistry, materials science, and engineering.

Over the past ten years, deep clustering advancements have primarily relied on maximizing mutual information (MI) as an unsupervised training objective, increasingly supplemented by regularization techniques. While the impact of these regularizations has been extensively analyzed, the suitability of MI itself as a clustering metric has received scant attention. This paper demonstrates that maximizing MI often fails to produce effective clusters, identifying the Kullback-Leibler divergence as the primary cause. To address this, we propose Generalized Mutual Information (GEMINI), a family of metrics that modifies the core distance of MI for unsupervised neural network training. Unlike traditional MI, certain GEMINI variants do not require regularization, and several incorporate geometry-aware properties through distances or kernels in the data space. Furthermore, we show that GEMINI metrics can automatically determine an appropriate number of clusters, addressing a significant gap in deep clustering research where the cluster count is typically unknown.

This study examines the characteristics and performance of synthetic random graph models featuring inherent community structures, which are crucial for assessing and optimizing inherently unsupervised community detection algorithms. We introduce ABCDe, a multi-threaded realization of the ABCD (Artificial Benchmark for Community Detection) graph generator. Our analysis covers the algorithm's implementation specifics and contrasts it with both the existing sequential ABCD version and the parallel implementation of the widely adopted LFR (Lancichinetti--Fortunato--Radicchi) generator. Our findings demonstrate that ABCDe achieves performance over ten times faster than NetworKit's parallel LFR implementation and exhibits superior scalability. Furthermore, while ABCDe is significantly more efficient, the graphs it produces via the ABCD model retain properties similar to those of the original LFR algorithm, whereas NetworKit's parallelized LFR version generates graphs with distinctly different characteristics.

Daylight significantly influences the human wake/sleep cycle, which originates from biological systems governed by a circadian rhythm dictated by light and dark cycles. These oscillations can be represented by a higher-order non-linear van der Pol equation driven by a term simulating the light cycle. This study introduces noise into the illumination to examine its impact on the human circadian rhythm. The findings indicate that noise generally disrupts the sleep/wake rhythm, though specific parameter values may enhance regular oscillations. Depending on system parameters, noise can induce regularities such as stochastic resonance. When natural light is absent, an optimal noise intensity emerges that most severely degrades cycle regularity, a phenomenon termed anti-coherent resonance. Conversely, in the presence of natural light, stochastic resonance occurs, where an optimal noise intensity improves the wake/sleep system's evolution. However, a critical noise threshold exists beyond which the system transitions into chaos; at sufficiently high noise levels, the sleep/wake cycle becomes random and unpredictable, regardless of the external light parameters.

We present an analysis of the cosmic ray energy spectrum for particles exceeding $2.5{\times} 10^{18}$ eV, utilizing a dataset of $215,030$ events. Our findings reveal a change in the spectral index near $1.3{\times} 10^{19}$ eV, shifting from $2.51 \pm 0.03 \textrm{ (stat.)} \pm 0.05 \textrm{ (sys.)}$ to $3.05 \pm 0.05 \textrm{ (stat.)} \pm 0.10\textrm{ (sys.)}$, and further increasing to $5.1\pm0.3\textrm{ (stat.)} \pm 0.1\textrm{ (sys.)}$ above $5{\times} 10^{19}$ eV. Within the observable energy range, no notable declination dependence of spectral characteristics was detected. These spectral behaviors are consistent with models incorporating energy-dependent mass composition. Additionally, the cosmic ray energy density above $5{\times} 10^{18}$ eV is calculated to be $(5.66 \pm 0.03 \textrm{ (stat.)} \pm 1.40 \textrm{ (sys.)} ) {\times} 10^{53}~$erg Mpc$^{-3}$.

We report high-resolution ($0\farcs{14}$) ALMA observations of the CO(2$-$1) emission within the circumnuclear gas disk of UGC 2698, a nearby compact galaxy. The disk displays regular rotation, with projected velocities reaching up to 450 km s$^{-1}$ close to the galactic center. By fitting gas-dynamical models to the data cube under the assumption of a dynamically cold, thin disk where CO emission originates, we determined the supermassive black hole (BH) mass in UGC 2698 to be $M_{\mathrm{BH}} = (2.46 \pm{0.07}$ [$1\sigma$ stat] $^{+0.70}_{-0.78}$ [sys])$\times 10^9$ $M_\odot$. UGC 2698 belongs to a sample of local early-type galaxies considered potential $z\sim2$ red nugget remnants. While prior stellar-dynamical modeling of three other galaxies in this sample yielded BH masses consistent with the $M_{\mathrm{BH}}-\sigma_\star$ relation but appearing over-massive relative to the $M_{\mathrm{BH}}-L_{\mathrm{bul}}$ correlation—suggesting BHs may acquire most of their mass before their hosts form—UGC 2698 aligns with both scaling relations. Given that UGC 2698 possesses the largest stellar mass and effective radius in the local compact galaxy sample, it may have experienced more recent mergers that brought its properties into agreement with these relations. Alternatively, since the three previously measured compact galaxies are outliers from the $M_{\mathrm{BH}}-L_{\mathrm{bul}}$ relation whereas UGC 2698 is not, there could be substantial scatter at the sparsely sampled high-mass end of this correlation. Further gas-dynamical BH mass measurements for compact galaxies are necessary to enhance our understanding of BH$-$galaxy co-evolution.

Panoramic integral field unit (IFU) spectroscopy serves as a fundamental instrument in contemporary observational astronomy, with particular significance for galaxy physics. Recently, numerous large-scale IFU surveys—including SDSS MaNGA (10,000 targets), SAMI (3,000 targets), Califa (600 objects), and Atlas3D (260 objects)—have been completed and made accessible to the wider astronomical community. Although visualizing the full extent of these complex, massive spectral cube datasets is challenging, it remains essential for scientific progress. Drawing on our previous experience in visualizing spectral and imaging data within the VOxAstro Initiative, we are currently developing an online web service (ifu.voxastro.org) for the interactive exploration of IFU spectroscopic data. This platform offers streamlined access and visualization tools for spectral cubes from public surveys (MaNGA, SAMI, Califa, Atlas3D) and their modeling results, as well as derived parameter maps, utilizing a connected views architecture. This paper details the service's core components and functionality, featuring a REST API built on a Django+Postgres backend and a high-performance user interface developed with the Vue.js-based Quasar framework.

Establishing stroke correspondences between keyframes is a critical yet labor-intensive step in the hand-drawn inbetweening pipeline, placing a heavy burden on animators. We introduce a method that estimates these stroke correspondences between raster character images directly, bypassing the need for vectorization. Our approach first isolates closed regions within each keyframe and determines their correspondences by analyzing shape features, depth information, and connectivity between areas. Subsequently, stroke correspondences are derived from these established closed area matches. The efficacy of our method is validated through a user study and a comparison with traditional techniques.

Hyperfine interactions between nuclear and electron spins have long served as a sensitive probe for the local chemical environment in material science, organic chemistry, and structural biology by enabling the spatial identification of nuclear spins. Once these spins are identified, the isotropic and anisotropic components of these interactions provide distinct insights into the electronic ground-state properties of paramagnetic centers. Nevertheless, conventional ensemble measurements average hyperfine interactions across macroscopic populations of spins with varying geometrical positions and nuclear isotopes. In this study, we employ a scanning tunneling microscope (STM) integrated with electron spin resonance (ESR) to measure hyperfine spectra of hydrogenated titanium (Ti) atoms on MgO/Ag(100), thereby determining isotropic and anisotropic hyperfine interactions at the single-atom level. By combining vector-field ESR spectroscopy with STM-based atomic manipulation, we characterize the complete hyperfine tensor of individual Ti-47 and Ti-49 atoms, revealing significant spatial anisotropy in hyperfine interactions for both isotopes when adsorbed at low-symmetry binding sites. Density functional theory calculations indicate that this substantial hyperfine anisotropy stems from a highly anisotropic distribution of ground-state electron spin density. Our findings underscore the potential of ESR-STM-enabled single-atom hyperfine spectroscopy as a potent tool for elucidating ground-state electronic structures and atomic-scale chemical environments with nano-electronvolt resolution.

The MINOS experiment operated between 2003 and 2012, gathering a dataset comprising 10.71x10^20 protons-on-target (POT) of beam neutrinos, 3.36x10^20 POT of beam antineutrinos, and an atmospheric neutrino exposure of 37.88 kt-yrs. The final determination of the atmospheric neutrino oscillation parameters, dm^2_32 and theta_23, was derived from a comprehensive three-flavor oscillation analysis of the combined charged-current (CC) nu_mu and CC anti-nu_mu beam and atmospheric samples, as well as the CC nu_e and CC anti-nu_e appearance samples. This analysis produced the most precise measurement of the atmospheric mass splitting dm^2_32 to date. The results are |dm^2_32|=[2.28 - 2.46]x10^-3 eV^2 (68\%) and sin^{2}theta_23=0.35-0.65 (90\%) under the normal hierarchy, and |dm^2_32|=[2.32 - 2.53]x10^-3 eV^2 (68\%) and sin^{2}theta_23=0.34-0.67 (90\%) under the inverted hierarchy. As the successor to MINOS in the NOvA era at FNAL, MINOS+ is currently collecting data primarily in the 3-10 GeV range. An analysis of nu_mu disappearance utilizing the initial 2.99x10^20 POT of data yielded results highly consistent with those from MINOS. Future data collection will further validate the standard neutrino oscillation paradigm and enable enhanced searches for exotic phenomena, including sterile neutrinos, large extra dimensions, and non-standard interactions.

Recent advancements in sequencing technology have made it cost-effective and feasible to sequence genomes at high depth, enabling the detection of low-frequency variants. Nevertheless, sequencing errors necessitate ongoing research into algorithms capable of distinguishing true variants from noise. While LoFreq is a leading tool for identifying these low-frequency variants, it suffers from a longer runtime compared to alternatives. Furthermore, its parallel execution interface could be streamlined to support multithreading and job distribution across clusters. This work outlines specific contributions to LoFreq aimed at addressing these limitations.

The rise of Location-based Social Networks (LBSNs) has made Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation a critical task, focusing on learning user preferences and mobility patterns. While prior research indicates that integrating contextual factors like time and geography helps alleviate data sparsity, existing approaches typically rely solely on physical distance to model geographical influence, neglecting its temporal dynamics. This paper investigates user mobility patterns and reveals that check-ins cluster around specific centers that vary based on the user's current temporal state. Consequently, we introduce a spatio-temporal activity-centers algorithm to model user behavior with greater precision. We validate the efficacy of our contextual model, named STACP, by integrating it into a matrix factorization framework across two scenarios: static and temporal. Experiments conducted on two prominent real-world datasets from Gowalla and Foursquare demonstrate that STACP yields statistically significant performance gains over state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our results highlight the value of jointly capturing both geographical and temporal information to accurately model user activity centers.

The convergence of terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks holds the promise of bridging connectivity gaps for the unconnected while significantly improving experiences for those already linked, carrying profound long-term technological and societal impacts. Unifying ground, air, and space wireless communications presents a major challenge for both mobile and satellite sectors, requiring the definition and intelligent coordination of a novel 3D network architecture. This article explores the primary opportunities and challenges stemming from this evolution by highlighting disruptive use cases, essential building blocks, relevant standardization efforts, and open research questions. Furthermore, by examining two multi-operator scenarios, we demonstrate how terrestrial networks can be efficiently redesigned to support aerial services or enhanced by non-terrestrial infrastructure to expand their existing capabilities.

We calculate the non-perturbative normalisation factor $r_\mathrm{m}\equiv Z_{\rm S}/Z_{\rm S}^{0}$, defined by the ratio of the renormalisation parameters for flavour non-singlet and singlet scalar densities, respectively. This factor is essential for computing quark masses using Wilson fermions and for renormalising nucleon matrix elements involving scalar densities. Our approach utilizes finite-volume lattice QCD simulations employing the tree-level Symanzik-improved gauge action, $N_\mathrm{f} = 3$ mass-degenerate $\mathrm{O}(a)$ improved Wilson fermions, and Schrödinger functional boundary conditions. We extract the slope of the current quark mass relative to the subtracted Wilson quark mass in two distinct configurations: a unitary setup with nearly degenerate chiral valence and sea quark masses, and a non-unitary setup where valence flavours are chiral while sea quark masses remain small. Combining these slopes with $Z \equiv Z_{\rm P}/(Z_{\rm S}Z_{\rm A})$—determined via a novel chiral Ward identity—yields $r_\mathrm{m}$. Our findings span gauge couplings corresponding to lattice spacings under $0.1\,$fm, a regime typically explored in large-volume $N_\mathrm{f} = 2+1$ QCD simulations using the identical lattice action.

When a black hole tidally disrupts a star, it may launch a powerful relativistic jet. If this jet aligns closely with our line of sight, Doppler boosting significantly amplifies its brightness. Consequently, on-axis relativistic tidal disruption events (TDEs) offer a unique opportunity to detect quiescent cosmological black holes (with redshifts $z > 1$) and serve as excellent laboratories for studying radiative mechanisms in super-Eddington jets. In this study, we report multi-wavelength observations (spanning X-ray, UV, optical, and radio bands) of the transient \target, discovered optically at $z=1.193$. This object exhibits atypical X-ray characteristics, including a peak luminosity exceeding $10^{48}$ erg s$^{-1}$, rapid variability on timescales as brief as 1000 seconds, and a rest-frame duration surpassing 30 days; these traits are hallmarks of relativistic TDEs. Spectral energy distributions from X-rays to radio waves, measured 5 to 50 days post-discovery, are consistent with synchrotron radiation from a relativistic jet (radio), synchrotron self-Compton emission (X-rays), and thermal emission resembling that of low-redshift TDEs (UV/optical). Our modeling suggests a beamed, highly relativistic jet similar to those in blazars, yet it demands extreme matter domination—specifically, a high ratio of electron-to-magnetic field energy densities within the jet—thereby challenging current theoretical models of jet formation.

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a degenerative condition that compromises an individual's capacity to manage daily tasks. Its clinical presentation varies significantly regarding age, disease duration, progression speed, and the extent of memory and cognitive decline. Because of these inconsistencies, personalized treatment strategies and counseling regarding individual trajectories remain constrained. However, recent advancements in machine learning, which can uncover hidden patterns within complex, multi-dimensional data, offer substantial opportunities to meet this critical need. This study employs both supervised and unsupervised machine learning techniques to identify subtypes and forecast progression. By applying these methods to the extensive clinical records from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we aim to classify patient subtypes and predict disease evolution. Our analysis maps the progression landscape into low, moderate, and high severity zones. This approach facilitates the early detection and characterization of distinct disease subtypes driven by clinical heterogeneity. We expect these models to support patient counseling, refine clinical trial designs, and ultimately foster individualized medical care.

Applying a Fourier expansion to the integrand within the path integral formulation of the partition function for quantum systems yields a deterministic expression. Although this expression remains intricate, it is more manageable than the original functional integral, thereby enabling the resolution of previously unsolvable problems. This paper derives the formula and presents an initial application in the work titled "Simultaneous occurrence of off-diagonal long-range order and infinite permutation cycles in systems of interacting atoms," available at arXiv:2108.02659 [math-ph].

Business workflows often involve extracting critical information from form-based documents like bank statements, bills of lading, and purchase orders. Current automation methods typically require extensive datasets to function effectively. To address performance gaps in scenarios with limited training data (such as 10–250 documents), we introduce FieldSwap, a novel data augmentation strategy. This technique generates synthetic training examples by replacing key phrases from a source field with those from a target field. Our results indicate that FieldSwap can enhance extraction performance by achieving F1 score improvements ranging from 1 to 7 points.

As deep learning models are increasingly deployed in complex, high-stakes applications, the ability to interpret AI predictions has become increasingly vital. While saliency mapping is a widely used visual attribution technique, current approaches are often hindered by high computational costs or architectural limitations. To address these issues, we introduce Hierarchical Perturbation, a highly efficient and entirely model-agnostic method for generating robust saliency maps. Evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate that our approach produces saliency maps of equal or superior quality compared to existing model-agnostic techniques, while achieving a computational speedup of over twenty times.

Recovering 3D human pose and shape from a single RGB image remains a difficult challenge. Current learning-based approaches rely heavily on weak supervision signals, such as 2D and 3D joint locations, because paired 3D data from natural environments is scarce. However, ambiguities inherent in these weak labels often cause networks to converge to local optima during training. To address this, we mitigate ambiguity by optimizing multiple initializations through a three-stage framework called the Multi-Initialization Optimization Network (MION). In the first stage, we strategically generate various coarse 3D reconstruction candidates that align with the input's 2D keypoints; each candidate serves as a distinct initialization for a separate optimization branch. The second stage employs a Mesh Refinement Transformer (MRT) to refine each coarse result individually using self-attention mechanisms. Finally, a Consistency Estimation Network (CEN) selects the optimal reconstruction by assessing whether the visual evidence in the RGB image corresponds to the given 3D model. Experimental results show that our MION outperforms existing 3D mesh-based methods across several public benchmarks.

Although the axion was initially proposed to resolve the strong CP problem, new CP-violating phenomena beyond QCD could appear through a minute scalar component of the axion-nucleon interaction. This effect can be investigated in experiments searching for axion-mediated forces, a concept first suggested by J.E. Moody and F. Wilczek. In this note, I examine the physical basis of CP-violating axion couplings and highlight the unique function of the QCD axion as a low-energy gateway to high-energy sources of CP violation.

This study investigates the inverse scattering of time-harmonic point sources by an infinite rough surface, modeled as a local perturbation of a plane. A new approach to reverse time migration is introduced to determine the shape and position of this surface. The technique relies on a modified Helmholtz-Kirchhoff identity tailored for a specific rough surface, generating an imaging functional that consistently peaks at the rough surface's boundary for both sound-soft and penetrable scenarios, while reaching a minimum (nadir) for sound-hard cases. Numerical results demonstrate the method's superior imaging performance, particularly when utilizing multi-frequency data.

Triality is a classical geometric concept originating from Lie groups of type $D_4$, whereas Wilson triality emerges within the study of reflexible maps. This work establishes a connection between these two concepts by demonstrating how to derive an incidence geometry possessing triality from a map that supports a Wilson triality. Furthermore, the authors extend a finding by Jones and Poulton, proving that for any prime power $q$, the group ${\rm L}_2(q^3)$ contains maps exhibiting Wilson trialities yet lacking dualities.

Cross-lingual transfer between high-resource languages and their dialects or closely related varieties should naturally be aided by their inherent similarities. However, existing methods operating within embedding spaces fail to leverage this surface-level similarity. This study introduces a straightforward yet effective strategy to enhance cross-lingual transfer among closely related language varieties. We propose augmenting the data from the high-resource source language with character-level noise, thereby increasing the model's robustness against spelling variations. This approach yields consistent improvements across multiple languages and tasks, including zero-shot transfer for part-of-speech tagging and topic identification among varieties from the Finnic, West and North Germanic, and Western Romance language families. Our findings demonstrate the efficacy of simple surface-level noise in facilitating better transfer between language varieties.

This brief review outlines potential interaction processes between lower solar atmospheric plasma and embedded small-scale magnetic fields. After introducing the subject, we define key types of small-scale magnetic field elements, examine their formation and evolution, and describe their primary involvement in phenomena such as magnetic reconnection and the generation of magneto-hydrodynamic waves. These small-scale occurrences exhibit greater frequency and global coverage in the solar atmosphere than the more explosive events typically associated with solar active regions. Consequently, they serve as fundamental building blocks of solar activity, even during the weaker phases of the 11-year solar cycle. Specifically, comprehending these fine-scale components from the lower to the upper solar atmosphere is crucial for solving the enigmatic problem of solar coronal heating, which remains a central challenge in modern astrophysics.

Every person undergoes income changes throughout their life, which collectively establishes a statistical link between age and earnings across a society. This research examines income distribution patterns relative to age, revealing a consistent joint distribution function for both the United Kingdom and the United States. We introduce a versatile calibration approach utilizing panel and population survey data to highlight the distinct characteristics of these two nations. The proposed model offers practical applications for forecasting income trajectories and designing pension strategies.

Establishing a quantitative and predictive theory for quantum light-matter interactions in ultra-thin materials presents significant fundamental hurdles. A viable model must concurrently address the quantization of ultra-confined plasmonic modes amidst losses and describe electronic states based on first principles. This study introduces such a framework by integrating density functional theory (DFT) with macroscopic quantum electrodynamics. Using this approach, we demonstrate Purcell enhancements up to $10^7$ for intersubband transitions in few-layer transition metal dichalcogenides situated between graphene and a perfect conductor. Our methodology's broad applicability enables a quantitative evaluation of several standard approximation paradigms, including the dipole-approximation, the utilization of 1D quantum well model wave functions, and Fermi's Golden rule. The analysis reveals that the selection of wave functions is especially critical. Consequently, our work establishes the groundwork for practical, *ab initio*-based quantum treatments of light-matter interactions within realistic nanostructured materials.

Cuban science and technology have achieved significant milestones, especially within biotechnology and healthcare. In the latter half of the 20th century, the nation established a network of scientific institutions designed to tackle critical economic, social, cultural, and health challenges. Nevertheless, the severe economic crisis experienced over the past three decades has profoundly affected Cuban scientific research. Beyond reduced funding, the emigration of thousands of scientists—both young and experienced—has significantly diminished research output. Currently, no systematic study exists that examines scientific publications, citations, or patents attributed to Cuban authors during this era. This paper presents an analysis of Cuban scientific production from 1970 onward, with a specific focus on the period from 1990 to 2019. National metrics are benchmarked against global figures, with particular emphasis on Latin American counterparts. Preliminary findings indicate that while Cuban scientific publications have doubled, this growth rate is substantially lower than the five-fold average observed in several Latin American countries. Furthermore, since 2014, the annual volume of Cuban scientific publications has been declining. The analysis also reveals that the majority of young Cuban authors with the highest citation indices between 1990 and 2019 are currently working abroad. All data and code associated with this study are publicly accessible via GitHub (https://github.com/ypriverol/cubascience).

By applying the Ginzburg-Landau framework, we demonstrate that strain in a nematic superconductor induces a distinct nematic vorticity. In doped topological insulators, this vorticity manifests as a spin vortex. Our analysis identifies two topologically distinct spin vortex types: Type I enhances superconductivity away from the core, whereas Type II suppresses it. Utilizing the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations to investigate electronic states within these nematic superconductors hosting spin vortices, we observe that Type I vortices localize zero-energy states near the core, which correspond to Majorana Kramer pairs.
