We introduce NxMiFormer, a flexible compression framework that simultaneously applies sparsification and quantization via ADMM and STE-based QAT. Additionally, we propose a cost-effective, heuristic-driven search algorithm designed to identify optimal heterogeneous compression configurations that satisfy specific compression ratio constraints. Evaluation on the GLUE suite of NLU benchmarks demonstrates that our method can compress BERT encoders by up to 93% while preserving 98.2% of the original accuracy, fully leveraging hardware capabilities. Furthermore, the heterogeneous configurations identified by our search heuristic retain 99.5% of baseline accuracy while achieving an 87.5% compression ratio.

Contemporary processors dynamically regulate their clock speeds to optimize resource usage, conserve energy, and adhere to system constraints. When the running average of electrical or thermal metrics surpasses established thresholds during workload execution, the power management system reactively lowers the CPU frequency to maintain safe operating conditions. This paper demonstrates that such power-management-induced throttling creates a timing side-channel vulnerability, allowing attackers to deduce secret data from workloads designed for constant cycles. We emphasize that constant-cycle code implementations do not inherently guarantee consistent wall-clock execution times across different data inputs. This discrepancy arises because current throttling mechanisms make frequency adjustments dependent on data, thereby rendering execution time data-dependent as well. Consequently, this frequency throttling side-channel attack can be executed by both kernel-space and user-space adversaries, undermining security isolation. We validate our methodology through experiments on a constant-cycle AES-128 implementation across various systems. Our results show that attackers can successfully recover the AES key by correlating collected timing traces with theoretical timing estimates for key guesses, even under frequency throttling. Finally, we explore potential mitigation strategies for these attacks, analyzing their respective pros and cons.

Globally, breast cancer remains one of the most prevalent malignancies affecting women. Diagnosis involves pathologists analyzing biomarkers like the HER2 protein via immunohistochemistry on biopsy-derived tissue. By examining slides microscopically, these experts assess staining intensity and membrane integrity, assigning scores of 0, 1+, 2+, or 3+; this process relies on subjective interpretation. This study reports preliminary analysis of annotations from three pathologists reviewing the same dataset of 1,252 non-overlapping biopsy patches captured at 20x magnification. Using Fleiss' Kappa coefficient, we observed substantial agreement among the experts themselves (intra-expert) and moderate agreement between different experts (inter-expert). These findings represent an initial step toward establishing a gold standard for HER2 breast cancer biopsies through supervised learning models trained on multi-pathologist annotations.

We utilized an ac bridge method sensitive to nonlinear signals to measure third-order electrical conductivity in the organic conductor $\alpha$-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$I$_3$. A distinct third-order conductance, $G_3$, was detected even at low electric fields, with a notable critical enhancement occurring above the charge-order transition temperature ($T_{\rm CO}=136$~K). The frequency dependence of $G_3$ contradicts percolation models that attribute nonlinear conduction to Joule heating within random resistor networks. Instead, we propose that the nonlinearity arises from a field-dependent relaxation time, based on a phenomenological model for mobility in high-dielectric-constant materials. Under this framework, $G_3$ aligns with the third-order electric susceptibility, $\chi_3$. Given that nonlinear susceptibility serves as an indicator for higher-order multipole ordering, the observed divergence of $G_3$ above $T_{\rm CO}$ indicates a hidden quadrupole instability associated with the charge-order transition in this organic system.

This study provides a systematic analysis of Hilbert boundary value problems for hypermonogenic functions defined on a hyperplane, considering solutions of arbitrary integer orders at infinity. Notably, cases involving negative orders present novel findings, even within the context of the complex plane. The paper establishes explicit solution formulas and outlines the necessary solvability conditions. These results are derived by applying the Clifford symmetric extension method, which transforms Hilbert boundary value problems into Riemann boundary value problems.

In recent years, online incremental learning has attracted increasing attention, yet it faces three significant challenges. First, concept drift occurs when the probability distribution of streaming data shifts over time. Second, catastrophic forgetting happens when new knowledge acquisition leads to the loss of previously learned information. Third, the underutilization of latent representation is often overlooked, despite its critical role in enhancing model prediction accuracy. Our research addresses these issues by proposing Adaptive Online Incremental Learning for evolving data streams (AOIL). This approach employs an auto-encoder equipped with a memory module to extract latent features from inputs; simultaneously, the reconstruction loss within this module detects concept drift and triggers timely parameter updates. Furthermore, we partition hidden layer activation features into common and private components. This strategy allows the model to learn private features from new instances without discarding shared historical knowledge, thereby mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Finally, a self-attention mechanism is utilized to fuse these extracted features into a comprehensive vector, further refining the latent representation learning.

Small-scale processes are believed to play a crucial role in solar atmospheric dynamics. Although numerical resolution constraints prevent these features from being explicitly included in magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations, their signatures should remain detectable in real observations taken at the same nominal resolution. Consequently, synthetic observables derived from simulations at a specific resolution may not be directly comparable to real data at that same resolution. This study investigates how inferences drawn from synthetic spectra generated by simulations with varying numerical resolutions compare, specifically examining whether these discrepancies persist after spatially degrading the spectra to a uniform resolution. We aim to contrast synthetic spectra produced by realistic 3D radiative MHD (rMHD) simulations executed at three distinct resolutions using a shared initial atmosphere, employing straightforward techniques to infer line-of-sight velocities and magnetic fields. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of varying spatial resolution on results obtained from the STiC inversion code. Our findings indicate that while simple inference methods applied to all three simulations identify consistent large-scale trends, higher resolutions produce more detailed structures and more extreme localized values for line-of-sight velocities and magnetic fields, even after spatial smearing. We also observe evidence that sub-resolution effects imprint on degraded spectra cause systematic errors in inversions, with these errors growing as the magnitude of sub-resolution effects increases. However, we note that the inclusion of progressively finer sub-resolution yields diminishing additional effects, indicating a clear trend where the importance of these finer details decreases.

The rise of wearable technology has led to the use of inertial measurement unit (IMU) data for monitoring and assessing human mobility, including human activity recognition (HAR). However, training deep neural network (DNN) models for these applications demands extensive labeled data, which is difficult to obtain in uncontrolled settings. To address this data scarcity, we introduce CROMOSim, a cross-modality sensor simulator capable of generating high-fidelity virtual IMU data from motion capture systems or monocular RGB cameras. By employing a skinned multi-person linear model (SMPL) for 3D body pose and shape, the system supports simulation from any on-body location. A DNN is trained to map imperfect trajectory estimations derived from noisy 3D SMPL body tri-meshes—caused by measurement noise, calibration errors, occlusion, and other modeling artifacts—into accurate IMU data. We assessed the fidelity of CROMOSim's simulated data and its effectiveness in augmenting datasets across various HAR benchmarks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed model improves HAR performance by 6.7% compared to baseline methods.

Estimating parameters under a multivariate normal (MVN) mixture model remains a significant computational hurdle. A recently introduced maximum pseudo \b{eta}-likelihood estimator seeks to address this by adapting the minimum density power divergence (DPD) framework to MVN mixtures, offering a more tractable and efficient algorithm suitable for higher dimensions. This letter provides a rigorous derivation establishing the existence and weak consistency of this estimator for MVN mixtures, subject to a reasonable set of assumptions.

As large digitized collections of fine art become more accessible, the automated analysis and categorization of paintings have emerged as a compelling research field. Nevertheless, the unique characteristics of art, including implicit subjectivity, domain-specific nuances, and the subtle distinctions between art movements, present significant obstacles when applying machine learning methods. Residual networks, or their variations, are among the most widely used tools for image classification, capable of extracting pertinent features for clearly defined categories. This case study examines the classification of a specific artwork, "Portrait of the Painter Charles Bruni" by Johann Kupetzky, and evaluates the performance of the proposed classifier. Our findings demonstrate that features extracted during the training of residual networks can effectively enhance image retrieval capabilities within online art collection search systems.

Denoising diffusion models (DDMs) have revolutionized image generation, editing, and restoration with remarkable performance gains. However, current DDMs typically require massive datasets for training. In this work, we present a framework capable of training a DDM on just a single image. Our proposed method, SinDDM, captures the internal statistics of the source image through a multi-scale diffusion process. To facilitate the reverse diffusion, we employ a lightweight, fully-convolutional denoiser conditioned on both noise levels and scale. This architecture enables the generation of samples with arbitrary dimensions using a coarse-to-fine approach. As demonstrated, SinDDM produces diverse, high-quality outputs applicable to various tasks such as style transfer and harmonization. Moreover, it can be effectively guided by external supervision; notably, we show how text-guided generation from a single image can be achieved using a pre-trained CLIP model.

Assessing and quantifying the effectiveness of new environmental policies or specific interventions in both space and time is essential for improving air quality. The global lockdown measures implemented in 2020 to curb the spread of SARS-CoV-2 can be viewed as a policy intervention with indirect consequences on air quality. This paper introduces a statistical spatio-temporal model designed for intervention analysis, capable of accounting for weather conditions, other confounding variables, and the inherent spatial and temporal correlations within the data. Specifically, the study examines the relative change in nitrogen dioxide (NO$_2$) concentrations in northern Italy during March and April 2020, the period when lockdowns were enforced. The results include a series of weekly continuous maps illustrating the spatial distribution of NO$_2$ relative changes between 2019 and 2020. The findings indicate that during March and April 2020, the majority of the study area experienced negative relative changes, with median values near -25%, except for the first week of March and the fourth week of April, which showed median values around 5%. Since these variations cannot be attributed to weather effects, it is probable that they resulted from the lockdown measures.

This work establishes both the existence and multiplicity of concentrating solutions for a slightly supercritical pure Neumann problem defined on a ball, marking the first such result in the supercritical regime. Due to the mandatory zero-average compatibility condition, these solutions are necessarily sign-changing. The proofs utilize a Lyapunov-Schmidt reduction technique that integrates the zero-average constraint through appropriate symmetries. Furthermore, this methodology ensures the existence and multiplicity of solutions for subcritical Neumann problems within annuli, while also addressing more general symmetric domains, such as ellipsoids.

Word alignment across parallel corpora serves numerous purposes, such as deriving translation lexicons, enabling cross-lingual transfer of language tools, and facilitating the automatic evaluation or analysis of translations. Historically, most research has relied on unsupervised learning using parallel texts. Recently, however, studies have shown that pre-trained contextualized word embeddings from multilingual language models offer a compelling alternative, yielding competitive alignment results even without explicit training on parallel data. This paper explores strategies to combine these approaches: utilizing pre-trained language models while fine-tuning them on parallel text with specific objectives to enhance alignment quality, and developing methods to effectively extract alignments from these fine-tuned models. Experiments conducted on five language pairs demonstrate that our approach consistently surpasses previous state-of-the-art models across all categories. Furthermore, we show that robust multilingual word aligners can be trained to perform well across various language pairs. Our proposed aligner, AWESOME (Aligning Word Embedding Spaces of Multilingual Encoders), which utilizes pre-trained models, is accessible at https://github.com/neulab/awesome-align.

Heavy meson decays serve as a crucial arena for investigating both electroweak and QCD dynamics, potentially offering insights into nonperturbative QCD and physics beyond the Standard Model. While the factorization-assisted topological-amplitude approach was introduced to analyze two-body non-leptonic $D$ meson decays—filling a gap left by the lack of a first-principles QCD-inspired method—it has also been applied to $B$ meson decays, addressing challenges associated with subleading power contributions. By decomposing topological amplitudes into long-distance hadronic matrix elements (which are either parameterized or calculated) and short-distance Wilson coefficients, this framework effectively isolates nonperturbative dynamics. Incorporating significant flavor SU(3) breaking effects allows for precise fitting of decay branching ratios and CP asymmetries in $B$ decays. The extracted amplitudes further enable predictions for other observables, including CP asymmetries in $D$ decays and mixing parameters within the $D^0-\bar{D}^0$ system. This review outlines the theoretical formulation of the factorization-assisted topological-amplitude approach, summarizes its applications in $D$ and $B$ meson decays, and emphasizes its key achievements.

For many regularized models, the approximate leave-one-out (ALO) formula allows for efficient estimation of leave-one-out cross-validation. This study addresses the challenge of tuning hyperparameters to optimize ALO. We develop efficient formulas for calculating the gradient and Hessian of ALO, enabling the use of second-order optimization methods to determine optimal hyperparameters. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated by successfully tuning hyperparameters for regularized logistic regression and ridge regression across multiple real-world datasets.

This study examines the characteristics of mean-square solutions to the Airy equation when initialized with stationary random processes. It establishes findings regarding the solution's modulus of continuity and outlines the properties of its covariance function. Additionally, it provides bounds for the distributions of solution suprema under $\varphi$-sub-Gaussian initial conditions, supported by several illustrative examples. The work also extends these findings to the fractional Airy equation.

Pinpointing fine-grained location mentions in crisis tweets is essential for converting situational awareness data from social media into actionable insights. While previous research has primarily focused on identifying generic locations, it often overlooks their specific types. To advance the task of fine-grained location identification, we have created and manually annotated two crisis tweet datasets with distinct location categories: one comprising a mixed collection of crisis events and another focused on global COVID-19 pandemic tweets. We then evaluated the performance of state-of-the-art deep learning sequence tagging models on these datasets across both in-domain and cross-domain scenarios.

This work provides a theoretical investigation into the electronic structure of interface states within twisted stacks of three-dimensional topological insulators. Specifically, when the surface Dirac cone's center aligns with the midpoint of a Brillouin zone boundary side, the hybridization of surface states generates an array of nearly independent one-dimensional channels, despite the moiré pattern remaining isotropic. These two counter-propagating channels exhibit opposite spin polarizations and remain robust against scattering from spin-independent impurities. Furthermore, the coupling between parallel channels can be adjusted via the twist angle. These distinctive 1D states can be interpreted as effective Landau levels, where the twist angle functions as a fictitious magnetic field.

Assessing the efficacy of security awareness and training initiatives is essential for reducing human-related security risks within organizations. Drawing from a literature review and industry interviews, this discussion examines prevailing practices and establishes guidelines for measuring the success of security training and awareness programs implemented by organizations.

Fashion serves as a medium for individuals to present themselves to the world, reflecting personal choices and enabling distinction. This paper examines the fashion design process and extends computer vision applications in fashion beyond a Western-centric focus. It explores the history of Southern African se-Shweshwe fabric fashion, details the assembly of a se-Shweshwe dataset, and investigates the use of sketch-to-image generation for affordable design. Addressing this application raises technical challenges regarding training with limited data, as well as significant ethical considerations for computer vision beyond fairness. These include the creation and use of fashion datasets, how computer vision can support cultural representation, and the necessity of avoiding algorithmic cultural appropriation.

The expansion and adoption of scientific production platforms have been extensively studied, yielding significant insights into coauthorship behaviors within research groups. Researchers and their outputs can be conceptualized as coauthorship social networks, where individuals are connected through shared publications. Within this framework, analyzing these networks allows for the identification of patterns that define their structure. This study specifically examines and characterizes the coauthorship networks of academic Brazilian graduate programs in computer science. Data were gathered from the curricula of Brazilian researchers and modeled as coauthoring networks based on the graduate programs in which they participate. Each network's topology was evaluated using complex network metrics alongside three qualitative indices assessing publication quality. Furthermore, these networks were characterized in relation to CAPES evaluations, which assign qualitative grades to Brazilian graduate programs. The findings highlight key topological measures essential for program characterization, assess performance across various qualitative levels, and reveal patterns among the programs receiving the highest CAPES ratings.

**Objective:** Achieving precise visual classification of bladder tissue during Trans-Urethral Resection of Bladder Tumor (TURBT) is crucial for enhancing early cancer detection and treatment. During these procedures, clinicians utilize White Light Imaging (WLI) and Narrow Band Imaging (NBI) to detect lesions; each modality offers distinct visual cues that aid in identifying malignancies. Employing computer vision approaches that integrate both imaging techniques holds the potential to refine endoscopic diagnosis. This study tackles the specific challenge of tissue classification where annotations exist solely for WLI images, while the corresponding NBI images form an unpaired dataset lacking exact equivalents in the WLI domain.

**Method:** We introduce a semi-supervised Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) framework consisting of three primary modules: a teacher network trained on labeled WLI data, a cycle-consistency GAN designed for unpaired image-to-image translation, and a multi-input student network. To validate the fidelity of the synthetic images produced by this GAN, we conducted a comprehensive quantitative and qualitative assessment involving medical specialists.

**Conclusion:** The proposed method yielded an overall average classification accuracy of 0.90, precision of 0.88, and recall of 0.89 for tissue classification. In the unlabeled NBI domain, these metrics were 0.92 for accuracy, 0.64 for precision, and 0.94 for recall. Furthermore, the generated images demonstrated sufficient quality to deceive specialists.

**Significance:** This research demonstrates the efficacy of semi-supervised GAN-based classification in improving bladder tissue analysis, particularly in multi-domain scenarios where annotated data is scarce.

Complex systems are often modeled as networks, making the study of how these networks fragment into subnetworks or communities a subject of significant interest. Nevertheless, creating a method that is both rapid and precise for identifying nodes critical to community structure remains a difficult, unsolved challenge. This manuscript presents a novel framework for characterizing node importance within communities. Initially, we introduce a centrality metric that assesses node significance regarding community structure by analyzing the spectrum of the adjacency matrix; specifically, node importance is defined as the relative shift in the adjacency matrix's eigenvalues following the removal of a node. Secondly, we propose an index capable of differentiating between two distinct types of vital nodes: "community core" and "bridge." These indices rely exclusively on the graph matrix's spectrum and have been tested on numerous artificial and real-world networks. This new methodology offers a foundational solution to this challenging problem, yielding realistic outcomes.

Named Entity Recognition and Disambiguation (NERD) systems serve as a cornerstone for various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including information retrieval, question answering, and event detection. We present TweetNERD, a dataset comprising over 340,000 Tweets spanning from 2010 to 2021, designed to benchmark NERD systems specifically for social media content. As the most extensive and temporally varied open-source benchmark for Tweet-based NERD, this resource aims to advance research in the field. We outline an evaluation framework for three specific NERD tasks: Named Entity Recognition (NER), Entity Linking with True Spans (EL), and End-to-End Entity Linking (End2End), alongside reporting the performance of current public methods on designated TweetNERD splits. The dataset is accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6617192 under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license, with further details available at https://github.com/twitter-research/TweetNERD.

When scalar hair perturbations are present, the Cauchy horizon of a Reissner-Nordström black hole vanishes, giving way to a rapid collapse of the Einstein-Rosen bridge and resulting in a Kasner singularity [1,2]. This study examines the time evolution of holographic complexity—considering both volume and action proposals—across various models of hairy black holes. While volume complexity accesses only a region of the black hole interior distant from the Kasner singularity, numerical evidence indicates that its rate adheres to the Lloyd bound throughout the explored parameter space. In contrast, action complexity probes regions closer to the singularity. Specifically, the action complexity rate diverges at the critical time $t_c$, when the Wheeler-DeWitt patch intersects the singularity, and subsequently stabilizes to a constant value. We observe that the Kasner exponent does not directly influence the specifics of the divergence at $t=t_c$ nor the late-time behavior of the complexity. However, the action complexity rate violates the Lloyd bound at finite times due to this divergence at $t=t_c$. Conversely, the asymptotic action complexity rate satisfies the Lloyd bound across all investigated parameter spaces.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) are widely utilized across fields including computer security, natural language processing, and computational biology. Due to their popularity and status as black-box models, there is a growing demand for explaining their predictions. One effective strategy involves counterfactual reasoning, which aims to alter GNN outputs by making minimal modifications to the input graph. However, current methods for GNN counterfactual explanations are restricted to instance-specific local reasoning, resulting in two key drawbacks: an inability to provide global recourse policies and the overwhelming of human cognition with excessive information. This study investigates global GNN explainability via global counterfactual reasoning, specifically by identifying a compact set of representative counterfactual graphs that elucidate all input graphs. To achieve this, we introduce GCFExplainer, a new algorithm that leverages vertex-reinforced random walks on an edit map combined with a greedy summary. Extensive experiments on real-world graph datasets demonstrate that GCFExplainer's global explanations yield valuable high-level insights into model behavior, outperforming state-of-the-art local counterfactual explainers by achieving a 46.9% increase in recourse coverage and a 9.5% decrease in recourse cost.

Accurate and dependable ego-motion estimation is fundamental to most autonomous mobile systems, with numerous odometry techniques developed utilizing various sensors like cameras and LiDARs. This study introduces a robust method that leverages the redundancy of multiple odometry algorithms through a combination of a 3D LiDAR scanner and a monocular camera to ensure reliable state estimation for autonomous vehicles. The proposed system operates a parallel stack of odometry algorithms, selecting the most viable pose estimate by applying sanity checks based on the vehicle's dynamic and kinematic constraints, alongside a scoring mechanism comparing the current LiDAR scan against a locally constructed point cloud map. This strategy capitalizes on the strengths of diverse existing ego-motion estimation approaches. Evaluated on the KITTI Odometry dataset, the experimental results indicate that the method is highly resilient to failure scenarios and delivers superior overall performance compared to the individual odometry techniques used within the system.

We present findings from the LISA Pathfinder (LPF) free-fall mode experiment, where the control force used to counteract quasistatic differential forces on two test masses is applied intermittently as short-duration "impulse" forces separated by approximately 350 seconds of genuine free fall. This approach offers an alternative to the standard LPF operation, which applies the balancing force continuously, by enabling the measurement of acceleration noise without the actuation force, thereby removing related noise and calibration uncertainties. The differential acceleration noise data obtained during the free-fall mode aligns with measurements from the continuous actuation method, providing a crucial independent validation of the LPF results. Furthermore, an additional test employing larger actuation forces demonstrates that this technique effectively suppresses actuation noise when it is the primary limiting factor.
The primary objective of this paper is to determine the estimation of Vilenkin-Fourier coefficients.

This note establishes an explicit non-Quillen equivalence between the category of precubical sets and Gaucher's category of flows, utilizing a specific class of "realization functors" under mild assumptions regarding precubical cofibrations. Furthermore, we prove a Quillen equivalence between simplicial semicategories and flows, subsequently demonstrating that simplicial semicategories share many properties with flows. Finally, we introduce the category of boxed symmetric trees as presheaves, which may offer a more adaptable framework for concurrent computing than (pre)cubical sets; we then show that when equipped with degeneracies, this presheaf category constitutes a test category, albeit not a strict one.

Accurate awareness of road boundaries is essential for autonomous vehicle navigation. We introduce a robust method for curb detection and filtering that integrates dense LiDAR point clouds with camera-based semantic information. To ensure reliable feature extraction, multiple LiDAR sensors are fused. The semantic data relies on a modified EfficientNet architecture, trained on labeled images captured by onboard fisheye cameras. After projecting the point clouds into image space using a fisheye model, points are matched to the nearest curb segment via $L_2$-norm analysis. Subsequently, unsupervised density-based spatial clustering groups these points to identify distinct curb regions. As new curb points appear in consecutive frames, they are linked to existing clusters based on temporal reachability; if no such connection exists, a new cluster is created. This approach enables the detection of multiple curbs within multi-lane road segments visible to the sensors. Finally, Delaunay filtering is employed to remove outliers, with its performance benchmarked against traditional RANSAC-based filtering. The system's effectiveness is evaluated against a high-definition map containing ground truth curb data from a commercial provider. Results demonstrate that the proposed system successfully detects curbs of any orientation in complex urban environments, including straight roads, curves, and intersections with traffic islands.
We demonstrate that the chromatic number of any triangle-free graph with a maximum degree of $\Delta$ does not exceed $\left(1+o(1)\right)\Delta/\log \Delta$.

Neutron noise in nuclear reactors denotes minor fluctuations around the steady-state average neutron flux caused by time-varying perturbations within the core. While neutron noise equations in the frequency domain can be addressed via Monte Carlo simulations to yield reference solutions with minimal approximations, these methods face significant challenges regarding statistical convergence. Specifically, the necessity of using both positive and negative particles—dictated by the complex nature of the noise equations—results in catastrophically large variances in tallies. This study focuses on neutron noise arising from mechanical vibrations. First, we develop a novel exact sampling strategy for the noise source. Subsequently, leveraging prior research in related areas, we demonstrate that weight cancellation techniques are highly effective in managing negative weights, yielding substantial improvements in the figure of merit. We validate these findings using a benchmark setup featuring a fuel assembly with a vibrating pin and outline potential avenues for future enhancements.

We investigate the nature and origin of the $\sim$5 kpc spiral disk located at the center of NGC 1275, the giant elliptical galaxy dominating the Perseus cluster. By matching stellar absorption lines from long-slit optical spectra with synthetic spectra of single stellar populations, we determine that two distinct populations are required to fit the data. The first is a very young population ($0.15 \pm 0.05$ Gyr) confined within $\sim$720 pc of the nucleus, exhibiting a peak radial velocity of $\pm 250$ km s$^{-1}$ relative to the systemic velocity and a velocity dispersion significantly below 140 km s$^{-1}$. The second is an ancient population ($\sim$10 Gyr) characterized by a constant radial velocity matching the systemic velocity, a broad velocity dispersion of $\sim$250 km s$^{-1}$, and representing the main stellar body of NGC 1275 along this sight line. We identify the young population as a post-starburst component linked to the spiral disk, while the old population corresponds to the galaxy's primary stellar mass. If the disk represents the remnant of a cannibalized galaxy, its progenitor must have retained an extraordinary amount of gas despite intense ram-pressure stripping to achieve an initial stellar mass of $\sim 3 \times 10^9 \,M_\odot$. However, it is more probable that the central spiral consisted of a gaseous structure accreted from a residual cooling flow over the distant past, which underwent a starburst approximately 0.15 Gyr ago to form its current stellar population.

A matrix $A$, whether finite or infinite, is defined as image partition regular if, for any finite coloring of the natural numbers $\mathbb N$, there exists a vector $\vec{x}$ with entries in $\mathbb N$ such that every entry of the product $A\vec{x}$ falls within a single color class. In reference [6], it was established that the diagonal sum of a finite and an infinite image partition regular matrix retains this property. The same source demonstrated that centrally image partition regular matrices are closed under diagonal summation. However, by applying Theorem 3.3 from [2], it can be deduced that the diagonal sum of two infinite image partition regular matrices does not necessarily preserve image partition regularity. The current paper investigates the image partition regularity of the diagonal sums of specific infinite image partition regular matrices, often yielding additional examples of such matrices.

The heterostructure formed by the Mott insulator LaVO$_3$ and the band insulator SrTiO$_3$ represents a promising prospect for future photovoltaic technologies. In addition to the fact that LaVO$_3$'s direct excitation gap aligns effectively with the solar spectrum, its correlated characteristics and the predicted built-in potential—arising from the non-polar/polar interface when combined with SrTiO$_3$—provide significant benefits compared to traditional solar cells. Nevertheless, experimental evidence beyond the observation of a thickness-dependent metal-insulator transition remains limited, and a deep, microscopic comprehension of the system's electronic properties is still absent. Utilizing soft and hard X-ray photoemission spectroscopy alongside resistivity and Hall effect measurements, we investigate the electrical characteristics, band bending, and band alignment within LaVO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ heterostructures. Our results identify a critical LaVO$_3$ thickness of five unit cells, reveal that conducting electrons are confined exclusively to Ti 3$d$ states at the interface, and detect a potential gradient throughout the film. Based on these observations, we conclude that electronic reconstruction is the primary mechanism driving the formation of the metallic interface in LaVO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$.

We investigate the non-equilibrium quantum dynamics of a small number of interacting bosonic clouds within a two-dimensional asymmetric double-well potential under resonant tunneling conditions. At the single-particle level, this phenomenon involves tunneling through the barrier from a ground state in one well to an excited state in the other, coupling states with different geometries and properties when their energies align. In two dimensions, two distinct resonant tunneling mechanisms arise: longitudinal and transversal. Longitudinal tunneling occurs when the state in the target well is longitudinally excited relative to the source, while transversal tunneling involves transverse excitation. We demonstrate that inter-particle interactions significantly enrich two-dimensional resonant tunneling, analyzing these effects through the lens of junction coherence loss, fragmentation, and the coupling between transverse and longitudinal degrees of freedom and excitations. Our detailed analysis explores the time evolution of key physical quantities, including survival probability, occupation numbers of the reduced one-particle density matrix, and variances in position, momentum, and angular momentum for many-particle systems. Ultimately, we illustrate the influence of both transverse and longitudinal degrees of freedom on the tunneling dynamics of many-boson systems at resonant scenarios.

Matching echelle spectra with synthetic models has evolved into a complex computational statistics problem, as over ten thousand individual spectral lines characterize a typical cool star echelle spectrum. Scientific potential is often hindered by telluric artifacts, incomplete line lists, inaccurate continuum placement, and rigid models. This work introduces "blas\'e," an interpretable machine-learning framework designed to overcome these and other obstacles. The semi-empirical method functions as "transfer learning," initially pre-training on noise-free synthetic spectra and subsequently learning adjustments to line depths and widths through whole-spectrum fitting against observed data. Utilizing back-propagation, a core algorithm in modern Deep Learning and Neural Networks, the auto-differentiable model manages over 40,000 parameters that represent physically meaningful line profile attributes—such as amplitude, width, location, and shape—as well as radial velocity and rotational broadening. This hybrid data- and model-driven approach enables the simultaneous modeling of both stellar and telluric lines, representing a significant advancement in reducing near-infrared telluric contamination. Serving as both a deconvolution tool and a semi-empirical model, the general-purpose scaffold is extensible to various scientific fields, including precision radial velocities, Doppler imaging, chemical abundance analysis, and remote sensing. Built on a sparse-matrix architecture with GPU acceleration, blas\'e operates at high speed. The open-source PyTorch-based codebase provides tutorials, API documentation, and additional resources. The authors demonstrate the tool's integration within the existing Python spectroscopy ecosystem, showcase diverse astrophysical applications, and address current limitations and future development directions.

We examine the zeroes of a family of random holomorphic functions defined on the unit disc, characterized by their invariance under hyperbolic geometry. Our primary result identifies a transition in the limiting behavior of the zero count within large hyperbolic discs. Specifically, when the covariance decays beyond a certain critical threshold, the limiting distribution is normal; however, in the regime of 'long-range dependence' where covariance decays slowly, the limiting distribution becomes skewed. Additionally, we highlight a connection to Gaussian multiplicative chaos for a closely related model.

We introduce a novel 4D-OS128 modulation format, which is four-dimensional, orthant-symmetric, and 128-ary, achieving a spectral efficiency of 7 bits/4D-sym. This format bridges the performance gap between PM-8QAM and PM-16QAM. Numerical simulations indicate that 4D-OS128 surpasses two established 4D geometrically-shaped formats, 128SP-16QAM and 7b4D-2A8PSK, by up to 0.65 dB in bit-interleaved coded modulation at identical spectral efficiency. These advantages are experimentally validated in an 11$\times$233 Gbit/s WDM transmission system operating at 5.95 bits/4D-sym over distances of 6,000 km and 9,000 km under EDFA-only and hybrid amplification conditions, respectively. Compared to 128-ary set-partitioning 16QAM, this approach yields a 15% increase in transmission reach. Additionally, simulations compare the proposed 4D-OS128 against $\boldsymbol{D}_4$ lattice-based constellations and finite-blocklength probabilistically-shaped 16QAM.

Prince Rupert of Rhine famously observed three centuries ago the counterintuitive fact that a straight tunnel can be carved through a cube large enough to allow a second, identical cube to pass through it. A century later, P. Nieuwland extended this inquiry, seeking the maximum aspect ratio that permits a larger, scaled version of the same shape to be passed through a tunnel. We demonstrate that cubes and all rectangular boxes possess Rupert's passages in every direction not parallel to their faces. While it was previously assumed without proof that the optimal solution for Nieuwland's problem regarding a cube involves a tunnel perpendicular to its largest internal square, we prove this assumption holds true not only for the cube but also for all other rectangular boxes.

We examine deterministic algorithms addressing the well-established hidden subgroup problem ($\mathsf{HSP}$). Given a finite group $G$ and a finite set $X$, the input consists of a function $f:G \to X$ with the promise that $f(g_1) = f(g_2)$ if and only if $g_1H = g_2H$ for some subgroup $H \le G$. The decision task involves determining whether $H$ is trivial, while the identification task requires finding $H$. An effective algorithm must query $f(g)$ for $g \in G$ with minimal effort. Nayak \cite{Nayak2021} posed the question of whether deterministic algorithms achieving $O(\sqrt{\frac{|G|}{|H|}})$ query complexity exist for $\mathsf{HSP}$. We resolve this inquiry by proving the following results, which generalize the findings of Ref. [30] by not relying on prior knowledge of $H$: (i) For general finite Abelian groups, there exist algorithms that decide the triviality of $H$ using $O(\sqrt{\frac{|G|}{|H|}})$ queries and identify $H$ using $O(\sqrt{\frac{|G|}{|H|}\log |H|}+\log |H|)$ queries. (ii) Generally, no deterministic algorithm can identify $H$ with $O(\sqrt{\frac{|G|}{|H|}})$ query complexity, as certain $\mathsf{HSP}$ instances require $\omega(\sqrt{\frac{|G|}{|H|}})$ queries. \footnote{$f(x)$ is said to be $\omega(g(x))$ if for every positive constant $C$, there exists a positive constant $N$ such that for $x>N$, $f(x)\ge C\cdot g(x)$, indicating that $g$ is a strict lower bound for $f$.} Conversely, there are $\mathsf{HSP}$ instances with query complexities significantly lower than $O(\sqrt{\frac{|G|}{|H|}})$, specifically $O(\log \frac{|G|}{|H|})$ and even $O(1)$.

Heliospheric observations predominantly utilize in situ spacecraft measurements to generate time-series data. Although often examined visually, such data aligns more intuitively with human auditory perception. The most basic approach to transforming oscillatory data into sound is audification, which maps data points directly to audio samples without losing information, thereby providing an authentic representation of the original dataset. Nevertheless, standard audification can render magnetospheric ULF wave observations fleeting, making them difficult to listen to effectively. Consequently, we examine various audio time-scale modification techniques originally designed for music, applying them to spacecraft ULF wave data to investigate their impact on the resulting audio's characteristics. Through public engagement, we formulate recommendations for ULF wave researchers regarding the audible rendering of these waves and explore the scientific and educational potential of these novel methods.

Demonstrating quantum error correction (QEC) represents a critical step toward building fully functional quantum computers, with recent experimental efforts focusing on surface codes. However, protecting logical quantum information beyond the physical coherence time remains unachieved. This study presents a comprehensive simulation of QEC using rotated surface codes with a distance of 5, which utilize 49 qubits and are compatible with current state-of-the-art hardware. Specifically, we assess the logical error probability under a realistic noise model that accounts for both stochastic Pauli errors and coherent errors arising from systematic control issues or unintended interactions. Although directly simulating 49 qubits is computationally prohibitive, we reduced the requirement to 26 qubits by delaying syndrome measurements. Combined with the GPU-accelerated Qulacs simulator, this approach enables the simulation of full QEC under arbitrary local noise within feasible timeframes. Furthermore, based on our numerical results, we developed and validated an effective model that integrates coherent error effects into a stochastic noise framework. This allows for the analysis of coherent error impacts on logical error probabilities at a large scale without relying on detailed full-scale simulations. Ultimately, this simulation framework and effective model, capable of handling arbitrary local noise, will be essential for identifying the physical parameters that future experimental QEC must optimize.

This study integrates network flexibility into chance-constrained economic dispatch (CCED). The proposed model treats both power generation and line susceptances as variables to minimize expected generation costs while ensuring a low probability of constraint violations regarding generation and line flows amidst renewable uncertainties. By analyzing the analytical form of CCED, we elucidate the mechanism through which network flexibility counters uncertainties. Specifically, renewable uncertainties reduce usable line capacities within flow constraints, thereby worsening transmission congestion; conversely, network flexibility alleviates this congestion by adjusting base-case line flows and diminishing the capacity reduction induced by uncertainties. Additionally, we develop an efficient alternate iteration solver utilizing duality theory to formulate two convex subproblems concerning generation-related and network-related variables, respectively. Alternating solutions to these subproblems yield a satisfactory result. Case studies on the IEEE 14-bus and IEEE 118-bus systems demonstrate that network flexibility significantly enhances operational economy under conditions of renewable uncertainty.

This study examines multiple theoretical models of the pion vector form factor to achieve the optimal fit for two-pion cross sections, thereby minimizing uncertainties in calculating the two-pion contribution to the muon anomalous magnetic moment. By incorporating a polynomial description of the pion vector form factor, we derive the best fit using the Gounaris-Sakurai (or K\"uhn-Santamaria) model for experimental data up to 1 GeV. As a result, the branching ratio for $\omega \to \pi\pi$ is determined to be $\text{Br}(\omega\to\pi\pi)=(1.52\pm 0.06) \%$, which aligns with Particle Data Group values. Utilizing this optimal fit, we calculate the muon anomalous magnetic moment from the two-pion contribution as $a_{\mu}^{\mathrm{HVP,\; LO}}(\pi^{+} \pi^{-} \leq 1\ \text{GeV}) = (497.76\pm3.15) \times 10^{-10}$, a result consistent with previous studies.

This paper focuses on constructing a fractal interpolation function (FIF) over the product of two Sierpiński gaskets. Additionally, we present findings concerning the smoothness of the resulting FIF, specifically proving that these functions are Hölder continuous under certain conditions. In the concluding section, we derive bounds for the fractal dimension of the FIF.

Precise neutron star mass measurements are essential for validating binary evolution theories and restricting the neutron star equation of state. For pulsar binaries lacking measurable post-Keplerian parameters, determining the system's inclination and the companion's radial velocity requires alternative methods beyond pulsar timing. This paper introduces a novel technique for measuring radial velocity using the binary synthesis code Icarus, which constructs a model spectrum of a tidally distorted, irradiated star based on a specific binary configuration. Applying this method to the optical spectra of the newly identified black widow PSR J1555-2908, alongside optical photometry, yields a companion radial velocity of $397\pm4$ km s$^{-1}$ (at 95\% confidence) and an inclination greater than $75^{\rm o}$. When integrated with $\gamma$-ray pulsation timing data, these results indicate a neutron star mass of $1.67^{+0.15}_{-0.09}$ M$_\odot$ and a companion mass of $0.060^{+0.005}_{-0.003}$ M$_\odot$, positioning PSR J1555-2908 at the observed upper mass limit for black widow systems.

The varying orientations of $\alpha$-clustered carbon nuclei during collisions with heavy ions can lead to substantial fluctuations in anisotropic flow values. Consequently, photon flow observables from collisions involving clustered ${\rm^{12}C}$ and ${\rm^{197}Au}$ offer a promising avenue for investigating the `direct photon puzzle'. Utilizing a hydrodynamic model framework at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=200$ GeV at RHIC, we computed the transverse momentum spectra and anisotropic flow coefficients ($v_n$) for thermal photons produced in triangular $\alpha$-clustered carbon-gold collisions, comparing these findings with those from unclustered systems. While the slope of the thermal photon spectra shows only moderate variation across different collision orientations, we observed that the elliptic ($v_2$) and triangular ($v_3$) flow coefficients for specific configurations are markedly higher and are primarily generated by QGP radiation. Furthermore, within an event-by-event framework for $\alpha$-clustered ${\rm C+Au}$ collisions, a strong anti-correlation between initial spatial ellipticity and triangularity emerges. These distinctive characteristics present a unique opportunity to detect the exotic cluster structure within the carbon nucleus using photon probes in future experiments.

This study examines the perturbative quantization of the spectral action within noncommutative geometry, demonstrating its one-loop renormalizability in a generalized sense while adhering to the spectral framework. Our findings rely on expanding the spectral action using higher Yang-Mills and Chern-Simons forms. Following the approach of random noncommutative geometries, we evaluate the path integral involving matrix fluctuations around a fixed noncommutative gauge background. We show that the resulting one-loop counterterms share the same structure, allowing them to be subtracted from the spectral action without issue. Furthermore, appropriate Ward identities play a pivotal role, enabling a complete spectral formulation of the quantum theory at the one-loop level.

We present a comprehensive theoretical framework explaining the recently observed metallic states with broken spin/valley symmetry in ABC trilayer graphene subjected to a significant transverse displacement field. By integrating insights from electronic structure models and mean-field theory, and aligning them with precise measurements of Fermi-surface areas via magneto-oscillations, we demonstrate that the system's physics is governed by momentum-space condensation. This principle promotes Fermi surface reconstructions driven by broken spin/valley flavor symmetries, particularly when single-particle bands form thin annular Fermi seas. Specifically, we identify a large outer Fermi surface composed of majority-flavor states alongside one or more small, inner hole-like surfaces made of minority-flavor states, which are the primary drivers of nematic order. These smaller surfaces can either rotate along a ring of van-Hove singularities or reconstruct into multiple Fermi surfaces with minimal energy cost. We attribute the experimentally observed fractionalization of quantum oscillation frequencies in certain regions of the carrier-density/displacement-field phase diagram to this latter reconstructive property.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) techniques are increasingly allowing deep learning models to be trained on image datasets in areas where obtaining labels is challenging. However, these methods currently face difficulties scaling to the high resolutions required by medical imaging datasets, where such scaling is essential for achieving strong generalization on label-scarce data. This study introduces the Histopathology DatasetGAN (HDGAN) framework, an adaptation of the DatasetGAN semi-supervised approach designed for image generation and segmentation that effectively handles large-resolution histopathology images. We implemented several modifications to the original framework, including updating the generative backbone, selectively extracting latent features from the generator, and utilizing memory-mapped arrays. These enhancements significantly reduce memory usage, thereby expanding the framework's applicability to medical imaging. We evaluated HDGAN on a high-resolution tile dataset for thrombotic microangiopathy, demonstrating robust performance in generating annotations for high-resolution images. We anticipate that this work will facilitate broader application of deep learning models to medical datasets and encourage further investigation into self-supervised frameworks within the medical imaging field.

This work presents a novel second-order stochastic algorithm designed to estimate the entropically regularized optimal transport cost between two probability distributions. While the source distribution can be arbitrary (either absolutely continuous or discrete), the target distribution is assumed to be discrete. To address the semi-dual formulation of this semi-discrete, regularized transport problem, we propose a stochastic Gauss-Newton method that utilizes data sequences sampled from the source measure. This approach is demonstrated to adapt effectively to the geometry of the underlying convex optimization problem without requiring the precise tuning of significant hyperparameters. Furthermore, we prove the almost sure convergence and asymptotic normality of various estimators derived from this algorithm, as well as their non-asymptotic convergence rates regarding the expected quadratic risk, even when the objective function lacks strong convexity. Finally, numerical experiments on simulated data illustrate the finite-sample performance of this stochastic Gauss-Newton method for regularized optimal transport and highlight its superiority over stochastic gradient descent, stochastic Newton, and ADAM algorithms.

Hardware heterogeneity is now an inevitable reality for high-performance computing. Contemporary large-scale systems feature multiple GPU accelerators per node and are poised to adopt even more specialized hardware in the future. While this evolution in the computing landscape presents significant opportunities for performance gains, it simultaneously complicates programming for such architectures. This study presents a runtime framework designed to simplify programming for heterogeneous systems while ensuring efficient hardware utilization. Integrated into a distributed and scalable runtime environment, the framework promotes performance portability across diverse nodes. In addition to detailing the design, the paper outlines the implementation and optimizations, which yield up to a 300% boost in shared memory benchmarks and up to a tenfold increase in distributed device communication. Initial findings suggest that the software imposes minimal overhead, delivering a 40% improvement in a distributed Jacobi proxy application while effectively abstracting hardware-specific quirks.

We investigate the degree to which all dark, compact astrophysical objects are necessarily black holes governed by Kerr geometry, a premise known as the "Kerr hypothesis." By questioning this assumption, we first outline its rationale and relevance before establishing a minimal set of reasonability criteria for alternative dark compact object models. As a proof of principle, we examine specific, dynamically stable non-Kerr black holes and horizonless mimickers that (1) satisfy fundamental theoretical and dynamical constraints, (2) align with current astrophysical observations, and (3) manifest only at macroscopic scales. These examples demonstrate how the purported universality of the Kerr hypothesis across all macroscopic scales can be challenged.

The two-dimensional Dirac equation plays a central role in the study of graphene, topological insulator surfaces, and notably, quantum scarring. Despite a numerical method for handling arbitrary confinement problems being introduced years ago, several foundational challenges remain to be fully comprehended and resolved. This study identifies and overcomes these obstacles, culminating in a comprehensive approach that has been validated through comparison with analytical solutions.

This paper introduces IRON (Invariant-based global Robust estimation and OptimizatioN), a highly robust, non-minimal solution designed for point cloud registration scenarios involving a large volume of outlier correspondences. To achieve this, the registration task is decomposed into separate estimations for translation, rotation, and scale. Our primary contribution is RANSIC (RANdom Samples with Invariant Compatibility), which utilizes invariant compatibility to identify inliers from random samples and simultaneously robustly estimates the scale between two point cloud sets. Following scale estimation, our second contribution involves relaxing the non-convex global registration problem into a certifiable convex Semi-Definite Program (SDP) via Sum-of-Squares (SOS) Relaxation, demonstrating that this relaxation is tight. For robust estimation, we introduce RT-GNC (Rough Trimming and Graduated Non-Convexity), a global outlier rejection heuristic that offers superior robustness and time efficiency compared to traditional GNC methods, constituting our third contribution. These advancements culminate in the IRON algorithm. Experimental results on real datasets demonstrate that IRON is efficient, highly accurate, and resilient against up to 99% outliers, regardless of whether the scale is known or unknown, thereby surpassing existing state-of-the-art algorithms.

This paper introduces differentially private algorithms for stochastic linear bandits across the central, local, and shuffled frameworks. In the central model, our approach yields nearly identical regret to optimal non-private methods, effectively providing privacy at no cost; specifically, we attain a regret of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T}+\frac{1}{\epsilon})$, which aligns with the established lower bound for private linear bandits and improves upon the best prior algorithm's $\tilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\sqrt{T})$. For the local setting, we achieve a regret of $\tilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon}{\sqrt{T}})$, matching non-private performance when $\epsilon$ is constant but incurring a penalty for small $\epsilon$. In the shuffled model, we also reach a regret of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T}+\frac{1}{\epsilon})$ for small $\epsilon$, surpassing the previous best algorithm which suffered $\tilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon}{T^{3/5}})$. Our numerical experiments confirm these theoretical findings.

Ensuring strict safety over long operational periods is a common challenge for control systems. Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) represent a promising method for designing simple, safe control strategies. This paper introduces a framework to verify that CBFs ensure safety indefinitely and to synthesize such functions with provable safety within polynomial control systems. The methodology demonstrates that CBF safety corresponds to the non-existence of solutions to a specific family of polynomial equations, which, according to the Positivstellensatz from algebraic geometry, is equivalent to a pair of sum-of-squares constraints. We extend this Positivstellensatz-based verification to handle high-degree systems and multiple CBF constraints. Additionally, we propose several heuristics for CBF synthesis, including an alternating-descent algorithm, a tailored method for compact safe regions, and a technique for convex unsafe regions. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through two numerical case studies.

Detecting extensive air showers (EAS) via radio waves generated by cosmic-ray interactions in the atmosphere offers a valuable method for studying particle origins and interaction physics. Previous studies using the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR) and the Owens Valley Long Wavelength Array (OVRO-LWA) have shown that dense cores in low-frequency radio telescopes provide detailed radiation ground patterns, enabling the reconstruction of EAS properties and the inference of primary cosmic-ray composition. In this work, we introduce a specialized observation mode for the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) designed to capture the sub-microsecond coherent radiation bursts from EAS. We demonstrate that data recorded at 0.1 ms resolution using the MWA's voltage capture system (VCS) across a 30.72 MHz bandwidth (comprising 3072 channels of 10 kHz) can be synthesized to achieve the full bandwidth Nyquist resolution of 16.3 ns. This technique, which utilizes the inversion of two polyphase filterbanks, preserves 90.5% of the signal-to-noise ratio inherent to cosmic-ray signals. Furthermore, we validate the timing and positional precision of this mode by locating a calibrator pulse with an accuracy of 5 meters. Preliminary results also indicate that the rate of nanosecond radio-frequency interference (RFI) is only 0.1 Hz, significantly lower than rates observed at other cosmic-ray radio telescope sites. Consequently, we conclude that identifying cosmic rays using the MWA—and by extension, the low-frequency component of the Square Kilometre Array—is feasible with minimal efficiency loss due to RFI.

This work introduces a technique for identifying symmetry groups within the Yukawa sector of the three-Higgs-doublet model and analyzing their consequences for lepton masses and mixing. The approach is flexible enough to handle various hypotheses regarding group representation assignments, thereby facilitating the investigation of potential symmetry groups. Applying this computer-aided method to a specific representation scheme, we scanned all discrete groups with orders below $10^{35}$. It has been demonstrated that no such group establishes a flavor symmetry compatible with experimental lepton data regarding masses and neutrino mixing angles, though several instances were identified that show partial or approximate consistency.

The performance of a small cylindrical drift chamber (CDC) prototype, intended for the COMET Phase-I experiment, was evaluated using an electron beam. This prototype featured an alternating all-stereo wire configuration and utilized a He-iC$_{4}$H$_{10}$ (90/10) gas mixture in the absence of a magnetic field. Key parameters, including the drift space-time relationship, drift velocity, $dE/dx$ resolution, hit efficiency, and spatial resolution relative to the wire distance, were analyzed. At applied voltages exceeding 1800 V, the system achieved an average spatial resolution of 150 $\mu$m and a hit efficiency of 99%. These results confirm that the prototype's design and gas composition are suitable for the operational requirements of the COMET CDC.

The integration of Monte-Carlo tree search with Deep Neural Networks, refined via self-play, has achieved state-of-the-art performance in automated game-playing across numerous board games. Although these training and search algorithms are universal, applying them to specific games traditionally necessitates domain-specific knowledge to define game rules and design neural network architectures, particularly regarding input and output tensor dimensions. Ludii serves as a versatile general game system hosting over 500 titles, expandable through its robust and accessible description language. Conversely, Polygames is a framework equipped with advanced training and search algorithms that has already generated superhuman players for various board games. This paper outlines the development of an interface connecting Ludii and Polygames, allowing Polygames to train and assess models for games executed within the Ludii environment. By leveraging our understanding of the Ludii system and its abstract state and move representations, we have created functions that automatically infer the correct tensor shapes for input and output, eliminating the need for game-specific domain knowledge. Furthermore, we present experimental outcomes from brief training sessions across a diverse range of board games and explore several unresolved challenges and potential directions for future research.

Switchbacks are Aflv'enic fluctuations in the solar wind characterized by significant magnetic field rotations. While initial insights into their properties and origins stem from the first two Parker Solar Probe (PSP) encounters, this early dataset may not accurately reflect the typical near-Sun solar wind, potentially skewing our current knowledge. A key characteristic is the direction of magnetic deflection; during the first encounter, the longest switchbacks predominantly deflected tangentially, a pattern cited as evidence and a testable prediction for various generation theories. This study re-evaluates the deflection directions across the first eight PSP encounters to verify if a systematic pattern exists. By identifying switchbacks with deflections exceeding a specific threshold and confirming their arc-polarization, we validate earlier findings. Consistent with the first encounter, we observe that clusters of longer switchbacks tend to deflect uniformly in one direction for several hours. However, unlike previous studies, we find no single unique deflection direction overall, though several encounters displayed a non-uniform distribution with a mild tangential preference. This outcome implies a systematic magnetic configuration underlying switchback generation, aligning with interchange reconnection as a source mechanism, while remaining compatible with alternative explanations such as wave mode expansion.

A locating-dominating set $D$ in a graph $G$ is a dominating set where every vertex outside $D$ possesses a distinct neighborhood within $D$. The Locating-Dominating Set problem determines whether such a set of bounded size exists. This problem is $\mathsf{NP-hard}$ for various restricted graph classes, including planar bipartite subcubic graphs, split graphs, and interval graphs. Conversely, it can be solved in polynomial time for trees and graphs with bounded cliquewidth. Although these findings offer significant insights into the problem's parameterized complexity, research regarding kernelization under structural parameters remains limited. This study addresses that gap by first demonstrating that the problem is $\mathsf{W}[1]$-hard when parameterized by the size of a minimum clique cover. We provide an exponential kernel for the distance to cluster parameterization and prove that, unless $\mathsf{NP} \subseteq \mathsf{coNP/poly}$, no polynomial kernel exists for parameters such as vertex cover or distance to clique. Furthermore, we investigate parameters beyond these bounds and establish a linear kernel for the max leaf number, identifying the feedback edge set parameterization as the main open question in this area.

This note provides a concise overview of the Lefschetz defect, a recently defined invariant for smooth Fano varieties. The invariant connects to the Picard number of the variety $X$ and to the Picard numbers of its prime divisors. We detail the definition and origins of the Lefschetz defect $\delta(X)$, summarize existing results—primarily concerning cases where $\delta(X) > 1$—and present several examples, particularly in dimensions 3 and 4. Specifically, we demonstrate how findings regarding the Lefschetz defect enable the recovery of Mori and Mukai's classification of Fano 3-folds with $\rho(X) > 4$. Additionally, we examine known examples of Fano 4-folds with $\rho(X) > 5$, which are notably scarce; excluding products and toric cases, only six families exist, characterized by Picard numbers in the set $\{6, 7, 8, 9\}$.

Experimental demonstration and analysis confirm the existence of a negative lens formed by gas within a steady, axisymmetric flow. This device holds promise for high-intensity laser optics, offering the ability to adjust focusing characteristics on a sub-millisecond scale. Furthermore, it functions effectively in environments that would compromise traditional optical components.

The appearance of $R^2$ (Starobinsky) inflation, arising from semi-classical gravity modifications driven by the trace anomaly of matter quantum fields, underscores the critical role of fundamental physics and first principles in building viable cosmological models. Beyond its observational success, $R^2$ gravity represents a significant progression beyond General Relativity (GR) toward quantum gravity. Moreover, various contemporary quantum gravity frameworks suggest that non-locality emerges at microscopic scales of time and length. In this context, the ultraviolet (UV) completion of $R^2$ inflation has recently been explored within a string theory-inspired, ghost-free analytic non-local gravity framework. We examine the compelling theoretical forecasts of non-local $R^2$-like inflation regarding essential observables, specifically the tensor-to-scalar ratio and tensor tilt, which characterize the spectrum of primordial gravitational waves, as well as scalar Non-Gaussianities, which describe three-point correlations in Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) fluctuations. Detecting any signature of non-local physics in the early universe would substantially enhance our comprehension of fundamental physics at high-energy UV scales and the nature of quantum gravity.

This paper demonstrates that both coloured Jones and coloured Alexander polynomials can be derived from a single geometric framework involving two Lagrangians within a symmetric power of a surface. Specifically, the $N^{th}$ coloured Jones and $N^{th}$ coloured Alexander polynomials arise as specialisations of a graded intersection between two explicit Lagrangian submanifolds located in the symmetric power of a punctured disc. This graded intersection is determined by the intersection points of these Lagrangians, with a specific grading applied via the diagonals of the symmetric power. As a particular instance, the original Jones and Alexander polynomials are recovered as two specialisations of a graded intersection between two Lagrangians in a configuration space, where their geometric supports correspond to Heegaard diagrams.

Detecting brain tumors is a critical factor in determining life or death. While deep learning-based detection methods have recently attracted significant attention due to their superior performance, achieving optimal results demands vast quantities of labeled images for training. Acquiring such data is often tedious, time-intensive, and prone to human error, which can impede the adoption of these advanced techniques. This paper presents a novel framework for brain tumor detection and classification centered on generating a large synthetic MRI dataset that mirrors the typical patterns of real scans derived from a small, class-imbalanced collection. This synthesized dataset is subsequently used to train a deep learning model for both detection and classification. The approach utilizes two distinct deep models: first, a generative model designed to capture the distribution of key features within the limited, unbalanced set of brain MRIs, enabling the synthesis of an unlimited number of images for each class to automatically transform a small, skewed dataset into a larger, balanced one. Second, a classifier trained on this expanded balanced dataset detects tumors in MRI images. The proposed framework achieves an overall detection accuracy of 96.88%, underscoring its potential as a precise, low-overhead solution for brain tumor detection.

A total coloring of a graph $G$ assigns colors to both vertices and edges such that no two adjacent vertices, no two incident edges, and no vertex-edge pairs sharing an endpoint share the same color. An interval total $t$-coloring extends this by using the color set $\{1, \ldots, t\}$, ensuring all colors are utilized, and requiring that for every vertex $v$, the set consisting of $v$ and its incident edges is colored with $d_{G}(v)+1$ consecutive integers, where $d_{G}(v)$ denotes the degree of $v$. This paper establishes that all complete multipartite graphs with uniformly sized parts admit an interval total coloring. Furthermore, we derive bounds for the minimum and maximum spans of such colorings for these graphs. We also examine interval total colorings in hypercubes $Q_{n}$, proving that for $n \geq 3$, $Q_{n}$ possesses an interval total $t$-coloring if and only if $n+1 \leq t \leq \frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2}$.

Code diffs are integral to daily code review, inspection, and auditing processes, often supplemented with explanations that clarify the program's changes. Since creating high-quality explanations manually is labor-intensive, researchers have developed automatic techniques to generate these descriptions. However, current methods rely exclusively on static analysis, ignoring runtime data to explain modifications. This paper introduces Collector-Sahab, a new tool that enriches code diffs with runtime difference information. By comparing program states between the original and patched versions to identify unique variable values, Collector-Sahab integrates this dynamic data into the diff output for use in code review systems. In an evaluation involving 587 code diffs from Defects4J bugs, the tool successfully augmented 90.6% (532 out of 587) of them. Furthermore, a manual analysis of 29 diffs from 10 real-world projects confirmed that Collector-Sahab produces correct, causally relevant, and comprehensible augmented diffs. Collectively, these results demonstrate the tool's effectiveness and utility in enhancing code diffs with runtime insights. Collector-Sahab: https://github.com/algomaster99/collector-sahab

The enumeration of Skew Dyck paths excludes the 'up-down-left' pattern, and subsequently, the frequency of this specific contiguous subword is calculated. This approach clarifies and generalizes findings previously documented in the Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences.

We present a bulging triangle as a generalization of the Reuleaux triangle. While multiple methods for creating such shapes exist, this paper focuses on a specific approach where the vertices remain identical to those of the original triangle. We derive several properties and theorems for these bulging triangles, and we use calculus to examine whether fundamental geometric principles, such as the triangle inequality and the Pythagorean theorem, apply to them.

Black hole echoes serve as a crucial observable for advancing our comprehension of gravitational theories. We demonstrate that non-linear electrodynamic black holes can support a multi-peaked effective potential for scalar perturbations, thereby generating echoes. By selecting appropriate parameters, this potential can display a structure containing more than two peaks. When an initial wave packet is released outside these peaks, the time-domain profile of the echo fragments as the effective potential transitions from having two peaks to three. This phenomenon, observable in black hole echoes, could potentially allow us to infer the geometric structure of the black hole via gravitational wave detection.

This paper investigates the spectrum of self-adjoint Schrödinger operators in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$ subject to a novel class of transmission conditions defined along a smooth, closed curve $\Sigma\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$. While these *oblique* conditions resemble $\delta'$-conditions on $\Sigma$—differing only in that the Wirtinger derivative replaces the normal derivative—their spectral characteristics are markedly distinct. Specifically, attractive interaction strengths invariably result in a discrete spectrum that is unbounded from below. Beyond this surprising spectral phenomenon, the study identifies the essential spectrum and establishes both a Krein-type resolvent formula and a Birman-Schwinger principle. Additionally, we demonstrate that Schrödinger operators with these oblique transmission conditions emerge naturally as non-relativistic limits of Dirac operators featuring electrostatic and Lorentz scalar $\delta$-interactions, thereby validating their utility as quantum mechanical models.

A key unresolved challenge in the design of superconducting quantum circuits involves reducing the full circuit Hamiltonian, which governs their dynamics, into an effective two-level qubit Hamiltonian suitable for quantum information manipulation. Although numerical techniques for simulating the spectral properties of multi-element circuits have advanced, existing literature lacks a consistent and effective approach for deriving the effective qubit Hamiltonian. This work addresses that gap by presenting a novel local basis reduction method. Unlike previous approaches, this technique does not rely on ad hoc assumptions regarding the Hamiltonian's structure, such as its linear response to external fields. We numerically benchmark this method against established reduction techniques and demonstrate specific cases of superconducting qubits, including the capacitively-shunted flux qubit, where standard methods fail. Furthermore, by integrating the local basis reduction method with the Schrieffer-Wolff transformation, we extend its utility to interacting qubit systems, successfully extracting non-stoquastic two-qubit Hamiltonians and three-local interaction terms within three-qubit Hamiltonians.

Communication-enabled cooperative driving is anticipated to greatly enhance transportation safety and efficiency. Currently, Cooperative Adaptive Cruise Control (CACC) and platooning represent two primary cooperative applications being investigated, both offering substantial advancements over existing Advanced Driver Assistance Systems like Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC). The core objectives of CACC and platooning are to alleviate traffic congestion while optimizing traffic flow, throughput, and highway capacity. To achieve these goals, an efficient controller is essential—one that balances computational costs with the need for driving comfort and rapid responsiveness.
