By applying combinatorial methods to solve the modified Smoluchowski equations derived from the hydrodynamic limit as $n \to \infty$, and utilizing the multidimensional Lambert-Euler inversion, we prove the occurrence of gelation and derive a closed-form expression for the gelation time. Additionally, we determine the asymptotic length of the minimal spanning tree for a wide variety of graphs endowed with random edge lengths.

Group-fairness in classification seeks to ensure predictive utility is equal across various sensitive sub-populations, such as those defined by race or gender. However, imposing equality or near-equality constraints often degrades both overall utility and the performance of the most disadvantaged groups. This paper applies Pareto-efficiency and least-difference principles to accuracy, introducing the "Rawls classifier," which minimizes the error rate for the worst-off sub-population. Mathematically, this classifier uniformly thresholds an ideal feature score, reflecting the concept of fair equality of opportunity. In practice, these scores are frequently generated by black-box models that are effective yet biased. Our second contribution is a practical method for adapting any existing black-box deep learning model to Rawlsian fairness without altering the underlying scores or feature representations. Given any score function or feature representation along with its second-order statistics across sensitive groups, we identify a threshold classifier (or linear threshold classifier for feature representations) that achieves the Rawls error rate within that specific hypothesis class. Technically, we formulate these challenges using ambiguous chance constraints and develop efficient algorithms for Rawlsian fair adaptation, accompanied by provable upper bounds on the error rate. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art group-fair algorithms, even without retraining the models for fairness.

This paper generalizes the established iterated mapping cone technique to monomial ideals within strongly Koszul algebras. We investigate monomial ideals in commutative Koszul algebras, demonstrating that the linear strand of those generated by linear forms appears as a subcomplex of the Priddy complex. For strongly Koszul algebras, this implies that the minimal free resolution of a monomial ideal with linear quotients arises from an iterated mapping cone, thereby extending prior results from polynomial rings to this broader class. Furthermore, we examine monomial ideals possessing a "regular ordering," which generalizes regular decomposition functions, proving that the comparison maps in the iterated mapping cone construction can be calculated explicitly. Consequently, this yields a closed-form expression for the minimal free resolution of such ideals over strongly Koszul algebras.

This presentation introduces Gopcaml-mode, the inaugural structural editing plugin for OCaml. We will explore the plugin's primary features, examining its internal architecture and its integration with current OCaml and GNU Emacs toolchains.

This study investigates particle generation driven by cosmic expansion, employing two Bianchi type I anisotropic models for spin-0 and spin-1/2 particles. The inherent rotational symmetry of these cosmological frameworks enables an exact solution to the equations of motion. Furthermore, the number density of the produced particles is determined using Bogolubov transformations.

To harness the potential of immersive network analytics for effective and engaging exploration, we advocate for the "egocentrism" metaphor, which adapts data representation and interaction to the user's perspective within a 3D network. This approach has the capacity to mitigate common drawbacks of virtual environments, such as visual clutter and cyber-sickness. To assess the impact of this metaphor, we designed and tested interfaces with varying levels of egocentrism. A user study examined how these interfaces influence visual search tasks, network traversal efficiency, spatial orientation, and cyber-sickness. The results indicate that a simple egocentric interface significantly enhances visual search efficiency and navigation performance without negatively affecting spatial orientation or increasing cyber-sickness. An occlusion-free Ego-Bubble view of the immediate neighborhood yielded only marginal performance improvements. We consolidate these findings in an open online tool for egocentric network exploration, offering actionable insights into the benefits of this metaphor.

Significant discourse exists regarding 2D and 3D representation learning for 3D medical imaging. While 2D methods leverage large-scale pretraining, they often fail to capture extensive 3D contexts. Conversely, 3D methods inherently handle 3D contexts well but are hindered by the scarcity of large, diverse public datasets required for universal 3D pretraining. Hybrid (2D + 3D) approaches also suffer from inherent limitations in both their 2D and 3D components. This study bridges the divide by reimagining 2D convolutions. We introduce ACS (axial-coronal-sagittal) convolutions, which enable native 3D representation learning while utilizing pretrained weights from 2D datasets. In ACS convolutions, 2D kernels are partitioned by channel into three segments, which are then convolved independently across the axial, coronal, and sagittal views of 3D data. Theoretically, any 2D CNN architecture (such as ResNet, DenseNet, or DeepLab) can be transformed into a 3D ACS CNN with equivalent parameter sizes and pretrained weights. Extensive experiments across various medical benchmarks—including classification, segmentation, and detection—demonstrate the consistent superiority of pretrained ACS CNNs over their 2D and 3D counterparts, regardless of pretraining status. Furthermore, even without pretraining, ACS convolutions serve as an efficient, plug-and-play alternative to standard 3D convolutions, offering reduced model size and computational cost.

When dealing with extensive missing data, one must typically model two separate data-generating mechanisms: the process producing the response and the mechanism governing data visibility. However, under Rubin's (1976) ignorability condition, likelihood-based inference for the response process becomes independent of the missing data mechanism, necessitating estimation only of the former. This simplification often makes ignorability a standard baseline assumption. This paper examines the consequences of Bayesian ignorability when high-dimensional nuisance parameters are present, arguing that ignorability is generally incompatible with reasonable prior beliefs regarding selection bias. We demonstrate that in many scenarios, ignorability forces the prior on selection bias to be tightly concentrated around zero. This is illustrated across several practical models, and the impact of ignorability on posterior distributions is analyzed specifically for high-dimensional linear models employing a ridge regression prior. Finally, we present methods for constructing high-dimensional models that incorporate sensible beliefs about selection bias and identify specific, narrow conditions under which ignorability remains less problematic.

To develop a biologically realistic model of machine listening, we examine how a wavelet scattering network represents multicomponent stationary signals. Initially, we demonstrate that renormalizing second-order nodes by their first-order parents provides a straightforward numerical metric for determining psychoacoustic interference between adjacent components. Next, we apply the Isomap manifold learning algorithm to scattering coefficients to map the similarity space inherent in parametric additive synthesis. Finally, we extend the "one or two components" framework to accommodate three or more sine waves, proving that the effective scattering depth of a Fourier series increases logarithmically with its bandwidth.

This research investigates automated intrusion prevention via reinforcement learning. We adopt a novel framework that models the dynamic interaction between attackers and defenders as an optimal stopping game, allowing both strategies to evolve through self-play and reinforcement learning. This game-theoretic lens enables the discovery of robust defender strategies capable of countering dynamic adversaries, while the optimal stopping formulation reveals that these strategies exhibit threshold characteristics. To derive these optimal strategies, we propose T-FP, a fictitious self-play algorithm that identifies Nash equilibria using stochastic approximation. Our results demonstrate that T-FP surpasses existing state-of-the-art algorithms in this specific context. Our comprehensive methodology for strategy learning and evaluation comprises two integrated systems: a simulation environment for the incremental learning of defender tactics and an emulation system that generates statistical data to drive simulations and assess the performance of learned strategies. We conclude that this approach yields effective defender strategies suitable for practical IT infrastructure.

In quantum key distribution (QKD), a passive light-source side channel renders quantum signals more distinguishable, thereby granting an eavesdropper additional information. Previous explicit eavesdropping strategies targeting this passive channel were restricted to measuring it independently of the operational degree of freedom. This work demonstrates how to address joint eavesdropping attacks that target both the operational degree of freedom and the generic passive side channel simultaneously. Specifically, we employ optimal phase-covariant cloning of the signal photon state—the most potent attack against the BB84 protocol absent side channels—followed by a collective joint measurement of the side channel and the operational degree of freedom. To assess QKD security under this specific attack, we introduce an effective error method and demonstrate its utility for the BB84 decoy-state protocol.

This research investigates how dark matter halos influence the orbital and escape behaviors of stars within the central regions of barred galaxies. To achieve this, a three-dimensional gravitational model incorporating a central bulge, bar, disc, and dark matter halo was constructed and analyzed using open Hamiltonian systems. The model was specifically evaluated using two distinct dark halo profiles: oblate and NFW. In both scenarios, an escape mechanism was identified near the phase space saddle points, which align with the bar ends. Star escape dynamics were visualized through orbital maps and Poincaré surface section maps across various phase planes. Furthermore, the study explored the connection between chaos and dark halo parameters, including mass, size, circular velocity, and structural nature. The results indicate that oblate dark halos better explain the formation of complete spiral arms and extended dark halo distributions in giant spiral galaxies hosting supermassive black holes (SMBHs). Similarly, oblate halos effectively account for weaker spiral arms and core-dominated dark halo distributions in dwarf and low surface brightness (LSB) galaxies lacking central SMBHs. Conversely, generating spiral patterns with NFW halos demands extreme central baryonic feedback, suggesting these halos are more suitable for galaxies with highly energetic centers.

This paper investigates the partitioning of agents into coalitions based on their additively separable preferences, a framework equivalent to a hedonic game. We examine three increasingly permissive solution concepts: envy-freeness, weakly justified envy-freeness, and justified envy-freeness. While trivial solutions exist for these concepts when coalition sizes are unrestricted, this motivates our restriction to coalitions of exactly three members. We analyze both the existence and computational complexity of finding partitions that satisfy these envy-free conditions. Our work offers a comprehensive complexity classification relative to restrictions on agents' preferences, revealing a consistent pattern: for the three successively weaker solution concepts, the conditions for existence and polynomial-time solvability also become progressively weaker.

The LHC Effective Field Theory (EFT) working group unites LHC experimenters and theorists to establish a framework for interpreting LHC data through the lens of EFT. This note examines experimental observables and their corresponding measurements within analyses of Higgs, top, and electroweak data at the LHC. It reviews the connection between operators and measurements essential for interpreting experimental results in the context of a global SMEFT analysis. A primary objective of this ongoing effort is to bridge the divide between the theoretical and experimental EFT communities, particularly regarding optimized analyses. Serving as a guide to the measurements and observables required for EFT fits, this document establishes best practices but does not provide authoritative instructions on how to execute those measurements.

We introduce a fully discrete, convergent finite difference method for liquid crystal Q-tensor flow, building upon the energy-stable semi-discrete framework established by Zhao, Yang, Gong, and Wang (Comput. Methods Appl. Mech. Engrg. 2017). This work establishes the scheme's stability properties and demonstrates its convergence toward weak solutions of the Q-tensor flow equations, with numerical simulations provided to illustrate its performance.

Although current Math Word Problem (MWP) solvers demonstrate high accuracy on benchmark datasets, previous research indicates they rely on superficial cues and lack generalization capabilities. This paper presents experiments demonstrating that such limitations stem primarily from the restricted size and diversity of existing MWP datasets. Consequently, we introduce several data augmentation techniques, broadly classified into Substitution and Paraphrasing methods. Applying these strategies expands the size of current datasets by five times. Extensive evaluations across two benchmark datasets and three state-of-the-art solvers reveal that our methods enhance both the generalization and robustness of these systems. On average, the proposed approaches improve state-of-the-art benchmark results by more than five percentage points, while solvers trained on augmented data also perform superiorly on challenge test sets. Furthermore, we validate the efficacy of our techniques through ablation studies and confirm the quality of the generated samples via human evaluation.

Bayesian computation is essential in modern statistics and machine learning for handling uncertainty, with a primary challenge lying in efficiently approximating or sampling from posterior distributions. Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) has emerged as a powerful solution for approximate inference. However, standard SVGD relies on calculating the gradient of the target density, making it inapplicable when gradients are inaccessible or prohibitively expensive. This paper addresses this limitation by constructing a local surrogate for the target distribution where gradients are computationally tractable. Specifically, we approximate the forward model using a deep neural network (DNN) trained on a strategically selected dataset, which influences the surrogate's quality. We propose a general adaptation procedure to refine this local approximation online while maintaining the convergence of the resulting SVGD. This approach significantly lowers the computational burden of SVGD, yielding a suite of easy-to-implement algorithms. The proposed method is demonstrated on challenging Bayesian inverse problems, with numerical experiments confirming clear improvements in both performance and applicability compared to standard SVGD.

This study utilizes spatially resolved data from the TYPHOON program to analyze gas-phase metallicity, ionization parameters, and interstellar medium (ISM) pressure across six local, face-on spiral galaxies known for star formation. By employing an iterative method, we simultaneously generate self-consistent maps for these three parameters to effectively characterize local chemical abundances and their connection to specific ISM conditions. To assess azimuthal metallicity variations, we calculated residual offsets, $\Delta$(O/H), by removing linear fits from radial metallicity profiles. Our results indicate only weak evidence for such variations in most galaxies, characterized by a minimal mean scatter of 0.03 dex. Instead, HII regions displaying both elevated and depleted abundances are scattered throughout the galactic disks. Although spiral structures help organize the ISM, they do not solely account for the observed uniformity in azimuthal variations; rather, differences in metal abundance appear primarily driven by strong correlations with local physical conditions. We identified a robust positive correlation between the ionization parameter and local abundances, as measured by the relative metallicity offset $\Delta$(O/H), underscoring a tight link between local physical environments and localized ISM enrichment. Furthermore, we examined how unresolved observations affect measured ISM properties by rebinning datacubes to mimic the low resolution (1 kpc) typical of large integral field unit (IFU) surveys. Our findings show that reducing resolution impacts ionization parameter and ISM pressure diagnostics, causing their measured values to appear larger compared to those derived at sub-HII region scales.

Serverless cloud platforms distribute workloads from various users across a shared resource pool, allowing providers to minimize resource consumption by transparently aggregating similar tasks within specific contexts, such as video processing, where computations overlap. Accurately quantifying the time savings achieved through such aggregation is vital; without this insight, uninformed scheduling and merging decisions may result in missed deadlines for both combined and subsequent tasks. Consequently, this paper investigates the estimation of execution-time reductions resulting from task merging, using video processing as a case study. To understand time savings across different merging scenarios, we created a suite of benchmark videos and evaluated a broad range of processing tasks with and without aggregation. Our findings indicate that while merging can reduce execution time by as much as 44%, the vast number of potential merging configurations makes exhaustive analysis intractable. Therefore, we utilized our benchmarking data to develop a Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT) model capable of predicting time savings for any given merging scenario. Experimental validation demonstrates that this method achieves an estimation error rate of only 0.04, as measured by Root Mean Square Error (RMSE).

Recent years have seen a growing focus on object detection within remote sensing imagery. Nevertheless, conventional optical detection remains highly vulnerable to variations in illumination and adverse weather conditions. Effectively leveraging cross-modality information from multi-source images—particularly the combination of optical and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data—to achieve high-accuracy, rapid, all-day, and all-weather detection remains a significant challenge. To address this, the current study proposes a fast multi-source fusion detection framework. This approach introduces a novel distance-decay intersection over union metric to encode target shape properties with scale invariance, enabling accurate pairing of the same target across different image sources. Additionally, the framework employs weighted Dempster-Shafer evidence theory to integrate optical and SAR detection results, thereby circumventing the limitation of feature-level fusion, which typically demands extensive paired datasets. The proposed algorithm is validated using paired optical and SAR images of the container ship *Ever Given* after it ran aground in the Suez Canal. Evaluation on a self-constructed dataset demonstrates that the average precision of the proposed fusion detection framework exceeds that of optical detection alone by 20.13%.

Pulsars act as prolific sources of relativistic electrons and positrons that travel outward, eventually saturating our Galaxy. The mechanisms driving the acceleration and movement of these particles remain a subject of significant scientific debate. Recently, direct observation of these particles being injected into the interstellar medium has become possible through the identification of gamma-ray halos surrounding pulsars. These unique gamma-ray emitters arise when electrons and positrons diffuse from the pulsar wind nebula and interact with ambient photon fields via scattering. This emerging research area is supported by multi-wavelength observations and constraints, alongside diverse theoretical models that explain the properties of these halos. We analyze the cosmic ray propagation characteristics derived from halo observations and explore their local and global implications for particle transport within the Galaxy. Furthermore, we discuss the potential for studying these sources using upcoming facilities such as LHAASO, CTA, and SWGO.

Within evolutionary robotics, selecting an appropriate encoding is particularly challenging, especially when evolving both morphology and behavior simultaneously. To enhance our comprehension of how encodings map to functional robots, we introduce the biological concept of heritability, which quantifies the phenotypic variation resulting from genotypic changes. Our analysis measures heritability in the initial generation of robots evolved from two distinct encodings: direct and indirect. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between heritability and phenotypic diversity throughout a complete evolutionary run. Specifically, we explore how direct and indirect genotypes may favor exploration or exploitation strategies over time. We find that the tradeoff between exploration and exploitation becomes clearer when analyzing patterns in heritability and phenotypic diversity. Ultimately, we demonstrate that heritability serves as a valuable tool for understanding genotype-phenotype relationships, particularly when designing complex systems where individuals and environments dynamically adapt and influence one another.

The binary channel involving a white dwarf (WD) and a helium (He) star is a critical component of the single degenerate model for type Ia supernova (SN Ia) progenitors. While earlier research on WDs paired with main sequence stars indicated that magnetic fields can substantially impact accretion and nuclear burning, this study specifically examines the evolution of magnetized WD + He star binaries using detailed stellar evolution and binary population synthesis (BPS) methods. In systems with magnetized WDs, magnetic fields can fragment the inner accretion disk, direct accretion flow toward polar caps, and restrict helium burning to these regions. Our findings reveal that for WDs with sufficiently strong magnetic fields, the viable parameter space for SN Ia progenitors shifts toward shorter orbital periods and lower donor masses compared to non-magnetized scenarios. This occurs because magnetic confinement typically operates at higher mass transfer rates, which can induce intense wind mass loss from the WD, thereby reducing the efficiency of He-rich mass accumulation. Consequently, surviving companion stars are likely to be low-mass at the time of explosion, offering a potential explanation for the lack of observed surviving companions or remnants within SN Ia sites. However, the predicted Galactic SN Ia birthrate in our high-magnetic models is approximately (0.08–0.13) × 10⁻³ yr⁻¹ (compared to ~0.17–0.28 × 10⁻³ yr⁻¹ for non-magnetic models), which remains significantly lower than the observed rate.

Magnetic fields are fundamental to protoplanetary disks, particularly within the disk atmosphere where they drive wind-launching mechanisms. This study investigates the polarization of light scattered by magnetically aligned grains in the atmosphere, specifically examining deviations from the standard azimuthal orientation that could be detected via near-infrared polarimetry using instruments like VLT/SPHERE. Using a simplified disk model, we demonstrate that polarization can align radially rather than azimuthally, a phenomenon especially prevalent in highly inclined disks dominated by toroidal magnetic fields. This "polarization reversal" stems from the anisotropic polarizability of aligned grains, serving as a definitive indicator of their presence. Our analysis reveals that at the $\tau=1$ surface, near-infrared scattering is primarily driven by grains smaller than a few micrometers; these grains can achieve magnetic alignment if they contain superparamagnetic inclusions. To facilitate comparison with observations, we produce synthetic maps of the $U_\phi/I$ and $Q_\phi/I$ ratios. These maps suggest that a negative $Q_\phi$ (indicating polarization reversal) and/or a substantial $U_\phi/I$ ratio can confirm the presence of magnetically aligned grains. Furthermore, we find that two observed features in existing data—an asymmetric $U_\phi$ distribution relative to the disk's minor axis and a spatially consistent positive or negative $U_\phi$—contradict scattering models involving spherical grains in an axisymmetric disk, thereby offering indirect evidence for scattering by aligned, non-spherical grains.

This study introduces CODER, a framework leveraging contrastive learning on knowledge graphs to generate cross-lingual medical term representations. Designed to facilitate medical term normalization, CODER creates dense vector embeddings that align terms representing identical or analogous medical concepts across languages. The model is trained using the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) knowledge graph, where similarity is derived from both textual terms and relational triplets. Incorporating relations during training infuses domain-specific medical knowledge into the embeddings, enhancing their utility as machine learning features. Evaluation on zero-shot term normalization, semantic similarity, and relation classification benchmarks demonstrates that CODER surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in biomedical word embeddings, concept embeddings, and contextual embeddings. The source code and models are accessible at https://github.com/GanjinZero/CODER.

This study outlines a comprehensive analysis of global stopping and fragment production in heavy-ion collisions occurring between 50 and 1000 MeV/nucleon. The investigation examines dependencies on excitation functions, impact parameters, system size, isospin asymmetry, and the equation of state, specifically within the context of symmetry energy and isospin-dependent cross sections. Results indicate that while the degree of stopping is only weakly influenced by symmetry energy, it is strongly affected by the isospin-dependent cross section. Conversely, both factors exert a significant impact—exceeding 10%—on the emission of light charged particles (LCPs). Consequently, nuclear stopping and LCP emission serve as effective probes for determining the isospin-dependent cross section. Notably, a strong correlation exists between LCP emission and global stopping when symmetry energy is present.

Lin's theorem asserts that for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that for any $n \geq 1$, if self-adjoint contractions $A, B \in M_n(\mathbb{C})$ satisfy $\|[A,B]\|\leq \delta$, then one can find commuting self-adjoint contractions $A', B' \in M_n(\mathbb{C})$ with $[A',B']=0$ and $\|A-A'\|,\|B-B'\|<\epsilon$. We provide comprehensive details of the methodology outlined in arXiv:0808.2474, which appears to be the result most akin to a general constructive proof of Lin's theorem. Additionally, we discuss constructive findings for specific instances and explore applications regarding almost commuting matrices where $B$ is normal, as well as their relevance to macroscopic observables.

This study aims to prove the existence of solutions with a specified norm for a specific class of nonlinear equations that incorporate mixed fractional Laplacians. Such equations are significant across diverse domains, including biophysics and population dynamics. Given the critical nature of these applications, the subject has recently garnered substantial attention. The approach presented here is innovative and encompasses all prior results.

Shared e-mobility initiatives have been extensively piloted worldwide and are now integral to contemporary urban planning. This research addresses a critical challenge within these systems: determining how to deploy and manage infrastructure spatially and temporally to ensure both widespread user accessibility and financial sustainability. In practice, however, assessing various deployment strategies to identify the optimal plan is often prohibitively costly, as numerous trial-and-error iterations are frequently infeasible. To overcome this, we developed a high-fidelity simulation environment that abstracts key operational details at a fine granularity and is calibrated with real-world data. This tool enables the testing of arbitrary deployment strategies to derive optimal solutions for specific contexts prior to real-world implementation. Specifically, we introduce a novel multi-agent neural search method featuring a hierarchical controller that generates tentative deployment plans. These plans are evaluated through a multi-simulation paradigm involving parallel assessments, with the results utilized to train the controller via deep reinforcement learning. This closed-loop system guides the controller to increasingly produce superior deployment plans over successive iterations. Extensive evaluations within our simulation environment demonstrate that this approach outperforms baselines, including human expertise and state-of-the-art heuristic optimization methods, in terms of both service coverage and net revenue.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) are an emerging meta-surface technology capable of establishing additional communication links by reflecting signals, positioning them as a promising candidate for 6G mobile systems. Recently, integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) with RIS has been acknowledged to significantly boost reconfiguration capabilities and improve robustness against complex transmission environments. Beyond traditional model-driven methods, AI offers a data-driven approach to existing signal processing challenges by extracting inherent patterns from real-world data. Consequently, AI is uniquely suited for handling signal processing issues in RIS networks under non-ideal conditions, such as modeling mismatches, limited resources, hardware impairments, and dynamic transmissions. As one of the pioneering survey papers on this topic, we explore the convergence of AI and RIS, termed AIRIS, across various signal processing domains including environmental sensing, channel estimation, beamforming design, and resource scheduling. Furthermore, we examine the challenges associated with AIRIS and outline potential future research directions.

Precise localization is critical for the autonomy and safety of self-driving vehicles, particularly in complex urban settings and subterranean search-and-rescue scenarios where high-precision GPS is unavailable. However, current odometry estimation often suffers from drift during long-term navigation if robust global localization is not implemented. Key challenges include handling scene divergence caused by dynamic environments and effectively perceiving variations in object layouts and observations from different viewpoints. To address these issues, we introduce PSE-Match, a viewpoint-independent place recognition approach that relies on parallel semantic analysis of isolated attributes derived from 3D point-cloud models. Unlike original point clouds, the variance of these semantic attributes is significantly reduced. PSE-Match utilizes a divergence place learning network to capture diverse semantic attributes simultaneously within the spherical harmonics domain. Experimental results on both established benchmark datasets and two newly collected field datasets demonstrate that the method achieves an average recall of over 70% for top-one retrieval and over 95% for top-ten retrieval. Furthermore, PSE-Match exhibits strong generalization capabilities even when trained on limited datasets.

We establish the stellar-to-halo mass relation (SHMR), defined as $f_\star\propto M_\star/M_{\rm h}$ plotted against $M_\star$ and $M_{\rm h}$, for early-type galaxies using their near-IR luminosities to determine stellar mass and the kinematic properties of their globular cluster systems to infer halo mass. Our specific $M_{\rm h}$ estimates rely on fitting dynamical models using action-angle variables, constrained by a prior on $M_{\rm h}$ derived from the concentration-mass relation within the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmological framework. Our results indicate that the SHMR for early-type galaxies peaks at $M_\star\sim 5\times 10^{10}M_\odot$ and $M_{\rm h}\sim 10^{12}M_\odot$ (comparable to the Milky Way's mass) before declining with increasing mass. This finding aligns with SHMRs for the general galaxy population derived via abundance matching and matches earlier, less precise studies of early types. In contrast, this trend differs significantly from the monotonically increasing SHMR observed for late-type galaxies based on extended HI rotation curves and the same $\Lambda$CDM prior. The SHMR transitions smoothly from rising to falling as galaxies evolve from late to early types, characterized by decreasing disc fractions and Hubble types. Furthermore, the distinct SHMRs for early and late types remain consistent with their respective stellar velocity-mass scaling relations (Faber-Jackson and Tully-Fisher), as differences in the relations between stellar and halo virial velocities account for this similarity. We propose that these empirical observations naturally arise from a formation scenario where galactic discs form through smooth, gradual inflow regulated by feedback from young stars, whereas galactic spheroids develop through a synergy of merging, black-hole fueling, and feedback from active galactic nuclei.

We demonstrate that completeness at higher levels within the theory of the reals is a resilient concept, even when the signature is altered or the quantifier domains are restricted. This finding fills acknowledged gaps in the hierarchy and yields more powerful completeness theorems for diverse computational issues. We present multiple families of complete problems suitable for advancing future research in the real hierarchy. Furthermore, we apply these insights to refine certain findings by Bürgisser and Cucker regarding the complexity of semialgebraic set properties, including the Hausdorff distance problem previously examined by Jungeblut, Kleist, and Miltzow.

We systematically investigate how non-Gaussianities influence the mass fraction of primordial black holes (PBHs) at formation by incorporating these effects into the one-point probability distribution function of the primordial curvature perturbation. Focusing on the bispectrum and trispectrum, we derive expressions for their impact on the distribution's skewness and kurtosis. For narrowly peaked spectra, we establish simplified formulas that succinctly capture the contributions of bi- and trispectra. Specifically, we demonstrate that in the narrow spectral limit, the non-Gaussianity parameters associated with various bispectrum types combine linearly with the trispectrum parameters $g_{\rm NL}$ and $\tau_{\rm NL}$ to form an effective parameter, $f_{\rm NL}^{\rm eff}$, which governs the PBH mass fraction.

We extend the unifying relations applicable to tree-level amplitudes to encompass $1$-loop Feynman integrands. Utilizing the $1$-loop Cachazo-He-Yuan (CHY) formula, we develop differential operators capable of transforming the $1$-loop gravitational Feynman integrand into those of various theories, including Einstein-Yang-Mills, Einstein-Maxwell, pure Yang-Mills, Yang-Mills with scalars, Born-Infeld, Dirac-Born-Infeld, bi-adjoint scalar, non-linear sigma model, and special Galileon theories. This establishes a unified framework at the $1$-loop level. Furthermore, we examine how these $1$-loop operators factorize into two tree-level operators under the standard unitarity cut condition.

This letter aims to substantiate two assertions regarding the gradient expansion in relativistic hydrodynamics. First, for a non-conformal fluid, the sequence of transverse derivatives holds no significance. Second, within the gradient expansion of a conformal fluid, the longitudinal projection of the Weyl covariant derivative can be discarded; however, this rule does not extend to curvature tensors. Furthermore, in the conformal context, the order in which Weyl covariant derivatives appear is inconsequential.

Person re-identification (re-ID) has increasingly attracted attention because of its extensive use in intelligent video surveillance. However, current mainstream deep learning approaches rely heavily on large amounts of labeled data, and manual annotation is costly in real-world settings. Furthermore, domain shifts between datasets cause a sharp decline in performance when models trained on data-rich source domains are directly applied to unlabeled target domains. To address these challenges, we propose solutions in both data and methodology. First, we created a system to automatically generate synthetic re-ID samples within a computer game environment and an automated annotator to label them, thereby eliminating the need for labor-intensive human data collection and annotation. Using this system, we established two synthetic person re-ID datasets of varying sizes: "GSPR" and "mini-GSPR." Second, we introduced a synthesis-based multi-domain collaborative refinement (SMCR) network. This architecture includes a synthetic pretraining module and two collaborative-refinement modules designed to fully leverage valuable knowledge across multiple domains. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our framework achieves significant performance gains over state-of-the-art methods on various unsupervised domain adaptation tasks for person re-ID.

We introduce a highly efficient approach for pretraining large-scale autoencoding language models by leveraging training signals from an auxiliary model. Building upon the ELECTRA framework, this strategy has proven effective for pretraining models with hundreds of millions of parameters. This study presents a comprehensive empirical analysis and proposes a new methodology called "Model generated dEnoising TRaining Objective" (METRO). METRO integrates several recent advanced modeling techniques designed to accelerate, stabilize, and improve pretrained language models without sacrificing their performance. The resulting METRO-LM models, which scale up to 5.4 billion parameters, establish new state-of-the-art results on the GLUE, SuperGLUE, and SQuAD benchmarks. Crucially, these models demonstrate significant efficiency by frequently surpassing previous larger models while utilizing substantially smaller architectures and incurring lower pretraining costs.

On April 1, 2019, the Advanced Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (aLIGO) commenced its third observing run alongside the Advanced Virgo detector, initiating a year-long campaign dedicated to detecting gravitational radiation. The LIGO facilities have attained unprecedented sensitivity and duty cycles for gravitational wave detection; specifically, LIGO Hanford reached an angle-averaged sensitivity to binary neutron star mergers of 111 Mpc, while LIGO Livingston achieved 134 Mpc, operating at duty factors of 74.6% and 77.0%, respectively. These enhancements in stability and sensitivity stem from multiple detector upgrades, such as doubling intracavity power, integrating an in-vacuum optical parametric oscillator for squeezed-light injection, swapping core optics and end test masses, and installing acoustic mode dampers. This study examines the rationale behind these improvements and details the noise sources currently constraining the sensitivity of each detector, to the best of our knowledge.

Modern data-intensive physics facilities depend heavily on large-scale, heterogeneous computing and data processing infrastructures to manage the massive volumes of data required for collection, distribution, filtering, and analysis. These operations frequently occur within hard or quasi-real-time pipelines, imposing stringent constraints on system design and parameter choices. As a result, designing, building, and operating such facilities presents a wide array of significant challenges. This is particularly evident at the energy and intensity frontiers of particle physics, where raw data bandwidths can surpass 100 TB/s, originating from over 300 million individual sensors comprising high-dimensional, heterogeneous information. The data filtering and compression algorithms employed at these sites often operate with a precision of one part in $10^5$; once executed, these algorithms dictate the data curation workflow, underscoring the critical role these systems play in the overall physics impact of these endeavors. This White Paper seeks to outline the challenges associated with designing trigger and data acquisition instrumentation and systems, as well as the difficulties involved in their installation, commissioning, integration, and operation. Furthermore, it addresses the need to cultivate the necessary domain knowledge and technical expertise to execute these tasks effectively.

We present STAR-MELT, a Python package designed to streamline the analysis of time-resolved emission line spectroscopy for young stellar objects (YSOs). This tool automatically extracts, identifies, and fits emission lines. Our methodology leverages the time domain of high-resolution stellar spectra to examine line profile variability and the associated emitting regions, thereby probing the innermost discs and accretion structures of YSOs. Physical parameters such as local temperatures and densities are derived using Boltzmann statistics, the Saha equation, and the Sobolev large velocity gradient approximation. STAR-MELT enables the extraction of new insights from archival data and supports the prompt analysis of incoming observations. We apply STAR-MELT to three YSOs using spectra from UVES, XSHOOTER, FEROS, HARPS, and ESPaDOnS, demonstrating its capabilities across varied time sampling, stellar inclinations, and variability types. For EX Lupi, we confirm a localized, stable stellar-surface hot spot linked to the accretion column footprint. In GQ Lupi A, we identify a correlation between the maximum infall rate from an accretion column and lines formed in the coolest regions. For CVSO109, we investigate the rapid temporal variability of a redshifted emission wing, signaling rotating and infalling material in the inner disc. These findings illustrate that STAR-MELT is a valuable instrument for this type of analysis and other emission line applications.

This note offers a proof of the generalized Green-Julg theorem by employing the framework of twisted localization algebras developed by G. Yu. The approach is designed for readers interested in coarse geometry who may lack extensive familiarity with KK-theory or E-theory.

As quantum circuits expand in size and depth, correlations within noisy systems become an unavoidable consequence. Randomized Benchmarking (RB) stands out as a straightforward approach for evaluating device performance and detecting temporal correlations, known as non-Markovianity; yet, once such correlations are identified, operationally quantifying them has remained difficult. This work introduces a technique leveraging machine learning and matrix product operators to determine the minimal average non-Markovianity from RB experimental data. We argue that this method is applicable to any compatible gate set and can be specifically adapted for the majority of targeted RB protocols.

Let {\Lnk} denote the collection of all real solvable Lie algebras of dimension $n$ with derived ideals of dimension $k$. While the authors and their colleagues provided a classification in 2020 of non-2-step nilpotent Lie algebras within {\Li}, this paper focuses on investigating the representations of these algebras and their associated connected, simply connected Lie groups. Specifically, we establish an upper bound for the minimal degree of a faithful representation for each algebra and offer a geometric characterization of the coadjoint orbits of the corresponding groups. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a key property of the family of maximal dimensional coadjoint orbits for MD-groups, previously identified by K. P. Shum and the second author, holds true for the Lie groups under consideration: the family of maximal dimensional coadjoint orbits constitutes a measurable foliation in the sense of Connes. Finally, we present the topological classification of these foliations.

This paper presents a numerical investigation into the wave turbulence of surface gravity waves using the Euler equations for a free surface. The primary objective is to examine how spectral scaling with wavenumber $k$ and energy flux $P$ varies across different nonlinearity levels and forcing or free-decay conditions. Across all scenarios considered—including free decay and both narrow- and broadband forcing—we observe that at high nonlinearity levels, the spectral forms converge toward the wave turbulence theory (WTT) predictions of $S_\eta\sim k^{-5/2}$ and $S_\eta\sim P^{1/3}$. As nonlinearity decreases, spectra for all cases steepen, with the narrow-band forcing scenario showing the most significant departure from WTT. To explain these spectral changes, we analyze two proposed mechanisms: bound waves and finite-size effects. Tri-coherence analysis reveals that a finite-size effect exists in all cases, driving the overall spectral steepening and reducing energy flux capacity at lower nonlinearity levels. While the proportion of bound waves generally declines as nonlinearity drops, the narrow-band case is an exception, displaying a transition at a critical nonlinearity level below which bound waves increase rapidly. This surge in bound waves is the primary cause of the fastest deviation from WTT observed in the narrow-band forcing scenario as nonlinearity diminishes.

This study provides a comprehensive analysis of active galactic nuclei in two Seyfert 1 galaxies, LEDA 3095839 and VII Zw 244. These objects were initially observed as part of the photometric reverberation mapping project conducted at the Special Astrophysical Observatory of the Russian Academy of Sciences (SAO RAS), where the supermassive black hole (SMBH) masses were previously determined. Subsequently, both galaxies were observed using spectropolarimetric and polarimetric modes on the 6-meter BTA telescope at SAO RAS, equipped with the SCORPIO-2 focal reducer, to measure the linear polarization of the continuum and broad Balmer lines. The findings indicate that (i) LEDA 3095839 shows no evidence of equatorial scattering in its broad H-alpha line, allowing for the estimation of the SMBH spin and disk magnetic field strength based on continuum polarization levels; (ii) in contrast, VII Zw 244 exhibits signs of equatorial scattering, which enabled an independent measurement of the SMBH mass, determination of the system's inclination angle, and estimation of the spin value.

To enable quantum computing capabilities on personal edge devices, the optimal strategy involves using simple, non-error-corrected terminals that delegate computational work to scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computers via edge servers equipped with cryogenic components. Consequently, network elements utilize various encoding protocols. This article introduces quantum terminals designed to be compatible with these diverse protocols, facilitating the realization of mobile edge-quantum computing. By integrating an atomic lattice processor within a cavity, the system employs Rydberg-Fermi cavity-QED technology to generate entanglement. The operation relies on Fermi scattering of a Rydberg electron from the plaquette atoms that host the physical qubits. Different logical-qubit arrangements cause the central atom to occupy distinct eigenstates, resulting in photon emission at varying times due to quantum interference. Applying an entanglement-swapping gate to these emitted photons entangles distant qubits irrespective of their specific encoding protocols. This gate serves as a universal photonic interface for clustering processors and linking them with quantum memories and the quantum cloud, ensuring compatibility across different encoding formats.

Ternary Neural Networks (TNNs) have garnered significant interest for their potential to achieve inference speeds and power efficiency orders of magnitude higher than full-precision models. However, encoding ternary values with just three quantization levels necessitates 2 bits, causing conventional TNNs to match the memory usage and speed of standard 2-bit models while offering inferior representational power. Furthermore, a substantial accuracy gap between TNNs and full-precision networks remains, hindering their practical deployment. To address these issues, this study first demonstrates that the computational complexity of ternary inner products can be halved under mild constraints. Second, an implementation-specific ternary quantization algorithm is designed to bridge the performance divide. This approach, named Fast and Accurate Ternary Neural Networks (FATNN), shows in image classification experiments that it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy. Additionally, speedup evaluations across various platforms compared to different precisions provide a robust benchmark for future research.

Denoising serves as a critical component in distant supervision-based named entity recognition (NER). Existing methods primarily rely on instance-level confidence statistics, often overlooking the diverse noise distributions across different datasets and entity types; consequently, they struggle to perform well in high-noise environments. This paper introduces Hypergeometric Learning (HGL), a denoising algorithm for distant supervision NER that simultaneously accounts for noise distribution and instance-level confidence. Specifically, during neural network training, the model naturally treats noise samples within each batch as following a hypergeometric distribution defined by the noise rate. Each instance is then classified as either correct or noisy based on its label confidence from the preceding training step and the noise distribution of the current batch. Experimental results demonstrate that HGL effectively cleans weakly-labeled data obtained through distant supervision, leading to significant enhancements in model performance.

A multidimensional analysis of the structure function ratio $\sigma_{LT'}/\sigma_{0}$ has been conducted for the hard exclusive $\vec{e} p \to e^\prime n \pi^+$ reaction, extending beyond the resonance region. Utilizing beam-spin asymmetry data from the CLAS12 spectrometer at Jefferson Lab, the study employed a 10.6 GeV electron beam incident on a liquid-hydrogen target. The investigation targets the very forward kinematic regime ($t/Q^{2} \ll$ 1), covering a broad range of valence $x_{B}$ values between 0.17 and 0.55, and virtualities $Q^{2}$ spanning from 1.5 to 6 GeV$^{2}$. Comparisons of these results with theoretical frameworks based on Generalized Parton Distributions (GPDs) reveal sensitivity to chiral-odd GPDs and the nucleon's tensor charge. Furthermore, the data were evaluated against an extended Regge formalism for high photon virtualities. The findings indicate that the Regge model offers a superior description at low $Q^{2}$, whereas the GPD model is more suitable at high $Q^{2}$.

Conventional pose transfer algorithms often fail to produce high-quality person images due to issues with unreliable geometric matching and content misalignment. To address this, we introduce Spatial Content Alignment GAN (SCAGAN), a novel framework designed to improve the consistency of garment textures and the fidelity of human details. Our approach first mitigates spatial misalignment by pre-transferring edge content to the target pose. Subsequently, we present a new Content-Style DeBlk module that progressively synthesizes photorealistic images by integrating appearance features from the source image, the target pose heatmap, and the prior edge-domain content. We demonstrate the superiority of our framework through both quantitative and qualitative comparisons against several state-of-the-art methods, with detailed ablation studies confirming the effectiveness of our contributions. The source code is publicly accessible at github.com/rocketappslab/SCA-GAN.

We introduce a new method for identifying a distinctive signal characterized by more than four muons, which arises from pair-produced vector-like leptons decaying into a muon-philic $Z^\prime$ boson. These hypothetical particles offer a promising explanation for anomalies observed in the muon anomalous magnetic moment and $b\to s\ell\ell$ transitions. Current LHC data rule out doublet and singlet vector-like leptons with masses below 1.3 and 1.0 TeV, respectively, assuming a branching ratio of $\mathrm{BR}(E\to Z^\prime \mu) = 1$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the excess of events with more than five leptons can be accounted for by this scenario if the vector-like lepton is a weak singlet with a mass near 400 GeV and $\mathrm{BR}(E\to Z^\prime \mu) = 0.25$. We also outline the potential for future discoveries at the HL-LHC.

Modern data science increasingly involves complex structures like time series, raising the fundamental question of statistical dependence between them. Existing methods often suffer from limitations, including reliance on parametric assumptions, detection of only linear associations, the need for multiple testing, or reduced power in high-dimensional, nonlinear scenarios. Furthermore, estimating the null distribution of test statistics is challenging because standard permutation tests are invalid in this context. This study combines distance correlation (Dcorr) and multiscale graph correlation (MGC) from independence testing with block permutation techniques from time series analysis to overcome these hurdles. The resulting nonparametric procedure is both valid and consistent; it leverages prior work by modeling relationship geometry, identifying the lag of maximum dependence, eliminating the need for multiple testing, and demonstrating superior power in high-dimensional settings with limited samples and nonlinear dynamics. Applied to fMRI data for neural connectivity, the method reveals linear dependencies within the visual and default mode networks, as well as nonlinear relationships in others. This research introduces a primary data analysis tool with open-source code, offering direct benefits to diverse scientific fields.

Evaluating and training fair classifiers presents significant challenges, primarily because relevant fairness metrics rely on both sensitive attributes and labels within the data. Frequently, acquiring large datasets containing this information is infeasible. A common workaround involves training a separate attribute classifier on available sensitive data and subsequently utilizing it within the machine learning pipeline to assess downstream bias. Although this decoupling strategy mitigates issues related to demographic scarcity, it introduces critical questions regarding how to train the attribute classifier and how to leverage it for precise bias estimation. This work addresses these issues through both theoretical analysis and empirical experimentation. We first show experimentally that the test accuracy of an attribute classifier does not necessarily correlate with its efficacy in estimating bias for a downstream model. To investigate this further, we examine an idealized theoretical model to characterize the structure of the optimal classifier. Our findings reveal counter-intuitive insights, suggesting that in specific scenarios, it may be advantageous to distribute the attribute classifier's errors unevenly across different subgroups. Building on this analysis, we propose heuristics for training and employing attribute classifiers in data-scarce environments, demonstrating their effectiveness on both real-world and simulated datasets.

This study introduces a quantum adaptation of the Monty Hall problem, grounded in quantum inferring acausal structures that extend the concept of Bayesian networks. Utilizing the formalism of quantum information theory, these structures represent density operators as quantum generalizations of probability distributions, with conditional relationships between quantum random variables defined by quantum conditional operators. By applying these quantum inferring structures to model a scenario analogous to the classic Monty Hall game, the paper highlights the distinctions between classical and quantum Bayesian reasoning.

Neural radiance fields have recently transformed novel view synthesis by learning directly from sparse inputs. However, rendering with this approach remains computationally expensive because accurately integrating the volume rendering equation necessitates a high density of samples per ray. While prior efforts have primarily accelerated network evaluations at individual sample points—often through caching radiance values into explicit spatial structures—such methods sacrifice model compactness. This paper introduces a novel dual-network architecture that pursues an alternative strategy by learning to minimize the required number of sample points. We achieve this by dividing the network into a sampling component and a shading component, which are trained jointly. Our training protocol utilizes fixed sample positions along each ray and gradually increases sparsity throughout the process, ensuring high-quality results even at low sample counts. Following fine-tuning with the target sample count, the resulting compact neural representation enables real-time rendering. Experimental results show that our method surpasses concurrent compact neural representations in both quality and frame rate, matching the performance of highly efficient hybrid representations. Code and supplementary materials are available at https://thomasneff.github.io/adanerf.

This work reviews the formalism for modeling gravitational wave (GW) polarizations and the coordinate systems that define them. It clarifies the concept of the "polarization angle," distinguishing three conceptually unique definitions, and explains their interrelationships within GW data analysis, detailing the conventions adopted by LIGO and Virgo. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any GW signal can be decomposed into a superposition of elliptical (fully-polarized) states, analyzing the properties and parametrizations of these elementary modes. We evaluate various common parametrizations for fully-polarized modes by computing Jacobians for the associated coordinate transformations, assessing their suitability for different applications, such as unmodeled or semi-modeled signal reconstruction. We highlight that analyses parameterized directly by plus and cross mode amplitudes tend to implicitly favor high signal power and linearly-polarized waves along a fixed direction, making them suboptimal for face-on or face-off sources, which are typically circularly polarized. Finally, we discuss alternative parametrizations with applications ranging from continuous waves and ringdown studies to unmodeled analyses like BayesWave.

Isaak Moiseevich Yaglom established a complete classification of geometric spaces. In this work, the author formalizes Yaglom's methodology to construct a uniform theory of geometric spaces at the analytic level. Among its advantages are its universality and ease of application; notably, the theory is not restricted to specific dimensions. It serves as the foundation for the GeomSpace project (http://sourceforge.net/projects/geomspace/).

By employing non-relativistic Quantum Electrodynamics alongside the Keldysh-Schwinger formalism, we derive Kadanoff-Baym-like equations governing two-body field correlators. These equations describe the non-equilibrium evolution and spectral properties of heavy particle-antiparticle pairs undergoing ultra-soft transitions within a plasma environment where the temperature is significantly lower than the characteristic relative momentum of the pair. The study demonstrates that the dynamical equation for the pair's phase-space distribution—which accounts for recombination and dissociation driven by electric dipole interactions—is consistent with prior open quantum system approaches to bound states in the Coulomb limit of the two-body spectral function.

Reconstructing 3D human pose and shape from RGB images offers a compelling alternative to marker-based motion capture, which is often labor-intensive, costly, and restricted to lab settings. However, monocular vision methods remain hindered by rotational ambiguities and lack the precision required for healthcare applications. Although multi-view data fusion could resolve these issues, existing algorithms have yet to achieve clinically acceptable accuracy. This paper introduces a learnable volumetric aggregation method for reconstructing 3D human pose and shape from calibrated multi-view images. By employing a parametric body representation, our approach is directly applicable to medical contexts. Compared to prior methods, our framework demonstrates superior accuracy and greater potential for real-time performance due to its cost efficiency.

Since their initial introduction and analysis by Andrews, Lewis, and Lovejoy, many congruences concerning partitions with designated summands have been established. This paper explicitly characterizes the count of such partitions where no part is divisible by $2^\ell$, $2$, or $3^\ell$, specifically modulo $2$, $4$, and $3$, thereby significantly broadening existing findings. Throughout the study, we present several applications of these characterizations, including specific congruences and a computationally efficient recurrence relation. Furthermore, we demonstrate a previously unrecognized link between the number of partitions with designated summands and those featuring odd multiplicities.

To effectively support data-heavy applications like immersive digital experiences, optimizing in-device storage and computational resources is essential. This paper introduces a content delivery framework based on location-dependent multi-antenna coded caching, specifically designed for wireless immersive viewing. Initially, a new memory allocation strategy prioritizes content relevant to detected wireless bottlenecks, balancing local and global caching benefits and ensuring that users store unequal portions of location-specific media. Subsequently, during the delivery phase, a novel packet generation method addresses this asymmetric cache distribution; while the packet count per user remains constant, packet sizes scale proportionally with each user's specific cache ratio. Consequently, users receive location-tailored content through joint multicast beamforming and multi-rate modulation, leveraging both global caching and spatial multiplexing advantages. Both mathematical analysis and numerical simulations confirm that this approach yields substantial performance improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods.

We introduce a novel method to demonstrate that two-dimensional crystallization yields a square lattice within finite particle systems. This approach is applied to energy minimizers of configurational energies characterized by two-body short-ranged interactions and three-body angular potentials that prefer bond angles aligned with the square lattice. For every configuration, we construct a bond graph and modify it by grouping successive atoms into chains. This technique, termed stratification, simplifies the crystallization problem into a basic minimization task equivalent to proving the isoperimetric inequality in $\ell^1$ via slicing. Additionally, as a secondary result, we establish a fluctuation estimate for energy minimizers, referred to as the $n^{3/4}$-law.

Within modified gravity frameworks at the linear level, cosmic structure evolution is influenced by alterations to the Poisson equation and the background expansion rate. Previous studies indicate that these factors create a degeneracy that must be addressed to reliably constrain new large-scale forces or deviations from General Relativity. This paper demonstrates that, given current data, assumptions regarding the background expansion exert minimal influence on constraints placed on gravitational modifications. We achieve this by analyzing three scenarios: a standard $\Lambda$CDM universe, a universe with a generalized dark energy equation of state, and a completely model-independent expansion rate. Employing Gaussian Processes, we model deviations from Poisson's equation and, for the general expansion case, the redshift-dependent Hubble rate. We identify a degeneracy between Poisson equation modifications and the background matter density ($\Omega_M$), which can only be resolved by adopting a model-dependent expansion rate. Consequently, we find that current growth rate measurements constrain modifications to the Poisson equation between 10% and 20%, a range that varies depending on the assumed strength of the cosmic expansion model.

Over the last twenty years, Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) has seen significant advancement. ECC provides security levels equivalent to other asymmetric cryptosystems while utilizing much smaller key sizes. This survey offers a comprehensive overview of hardware implementations of ECC. It begins by examining various elliptic curves, point multiplication algorithms, and the underlying finite field operations over binary fields ($F_{2^m}$) and prime fields ($F_p$) utilized in existing literature. Subsequently, the methods, procedural steps, and design considerations for ECC implementation are detailed. These implementations are divided into two primary categories based on technology: Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) and Application Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC). Within these categories, implementations are further distinguished by the type of finite field used to facilitate clearer comparison and presentation. The most recent and efficient architectural structures found in the literature are described in detail to illustrate the approaches within each implementation group. High-speed performance is a critical factor for ECC applications such as network servers. Conversely, smart cards, Wireless Sensor Networks (WSN), and Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) tags necessitate low-cost and lightweight solutions; therefore, implementation methods tailored to these specific applications are explored. Additionally, previous works are classified according to their scalability, flexibility, performance, and cost-effectiveness. Finally, the survey concludes with insights and techniques regarding future research directions that warrant consideration.

Although the concept of employing stellar photometry to monitor the atmosphere for high-energy astrophysics optical experiments appears simple, achieving the high precision required to determine vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) to within 0.01 has been challenging. Wide-field photometry spanning various altitudes enables a rapid, calibration-independent VAOD calculation, while simultaneously serving as a valuable calibration by-product. By leveraging multi-year datasets from the FRAM (F/(Ph)otometric Robotic Atmospheric Monitor) telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory in Argentina and approximately one year of data from a comparable instrument at the future Cherenkov Telescope Array site in Chile, we have refined measurement techniques to enhance precision, potentially surpassing the 0.01 threshold. Crucially, this analysis relied on detailed laboratory assessments of the system's response to light spectrum and intensity, as the standard assumption of CCD detector linearity no longer holds under these specific observational conditions.

With robots gaining greater dexterity and autonomous capabilities, long-horizon task and motion planning has become increasingly critical. A primary difficulty in these scenarios is that initial decisions can render subsequent actions impossible. When search algorithms encounter dead-ends, traditional planners typically employ backtracking, which exhaustively re-evaluates motion-level steps and often leads to inefficient planning, particularly at large search depths. This paper introduces a method to learn backjumping heuristics that use supervised learning models to directly identify the problematic action, thereby guiding the task-level search. Evaluations across two distinct tasks demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances planning efficiency compared to standard backtracking and successfully generalizes to problems featuring novel object counts.

Motivated by recent discrepancies between experimental results and QCD factorisation-based theoretical predictions for various colour-allowed non-leptonic $B$-meson decays, we investigate the possible magnitude of new physics (NP) contributions in $b \to c \bar{u} d(s)$ transitions. Utilizing the most comprehensive effective Hamiltonian for these $b \to c \bar{u} d(s)$ processes, we calculate NP impacts on theoretical forecasts regarding $B$-meson lifetimes and $B$-mixing observables. The established lifetime ratio $\tau (B^+)/\tau (B_d)$ and the experimental limit on the semi-leptonic CP asymmetry $a_{sl}^d$ offer robust, complementary restrictions on specific NP Wilson coefficients.

The Weyl-node-driven, large anomalous Hall effect (AHE) observed in the kagome ferromagnet $\rm Co_{3}Sn_{2}S_{2}$ has prompted predictions that a $\rm Co$ kagome monolayer film could exhibit the quantum AHE, pending experimental confirmation. However, because Weyl nodes are bulk-specific topological singularities, their persistence in reduced-thickness films remains uncertain, and predicting band topology in films with distinct lattice and electronic structures is difficult. This study presents $ab \ initio$ calculations for $\rm Co_{3}Sn_{2}S_{2}$ thin films containing one to three $\rm Co$ layers, terminated by either $\rm Sn$ or $\rm S$, focusing on lattice and magnetic optimization. We find that $\rm Sn$-terminated films maintain a bulk-like ferromagnetic state and preserve the large AHE, which becomes quantified even at the monolayer limit. Conversely, $\rm S$-terminated films display magnetic states dependent on the number of $\rm Co$ layers, leading to significant topological variations, such as a zero-AHE interlayer antiferromagnetic state in the bilayer configuration. These findings encourage further experimental investigation into thin Weyl materials.

We present an operational semantics grounded in rewriting for strictly positive nested higher-order (co)inductive types. This approach incorporates the "limits" of infinite reduction sequences, effectively refining and extending the concept of productivity from term rewriting to environments involving higher-order functions and nested (co)inductive data specifications. Intuitively, this interprets lazy data structures within a higher-order functional language as potentially infinite terms representing their full unfoldings. We establish an approximation theorem asserting that if a term reduces to an arbitrarily large finite approximation of an infinite object within a coinductive type's interpretation, it infinitarily reduces to that infinite object in the limit. Furthermore, we propose a sufficient syntactic correctness criterion via a type system for finite terms annotated with type information. Leveraging the approximation theorem, we demonstrate that every well-typed term possesses a well-defined interpretation under our semantics.

This manuscript introduces a reduced order modeling (ROM) approach for subsurface multi-phase flow, leveraging the recently developed deep residual recurrent neural network (DR-RNN) [1]. As a physics-informed architecture for dynamical systems, the DR-RNN is modeled after iterative line search updates, stacking a fixed number of layers to minimize the residual of the governing physical equations. We integrate DR-RNN with proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and the discrete empirical interpolation method (DEIM) to significantly lower the computational cost of high-fidelity simulations. Specifically, POD generates an optimal set of reduced basis functions, while DEIM approximates nonlinear terms without dependency on the full-order model size. Validation is performed on two uncertainty quantification scenarios involving Monte-Carlo simulations of subsurface flow with random permeability fields. The results confirm that the DR-RNN coupled with POD-DEIM yields an accurate and stable reduced model at a fixed computational budget substantially lower than that required by standard POD-Galerkin approaches combined with DEIM for nonlinear dynamical systems.

The Vertex Locator (VELO), a silicon microstrip detector encircling the proton-proton interaction zone within the LHCb experiment, has undergone a performance review covering its initial years of physics operations. Operating in a vacuum with bi-phase CO2 cooling, the system positions its sensors just 7 mm from the LHC beam during data collection. This overview details the stability and performance of these operational characteristics, provides specifics on the material budget, and outlines the FPGA-based algorithms for timing calibration and data processing, effectively characterizing the system's overall performance. The sensors achieve a signal-to-noise ratio of roughly 20 and a best hit resolution of 4 microns at optimal track angles. In standard 2011 operating conditions, typical detector occupancy for minimum bias events was approximately 0.5%, with less than 1% of strips faulty. Due to the detector's close proximity to the beam, radiation damage has caused space-charge sign inversion in the inner regions of the n+-on-n sensors. Key performance metrics influencing the experiment's physics sensitivity are presented, including a track finding efficiency typically exceeding 98% and module alignment precision of 1 micron in the plane transverse to the beam. Furthermore, the system achieves a primary vertex resolution of 13 microns transversely and 71 microns along the beam axis for vertices containing 25 tracks, while resolving impact parameters of under 35 microns for particles with transverse momentum greater than 1 GeV/c.

Current dialogue benchmarks, including MultiWOZ 2.1 and Taskmaster-1, represent some of the most difficult challenges for existing models and are consequently standard for evaluating system performance. However, we pinpoint several critical flaws in these datasets, such as their reliance on independent history, heavy dependence on knowledge bases, and unclear system responses. Ultimately, we propose essential requirements for future datasets that we believe would better support the development of conversational artificial intelligence.

We investigate and introduce methods for mapping messages to constant-weight codewords by utilizing variable-length prefixes. We present formulas that can be computed in polynomial time to estimate the average number of redundant bits required by these schemes. Beyond providing exact formulas, we conduct an asymptotic analysis, showing that our approach employs $\frac12 \log n+O(1)$ redundant bits to encode messages into words of length $n$ with a weight of $(n/2)+{\sf q}$, where ${\sf q}$ remains constant.

We derive the fundamental non-relativistic string theory solutions for the Neveu-Schwarz (NS) brane by employing longitudinal T-duality as a method for generating solutions. By expanding the NS background fields into a full supergravity multiplet, we confirm that every solution obtained possesses half-supersymmetry. Both perturbative solutions identified represent the spacetime geometry exterior to a string-like entity; consequently, we label these non-Lorentzian backgrounds as the winding string and unwound string solutions. While the winding string belongs to the on-shell spectrum of non-relativistic string theory, the unwound string is valid only off-shell, serving as the mediator for instantaneous gravitational forces. From the perspective of nine dimensions, the winding string is sourced by a non-relativistic massive particle, whereas the unwound string is sourced by a massless Galilean particle with zero colour and spin. We detail how these two string configurations integrate into a discrete lightcone quantization framework of string theory. Additionally, we briefly examine the basic NS five-brane and Kaluza-Klein monopole solutions, demonstrating that both exhibit half-supersymmetry.

We demonstrate that for a generic measure-preserving action of a countable amenable group $G$, the scaling entropy cannot be dominated by any prescribed growth rate. Consequently, no topological action of $G$ exists where the collection of ergodic invariant measures is identical to the set of all ergodic measure-preserving $G$-systems with zero entropy. Furthermore, we establish that a generic action of a residually finite amenable group possesses scaling entropy that cannot be bounded from below by an arbitrary sequence. Finally, we present an example of an amenable group for which every free measure-preserving action admits such a lower bound.

Although self-supervised learning (SSL) has demonstrated empirical success, the specific representation traits responsible for high downstream performance remain poorly understood. This study defines the ideal properties SSL representations must possess. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions ensuring that any task invariant to specific data augmentations achieves perfect accuracy when evaluated with probes (such as linear or MLP models) trained on these representations. These findings create a unified conceptual framework to enhance existing SSL techniques and inspire new ones. For contrastive learning, the framework recommends meaningful yet straightforward upgrades, such as employing asymmetric projection heads. In the realm of non-contrastive learning, we leverage the framework to formulate a novel, simple objective. Consequently, our proposed SSL algorithms surpass baseline methods on standard benchmarks, notably achieving superior results with SwAV+multicrops on ImageNet linear probing.

This study investigates two recent contextualized word embedding techniques, ELMo and BERT, within the framework of open-domain argument search. We demonstrate, for the first time, how to harness these embeddings to classify and cluster arguments based on topic, yielding impressive performance across various datasets.
