In argument classification, we achieve state-of-the-art improvements on the UKP Sentential Argument Mining Corpus by 20.8 percentage points and on the IBM Debater - Evidence Sentences dataset by 7.4 percentage points. Furthermore, addressing the underexplored task of argument clustering, we introduce a pre-training step that enhances results by 7.8 percentage points over strong baselines on a new dataset and by 12.3 percentage points on the Argument Facet Similarity (AFS) Corpus.

The Fermilab Muon g-2 collaboration has announced a new measurement of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, revealing a $4.2\sigma$ deviation from the most accurate Standard Model predictions. Under the hypothesis that this discrepancy signals new physics, we examine a straightforward supersymmetric framework that simultaneously offers a dark matter solution within a previously uncharted region of parameter space. This specific region supports a Bino-like dark matter candidate consistent with existing direct detection limits for small to moderate Higgsino mass parameter values ($|\mu|$). Consequently, this scenario predicts the presence of light additional Higgs bosons and Higgsinos accessible to the high-luminosity LHC and future colliders. We present benchmark scenarios designed to be probed by the next generation of direct dark matter searches and LHC experiments.

A longstanding unresolved issue concerns whether tribocharging—the creation of electric charges on sand grains through particle collisions during electrification—significantly influences sand transport rates on Mars. Although earlier wind tunnel experiments and numerical simulations examined how external electric fields alter particle trajectories, the specific impact of sand electrification remained unclear. In this study, wind tunnel simulations conducted at an air pressure of 20 mbar demonstrate that surface charges on particles can substantially lower the minimum threshold wind shear velocity ($u^*_{ft}$) required to initiate sand transport. Our experiments utilized various samples, including glass beads as a model system and a Martian soil analog, alongside different triboelectrification scenarios. Additionally, we introduce a model grounded in inhomogeneously distributed surface charges to account for the observed $u^*_{ft}$ values. These findings suggest that on Mars, once sand transport ceases because wind shear velocity drops below the threshold for sustained movement, it can be more readily restarted than previously believed.

Single-file diffusion represents a framework for studying strongly correlated classical stochastic many-body dynamics, finding extensive use in soft condensed matter and biophysics. Yet, exact solutions for these systems remain scarce, typically restricted to the most basic cases. This work introduces an algorithm to compute the non-Markovian time-dependent conditional probability density function of a tagged particle within a single-file system of $N$ particles diffusing under a confining external potential. The method relies on an eigenexpansion of the full interacting many-body problem derived via the coordinate Bethe ansatz. Although formally exact, the Bethe eigenspectrum requires generating and evaluating permutations, a process that becomes computationally infeasible as the number of particles $N$ increases. By leveraging the exchange symmetries between particles located to the left and right of the tagged particle, we demonstrate that the algorithm's complexity can be reduced from the worst-case $\mathcal{O}(N!)$ to $\mathcal{O}(N)$. We provide C++ code implementing this algorithm to calculate the non-Markovian probability density function. The software includes ready-to-use solutions for simple model potentials, covering single-file diffusion in flat, tilted, and parabolic boxes. Notably, the program supports arbitrary external potentials, provided the user can supply the corresponding single-particle eigenspectra.

This call for participation outlines four benchmark tests designed to validate and compare numerical schemes for simulating single-phase flow in fractured porous media. By extending the two-dimensional benchmark suite introduced by Flemisch et al. in 2018, this work incorporates three-dimensional problems and includes transport simulations to evaluate flow discretization methods. Through this publication, we invite researchers to contribute by submitting results from their applied discretization methods for these test cases.

This study serves as the second installment in a research series initiated by [66] and continued by [67], dedicated to interpreting gravitational phenomena through a consistent stochastic fractal-based (intrinsically conformal) path-integral framework. Utilizing the Wiener stochastic process, we investigate the Brownian motion of fractal functions on a closed Riemannian manifold featuring dynamical geometry driven by Ricci flow. Our findings demonstrate that the Wiener measure naturally yields the Einstein-Hilbert action and the path-integral formulation of scalar quantum field theory at the first local approximation, suggesting a more fundamental basis for quantum field theory in the presence of gravity. Crucially, we show that the emergence of the Einstein-Hilbert action is independent of matter field interactions, arising instead as a purely entropic consequence of the Ricci flow's nature. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the cosmological constant expressed through the Ricci flow and Hamilton's theorem for 3-manifolds. We then examine the cosmological properties of FLRW solutions within the $\Lambda$CDM model using these derived Ricci flow equations, while also highlighting the correlation between our formulation and the entropic dimensions of gravity. Ultimately, we provide theoretical evidence supporting the assertion that the second law of thermodynamics is the fundamental origin of gravity, surpassing it in significance.

This paper introduces a novel concept termed Krasovskii's passivity and establishes a sufficient condition for a system to satisfy this property. Leveraging this condition, we examine various classes of port-Hamiltonian and gradient systems that exhibit Krasovskii's passivity. Furthermore, we present a new interconnection-based control strategy grounded in this passivity notion. This proposed technique is applicable even when constructing a standard passivity-based controller is unclear, as illustrated through examples involving a Boost converter and a parallel RLC circuit.

We present flat automata, a streamlined representation of standard finite automata, designed for the automated creation of tokenizers. This simplified format facilitates the construction, combination, and output of automata. By leveraging border functions, flat automata offer greater compactness than traditional automata when transitions involve character intervals, while also simplifying standard automata algorithms. We detail standard algorithms for building tokenizers using regular operations, determinization, and minimization, providing proofs of their correctness. These algorithms efficiently handle character intervals without increasing complexity compared to single-character processing. Additionally, deterministic automata can be easily converted into C++ code. All procedures have been implemented in C++ and are publicly accessible, having been successfully applied in both practical software and educational settings.

The Jarlskog invariant, which governs the magnitude of intrinsic CP violation in neutrino oscillation appearance experiments, undergoes modification due to Wolfenstein matter effects when neutrinos propagate through matter. This paper presents an exact factorization of the Jarlskog invariant in matter, expressing it as the product of the vacuum Jarlskog invariant and two distinct matter resonance factors that independently regulate matter effects for solar and atmospheric resonances. We compare the positions of the minima of these factorizing resonance factors with the precisely defined locations of the solar and atmospheric resonances; while they are not identical, the fractional differences are found to be less than 0.1%. Furthermore, we elucidate why symmetry polynomials involving the square of neutrino eigenmasses in matter, such as the inverse square of the Jarlskog invariant in matter, can be formulated as polynomials of the matter potential.

A collection of four distinct, non-zero polynomials in $\mathbb{Z}[i][X]$, denoted as $\{a, b, c, d\}$, constitutes a Diophantine $D(4)$-quadruple if the sum of the product of any two distinct elements and 4 yields a perfect square within $\mathbb{Z}[i][X]$. This paper establishes that every such $D(4)$-quadruple in $\mathbb{Z}[i][X]$ is regular, which is equivalent to demonstrating that the relation $(a+b-c-d)^2 = (ab+4)(cd+4)$ holds true for all $D(4)$-quadruples in this domain.

This study examines two models of random cones in high-dimensional spaces alongside their duals: the Donoho-Tanner cone, $D_{n,d}$, which consists of the positive hull of $n$ independent $d$-dimensional Gaussian vectors, and the Cover-Efron cone, $C_{n,d}$, defined similarly but conditioned on the cone not spanning the entire space. We analyze expectations of various combinatorial and geometric functionals for these structures, demonstrating that they obey limit theorems when $d$ and $n$ grow in a coordinated manner. These results encompass large deviation principles and both central and non-central limit theorems regarding the expected counts of $k$-faces and $k$-th conic intrinsic volumes, where $n$, $d$, and potentially $k$ all approach infinity simultaneously. Additionally, we establish the precise asymptotic behavior of the expected statistical dimension for both cone models, revealing a distinct high-dimensional phase transition. Finally, we apply these findings to derive limit theorems concerning the number of $k$-faces in high-dimensional polytopes formed by random Gale diagrams.

Recent developments in the online fashion sector have spurred a search for innovative methods to boost the shopping experience through enhanced personalization. A key challenge in this area is accurately predicting the correct item size, which is the focus of this study. Previous research in this domain has primarily relied on explicit fitment feedback or addressed only isolated aspects, such as specific brands or categories. More recent efforts have introduced advanced models—either content-based or sequence-based—that better capture item attributes or the customer's browsing journey. However, these approaches have limitations: sequence-based models struggle with unseen items, while content-based models fail when encountering new users.

To bridge these gaps, we introduce PreSizE, a new deep learning framework leveraging Transformers for precise size prediction. PreSizE integrates both content-based factors, like brand and category, and the buyer's purchase history to determine size preferences. Through extensive experiments on a large-scale e-commerce dataset, we show that PreSizE outperforms previous state-of-the-art baselines. By encoding item attributes, it effectively manages cold-start scenarios involving unseen items or users with limited purchase history. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that integrating PreSizE's size predictions into an existing production recommender system provides highly effective features and significantly enhances recommendation quality.

In recent years, estimating the 6D pose of object instances using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) has garnered significant attention. Existing literature is generally categorized into two approaches based on the use of intermediate cues: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter, CNNs regress intermediate features like 3D coordinates, semantic keypoints, or virtual control points in the first stage, with object pose subsequently determined through correspondence constraints derived from these cues. This paper focuses on refining the postprocessing stage of a two-stage pipeline by integrating projection grouping and correspondence learning to estimate poses in challenging scenarios. First, a local patch-based method predicts projection heatmaps representing the confidence distribution of 3D bounding box corners. A proposed projection grouping module then eliminates redundant local maxima across heatmap layers. Rather than directly applying the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) algorithm to 2D-3D correspondences, multiple correspondence hypotheses are sampled from local maxima and their neighborhoods, then ranked by a correspondence-evaluation network. Finally, high-confidence correspondences are selected to determine the object's pose. Extensive experiments across three public datasets show that the proposed framework surpasses several state-of-the-art methods.

Variational Bayes (VB) is a widely used method for Bayesian inference in statistical modeling. Recently, various VB algorithms have been developed to address intractable likelihoods, particularly in contexts like approximate Bayesian computation. This paper introduces several unbiased estimators derived from multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) to calculate the gradient of the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the posterior and variational distributions, specifically when the likelihood is intractable but admits an unbiased estimator. Unlike existing literature, where VB algorithms typically yield biased gradient estimators, our approach offers an unbiased alternative. Furthermore, we integrate randomized quasi-Monte Carlo (RQMC) sampling into these MLMC-based estimators, leveraging its known advantage in accelerating numerical integration convergence; theoretical guarantees for RQMC are also established within this framework. Numerical experiments demonstrate that incorporating RQMC significantly accelerates the VB algorithm and yields superior parameter estimates compared to several existing competitors.

Recent studies have investigated Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning (PETL), a technique that adapts pre-trained Vision Transformers (ViT) by updating a minimal subset of parameters to enhance storage efficiency. Existing PETL approaches demonstrate that tuning merely 0.5% of parameters can match or exceed the performance of full fine-tuning on downstream tasks. This paper seeks to further optimize PETL efficiency to address stringent storage constraints in practical applications. We introduce a tensorization-decomposition framework that converts ViT weights into a single 3D tensor and decomposes their updates into lightweight factors. During fine-tuning, only these factors are stored and updated, a method we term Factor-Tuning (FacT). Evaluated on the VTAB-1K benchmark, FacT achieves performance comparable to NOAH, the current state-of-the-art PETL method, while offering five times greater parameter efficiency. Additionally, we present a miniature variant requiring only 8K trainable parameters (0.01% of the ViT), which surpasses full fine-tuning and other PETL techniques like VPT and BitFit. In few-shot scenarios, FacT outperforms all PETL baselines using the fewest parameters, highlighting its robustness in low-data environments.

Simulations of three-dimensional cardiovascular fluid dynamics are often computationally intensive because they require calculating multiple cardiac cycles to achieve a periodic solution, and no standardized approach currently exists to identify when this state is reached. This study proposes utilizing an asymptotic error measure, based on lumped-parameter modeling, to quantify the deviation between simulation results and their ideal periodic state. Additionally, we demonstrate that selecting appropriate initial conditions is vital for minimizing computational time and present an automated framework that generates these conditions using a one-dimensional blood flow model. We validated our initialization strategy using six patient-specific models from the Vascular Model Repository. Our results show that this protocol achieves periodic convergence within one or two cardiac cycles, substantially lowering computational costs compared to conventional methods. All tools developed for this research are available on the open-source SimVascular platform, and our findings suggest that automatically generated initial conditions can markedly reduce computation times in cardiovascular fluid dynamics simulations.

A flow view represents a measurable conjugacy mapping a substitution or S-adic subshift to an exchange of infinitely many intervals (IIET) within [0,1]. This representation is constructed by transferring the natural refining sequence of partitions from the sequence space to [0,1] via a canonical addressing scheme, a fixed dual substitution, and a shift-invariant probability measure. In this flow view, sequences are depicted horizontally at a vertical level determined by the conjugacy. Because the IIET can be closely approximated by exchanges involving a finite number of intervals, both numerical and graphical analysis methods become feasible. The graphs of these IIETs exhibit self-similarity patterns, with a specific instance of this property being proven. The spectral characteristics of the conjugacy itself are of significant interest, and to illustrate its utility, spectral findings for constant-length substitutions are provided.

This paper introduces a method for consistently quantizing conformal gravity that manages conformal symmetry in a highly controlled manner. Initially, we examine local conformal symmetry within gravitational interactions, treating it as a specific instance of a general gauge theory. We also review early attempts to quantize conformal gravity and apply the covariant quantization framework developed by Faddeev and Popov. Furthermore, the study addresses key challenges, including the necessity of conformal gauge-fixing, complications arising from conformal third ghosts, and discontinuities inherent to conformal gravity. Finally, we clarify the original ad hoc computational techniques that are valid at the first quantum loop level in this theory.

The recent advancement of atomic-precision-advanced-manufacturing (APAM) enables the control of phosphorous doping in silicon at the atomic scale using scanning tunneling microscopy (STM). This capability allows for the precise tailoring of electronic devices, opening new avenues for Si electronics research. Key challenges in these applications involve identifying the exact locations of current flow and detecting leakage currents within or near APAM structures. Consequently, mapping and detecting current flow serves as a vital diagnostic method for ensuring reliability in digital-enhanced applications. In this study, we utilized nitrogen-vacancy (NV) wide-field magnetic imaging to detect stray magnetic fields generated by surface current densities in an APAM test device, achieving micron-level resolution across a millimeter-scale field of view. The process involved integrating a diamond containing a surface NV ensemble with the device, which consisted of two parallel millimeter-sized ribbons. Using a custom-built NV wide-field microscope, we mapped the magnetic fields produced by direct current injected into the APAM device. These two-dimensional magnetic field maps were then used to reconstruct surface current density, providing insights into current pathways, device failures such as choke points that impede flow, and current leakages extending beyond the P-doped regions defined by the APAM process. Analysis of the reconstructed current density map indicated a projected sensitivity of approximately 0.03 A/m, corresponding to a minimum detectable current of roughly 6 μA within a 200 μm-wide APAM ribbon. These findings highlight the potential of NV wide-field magnetometry for failure analysis in APAM materials and suggest its applicability to investigating other advanced microelectronic devices.

This article introduces a multi-simulation model designed to evaluate the performance of all Smart Grid perspectives as outlined in the IEEE P2030 standard. As a foundational step, a new Information Technology (IT) and communication multi-simulator was built based on the High Level Architecture (HLA) framework. To demonstrate its utility, the authors present a case study involving distribution network operations, utilizing real-world topological configurations and realistic communication traffic compliant with IEC 61850 standards. This multi-simulator enables the quantification of communication delays and system reliability when aggregating all traffic on a low-capacity Digital Mobile Radio (DMR) link during an LTE network failure. The study shows that such a tool facilitates the automated experimentation of new Smart Grid mechanisms and verifies their effects across all relevant perspectives. Most significantly, multi-simulation offers the ability to preemptively identify issues before implementing Smart Grid modifications or upgrades, thereby potentially lowering utility costs.

Compared to general event extraction, the domain of event extraction within commodity news remains under-explored; however, it holds significant value for various applications, including the analysis of event chains and the identification of inter-event relationships, which ultimately aid in forecasting commodity prices. Because events found in commodity news possess distinct characteristics compared to generic events, they present unique challenges for existing extraction methods. This study introduces an effective approach utilizing Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) combined with a pruned dependency parse tree, referred to as a contextual sub-tree, to enhance event extraction in this specific domain. The model is trained on feature embeddings derived from ComBERT, a BERT-based masked language model that underwent domain-adaptive pre-training on a corpus of commodity news. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of this proposed solution, which surpasses existing methods with F1 scores reaching up to 0.90. Additionally, our pre-trained language model achieves a 23% improvement over GloVe and a 7% improvement over BERT and RoBERTa in argument role classification. To ensure reproducibility, the code and trained models have been made publicly available.

This paper introduces the initial version of a system designed for the interactive creation of theatre play scripts. Built upon a standard GPT-2 model with specific modifications to address practical challenges, the system also outlines several other encountered issues reserved for future resolution. This prototype was successfully utilized to generate a script scheduled for its premiere in February 2021.

We establish tight bounds connecting the primal and dual dimensions of various combinatorial measures, including pseudo-dimension and fat-shattering dimension, specifically for multi-valued function classes. These dimensions are fundamental to learning theory. Our approach begins by reviewing established (folklore) results that constrain dual dimensions based on their primal counterparts, followed by the presentation of (almost) matching lower bounds. Notably, we extend a classic bound by Assouad (1983)—which links the primal and dual VC-dimensions of binary function classes—to appropriately cover multi-valued function classes.

We introduce a mechanism for defining and analyzing the syntax of datatypes, programming languages, and logical systems. Specifically, we investigate a concept of "signature" used to describe syntactic structures. Aligned with the principles of Initial Semantics, we define the "syntax generated by a signature" as the initial object within an appropriate category of models, provided such an object exists. Within our framework, the automatic generation of syntax for a given signature is not guaranteed; however, we utilize the concept of a "presentation of a signature" to characterize a broad class of signatures that successfully generate syntax. Our "presentable" signatures encompass traditional algebraic signatures (including those for languages with variable binding, like the pure lambda calculus) and expand to cover various other important syntactic examples. A central advantage of our definitions for signatures, syntax, and presentations is their high degree of compositionality, allowing complex instances to be constructed by combining simpler ones. Furthermore, the Initial Semantics approach ensures that, in addition to the standard algebra of terms, the framework yields well-behaved substitution rules along with the associated induction and recursion principles. This work extends ideas from a prior effort by Hirschowitz-Maggesi, which was itself inspired by earlier contributions from Ghani-Uustalu-Hamana and Matthes-Uustalu. The primary results of this paper have been verified using the UniMath system.

The relativistic energy shifts in hydrogenlike ions and muonic hydrogen caused by hadronic vacuum polarization are assessed using a semiempirical approach. This method employs a parametric hadronic polarization function, derived from experimental data on $e^-e^+$ annihilation into hadrons, to construct an effective relativistic Uehling potential. Energy corrections for low-lying states are computed using analytical Dirac-Coulomb wave functions alongside bound wave functions that incorporate finite nuclear size effects. The study yields closed-form expressions for both the hadronic Uehling potential of an extended nucleus and the relativistic energy shift for a point-like nucleus, subsequently comparing these findings with established analytic formulas from non-relativistic theory.

A Self-Organizing Map (SOM) is a competitive artificial neural network that maps high-dimensional input data from training samples into a low-dimensional space while maintaining topological relationships. This capability makes SOMs highly effective for organizing and visualizing complex datasets, leading to their widespread adoption across various disciplines. Despite their extensive use, SOMs face a significant challenge due to their inherent randomness; training on identical samples with the same parameters can yield different patterns each time. This variability raises usability concerns among practitioners and limits broader adoption. Addressing this issue, we introduce a deterministic approach to complement the standard SOM. Theoretical design and experimental results using satellite cloud data confirm that this proposed method effectively organizes and simplifies data with high efficiency.

This study examines the Schur algebra's influence on the Lie algebras of derivations within free Lie algebras and the resulting operad structures. We further demonstrate that the Lie algebra of derivations is generated by quadratic derivations and the Schur operad's action. Additionally, applications to specific subgroups of the automorphism group of a finitely generated free group are provided.

Kerr nonlinearity within nanophotonic cavities serves as a flexible foundation for investigating fundamental physics and creating advanced photonic technologies, enabled by precise dispersion management and substantial field enhancement in nanoscale architectures. While dispersion and pump engineering are established methods, directly manipulating Kerr nonlinearity offers a route to unlock the peak performance and functionality of photonic systems. This study presents the in situ regulation of integrated Kerr nonlinearity by exploiting its interaction with cascaded Pockels nonlinear processes. We successfully tune the nonlinearity across a 10 dB dynamic range without altering the underlying photonic structures. A nonlinear Fano resonance is observed, distinct from conventional linear transmission, which verifies quantum interference between competing optical nonlinear pathways. In addition to enhancing nonlinearity, we demonstrate the ability to suppress intrinsic material nonlinearity. Furthermore, utilizing this tunable nonlinearity allows for the control of single-photon generation spectral brightness and the coincidence-to-accidental ratio. These findings establish a pathway toward comprehensive nanoscale control of optical nonlinear processes at the quantum level.

We explore topological lasers by integrating nonlinear, non-Hermitian, and topological lattice systems through quench dynamics initiated at a single site. Specifically, we examine a topological laser within the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model featuring two edge states and a second-order topological laser in a breathing Kagome lattice characterized by three corner states. Upon stimulating any single site, all sites associated with the topological edge or corner states subsequently emit stable laser light after a delay, contingent upon the density of states, despite the absence of wave propagation from the stimulated location. Notably, the spatial profile of these topological states becomes observable through lasing intensity measurements. This phenomenon arises from the interplay between linear non-Hermitian loss and nonlinear non-Hermitian gain terms in the presence of topological edge or corner states.

K. S. S. Nambooripad introduced normal categories to provide a comprehensive description of regular semigroup structures. This paper examines the ideal categories of the regular semigroup $OX_n$, consisting of non-invertible order-preserving transformations on a finite chain $X_n=\{1\leq 2\leq \cdots \leq n \}$, specifically identifying which are normal categories. Furthermore, it demonstrates that the principal left ideal category of $OX_n$ corresponds to the power set category $P_o(X_n)$ of $OX_n$, while the principal right ideal category aligns with the $\prod_o(X_n)$ category of ordered partitions of $X_n$. Additionally, the cone semigroup $T\mathscr L(OX_n)$ is described, and its isomorphism to $OX_n$ is proven.

We introduce a straightforward extension to the GloVe representation learning framework that starts with general-purpose embeddings and refines them using data from a specific domain. Our findings demonstrate that these adapted representations facilitate faster convergence and yield superior performance across multiple tasks.

We present a method for continuously measuring electric field frequency utilizing the far-off-resonant AC Stark effect within a Rydberg atomic vapor cell. In this setup, a robust far-off-resonant local oscillator (LO) field induces a gain shift that moves the Rydberg energy level into a high-sensitivity regime. A weak incident signal field, differing from the LO by a few hundred kHz, mixes with the LO within the Rydberg system to produce an intermediate frequency (IF) signal, which is detected via Rydberg electromagnetically induced transparency (Rydberg-EIT) spectroscopy. Unlike resonant EIT-AT spectra, our approach enables electric field measurements across the 2 GHz to 5 GHz range using a single Rydberg state. The system achieves a minimum detectable field strength of 2.31 $\mu$V/cm and maintains a linear dynamic range exceeding 65 dB. This sensitivity is comparable to that of a resonant microwave-dressed Rydberg heterodyne receiver operating on the same platform, which reaches 1.45 $\mu$V/cm. Furthermore, the system exhibits inherent polarization selectivity. Our technique offers high sensitivity for electric field measurements and is adaptable for arbitrary frequency detection.

This study aims to define the expansion of $r$-hyperideals and generalize this notion to $\phi$-$\delta$-$r$-hyperideals. Let $\Re$ be a commutative Krasner hyperring with a nonzero identity. For a given expansion $\delta$ of hyperideals, a proper hyperideal $N$ of $\Re$ is termed a $\delta$-$r$-hyperideal if $a \cdot b \in N$ and $ann(a)=0$ imply $b \in \delta(N)$ for all $a, b \in \Re$. Consequently, given an expansion $\delta$ and a hyperideal reduction $\phi$, a proper hyperideal $N$ of $\Re$ is defined as a $\phi$-$\delta$-$r$-hyperideal if $a \cdot b \in N - \phi(N)$ with $ann(a)=0$ implies $b \in \delta(N)$ for all $a, b \in \Re$. We examine several properties of these structures and provide illustrative examples.

Topological phases in quantum materials are identified by topological invariants, which capture the global geometric features of quantum wave functions and remain unaffected by local disturbances. We introduce a strategy for measuring these invariants on quantum computers, demonstrating that it can be seamlessly combined with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). This integration allows for the characterization of topological properties in generic quantum many-body states using existing quantum hardware. We validate the method's robustness by measuring invariants across both non-interacting and interacting models, successfully mapping interacting quantum phase diagrams on quantum simulators and IBM quantum processors.

Machine learning image classifiers are vulnerable to adversarial attacks and corruption perturbations, where adding imperceptible noise can cause severe misclassifications. Since $L_p$-norms do not align well with human perception of similarity, optimal transport-based metrics such as the Wasserstein distance are increasingly adopted in adversarial robustness research. Robustness verification using the Wasserstein metric involves either certifying the absence of adversarial examples or demonstrating their presence via attacks. This work introduces a framework, building on Levine and Feizi's research, that adapts existing certification methods for convex polytopes or $L_1$-balls to the Wasserstein threat model; the completeness of this certification depends on the chosen geometric shape. Furthermore, we propose a novel Wasserstein adversarial attack utilizing projected gradient descent, which offers a substantially lower computational cost than current attack methodologies.

For real numbers $q$ satisfying $|q| < 1$, we examine the universal enveloping $C^*$-algebra of the $*$-algebra defined by $q$-canonical commutation relations ($q$-CCR). This algebra is generated by elements $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ obeying the relations $a_i^* a_j = \delta_{ij} 1 + q a_j a_i^*$. It possesses a distinguished representation known as the Fock representation, $\pi_F$, which is conjectured to be faithful. We denote the image of the universal enveloping $C^*$-algebra of $q$-CCR under this Fock representation as $\beth_q$. While prior literature has investigated whether a $C^*$-isomorphism exists between $\beth_q$ and $\beth_0$, proving it only for $|q| < 0.44$, this article demonstrates that $\beth_q \simeq \beth_0$ holds for the entire range $|q| < 1$.

This paper introduces Trust-ya, a cooperative multi-player betting game designed to model specific aspects of status dynamics within human groups. The game aims to provoke status-driven leader-follower interactions, allowing researchers to observe and influence social hierarchies. Modeled after a Bach/Stravinsky deference game, each participant can either invest in another player or wait to receive investment. Those who secure investment funds can gamble against a central pool for potential payoffs, which are then partially or fully redistributed to the investors; notably, larger gambles by those with more investors yield higher returns. Consequently, players naturally cluster around a "leader" who gambles but retains enough winnings to maintain investor loyalty, even though the leader is incentivized to maximize personal gain. Although the game is anonymous, players may purchase "status symbols" that hold no intrinsic game value but function as a communication tool. This study outlines the game's design, connects it to social psychology's status theories, and presents results from both simulations and human experiments demonstrating its utility in analyzing status processes and group dynamics.

This research examines the query complexity of quantum learning scenarios where oracles constitute a group $G$ of unitary matrices. In the most basic scenario of identifying the oracle, we derive a description of the optimal success probability for a $t$-query quantum algorithm using group characters. As an application, we demonstrate that identifying a random permutation in $S_n$ necessitates $\Omega(n)$ queries. More broadly, considering a fixed subgroup $H$ of the oracle group $G$, the task involves determining the coset of $H$ to which an oracle, sampled uniformly from $G$, belongs. We term this "coset identification," a problem that encompasses several established quantum algorithms such as Bernstein-Vazirani, the van Dam problem, and finite field polynomial interpolation. We present character-theoretic formulas for the optimal success probability attainable by a $t$-query algorithm for this task. One specific application utilizes the Heisenberg group to define a family of problems dependent on $n$, which demand $n+1$ classical queries but can be solved with just 1 quantum query.

The features of a proof-theoretic representation of a specific logic depend on various factors, including the selected proof formalism, the structure of logical rules and sequents, the fundamental concept of consequence, the expressive power of its linguistic tools, and the surrounding logical framework. It is established that standard one-dimensional logics, defined by non-deterministic logical matrices, can be axiomatized by analytic and potentially finite proof systems provided they meet a threshold of sufficient expressiveness. This paper presents a method for constructing a two-dimensional logical matrix (B-matrix) by combining two (potentially partial) non-deterministic matrices. We demonstrate that this combination can yield B-matrices with sufficient expressiveness, even when the individual input matrices lack this property in isolation. Consequently, we show that one-dimensional logics which are not finitely axiomatizable can become finitely axiomatizable within a two-dimensional context, effectively gaining finite axiomatizability through the addition of an extra dimension. We illustrate this construction using the well-known logic of formal inconsistency, mCi. First, we prove that mCi cannot be finitely axiomatized by a one-dimensional (generalized) Hilbert-style system. Subsequently, leveraging a known 5-valued non-deterministic matrix for mCi, we combine it with another appropriately selected matrix to create a B-matrix. This resulting B-matrix is axiomatized by a two-dimensional Hilbert-style system that is both finite and analytic.

High-fidelity replicas of artworks offer museums enhanced means to safeguard and disseminate cultural heritage. This study introduces an integrated system capable of capturing a painting's color, surface topography, and gloss, with the latter representing a primary innovation. By extending a 3D imaging setup that employs fringe-encoded stereo technology, the system captures spatially varying gloss through specular reflectance polarization. Gloss is quantified by sampling specular reflections near Brewster's angle, where light is effectively polarized, allowing separation from unpolarized diffuse reflectance. Measurements taken off-center are calibrated against central readings, while off-specular measurements resulting from local surface normal variations are masked using height maps and subsequently corrected; shadowed areas caused by 3D relief are handled in a similar manner. Each capture covers approximately 180x90mm at a resolution of 25x25 microns. Overlapping color regions are registered to stitch together aligned tiles of color, height, and gloss, which then serve as inputs for a 3D printer. The system's effectiveness and efficiency were verified by reproducing two paintings; one was scanned four times with consecutive 90-degree rotations to assess how geometric configuration affects gloss measurement. Experimental outcomes indicate that the method is fast enough for practical use, with results suitable for physical reproduction and other applications requiring first-order appearance estimates. Extending appearance scanning with gloss measurements adds significant practical value and perceptual realism to reproductions that already include color and topography data.

The gradient noise inherent in Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is widely recognized as a fundamental factor influencing its characteristics, such as escaping local minima and providing regularization. Previous studies have highlighted that the covariance of SGD error arising from minibatching is pivotal in governing these regularization and escape properties. However, the extent to which the error distribution itself shapes the algorithm's behavior remains underexplored. Building on emerging research in this domain, we demonstrate universality results by proving that noise classes sharing the same mean and covariance structure as minibatching SGD exhibit comparable properties. Our primary focus is the Multiplicative Stochastic Gradient Descent (M-SGD) algorithm introduced by Wu et al., which accommodates a broader class of noise than standard minibatching SGD. We derive nonasymptotic bounds for M-SGD, primarily relative to the Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) associated with minibatching SGD. Furthermore, we show that the M-SGD error approximates a scaled Gaussian distribution with a mean of $0$ at any fixed point of the algorithm. Additionally, we establish convergence bounds for M-SGD within the strongly convex setting.

Driven by the widespread success of deep learning, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a leading method for graph classification. Current GNN classifiers typically employ a global readout mechanism that aggregates node or node-cluster representations to generate a graph-level embedding for label prediction. However, this approach overlooks the structural information of individual nodes, leading to a loss of global structural details. Specifically, it restricts discriminative capability by applying uniform classifier weights to all node representations, despite their varying contributions to target classes based on their unique structural semantics. To address this, we introduce Structural Semantic Readout (SSRead), which summarizes node representations at the position level. This enables the modeling of position-specific weight parameters for classification and effectively captures global graph semantics. SSRead identifies structurally meaningful positions by aligning node semantics with structural prototypes that encode prototypical features for each position. During training, these prototypes are optimized to minimize alignment costs across all graphs, while other GNN parameters are trained to predict class labels. Experimental results show that SSRead significantly enhances both the classification performance and interpretability of GNN classifiers, while remaining compatible with diverse aggregation functions, architectures, and learning frameworks.

The Cohn-Elkies linear program, instrumental in resolving sphere packing for dimensions 8 and 24, is conjectured to fail as a sharp method in all other dimensions $d>2$. By translating feasible points from this infinite-dimensional framework into a finite-dimensional setting through discrete reduction, we establish a general approach for deriving dual bounds on the Cohn-Elkies program. This reduction limits the variable count to a finite number, thereby allowing the application of computational optimization tools. Employing this technique, we demonstrate that for dimensions $3 \leq d \leq 13$ (excluding the solved case $d=8$), the Cohn-Elkies bound falls significantly short of the best known packing densities. Specifically, our dual bounds confirm that the Cohn-Elkies approach cannot resolve the sphere packing problems in dimensions 3, 4, and 5.

We introduce TWIROLE, a hybrid classification model designed to support diverse research by identifying male, female, and brand-related (organization or institution) users on Twitter. This system integrates features from tweet content, user profiles, and profile images to determine user roles. Evaluated on two large existing Twitter datasets through both intra- and inter-comparison experiments, TWIROLE surpasses current methods and delivers more balanced performance across all categories. Furthermore, our findings confirm that user names and profile images serve as effective indicators for this task. This study advances prior research by incorporating brand-related users and provides valuable assistance for future evaluations that depend on self-labeled datasets.

Building on Frierson's powerful parameterization of order 3 associative magic squares, we constructed a family of six related order 9 compound (or composite) magic squares, some of which date back to antiquity. Inspired by Bellew's 1997 extension to order 27, we generalize these concepts to all orders that are powers of 3, deriving simple formulas for their matrix spectra and entropic measures. This construction exhibits fractal properties, and numerical results up to order 243 demonstrate that the information entropy for the lowest entropy members converges to a constant value of approximately 1.168. Additionally, we briefly examine the compounding of an order 4 magic square with the lowest entropy, observing a similar trend toward constant entropy.

Peridynamic (PD) theories have become widely adopted across numerous research fields because of their capacity to simulate the formation and evolution of discontinuities in materials. Despite certain modeling constraints, Bond-Based Peridynamics (BB-PD) remains a popular choice for numerical simulations, largely due to its ease of implementation, physical clarity, and stability. This paper reviews and examines various facets of bond-based peridynamic models, offering a comprehensive overview of the theory, its applications, and associated numerical frameworks. The study presents the integral kernels used in BB-PD, highlighting both their distinctions and shared characteristics, followed by an analysis of the implications arising from their mathematical structure. Critical discussion is provided on the kinematic implications of nonlocality, the connection between kernel architecture and material impenetrability, and the influence of kernel nonlinearity on predicting crack formation. Finally, the paper proposes extending BB-PD to fluid dynamics within the context of fading memory materials, offering insights for a more profound and holistic understanding of peridynamics in fluids.

Automatic medical report generation, which involves creating lengthy and coherent narratives from medical images, has become a focal point of growing research. Current methods predominantly rely on supervised learning, necessitating extensive datasets of paired images and reports. However, assembling such large-scale paired data in the medical field is both costly and time-intensive. To mitigate this dependency on paired data, we introduce an unsupervised model called the Knowledge Graph Auto-Encoder (KGAE), which utilizes independent sets of images and reports for training. The KGAE architecture comprises a pre-existing knowledge graph, a knowledge-driven encoder, and a knowledge-driven decoder. The knowledge graph functions as a shared latent space that connects visual and textual domains; the encoder maps medical images and reports to specific coordinates within this space, while the decoder generates a report based on a given coordinate. Because the encoder and decoder can be trained using separate image and report sets, the KGAE operates in an unsupervised manner. Experimental results demonstrate that the unsupervised KGAE produces high-quality medical reports without any image-report training pairs. Additionally, the model is flexible enough to operate in both semi-supervised and supervised settings by accepting paired data during training. Through further fine-tuning with image-report pairs, KGAE consistently surpasses existing state-of-the-art models across two datasets.

This paper investigates the Embedding Wirelength of an $n$-dimensional Hypercube $Q_n$ into a Cylinder $C_{2^{n_1}}\times P_{2^{n_2}}$, where $n_1+ n_2=n$, a problem designated as EWHC. We demonstrate that the wirelength associated with a Gray code embedding equals $2^{n_2}(3\cdot 2^{2n_1-3}-2^{n_1-1})+2^{n_1} (2^{2n_2-1}-2^{n_2-1})$. Furthermore, we establish that the Gray code embedding constitutes an optimal strategy for EWHC.
We extend Artin's three principal theorems on algebraicity to the realm of supergeometry, covering Artin approximation, the algebraization of formal moduli, and the algebraization of stacks.

Investigating photochemical reactions theoretically demands accurate mapping of excited-state energy landscapes, particularly in regions of degeneracy where state transitions occur. Although such systems are often too extensive for high-level multireference methods, and while time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) offers computational efficiency, it frequently lacks the necessary precision. This study applies a variational, time-independent density functional approach to the twisting of ethylene's double bond and its pyramidal distortion, serving as a standard model for photochemistry. By incorporating symmetry breaking, the resulting energy surfaces correctly reproduce the topology near the twisted-pyramidalized conical intersection, even with semilocal functionals. Furthermore, the inclusion of explicit self-interaction correction yields torsional energy curves that closely match established multireference data. These results suggest that a single-determinant, time-independent density functional method could effectively simulate nonadiabatic dynamics for large systems where multireference techniques are infeasible and TDDFT proves insufficient.

Inverse problems appear across numerous physical fields, ranging from aerospace engineering to medical imaging, with the objective of deducing an underlying state from observed data. When the forward model generating these observations is both nonlinear and stochastic, resolving the inverse problem becomes highly difficult. Neural networks offer a promising solution because they can be trained on noisy datasets and execute efficiently after training. Nevertheless, inverse model neural networks lack inherent guarantees of correctness, rendering them unsuitable for safety- and accuracy-critical applications. This study presents a method to verify the correctness of such networks by overapproximating the nonlinear, stochastic forward model using piecewise linear constraints and encoding both this overapproximation and the neural network inverse model as a mixed-integer program. We validate this verification process using a real-world case study involving an airplane fuel gauge. The capacity to verify and thereby trust inverse model neural networks facilitates their deployment across diverse domains, including aerospace and medicine.

We introduce a local-to-global framework for graph machine learning and network analysis that defines specific local node features and vector representations to enable deep neural networks to learn global metrics and properties. By expanding the concept of node degree through Breadth-First Search (BFS), we establish a general family of **parametric centrality functions** capable of identifying node importance. We also propose the **neighbors degree frequency (NDF)**, a locally defined embedding that maps nodes in undirected graphs to Euclidean spaces. This vectorized labeling captures the structural characteristics of local neighborhoods and supports graph isomorphism testing. Our method includes flexibility to accommodate dynamic graphs. Subsequently, BFS is employed to extend NDF vectors into two distinct matrix representations that encode higher-order neighborhood information. These matrix forms offer a novel approach to visualizing node neighborhood shapes and generate feature vectors compatible with standard deep learning algorithms. We validate that these embeddings retain meaningful node information by demonstrating, through multiple examples, that deep learning can successfully recover PageRank and closeness centrality from these local features. Our construction remains adaptable to evolving graphs, and we conclude by detailing how to extend these methods to directed graphs.

This research examines the magnetic moments of the hidden-charmed pentaquarks $P_{cs}(4338)$ and $P_{cs}(4459)$, emphasizing their connection to internal substructures. Using the QCD light-cone sum rules method, we calculated these moments for quantum numbers $I(J^P) = 0(1/2^-)$ and $I(J^P) = 0(3/2^-)$, corresponding to $P_{cs}(4338)$ and $P_{cs}(4459)$, respectively. Our findings predict a magnetic moment of $\mu_{P_{cs}} = 0.34 \pm 0.12~\mu_N$ for $P_{cs}(4338)$ and $\mu_{P_{cs}} = -1.67 \pm 0.58~\mu_N$ for $P_{cs}(4459)$. Additionally, we derived the magnetic moments for the isospin-1 partners of these states, yielding values of $\mu_{P_{cs}} = 0.63 \pm 0.21~\mu_N$ and $\mu_{P_{cs}} = -3.33 \pm 1.04~\mu_N$. Finally, our results for these color singlet-singlet type pentaquarks are compared against existing literature.

This study investigates the superconducting characteristics of multilayer thin films composed of the superconductor La$_{1.85}$Sr$_{0.15}$CuO$_4$ (LSCO) and the Mott insulator Sr$_2$IrO$_4$ (SIO), revealing enhanced superconductivity in optimized samples. Compared to single-layer LSCO films, these heterostructures exhibit a higher superconducting transition temperature ($T_C$). Additionally, the thermal activation, Arrhenius behavior, and variable-range hopping mechanisms governing SIO single layers across various temperature regimes were examined. Finally, the reduction in $T_C$ observed beyond an optimal LSCO thickness is analyzed using a model that attributes induced superconductivity at the SIO-LSCO interface to doping effects from La and/or oxygen deficiencies within the SIO layers.

The incidence of gastrointestinal (GI) cancer is rising sharply annually, resulting in a significant surge in mortality. Although endoscopy offers vital diagnostic assistance, identifying subtle lesions in the upper and lower GI tract remains challenging, often leading to substantial missed detections. This study utilizes deep learning to create a framework that enhances the localization of hard-to-spot lesions and reduces the rate of missed diagnoses. We introduce an end-to-end student-teacher learning architecture, wherein the class probabilities from a teacher model trained on a larger single-class dataset are used to penalize a multi-class student network. Our approach achieves superior mean average precision (mAP) on both the EDD2020 challenge and the Kvasir-SEG datasets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this learning paradigm ensures generalizability to unseen test sets, yielding higher accuracy for clinically critical neoplastic and polyp categories.

Active chiral viscoelastic materials display elastic responses orthogonal to applied stresses, a phenomenon known as odd elasticity. By employing a covariant framework for viscoelasticity alongside an entropy production analysis, we demonstrate that odd elasticity occurs not only in active systems but also across broad categories of passive chiral viscoelastic fluids. Conversely, we show that linear viscoelastic chiral solids necessitate activity to exhibit odd elastic responses. To model passive odd viscoelasticity, we introduce a chiral extension of the Jeffreys model. Furthermore, applying our covariant formalism allows us to derive the dispersion relations of hydrodynamic modes, revealing distinct signatures of odd viscoelastic behavior.

We introduce a data-driven method for automating audio signal processing by embedding stateful, third-party audio effects as layers inside a deep neural network. A deep encoder is trained to examine input audio and adjust effect parameters to achieve specific manipulations, utilizing only input-target paired data for supervision. To handle non-differentiable black-box effect layers, we employ a rapid, parallel stochastic gradient approximation scheme within a standard automatic differentiation framework, enabling efficient end-to-end backpropagation. We showcase the capabilities of this approach across three distinct automatic audio production tasks: tube amplifier emulation, automatic elimination of breaths and pops from vocal recordings, and automatic music mastering. Our results are validated through a subjective listening test, demonstrating that our method not only facilitates new automatic audio effect tasks but also produces outcomes comparable to specialized, state-of-the-art commercial music mastering solutions.

This study explores compressing quantum information relative to a specified set $\mathcal{M}$ of high-dimensional measurements. We introduce a concept of simulability requiring that the statistics generated by $\rho$ and $\mathcal{M}$ be exactly replicated by compressing $\rho$ into a lower-dimensional space before performing quantum measurements. Complete quantum compression, resulting in purely classical data, is feasible if and only if the set $\mathcal{M}$ is jointly measurable. Consequently, our definition of simulability serves as a dimensional quantification of measurement incompatibility. Following the establishment of these definitions, we present illustrative cases involving mutually unbiased bases and devise a semi-definite programming approach for building simulation models. Furthermore, we analytically derive optimal simulation models for all projective measurements under conditions of white noise or loss. Finally, we examine the connections between our methodology and other concepts related to quantum channels and correlations.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso problems. Building on the Graphical Lasso method introduced by (Friedman 2007) and further explored by (Yuan 2007; Banerjee 2008), this approach estimates a sparse inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma) \in \mathbb{R}^p$. While initially formulated by (Dempster 1972) as Covariance Selection, the framework has since been expanded to accommodate latent variables, as noted in (Chandrasekaran 2012), and more recently to enable the joint estimation of multiple inverse covariance matrices, exemplified by works such as (Danaher 2013; Tomasi 2018). The GGLasso package provides algorithms to solve this general formulation, covering key specific instances including the standard Graphical Lasso (with latent variables), Group Graphical Lasso, and Fused Graphical Lasso.

The interplay between genotype and phenotype is fundamental to establishing the function and robustness of biological systems. In this context, evolution drives changes in the genotype, while selection acts upon the phenotype, causing the genotype-phenotype mapping itself to evolve. Unlike the well-established theories regarding evolution on fitness landscapes defined by genotypes, theoretical frameworks for phenotypic evolution remain underdeveloped. This study introduces a statistical-physics approach to address this gap by employing replicas for both genotypes and phenotypes. We apply this method to an evolutionary model where phenotypes correspond to spin configurations, genotypes define the spin interaction matrices (Hamiltonian), and fitness is determined solely by the configuration of a specific subset of spins, termed the target. Using this new approach, which extends replica theory for spin-glasses to include spin-replicas for phenotypes and coupling-replicas for genotypes, we characterize the interaction between genetic and phenotypic variations mediated by noise. Within this framework, we derive a phase diagram of evolved phenotypes as a function of noise and selection pressure, distinguishing phases by their fitness levels and overlaps for both genotypes and phenotypes. Notably, we identify a "robust fitted phase," highly relevant to biological evolution, which emerges at intermediate noise levels (temperatures). In this phase, robustness against noise and genetic mutations are correlated due to replica symmetry. Furthermore, we observe a trade-off between maintaining high phenotypic fitness and developing robust genetic patterns, noting that this trade-off depends on the ratio of functional (target) spins to non-functional (non-target) spins. Finally, we find that the selection pressure required to achieve high fitness increases as the fraction of target spins grows.

This study utilizes ALMA data with 800 au resolution and radiative-transfer modeling to investigate the inner region ($r \approx 6000$ au) of the ionized accretion flow surrounding a forming compact star cluster within the luminous ultra-compact HII region G10.6-0.4. The flow was modeled as an ionized Keplerian disk, incorporating either radial motions in the outer regions or an external Ulrich envelope. Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) fitting of the data yields total stellar masses ($M_\star$) between 120 and 200 $M_\odot$, contrasted with significantly lower ionized-gas masses ($M_\mathrm{ion-gas}$) ranging from 0.2 to 0.25 $M_\odot$. The stellar mass is concentrated within the gravitational radius ($R_g \approx 1000$ to 1500 au), where the ionized gas remains bound. The system's inclination angle relative to a face-on view is estimated at 49 to 56 degrees. Radial velocities at radii beyond $R_g$ converge to approximately 8.7 km/s ($v_{r,0}$), roughly equal to the sound speed of ionized gas, suggesting the gas is at best marginally unbound. Based on constraints regarding the ionizing-photon rate and far-infrared luminosity, we deduce that the cluster comprises a few massive stars with masses between 32 and 60 $M_\odot$, or alternatively, a single star of this mass range alongside a population of lower-mass stars. Active accretion of ionized gas onto these massive (proto)stars appears to be residual. The inferred cluster density is exceptionally high, comparable to densities observed at similar scales in the Galactic Center, implying that stellar interactions are likely to occur within the next million years.

This study explores the Unruh-Fulling effect within a specific set of nonlocal field theories by evaluating both the number operator and Unruh-DeWitt detector approaches. Diverging from prior research, we employ Unruh quantization rather than the conventional Minkowski decomposition for the matter field. This method inherently respects time translational symmetry in the positive frequency Wightman function, thereby accounting for the system's thermal equilibrium. We examine the Unruh-Fulling effect for a massless real scalar field across both Lorentz-invariant and Lorentz-noninvariant nonlocal frameworks. In Lorentz-noninvariant theories, the detector response function and the expectation value of the number operator are altered by a global multiplicative factor. Conversely, in Lorentz-invariant theories, these quantities match those of the standard Unruh-Fulling effect. The temperature of the thermal bath remains constant across both nonlocal models. Consequently, when derived through Unruh quantization, the nonlocal Unruh-Fulling effect is universal regarding temperature, although the transition rate may vary.
We provide an elementary proof of the Riemann Hypothesis that requires only undergraduate-level mathematics.

This note offers a remark on the recent paper by Y.~Lai and Q.~Xu, titled "On the coefficient inequalities for a class of holomorphic mappings associated with spirallike mappings in several complex variables," which appeared in the journal {\it Results in Mathematics}. We demonstrate that a theorem in their work regarding the finite-dimensional space $\mathbb{C}^n$ follows directly from another result, rendering an independent proof unnecessary. Furthermore, we establish that a sharp norm estimate for the Fekete--Szeg\"{o} functional over spirallike mappings in a general Banach space can be derived from a finding in \cite{LX}.

This paper examines an optimal control problem defined over an infinite horizon with a quadratic cost functional for a linear system subject to known additive disturbances. The defining characteristic of this problem is that the control cost weight matrix within the cost functional is singular. Consequently, standard solution methods such as Pontryagin's Maximum Principle or the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman approach are inapplicable, classifying the problem as singular. Because the singular weight matrix is generally not entirely zero, only a subset of the control coordinates are singular, leaving the remainder regular. The solution employs a regularization method, which transforms the original dynamics equation into a new optimal control problem. The cost functional for this new problem comprises the original functional plus an infinite horizon integral of the squares of the singular control coordinates, weighted by a small positive coefficient. Given the smallness of this coefficient, the new problem constitutes a partial cheap control problem. A perturbation technique is then used to perform an asymptotic analysis of this partial cheap control problem. Based on this analysis, the infimum of the original cost functional is determined, and a sequence of minimizing state-feedback controls is constructed. The study concludes with an illustrative example involving singular trajectory tracking.

We demonstrate stability exceeding $7\times 10{}^{-17}$ for two independent optical lattice clocks utilizing the bosonic ${}^{88}$Sr isotope. The absolute frequency of the ${}^{1}S_{0}$ - ${}^{3}P_{0}$ transition, measured as 429228066418008.3(1.9)${}_{syst}$(0.9)${}_{stat}$~Hz, was determined using an optical frequency comb linked to the local UTC via a 330 km stabilized fiber optic connection. This outcome, confirmed through repeated measurements on the two distinct clocks, aligns with the recommendations of the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures.

**Context.** The mechanisms behind massive star formation remain uncertain, though a model involving accretion disks and molecular outflows—mirroring low-mass star formation on a larger scale—is taking shape. Investigating outflow activity across massive star-forming clumps at various evolutionary stages offers valuable insights into this process.

**Aims.** This study utilizes SEDIGISM data to survey outflows within ATLASGAL clumps, with the goal of compiling a substantial dataset of clumps displaying outflows across different evolutionary phases.

**Methods.** We identified high-velocity wings in 13CO spectra toward ATLASGAL clumps by (1) retrieving simultaneously observed 13CO and C18O spectra from SEDIGISM, and (2) subtracting Gaussian profiles fitted to opacity-corrected, scaled C18O data from the 13CO lines.

**Results.** High-velocity gas was detected in 1,192 out of 2,052 clumps, yielding a 58% overall detection rate. Outflow activity spans from the earliest quiescent stages (70$\mu$m weak) to the most evolved HII regions (8$\mu$m bright with massive star formation tracers). Detection rates rise with evolutionary progression: 51% for quiescent clumps, 47% for protostellar clumps, 57% for Young Stellar Objects (YSOs), and 76% for Ultra-Compact HII (UCHII) regions.

**Conclusion.** This represents the largest outflow sample identified to date. The high detection rate aligns with prior findings and reinforces the notion that outflows are a universal characteristic of massive star formation. The reduced detection rate in early stages likely stems from the weakness of outflows at these times, making them harder to observe. We have secured a statistically significant sample of outflow clumps for every evolutionary stage, particularly for those in the 70$\mu$m dark phase. This indicates that the lack of 70$\mu$m emission is not a reliable marker for starless or pre-stellar cores.

The scattered disk comprises a vast collection of trans-Neptunian minor bodies characterized by highly elongated, long-period orbits around the Sun. The stability of these objects is chiefly governed by a single factor: their perihelion distance. Although numerical simulations have long established the existence of a perihelion boundary distinguishing chaotic from regular motion in long-period orbits, the theoretical underpinnings of this boundary and its dependence on the semi-major axis remain unclear. This study presents an analytical model for the dynamics of distant trans-Neptunian objects, demonstrating that the scattered disk's architecture is defined by an infinite series of $2:j$ resonances with Neptune. As the perihelion distance nears Neptune's semi-major axis, the widths of these resonances expand; their overlap subsequently induces chaotic behavior. Based on this framework, we derive an analytic criterion for the instability of long-period orbits, showing that rapid dynamical chaos occurs when the perihelion falls below a critical threshold:
$q_{\rm{crit}}=a_{\rm{N}}\,\big(\ln((24^2/5)\,(m_{\rm{N}}/M_{\odot})\,(a/a_{\rm{N}})^{5/2})\big)^{1/2}$.
This formula delineates the boundary between the "detached" and actively "scattering" sub-populations of distant trans-Neptunian minor bodies. Furthermore, we observe that within the stochastic layer, the Lyapunov time of scattered disk objects converges toward their orbital period, and we establish that the semi-major axis diffusion coefficient can be approximated by:
$\mathcal{D}_a\sim(8/(5\,\pi))\,(m_{\rm{N}}/M_{\odot})\,\sqrt{\mathcal{G}\,M_{\odot}\,a_{\rm{N}}}\,\exp\big[-(q/a_{\rm{N}})^2/2\big]$.
Our findings are validated through numerical simulations, which also reveal the connections between scattered disk dynamics and the Chirikov Standard Map. Finally, the implications of these results for the long-term evolution of the distant solar system are discussed.

We derive non-linear dynamical equations for an augmented electromagnetic railgun, where the augmentation circuit is inductively coupled to the gun circuit. These differential equations are solved numerically using representative parameter values. Our analysis reveals a complex interaction between the augmentation circuit, the gun circuit, and the mechanical degrees of freedom, resulting in a challenging optimization problem. For specific parameter values, the augmented railgun exhibits armature kinetic energy that is 42% greater than that of a standard railgun without an augmentation circuit. Further optimization of these parameters could potentially enhance performance even more.

Superconducting microresonators have proven effective as detection components across numerous applications. As the most scalable low-temperature detector technology available, they can support over 1,000 detectors on a single transmission line. While high-throughput scenarios may couple fewer detectors to a wire to increase individual bandwidth, existing designs suffer from fabrication tolerance variations that cause non-uniform shifts in resonance frequency and sensitivity, thereby restricting bandwidth efficiency. This work introduces the design, implementation, and preliminary characterization of a readout system for superconducting microresonators that incorporates two tunable inductances per detector. We show that these elements enable independent adjustment of both detector frequency and sensitivity, optimizing transmission line bandwidth usage. Additionally, we address the integration of these detectors into a multilayer fabrication stack for the high-speed readout of the D-Wave quantum processor, emphasizing the use of single flux-quantum loop control and routing circuitry to reduce the number of control wires required at the lowest temperature stage.

This study illustrates the efficacy of our experimentation platform (XP), which prioritizes democratization and computational efficiency, by introducing four novel models: Weighted least squares, Quantile bootstrapping, Bayesian shrinkage, and Dynamic treatment effects. Although each model addresses a distinct business challenge, they remain both generalizable and extensible. The platform's modular architecture fosters independent advancements in both statistical techniques and computational algorithms. Practically, this creates a synergistic cycle where sophisticated user contributions drive software innovations, which subsequently facilitate further methodological enhancements. This iterative loop amplifies the XP's overall value in delivering business solutions.

Machine learning has recently become a focal point of research for solving AC optimal power flow (OPF) problems, driven by the dramatic speed gains achieved by circumventing conventional optimization methods. Nevertheless, guaranteeing the feasibility of these predictions without sacrificing such efficiency remains a difficult, unresolved challenge. This paper presents a neural network trained to mimic an iterative solver, enabling rapid and approximate progression toward the optimal solution. Upon nearing convergence, a power flow calculation is performed to secure a globally AC-feasible result. Experimental results on networks comprising up to 1,354 buses demonstrate that this approach can identify feasible, near-optimal AC OPF solutions in milliseconds on standard laptop hardware. Furthermore, the method proves capable of resolving "difficult" AC OPF cases that typically cause flat-start or DC-warm-start algorithms to diverge.

We examine a variation of the SSH model featuring an SSH chain incorporating an embedded Aharonov-Bohm quantum ring. This ring generates domain wall states located within the band gap, where certain states exhibit a dependence on the ring's magnetic flux that enables control over the entanglement between the two SSH edge fermion modes. The concurrence of these edge modes varies periodically with the magnetic flux. Within the deep topological regime, specific flux values allow the concurrence to reach extreme values of 0 and 1, representing states of zero and maximal entanglement, respectively. Consequently, the QR-SSH system provides a tunable mechanism capable of functioning as either an entanglement switch or an entanglement modulator.

The KOALA experiment determines the differential cross section for (anti)proton-proton elastic scattering across a broad spectrum of four-momentum transfer squared, spanning 0.0008 < |t| < 0.1 (GeV/c)$^2$. By examining the distinctive shape of the differential cross-section spectrum, researchers can derive the forward scattering parameters and absolute luminosity. Operating under fixed-target kinematics, the setup employs an internal hydrogen cluster jet target. To cover the extensive |t| range, the experiment measures the total kinetic energy of recoil protons detected near 90 degrees using a recoil detector composed of silicon and germanium single-sided strip sensors, achieving an energy resolution superior to 30 keV (FWHM). Additionally, a forward detector made of two layers of plastic scintillators captures elastically scattered beam particles close to the beam axis. This component mitigates significant background noise at small recoil angles and enhances the identification of elastic scattering events in the low |t| region. Installed and commissioned at COSY, the KOALA configuration has been validated through proton-proton elastic scattering measurements, the results of which are detailed herein.

Amidst the expanding and diverse landscape of contemporary music, locating specific songs has grown increasingly challenging, a task significantly aided by the singer's identity. This project addresses singer identification through various feature extraction techniques, with a specific introduction of the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), marking its first application in this context to our knowledge. The methodology comprises three essential stages: first, isolating the vocal track from background music using Robust Principal Component Analysis (RPCA); second, extracting features from the isolated vocals to evaluate DWT against the standard Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficient (MFCC); and third, identifying the singer using either Support Vector Machine (SVM) or Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). Our findings indicate that for a dataset comprising 4 singers and 200 songs, the optimal system combines the novel DWT (db4) feature extraction with a linear SVM classifier, achieving a mean accuracy of 83.96%.

This paper investigates pseudo-parallel contact CR-submanifolds, defined both in the sense of Chaki and Deszcz, within Kenmotsu manifolds using the Levi-Civita connection and the semisymmetric metric connection, and establishes the equivalence of these two classes under specific conditions.

This study evaluates and compares numerous numerical techniques for addressing stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics, which rely on combinations of deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. Leveraging recent work by the authors, the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion is employed to analyze sampling accuracy and quantify stepsize-dependent biases in configurational averaging. For harmonic oscillators, specific schemes yield exact configurational averaging, potentially enhancing the modeling of biomolecules where bond stretching is critical. In general systems, an optimal method is identified that exhibits significantly lower bias than alternatives. Simulations of the alanine dipeptide (both solvated and unsolvated) demonstrate that this approach achieves higher accuracy without sacrificing computational efficiency, supports larger timesteps, and maintains the conformational exploration rate. The proposed scheme represents a uniformly superior algorithm for molecular sampling, offering practical timestep increases of over 25% in vacuum and reducing errors in configurational averages by more than a factor of ten in solvated simulations at large timesteps.

The consensus algorithm serves as a fundamental element of any blockchain or distributed ledger technology (DLT) platform, acting as the primary mechanism for nodes to achieve agreement. Although numerous consensus algorithms have recently been proposed—primarily for private and permissioned networks—their performance and reliability under hostile conditions or in the presence of Byzantine and other network failures remain poorly understood. Furthermore, validating blockchain applications presents significant technical hurdles. This paper employs chaos engineering and testing to assess consensus algorithm performance across various load levels, Byzantine failures, and communication breakdowns. Specifically, we evaluate three distinct consensus algorithms (PBFT, Clique, and Raft) and their associated platforms using chaos engineering. Our methodology involves measuring network throughput, latency, and success rates during chaos and load tests, utilizing lightweight blockchain applications deployed in a semi-production environment. Our findings indicate that chaos engineering effectively reveals how different consensus algorithms behave in unreliable or hostile settings and highlights the limitations of blockchain platforms. Ultimately, this work underscores the advantages of applying chaos engineering to test complex distributed systems like blockchain networks.

Future CMB mission data might reveal a lower tensor-to-scalar ratio than current measurements suggest. This outcome can be modeled using single-field chaotic inflation, the curvaton mechanism, quantum gravity effects, or a combination thereof.
