Furthermore, the approach is adapted to verify whether the heteroscedasticity assumption adequately identifies parameters in SVAR models. A Monte Carlo simulation evaluates the method's performance under non-Gaussian error distributions and misspecified VAR orders, demonstrating that the test maintains an asymptotically correct size. Additionally, the results indicate that the test's power renders it well-suited for empirical applications.

We focus on assessing systems that generate image descriptions and introduce a new, image-aware metric called VIFIDEL. This metric gauges how faithfully a generated caption aligns with the actual image content by calculating the semantic similarity between image object labels and words in the description. Additionally, VIFIDEL can incorporate the relative importance of objects as highlighted in human reference descriptions. Notably, even without access to human references, VIFIDEL remains capable of reliably evaluating system outputs. On two established datasets, the metric demonstrates a strong correlation with human judgments and performs competitively against methods that rely on human references.

We have modeled the velocity-resolved reverberation response of the H\textit{\eta} broad emission line in nine Seyfert 1 galaxies from the 2016 Lick AGN Monitoring Project sample to infer the geometry, structure, and mass of the central supermassive black hole within the low-ionization broad-line region (BLR). Our results indicate that the H\textit{\eta} BLR is typically a thick disk observed at low to moderate inclinations. By combining our data with previous studies, we examined how line-profile shape metrics, such as $\log_{10}(\text{FWHM}/\sigma)$, relate to BLR structure and kinematics, as well as potential trends linked to BLR luminosity. We observed marginal evidence for an anticorrelation between the shape of the broad H\textit{\eta} emission line and the Eddington ratio when utilizing the root-mean-square spectrum. However, no luminosity-dependent trends were identified, leading us to conclude that AGNs exhibit diverse BLR structures and kinematics, which supports the hypothesis of transient AGN/BLR conditions over systematic trends.
Because prior findings establish that contact varieties are isomorphic to specific varieties, the momentum polytopes associated with contact manifolds are convex.

This study presents a computational analysis of a fully passive energy harvesting foil. An internal second-order finite volume CFD code, MaPFlow, is tightly integrated with a rigid body dynamics solver to examine the foil's behavior under uniform and sheared inflow conditions, both with and without a free surface. The computational mesh adapts to the airfoil's movement using a radial basis function (RBF) mesh deformation technique. First, MaPFlow results are benchmarked against existing experimental and numerical data from the literature, demonstrating reasonable agreement. Subsequently, one-phase simulations are conducted for linearly sheared inflows across various shear rates, revealing that foil performance improves under sheared conditions. Finally, two-phase simulations incorporating the free surface are performed for both uniform and sheared inflows. The findings indicate a marked decline in system performance when the foil operates beneath the free surface, attributed to the interaction between shed vorticity and the free surface.

The computational cost of traditional numerical methods for solving Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) escalates dramatically with increased resolution. A critical example is climate modeling, which demands fine spatio-temporal grids to capture all turbulent fluid scales; however, accurately resolving these scales remains computationally infeasible even for state-of-the-art supercomputers. Consequently, current models rely on overly coarse grids (ranging from 3km to 200km per side), compromising prediction accuracy and utility. This paper introduces a novel architecture based on recent Implicit Neural Representation (INR) advancements, designed to predict the spatially continuous solution of a PDE at any queried position. By integrating Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with coordinate-based frameworks, we achieve zero-shot generalization to new, non-uniform meshes and enable physically consistent long-term forecasting up to 250 frames ahead. Our proposed Mesh Agnostic Neural PDE Solver (MAgNet) delivers accurate predictions across diverse PDE datasets, outperforming existing baselines. Furthermore, MAgNet demonstrates robust generalization to varying mesh structures and resolutions up to four times higher than those used during training.

We establish a general formula for the electric and magnetic components of the near-field energy density for $N$ dipoles at temperatures $T_1, \ldots, T_N$ situated within a background field of temperature $T_b$. Unlike previous formulations, this approach incorporates the background field, enabling the calculation of energy density for heated or cooled isotropic dipolar objects in arbitrary environments thermalized at a distinct temperature. Additionally, we demonstrate the relationship between energy density and the local density of states. Applying this general expression, we investigate the near-field enhanced energy density at the edges and corners of one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chains and two-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattices composed of plasmonic InSb nanoparticles during the transition from a topological trivial to a non-trivial state. Finally, we examine the robustness of these modes against defects and assess the feasibility of measuring the topological edge and corner modes.

Adult tissue maintenance and regeneration depend on stem cell self-renewal, yet preventing over-proliferation during regeneration necessitates precise control over their proliferation and differentiation. The specific regulatory mechanisms across various tissues and how to integrate them into stem cell population dynamics models remain largely unclear. While the critical birth-death (CBD) process is a common modeling tool that captures phenomena like scaling laws in clone size distributions, it fails to account for regulatory mechanisms. This study introduces the birth-death process with volume exclusion (vBD), a modified approach that incorporates crowding effects, such as those resulting from limited space within a stem cell niche. Although deterministic rate equations for vBD predict a single non-trivial steady state, the master equation forecasts extinction and transient distributions exhibiting three potential behaviors: a long-lived quasi-steady state, or short-lived bimodal and unimodal distributions. We approximate solutions to the vBD master equation using a renormalized system-size expansion, the quasi-steady state approximation, and the WKB method. Our findings indicate that stem cell population size distributions contain signatures useful for identifying negative feedback mediated by volume exclusion.

Deep Learning Gaussian Processes (DL-GP) are introduced as a method to analyze and approximate computer models that generate high-dimensional, heteroskedastic outputs. These simulation models find applications across diverse fields such as engineering, physics, biology, environmental science, agriculture, and socio-economic processes. The proposed approach employs deep learning to deterministically transform inputs, while traditional Gaussian Processes are used to generate predictions. The methodology is demonstrated through simulations of motorcycle accidents and an Ebola outbreak, with the paper concluding by outlining directions for future research.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have become fundamental to numerous mobile applications, but achieving high accuracy often necessitates extremely deep architectures with hundreds or thousands of layers. This complexity results in significant computational and memory demands during inference. While operator fusion is a critical optimization strategy in leading frameworks like TensorFlow, TVM, and MNN, these systems typically rely on rigid pattern-matching rules that fail to address the full diversity of operators and layer interconnections. Conversely, polyhedral-based loop fusion methods operate at a low-level computational view lacking operator-specific context, causing them to overlook viable fusion possibilities. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces DNNFusion, a comprehensive loop fusion framework. DNNFusion operates at the operator level but expands fusion potential by classifying both individual operators and their combinations. Its key components include: 1) a novel graph rewriting framework based on mathematical properties to lower evaluation costs and streamline fusion; 2) an integrated fusion planning module that combines high-level analysis with accurate, lightweight profiling; and 3) further optimizations during code generation. Extensive testing across 15 diverse DNN models reveals that DNNFusion identifies up to 8.8 times more fusion opportunities than existing methods. Furthermore, it outperforms four state-of-the-art frameworks by achieving a 9.3x speedup. These improvements in memory efficiency and performance facilitate the execution of complex models on mobile devices, enabling their integration into real-time applications.

Autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) relying on inertial navigation face a critical reliance on Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS); without these signals, they experience a gradual yet inevitable position drift that can result in total platform loss if recovery via remote control is not possible before signal restoration or reaching a safe location. This paper details a stochastic, high-fidelity simulation of a low SWaP (size, weight, and power) fixed-wing autonomous UAV operating in turbulent and changing weather conditions, designed to evaluate and validate various navigation algorithms under GNSS-denied scenarios. The project's open-source C++ implementation is publicly accessible. The simulation incorporates onboard sensors such as accelerometers, gyroscopes, magnetometers, a Pitot tube, air data systems, a GNSS receiver, and a digital camera, ensuring validity for inertial, visual, and visual-inertial navigation systems. Two specific GNSS-outage scenarios are modeled: the first addresses the difficulties of aborting a mission and navigating to a remote recovery point amidst varying weather, while the second simulates mission continuation through a sequence of closely spaced bearing adjustments. To maximize result realism, all simulation modules were modeled with minimal simplifications. Although the aircraft performance and control system implementations are deterministic, all other modules—including mission parameters, sensors, weather, wind, turbulence, and initial estimations—are fully stochastic. This approach facilitates a robust assessment of each navigation system using Monte-Carlo simulations that require a large number of scenario executions.

We present a learning-driven algorithm designed for the distributed formation control of networked multi-agent systems characterized by unknown, nonlinear dynamics. Unlike most existing methods that either rely on specific parametric assumptions for unknown dynamics or require excessively large control inputs to ensure theoretical validity, our approach overcomes these limitations by combining neural network-based learning with adaptive control in a two-stage process. Initially, each agent trains a neural network controller using data generated from various formation tasks and agent parameters, which are obtained by perturbing nominal parameters and a target formation task, respectively. Subsequently, each agent integrates this trained network into an online adaptive control strategy, ensuring the closed-loop multi-agent system fulfills the desired formation requirements. Both the learning phase and the adaptive control policy operate in a distributed manner, meaning each agent determines its actions solely based on local information from neighboring agents. Notably, the proposed method requires no prior knowledge of the agents' unknown dynamic terms or any approximation techniques. Furthermore, we establish formal theoretical guarantees regarding the successful execution of the formation task.

Visual object tracking is a critical function for intelligent robots. However, most current methods overlook online latency, which can significantly degrade performance during real-world operations. This issue is particularly critical for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), where robust tracking is inherently difficult and onboard computational resources are constrained; in such scenarios, latency can be fatal. This paper introduces a straightforward, end-to-end framework for latency-aware tracking called Predictive Visual Tracking (PVT++). PVT++ transforms state-of-the-art trackers into predictive ones by adding an online predictor module. Unlike previous model-based solutions, our framework is learnable, allowing it to utilize motion data, visual cues, or a combination of both as inputs. Furthermore, because PVT++ is fully end-to-end optimizable, joint training enhances its latency-aware tracking capabilities. We also provide an extended benchmark for evaluating any-speed trackers in online environments. Empirical results from robotic platforms with an aerial perspective demonstrate that PVT++ can improve various trackers by up to 60% and outperform prior model-based approaches in robustness, effectively mitigating performance degradation caused by latency. The code and models will be released publicly.

This work investigates computational techniques for approximating special functions that appear frequently in geometric function theory and quasiconformal mapping theory. These functions are characterized as either quotients or inverses of quotients of complete elliptic integrals. Specifically, we examine the distortion function $\varphi_K(r)$, which serves as an upper bound for $|f(x)|$ for any quasiconformal mapping $f: \mathbb{B}^2 \to \mathbb{B}^2$ satisfying $f(0)=0$. Notably, the proposed approximation method is remarkably efficient, requiring only five iterations of Landen's algorithm to attain machine precision.

Advancing particle physics necessitates a stable and thriving society, which is currently facing escalating threats from global climate change. Human-driven alterations to the climate have already disrupted weather patterns, and without substantial reductions in CO$_2$ and other greenhouse gas emissions, global warming will intensify. Consequently, both current and future endeavors in particle physics must be evaluated in light of this reality, either on moral grounds regarding our duty to preserve a habitable planet for future generations, or on practical grounds recognizing that large-scale projects will face scrutiny over their environmental impact. This white paper, prepared for the U.S. Particle Physics Community Planning Exercise ("Snowmass"), investigates various areas where particle physics influences the climate, including facility construction, detector design and operation, large-scale computing, and scientific research. We propose recommendations to foster climate-conscious practices within the field, aiming to minimize our environmental footprint. Furthermore, we call upon community members to endorse a sustainable particle physics future (https://indico.fnal.gov/event/53795/).

Effective object tracking relies on understanding an object's appearance, motion, and temporal evolution. While motion offers unique and complementary data—particularly for rapidly moving targets—most contemporary tracking systems prioritize appearance information. This paper introduces TRAT (TRacking by ATtention), a two-stream deep neural network tracker that integrates both spatial and temporal features. Built upon the ATOM framework, the architecture employs two backbones: a 2D-CNN to extract appearance features and a 3D-CNN to capture motion dynamics. These features are combined via an attention-based Feature Aggregation Module (FAM). Because the design is unified, the entire system supports end-to-end training. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that TRAT achieves state-of-the-art results across most benchmarks, significantly surpassing the baseline ATOM tracker.

Reference [1] provided a comprehensive analysis of the long-term asymptotic behavior of the total mass for the parabolic Anderson model on a supercritical Galton-Watson random tree, featuring an independent and identically distributed random potential with a double-exponential marginal distribution. Assuming a bounded support for the degree distribution, two terms in the asymptotic expansion were established under the quenched law—conditional on the specific realizations of both the tree and the potential. The second term included a variational formula, demonstrating that the solution concentrates on a subtree characterized by minimal degrees according to a computable profile. This paper extends that analysis to accommodate degree distributions with unbounded support. We determine the weakest tail condition on the degree distribution that allows the arguments from [1] to remain valid. Achieving this requires controlling the occurrence of large degrees uniformly across large subtrees within the Galton-Watson tree.

Bayesian neural networks predict nuclear masses by learning the mass surface of even-even nuclei and their correlation energies with neighboring nuclei. By integrating established physics from various sophisticated mass models and carefully designing the neural network architecture, the proposed Bayesian machine learning (BML) model achieves a precision of 84 keV, surpassing the 100 keV accuracy threshold within the experimentally known region. The study further demonstrates that prediction uncertainties are appropriately quantified, rising by approximately 50 keV at each step along isotopic chains as one moves toward uncharted regions. Additionally, shell structures in the known domain are accurately described, while several key features in the unknown region are forecasted, including new magic numbers near N = 40, the stability of the N = 82 shell, the weakening of the N = 126 shell, and smooth separation energies around N = 104.

This dissertation explores and improves Deep Learning (DL) methods for detecting objects such as pedestrians, cells, or vehicles in static images and video frames. A primary focus was addressing the scarcity of training data, which limits the scalability of current supervised neural network solutions due to restricted labeling budgets. This data shortage causes significant performance degradation when algorithms encounter new scenarios. To overcome these hurdles, we proposed multi-faceted solutions: generating automatically labeled datasets from virtual environments, implementing Domain Adaptation strategies to bridge distribution gaps between training and test data, and developing a counting approach for weakly labeled data where annotator disagreement is substantial. Additionally, we addressed the engineering complexities of deploying Convolutional Neural Networks on power-constrained devices, enabling direct counting of vehicles and pedestrians on embedded vision systems with limited computational resources.

Time series data serves as the primary input for educational prediction tasks. Most existing research relies on manually engineered features created by experts to ensure both interpretability and predictive performance; however, extracting these features is resource-intensive for both humans and machines. This paper introduces an approach leveraging irregular multivariate time series modeling with graph neural networks to achieve accuracy comparable to or exceeding that of hand-crafted features when using raw time series clickstreams. Additionally, we extend concept activation vectors to enhance interpretability within raw time series models. We apply these advancements to the education sector, specifically targeting early student performance prediction to facilitate downstream interventions and instructional support. Our experiments, conducted across 23 MOOCs involving millions of interactions across six behavioral dimensions, demonstrate that our models can (i) outperform state-of-the-art educational time series baselines without feature extraction and (ii) offer interpretable insights for personalized interventions. Source code: https://github.com/epfl-ml4ed/ripple/.

We introduce the inaugural systematic investigation into Concealed Object Detection (COD), a task dedicated to identifying items seamlessly integrated into their surroundings. The inherent visual similarity between hidden objects and their backgrounds renders COD significantly more difficult than conventional object detection or segmentation. To address this, we have compiled COD10K, a large-scale dataset comprising 10,000 images featuring concealed objects across 78 categories within various real-world contexts. This dataset includes comprehensive annotations, such as object categories, precise boundaries, challenging attributes, and both object-level and instance-level labels. As the most extensive and richly annotated COD dataset to date, COD10K facilitates deep understanding of concealed objects and supports advancements in related vision tasks like classification, segmentation, and detection. Inspired by natural hunting behaviors, we developed the Search Identification Network (SINet), a robust yet straightforward baseline. Without complex modifications, SINet surpasses 12 state-of-the-art methods across all tested datasets, establishing itself as a reliable and generalizable architecture to propel future COD research. We also present key insights, potential applications, and future research directions. To foster progress in this emerging field, our code, dataset, and online demo are accessible at http://mmcheng.net/cod.

The intricate architecture of Remeika phases, combined with their fascinating quantum behaviors and minimal carrier densities, provides a compelling drive to explore their superconducting characteristics. This study examines the microscopic attributes of the superconducting state in single-crystalline Lu$_3$Os$_4$Ge$_{13}$ using muon-spin relaxation and rotation ($\mu$SR) techniques. Zero-field $\mu$SR results indicate the existence of spontaneous static or quasi-static magnetic fields within the superconducting state, which violates time-reversal symmetry; notably, the magnitude of these internal magnetic fields is unusually high (approximately 0.18~mT). Additionally, transverse-field $\mu$SR data from the vortex state suggest a complex gap function characterized by varying strengths across different sections of the Fermi surface. Although these findings do not fully resolve the order parameter, they robustly suggest that electron-electron interactions are crucial for stabilizing the pairing mechanism, thereby confirming the unconventional nature of this system.

Near a quantum critical point, quenched disorder can induce a quantum Griffiths phase, characterized by exotic power-law scaling and a dynamical exponent that varies continuously and diverges as temperature approaches zero. In this study, we examine a nematic quantum critical point in the iron-based superconductor FeSe$_{0.89}$S$_{0.11}$ through the application of hydrostatic pressure. We observe an anomalous crossing of magnetoresistivity isotherms in the normal, non-superconducting state, which exhibits a continuously varying dynamical exponent across a broad temperature range. We attribute these findings to a quantum Griffiths phase arising from nematic islands generated by the local distribution of Se and S atoms. At low temperatures, however, the Griffiths phase is obscured by the onset of a Fermi liquid phase, driven by strong nematoelastic coupling and a Lifshitz transition that alters the Fermi surface topology.
We derive $H^{p}_{w} - L^{q}_{w^{q/p}}$ bounds for specific fractional operators.

GADTs may be modeled either through Church encodings in the style of Atkey or as fixpoints following Johann and Polonsky. Although a GADT using a Church encoding does not necessarily require a map function that adheres to functor laws, a fixpoint-based GADT must possess such a map function to be well-defined. Consequently, these two representations are not generally equivalent. This distinction necessitates a choice of representation for data types in languages that support GADTs. This paper demonstrates that selecting between Church encodings and fixpoints determines whether a GADT-supporting language can possess parametric models. Therefore, this decision significantly impacts how we program with and reason about these sophisticated data structures.

This study details measurements of groomed jet substructure in proton-proton (pp) and lead-lead (Pb-Pb) collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV using the ALICE detector. The Soft Drop algorithm isolates hard parton splittings within jets by eliminating soft, wide-angle radiation. We present results for the groomed jet momentum splitting fraction, $z_{\rm g}$, and the scaled groomed jet radius, $\theta_{\rm g}$. Charged-particle jets were reconstructed at midrapidity employing the anti-$k_t$ algorithm with resolution parameters of $R = 0.2$ and $R = 0.4$. In heavy-ion environments, the substantial underlying event complicates the measurement of groomed jet observables, as background fluctuations can lead to the misidentification of groomed parton splittings. By applying stringent grooming criteria to suppress this background, we provide the first fully corrected measurements of these observables, accounting for both detector effects and background fluctuations. We observe a narrowing of the $\theta_{\rm g}$ distribution in Pb-Pb collisions relative to pp collisions, offering direct evidence of altered angular jet structures within the quark-gluon plasma. Conversely, no significant modification of the $z_{\rm g}$ distribution is detected in Pb-Pb collisions compared to pp collisions. These findings are benchmarked against various theoretical models of jet quenching, thereby constraining mechanisms of jet energy loss and coherence effects in the quark-gluon plasma.

The occurrence of particle production in integrable field theories relies on the specific vacuum defining the excitations. To address this and related challenges using standard field theoretical methods, we examine the integrable $SU(2)$ $\lambda$-deformed model incorporating a timelike coordinate. We construct the associated four-dimensional plane wave background, retaining post-plane wave corrections and full $\lambda$-dependence. By enforcing the light-cone gauge and Virasoro constraints, we derive an interacting field theory for massive transverse physical modes. We explicitly show that particle production is absent to leading order in the large $k$-expansion, a result fundamentally tied to the structure of interaction vertices and their $\lambda$-dependence. Furthermore, we calculate the exact $S$-matrix for two-particle elastic scattering in terms of $\lambda$ and to leading order in the large $k$-expansion. This approach is applicable to any integrable theory possessing at least one isometry.

To effectively model the spatial arrangements of multiple species observed in nature, we propose the saturated pairwise interaction Gibbs point process. This model's primary advantage is its capacity to represent both attraction and repulsion forces, both within and across species, across varying scales, making it ideal for analyzing associations in complex ecosystems. Drawing from current literature, we offer a straightforward fitting procedure and a method for inferring model parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the point process is locally stable under specific conditions, enabling the use of the well-established "coupling from the past" algorithm to generate samples. Numerical experiments confirm the model's robustness. Finally, we analyze three distinct ecological datasets, illustrating in each case how our model effectively distinguishes between competing ecological influences on species distribution.

We present a quantum key distribution system utilizing subcarrier wave encoding within a Plug&Play setup. Our comprehensive analysis examines the performance of subcarrier encoding under Rayleigh back-scattering, chromatic dispersion, and other adverse experimental conditions typical of this configuration. We introduce and experimentally validate a new operational regime for subcarrier wave encoding that merges the simultaneous detection of two logical states in a single basis with the inherent robustness and simplicity of the original protocol. This deep modulation approach ensures reliable quantum communication despite losses reaching 20 dB and offers a predicted doubling of the secret key generation rate compared to standard subcarrier wave quantum key distribution in either one-way or Plug&Play configurations.

As quantum computing advances, practical utility becomes increasingly vital. Many quantum applications will be hybrid, with classical computers remaining essential for operation and utilization. However, the term "hybrid" is ambiguous and open to multiple interpretations. This work defines two distinct classes of hybrid quantum-classical computing: vertical and horizontal. The vertical class is application-agnostic and pertains to the use of quantum computers in general, while the horizontal class is application-specific and relates to executing particular algorithms. For both categories, we provide further subdivisions into various types of hybrid quantum-classical computing and introduce specific terminology for each.

This proposal outlines an M-class mission for ESA's 2021 science programme call, featuring diverse fundamental physics goals such as verifying the Equivalence Principle and Lorentz Invariance, investigating Ultralight Dark Matter, and exploring Quantum Mechanics.

Wireless communication has historically operated as a broadcast medium, creating inherent security and privacy vulnerabilities at the physical layer between transmitting and receiving pairs. As we transition toward advanced spectrum sharing techniques connecting billions of devices, it becomes critical to ensure that wireless signals remain secure, allowing only the intended receiver to access the signal's properties. This paper introduces Rand-OFDM, a novel waveform secured by a shared secret key, enabling signal property recovery exclusively at the legitimate receiver. We achieve signal-level security by altering the OFDM signal in the time domain, which eliminates standard OFDM characteristics and obscures the signal from eavesdroppers. Furthermore, we present a key-based training signal for channel estimation, accessible only to the intended receiver who possesses the secret key. Finally, a clustering-based method is employed to correct the phase of the received signal for recovery. Cryptanalysis indicates that Rand-OFDM is particularly well-suited for future wideband applications. Extensive simulations and over-the-air experiments demonstrate that Rand-OFDM performance is comparable to legacy OFDM, with an SNR penalty ranging from 1-4 dB due to the secured waveform. In all tested scenarios, the adversary remains unable to recognize the signal, even at maximum SNR levels.

Aggregated human judgments forecasting public health-critical COVID-19 targets prove accurate and frequently surpass computational models. Our research demonstrates that aggregated human forecasts for infectious agents are prompt, precise, and flexible, serving as an effective tool to support public health decision-making during outbreaks.

Bulk dielectric loss is a primary constraint on the lifetimes of advanced superconducting qubits. While recent experiments suggest upper limits for bulk dielectric loss tangents around $100$ parts-per-billion (ppb), these findings rely on fully fabricated devices containing multiple loss pathways, preventing a definitive attribution to dielectrics. To address this uncertainty, we developed a technique called the "dielectric dipper," which achieves a sensitivity of $5$ ppb. This method allows for the in-situ insertion of dielectric samples into high-quality microwave cavity modes; by smoothly adjusting the sample's participation factor, we perform differential measurements of the dielectric loss tangent. This approach probes low-power dielectric behavior at cryogenic temperatures without requiring lithography, facilitating controlled comparisons of various substrate materials and fabrication processes. Using this method, we measured EFG sapphire, determining a bulk loss tangent of $62(7) \times 10^{-9}$ and a substrate-air interface loss tangent of $12(2) \times 10^{-4}$. For a standard transmon, this bulk loss would restrict device quality factors to under $20$ million, indicating that bulk loss likely dominates in the longest-lived sapphire-based transmons. Additionally, we applied the technique to HEMEX sapphire, constraining its bulk loss tangent to below $15(5) \times 10^{-9}$. Since this bound is approximately four times lower than that of EFG sapphire, utilizing HEMEX sapphire as a substrate could raise the bulk dielectric coherence limit of a typical transmon qubit to several milliseconds.

Drawing inspiration from the research of Luk and Yau, as well as Huneke and Wiegand, this paper examines several facets of the cohomological rigidity inherent in tensor products of modules defined over commutative Noetherian rings. We establish conditions where the vanishing of one local cohomology module for a tensor product necessitates the vanishing of all lower-degree modules, and we uncover novel relationships between the local cohomology of tensor products and Tate homology. Furthermore, our approach provides bounds for the depth of tensor product modules and offers criteria for module freeness over complete intersection rings. Additionally, we present a splitting criterion for vector bundles situated on smooth complete intersections.

A recently introduced concept known as "ghost dark energy" aims to account for the current accelerated expansion of the universe. Derived from the Veneziano ghost in QCD, the energy density of this model is directly proportional to the Hubble parameter, expressed as $\rho_D=\alpha H$, where $\alpha$ represents a constant linked to the QCD mass scale. This study demonstrates a correspondence between ghost dark energy and the energy density of a quintessence scalar field. By establishing this link, we can derive the potential and dynamics of the quintessence field based on the evolution of the ghost energy density.

Interactions between objects are pivotal in shaping their behavior across numerous domains. While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) offer a potent means of modeling these interactions, they frequently introduce significant complexity and latency. This paper addresses spatial interaction modeling specifically for predicting the movement of actors around autonomous vehicles, exploring alternatives to GNNs. We re-examine 2D convolutions and demonstrate that they can match GNN performance in capturing spatial interactions while reducing latency, making them a viable and efficient solution for time-sensitive systems. Additionally, we introduce a new interaction loss function to further enhance the interaction modeling capabilities of the evaluated methods.

In the context of trajectory space, dynamical heterogeneities observed in glass-forming liquids are characterized by a dynamical phase transition between an active phase lacking local structure and an inactive phase abundant in it. This hypothesis is validated through an investigation of a model additive mixture of Lennard-Jones particles, specifically examining how the selection of pertinent structural and dynamical observables influences this transition. The results indicate that the low-mobility, structure-rich phase is primarily governed by icosahedral order. Furthermore, by employing a nonequilibrium rheological protocol, we establish a link between local structural order and the development of mechanical rigidity.

Device-independent quantum key distribution (DIQKD) utilizes the violation of Bell inequalities to generate secure keys, even when the users' hardware is untrusted. However, existing DIQKD protocols are currently limited by a secret key capacity bound, meaning the key generation rate increases only linearly with the users' channel transmittance. In this work, we introduce a heralded DIQKD protocol utilizing entangled coherent states, which enhances entanglement generation rates by creating long-distance entanglement through single-photon interference. Our proposed scheme achieves a secret key rate that significantly exceeds that of traditional two-photon Bell-state measurement methods and, crucially, breaks the aforementioned capacity limit. Consequently, this protocol represents a significant advancement toward practical DIQKD implementation and serves as a promising candidate for entanglement swapping in future quantum internet architectures.

Based on fundamental principles, I demonstrate the classical ultraviolet catastrophe, proving that source-free General Relativity must be quantized, a novel finding that contradicts certain respected views and addresses complex subtleties.

This paper reports the successful enumeration in Magma of representatives for the 195,826,352 conjugacy classes of transitive subgroups within the symmetric group $S_{48}$. We identified that 25,707 of these groups are minimal transitive and 713 are elusive. These minimal transitive examples facilitated the enumeration of vertex-transitive graphs of degree 48, totaling 1,538,868,366, with only 0.1625% not being Cayley graphs. Furthermore, we determined that the maximum number of generators required for any of these groups is 10, a finding that improves the third author's previous general bounds on the generation of arbitrary transitive permutation groups of a given degree; the proof of this improved bound will be published separately by the third author.

Let $X_N$ denote an $N$-dimensional subspace within $L_2$ functions defined over a probability space $(\Omega, \mu)$, generated by a uniformly bounded Riesz basis $\Phi_N$. For any integer $v$ where $1\leq v\leq N$ and exponent $q$ where $1\leq q\leq 2$, we establish a universal discretization for the $L_q(\Omega,\mu)$ integral norms of functions belonging to every subspace of $X_N$ formed by $v$ elements of $\Phi_N$. The required number of points $m$ satisfies $m\ll v(\log N)^2(\log v)^2$. This upper bound on $m$ significantly improves upon prior results, which were quadratic in $v$. The proof relies on a conditional theorem regarding universal sampling discretization alongside an inequality linking entropy numbers to greedy approximation with respect to dictionaries.

Grasping crystal morphology is a cornerstone of surface science, traditionally explained by how chemical bonding influences surface energies relative to orientation. However, the emergence of topological materials introduces a new framework, suggesting that topological surface states might alter surface energies and crystal facets in novel ways. We demonstrate that for glide-symmetric topological crystalline insulators (TCIs), surface energy exhibits a unique dependence on orientation, dictated specifically by the parity of the Miller index. This singular energy profile directly impacts equilibrium crystal shapes, giving rise to distinctive facets exclusive to these materials. Notably, this phenomenon arises from glide symmetry protection, distinguishing it from TCIs protected by mirror symmetry. Furthermore, we confirm through first-principles calculations that such singular states can be realized in KHgSb under glide symmetry. These findings offer a foundational approach for designing and controlling crystal facets by leveraging both symmetry and topology.

Although recent automated systems have achieved diagnostic accuracy comparable to board-certified dermatologists, they typically treat skin cancer diagnosis as a standalone classification problem, neglecting the advantages of lesion segmentation. We contend that precise segmentation can enhance classification by providing additional lesion characteristics such as asymmetry, borders, intensity, and size, while accurate classification can simultaneously aid segmentation by highlighting discriminative features. Consequently, we introduce MT-TransUNet, a novel multi-task framework that leverages Transformer-based multi-task tokens to collaboratively perform both segmentation and classification. Additionally, we incorporated dual-task and attended region consistency losses to utilize images lacking pixel-level annotations, thereby improving robustness against data augmentation. Experimental results on the ISIC-2017 and PH2 datasets demonstrate that MT-TransUNet outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in both tasks. Notably, it maintains superior computational efficiency with significantly fewer parameters (48M vs. 130M) and faster inference times (0.17s vs. 2.02s per image). The code will be accessible at https://github.com/JingyeChen/MT-TransUNet.

We confirm M. Barge's 1989 entropy conjecture by demonstrating that for any $r\in [0,\infty]$, there exists a pseudo-arc homeomorphism $h$ with topological entropy equal to $r$. Previously, the only known entropy values for pseudo-arc homeomorphisms were $0$ and $\infty$.

This paper offers a formal examination of temporally sensitive counterfactual conditionals. We identify several crucial metaphysical and conceptual issues concerning the intersection of counterfactual statements and time. In light of these challenges, we propose the most parsimonious framework combining Ockhamist branching time temporal logic with the minimal counterfactual logic P, and we advocate for this straightforward solution.

Evaluating machine learning initiatives necessitates assessing both the projected business return on investment and the technical complexity involved in constructing a model with specific attributes. This paper introduces a method for determining the essential performance metrics of a predictive model based on its intended application context. By employing this approach, organizations can conduct reliable and unbiased comparisons across different project proposals. These calculated estimates empower data scientists and management to assess the viability of a machine learning initiative prior to commencing any development work. The methodology has been operationalized within the open-source tool MinViME (Minimum Viable Model Estimator), accessible either through the PyPI Python package index or directly from its GitHub repository at https://github.com/john-hawkins/MinViME.

Determining the rank of an elliptic curve $E/\mathbb{Q}$ is a challenging task; consequently, applications such as searching for high-rank curves often depend on heuristics to estimate the analytic rank, which corresponds to the algebraic rank under the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture. This paper introduces rank classification heuristics based on deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Modeled similarly to the widely used Mestre-Nagao sums, the proposed method accepts the conductor of $E$ and a sequence of normalized $a_p$ values (where $a_p = p + 1 - \#E(\mathbb{F}_p)$ for primes of good reduction) within a specific range ($p < 10^k$ for $k=3, 4, 5$) to predict the rank or identify curves with "high" ranks. The model was trained and evaluated on two datasets: the LMFDB and a custom collection of elliptic curves with trivial torsion, conductors up to $10^{30}$, and ranks up to 10. For comparison, eight distinct neural network models utilizing Mestre-Nagao sums were also developed. Experimental results indicate that the CNN outperformed the individual Mestre-Nagao sums on the LMFDB dataset, particularly when the network processed all sums simultaneously, whereas performance was roughly equivalent on the custom dataset.

Recent breakthroughs in material synthesis have enabled the creation of two-dimensional monolayers of promising quantum spin liquid (QSL) candidates, including $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$, 1T-TaSe$_2$, and 1T-TaS$_2$. This study introduces an experimental configuration utilizing nonlocal electrical probes to investigate the transport characteristics of a gapless QSL. The proposed method involves a spinon-mediated drag experiment where current is injected into one layer and voltage is measured across a second metallic film. The underlying momentum transfer occurs via a two-step mechanism mediated by Kondo interactions between the local moments within the QSL and the spins of conduction electrons. While we initially calculated the drag relaxation rate for Kitaev, $\mathbb{Z}_2$, and U(1) QSLs using Aslamazov-Larkin diagrams under the assumption of negligible momentum relaxation within the QSL layer, we determined that dominant momentum relaxation is the more physically relevant scenario. Consequently, we developed a model grounded in the Boltzmann kinetic equation to describe the setup. Using this framework, we computed the low-temperature scaling of drag resistivity for both U(1) and $\mathbb{Z}_2$ QSLs possessing Fermi surfaces. Our results reveal a crossover in temperature scaling that distinguishes between $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and U(1) QSLs, driven by the non-Fermi liquid nature of the U(1) phase and distinct momentum relaxation mechanisms. These findings indicate that system parameters can be adjusted to ensure spinon-mediated drag constitutes a substantial portion of the total transresistance.

This work investigates the significant link between the cohomology ring ${\rm H^{\ast}(Gr}(d, d+r),\Z)$ of the Grassmannian ${\rm Gr}(d,d+r)$ and the lattice points within the dilated standard $d$-simplex, $r\Delta_{d}$. The inherent grading of the cohomology ring generates distinct gradings for the lattice points of $r\Delta_{d}$, resulting in various refinements of the Ehrhart polynomial $L_{\Delta_{d}}(r)$ for the standard simplex. We examine two specific refinements based on the weight sets $(1,1,\dots,1)$ and $(1,2,\dots, d)$. One of these refinements characterizes the Poincaré polynomial ${\rm P(Gr}(d,d+r),z)$ as a count of lattice points situated on the slicing hyperplanes of the dilation $r\Delta_d$. Consequently, at the combinatorial level, the Poincaré polynomial of the Grassmannian ${\rm Gr}(d,d+r)$ serves as a refinement of the Ehrhart polynomial $L_{\Delta_d}(r)$ for the standard $d$-simplex $\Delta_{d}$.

Modeling and comprehending the dynamics of BitTorrent (BT) remains a persistent area of research, driven by the system's inherent complexity and significant practical utility. Throughout history, various models have revealed diverse phenomena within the system, many of which directly influence its performance. This paper identifies and characterizes a previously unobserved phenomenon: homogeneous peers (those with similar upload capacities) experience heterogeneous download times. This behavior significantly affects peer and system performance, resulting in high variability in download durations, unfairness regarding peer arrival order, bursty departures, and content synchronization issues. To characterize this phenomenon, we conducted detailed packet-level simulations and prototype-based experiments on the Internet. Furthermore, we developed a mathematical model that accurately forecasts the heterogeneous download rates of homogeneous peers based on their content. Additionally, we utilized this model to determine lower and upper bounds for the number of bursty departures. These heterogeneous download rates are more prevalent in unpopular swarms, which typically contain very few peers. Although few studies have addressed such swarms, they currently represent the most common type of swarm in BitTorrent.

The $S$-matrix framework suggests that embedding a de Sitter state consistently within quantum gravity is feasible only as an excited quantum state built upon a valid $S$-matrix vacuum, such as Minkowski space. This paper presents such a construction, realizing de Sitter as a coherent state of gravitons. Distinguishing itself from prior attempts, our approach prioritizes BRST invariance as the criterion for physicality. To derive universal rules for gauge consistency, we examine the BRST-invariant formation of coherent states generated by both classical and quantum sources in QED and linearized gravity. By introducing $N$ copies of scalar matter coupled to gravity, we can access a specific double scaling limit known as the species limit. Within this limit, our de Sitter construction becomes exact: irrelevant quantum gravitational effects disappear, while collective phenomena, including Gibbons-Hawking radiation, become calculable.

The exponential growth in scientific literature has made it increasingly challenging for researchers across various disciplines to stay current with recent developments in their fields. While automated processing of articles has been suggested as a remedy, its accuracy remains inadequate for complex extraction tasks beyond basic ones. Few initiatives have attempted to address the root cause by reforming publication practices to ensure articles are machine-interpretable from the outset through the use of formal semantics. This study demonstrates that high-level scientific claims can be formally published in logic and disseminated via a special journal issue. Leveraging nanopublications, we represent not only submissions and final papers in an RDF-based format but also the entire lifecycle, including reviews, author responses, and editorial decisions. To achieve this, we conducted a field study using "formalization papers," which provide novel logical formalizations of previously published claims. The project received 15 submissions from 18 authors, who navigated the full publication process until their contributions were published in the special issue. Our evaluation confirms the technical and practical viability of this approach. Participating authors exhibited high levels of interest and confidence, finding the process relatively straightforward despite the technical nature of the existing interfaces. These findings suggest that publishing scientific results with machine-interpretable semantics from the start is feasible, potentially unlocking countless opportunities to significantly enhance the future efficiency and effectiveness of the scientific enterprise.

Surface electric noise, driven by fluctuations in surface charge density and the electrostatic potential at the crystal boundary, significantly impacts spin defects. Notably, the two-point correlation functions governing both charged particle positions and the surface electrostatic potential critically determine the polynomial decay power of the electric noise spectral density, a factor not exclusively defined by the nature of the charge fluctuators. Furthermore, the time-dependent crossover observed near the fluctuators' correlation time—specifically regarding spin defect relaxation and decoherence—serves as a quantitative indicator of the diffusive behavior of surface charged particles.

This study theoretically examines the optical conductivity of a tight-binding model featuring two distinct hopping integrals arranged according to a Fibonacci sequence. The absence of translational symmetry results in numerous peak structures within both the optical conductivity and the density of states. When the ratio between the two hopping integrals is sufficiently large, a self-similar pattern emerges in the optical conductivity. This phenomenon indicates that the optical response of high-energy bands is linked to that of low-energy bands, a connection attributed to critical behavior in the wave functions. Furthermore, the impact of disorder on optical conductivity is analyzed to demonstrate that self-similarity does not occur when the hopping sequence is random.

User scheduling and beamforming design are two interdependent critical components in wireless communication systems, often optimized independently using traditional methods. This paper introduces a novel cross-layer optimization framework that jointly addresses user scheduling and beamforming for multicell multiuser joint transmission networks, adhering to per-user Quality of Service (QoS) constraints and maximum transmit power limits. The objective is to maximize the system's sum rate through a mixed discrete-continuous variable optimization problem. To resolve the inherent non-convexity and dynamic solution space, the original problem is first converted into a 0-1 integer and continuous variable optimization task, which is then reformulated into a tractable continuous form by leveraging 0-1 constraint properties. An alternating optimization algorithm is subsequently employed to simultaneously determine the scheduled users and optimal beamforming vectors. Theoretical analysis confirms that base stations assign zero power to unscheduled users. Additionally, two heuristic algorithms based on brute-force and greedy search strategies are proposed. Numerical simulations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods, showing that the optimization approach yields relatively balanced performance compared to the alternative strategies.

This study seeks to reduce average file transmission delay through joint optimization of bandwidth allocation and cache placement within two-tier heterogeneous networks constrained by limited storage (comprising both cache and buffer capacities). For the specific case of fixed bandwidth allocation, the nonconvex average delay minimization problem yields a closed-form optimal solution by evaluating all locally optimal points derived from the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions. To address the joint optimization of bandwidth and caching, the optimal bandwidth allocation is first determined and substituted into the original formulation. The analysis reveals that the optimal caching strategy prioritizes files with high popularity over those with larger sizes. Leveraging this structural insight, we propose a low-complexity iterative algorithm that generates a suboptimal solution with a closed-form expression at each iteration. Numerical evaluations demonstrate that our approach outperforms conventional caching strategies that ignore the trade-off between cache and buffer capacities, specifically regarding delay reduction.

Advancements in computational capabilities and the emergence of cutting-edge deep learning algorithms have made appearance-based gaze estimation increasingly popular. Although these methods perform effectively on curated laboratory datasets, they encounter significant hurdles when applied to real-world scenarios. A primary challenge involves estimating gaze for individuals unknown to the model during training. To evaluate performance in such cases, we simulated a calibration mechanism using the MPIIGaze dataset. By training a multi-modal convolutional neural network and analyzing its performance both with and without calibration, this study provides clear insights into how calibration enhances the model's ability to estimate gaze in uncontrolled environments.

This paper establishes a connection between remote almost periodicity and quasi-asymptotical almost periodicity, demonstrating that a remotely almost periodic function is essentially a bounded, uniformly continuous quasi-asymptotically almost periodic function. We define and examine several novel classes of remotely $c$-almost periodic functions in ${\mathbb R}^{n}$, slowly oscillating functions in ${\mathbb R}^{n}$, and further investigate the recently proposed class of quasi-asymptotically $c$-almost periodic functions in ${\mathbb R}^{n}$. Additionally, we apply these theoretical findings to abstract Volterra integro-differential equations and ordinary differential equations.

We conducted photometric analysis on four Galactic globular clusters (NGC 4147, NGC 4590, NGC 5053, and NGC 7492) utilizing the far-UV and near-UV filters of the Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (UVIT) aboard AstroSat. By examining color-magnitude diagrams, we identified 150 blue horizontal branch stars and 40 blue straggler stars within these clusters. Our study further investigates the temperature and radial distribution patterns of both BHBs and BSS across the four GGCs.

This study analyzes the radial changes in correlation lengths parallel (\(\lambda_C^{\parallel}\)) and perpendicular (\(\lambda_C^{\perp}\)) to the magnetic field, utilizing solar wind magnetic data from the Parker Solar Probe (PSP) during its first eight orbits, as well as data from Helios 1, ACE, WIND, and Voyager 1. Correlation lengths are categorized based on the alignment angle (\(\Theta_{\rm BV}\)) between the magnetic field and solar wind velocity vectors. Specifically, parallel and perpendicular angular channels are defined by the ranges \(0^{\circ}~<~\Theta_{\rm BV}~<~40^{\circ}\) and \(50^{\circ}~<~\Theta_{\rm BV}~<~90^{\circ}\), respectively. Our findings reveal anisotropy in the inner heliosphere within 0.40 au, where the ratio \(\lambda_C^{\parallel} / \lambda_C^{\perp}\) is approximately 0.75 at 0.10 au. As heliocentric distance increases, this anisotropy diminishes, and the correlation lengths become roughly isotropic by 1 au. Data from ACE and WIND suggest a reversal of this anisotropy, resulting in a ratio of \(\lambda_C^{\parallel} /\lambda_C^{\perp} \approx 1.29\) at 1 au. Beyond 1 au, the ratio appears stable, though the limited number of parallel intervals in the Voyager dataset prevents definitive conclusions. This research offers insights into the radial evolution of large-scale, energetic turbulent fluctuations in the heliosphere. Furthermore, we highlight the critical need to account for changes in PSP sampling directions as the spacecraft nears the Sun when investigating turbulence evolution. Addressing this factor is essential for understanding the complex dynamics of the inner heliospheric solar wind and for enhancing related simulations.

Traditionally, the strong-$CP$ problem is treated as a naturalness issue, often regarding the axion as an ad hoc remedy, with gravity either neglected or seen as a danger to the global Peccei-Quinn symmetry. We argue that the reality is fundamentally distinct. Within a gravitational framework, the axion arises from $S$-matrix consistency, requiring that every gauge sector contain an axion that precisely relaxes the associated $\bar{\theta}$. This perspective supports a remarkably simple alternative formulation of the axion, entirely determined by QCD's gauge redundancy and independent of any global symmetry. The axion mechanism functions as a Higgs effect for the QCD $3$-form, guaranteeing that physical laws remain independent of $\bar{\theta}$ to all orders in the operator expansion. Furthermore, a near-future experimental observation of the neutron EDM would serve as definitive evidence for $CP$-violating physics beyond the Standard Model, with the axion coupling directly linked to the scale of gravity.

In 1968, Atkinson demonstrated the existence of functions satisfying all S-matrix axioms in four spacetime dimensions. His constructive proof remains, to our knowledge, the sole result of this kind; however, the techniques he employed have never been practically implemented. This paper examines the feasibility of those methods within the more tractable context of two-dimensional S-matrices. We address the reconstruction of scattering amplitudes from specified particle production probabilities by applying two numerical iterative approaches: fixed-point iteration and Newton's method. These schemes iterate through unitarity and dispersion relations until converging on solutions that satisfy S-matrix axioms. We map the region in amplitude-space where our algorithms converge and identify a fractal pattern linked to CDD ambiguities, which we term the "CDD fractal." Surprisingly, convergence issues align with recent investigations into coupling maximization within the two-dimensional S-matrix bootstrap. The methodologies presented here establish a foundation for extending these applications to higher dimensions and highlight potential hurdles that must be addressed.

This study introduces a Reduced-Order Model for hierarchical deep-learning neural networks (HiDeNN) utilizing Proper Generalized Decomposition (PGD). The resulting HiDeNN-PGD approach retains the distinct benefits of both HiDeNN and PGD techniques. Thanks to automatic mesh adaptivity, HiDeNN-PGD surpasses both the Finite Element Method (FEM) and traditional PGD in accuracy while utilizing only a fraction of the degrees of freedom required by FEM. Theoretical and numerical analyses, alongside comparisons with FEM, PGD, HiDeNN, and Deep Neural Networks, confirm the method's accuracy and convergence. Theoretically, it has been demonstrated that PGD converges to FEM as the number of modes increases, with the PGD error representing a direct sum of FEM error and mode reduction error. Ultimately, HiDeNN-PGD delivers high accuracy with orders of magnitude fewer degrees of freedom, indicating significant potential for rapid, high-precision computations in large-scale engineering applications.

This study details the computation of massless three-loop three-point integrals at the symmetric point, aiming to generalize established two-loop results to the three-loop level. The derived outcomes are applicable to QCD calculations within the regularization-invariant symmetric point momentum-subtraction (RI/SMOM) scheme, specifically for determining renormalization group functions and various composite operator matrix elements. Our methodology involves solving differential equations for auxiliary integrals by converting the system into the $\varepsilon$-form. The resulting integrals are expressed using a basis of functions characterized by uniform transcendental weight. Furthermore, we present an expansion of these basis functions up to transcendental weight six, formulated in terms of harmonic polylogarithms with a six-root of unity argument.

Acrylic plastic (PMMA) acoustic lenses have historically been employed to expand the acceptance angle of large, sensitive detectors and enhance lateral resolution; however, they often generate image artifacts caused by internal ultrasound reflections. This study addresses this limitation by evaluating a novel lens material, Stycast 1090SI. We compared the acoustic properties of Stycast 1090SI against PMMA, testing detector performance with negative lenses of both materials through finite element simulations and experimental validation. Additionally, image quality within a photoacoustic tomography system was assessed using both k-Wave simulations and physical experiments. Our characterization revealed that Stycast 1090SI exhibits tissue-mimicking acoustic impedance, a high speed of sound, and low acoustic attenuation. While both lens types successfully enlarged the detector's acceptance angle and improved lateral resolution, the proposed Stycast 1090SI lens significantly reduced image artifacts compared to the traditional PMMA lens.

We demonstrate that the real components of equivariant (yet non-invariant) eigenfunctions associated with generic bundle metrics on principal $S^1$ bundles over manifolds of arbitrary dimension possess connected nodal sets and precisely two nodal domains. This finding extends our previous work on the three-dimensional case. We illustrate the limitations of these results when $S^1$ actions are not free using even-dimensional spheres, specifically through one-parameter rotation subgroups where the fixed point set comprises two antipodal points.

This study examines the existence of almost periodic traveling fronts within one-dimensional almost periodic media for Fisher-KPP lattice equations. Utilizing the Lyapunov exponent of the linearized operator near the unstable steady state, we establish a sufficient condition for the minimal speed of these traveling fronts. Additionally, it is demonstrated that almost periodic traveling fronts exhibit the same recurrence characteristics as the underlying media structure. In terms of applications, we present several typical examples possessing minimal speed, with the proof relying on a dynamical systems approach to almost periodic Schrödinger operators.

Research into learning first-order planning models from unstructured data has primarily followed two paths: combinatorial methods that derive crisp action schemas from state space structures, and deep learning techniques that generate schemas from image-based state representations. While combinatorial approaches produce schemas resembling manually crafted rules, deep learning excels by grounding learned predicates in images, enabling the specification of new instances via visual input. This paper introduces a novel framework for learning crisp first-order planning models grounded in parsed images, effectively merging the strengths of both methodologies. The approach utilizes a simplified O2D language to represent parsed images, employing a limited set of unary and binary predicates such as "left," "above," and "shape." Following the learning process, planning instances can be defined using pairs of parsed images to denote initial and goal states. The study presents learning and planning experiments across multiple domains, including Blocks, Sokoban, IPC Grid, and Hanoi.

Understanding the statistical correlations between nodes relies heavily on the topology of a quantum network, yet this structural information is often unavailable or requires verification beforehand. This paper introduces an efficient protocol for inferring such network topology by uniquely characterizing it through entropic quantities, specifically von Neumann entropy and measured mutual information. Because the method relies solely on local measurements, it is practical and immediately applicable to quantum hardware. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the protocol remains completely robust against independent depolarizing noise provided that qubit measurements are accessible.

The rapid expansion of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) applications in daily life makes the detection of these drones and their pilots a critical requirement. Numerous UAVs utilize frequency hopping spread spectrum (FHSS) technology to communicate securely and efficiently with their radio controllers (RC), employing a hopping pattern to mitigate interference. To accurately distinguish between frequency hopping (FH) RC signals, it is essential to account for real-world radio propagation conditions, as long-distance communication between UAVs and RCs often involves both slow and fast fading phenomena. Unlike previous literature, this study examines a system operating under realistic conditions by capturing over-the-air signals in hilly suburban environments containing foliage. We employ the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) to extract the hopping sequence of each signal. Additionally, time guards for every hopping sequence are determined using the autocorrelation function (ACF) of the STFT, enabling precise differentiation of individual UAV RC signals. To validate the proposed method's performance, we present normalized mean square error (MSE) results across varying signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), window sizes, and transmitter-receiver separation distances.

We introduce the ELITR ECA corpus, a multilingual dataset extracted from publications by the European Court of Auditors. By combining automatic translation with Bleualign, we identified parallel sentence pairs across all 506 translation directions. The resulting corpus contains 264k document pairs and 41.9M sentence pairs.

Automated systems designed to negotiate with humans hold significant potential in conversational AI and education. To foster the creation of practical negotiation tools, we introduce CaSiNo, a new corpus comprising over 1,000 English-language negotiation dialogues. In this setup, participants assume the roles of campsite neighbors bargaining for essential supplies like food, water, and firewood for an upcoming journey. Our design ensures a diverse and linguistically varied dataset within a manageable, closed-domain setting. Drawing inspiration from human-human negotiation research, we annotate persuasion strategies and conduct correlation analyses to explore the link between dialogue behaviors and negotiation outcomes. Additionally, we develop and assess a multi-task framework for identifying these strategies within specific utterances. Our findings indicate that multi-task learning significantly enhances performance across all strategy labels, with notable gains for those that are most imbalanced. We are releasing the dataset, annotations, and source code to advance future research in human-machine negotiations: https://github.com/kushalchawla/CaSiNo

Controlling open quantum systems presents a significant challenge yet holds the potential to advance current quantum information processing technologies. We propose a comprehensive Reinforcement Learning framework designed to identify optimal thermodynamic cycles that maximize the power output of out-of-equilibrium quantum heat engines and refrigerators. Utilizing the soft actor-critic algorithm, we applied this method to three distinct systems: a standard two-level heat engine where we recovered the known optimal cycle; an experimentally viable superconducting qubit refrigerator that generates coherence, where our approach yielded a non-intuitive control sequence surpassing existing literature; and a quantum harmonic oscillator heat engine, where we discovered a complex cycle outperforming the optimized Otto cycle. Finally, we assessed the efficiency of these systems at maximum power.

This study investigates variable stars within the young open cluster NGC 1893 using a multi-year photometric survey spanning a $31' \times 31'$ field of view. Data reduction was performed on over 23,000 $V$-band images collected from January 2008 to February 2017 using various telescopes, supplemented by 90 $B$-band images from 2014 and 2017. Light curves for 5,653 stars were generated, leading to the detection of 147 variable stars, 85 of which are new discoveries. These include 110 periodic variables, 15 eclipsing binaries, and 22 non-periodic variables. By examining proper motions, radial velocities, and color-magnitude and two-color diagrams, 84 of these variables were confirmed as cluster members. These periodic members were classified based on their magnitudes, variability periods, and positions in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, specifically for early-type stars. Among the main-sequence periodic members, we identified five $\beta$ Cep candidates, seven slowly pulsating B-type candidates, and thirteen fast-rotating pulsating B-type (FaRPB) candidates, including one confirmed classical Be star. While most FaRPB stars resemble those found in NGC 3766 by Mowlavi et al. (2013), five exhibit periods under 0.1 days, contrary to expectations. Further characterization through additional spectroscopic observations is recommended. Additionally, a binary candidate containing a $\delta$-Scuti candidate was identified.

The swift expansion of behind-the-meter (BTM) distributed generation has prompted reforms in net energy metering (NEM) policies to tackle critical issues such as escalating electricity costs, equitable cost distribution, and the sustainable growth of distributed energy resources. This paper introduces an analytical framework for determining optimal prosumer consumption strategies through an inclusive NEM X tariff model that encompasses both current and proposed tariff structures. The resulting optimal consumption policy facilitates near closed-form solutions, making it highly suitable for practical energy management systems capable of responding to stochastic BTM generation and dynamic pricing. Furthermore, the study evaluates the short-term and long-term performance of NEM and feed-in tariffs (FiT) within a sequential rate-setting context. Additionally, numerical results are provided to analyze social welfare distributions, cross-subsidies, and long-term solar adoption outcomes for specific NEM and FiT policy designs.

This study investigates the adiabatic exponent $\Gamma_1$ within the partially ionized plasma of the solar convection zone, focusing on how heavy elements influence its profile. Using the SAHA-S equation of state, we computed $\Gamma_1$ for various chemical compositions to analyze the specific contributions of individual elements. Our methods involved comparing the reduction in $\Gamma_1$ caused by the ionization of heavy elements against that of a pure hydrogen-helium plasma. These differences, termed "Z contributions," were examined for eight specific elements (C, N, O, Ne, Mg, S, Si, and Fe) and for mixtures reflecting solar composition. We further tested linear combinations of these individual contributions against exact values and employed a least-squares approach to decompose the total Z contribution into individual components to derive heavy element mass fractions.

The results indicate that the Z contribution from heavy elements can be accurately represented as a linear combination of individual-element contributions, achieving a precision of $5 \times 10^{-6}$. We also addressed the inverse problem of inferring heavy element mass fractions from a known $\Gamma_1$ profile using solar-type mixtures. In ideal numerical simulations, the mass fractions of the most abundant elements can be determined with a relative accuracy superior to a few tenths of a percent. However, the presence of random or systematic errors in the $\Gamma_1$ profile significantly reduces this accuracy. Specifically, if error amplitudes remain below $1 \times 10^{-4}$, it is feasible to determine the oxygen abundance with a relative error of approximately 10%.

Photonic graph states, characterized by mutual entanglement among multiple photons, serve as fundamental resources for optical quantum technologies, particularly in error-corrected measurement-based computing and all-optical networks. Within the discrete variable framework, these applications demand the high-efficiency creation of cluster states composed of indistinguishable photons. While such states can be produced using heralded single-photon sources and probabilistic gates, these methods face significant challenges regarding efficiency and scalability. Conversely, spin-photon entanglement offers a pathway to deterministically generate linear cluster states. Initial demonstrations utilizing semiconductor spins have achieved high photon indistinguishability, and recent work with atomic systems has attained high collection efficiency and record-breaking lengths. This study reports the efficient generation of three-partite cluster states involving one semiconductor spin and two indistinguishable photons. We utilize a semiconductor quantum dot embedded in an optical cavity to ensure efficient photon collection and electrical control for superior indistinguishability. We verify two- and three-particle entanglement with fidelities of 80% and 63%, respectively, and an indistinguishability of 88%. Furthermore, the entanglement rates for spin-photon and spin-photon-photon systems surpass the previous state of the art by two and three orders of magnitude, respectively. Our proposed monolithic solid-state device, controlled via a resource-efficient and simple experimental setup, shows great promise for future scalable applications.

We have performed a comprehensive $k$-mode analysis of single-inflaton slow-roll inflationary perturbations, incorporating quantum fluctuations. This was achieved by formulating non-linear coupled differential equations for the inflaton field ($\phi$), its perturbation ($\delta\phi$), and the metric perturbation (Bardeen potential, $\Phi_B$). Using $E$-model $\alpha$-attractor potentials, which exhibit slow-roll behavior, we calculated the number of e-folds ($N$), scalar spectral index ($n_s$), tensor spectral index ($n_h$), scalar power spectrum ($\Delta_s$), tensor power spectrum ($\Delta_h$), tensor-to-scalar ratio ($r$), and Hubble parameter ($H$) for various $k$ values at horizon crossing. Our derived values for $n_s$ and $r$ align with established universal $\alpha$-attractor formulae. Specifically, for a potential parameter $n=1$, we obtained $n_s = 0.956908$ and $r = 0.005571$ at $k = 10^6$ Planck units. These results are consistent with observational data from Planck-2018 ($n_s = 0.9649 \pm 0.0042$ at $68\%$ CL, $r < 0.064$ at $95\%$ CL) and ACT-2020 ($n_s = 0.9691 \pm 0.0041$ at $68\%$ CL).

How can we achieve efficient planning in large, complex environments under tight time constraints? Since the original environment simulator can be computationally intensive, we propose learning an online, approximate simulator that becomes increasingly faster and more accurate over time. To ensure reliable and efficient planning while this approximation is still learning, we introduce a method that adaptively selects the appropriate simulator for each step based on a statistical metric of the approximate simulator's accuracy. This strategy allows the system to substitute the original simulator with the faster approximate version whenever the latter is sufficiently accurate for the current context, effectively balancing simulation speed against accuracy. Experimental results across two large domains demonstrate that, when integrated with POMCP, our approach enables planning with progressively improving efficiency over time.

It has recently been suggested that neural networks can approximate high-dimensional probability distributions found in statistical mechanics and lattice field theories. These networks serve as variational approximators for calculating extensive system properties, such as free energy, and as samplers for Monte Carlo simulations. However, their practical utility is hindered by poor scaling of both computational cost and memory usage relative to system size. This limitation stems from the original method, which required neural network width to scale with the total number of degrees of freedom (e.g., $L^2$ for a two-dimensional $L \times L$ lattice). In this study, we introduce a hierarchical mapping of physical degrees of freedom, such as spins, to neurons, changing the scaling to depend on the system's linear dimension $L$. We validate this approach using the two-dimensional Ising model, successfully simulating lattices up to $128 \times 128$ spins with benchmarks extending to $512 \times 512$. Our results show that this method enhances training quality, yielding a probability distribution closer to the target than previously possible. Consequently, the variational free energy aligns more closely with theoretical expectations, and when integrated into Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms, the autocorrelation time decreases. Furthermore, substituting a single large network with a hierarchy of smaller ones significantly lowers memory demands.

This work quantifies the impact of private key leakage and randomness generated during quantum key distribution. We establish straightforward lower bounds for the one-way distillable key following the detection of such leakage. Additionally, we demonstrate that distributed private randomness decreases by no more than twice the number of qubits in the traced-out system.
