We are observing a significant increase in remote privacy attacks targeting laptop computers, which frequently utilize malware to access microphones and webcams for surveillance. Although commercial webcam covers provide some protection, effective solutions for mitigating microphone attacks remain scarce despite recent industry initiatives. To address this vulnerability, we introduce TickTock, a novel system designed to detect microphone on/off states. TickTock achieves this by externally analyzing electromagnetic (EM) emissions originating from laptop connectors and cables that transmit microphone clock signals; these signals are emitted exclusively during active recording. We have designed and implemented a proof-of-concept system to validate TickTock's feasibility. Additionally, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation across 30 popular laptops running various applications, successfully detecting microphone status in 27 devices. In these cases, TickTock consistently identified recording activity with high true positive and negative rates.

This paper introduces a projection-based framework designed to solve a thermodynamically-consistent Cahn-Hilliard Navier-Stokes system for two-phase flows. Building upon the fully implicit method by Khanwale et al. (2020), we extend the approach to a block iterative hybrid scheme. Specifically, we employ a projection-based semi-implicit time discretization for the Navier-Stokes equations and a fully-implicit scheme for the Cahn-Hilliard equation. Spatially, we utilize a conforming continuous Galerkin (cG) finite element method augmented with a residual-based variational multiscale (RBVMS) formulation. By decoupling pressure through a projection step, we obtain two linear positive semi-definite systems for velocity and pressure, avoiding the saddle point system typical of pressure-stabilized methods. All resulting linear systems are resolved efficiently and scalably using an algebraic multigrid (AMG) method. Implemented on a massively parallel platform with adaptive octree-based meshes, this strategy enables larger time steps and significantly faster solution times. Comprehensive numerical experiments are provided, offering detailed comparisons with existing literature for canonical scenarios such as single bubble rise and Rayleigh-Taylor instability.

A moving dielectric medium can shift the optical path of light traversing it, a phenomenon recognized as the Fresnel-Fizeau optical drag effect, where the displacement scales with the medium's velocity. In this article, we present an anomalous optical drag effect, in which the displacement remains proportional to the medium's speed but occurs in the direction opposite to its motion. We performed an optical drag experiment under electromagnetically-induced transparency conditions and observed the transition from normal to null to anomalous optical drag by adjusting the two-photon detuning.

As data volumes expand, clustering and outlier detection algorithms are becoming progressively slower. Traditional index structures for neighbor search are no longer viable because of the "curse of dimensionality." Conversely, approximate index structures present a promising solution to substantially speed up neighbor search for these algorithms while minimizing result errors. Locality-sensitive hashing is a prime example of such an approach. We outline directions for modeling the characteristics of LSH.

This paper addresses the robust output feedback stabilization of invertible multi-input multi-output nonlinear systems featuring output-dependent multipliers. Initially, an "ideal" state feedback control is constructed based on specific mild assumptions. Subsequently, a collection of extended low-power high-gain observers is methodically developed to accurately estimate this ideal feedback law. Consequently, a robust output feedback stabilizer is achieved, ensuring that the closed-loop system's origin is semiglobally asymptotically stable; this approach also enhances numerical implementation by utilizing high-gain parameters raised to a power of up to 2.

Few-Shot Object Detection (FSOD) represents a rapidly expanding area within computer vision, focused on identifying instances of specific classes using only a limited number of annotated examples per class. While numerous methods have been developed to tackle this challenge, the majority rely on attention mechanisms. However, the diverse landscape of traditional object detection frameworks and training strategies complicates performance comparisons across different approaches. This difficulty is particularly pronounced when evaluating how various attention mechanisms affect results in attention-based FSOD methods. This paper seeks to address this gap by proposing a flexible framework capable of implementing most attention techniques found in the literature. To facilitate the introduction of this framework, the paper first provides a comprehensive review of existing FSOD methods. Subsequently, several distinct attention mechanisms are reimplemented within the proposed framework and compared while keeping all other parameters constant.

We present a flow-augmentation algorithm for directed graphs, demonstrating the existence of a polynomial-time procedure that, given a directed graph $G$, source and target vertices $s,t \in V(G)$, and an integer $k$, randomly adds arcs to $G$. This augmentation ensures that for every minimal $st$-cut $Z$ in the original graph with size at most $k$, the set $Z$ becomes a minimum $st$-cut in the modified graph with probability $2^{-\mathrm{poly}(k)}$. This directed flow-augmentation technique enables us to establish the fixed-parameter tractability of several problems parameterized by deletion set size, addressing long-standing open questions regarding their parameterized complexity. Specifically, these problems include: (1) Chain SAT, introduced by Chitnis, Egri, and Marx [ESA'13, Algorithmica'17]; (2) various weighted versions of classic directed cut problems, such as Weighted $st$-Cut, Weighted Directed Feedback Vertex Set, and Weighted Almost 2-SAT. Furthermore, by proving that Chain SAT is fixed-parameter tractable, we validate a conjecture by Chitnis, Egri, and Marx stating that for any graph $H$, if the List $H$-Coloring problem is solvable in polynomial time, then the associated vertex-deletion problem is also fixed-parameter tractable.

This study tackles the challenge of discrete-time average consensus among agents communicating over unreliable links. We improve the Robustified Ratio Consensus algorithm by integrating the Automatic Repeat ReQuest (ARQ) protocol, enabling agents to achieve asymptotic average consensus even in unreliable directed networks. Beyond managing time-varying delays caused by retransmissions (which the Robustified Ratio Consensus already addresses), this approach also handles packet losses resulting from exceeding a predefined ARQ retransmission limit. Utilizing the ARQ protocol allows nodes to: (a) leverage error-free acknowledgement feedback to initially determine or subsequently update their out-degrees, (b) confirm packet arrival status, and (c) establish a local upper bound on delays dictated by the retransmission constraint. By modifying the network's weighted adjacency matrix to accommodate time-varying but bounded delays and potential packet drops, we demonstrate that the proposed ARQ-based Ratio Consensus algorithm ensures asymptotic average consensus despite unreliable communication links. To our knowledge, this represents the first consensus algorithm to incorporate a real-world communication protocol with feedback for error control.

Fast radio bursts (FRBs) represent short, intense, extragalactic radio flashes, yet their origins remain largely unidentified. While analyzing the FRB population is crucial for understanding these astrophysical events, such research has historically been hindered by the scarcity of FRBs and uncharacterized observational biases. Leveraging the newly released catalog of 536 FRBs from the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment/Fast Radio Burst (CHIME/FRB) collaboration, this study investigates the FRB population while correcting for selection effects. Adopting a Schechter luminosity function, we derive a characteristic energy cutoff of $E_\mathrm{char} = 2.38^{+5.35}_{-1.64} \times 10^{41}$ erg and a differential power-law index of $\gamma = -1.3^{+0.7}_{-0.4}$. Concurrently, we estimate a volumetric rate of [$7.3^{+8.8}_{-3.8}$(stat.)$^{+2.0}_{-1.8}$(sys.)]$\times 10^4$ bursts per Gpc$^{-3}$ year$^{-1}$ for events exceeding a pivot energy of 10$^{39}$ erg and occurring below a 10 ms scattering timescale at 600 MHz; however, we cannot significantly constrain cosmic evolution relative to the star formation rate. By modeling the host dispersion measure (DM) as a log-normal distribution with an assumed Galactic contribution of 80 pc cm$^{-3}$, we determine a median $\mathrm{DM}_\mathrm{host}$ of $84^{+69}_{-49}$ pc cm$^{-3}$, a value consistent with standard literature figures. Proposed FRB progenitor models must align with the energetics and abundance of the full FRB population predicted here. Furthermore, we infer the redshift distribution of CHIME-detected FRBs, a prediction that will be validated using localization and redshift data from the upcoming CHIME/FRB Outriggers project.

To bridge the gap in healthcare access and quality between urban and rural areas, it is essential to address significant challenges such as high chronic disease prevalence, limited provider availability, and the ongoing closure of rural hospitals. Consequently, Appalachian cancer patients must increasingly rely on health information technology (HIT). Existing tools like the NCCN Distress Thermometer and Problem List (DT) suffer from being under-utilized, lacking patient-centeredness, failing to account for provider needs, and becoming obsolete in today's digital environment. Transitioning to digital distress screening offers key benefits, including more frequent assessments, the elimination of geographical obstacles, and enhanced autonomy for rural patients. This paper explores how insights from patient-centered design informed the development of a rural remote patient monitoring application, creating an engaging and informative experience for its users.

The Ce$^{3+}$ pseudospin-$\frac{1}{2}$ degrees of freedom in the pyrochlore magnet Ce$_2$Zr$_2$O$_7$ exhibit dipole-octupole (DO) characteristics, positioning the material as a potential candidate for novel quantum spin liquid (QSL) ground states at low temperatures. This study presents new low-temperature polarized neutron diffraction data and heat capacity ($C_p$) measurements on single-crystal Ce$_2$Zr$_2$O$_7$. The diffraction results show both parallels and distinctions when compared to the canonical dipolar spin ice compound Ho$_2$Ti$_2$O$_7$, while the heat capacity rises sharply at low temperatures, forming an initial plateau near 0.08 K before decreasing toward a high-temperature zero beyond 3 K. Above approximately 0.5 K, the $C_p$ data aligns with quantum numerical linked cluster (NLC) calculations performed to the 4$^{\mathrm{th}}$ order, enabling estimates for the near-neighbour XYZ Hamiltonian terms expected in such DO pyrochlore systems. This analysis is supported by fitting the same theoretical model to the temperature dependence of magnetic susceptibility and unpolarized neutron scattering. Comparing the optimal NLC fit with polarized neutron diffraction reveals both agreement and discrepancies, particularly regarding zone-boundary diffuse scattering in the non-spin flip channel, which are attributed to interactions extending beyond near-neighbours. The absence of a thermodynamic anomaly, combined with constraints on the near-neighbour XYZ Hamiltonian, suggests that Ce$_2$Zr$_2$O$_7$ realizes a U(1)$_\pi$ QSL state at low temperatures, likely situated near the boundary between dipolar and octupolar character.

Mobile Edge-Cloud Computation Offloading (MECCO) is considered a vital solution for supporting latency-sensitive applications in current and future Internet of Things (IoT) networks. Nevertheless, offloading tasks to the cloud presents security vulnerabilities, particularly when malicious mobile devices (MDs) are involved. Addressing the dual challenge of reducing computational burdens on MDs while ensuring robust security within a mobile edge cloud environment remains a difficult task. This paper explores both security and computation offloading in a multi-user MECCO system enhanced by blockchain technology. First, to enhance offloading security, we introduce a blockchain-based trustworthy access control mechanism designed to safeguard cloud resources from unauthorized offloading attempts. Subsequently, to manage computation for authorized MDs, we formulate an offloading optimization problem that jointly determines offloading decisions, allocates computing resources and radio bandwidth, and utilizes smart contracts. The objective of this optimization is to minimize the long-term system costs regarding latency, energy consumption, and smart contract fees across all MDs. To address this problem, we devise an advanced deep reinforcement learning algorithm employing a double-dualing Q-network. Experimental evaluations and numerical simulations confirm that our proposed scheme offers significant improvements over existing methods.

For a wide sense stationary signal sampled across a full linear array, the ensemble covariance matrix is both Toeplitz and positive semi-definite. In contrast, the direct augmented covariance matrix of an augmentable sparse array, while Toeplitz, fails to be positive semi-definite, leading to negative eigenvalues that complicate tasks such as source localization and model order estimation. Although existing methods based on positive eigenvalues offer robustness, they become unattainable when the direct augmented matrix possesses negative noise eigenvalues. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a robust covariance matrix for augmentable sparse arrays that utilizes both positive and negative noise eigenvalues. This proposed estimate integrates effectively with subspace-based algorithms and adaptive beamformers to achieve precise signal direction estimates.

Conway and Sloane's book identifies a subalgebra within the Hurwitz quaternionic integers ($\mathscr{H}$)—the set of quaternions over integers and half-integers—that is isomorphic to the alternating group $2 \cdot A_4$. Building on this foundation, this paper extends the concept of quaternions over integers and half-integers to incorporate duality, demonstrating that a subalgebra within this extended structure is isomorphic to the Exceptional Weyl group $W(F_4)$. Furthermore, a construction method for the $16$-dimensional lattice $\Lambda_{16}$ is presented using Dual Quaternions; this lattice appears to be isomorphic to the highly dense Barnes-Wall lattice $\Lambda_{\text {Barnes-Wall }}$, a claim that warrants further discussion. Finally, the paper briefly outlines a procedure for constructing the Exceptional Weyl group $W(E_8)$ by utilizing Octonions and Dual Quaternions.

Future plans for the High Energy Photon Source (HEPS) include up to 90 beamlines, making it crucial to reduce individual beamline workloads and maximize the transferability of knowledge across them to lower overall control complexity. This paper outlines our efforts to meet these objectives by developing straightforward utilities and mechanisms to automate tasks, prioritizing simplicity and clarity in our automation solutions. Following an introduction to our selected EPICS-based software, we discuss the challenges and solutions related to integrating package management into EPICS modules, along with a concise overview of our packaging system's design and implementation. We then present our work on reducing the need for custom multi-device EPICS IOC applications through reusable modular executables, followed by an explanation of our maintainable multi-IOC setups achieved by separating and minimizing individual user configurations. Finally, we introduce the ongoing project for comprehensive HEPS beamline services aimed at further simplifying configuration management across multiple scales, from single devices to the entire facility.

Low-temperature calorimeters utilizing Transition Edge Sensors (TESs) and operating below 100 mK are ideal for rare event detection, offering exceptional resolution and sensitivity. This paper details initial experimental outcomes from two prototype detectors employing a new thermometer coupling design called remoTES. This innovation broadens the scope of TES technology by accommodating a diverse range of absorber materials that would otherwise be incompatible with direct TES fabrication due to factors like hygroscopicity, low hardness, or low melting points. This capability is particularly significant for the COSINUS experiment (Cryogenic Observatory for SIgnals seen in Next-Generation Underground Searches), which utilizes sodium iodide (NaI) as an absorber. Testing two remoTES prototypes in an above-ground R&D setting yielded energy resolutions of $\sigma=87.8$ eV for a 2.33 g silicon absorber and $\sigma = 193.5$ eV for a 2.27 g $\alpha$-TeO$_{2}$ absorber. Beyond enabling a wider selection of absorber materials, remoTES calorimeters provide a more streamlined production process, improved reproducibility for large-scale detector arrays, and superior radiopurity standards.

Creating immersive, 3D communication environments demands a method to generate photo-realistic 360-degree human avatars, ideally using only consumer-grade hardware such as smartphone cameras. To ensure realistic rendering from every angle, training data and camera poses from all directions are essential; however, traditional pose estimation often fails when trackable features are absent in the foreground or background, particularly when viewing the head from the side or rear. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel landmark detector trained on synthetic data, designed to infer camera poses from 360-degree mobile videos of human heads. These pose estimates feed into a multi-stage optimization pipeline that produces photo-realistic avatars. We validate our approach using synthetic datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness by generating 360-degree avatars from mobile phone video recordings.

A submanifold $M^m$ embedded in a Euclidean space $R^{m+p}$ is defined as having harmonic mean curvature if its mean curvature vector field $\vec{H}$ satisfies $\Delta \vec{H}=0$, where $\Delta$ denotes the rough Laplacian on $M$. Bangyen Chen proposed a conjecture asserting that any submanifold in a Euclidean space with a harmonic mean curvature vector field must be minimal. This paper demonstrates that weakly convex hypersurfaces—those with nonnegative principal curvatures—possessing harmonic mean curvature vectors in Euclidean spaces are indeed minimal. Additionally, we establish that weakly convex biharmonic hypersurfaces situated in space forms with nonpositive curvature are also minimal.
We characterize specific Lagrangian fibrations involving Prym varieties on holomorphic symplectic varieties that deform into compactifications of Sp-Hitchin systems.

This study reports the identification of SDSS J095909.51+460014.3 (J0959+4600, $z$ = 0.399) as a new $\gamma$-ray emitting narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy ($\gamma$-NLS1), confirmed by linking it to the $\gamma$-ray source 4FGL 0959.6+4606. Although its low-energy counterpart was previously attributed to the radio galaxy 2MASX J09591976+4603515 (J0959+4603), long-term *WISE* light curves reveal distinct infrared variability patterns between the two. J0959+4600 exhibits violent infrared fluctuations with amplitudes reaching one order of magnitude, whereas J0959+4603 shows only mild variability. Crucially, the peak of the infrared flare in J0959+4603 coincides with the brightening of 4FGL 0959.6+4606, yet J0959+4603 remains in a quiescent flux state during this event. Analysis of 15 months of Fermi-LAT data focused on the high $\gamma$-ray flux state identifies a significant source (TS = 41). Localization results indicate that only J0959+4600 lies within the uncertainty region, reinforcing the revised association. Furthermore, the broadband spectral energy distribution of J0959+4600 is well modeled by a classic single-zone homogeneous leptonic jet model, and its jet properties are found to be consistent with those of other $\gamma$-NLS1s.

Adversarial Examples (AEs) created by perturbing original training data are valuable for enhancing the robustness of Deep Learning (DL) models. However, most existing approaches produce AEs that are either lexically flawed or deviate significantly in semantics and function from the originals. This paper introduces ReinforceBug, a reinforcement learning framework that learns a transferable policy capable of generating utility-preserving AEs that remain effective across unseen datasets and different models. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves a 10% higher success rate on average compared to the state-of-the-art TextFooler attack. Furthermore, target models exhibit an average confidence of 73.64% in their incorrect predictions, while the generated AEs maintain functional equivalence and 83.38% semantic similarity to the original inputs. Additionally, these AEs show transferability to other models with an average success rate of 46%.

Applying Wang-Landau sampling (WLS) to extensive systems typically involves partitioning the energy spectrum into "windows" and merging the outcomes from each segment. However, this approach yields density of states and related thermodynamic properties that are compromised by boundary artifacts when simulating lattice polymers and the five-state Potts model. In this study, we introduce an adaptive windowing strategy for WLS. Rather than relying on static energy intervals (or fixed regions in the energy-magnetization plane for the Potts model), the window boundaries dynamically adjust based on the energy values at which the histogram achieves flatness at each simulation stage. By repositioning the windows whenever the modification factor $f$ decreases, we successfully eradicate the border effects inherent to fixed-window methods. Consequently, adaptive windows substantially broaden the range of system sizes that can be investigated with reliability using WLS.

The CMS detector at the LHC measured the production cross sections of $B^0_\mathrm{s}$ mesons and their charge conjugates in both proton-proton (pp) and PbPb collisions through the exclusive decay channel $B^0_\mathrm{s} \to \mu^+\mu^-K^+K^-$. These measurements were conducted at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair, restricted to the rapidity range $|y| < 2.4$. For pp collisions, the cross section was analyzed as a function of the $B^0_\mathrm{s}$ transverse momentum ($p_\mathrm{T}$) between 7 and 50 GeV/$c$, with results compared to perturbative QCD predictions. In PbPb collisions, the $B^0_\mathrm{s}$ yield was determined in two $p_\mathrm{T}$ intervals (7–15 and 15–50 GeV/$c$) and contrasted with the pp yield within the same kinematic regions. The resulting nuclear modification factor ($R_\mathrm{AA}$) was found to be $1.5 \pm 0.6\,(\text{stat}) \pm 0.5\,(\text{syst})$ for the 7–15 GeV/$c$ range and $0.87 \pm 0.30\,(\text{stat}) \pm 0.17\,(\text{syst})$ for the 15–50 GeV/$c$ range. Within current uncertainties, these findings align with models predicting strangeness enhancement and the suppression previously observed in $B^+$ mesons.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are susceptible to adversarial examples that trick them into making prediction errors through minimal perturbations in input images. Researchers have focused on advancing universal adversarial perturbations (UAPs), specifically those that do not rely on gradients or prior knowledge of data distributions. One such approach is procedural adversarial noise attack, a data-free method for generating universal perturbations. This paper introduces two UAP generation techniques based on procedural noise functions: Simplex noise and Worley noise. Our framework utilizes rendering technology to create shading that disrupts visual classification. Crucially, while maintaining semantic integrity, the adversarial examples produced by our methods demonstrate superior attack performance.

This work addresses the challenge of learning a rotation-invariant latent factor model from training data consisting of lower-dimensional projections within the original feature space. The primary objective is to identify a set of 3-D basis poses capable of characterizing the manifold of primitive human motions, known as movemes, derived from a collection of 2-D projected poses captured in still images across various camera angles. The proposed approach for discovering these bases is data-driven instead of being manually designed. The resulting representation achieves rotation invariance and enables the reconstruction of any training instance from multiple viewing perspectives. We evaluate our method on modeling human poses in sports using the Leeds Sports Dataset, demonstrating the utility of the learned bases in diverse applications including activity classification, dynamic inference from single frames, and the synthetic representation of movements.

Vision Transformers process images by dividing them into patches, where the patch dimensions dictate a tradeoff between speed and accuracy. Smaller patches enhance accuracy but increase computational demands, and typically, adjusting patch sizes necessitates retraining the model. This paper introduces a method where randomizing patch sizes during training yields a single set of weights that performs effectively across various patch dimensions. This approach, named FlexiViT, allows models to be adapted to different compute constraints at deployment without retraining. Extensive evaluations across diverse tasks—such as classification, image-text retrieval, open-world detection, and both panoptic and semantic segmentation—show that FlexiViT generally matches or exceeds the performance of standard ViT models trained with fixed patch sizes under identical conditions. Consequently, FlexiViT offers a straightforward, drop-in enhancement for ViT-based architectures, enabling compute-adaptive capabilities. The associated code and pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/google-research/big_vision.

This study presents B-CANF, a novel B-frame coding framework leveraging conditional augmented normalizing flows. Since learned B-frame coding remains an under-explored and difficult area, B-CANF builds upon recent progress in conditional P-frame coding to become the first application of flow-based models to both conditional motion and inter-frame coding. The framework incorporates frame-type adaptive coding to optimize bit allocation for hierarchical B-frame structures and introduces a specialized B*-frame designed to emulate P-frame coding. Experimental results on standard datasets demonstrate that B-CANF achieves state-of-the-art compression performance, delivering BD-rate metrics (PSNR-RGB) comparable to HM-16.23 within the random access configuration.

Current self-supervised monocular depth estimation methods either neglect independently moving objects or require an additional segmentation stage to detect them. We introduce MonoDepthSeg, a framework that simultaneously estimates depth and segments moving objects from monocular video without relying on ground-truth annotations. Our approach partitions the scene into a fixed set of components, where each component represents a specific image region governed by its own motion transformation matrix. Using a shared encoder, we efficiently estimate both the motion and mask for each component. Experiments on three driving datasets demonstrate that our model significantly enhances depth estimation accuracy by decomposing the scene into distinct moving parts.

Rare $b$-hadron decays serve as powerful tools for investigating microscopic new semileptonic four-fermion interactions, yet these same interactions also modify the high-mass tails of the Drell-Yan process. This study revisits the potential of rare $b$ decays by examining this complementarity to map out viable short-distance new physics scenarios. We incorporate the most recent measurements of $b \to q \ell^+ \ell^-$ transitions (with $q = d, s$ and $\ell = e, \mu$), specifically including the latest LHCb $R_{K^{(*)}}$ results, alongside updated high-mass Drell-Yan data for both charged ($p p \to \ell \nu$) and neutral ($p p \to \ell^+ \ell^-$) currents. Utilizing a sophisticated analysis pipeline within the flavio framework, we efficiently explore the multidimensional SMEFT parameter space. To demonstrate flavio's enhanced capabilities, we develop explicit models based on $Z'$ bosons or leptoquarks that resolve the tension in $b \to s \mu^+ \mu^-$ angular distributions and branching ratios while predicting lepton flavor universality ratios consistent with the Standard Model, $R_{K^{(*)}} \approx R^{{\rm SM}}_{K^{(*)}}$, as suggested by recent observations. Finally, these models are tested against the global likelihood, which includes high-mass Drell-Yan constraints, to determine whether they exhibit tensions or remain compatible with existing data.

The emergence of magnetic flux is broadly acknowledged as a critical factor in triggering coronal mass ejections. The Chen-Shibata (2000) framework, which links emerging flux to flux rope eruptions, is utilized here in numerical simulations to examine how photospheric flux emergence influences the eruption of pre-existing coronal flux ropes. A parameter study explores the model's sensitivity to initial conditions and reconnection micro-physics, with a specific focus on the stability of the coronal flux rope during X-point collapse and the impact of boundary driving within both unstratified and stratified atmospheres. In scenarios without driving, the behavior of waves near the X-point is analyzed. When boundary driving is introduced, the study investigates how reconnection micro-physics and atmospheric stratification affect the eruption. Results indicate that the Chen-Shibata equilibrium can become unstable to X-point collapse even without driving, caused by wave accumulation at the X-point; however, this instability can be mitigated by reducing plasma compressibility, enabling small-amplitude waves to traverse the X-point without accumulating. Simulations incorporating photospheric boundary driving reveal that the system's evolution is governed primarily by the global magnetic field structure, showing minimal sensitivity to reconnection micro-physics. Furthermore, within a stratified atmosphere, a new mechanism is identified that generates quasi-periodic behavior at the reconnection site behind a rising flux rope, offering a potential explanation for similar phenomena observed in solar and stellar flares.

Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) generate unique identifiers for physical objects by leveraging inherent physical randomness. However, Gao et al. highlighted that many existing PUFs are susceptible to advanced machine learning attacks. To overcome this limitation, we propose integrating classical PUFs with established quantum communication technologies. This paper introduces a generic framework for provably secure PUFs, termed Hybrid Locked PUFs (HLPUFs), offering a practical method to enhance the security of classical PUFs. An HLPUF combines a classical PUF (CPUF) with the encoding of its output into non-orthogonal quantum states, effectively concealing the CPUF's results from potential adversaries. We further implement a quantum lock to safeguard HLPUFs against general threats. By utilizing the indistinguishability of non-orthogonal quantum states alongside the quantum lockdown mechanism, we prevent adversaries from accessing CPUF outcomes. Additionally, we demonstrate that leveraging the non-classical properties of quantum states enables the server to reuse challenge-response pairs for extended client authentication. This approach offers an efficient solution for long-term PUF-based authentication while maintaining a compact challenge-response database on the server side. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings by instantiating the HLPUF design using readily available real-world CPUFs. By employing optimal classical machine-learning attacks to forge both CPUFs and HLPUFs, we confirm a security gap through numerical simulations, demonstrating a construction ready for practical implementation.

This paper investigates smooth minimax optimization problems defined as $\min_{\bf x}\max_{\bf y} f({\bf x},{\bf y})$, where the objective function $f$ is $\ell$-smooth, strongly concave with respect to ${\bf y}$, but potentially nonconvex in ${\bf x}$. While prior research predominantly targets first-order stationary points of either $f({\bf x},{\bf y})$ or the primal function $P({\bf x})\triangleq \max_{\bf y} f({\bf x},{\bf y})$, few address the achievement of second-order stationary points. We introduce Minimax Cubic Newton (MCN), a new methodology capable of locating an $\big(\varepsilon,\kappa^{1.5}\sqrt{\rho\varepsilon}\,\big)$-second-order stationary point of $P({\bf x})$. This approach utilizes ${\mathcal O}\big(\kappa^{1.5}\sqrt{\rho}\varepsilon^{-1.5}\big)$ second-order oracle calls and $\tilde{\mathcal O}\big(\kappa^{2}\sqrt{\rho}\varepsilon^{-1.5}\big)$ first-order oracle calls, where $\kappa$ denotes the condition number and $\rho$ represents the Lipschitz constant of the Hessian of $f({\bf x},{\bf y})$. Furthermore, to address high-dimensional challenges and reduce reliance on costly second-order oracles, we propose an inexact MCN variant. This method solves the cubic sub-problem approximately using gradient descent and matrix Chebyshev expansion, achieving the desired second-order stationary point with high probability while requiring only $\tilde{\mathcal O}\big(\kappa^{1.5}\ell\varepsilon^{-2}\big)$ Hessian-vector oracle calls and $\tilde{\mathcal O}\big(\kappa^{2}\sqrt{\rho}\varepsilon^{-1.5}\big)$ first-order oracle calls. To our knowledge, this study presents the first analysis of non-asymptotic convergence for finding second-order stationary points in minimax problems without relying on convex-concave assumptions.

When collaborating with humans, robots must focus not only on their environment and tasks but also on comprehending their partner's reasoning. To aid humans in complex scenarios, robots can share their knowledge; however, indiscriminately communicating everything can be distracting or annoying, as humans may already possess some information, and not all data is pertinent to the current context. The concept of Theory of Mind-based Communication addresses the critical questions of when and what information to share by selecting actions based on relevance assessments and estimates of human beliefs. We integrated this concept into a communication assistant to support cooperative settings and evaluate its performance benefits. We designed a challenging human-robot sushi-making task that creates situations where human unawareness occurs, making communication advantageous. A user study evaluated how this human-centric communication approach influences performance. Compared to conditions without information exchange, participants receiving assistance recovered from unawareness significantly earlier. This approach effectively balances interruptions and respects communication costs, outperforming other methods. By providing situationally adapted information, the robot enables rather than instructs, empowering humans to make optimal decisions.

Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) is a core task aimed at predicting emotion labels from audio data. Recent research predominantly relies on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to extract local attention maps from fixed-scale features by treating time-varying spectral data as images. However, existing CNNs struggle to effectively capture rich emotional features across various scales and crucial global information. To address this, we introduce a novel Global-Aware Multi-scale (GLAM) neural network, available at https://github.com/lixiangucas01/GLAM, which learns multi-scale representations using a global-aware fusion module to focus on emotional cues. Specifically, GLAM iteratively employs convolutional kernels of varying sizes to generate multiple feature representations. Subsequently, rather than relying on attention-based techniques, it utilizes a simple yet effective global-aware fusion module to extract the most significant global emotional information. Experiments conducted on the IEMOCAP benchmark corpus across four emotion categories demonstrate that our model outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods, achieving improvements of 2.5% to 4.5% on four standard metrics.

This work establishes a canonical form for block matrices, enabling streamlined calculations of determinants, inverses, higher powers, logarithms, and exponentials. These advancements are especially beneficial for block covariance and correlation matrices, significantly simplifying Gaussian log-likelihood evaluations and estimation processes. An empirical study using daily asset returns demonstrates these applications. Furthermore, this representation offers novel approaches for regularizing large covariance or correlation matrices, testing block structures within matrices, and estimating regressions involving numerous variables.

A graph is defined as $\alpha$-excellent when each of its vertices belongs to at least one maximum independent set. This paper provides two distinct characterizations for $\alpha$-excellent $2$-trees.

We establish explicit, sharp two-sided bounds for the transition density of the Langevin process under a quadratic potential, conditioned to remain within the interval (0,1). Additionally, we derive the long-term asymptotic behavior of this density, which demonstrates that the associated killed semigroup exhibits uniform conditional ergodicity.

The Richards equation, widely utilized for simulating water and air movement within soil and acting as a fundamental model for multiphase flow in porous media, is a nonlinear advection-reaction-diffusion equation characterized by both parabolic-hyperbolic and parabolic-elliptic degeneracies. This study establishes reliable, fully computable, and locally space-time efficient a posteriori error bounds for numerical solutions to the fully degenerate Richards equation. To demonstrate global reliability, a nonlocal-in-time error estimate is derived separately for the time-integrated $H^1(H^{-1})$, $L^2(L^2)$, and $L^2(H^1)$ errors, with the latter utilizing a maximum principle and a degeneracy estimator. Subsequently, global and local space-time efficiency bounds are established within the standard $H^1(H^{-1})\cap L^2(H^1)$ norm. When the equation lacks nonlinearity, the norms for reliability and efficiency align. Furthermore, the analysis isolates and identifies specific error contributors, including flux nonconformity, time discretization, quadrature, linearization, and data oscillation. These estimates remain valid even when iterative linearization with inexact solvers is applied. Numerical experiments were performed on nondegenerate and degenerate cases with known exact solutions, as well as a realistic scenario, demonstrating that the estimators accurately pinpoint errors within a factor of order unity.

An infinite-type surface $\Sigma$ belongs to type $\mathcal{S}$ if it possesses an isolated puncture $p$ and supports shift maps; this category encompasses all such surfaces with an isolated puncture, excluding only two sporadic exceptions. For these surfaces, we establish an infinite collection of intrinsically infinite-type mapping classes that act loxodromically on the relative arc graph $\mathcal{A}(\Sigma, p)$. While J. Bavard previously demonstrated the existence of such an element for the plane minus a Cantor set, our work provides the inaugural examples for all remaining surfaces of type $\mathcal{S}$. Our constructed elements arise as the composition of three shift maps on $\Sigma$, and we also offer an alternative characterization defining them as the composition of a pseudo-Anosov map on a finite-type subsurface of $\Sigma$ with a standard shift map. Furthermore, we explicitly determine their limit points on the boundary of $\mathcal{A}(\Sigma,p)$ and their associated limiting geodesic laminations. Ultimately, we demonstrate that these infinite-type elements enable the proof that $\text{Map}(\Sigma,p)$ admits an infinite-dimensional space of quasimorphisms.

Over the past few years, energy harvesting has garnered significant interest within wireless communication research. However, the inherent stochasticity of renewable energy sources has emerged as a critical challenge, prompting the proposal of energy storage as a viable solution. Initially, researchers utilized idealized battery models that ignored storage losses due to their simplicity and analytical compatibility. Yet, to address practical realities, battery models must now account for energy dissipation. This paper examines a wireless communication system incorporating a battery with losses during both charging and discharging cycles. We treat energy underflows—instances where battery levels drop below a specific threshold—as the primary management issue, characterizing the underflow probability through a simple exponential formulation derived from the large deviation principle and queueing theory. By leveraging the parallels between battery and data buffer models, we introduce the "available space decay rate" as a metric for energy consumption performance. Furthermore, we propose a method to establish energy demand policies that satisfy management requirements by constraining the underflow probability. Finally, we validate our analytical results with numerical simulations, comparing the transmission performance of a system utilizing a lossy battery against one that consumes harvested energy immediately.

The interplay between supermassive black holes and their surroundings is most clearly observed through the hot atmospheres of dark matter halos. As these hot atmospheres cool, they supply fresh gas to the central regions, triggering active galactic nuclei (AGN) that operate with extended duty cycles. In response, outflows from the central engine interact tightly with the surrounding gas, acting as the primary heating mechanism that prevents runaway cooling by creating cavities and generating shocks. This AGN feedback loop is a fundamental component of contemporary galaxy evolution models. In this review, we examine the current understanding of AGN feedback specifically within galaxy groups, which are uniquely positioned to constrain the mechanisms balancing cooling and heating. Unlike in more massive halos, the energy injected by the central AGN into the hot intragroup medium can surpass the gravitational binding energy of the halo gas. We present the latest observational evidence and theoretical models regarding this heating-cooling balance in galaxy groups. Furthermore, we outline how insights into AGN feedback influence galaxy evolution simulations and the distribution of baryons on large scales. Finally, we discuss how upcoming instrumentation will address critical open questions in this field.

Few-shot algorithms are designed to master new tasks using only a limited number of training examples. This study explores few-shot learning within a context where data consists of token sequences, introducing an efficient Transformer-based learning method. In its most basic form, a task-specific token is appended to the input sequence, allowing the embedding of this token to be optimized dynamically with minimal labeled data. Unlike other meta-learning or few-shot approaches, our method avoids complex architectural modifications like adapter layers or the computation of second-order derivatives. We evaluate this approach across various tasks, analyzing the generalization capabilities of different model variants and baselines. Specifically, we demonstrate that using compositional task descriptors enhances performance. Experimental results indicate that our method achieves performance comparable to existing techniques while offering superior computational efficiency.

We conduct a detailed analysis of superconductivity within an extended Hubbard model representing a multiband system characterized by repulsive interactions. Our findings demonstrate that virtual interband processes generate an effective attractive interaction at small momentum transfers, a phenomenon rarely observed in standard superconductivity models based on repulsion. This attraction originates, in real space, from correlated hopping terms driven by interband polarization. We elucidate this mechanism using strong-coupling expansions and many-body perturbation theory, supported by numerical computations. Furthermore, we highlight notable parallels with interacting electrons in twisted bilayer graphene, underscoring the significance of interband contributions to superconductivity.

It is widely assumed that enforcing invariance enhances generalization, yet a rigorous theoretical proof of this advantage has only recently emerged. This study extends the function space framework proposed by Elesedy and Zaidi (arXiv:2102.10333) to demonstrate a strictly positive generalization gain when incorporating invariance into kernel ridge regression for targets invariant under a compact group's action. By examining invariance through feature averaging, we reveal that generalization is controlled by an effective dimension resulting from the interaction between the kernel and the group. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the group's action creates an orthogonal decomposition of both the reproducing kernel Hilbert space and its associated kernel, a finding that may hold independent significance.

Controlling large-scale quantum many-body systems presents significant challenges. A promising strategy involves entangling these systems with diluted counterparts containing a minimal number of particles. Such entangled states can be effectively prepared either as the ground state of a many-body Hamiltonian or as the steady state of an open many-body quantum system. This study investigates two-site lattice models featuring a conserved boson number, specifically biased to exhibit high occupancy at one site. Analysis of the Von Neumann entanglement entropy and logarithmic negativity reveals a characteristic power-law decay with respect to $R$, the occupancy ratio between the two sites. These findings suggest that it is indeed feasible to entangle a large many-body system with a single atom, a possibility recently confirmed by experimental reports.

SemEval-2020 Task 12, known as OffenseEval, focused on identifying offensive language in social media across multiple languages (Zampieri et al., 2020). This competition was split into three sub-tasks: detecting offensive language, automatically categorizing offense types, and identifying the targets of offenses. I contributed to Task-C, which involved offense target identification. To develop my system, I utilized Deep Learning architectures such as LSTMs and the Keras framework. The approach combined a bag-of-words model with automatically generated sequence-based features alongside manually extracted features from the dataset. Training on 25% of the total data yielded a macro-averaged F1 score of 47.763%.

To remedy the widespread lack of familiarity with nuclear history among engineers and physicists, we present the design and implementation of a special-topics course titled "NE290: Nuclear History, Politics, and Futures." This course contextualizes the field's significance regarding its origins, contemporary relevance, and future applications. We first examine deficiencies in secondary education concerning nuclear history and their implications for non-technical engineering standards. Subsequently, we align ABET specifications as pedagogical goals to establish specific student learning objectives. The course syllabus is then detailed, including assignments and a chronological overview of content. We provide an in-depth description of the instructional materials and methodologies for the four core units: 20th-Century Physics, Physics in WWII, the Early Cold War, and the Late Cold War and Modern Era. The sequence of lectures and historical timelines are outlined, culminating in a showcase of final projects that reflect the innovative nature of the course. Since NE290 debuted in Spring 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic, it incorporated additional remote learning tools, such as videoconferencing to engage geographically diverse guest speakers and the MIRO platform for virtual whiteboarding. Finally, we report on course outcomes based on student feedback, which, alongside the comprehensive course materials, supports the integration of nuclear history into the broader nuclear engineering and physics curricula.

We computed electron energy loss spectra (EELS) for composite plasmonic systems utilizing silicene and germanene. Multiscale EELS calculations for these materials on silver substrates were executed using a continued-fraction representation of the effective dielectric function. A notable shift in plasmonic behavior is observed when the germanene or silicene surface layer exceeds three atoms in thickness. These variations can be leveraged through spectroscopic analysis to verify the successful fabrication of few-layer coatings.

Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) requires users to manually define reward functions, a process that is both time-consuming and technically demanding. This paper proposes an alternative RL framework where users specify tasks by providing examples of desired outcomes rather than explicit reward functions. We introduce a control algorithm designed to maximize the likelihood of these successful outcomes in the future. Unlike previous two-stage approaches that first learn a reward function and then optimize it, our method directly learns a value function from state transitions and outcome examples, bypassing the need for an intermediate reward function. This streamlined approach reduces the number of hyperparameters to tune and minimizes debugging efforts. We demonstrate that our method adheres to a novel data-driven Bellman equation, substituting the standard reward term with outcome examples. Experimental results indicate that our approach surpasses prior methods reliant on explicit reward function learning.

The triumph of deep learning has driven interest in enhancing relational table tasks, such as data preparation and search, using table representation models trained on extensive corpora. However, current corpora mainly consist of tables scraped from HTML, which restricts their ability to represent offline database tables. To develop and assess high-capacity models for applications extending beyond the web, there is a need for resources featuring tables that mirror relational database structures. We present GitTables, a corpus comprising 1 million relational tables extracted from GitHub, with ongoing efforts to expand this to at least 10 million tables. Analyses reveal that GitTables' structure, content, and topical coverage differ substantially from existing corpora. We annotate GitTables' table columns with semantic types, hierarchical relations, and descriptions sourced from Schema.org and DBpedia. Evaluations of our annotation pipeline on the T2Dv2 benchmark demonstrate performance comparable to human annotations. We showcase three applications of GitTables, highlighting its utility for learned semantic type detection, schema completion, and benchmarks for table-to-KG matching, data search, and preparation. The corpus and associated code are accessible at https://gittables.github.io.

Motzkin paths are defined by up-steps, down-steps, and level-steps, remaining non-negative throughout and terminating on the $x$-axis. The notion of a skew Dyck path \cite{Deutsch-italy} is adapted to skew Motzkin paths by permitting an additional left step $(-1,-1)$, provided the path does not intersect itself. While the enumeration of these structures was previously established \cite{Qing}, this work employs the kernel method to generalize those findings by allowing paths to conclude at a specific level $j$. The methodology relies entirely on generating functions, and the study also provides asymptotic formulas for both the total count of such objects and their average height.

Recommendation Systems enable users to discover trending items within a community that are both timely and aligned with their expectations. Depending on the specific goals of a system, the nature of the recommendations required varies across different use cases. While some systems prioritize popular items, others focus on suggesting content similar to a user's specific interests. To achieve higher-quality recommendations, researchers have developed various approaches, including Content-based filtering, Collaborative filtering (both user-to-user and item-to-item), and more recently, Deep Learning methods.

Although each of these techniques performs well on its own, efforts have been made to overcome their individual limitations. By adopting a hybrid approach in model and architecture design, researchers have sought to enhance the capabilities of standard systems, delivering more effective recommendations that also offer greater business profitability. This paper reviews novel models and architectures within hybrid Recommendation Systems. It examines opportunities to expand the capabilities of baseline models, along with the specific advantages and drawbacks of each approach, illustrated through selected use cases.

We tackle the challenge of jointly demosaicking and deblurring noisy raw images by adapting a learning-based RGB deblurring framework. This adaptation introduces a novel, interpretable module designed to perform both tasks simultaneously. The model is trained using RGB images synthetically converted to raw format via a realistic, invertible camera pipeline. Our results demonstrate superior performance compared to two-stage methods that sequentially stack demosaicking and deblurring components, validated on quantitative benchmarks. Furthermore, we utilize this approach to eliminate the inherent color-dependent blur (point-spread function) found in real camera captures, effectively sharpening images.

Standard double-copy procedures for multi-loop amplitudes with massive matter coupled to gauge theories typically yield gravitational amplitudes that include unwanted contributions from propagating antisymmetric tensors and dilatons, even at tree level. We introduce a graph-based methodology that integrates maximal cuts with double-copy construction to provide a systematic framework for isolating pure Einstein-Hilbert gravitational terms at the loop level. This approach enables the bootstrapping of pure-gravity results derived from the double-copy of massive scalar-QCD. Applying this method, we derive a novel $D$-dimensional one-loop five-point QFT integrand relevant in the classical limit, which is essential for generating observables related to the radiative effects of massive black-hole scattering within pure Einstein-Hilbert gravity.
We introduce the concept of a Manifold equipped with a complex Lie structure at infinity, a category that encompasses the significant class of ACH manifolds.

The multi-role judicial debate, involving the plaintiff, defendant, and judge, constitutes a vital component of judicial trials. Distinct from other dialogues, questions are initiated by the judge, while the plaintiff, their agent, the defendant, and their agent engage in debate to ensure the trial proceeds orderly. Question generation is a critical task in Natural Language Generation; within the judicial context, it enables judges to formulate efficient inquiries, thereby gaining a clearer grasp of the case. This study introduces an innovative end-to-end question generation model, the Trial Brain Model (TBM), designed to construct a "Trial Brain" capable of generating the judge's desired questions based on the historical dialogue between the plaintiff and defendant. Unlike previous approaches in natural language generation, our model learns the judge's questioning intentions through predefined knowledge. Experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate that our model yields more accurate questions in multi-role court debate scenarios.

The study investigates the evolution of a subsystem's reduced density matrix to quantify deviations from Markovian behavior within a closed chain of $N$ oscillators, where one oscillator acts as the subsystem. Numerical analysis explores how these deviations depend on $N$ and the coupling between the two subsystems. The results indicate that these deviations are heavily influenced by both $N$ and the coupling strength. In the most favorable scenario, with $N-1=100$ and a randomized coupling structure, deviations decrease over time to as low as 3%. Conversely, in other configurations, deviations remain substantial, often reaching 30% or higher.

Standard knowledge distillation for classification relies on class correlations within soft labels, a mechanism unavailable in regression tasks such as predicting stock trading volumes. To address this limitation, we introduce a new distillation framework designed to train a lightweight student model for volume prediction using historical transaction data. By transforming the regression task into a probabilistic forecasting problem where models predict a Gaussian distribution for the trading volume, the student can learn from the teacher at a distributional level by aligning its predicted distributions with those of the teacher. Additionally, two correlation-based distillation objectives are implemented to ensure the student maintains consistent pairwise relationships with the teacher. Evaluated on a real-world stock volume dataset across two different time window configurations, the framework outperforms strong baselines by reducing model size by 5x while sustaining 99.6% prediction accuracy. Comprehensive analysis further indicates that this approach is more effective than traditional distillation methods in low-resource settings.

Effective feature representation is crucial for instance image retrieval. Current methods typically rely on deep models pre-trained on standard benchmarks or fine-tuned using task-specific labeled auxiliary data. While these approaches yield promising results, they are constrained by two main challenges: the domain gap between benchmark datasets and the target retrieval dataset, and the difficulty of acquiring the necessary auxiliary data. Addressing these limitations, this study explores an underinvestigated strategy: learning feature representations specifically tailored to a given retrieval task. Our findings are positive; by incorporating an object proposal generator to create image regions for self-supervised learning, the proposed method successfully learns dataset-specific representations. Furthermore, integrating image similarity information mined from the dataset enhances the effectiveness of these features. Experimental results demonstrate that this straightforward "self-supervised learning plus self-boosting" approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art retrieval methods. Additionally, ablation studies highlight the method's advantageous characteristics and its limitations regarding cross-dataset generalization.

The ATLAS detector has conducted a search for the decay of the Standard Model Higgs boson into a $b\bar{b}$ pair, specifically when produced in association with a $W$ or $Z$ boson. This analysis utilized data from 79.8 $\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collisions recorded during Run 2 of the Large Hadron Collider at a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. For a Higgs boson mass of 125 GeV, an excess of events over the expected background from other Standard Model processes was observed with a significance of 4.9 standard deviations (4.3 expected). By combining these Run 2 results with previous searches from Run 1 and Run 2 for the Higgs boson in the $b\bar{b}$ channel, an overall observed (expected) significance of 5.4 (5.5) standard deviations was achieved, confirming the direct observation of the Higgs boson decaying into $b$-quarks. The measured event yield for this decay mode relative to the Standard Model prediction is $1.01 \pm 0.12 \mathrm{(stat.)} ^{+0.16}_{-0.15} \mathrm{(syst.)}$. Furthermore, a combination of Run 2 results for the vector boson-associated production of the Higgs boson resulted in an observed (expected) significance of 5.3 (4.8) standard deviations.

This paper investigates CDF $W$-mass, muon $g-2$, and dark matter observables within a local $U(1)_{L_\mu-L_\tau}$ framework featuring three vector-like leptons ($E_1, E_2, N$), a new gauge boson $Z'$, a symmetry-breaking scalar $S$, and a scalar dark matter particle $X_I$ alongside its partner $X_R$. Our analysis indicates that the CDF $W$-mass data disfavors scenarios where $m_{E_1} = m_{E_2} = m_N$ or where the mixing parameters for left- and right-handed fields ($s_L, s_R$) vanish. Conversely, a significant mass splitting between $E_1$ and $E_2$ is preferred when the difference between $s_L$ and $s_R$ is minimal. We demonstrate that the muon $g-2$ anomaly can be resolved simultaneously under specific conditions involving the disparity between $s_L(m_{E_1})$ and $s_R(m_{E_2})$, although certain parameter regions are ruled out by diphoton signals from the 125 GeV Higgs. When combined with CDF $W$-mass, muon $g-2$, and other constraints, the viable dark matter relic density is primarily achieved through two mechanisms: (i) annihilations into $Z'Z'$ or $SS$ for $m_{Z'}(m_S) < m_{X_I}$, and (ii) co-annihilation processes when the lightest mass among $E_1, E_2, N,$ and $X_R$ is close to $m_{X_I}$. Finally, we utilize LHC direct searches for $2\ell + E_T^{miss}$ events to constrain the model, delineating the permissible mass ranges for vector-like leptons and dark matter.

Given that linear-optical two-photon gates operate probabilistically, measurement-based approaches are ideally suited for photonic systems, where computation is executed by consuming a large, highly entangled resource known as a graph state via measurements. The primary hurdle lies in generating these graph states. While various methods utilizing interacting quantum emitters or efficient spin-photon interfaces have been suggested for deterministic creation, they remain experimentally unattainable, with current capabilities limited to linear graph states. In this work, we present near-deterministic generation techniques for graph states leveraging existing quantum emitter technologies. We propose a hybrid strategy that combines quantum-emitter-based generation with all-photonic fusion gates to produce graph states of complex topologies with near-deterministic reliability. These findings are expected to facilitate the practical realization of resource-efficient quantum information processing, encompassing measurement-based quantum communication and computing.
We demonstrate an extension of the Bogomolov-Tian-Todorov theorem applicable to Calabi-Yau categories.

For centuries, rogue ocean waves have captivated observers. Despite their elusive and awe-inspiring nature, along with their capacity to cause catastrophic destruction, these waves remain unpredictable and only partially understood. To deepen our comprehension of their behavior, we examined over 3.4 billion ocean surface waves to calculate the statistical distribution of the largest ones. Our findings reveal that the distribution governing rare events—specifically the one that resolves the St. Petersburg paradox—also accurately describes the relative heights of these massive waves. This discovery will enhance models of ocean surface dynamics and increase the precision of marine weather forecasting.

Deep learning training datasets typically feature objects in familiar environments, such as horses on grass or ships in water, because they are usually gathered by randomly scraping the web. Consequently, rare or uncommon scenarios, like planes on water or cars in snow, are significantly underrepresented. This imbalance can introduce a bias toward common settings and create a misleading impression of model accuracy. To address this, we present FOCUS (Familiar Objects in Common and Uncommon Settings), a dataset designed to stress-test the generalization capabilities of deep image classifiers. Utilizing modern search engines, we intentionally compiled data featuring objects across both common and uncommon settings, spanning diverse locations, weather conditions, and times of day. Our analysis evaluates the performance of several popular image classifiers on this dataset, revealing a distinct decline in accuracy when processing images from uncommon scenarios. Furthermore, by examining the models' deep features, we demonstrate that these failures often stem from reliance on spurious features. We anticipate that the FOCUS dataset will assist researchers in better understanding the limitations of deep models in generalizing to rare settings and encourage future efforts to enhance their distributional robustness.

We investigate federated learning with personalization, where clients aim to optimize both a global goal and their own unique local objectives. This problem is addressed within a general continuous action space framework, assuming objective functions reside in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We introduce algorithms utilizing surrogate Gaussian process (GP) models that attain the optimal regret rate (modulo polylogarithmic terms). Additionally, we demonstrate that sparse GP approximations substantially lower inter-client communication overhead.

Topographic maps serve as neural structures that link pre-synaptic and post-synaptic brain areas. Their development relies on Hebbian-based plasticity mechanisms interacting with spontaneous neural activity patterns originating in the pre-synaptic regions. Research on mice indicates that these spontaneous patterns can display intricate space-time structures that current models fail to capture. Because of the dense connectivity between regions, neural field theories provide a suitable modeling framework for topographic systems; these can be enhanced with a flexible plasticity rule capable of representing complex time-varying dynamics. We introduce a theoretical framework to investigate topographic development under conditions of complex spatial-temporal activity flowing from pre- to post-synaptic zones. Model analysis yields an analytic solution supporting the conclusion that activity drives the refinement of topographic projections. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that biological noise plays a role in stabilizing developmental dynamics. Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) simulations were employed to examine differences in topographic refinement between wild-type mice and $\beta2$ knock-out mutants. In this context, the synaptic plasticity window time scale was estimated at 0.56 seconds, achieving a model fit of $R^2 = 0.81$.

This paper focuses on constrained mechanical systems, defined as one-dimensional field theories. The classical analysis also addresses systems with infinite-dimensional targets, thereby covering higher-dimensional field theories within the Hamiltonian framework. The study provides a detailed examination of the Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) action, supported by explicit computations of several examples, such as nonabelian Chern-Simons theory, where the HJ action corresponds to the gauged Wess-Zumino-Witten action. Perturbative quantization, restricted here to finite-dimensional targets, is conducted using the Batalin-Vilkovisky (BV) formalism in the bulk and the Batalin-Fradkin-Vilkovisky (BFV) formalism at the boundaries. The method's validity is confirmed by demonstrating that the semiclassical contribution to the physical evolution operator remains governed by the HJ action. Multiple explicit examples are calculated, notably showing that toy models for nonabelian Chern-Simons theory and 7D Chern-Simons theory with nonlinear Hitchin polarization yield no quantum corrections in the physical sector (with extensions to the full cases discussed in a companion paper, arXiv:2012.13983). Additionally, the paper supplies necessary background on the classical aspects (including symplectic geometry, generalized generating functions, HJ actions, and their extension to infinite-dimensional manifolds) and the quantum aspects (the BV-BFV formalism).

Catastrophic forgetting, the tendency for neural networks to lose previously acquired knowledge when learning new tasks, remains a significant limitation. Despite numerous proposed continual learning methods to address this issue, the fundamental cause of the phenomenon is still unclear. This study seeks to identify the root cause by formulating and testing hypotheses regarding the specific nature of internal representations within neural models. We conducted empirical evaluations comparing the robustness of representations in both discriminative and generative models against catastrophic forgetting. Our findings reveal that representations from discriminative models are significantly more susceptible to forgetting than those from generative models, highlighting the potential benefits of generative approaches for continual learning. Ultimately, this research suggests new avenues for utilizing generative models in continual learning, extending beyond simple replay strategies.

In domains like healthcare, finance, and safety-critical systems such as autonomous vehicles, grasping the decision-making logic of complex "black box" machine learning models is essential, driving recent growth in interest toward explainable AI (xAI) tools. Yet, the efficacy of current xAI frameworks, particularly those applied to data rather than images, remains an unresolved research challenge. To bridge this gap, this study evaluates the Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) framework—a widely cited model-agnostic approach—with a specific emphasis on enhancing the interpretability of tabular models. We apply several state-of-the-art algorithms to a tabular dataset to illustrate how LIME complements traditional performance metrics. Furthermore, we assess the comprehensibility of LIME's output through a usability study with participants unfamiliar with the tool, alongside an overall usability evaluation based on the ISO 9241-11:1998 standard.

We conduct a bordism calculation to demonstrate that the $E_{7(7)}(\mathbb{R})$ U-duality symmetry of four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=8$ supergravity might possess an anomaly undetectable by perturbative techniques, before proving that this anomaly is actually trivial. This result is achieved by calculating the pertinent bordism group via the Adams and Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequences and verifying the vanishing of the anomaly through the computation of $\eta$-invariants on the Wu manifold, which serves as the generator of the bordism group.

To support the advancement of machine learning techniques for automatically classifying spectroscopic data, we have created a universal synthetic dataset intended for model validation. This collection includes artificial spectra mimicking experimental data from various methods, such as X-ray diffraction, nuclear magnetic resonance, and Raman spectroscopy. The generation process incorporates customizable parameters, including scan length and peak count, allowing users to tailor the data to specific problems. As a starting benchmark, we simulated a set of 35,000 spectra derived from 500 distinct classes. To automate the classification of this data, we assessed eight different machine learning architectures, and our findings highlight the key factors necessary for achieving optimal performance in this task. To facilitate the development of more advanced models for spectroscopic analysis, the scripts for generating synthetic spectra, along with the benchmark dataset and evaluation routines, are now publicly available.

Differentiable architecture search (DAS) is widely adopted in Neural Architecture Search (NAS) due to its simplicity and efficiency, primarily operating through two dominant paradigms: multi-path algorithms and single-path methods. While the multi-path framework (exemplified by DARTS) is intuitive, it is hindered by high memory consumption and training collapse. Conversely, single-path methods (such as GDAS and ProxylessNAS) address memory constraints and narrow the gap between search and evaluation, yet they compromise performance. This paper introduces a conceptually straightforward and efficient approach to reconcile these two paradigms, termed Mutually-aware Sub-Graphs Differentiable Architecture Search (MSG-DAS). The framework's core relies on a differentiable Gumbel-TopK sampler that generates multiple mutually exclusive single-path sub-graphs. To mitigate the severe skip-connection issues arising from multiple sub-graphs, we propose a Dropblock-Identity module to stabilize optimization. Furthermore, to maximize the utility of available models (the super-net and sub-graphs), we implement a memory-efficient super-net guidance distillation technique to enhance training. The resulting framework achieves a balance between flexible memory usage and search quality. Experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR10 demonstrate the method's effectiveness, with searched models achieving performance comparable to the most recent state-of-the-art approaches.

Let $c(G)$ represent the count of cyclic subgroups within a finite group $G$. A group $G$ is termed {\em $n$-cyclic} when $c(G)=n$. This paper establishes that $c(G)=11$ if and only if $G$ is isomorphic to $H$, where $H$ belongs to the set $\{\mathbb{Z}_{p^{10}}, \mathbb{Z}_{27}\times \mathbb{Z}_3, \mathbb{Z}_{27}\rtimes \mathbb{Z}_3, Dic_7,\mathbb{Z}_{7}\rtimes \mathbb{Z}_9, \mathbb{Z}_3\times S_3, \mathbb{Z}_{5}\rtimes \mathbb{Z}_8,\mathbb{Z}_{3}\rtimes \mathbb{Z}_{16}\}$ and $p$ denotes a prime number.

We introduce stack graphs, an extension of the scope graphs framework developed by Visser et al. These graphs enable Precise Code Navigation on GitHub, facilitating the traversal of name binding references both within and across repositories. Similar to scope graphs, stack graphs represent program name binding information through a graph structure where paths denote valid bindings; resolving references to their definitions is achieved via straightforward path-finding searches.

Given that GitHub hosts millions of repositories totaling petabytes of code across hundreds of languages, with thousands of pushes occurring every minute, we have optimized graph construction and path-finding to be file-incremental. For every source file, we generate an isolated subgraph independent of other files, thereby eliminating the computational and storage overhead of reanalyzing previously processed file versions. Since most commits affect only a small subset of files, this approach significantly amortizes the indexing costs for large, frequently updated repositories. To manage type-directed name lookups—which involve pausing the current search to resolve another name—our algorithm utilizes a stack to track pending lookups. Stack graphs are built through purely syntactic analysis of source code using a novel declarative graph construction language. This allows us to extract name binding data for all repositories without requiring per-package configuration or invoking arbitrary, untrusted, package-specific build processes.

Current state-of-the-art solutions for spelling correction typically involve Transformer-based Seq2Seq models, which demand extensive training data and exhibit slow inference speeds, or sequence labeling models utilizing Transformer encoders like BERT. The latter relies on token-level labels, necessitating a substantial pre-defined vocabulary. In this paper, we introduce HCTagger, a Hierarchical Character Tagger designed for correcting spelling errors in short texts. Our method employs a character-level pre-trained language model as an encoder and predicts character-level edits to convert erroneous text into a corrected form, utilizing a significantly reduced label space. To address long-tail label distribution issues during decoding without adding extra parameters, we propose a hierarchical multi-task strategy. Experimental results on two public misspelling correction datasets show that HCTagger achieves high accuracy and offers substantially faster performance compared to many existing models.

This work introduces the concept of conformal blocks for modules within vertex operator algebras. We demonstrate that the space of intertwining operators linking three such modules is isomorphic to the corresponding space of conformal blocks. Furthermore, we derive a novel proof of an alternative formulation of the fusion rules theorem, which establishes the fusion rules for modules over a vertex operator algebra through the use of $A(V)$-bimodules.

We introduce a new methane sensor utilizing a "sensing without detection" approach, originally developed for quantum imaging. This technique exploits interference effects in three-wave mixing, where pump and idler signals traverse a nonlinear crystal twice. It enables sensing at wavelengths with weak detector performance and detection at wavelengths suitable for high photon-counting sensitivity. This compact interferometer, potentially adaptable for portable field units, could identify low methane concentrations from distances up to 100 meters. Signal-to-noise ratio analysis indicates that the method's sensitivity surpasses that of integrated path differential absorption direct sensing under high non-linear gain conditions.

Domain decomposition techniques are widely employed to parallelize solvers for partial differential equations. While convergence is well-understood for elliptic equations, results for parabolic equations on general Lipschitz domains in two or higher dimensions remain scarce. Consequently, this work aims to establish a new framework for analyzing nonoverlapping domain decomposition methods applied to the heat equation within a space-time Lipschitz cylinder. Drawing inspiration from recent research on space-time finite elements involving Sobolev spaces with fractional time regularity, the proposed framework utilizes a variational formulation. Within this setting, time-dependent Steklov–Poincaré operators are defined and their fundamental properties are demonstrated. The study subsequently derives the interface interpretations of Dirichlet–Neumann, Neumann–Neumann, and Robin–Robin methods, confirming their well-defined nature. Finally, convergence for the Robin–Robin method is proven, and a modified version with enhanced convergence characteristics is introduced.

This study generates a new equation of state table that incorporates Bose-Einstein condensation of $K^{-}$ mesons for simulations of core collapse supernovae and neutron star mergers. The model describes non-uniform matter containing nuclei and interacting nucleons using an extended nuclear statistical equilibrium framework that accounts for excluded volume effects, while uniform matter at higher densities is modeled via relativistic hadron field theory with density-dependent couplings.
