Unlike prior work, which primarily targeted classification on extensive natural image datasets like MNIST and CIFAR-10, we apply these methods to both classification and segmentation tasks using the smaller ISIC 2018 medical imaging dataset. Our results demonstrate that the derived bounds are competitive against simpler baselines while offering greater interpretability and eliminating the requirement for separate holdout sets.

Utilizing the COVID-19 Trends and Impacts Survey, this study analyzes how vaccinations influenced self-reported depression, anxiety, isolation, and health concerns among vaccine-accepting participants in February 2021. Under the assumption of no unmeasured confounding, vaccinations are estimated to have reduced these outcomes by 3.9 (95% CI: -4.2, -3.7), 3.4 (95% CI: -3.7, -3.1), and 4.1 (95% CI: -4.4, -3.8) percentage points, respectively. Given these findings, the pandemic is attributed to at least a 25% rise in reported depression and anxiety during that month. Additionally, the reduction in depression was most pronounced among individuals aged 18 to 24. We propose a framework suggesting that vaccinations impact depression through pathways involving health worries, isolation, and a direct mechanism. Our estimates indicate that addressing social isolation could account for 38.1% (95% CI: 35.3, 41.0) of the total effect, compared to only 7.6% (95% CI: 6.7, 8.5) for health worries, implying that isolation is a more significant mediator. Finally, we note that the causal conclusions drawn here depend heavily on strong assumptions.

We introduce a family of propositional constructive modal logics, each aligned with a distinct classical modal system. Modeled after Wijesekera's constructive modal logic, these systems are grounded in both proof theory and semantics. Specifically, they reflect the single-succedent restriction found in standard sequent calculi for classical modal logics. Simultaneously, they arise by integrating the hereditariness characteristic of intuitionistic Kripke models into the classical satisfaction rules for modal formulas. We demonstrate that for the classical logics under consideration, both the proof-theoretical and semantical methods yield identical constructive systems.

Place recognition enables SLAM systems to mitigate cumulative errors. However, unlike images rich in texture, point clouds consist primarily of geometric data, making semantic-based place recognition difficult. Current approaches typically rely on encoding low-level features like coordinates, normals, and reflection intensity into local or global descriptors, often neglecting translation adjustments during matching. In contrast, this work leverages high-level semantic features to enhance descriptor representation and explicitly corrects translations to improve matching accuracy. Specifically, we introduce a novel global descriptor called Semantic Scan Context, which utilizes semantic information for more effective scene representation. Additionally, we propose a two-step global semantic ICP method to estimate the 3D pose (x, y, yaw) for aligning point clouds and boosting performance. Experiments on the KITTI dataset demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques. The code is available at: https://github.com/lilin-hitcrt/SSC.

Observations of the Sun at sub-millimeter, millimeter, and centimeter wavelengths provide a direct diagnostic of atmospheric physical conditions. This is because they measure brightness temperature, which, for optically thick regions, directly reflects the intrinsic temperature—a distinct advantage over diagnostics in other spectral ranges. Consequently, the Atacama Large Millimeter and sub-millimeter Array (ALMA) has unlocked a previously underexplored spectral window for investigating the mysterious solar chromosphere. This review examines early ALMA studies of the quiet chromosphere, utilizing both single-dish and compact-array interferometric modes. We present findings regarding the chromosphere's temperature structure, compare these results with classic empirical models, and detail observations of the chromospheric network and spicules. Additionally, we explore future prospects, noting that ALMA's capabilities are continuously evolving to offer higher angular resolution, broader wavelength coverage, and polarization measurements for magnetometry.

SN 2011fe stands as the closest and most thoroughly observed type Ia supernova in recent decades, providing high-resolution data that starkly contrasts with previously fragmented datasets. Looking back, our understanding of type Ia supernova spectroscopic evolution has been hindered more by irregular and sparse temporal sampling than by issues like low signal-to-noise ratios, atmospheric interference, or limited sample sizes. Consequently, research has largely focused on discrete parameters derived from snapshots near peak brightness. This work outlines the essential next steps for consistently modeling and directly measuring spectroscopic observables in type Ia supernovae. Furthermore, we examine existing spectroscopic data within a parameter space defined by empirical metrics, a framework that will remain valuable even as progenitor observations emerge and theoretical models are refined.

Achieving collision avoidance in UAV swarms is difficult because it requires strict coordination among members to ensure safe path planning. Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) within Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) offers a promising solution, though the primary hurdle remains learning decentralized policies that cooperatively maximize global rewards. We introduce MACA, a novel critic-actor learning framework designed for UAV swarm collision avoidance. This approach employs a centralized critic to optimize a discounted global reward that balances safety and energy efficiency, alongside a dedicated actor for each UAV to derive decentralized collision-avoidance policies. To address the credit assignment issue inherent in CTDE, we developed a counterfactual baseline that marginalizes both individual agent states and actions, allowing for an accurate assessment of each agent's contribution within the joint observation-action space. To facilitate training and evaluation, we created a custom simulation environment, MACAEnv, which realistically mimics UAV swarm dynamics. Experimental results demonstrate that MACA outperforms two leading MARL algorithms by achieving an average reward increase of over 16%. Furthermore, compared to traditional UAV swarm collision avoidance methods, MACA reduces the failure rate by 90% and cuts response time by more than 99% across all tested scenarios.

As self-adaptive systems become more prevalent across different fields, there is a heightened demand for methods to verify their proper functioning. Specifically, self-healing systems designed to ensure resilience and fault tolerance frequently encounter unforeseen failures within critical, highly dynamic settings. Their reactive and intricate nature complicates the assessment of whether they align with intended objectives. Recently, numerous researchers have highlighted the absence of systematic evaluation techniques for self-healing behaviors.

This paper introduces CHESS, a framework for the systematic assessment of self-adaptive and self-healing systems rooted in chaos engineering. Chaos engineering involves exposing systems to unexpected conditions and scenarios, a practice that has proven effective in fostering resilient microservice architectures and cyber-physical systems. CHESS reverses this concept by leveraging chaos engineering to test how robustly a self-healing system can endure such disturbances. We examine the feasibility of this method through an exploratory study involving a self-healing smart office environment. This investigation allows us to analyze the potential and constraints of the approach while pinpointing areas requiring further research. The paper concludes with a summary of key lessons derived from the study.

A long-standing hypothesis posits that global symmetries cannot exist within quantum gravity. By examining extensive families of four-dimensional Type IIB $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, we identify potential generalized global symmetries and demonstrate how they are circumvented. A key component in these theories involves generalized $\theta$-terms, which establish non-linear interactions between axion fields and gauge field strength terms quadratic in topology, thereby disrupting a significant portion of global symmetries. Furthermore, assuming the presence of charged states can break any remaining residual symmetries. However, we show that generalized $\theta$-terms induce a generalized Witten effect, implying that the charged state spectrum forms an infinitely populated lattice. We also demonstrate that this lattice arises from the monodromy transformation acting on the moduli space boundary where the effective theory is defined.

This paper presents an AI-driven solution designed to facilitate a cross-sector, cross-border eGovernance framework for sharing public services. The approach empowers beneficiaries to engage in a decentralized network that ensures efficient big data exchange and service delivery, adhering to the "once-only" principle while being inherently digital, efficient, cost-effective, interoperable, and secure. The proposed system includes four key components: (i) a robust decentralized mechanism for data sharing that handles complex processes and high resource demands; (ii) a stakeholder-focused ecosystem for delivering mobile services; (iii) a single sign-on wallet system for managing transactions across multiple services; and (iv) an intercommunication layer ensuring secure information exchange between existing and newly developed eGovernment systems. An illustrative application scenario demonstrates the potential of this methodology.

Collaborative filtering (CF), a cornerstone of recommender systems, typically relies on latent factor models with learnable parameters to forecast user-item preferences. However, constructing an optimal CF model for specific datasets is challenging due to the high diversity of data characteristics. Drawing inspiration from recent advancements in automated machine learning (AutoML), this paper proposes designing data-specific CF models using AutoML techniques. Central to this approach is a novel framework that unifies state-of-the-art (SOTA) CF methods by decomposing them into distinct stages: input encoding, embedding, interaction, and prediction. We further introduce a user-friendly, robust, and efficient search strategy that leverages random search combined with a performance predictor to navigate this framework effectively. This methodology enables the combinatorial generation of previously unexplored, data-specific CF models based on SOTA architectures. Extensive experiments across five real-world datasets show that our approach consistently outperforms existing SOTA methods for various CF tasks. Additional experiments confirm the validity of the proposed framework and the efficiency of the search strategy. Furthermore, the discovered models offer valuable insights for developing more effective methods in the future.

Mixtures of microtubules and molecular motors create active materials exhibiting diverse dynamical behaviors determined by the molecular characteristics of their components. We have mapped the non-equilibrium phase diagram for systems comprising microtubules and kinesin-4 motors that accumulate at tips. Our findings indicate that kinesin-4 drives either global contractions or turbulent-like extensile dynamics, contingent upon the concentrations of microtubules and a bundling agent. Additionally, we identified various spatially heterogeneous non-equilibrium phases, such as finite-sized radial asters, 1D wormlike chains, extended 2D bilayers, and system-spanning 3D active foams. Furthermore, we outline complex kinetic pathways leading to microphase-separated structures, which result from the inherent frustration between the orientational order of filamentous microtubules and the positional order of tip-accumulating motors. Our research demonstrates that the specific forms of active stresses and phases within cytoskeletal networks depend not only on the properties of individual motors and filaments but also on the concentrations and spatial arrangement of the constituents.

The cosmological phenomenology of loop quantum gravity largely relies on holonomy corrections applied to the Hamiltonian constraint, which directly alter the Friedmann equations. This study examines corrections that extend beyond those standard in loop quantum cosmology. Our findings indicate that sufficiently long inflationary periods can arise solely from quantum geometric effects, though we also highlight the constraints of this approach. Furthermore, we analyze how these generalized holonomy corrections impact an inflationary phase driven by a massive scalar field. Finally, we provide a detailed investigation into the implications for the primordial scalar power spectrum at the level of perturbations.

This paper investigates the relationship between discrete Morse theory and persistent homology within shape reconstruction techniques. Specifically, we examine the Wrap complex, a subcomplex of the Delaunay complex introduced by Edelsbrunner, alongside the lexicographically optimal homologous chains proposed by Cohen-Steiner, Lieutier, and Vuillamy. We demonstrate that for any cycle existing in a Delaunay complex at a specific radius threshold, the corresponding lexicographically optimal homologous cycle is contained within the Wrap complex at that same threshold, thus revealing a strong link between these two approaches. This finding arises from a broader connection between cycle reduction in persistent homology computations and gradient flows in the algebraic extension of discrete Morse theory, a result that holds independent significance.

Graphs serve as a fundamental data structure in data science, extensively utilized in domains such as social networks, knowledge representation, and recommendation systems. When analyzing datasets comprising one or multiple weighted graphs, the initial objective is typically to identify clusters within them. This paper details our ongoing research on graph clustering algorithms designed for weighted graph datasets, specifically proposing the Weighted Graph Node Clustering via Gumbel Softmax method (abbreviated as WGCGS). We applied WGCGS to the Karate club weighted network dataset, and our experiments confirm that the algorithm efficiently and effectively discovers clusters within this dataset. The effectiveness of our approach is validated through (1) a comparison of the generated clustering results against the dataset's provided labels, and (2) an evaluation of various performance metrics contrasting our algorithm with other state-of-the-art graph clustering methods.

Many fingerprint recognition systems capture four fingerprints in a single image, necessitating that the processing pipeline first segment these multi-fingerprint slaps into individual prints. However, most existing segmentation algorithms have been designed and tested primarily on adult datasets. To address this, we created a human-annotated in-house dataset comprising 15,790 slaps, including 9,084 adult samples and 6,706 samples from children aged 4 to 12. We first used this dataset to evaluate the matching performance of the NIST-developed NFSEG system on slaps from both adults and juveniles, revealing that NFSEG performs significantly worse on juvenile subjects. Leveraging our novel dataset, we subsequently developed the Mask-RCNN-based Clarkson Fingerprint Segmentation (CFSEG). Matching results obtained using the Verifinger matcher demonstrate that CFSEG outperforms NFSEG for both adult and juvenile slaps. The CFSEG model is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/keivanB/Clarkson_Finger_Segment}.

Determining the nuclear parton distribution functions (nPDFs) for gluons is challenging when relying solely on fits of deep inelastic scattering (DIS) and Drell-Yan (DY) data. Consequently, the nCTEQ15 study incorporated inclusive neutral pion production data from RHIC to better constrain the gluon distribution. In this work, we introduce a new global analysis of nuclear PDFs utilizing an expanded dataset of single inclusive light hadron measurements from both RHIC and the LHC. By employing our updated nCTEQ++ code alongside an optimized version of INCNLO, we systematically examine theoretical limitations and assess the influence of fragmentation function uncertainties.

Federated Learning (FL) represents a distributed approach for training global or personalized models using decentralized data on edge devices. However, within the computer vision domain, FL performance lags significantly behind centralized training due to insufficient exploration across diverse tasks under a unified framework. Consequently, FL has seldom been successfully applied to advanced vision tasks like object detection and image segmentation. To address this gap and advance FL in computer vision, we introduce FedCV, a federated learning library and benchmarking framework designed to evaluate FL on three key tasks: image classification, image segmentation, and object detection. This resource includes non-I.I.D. benchmark datasets, pre-trained models, and various reference FL algorithms. Our benchmarking study highlights several critical challenges for future research: centralized training techniques often fail to translate directly to FL; non-I.I.D. data can degrade model accuracy across different tasks; and enhancing system efficiency remains difficult due to the high parameter count and per-client memory demands. We argue that a standardized library and benchmark are essential for achieving meaningful progress in computer vision via FL. FedCV is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/FedML-AI/FedCV.

Achieving consensus—defined as a macroscopic state where all system components share an identical microscopic state—is essential for the proper operation of various complex socio-technical and techno-economic systems. In numerous distributed environments, such as blockchain applications, the formation of consensus is vital not only for establishing a dominant majority but also for the system's fundamental functionality. We have developed a minimal network model to analyze consensus formation in blockchain systems, specifically to quantify how central nodes, based on their average distance to others, can exploit their strategic positions to gain competitive advantages. Our findings demonstrate that across a broad spectrum of network topologies, the likelihood of achieving a majority can increase substantially depending on the centrality of the nodes that initiate the information spread. Additionally, we examined the influence of network topology on the consensus process, revealing that in scale-free networks, central nodes can secure consensus even if they broadcast their states significantly later than peripheral nodes.

Creating effective approximate models for analyzing and simulating intricate nonlinear systems holds significant practical value. This study investigates the utility of a broad category of nonlinear stochastic models, termed the conditional Gaussian nonlinear system (CGNS), serving as both a low-cost surrogate and a rapid preconditioner to address computationally demanding challenges. The CGNS largely retains the underlying physical dynamics and effectively captures intermittency, extreme events, and other non-Gaussian characteristics found in various complex systems from real-world applications. The research focuses on three interconnected areas. First, it derives closed-form analytic solutions for conditional statistics, enabling an efficient and precise data assimilation framework. Results demonstrate that a well-tuned CGNS approximate forecast model achieves superior data assimilation performance compared to ensemble methods applied to perfect models with strong nonlinearity, particularly avoiding the filter divergence issues that plague the latter. Second, the CGNS facilitates a rapid algorithm for jointly estimating parameters and unobserved variables with uncertainty quantification, even when data is partially observed. Using a suitable CGNS as a preconditioner markedly lowers the computational expense required to accurately estimate parameters within the original complex system. Finally, the CGNS enables swift and statistically robust algorithms for calculating probability density functions and sampling trajectories of unobserved state variables. These efficient algorithms support the creation of a data-driven approach that accurately predicts the linear response of the original system to parameter perturbations, leveraging a CGNS-based preconditioner.

Spin defects within hexagonal Boron Nitride (hBN) have gained significant attention for quantum technology due to their role as optically addressable qubits in van der Waals materials. Specifically, negatively charged boron vacancy centers (${V_B}^-$) in hBN have demonstrated potential as sensors for static magnetic fields, pressure, and temperature. Nevertheless, the utility of these defects is currently constrained by their brief spin coherence times. In this study, we utilize dynamical decoupling methods to mitigate magnetic noise, thereby extending the spin coherence time by almost two orders of magnitude and nearing the fundamental $T_1$ relaxation limit. Leveraging this enhancement, we achieve sophisticated spin manipulation and implement quantum sensing protocols capable of detecting MHz-range electromagnetic signals with sub-Hz resolution. These findings establish a groundwork for nanoscale sensing using spin defects in exfoliable materials and pave the way for integrating quantum sensors and networks into ultra-thin structures.

Onboard visual sensing is extensively utilized in unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), which can be modeled as dynamic systems on SE(3). While sensing outputs typically yield relative positions between feature marks and the system, they often include explicit bearing constraints. These geometric constraints complicate the design of visual observers on SE(3), primarily because the visible set of feature marks varies in size and composition along different trajectories, leading to time-varying or switching dynamics. Furthermore, issues such as misidentified features and modeling uncertainties can cause estimation errors to diverge. This paper introduces a novel robust observer design capable of handling these uncertainties inherent in onboard visual sensing. The core approach involves estimating the visible set and detecting misidentified features from the measurements. Leveraging these identified uncertainties, a switching strategy is developed to guarantee bounded estimation errors for any trajectory within a fixed time interval. Simulation results are presented to validate the effectiveness of this proposed robust observer.

Cascaded speech translation systems depend on discrete, non-differentiable transcription to provide source-side supervision and facilitate the conversion from source speech to target text, though this approach is prone to error propagation between the Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Machine Translation (MT) stages. While direct speech translation offers a solution to avoid such propagation, it often yields inferior performance compared to cascaded systems. Previous attempts to maintain end-to-end trainability utilized two-stage architectures by feeding ASR hidden vectors directly into the MT decoder while bypassing the MT encoder. This study investigates the viability of consolidating the entire cascade into a single, fully end-to-end trainable model by jointly optimizing all parameters of both ASR and MT without discarding any learned weights. This tightly integrated framework transmits renormalized source word posterior distributions as soft decisions rather than one-hot vectors, thereby enabling backpropagation. Consequently, the model generates both transcriptions and translations with high mutual consistency. Experiments across four tasks with varying data conditions demonstrate that this approach surpasses cascade models by up to 1.8% in BLEU and 2.0% in TER, while also outperforming direct models.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become a standard solution for major computer vision challenges. While researchers continue to develop new architectures and refine existing ones to boost performance, there is a growing tendency to prioritize results at the expense of critical factors like simplicity, versatility, fair comparison, and energy efficiency. Ignoring these variables during design and evaluation fosters research bias and causes substantial environmental harm, potentially counteracting the benefits of deep learning in addressing climate change. This paper presents a comprehensive and impartial empirical study of various proposed techniques to assess their effectiveness for segmentation and classification. Our results reaffirm the value of prioritizing simplicity over complexity (Occam's Razor) in model design. Additionally, we demonstrate that adopting simple, standardized practices can markedly reduce environmental impact with minimal performance loss. We emphasize the urgent need to reconsider how CNNs are designed and evaluated to mitigate research bias and lower carbon emissions.

This paper presents an enhanced visible light communication (VLC) channel model designed for ranging applications. For indoor VLC scenarios, distance estimation relies on received signal strength, where shot noise is treated as a parameter dependent on distance to improve range estimation accuracy. Furthermore, the Cramer-Rao lower bound is calculated to establish theoretical performance limits for any unbiased estimator within this framework. Using this model, the impacts of both horizontal and vertical distances are analyzed, alongside the influence of transmitted power on received signal strength and the corresponding CRLB.

This research examines the breaking of residual flavor symmetries occurring at moduli space fixed points within supersymmetric modular invariant theories. It posits that a slight shift of the modulus away from these fixed points is necessary to generate fermion mass hierarchies and significant CP-violation. We explore the possibility of dynamically stabilizing moduli values near these fixed points within Type IIB string theory. Our findings indicate that the string landscape statistically favors a CP-breaking vacuum, with the complex structure modulus deviating from all fixed points by approximately $|\delta \tau| \simeq 10^{-5}$. To demonstrate the phenomenological consequences of moduli distributions around these fixed points, we perform an analysis of the lepton sector using a specific $A_4$ modular flavor model.

Although the Sun has gradually brightened over time, Earth has maintained a climate suitable for life throughout its history, a phenomenon known as the Faint Young Sun Problem (FYSP). While the carbonate-silicate cycle is a recognized mechanism, recent studies propose that long-term cloud feedbacks may also contribute to resolving the FYSP. However, previous research relied on general circulation models that could not explicitly simulate convection and clouds. This study re-examines cloud dynamics using a near-global model that permits explicit cloud resolution without cumulus convection parameterization. The findings confirm the existence of a stabilizing shortwave cloud feedback, with a magnitude of approximately 6 W m$^{-2}$. This value represents about 14% of the energy needed to counteract a Sun 20% fainter than today, or roughly 10 W m$^{-2}$ (16%) for a Sun 30% fainter. Furthermore, as insolation rises and CO$_2$ levels fall, low-level clouds increase, enhancing planetary albedo to stabilize the climate; the reverse occurs under opposite conditions.

The classical No-Three-In-Line problem aims to determine the maximum number of points that can be chosen from an $n\times n$ grid without forming a collinear triple, a maximum known to grow linearly with $n$. Addressing a query by Erde, we investigate the selection of high-density subsets from the infinite integer grid $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ that avoid collinear triples. We demonstrate the existence of such a set containing $\Theta(n/\log^{1+\varepsilon}n)$ points within the $[1,n]^{2}$ region for all $n$, where $\varepsilon>0$ is an arbitrarily small real constant. Additionally, computational results indicate that a set of lattice points might exist with at least $n/2$ points on every sufficiently large $n\times n$ grid.

Foams represent unstable, jammed systems that change over durations similar to their intended lifespan, making the investigation of their destabilization processes vital for practical applications. Typically composed of viscoelastic fluids, many foams exhibit extended lifetimes; however, the specific coarsening mechanisms within these systems remain poorly understood. This study examines how the viscoelasticity of the continuous phase influences foam coarsening using foamed emulsions. Our findings demonstrate that bubble size evolution is significantly retarded and the foam's structure is profoundly altered. The primary drivers are the lack of continuous phase redistribution and a complex relationship between foam architecture and mechanical properties, which together result in spatially heterogeneous coarsening. Beyond aiding in the design of foamy materials, these results provide a macroscopic perspective on phase separation within viscoelastic media.

Constructing an ideal multi-secret sharing scheme for general access structures is a challenging task. This paper addresses an open problem recently posed by Spiez et al. [Finite Fields and Their Application, 2011(17) 329-342] by designing an algorithm to identify privileged coalitions of any length, provided they exist. Additionally, we demonstrate that many existing multi-secret sharing schemes based on Shamir threshold secret sharing are imperfect by analyzing the works of Yang et al. and Pang et al. in the context of privileged coalitions. Finally, utilizing the aforementioned algorithm, we develop an ideal multi-secret sharing scheme for families of access structures that features a more diverse set of authorized participants compared to threshold schemes.

We present two findings concerning the Schwarz lemma within complex geometry. Initially, we demonstrate that if the inequality associated with the Schwarz lemmas of Yau, Royden, and Tosatti attains equality at a single point, this equality extends across the entire manifold; consequently, the holomorphic map becomes totally geodesic and maintains a constant rank. Furthermore, we investigate holomorphic sectional curvature on almost Hermitian manifolds and formulate a Schwarz lemma specifically utilizing holomorphic sectional curvatures within this framework.

Using QCD sum rules, we investigate tetraquark states characterized by $I^G J^{PC}=1^- 1^{-+}$. Having examined all feasible flavor configurations, we apply both SVZ and finite energy sum rule methods. Both techniques yield a predicted mass of approximately 1.6 GeV for the $q q q_{bar} q_{bar}$ configuration and roughly 2.0 GeV for the $q s q_{bar} s_{bar}$ configuration. The flavor structure $3_{bar} * 6_{bar} + 6 * 3$ is favored by our findings. Our results strongly suggest that $\pi_1(1600)$ and $\pi_1(2015)$ are compatible with an exotic tetraquark interpretation, despite their occasional classification as $1^{-+}$ hybrid meson candidates. Furthermore, a primary decay channel for these states involves pairs of axial-vector and pseudoscalar mesons, such as $b_1(1235) \pi$, a mode often associated with hybrid mesons.

This study investigates a hidden charmed pentaquark candidate containing two strange quarks. The research is divided into two sections: the first predicts the state's mass, while the second calculates its partial decay widths for the $P_{css}\rightarrow \Xi^0 J/\psi$ and $P_{css}\rightarrow \Xi_c^+ D_s^-$ transitions. To derive these values, two-point and three-point QCD sum rule techniques are employed for the mass and width calculations, respectively. The analysis yields a mass of $m_{P_{css}}=4600 \pm 155$ MeV and a corresponding current coupling constant of $\lambda_{P_{css}}=(0.81 \pm 0.21)\times 10^{-3}$ GeV$^6$. Utilizing these parameters, the partial widths for the specified decay channels are evaluated, resulting in a total width of $\Gamma = 12.29\pm 2.94 $ MeV. These findings could guide future experimental efforts in detecting similar states and offer criteria to distinguish between potential observations.

Model selection plays a crucial role in data analysis, particularly for tasks involving fitting and prediction. This paper addresses model selection within a general linear regression framework where the parameter matrix exhibits a block-sparse structure; that is, non-zero entries are grouped into clusters, and the count of these blocks is minimal relative to the total parameter dimension. Additionally, the study operates in a high-dimensional context where the parameter dimension significantly exceeds the number of observations. To facilitate model selection under these conditions, we introduce an information criterion that extends the Extended Bayesian Information Criterion-Robust (EBIC-R), incorporating both the block structure and high-dimensionality. We provide the analytical derivations for this adapted EBIC-R. Simulation results indicate that the proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods and demonstrates empirical consistency at large sample sizes and/or high signal-to-noise ratios.

This study introduces a natural-language agent-based model of argumentation (ABMA) utilizing artificial deliberative agents (ADAs) built upon recent neural language models from AI and computational linguistics. These agents operate with a minimalist belief system and are capable of generating and submitting original contributions to discussions. Unlike formal models that rely on mathematical representations, this natural-language ABMA simulates collective deliberation using actual arguments, reasons, and claims in English. The research employs this model to evaluate the robustness of formal reason-balancing frameworks [Maes & Flache 2013, Singer et al. 2019]. Findings indicate that while confirmation bias and homophily updates lead to polarization when ADAs remain passive—aligning with formal model results—the dynamics shift once agents actively create new content. In such cases, the evolution of the conversation is primarily driven by the properties of the agents as authors. This highlights that the generation of new arguments, reasons, and claims critically influences conversational dynamics and is essential for understanding collective deliberation. The paper concludes by outlining potential future applications and research challenges.

Driven by the potential of antiferromagnetic skyrmions as fundamental components for future data storage and computing technologies, this study presents a theoretical and computational investigation of a spin-orbit coupled correlated magnet situated on a triangular lattice. Our analysis, conducted through Monte Carlo simulations on an effective magnetic model derived from a microscopic electronic Hamiltonian—incorporating Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Hund's rule coupling to large classical spins—reveals that two distinct antiferromagnetic skyrmion crystal (AF-SkX) phases can be stabilized at low temperatures under an external magnetic field. These two AF-SkX phases emerge from a classical spin liquid state present at low but finite temperatures. Furthermore, these states can be readily differentiated experimentally via neutron scattering, which measures the spin structure factor and identifies peaks at unique momenta for each phase. Finally, we explore specific material candidates where this model and the resulting dual AF-SkX states could be physically realized.

As we increasingly identify scenarios where existing noisy quantum devices outperform classical ones, the efficient utilization of quantum resources becomes paramount. Quantum autoencoders were introduced as a method to compress quantum data and minimize these resource demands. In this work, we propose a strategy that employs evolutionary algorithms to design quantum autoencoders capable of transforming quantum information into lower-dimensional representations. We successfully apply this algorithm to compress various families of quantum states. Notably, we demonstrate that restricting the gate set within the algorithm facilitates the efficient simulation of the resulting circuits. This methodology enables the use of classical logic to identify compact representations of quantum data with reduced computational overhead.

We examine a multi-agent network where each participant minimizes a private objective comprising two potentially nonsmooth convex terms, one involving a linear operator. During each iteration, agents conduct local computations and exchange information solely with their neighbors. A key difficulty in this study arises because the smooth component of each agent's cost function is defined as an expectation, accessible only through a heavy-tailed stochastic oracle. To address this sampling-based optimization challenge, we introduce a stochastic variant of the triangular preconditioned primal-dual algorithm. We establish the almost sure convergence of the proposed method and corroborate its efficacy through numerical experiments.

The paper demonstrates an equivalence between the category of \emph{pseudo-actions} and the category of \emph{semi-biproducts} of monoids. A semi-biproduct represents a novel concept derived by extending the biproduct of commutative monoids; this generalization involves abandoning commutativity and allowing certain homomorphisms in the biproduct diagram to be merely identity-preserving maps. Similarly, a pseudo-action is a new concept composed of three components: a pre-action, a factor system, and a correction system. Notably, within the category of groups, all correction systems are trivial, which may explain why this notion has, to the author's knowledge, remained unexplored in prior literature.

The recent identification of higher-order topology has significantly expanded the classification of topological materials. While theoretical and experimental research has already revealed various higher-order topological insulators featuring topologically protected corner or hinge states, the extension of this concept to topological semimetals is a more recent development. Currently, realistic models and experimental confirmations for higher-order topological semimetals remain scarce. In this study, we design and demonstrate a three-dimensional photonic crystal that achieves a higher-order Dirac semimetal phase. Numerical analysis of the band structure indicates that the crystal supports two four-fold Dirac points, whose momentum-space projections along an edge are linked by higher-order hinge states. This higher-order topology is characterized by calculating the $\chi_6$ topological invariant across different $k_z$ values. Furthermore, we present a microwave-frequency experiment to measure the dispersion of the hinge states. Our findings confirm the physical realization of a higher-order Dirac semimetal phase and open new avenues for investigating higher-order topological semimetal phases within three-dimensional photonic systems.

This research investigates wave-particle duality within a general Mach-Zehnder interferometer featuring an asymmetric beam splitter, utilizing the framework of quantum information theory. We derive the correlations—encompassing both classical and quantum aspects—between the particle and its which-path detector for both pure and mixed states at the interferometer's output. Our findings indicate that fringe visibility and these correlations are influenced by the asymmetry of the beam splitter and the particle's initial state. Furthermore, we establish the complementary relationships between fringe visibility and the correlations.

Let $n$ denote the order of a (quaternary) Hadamard matrix. It has been demonstrated that a projective plane of order $n$ exists if and only if there exists a balancedly multi-splittable (quaternary) Hadamard matrix of order $n^2$.

This study introduces a mathematical framework for modeling shock wave propagation within graded density profiles, a phenomenon observed across diverse astrophysical events, including planetary and stellar atmospheric collisions, common envelope explosions, and specific Type Ia supernovae. The evolution of these shock waves is characterized by Type II self-similar solutions, which rely on boundary conditions at the shock front and a singular point within the shocked region. We demonstrate how to determine this evolution for various equations of state and density profiles, comparing the results against numerical simulations. Furthermore, these findings are applied to multiple astrophysical scenarios to validate their applicability.

With the initiation of Run II data collection, it is beneficial to highlight outstanding inquiries by examining recent findings from Run I analyses. Additionally, preliminary outcomes from the ongoing data gathering and medium-term projections are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the acquisition and analysis workflow.

This note introduces explicit canonical forms for every element of the two-qubit CNOT-Dihedral group, utilizing the minimal count of controlled-S (CS) and controlled-X (CX) gates based on the generating set {X, T, CX, CS}. We also present an algorithm for the successive construction of the n-qubit CNOT-Dihedral group, which guarantees an optimal number of controlled-X (CX) gates. These findings are essential for estimating gate errors through non-Clifford randomized benchmarking and could support additional applications in circuit optimization for fault-tolerant gate sets.

The mirror twin Higgs model serves as a candidate for strongly-interacting complex dark matter, featuring interactions with the Standard Model (SM) analogous to heavier quarks. This framework predicts the existence of mirror neutron stars—exotic, electromagnetically invisible objects composed solely of mirror matter that are significantly more compact than ordinary neutron stars. While mergers of two such mirror neutron stars are distinct and detectable via gravitational waves, the paper investigates whether we can observationally differentiate regular neutron stars from those containing mirror matter components. The study examines two scenarios: (i) mirror matter captured within a neutron star and (ii) the coalescence of a mirror neutron star with a standard neutron star. For the first scenario, we find that non-rotating neutron stars with mixed mirror matter do not follow a single mass-radius relation but instead occupy a two-dimensional mass-radius plane. In the second scenario, binary systems involving mirror neutron stars exhibit a broader distribution of chirp masses and unique binary Love relations, potentially resulting in merger remnants that are exceptionally light black holes. Consequently, gravitational wave data from advanced LIGO and Virgo, alongside X-ray observations from NICER, could detect or place constraints on mirror matter by expanding the range of model parameters and priors used in searches.

Noisy labels in real-world datasets significantly degrade the performance of deep learning models. While extensive research has focused on enhancing robustness against label noise in classification, the issue remains unresolved in deep metric learning (DML). This paper introduces PRISM, a noise-resistant training technique for DML. PRISM detects noisy samples within a minibatch by evaluating their average similarity to image features stored in a memory bank, which contains representations from multiple prior network iterations. To mitigate the computational overhead associated with the memory bank, we propose an acceleration strategy that substitutes individual data points with class centers. Extensive evaluations against 12 existing methods under both synthetic and real-world noisy label conditions demonstrate that PRISM achieves superior performance, improving Precision@1 by up to 6.06%.

Tracer-kinetic models enable the calculation of kinetic parameters, including blood flow, by analyzing dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance (MR) images. Utilizing multi-compartment exchange models to fit observed data is preferred because these models align with physiological reality and directly estimate blood flow and microvascular function. Nevertheless, the accuracy of such fitting is constrained by factors like low signal-to-noise ratios, limited temporal resolution, and short acquisition durations, which can lead to erroneous parameter estimates.

This study proposes physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a robust method for quantifying myocardial perfusion via MR, offering a flexible framework for inferring kinetic parameters. These networks are trained to match observed perfusion MR data while adhering to the physical conservation laws defined by multi-compartment exchange models. The paper presents a specific framework for implementing PINNs in myocardial perfusion MR analysis.

The proposed approach was validated through both in silico and in vivo experiments. The in silico results showed a significant reduction in mean-squared error relative to ground-truth parameters compared to standard non-linear least squares fitting. Furthermore, the in vivo study confirmed that the method yields parameter values consistent with existing literature and generates parameter maps that align with clinical patient diagnoses.

While the advancement of certain AI frameworks, including deep learning, correlates with an exponential rise in parameter counts, it remains uncertain whether this equates to a similarly exponential surge in energy usage. To address this, our analysis prioritizes inference over training costs, given that inference incurs the majority of computational expenses due to multiplicative factors. Beyond algorithmic improvements, we also incorporate the impact of more potent hardware with higher FLOPS, which typically includes significant energy efficiency enhancements. Furthermore, rather than examining the initial implementation of a breakthrough, we evaluate the consolidated versions of these techniques developed one to two years later. From this comprehensive standpoint, analyzing models in computer vision and natural language processing reveals that sustained performance gains are accompanied by a considerably slower increase in energy consumption than previously expected. The primary concern remains the multiplicative factor, as AI's expanding penetration and ubiquity could amplify future energy demands.

Internal chemical mixing within intermediate- and high-mass stars introduces a significant uncertainty into stellar evolution models. Beyond prolonging the main-sequence lifetime, this mixing notably augments the mass of the stellar core. Although various studies have attempted to calibrate the efficiency of different convective boundary mixing mechanisms, their results often appear contradictory. Our objective is to show that standard stellar models consistently underestimate convective core masses. We achieved this by compiling convective core mass and fractional hydrogen content estimates from numerous independent binary and asteroseismic studies, then comparing them against stellar evolution models generated using the MESA code. Our findings reveal that literature-based core mass inferences are universally higher than those predicted by models lacking or possessing minimal convective boundary mixing. Consequently, regardless of the specific mixing mechanism, stellar models must incorporate an efficient process that generates more massive cores throughout the main sequence to align with high-precision observations. This requirement has profound implications for the post-main-sequence evolution of all stars that possess a well-developed convective core during their main-sequence phase.

This study introduces a deep neural network architecture designed to efficiently approximate classical elasto-plastic constitutive relations. By integrating essential physical principles of elasto-plasticity—specifically the additive separation of elastic and plastic strains and nonlinear incremental elasticity—the network functions as a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN), termed the Elasto-Plastic Neural Network (EPNN). Comprehensive analyses indicate that embedding these physical constraints into the network structure streamlines training with reduced data requirements and significantly improves extrapolation capabilities for loading conditions beyond the training set. The EPNN framework is model- and material-agnostic, allowing adaptation to various elasto-plastic materials, such as metals and geomaterials, with the potential to utilize experimental data directly for training. To validate the architecture's robustness, the general framework was applied to model the elasto-plastic behavior of sands. The network was trained using synthetic data derived from material point simulations based on an advanced dilatancy-based constitutive model for granular materials. The study further investigates the advantages of EPNN over standard neural network architectures by predicting unseen strain-controlled loading paths for sands exhibiting different initial densities.

This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to identify individuals with COVID-19 based on their cough sounds. The proposed methodology consists of two primary stages. Initially, a cough sound representation is generated by merging an embedding from a pre-trained model with handcrafted features derived from the audio recording, a process termed front-end feature extraction. Subsequently, these combined features are input into various back-end classification models to detect positive cases. Experimental results on the Track-2 dataset of the Second 2021 DiCOVA Challenge secured the second-highest ranking, achieving an AUC score of 81.21 and the top F1 score of 53.21 on a Blind Test set. These outcomes represent improvements of 8.43% and 23.4% over the challenge baseline, respectively, demonstrating the system's deployability, robustness, and competitiveness against state-of-the-art solutions.

The Non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE) is an emerging phenomenon in non-Hermitian systems. We present an experimental observation of NHSE, distinguishing our approach from prior non-reciprocal circuit implementations that relied on logic components; instead, we constructed one-dimensional (1D) circuits using exclusively linear components. Non-reciprocity was achieved by proportionally adjusting component parameter values. By measuring the voltage response at each site, we mapped the eigenstate information. Results indicate that the voltage response is consistently higher at one end of the circuit, regardless of where the voltage driving is applied, providing clear evidence of NHSE. Additionally, we simulated the interaction between NHSE and Anderson localization (AL) by introducing disorder. As disorder strength increased, we observed a transition from the skin effect phase to the localized phase. In the skin effect phase, eigenstates localize entirely at one edge, whereas in the localized phase, eigenstates are influenced by the voltage supply input. These findings reveal a promising new pathway for simulating topological phenomena in non-Hermitian systems.

This study investigates flavour-changing neutral current (FCNC) interactions between a top quark, another up-type quark ($q=u$ or $c$), and the Standard Model Higgs boson, specifically analyzing the decay channel $H \rightarrow \tau^+\tau^-$. The analysis utilizes a dataset from $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, comprising an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. Two production mechanisms are examined: single top quark FCNC production accompanied by a Higgs boson ($pp\rightarrow tH$), and top quark pair production where one top decays via the standard $Wb$ mode while the other undergoes FCNC decay into $qH$. Event selection requires either two hadronically decaying $\tau$-lepton candidates or at least one such candidate alongside an additional lepton ($e$, $\mu$) and multiple jets. A multivariate discriminant leveraging event kinematics distinguishes the signal from background processes. A slight data excess with a significance of 2.3$\sigma$ relative to the expected Standard Model background is noted, leading to the derivation of 95% confidence level (CL) upper limits on $t\to qH$ branching ratios. The observed (expected) 95% CL upper limits for $t\to cH$ and $t\to uH$ branching ratios are determined to be $9.4 \times 10^{-4}$ ($4.8^{+2.2}_{-1.4}\times 10^{-4}$) and $6.9\times 10^{-4}$ ($3.5^{+1.5}_{-1.0}\times 10^{-4}$), respectively. Correspondingly, the combined observed (expected) upper limits on the dimension-6 operator Wilson coefficients for the effective $tqH$ couplings are established as $C_{c\phi} <1.35$ ($0.97$) and $C_{u\phi} <1.16$ ($0.82$).

This study examines seven spectroscopically confirmed Ly$\alpha$-emitting galaxies at a redshift of $z\simeq6$ using James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) NIRCam imagery. These galaxies, which exhibit a broad spectrum of Ly$\alpha$ luminosities, were recently surveyed across various NIRCam broad- and medium-band filters. By combining NIRCam photometry with archival Hubble Space Telescope data, we determined the continuum and H$\alpha$ line characteristics of these objects. Our findings indicate that galaxies with bluer UV continuum slopes likely possess higher Ly$\alpha$ photon escape fractions. Additionally, galaxies showing stronger Ly$\alpha$ line emission demonstrate more efficient production of ionizing photons. The most Ly$\alpha$-bright galaxy in our sample displays an ionizing photon production efficiency of log$_{10} \xi_{\rm ion, 0}$ (Hz erg$^{-1}$) exceeding 26. These results suggest that Ly$\alpha$ galaxies played a significant role in cosmic reionization. Consequently, blue and luminous Ly$\alpha$ galaxies represent prime candidates for future JWST spectroscopic follow-up.

Recent discussions have questioned whether $\overline{\text{MS}}$ parton densities strictly adhere to positivity bounds, such as the Soffer bound, and whether these bounds should constrain global fits and nonperturbative calculations. A recent study (JHEP ${\bf \text{11}}$ (2020) 129) claimed to prove positivity, contradicting previous findings. Upon reviewing their derivation, we identify a critical flaw in the assertion that bare parton distribution functions (pdfs) are invariably positive, a claim we demonstrate fails under the specific conditions of their proof. Using elementary calculations within a model quantum field theory, we illustrate how such violations can generically occur. Furthermore, we note that the derivation methods share characteristics with much, though not all, existing work on factorization. Our analysis reveals significant issues with these methods, rendering them either incorrect or highly problematic, and underscores how they can produce phenomenologically significant erroneous results regarding positivity. Finally, our study delineates the specific circumstances under which positivity may be violated.

We examine thick brane configurations within Horndeski gravity by deriving analytical solutions using the first-order formalism applied to two scalar fields: one arising from non-minimal scalar-tensor coupling and the other from the matter sector. Based on these solutions, we analyze symmetric thick branes in a four-dimensional geometric framework. In this context, we assess gravity fluctuations to identify nearly massless modes across all Horndeski parameter values. These modes are subsequently employed to calculate corrections to the Newtonian potential and determine the limit of four-dimensional gravity.

This research presents a heuristic investigation into the distribution of prime numbers within short intervals. By modeling the occurrence of primes in these intervals as a counting experiment, we have offered both an experimental validation and an extension of the Montgomery and Soundararajan conjecture. This work represents a condensed version of my bachelor's thesis, which was submitted to the University of Valencia.

Over the past few years, empirical game-theoretic analysis (EGTA) has become a vital method for studying games where exact utility functions are unknown. Rather than relying on precise specifications, EGTA utilizes an oracle or simulator to obtain unbiased, noisy samples of player utilities for specific strategy profiles, allowing for empirical utility estimation through repeated queries. Recently, several progressive sampling (PS) algorithms have been developed to achieve PAC-style learning guarantees, such as identifying approximate Nash equilibria with high probability, while minimizing simulator queries. A recent study introduced "regret-pruning," a technique designed to further reduce the number of queries required in PS algorithms targeting pure Nash equilibria. However, this paper identifies a critical flaw in the original regret-pruning method: it only ensures that true pure Nash equilibria of the empirical game approximate those of the true game, offering no strong guarantees for approximate pure Nash equilibria. This limitation is significant because pure Nash equilibria are often computationally intractable or nonexistent in many games. To address this, we propose three novel regret-pruning variations. The first two extend the original approach to provide guarantees for approximate pure Nash equilibria within the empirical game, while the third variation offers robust guarantees for all approximate mixed Nash equilibria. Leveraging these variations, we developed two new progressive sampling algorithms, PS-REG+ and PS-REG-M. Experimental results demonstrate that these algorithms outperform the current state-of-the-art methods for learning pure and mixed equilibria in simulation-based games.

This manuscript investigates a Leslie-Gower predator-prey model characterized by a hyperbolic functional response and a weak Allee effect. The findings demonstrate that the system allows for the coexistence and oscillatory dynamics of both predator and prey populations. Furthermore, we delineate specific regions within the parameter space where various bifurcation types occur, including saddle-node, Hopf, and Bogdanov-Takens bifurcations.

The seven-equation model represents a compressible multiphase framework capable of handling disequilibrium in both pressure and velocity between phases. Utilizing a diffused interface method to simulate resolved multiphase flows, this approach introduces novel extensions to account for surface tension, viscosity, multi-species interactions, and chemical reactions. The model's ability to sustain pressure non-equilibrium enhances numerical stability during strong shocks and permits the use of arbitrary, independent equations of state. Fluxes are calculated via a discrete equations method (DEM), which demonstrates that stiff solvers for pressure and velocity relaxation are unnecessary because non-conservative fluxes are accurately captured. An interface compression scheme is employed to manage numerical diffusion at the interface, with its impact on the solution analyzed. Validation of the computational method is achieved through various test cases, including multiphase shock tubes, shock propagation across material boundaries, surface-tension-induced droplet oscillations, droplet acceleration in viscous fluids, and shock-detonation interactions with deforming droplets. Where feasible, simulation outcomes are benchmarked against exact solutions and experimental data.

It is established in the literature that the momentum space corresponding to the $\kappa$-Poincaré algebra is represented by the Lie group $\mathsf{A}\mathsf{N}(3)$. In this letter, we demonstrate that the complete $\kappa$-Poincaré Hopf algebra structure can be derived through relatively simple group-theoretic operations based on the Iwasawa decomposition of the $\mathsf{SO(1,4)}$ group.

Commissioned in 2022, LCLS-II stands as the world's first operational Continuous Wave (CW) hard X-Ray Free Electron Laser (XFEL). To propel electrons to an energy of 4 GeV, the facility employs 280 TESLA-type superconducting radio frequency (SRF) cavities operating at a few kilowatts with a loaded quality factor ($Q_L$) of $4 \times 10^7$, which results in a cavity bandwidth of 32 Hz. Maintaining the resonance frequency within this narrow bandwidth is critical to prevent a substantial rise in drive power. In superconducting accelerators, mechanical microphonic vibrations are a primary cause of resonance frequency shifts, often originating from rotary equipment like vacuum pumps and HVAC systems. Narrowband Active Noise Control (NANC) offers a viable solution for mitigating these disturbances, having previously been validated at DESY/CMTB and Cornell/CBETA. This paper details the adaptation of a NANC controller for the LCLS-II Low Level RF (LLRF) system and presents test results demonstrating the effective rejection of LCLS-II microphonic noise.

In our previous work at https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4887, we identified necessary conditions for a Riemannian manifold to support a local limiting Carleman weight (LCW), utilizing the Cotton-York tensor in three dimensions and the Weyl tensor in four dimensions. This paper extends those findings by deriving additional necessary conditions for local LCWs that are frequently sufficient. For manifolds in dimensions 3 and 4, we classify the corresponding Cotton-York and Weyl tensors and outline a procedure to determine LCW existence for each tensor type. Specifically, we demonstrate that a product of two surfaces admits an LCW if and only if at least one of the surfaces is of revolution. This result yields an example of a manifold that satisfies the eigenflag condition described in \cite{AFGR} yet fails to admit an LCW.

The Move language offers programming abstractions for digital assets by combining value and reference semantics. Although guaranteeing memory safety in programs where references interact with a shared, mutable global ledger is challenging and crucial for Move's intended applications, the language overcomes this hurdle through a unique memory model and a modular, intraprocedural static analysis of reference safety that exploits specific memory characteristics. This analysis guarantees that no memory safety violations occur in any Move program—including those linking to untrusted code—by executing as a bytecode verification step during the loading process, akin to mechanisms in the JVM and CLR. The authors have formalized this static analysis and demonstrated that it satisfies three key properties: the elimination of dangling references, referential transparency for immutable references, and the prevention of memory leaks.

The Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) framework seeks to learn invariant features across multiple environments to address out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. This approach relies on the premise that causal components of data generation remain stable across environments or that data overlaps sufficiently to identify these meaningful features. However, when this overlap assumption fails, the identified invariant features may fall short of optimal predictive performance, a limitation that naturally occurs in networked and hierarchical data-generating models, rendering IRM suboptimal in such contexts. To address this failure mode, we propose a partial invariance framework. The core strategy involves introducing flexibility into IRM by segmenting environments based on hierarchical distinctions and enforcing invariance only within these local partitions. We illustrate this framework within classification scenarios involving causal distribution shifts. Our findings demonstrate that partial invariant risk minimization can effectively balance the trade-off between fairness and risk in specific settings.

We demonstrate that a minimal framework, employing solely the graviton as an intermediary between the inflaton, the dark sector, and the Standard Model (SM), can simultaneously account for the observed dark matter (DM) relic density, generate baryon asymmetry via leptogenesis, and establish a sufficiently hot thermal bath post-inflation. Assuming an inflaton potential of the form $V(\phi)\propto \phi^k$ near its minimum at the end of inflation, we address the fact that previous constraints on dark radiation have ruled out simple reheating via minimal gravitational interactions due to excessive inflationary gravitational waves. Consequently, we expand the minimal model through several modifications: i) incorporating non-minimal gravitational couplings, which suggests a parameter space for DM masses $M_{N_1} \simeq 2-10$ PeV, right-handed neutrino masses $M_{N_2} \simeq (5-20) \times 10^{11}$ GeV, and reheating temperatures $T_\text{rh} \lesssim 3 \times 10^5$ GeV (for $k \le 20$); ii) offering an explanation for the PeV excess detected by IceCube when DM possesses a direct yet small Yukawa coupling to the SM; and iii) introducing a novel two-step mechanism for gravitational DM production, initially creating two scalars that subsequently decay into fermionic DM. In this scenario, the lack of helicity suppression boosts DM and baryon asymmetry production, permitting a broad range of parameters, including sub-MeV DM masses where warmness could be detectable via cosmic 21-cm lines, even if gravitational interactions drive reheating. Furthermore, we indicate that detectable primordial gravitational wave signals offer a pathway to probe this scenario for $T_\text{rh}\lesssim 5\times 10^6$ GeV in upcoming experiments such as BBO, DECIGO, CE, and ET.

This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of transition form factors for axial-vector meson production through the two-photon fusion process $\gamma^* \gamma^* \to 1^{++}$, involving space-like virtual photons in the initial state and a $P$-wave axial-vector quarkonium in the final state. The analysis utilizes light-front quarkonium wave functions derived from solving the Schr\"odinger equation for various interquark potentials describing $Q \bar Q$ interactions. We determine the helicity structure and covariant decomposition of the matrix elements, which are broadly applicable to any $q \bar q$ axial-vector meson $\gamma^* \gamma^* \to 1^{++}$ transition, with numerical results specifically provided for the phenomenologically significant charmonium $\chi_{c1}$ state. The helicity form factors are presented as functions of both photon virtualities. Additionally, we find that the ratio $Q F_{\rm LT}(Q^2,0)/F_{\rm TT}(Q^2,0)$ remains constant.

The WZ production cross section has been measured in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV using data from the CMS detector, which corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. The inclusive cross section is determined to be $\sigma_{\text{tot}}$(pp $\to$ WZ) = 48.09 $^{+1.00}_{-0.96}$ (stat) $^{+0.44}_{-0.37}$ (theo) $^{+2.39}_{-2.17}$ (syst) $\pm$ 1.39 (lumi) pb, yielding a total uncertainty range of $-$2.78/$+$2.98 pb. Additionally, fiducial cross sections and ratios of charge-dependent cross sections are presented. The analysis also includes differential cross section measurements as a function of three variables: the Z boson transverse momentum ($p_\mathrm{T}$), the leading jet $p_\mathrm{T}$, and the $m$(WZ) variable, defined as the invariant mass of the system comprising the three leptons and the missing transverse momentum. Furthermore, differential measurements relative to the W boson $p_\mathrm{T}$, categorized by charge, are provided. The results align with Standard Model predictions, showing better agreement with next-to-next-to-leading-order calculations than with next-to-leading-order ones. Constraints on anomalous triple gauge couplings are established through a binned maximum likelihood fit applied to the $m$(WZ) distribution.

This study examines the $W^{s,p}$-boundedness of stationary wave operators associated with the Schrödinger operator featuring an inverse-square potential, defined as $\mathcal L_a=-\Delta+\tfrac{a}{|x|^2}$ for $a\geq -\tfrac{(d-2)^2}{4}$ in dimensions $d\geq 2$. We define these stationary wave operators using integrals involving Bessel functions and spherical harmonics, demonstrating their $W^{s,p}$-boundedness for specific values of $p$ and $s$ that vary with $a$. As corollaries, we resolve several open issues related to $\mathcal L_a$, including dispersive and local smoothing estimates across dimensions $d\geq 2$. Furthermore, we extend established results—such as uniform Sobolev inequalities, the equivalence of Sobolev norms, and the Mikhlin multiplier theorem—to a broader range of indices. These findings are significant for characterizing both linear and nonlinear dynamics in dispersive equations subject to an inverse-square potential.

Respiratory rate (RR) serves as a clinical indicator for evaluating general health and physical condition. An individual's RR may deviate from their baseline due to chronic conditions like asthma or congestive heart failure, acute illnesses such as infection-induced breathlessness, or daily fluctuations caused by physical fatigue during high exertion. Remotely estimating RR provides a cost-efficient means to monitor disease progression and cardio-respiratory fitness over time. This study examines a model-driven technique to estimate RR from brief audio clips recorded after physical activity in healthy adults. Data were gathered from 21 participants using microphones in near-field headphones, capturing recordings before, during, and after strenuous exercise. RR values were manually annotated by counting perceived breaths. A multi-task Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network incorporating convolutional layers was developed to process mel-filterbank energies, estimate RR amidst varying background noise, and predict heavy breathing defined as an RR exceeding 25 breaths per minute. This multi-task architecture handles both classification and regression using a combination of loss functions. Results indicate that RR can be estimated with a concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) of 0.76 and a mean squared error (MSE) of 0.2, confirming that audio signals are a viable medium for approximating respiratory rate.

By applying the external field technique—specifically by calculating the effective action $V_{\mathrm{eff}}$ for constant, homogeneous fields of arbitrary strength—we investigate nonperturbative aspects of QED with a general gyromagnetic ratio $g$. Our analysis reveals a cusp at $g = 2$ within: a) the QED $b_0$ renormalization group coefficient, and b) a subset of light-light scattering coefficients, including the pseudoscalar ${\cal P}^{2n}= (\vec E\cdot\vec B)^{2n}$, in the infinite wavelength limit. Furthermore, the characteristics of $b_0$ suggest that asymptotic freedom can occur in Abelian theories for specific ranges of $g$.

This work investigates a collaborative multi-agent stochastic linear bandit framework where $N$ networked agents communicate locally to minimize collective regret. In this environment, each agent faces a distinct linear bandit problem with its own reward parameter, aiming to identify the optimal global action relative to the average of these parameters. During every round, agents submit action proposals, one of which is randomly chosen and executed as the network-wide action. All agents then observe the resulting rewards and employ an accelerated consensus mechanism to estimate the mean reward across the network. We introduce a distributed Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithm and establish a high-probability regret bound for $T$ rounds, which accounts for a linear regret component tied to each communication step. The derived regret bound scales as $\mathcal{O}\Big(\sqrt{\frac{T}{N \log(1/|\lambda_2|)}}\cdot (\log T)^2\Big)$, where $\lambda_2$ represents the second largest eigenvalue of the communication matrix in absolute value.

We have investigated how thermal conduction influences the structure of viscous and resistive advection-dominated accretion flows (ADAFs). Observations of hot gas surrounding Sgr A$^*$ and other nearby galactic nuclei confirm the significance of thermal conduction in hot accretion flows. In this study, we model thermal conduction using a saturated form, which is suitable for weakly-collisional systems. We assume that viscosity and magnetic diffusivity arise from turbulence and dissipation within the flow, with viscosity specifically facilitating angular momentum transport. Unlike constant values, both magnetic diffusivity and kinematic viscosity vary spatially and are defined via an $\alpha$-prescription. The governing equations were solved using the steady self-similar method. The resulting solutions indicate that radial velocities are highly subsonic and rotational velocities are sub-Keplerian. Furthermore, for a specific thermal conduction coefficient, the rotational velocity drops to zero; this critical conductivity value depends heavily on the magnetic pressure fraction, magnetic Prandtl number, and viscosity parameter. Comparing energy transport mechanisms reveals that thermal conduction can be a dominant energy process in resistive, magnetized ADAFs, a finding supported by non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) simulations.

Leveraging increased bandwidth, Terahertz (THz) communication is poised to meet the explosive ultra-high-speed demands of future 6G wireless systems. To mitigate high-frequency path loss, massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) technology is employed to achieve high array gains through beamforming. However, the reliance on numerous analog phase shifters for analog beamforming in current THz massive MIMO systems results in substantial energy consumption. This paper proposes a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-based hybrid precoding architecture for THz communication, substituting the energy-intensive phased array with an energy-efficient RIS to perform analog beamforming. Building on this architecture, the study investigates a sum-rate maximization problem for hybrid precoding. Given that practical RIS phase shifts are discrete, this non-convex constrained optimization problem is inherently challenging. To address this, the problem is reformulated as a parallel deep neural network (DNN)-based classification task, solvable via a proposed low-complexity deep learning-based multiple discrete classification (DL-MDC) hybrid precoding scheme. Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed DL-MDC scheme performs effectively under both the theoretical Saleh-Valenzuela and practical 3GPP channel models. Compared to existing iterative search algorithms, the proposed DL-MDC scheme significantly reduces computational runtime while incurring negligible performance loss.

The CMS experiment at the LHC reports a measurement of the $\mathrm{Z}/\gamma^{*} \to \tau\tau$ cross section from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, utilizing an integrated luminosity of 2.3 fb$^{-1}$. The product of the inclusive cross section and the branching fraction is determined to be $\sigma(\mathrm{pp} \to \mathrm{Z}/\gamma^{*}\text{+X}) \, \mathcal{B}(\mathrm{Z}/\gamma^{*} \to \tau\tau) = $ 1848 $\pm$ 12 (stat) $\pm$ 67 (syst+lumi) pb, which aligns with standard model predictions calculated at next-to-next-to-leading order in perturbative quantum chromodynamics. This result serves to validate novel analysis methods pertinent to future studies of $\tau$ lepton production and establishes the reconstruction efficiency and energy scale for $\tau$ decays into hadrons plus $\nu_{\tau}$, with relative uncertainties of 2.2% and 0.9%, respectively.

Gravitational wave interferometers attain exceptional sensitivity by integrating Michelson interferometers with optical cavities, suspended masses, and squeezed quantum states of light. By modifying the measurement processes in LIGO, VIRGO, and GEO600, these states mitigate quantum noise that obscures astrophysical signals, making further advancements in squeezing crucial for expanding our gravitational perspective of the universe. To achieve even greater noise reduction, it is necessary to minimize decoherence caused by losses and employ more advanced techniques to counteract quantum back-action from radiation pressure. Both objectives demand a comprehensive understanding of the physical interactions between squeezed light and the various components of kilometer-scale interferometers. Consequently, data from both LIGO observatories during observing run three are analyzed using frequency-dependent metrics to evaluate each detector's quantum response to squeezed states. These derived metrics effectively describe the physical mechanisms underlying squeezing's concurrent interaction with transverse-mode selective optical cavities and the quantum radiation pressure noise of suspended mirrors. Such metrics and their associated analyses are widely applicable to cavity-enhanced optomechanics experiments utilizing external squeezing and, for the first time, provide physical descriptions of all observed features in the quantum noise of LIGO detectors.

We consider $N\subset GL(n,R)$, the group of upper triangular matrices with unit diagonal entries, endowed with its standard Carnot group structure. We demonstrate that for $n \geq 4$, quasiconformal homeomorphisms between open subsets of $N$—and more broadly, Sobolev mappings possessing a nondegenerate Pansu differential—exhibit rigidity. This finding confirms the Regularity Conjecture for these groups. The proof relies on a rigidity theorem concerning the manifold of complete flags in $R^n$. Analogous conclusions apply to both complex and quaternionic settings.

This work introduces the integration of the safe C dialect, Checked C, into the RIOT Internet of Things operating system. By converting specific sections of the RIOT network stack to Checked C, we achieve spatial memory safety within those code segments. Consistent with previous research on safe C dialects for IoT OSs, our integration is fully optional, allowing compilation with standard C compilers that lack support for Checked C extensions. To our knowledge, this marks the first proposed integration of a safe C dialect for RIOT. We detail an incremental methodology for migrating RIOT modules to Checked C, assess the performance overhead resulting from these conversions, and share insights regarding the practical application of Checked C within the IoT domain.

This study introduces the inaugural Entity Linking corpus for Icelandic. We detail a methodology that integrates the multilingual entity linking model mGENRE with the Wikipedia API Search (WAPIS) for data labeling, contrasting it against a baseline utilizing WAPIS alone.
