Our findings indicate that the combined approach achieves a 53.9% coverage rate, significantly outperforming the 30.9% attained by using WAPIS in isolation. Furthermore, we examine these outcomes to highlight the benefits of employing multilingual systems for Icelandic tasks and investigate the characteristics of the remaining unlabeled data, identifying patterns that contribute to annotation difficulties.

Square-root topology represents a newly developed area of study concerning insulators and superconductors that exhibit topological properties only after their Hamiltonians are squared; specifically, the finite-energy edge states of the original square-root model derive their topology from the zero-energy edge states of a recognized topological insulator or superconductor found in the squared version. By examining one-dimensional systems, we demonstrate how this principle extends to $2^n$-root topological insulators and superconductors for any positive integer $n$, establishing a systematic framework for their construction. Drawing on graph theory, we define the "arborescence" of these $2^n$-root systems, which maps the Hamiltonian of the initial model to that of the known topological parent through successive squaring operations and constant energy shifts. This research lays the groundwork for expanding $2^n$-root topology into higher-dimensional contexts.
The motivic Donaldson-Thomas series for an elliptic Sklyanin algebra, which corresponds to a point of order two, does not align with the series proposed in Conjecture 3.4 of 1510.08116.

Creating realistic mock galaxy catalogs is vital for preparing large-scale galaxy surveys, as it allows researchers to test theoretical models and evaluate systematic errors. We introduce an updated mock catalog derived from the Millennium-XXL simulation, employing a halo occupation distribution (HOD) approach to assign r-band magnitudes and g-r colours. Several adjustments were implemented to enhance consistency with data from the SDSS and GAMA surveys. Specifically, we replaced the original cubic interpolation method, which caused extreme velocity variations between snapshots, with linear interpolation; this change improves quadrupole measurements of the correlation function on small scales. Additionally, the g-r colour distributions have been refined to better match GAMA observations, especially for faint galaxies. As a demonstration of the catalog's scientific utility, we analyzed the luminosity function's dependence on environment and colour, finding strong agreement with GAMA measurements. Designed for the ongoing Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Bright Galaxy Survey (BGS), this full-sky mock is complete down to a magnitude limit of r=20.2.

New searches for muon-to-electron conversion aim to improve limits on charged lepton flavor violation (CLFV) by four orders of magnitude. By analyzing P and CP selection rules alongside the structure of charge and current densities, we identify that conversion rates depend on six nuclear responses. To formulate these responses microscopically, we construct the CLFV interaction at the nucleon level using non-relativistic effective theory (NRET) and embed it within a nucleus. We review prior studies, highlighting the absence of a systematic approach to handling various small parameters.

Given that momentum transfer is comparable to the inverse nuclear size, a comprehensive multipole expansion of response functions is required—a challenging task involving Coulomb-distorted electron partial waves. We execute this expansion with high precision by introducing a simplified local electron momentum to treat the complete set of 16 NRET operators. Previous efforts were restricted to basic charge and spin operators, often neglecting Coulomb distortion or truncating partial wave expansions, and omitted the nucleon velocity operator, which contributes to three response functions; these omissions led to inconsistencies in treating small parameters. We derive a "master formula" for muon-to-electron conversion that correctly accounts for all such effects, including muon velocity. We calculate conversion rates for various experimental targets to establish bounds on CLFV operator coefficients.

We also address the nuclear physics involved, noting how two types of coherence amplify specific CLFV operators while selection rules render elastic muon-to-electron conversion insensitive to others. Furthermore, we discuss the matching of NRET to higher-level effective field theories and the connection to other CLFV tests. Finally, we present a publicly available script for computing muon-to-electron conversion rates in nuclear targets.

Masers, which function as the microwave counterpart to lasers, offer ultra-low noise amplification for applications ranging from medical MRI to deep-space communication. Modern research in this field has been revitalized by the identification of room-temperature operable gain media, eliminating the need for the bulky cryogenic systems that previously limited their utility. Despite this breakthrough, progress in discovering entirely new room-temperature materials has been limited, with only pentacene-doped para-terphenyl and negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy defects in diamond currently recognized. This study presents the discovery of 6,13-diazapentacene doped in para-terphenyl as a novel maser gain medium capable of operating at room temperature without an external magnetic field. With a measured pulse power of -10 dBm, this material matches the absolute power output of its pentacene-based predecessor while offering significant advantages, including a faster amplification startup time, excitation via longer 620 nm wavelengths, and enhanced chemical stability due to nitrogen incorporation. Additionally, the maser bursts enable this material to achieve the strong coupling regime in cavity quantum electrodynamics, demonstrating a high cooperativity of 182. By analyzing the optical and microwave spin dynamics, we observe fast intersystem crossing and a favorable triplet quantum yield, confirming its effectiveness as a gain medium. These findings not only facilitate the future identification of similar maser materials but also establish them as promising candidates for investigating cavity quantum electrodynamic effects at ambient temperatures.

This work introduces bicategorical counterparts to various geometric concepts derived from spectral theory. Initially, we define local right biadjoints and demonstrate their equivalence to bistable pseudofunctors, thereby categorifying a previously established 1-categorical result. We further examine additional laxness conditions to elucidate properties of known lax familial pseudofunctors. Additionally, we outline 2-dimensional analogs of orthogonality and factorization systems, utilizing these to generate examples of bistable pseudofunctors via the inclusion of left objects and maps. By applying this construction to factorization systems of geometric morphisms, we establish geometry-like structures within Grothendieck topoi. Notably, we prove a novel factorization theorem for geometric morphisms (specifically in the terminally connected, pro-etale context), which aligns with a specific local geometry integral to the broader construction of spectra.

Reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted communication emerges as a promising enabler for sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks, offering a novel approach to optimize system performance. This study addresses a critical gap in existing literature by presenting a precise, source-based, and broadly applicable RIS channel model tailored for millimeter-wave frequencies. The proposed model is versatile, accommodating diverse indoor and outdoor scenarios while incorporating the physical dynamics of wireless propagation with RIS and addressing practical 5G channel modeling challenges. Furthermore, this paper introduces the open-source SimRIS Channel Simulator, a comprehensive tool designed for simulating RIS-assisted communication systems.

This study identifies the optimal learning scenario for training agent teams to compete against various opposing strategies. We assess cooperative value-based approaches within a mixed cooperative-competitive setting, specifically focusing on a symmetric, partially observable, two-team Markov game. Three training methods adhering to the centralized training and decentralized execution (CTDE) paradigm—QMIX, MAVEN, and QVMix—were selected. For each method, we examined three learning scenarios distinguished by the diversity of team policies encountered during training. To facilitate these experiments, we adapted the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge environment to establish competitive settings where both teams could learn and compete concurrently. Our findings indicate that training against multiple evolving strategies yields the best outcomes when team performance is evaluated against a variety of opposing strategies.

Data cleaning remains a widespread challenge for organizations seeking to leverage their data assets. Driven by recent breakthroughs in networking and cloud computing, a new paradigm known as Database-as-a-Service has emerged, enabling data management tasks to be delegated to major service providers. This paper introduces a Data Cleaning-as-a-Service framework where clients interact with providers hosting both curated and sensitive datasets. We propose PACAS, a Privacy-Aware Data Cleaning-as-a-Service model that orchestrates interactions between clients and providers through a pricing mechanism based on data sensitivity. Additionally, we introduce extensions to the model that define generalized data repairs to obfuscate sensitive information, thereby facilitating secure data sharing. We also develop a novel semantic distance metric to assess the utility of these repairs and redefine consistency within the context of generalized values. The PACAS model employs (X,Y,L)-anonymity, an advancement over traditional data publishing methods that incorporates semantic data characteristics while protecting sensitive attributes. Empirical evaluations using real-world data demonstrate that PACAS effectively safeguards semantically related sensitive values and achieves lower repair errors than current privacy-aware cleaning techniques.

Continuous-Variable (CV) systems offer a compelling avenue for realizing large-scale quantum information protocols. Within this context, we establish a general quantum computational framework grounded in CV hardware, comprising vacuum inputs, a limited collection of gates (which include non-Gaussian components), and homodyne detection. We demonstrate that this architecture supports encodings capable of enabling probabilistic, fault-tolerant universal quantum computation. Additionally, we illustrate how the model can be configured to generate sampling tasks that are classically intractable unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses. This insight provides a straightforward paradigm for near-term experimental investigations into quantum advantage, utilizing Gaussian states, homodyne detection, and specific non-Gaussian evolutions. Finally, we examine the recently proposed Instantaneous Quantum Computing model for CV systems and confirm that its computational hardness remains robust against certain experimentally feasible simplifications.

The successful operation of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) over the past two years enabled the investigation of particle interactions within a novel energy regime. The LHC experiments conducted measurements of key Standard Model processes, including the production of high-\pt\ jets, $W$ and $Z$ bosons, and top and $b$-quarks. Furthermore, the high collision energy facilitated a search for new particles in previously unexplored mass regions, leading to significant constraints on the existence of new particles predicted by various physics beyond the Standard Model. With integrated luminosities approaching 5 \ifb\ in 2011, the experiments also achieved the sensitivity necessary to probe the existence of the Standard Model Higgs boson across a broad mass range. This report summarizes the major physics results obtained by the two general-purpose experiments, ATLAS and CMS.

Over the past twenty years, significant advances have been made in comprehending the geometry of smooth Gaussian fields. This survey focuses on a specific research trajectory: the large-scale behavior of level and excursion sets and their hypothesized link to percolation theory.

Over the last twenty years, Complex Event Recognition (CER) systems have gained popularity for their capacity to instantly identify patterns within real-time event streams. Nevertheless, there remains a gap in methodologies capable of predicting when a pattern will occur prior to its actual detection by a CER engine. This paper introduces a formal framework designed to tackle Complex Event Forecasting (CEF). The proposed approach integrates two formalisms: symbolic automata, which encode complex event patterns, and prediction suffix trees, which offer a concise probabilistic representation of an automaton's behavior. When compared to state-of-the-art techniques, our method demonstrates superior accuracy and efficiency. Specifically, as variable-order Markov models, prediction suffix trees can capture long-term dependencies in a stream by retaining only past sequences that hold sufficient information. Experimental results highlight the accuracy benefits derived from capturing these long-term dependencies. This is accomplished by increasing the model order beyond the limits of full-order Markov models, which require exhaustive enumeration of all possible past sequences of a specific order. Furthermore, the paper provides an extensive discussion on the optimal evaluation metrics for CEF solutions, focusing specifically on forecast quality.

Deriving query-document relevance from sparse and biased click logs remains a foundational challenge in web search systems. Existing approaches primarily rely on semantic features of queries and documents to learn relevance models, often neglecting direct counterfactual evaluation derived from click logs. While these semantic matching models can signal relevance for tail queries when features are present, they lack the ability to introspectively correct biased relevance estimates when they conflict with abundant implicit user feedback. Conversely, counterfactual evaluation methods guarantee unbiased relevance estimation given sufficient click data but struggle with the sparsity or absence of clicks inherent in long-tailed query distributions. This paper proposes unifying counterfactual evaluation and learning to achieve unbiased relevance estimation across queries of varying popularity. Specifically, we theoretically construct a doubly robust estimator with minimized bias and variance, strategically merging the advantages of current evaluation and learning paradigms. We further implement this unbiased relevance estimation framework within Baidu search, incorporating comprehensive practical solutions for click behavior tracking data pipelines and online relevance estimation using an approximate deep neural network. Finally, extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate the framework's practical robustness and its substantial improvement in online ranking performance.

This work re-examines the multi-agent epistemic logic introduced in [10], substituting agents and agent sets with abstract, intensional "names." Our contributions are threefold. First, we analyze its model theory by establishing appropriate concepts of bisimulation and frame morphisms to investigate the logic's expressive capabilities and definability. Second, we demonstrate that the logic admits a natural neighborhood semantics, which proves that the axiomatization in [10] avoids reliance on potentially contentious introspective properties of knowledge. Finally, we expand the logic to include common and distributed knowledge operators, delivering sound and complete axiomatizations for both extensions. Collectively, these findings reposition the original epistemic logic with names within a contemporary framework and pave the way for logically analyzing epistemic scenarios where group membership is uncertain or fluctuating.

Boolean automata networks (BANs) extend the concept of Boolean cellular automata, making any theorem regarding their information processing capabilities a versatile tool applicable to diverse computational models. This paper investigates an approach to BANs that incorporates external inputs into the fundamental model through modules and, crucially, connects networks via these inputs using wirings. Our objective is to establish a robust formalism for the (de)composition of BANs. We present two key findings: first, demonstrating that our definition of modules and wirings is complete, and second, utilizing these components to derive simulation results between BANs.

Standard Natural Language Processing (NLP) evaluation typically involves independently averaging the scores of competing systems across a shared set of test instances. This work challenges the practice of using averages—or even medians—to aggregate these scores into a single metric for determining the best system, as these methods overlook the inherent pairing of scores derived from identical test instances. We highlight the necessity of accounting for this instance-level pairing and demonstrate, through both theoretical analysis and empirical evidence, the benefits of aggregation strategies based on pairwise comparisons, such as the Bradley-Terry (BT) model, which estimates the probability that one system outperforms another on the test set. By re-evaluating 296 real-world NLP setups spanning four tasks and 18 metrics, we reveal that the choice of aggregation method significantly impacts results, leading to different conclusions about state-of-the-art systems in approximately 30% of cases. To support the implementation of pairwise evaluation, we have released a practical tool capable of conducting comprehensive analyses using mean, median, BT, and two BT variants (Elo and TrueSkill), along with features for appropriate statistical testing.

We introduce a novel modal logic featuring a straightforward deductive framework designed to interpret Aristotle's theory of modal syllogisms. Drawing inspiration from standard propositional modal logic, this system operates as a logic of terms and supports a sound extensional semantics based on possible states-of-affairs within a specific world. When applied to Aristotle's modal syllogistic as presented in the \emph{Prior Analytics} A8-22, it illuminates several nuanced distinctions; recognizing these distinctions resolves ambiguities and yields a fully consistent system capable of validating all modal syllogisms Aristotle deemed correct. Additionally, this logic establishes a bridge to the axioms of contemporary propositional modal logic, revealing the extent to which these principles are implicit in Aristotle's reasoning. Future research will focus on determining the completeness of this logic (or its variants) and expanding it to encompass a calculus of relations, such as the relational syllogistic discussed in Galen's \emph{Introduction to Logic}, which Slomkowsky contends is already present in the \emph{Topics}.

ArCo serves as the Italian Cultural Heritage knowledge graph, comprising a network of seven vocabularies and 169 million triples that describe approximately 820,000 cultural entities. It is distributed alongside a SPARQL endpoint, software for transforming catalogue records into RDF, and an extensive collection of documentation materials, including testing guides, evaluations, tutorials, and examples. Built upon the official General Catalogue of the Italian Ministry of Cultural Heritage and Activities (MiBAC)—along with its associated encoding regulations—ArCo collects and validates records for virtually all Italian cultural heritage properties (excluding libraries and archives), contributed by heritage administrators across the country. This presentation outlines its architecture, design methodologies, and supporting tools, highlights its expanding community, and defines its significance, quality, and impact.

Quantum causality represents a distinct quantum phenomenon that defies classical cause-and-effect intuitions, setting it apart from other effects like entanglement and nonlocality. To address the detection loophole inherent in testing quantum causality, we investigate the necessary detection efficiencies for observing such violations. First, we demonstrate that existing classical causal inequalities demand detection efficiencies of at least 95.97% (89.44%) to reveal violations using quantum (nonsignaling) correlations. We then introduce a new classical causal inequality, $I_{222}$, which lowers these thresholds to 92.39% for quantum correlations and 81.65% for nonsignaling correlations, thereby significantly easing detection requirements. Following an extension of this inequality to multiple measurement settings and an analysis of the associated efficiency, we note that prior quantum causal inequalities require a minimum of 94.29% efficiency to violate nonsignaling correlations. Subsequently, we derive a novel quantum causal bound, $J_{222}$, which reduces the necessary detection efficiency to 91.02% for nonsignaling violations. Ultimately, our research facilitates future experimental verification of quantum causality and highlights that causal inequalities differ notably from Bell inequalities regarding their detection efficiency demands.

We introduce a practical approach to achieve rate points on the dominant face of the multiple access channel capacity using a standard, low-complexity decoder. This method is grounded in recent theoretical work by Zhu and Gastpar on compute-forward multiple access (CFMA), which attains channel capacity via a sequential decoder. We demonstrate the strategy using standard LDPC codes. The decoding process occurs in two stages: first, the receiver recovers a linear combination of the transmitted codewords using the sum-product algorithm (SPA); second, leveraging this recovered sum as side information, the receiver retrieves one codeword via a modified SPA, thereby recovering both. The primary advantage of decoding the sum of codewords rather than individual codewords is the ability to reach points on the dominant face of the capacity region without requiring rate-splitting or time-sharing, all while maintaining complexity comparable to a standard point-to-point decoder. This property is particularly vital for certain applications, such as interference channels. Furthermore, simulation results with single-layer binary codes indicate that our proposed strategy stays within 1.7 dB of theoretical limits, even without explicit optimization of the off-the-shelf LDPC codes.

Precise road network prediction from satellite imagery demands a comprehensive grasp of network topology. To achieve this, we introduce a graph-based framework that leverages reinforcement learning (RL) to simulate the sequential addition of graph edges. Specifically, provided with a partially constructed graph corresponding to a satellite image, an RL agent selects modifications that optimize cumulative rewards. Unlike conventional supervised methods constrained by standard surrogate losses, our approach allows rewards to be defined by diverse, complex, and potentially non-continuous metrics, thereby offering greater flexibility to encode problem-specific knowledge. Empirical evaluations across multiple benchmark datasets reveal improved performance and superior high-level reasoning regarding graph topology when employing tree-based search. Additionally, we present a new synthetic benchmark dataset to demonstrate the robustness and superiority of our method under significant occlusion conditions.

Monocular depth estimation has advanced significantly in recent years, enabling a deeper understanding of three-dimensional environments from single images. Despite this progress, the task remains ill-posed due to the challenge of inferring depth directly from 2D inputs, a hurdle that deep learning techniques have helped overcome. However, most existing approaches suffer from detail loss caused by continuous downsampling during the transition from RGB to depth space. To address this, we propose the Multi-scale Features Network (MSFNet), which integrates an Enhanced Diverse Attention (EDA) module and an Upsample-Stage Fusion (USF) module. The EDA module utilizes spatial attention to capture key spatial features, while the USF module enhances prediction quality by fusing multi-scale features, combining high-level semantics with low-level details. Furthermore, to mitigate the difficulty in converging on hard samples that are often neglected in favor of simpler ones, we introduce a batch-loss mechanism that assigns higher loss weights to challenging instances within a batch. Experimental results on the NYU-Depth V2 and KITTI datasets confirm that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in both qualitative and quantitative metrics.

Frequency encoding is rapidly emerging as a promising option for quantum information protocols due to its larger Hilbert spaces and superior noise resilience compared to other photonic degrees of freedom. To fully realize frequency encoding as a practical paradigm for quantum information processing, an efficient and straightforward source of frequency entanglement is essential. We introduce a single-pass source of discrete frequency-bin entanglement that avoids the use of filtering or resonant cavities. Utilizing a domain-engineered nonlinear crystal, we generate an eight-mode frequency-bin entangled source at telecommunication wavelengths. This method capitalizes on the high heralding efficiency and simplicity characteristic of bulk crystal sources.

High-speed, high-resolution stereoscopic (H2-Stereo) video enables the perception of dynamic 3D content with fine granularity, yet acquiring such video using standard cameras remains difficult. Current approaches relying on spatial super-resolution or temporal frame interpolation offer incomplete solutions, sacrificing either temporal or spatial fidelity. To address this, we introduce a dual-camera setup: one captures low-frame-rate, high-spatial-resolution (LSR-HFR) footage rich in spatial detail, while the other records high-frame-rate, low-spatial-resolution (HFR-LSR) videos ensuring smooth temporal continuity. We then develop a Learned Information Fusion network (LIFnet) that leverages cross-camera redundancies to boost both views to high spatiotemporal resolution (HSTR) for effective H2-Stereo reconstruction. Utilizing a disparity network capable of handling large disparities, we implement disparity-guided flow-based warping for the HFR-LSR view and complementary warping for the LSR-HFR view. Additionally, a multi-scale feature-domain fusion technique minimizes occlusion-induced artifacts like warping ghosts and holes in the LSR-HFR view. Trained end-to-end on a high-quality Stereo Video dataset collected from YouTube, the LIFnet significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on both synthetic and real-world large-disparity data. Comprehensive ablation studies further investigate the system's performance regarding spatiotemporal resolution, camera baseline, desynchronization, exposure settings, and various applications to fully assess its potential.

This paper investigates dynamic network selection for mobile users within an Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS)-enabled wireless environment. Specifically, users dynamically choose among various Service Providers (SPs) and network services over time, where these services comprise both IRS resources and transmit power. To model this selection process, we employ an evolutionary game framework, allowing users to adjust their network choices based on achieved utilities, with replicator dynamics utilized to simulate this adaptation. Furthermore, to incorporate users' past service experiences into their decision-making, we introduce an enhanced approach known as the fractional evolutionary game. This method integrates a memory effect that reflects users' recollection of their past decisions. We theoretically demonstrate that both game models possess a unique equilibrium. Finally, numerical results validate the efficacy of our proposed approaches, revealing key insights such as the fact that the inclusion of a memory effect enables users to attain higher utilities compared to scenarios without it.

Reversible computing represents a computational paradigm where processes are deterministic in both forward and backward directions, ensuring programs possess well-defined semantics for both execution paths. This study examines the formal semantics of the reversible functional language Rfun by introducing join inverse rig categories, a synthesis of join inverse categories and rig categories. We demonstrate that, under reasonable assumptions, these categories can effectively model Rfun. Furthermore, they prove to be a particularly natural framework for reversible computing as a whole, as they also encompass models for other reversible languages, including Theseus and reversible flowcharts. This indicates that join inverse rig categories likely constitute the fundamental categorical models for reversible computing.

This paper aims to establish a general framework for estimating fluid motion through a constraint-based refinement method. We show that with a specific constraint selection, our approach closely mimics continuity equation-based fluid flow, a claim supported theoretically by a modified augmented Lagrangian method and confirmed via numerical validation. In addition to the continuity constraint, the model accommodates other geometric constraints. The system's mathematical well-posedness is analyzed within a Hilbert space context. A distinctive aspect of our framework is its ability to diagonalize the system using the Cauchy-Riemann operator, converting it into a diffusion process involving the flow's curl and divergence. By applying semigroup theory to this decoupled system, we demonstrate that the method preserves the spatial properties of divergence and vorticity. Finally, we present results from multiple numerical experiments across various datasets.

Text style transfer presents a difficult text generation challenge that involves modifying a sentence's style to match a target while maintaining its original meaning. Due to the natural lack of parallel datasets, recent research has primarily focused on unsupervised solutions. However, existing gradient-based methods typically face two key limitations: (1) Content migration, where the absence of explicit content invariance modeling makes these approaches prone to unintended content shifts between the source and target sentences; and (2) Style misclassification, a drawback of gradient-guided methods where the inference process resembles adversarial attacks, causing latent optimization to potentially exploit the classifier and hinder high transfer accuracy. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a novel gradient-guided model utilizing a contrastive paradigm to explicitly cluster semantically similar sentences and a siamese-structured style classifier to mitigate both issues. Experimental results on two datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

This study numerically examines how disorder influences the quantum Hall effect (QHE) and quantum phase transitions in silicene using a lattice model. Results indicate that a pristine silicene sample displays an unconventional QHE near the band center, characterized by plateaus at $\nu=0,\pm2,\pm6,\ldots$, alongside a conventional QHE near the band edges. When disorder is introduced, Hall plateaus can be eliminated via the "float-up" of extended states toward the band center, causing higher plateaus to vanish first. Notably, the $\nu=0$ plateau at the center proves more fragile to disorder, disappearing even at relatively low disorder strengths. Furthermore, the interplay between an electric field and intrinsic spin-orbit interaction (SOI) can induce quantum phase transitions from a topological insulator to a band insulator at the charge neutrality point (CNP), resulting in additional quantum Hall conductivity plateaus.

The study of Lagrangian geometry within matroids began in [ADH20] with the development of the conormal fan for a matroid $M$. Leveraging this fan, we provided a Lagrangian-geometric framework for interpreting the $h$-vector of $M$'s broken circuit complex; specifically, its components correspond to the degrees of mixed intersections between specific convex piecewise linear functions, $\gamma$ and $\delta$, defined on the conormal fan. By establishing that the conormal fan adheres to the Hodge-Riemann relations, we confirmed Brylawski's conjecture regarding the log-concavity of this $h$-vector sequence. This follow-up work advances the Lagrangian combinatorics of matroids by deepening the analysis of biflats and biflags and connecting them to the theory of basis activities pioneered by Tutte, Crapo, and Las Vergnas. Our primary achievement is a refined combinatorial formula for the $h$-vector: we express the $k$-th mixed intersection of $\gamma$ and $\delta$ explicitly as a summation over biflags associated with non-broken circuit bases possessing internal activity $k+1$.

This study offers a comprehensive investigation of high-pressure, high-temperature synthesized silver bismuthate (Ag$_2$BiO$_3$), a material recently theorized to exhibit complex topological electronic states. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy reveals two distinct bismuth valence states, while oxygen $K$-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy indicates holes within the oxygen bands. These findings corroborate a bond-disproportionated state characterized by oxygen-localized holes. Optical conductivity measurements estimate the band gap at approximately 1.25 eV, a value consistent with density functional theory calculations performed on the non-symmorphic space group $Pnn2$, which accommodates two inequivalent bismuth sites. Theoretical band structure analysis suggests that the disproportionated form of Ag$_2$BiO$_3$ hosts Weyl nodal chains, with one chain positioned roughly 0.5 eV below the Fermi level. Additionally, we draw parallels between Ag$_2$BiO$_3$ and the established disproportionated bismuthate BaBiO$_3$, noting shared breathing phonon modes of similar energy. Although hybridization of Bi-$6s$ and O-$2p$ orbitals significantly influences the band structure in both compounds, a key distinction lies in the band contributions: whereas Ba-$5p$ states are prominent in BaBiO$_3$, Ag-$4d$ bands in Ag$_2$BiO$_3$ extend up to the Fermi level.

Deep learning is rapidly becoming integral to healthcare, particularly in medical image analysis, where it aims to enhance patient outcomes. While these models achieve state-of-the-art predictive accuracy, their "black box" inference processes pose a significant barrier to widespread adoption in clinical settings. To build stakeholder confidence and support informed clinical decisions, attribution methods are essential for explaining model predictions. This study addresses the critical question of what deep neural networks actually learn from medical images. To this end, we introduce a novel attribution framework based on adaptive path-based gradient integration. Our results indicate that this approach can foster trust among domain experts by enabling them to grasp the correlations between inputs and predictions, identify new biomarkers, and uncover potential model biases, ultimately contributing to improved healthcare outcomes.

This study theoretically examines low-energy collisions within Rydberg atom-ion systems. We delineate the parameter space for various dynamical approaches, including quantum, Langevin, and classical exchange regimes, demonstrating that classical methods are suitable for the lowest attainable temperatures. Utilizing a quasi-classical trajectory method, we analyze charge exchange cross sections for Li$^*$-Li$^+$ and Li$^*$-Cs$^+$ pairs at collision energies as low as $1\,$K. Our findings for cold collisions indicate that the charge exchange cross section diverges from the expected $n^4$ geometric scaling. Additionally, in the low-energy regime, we observe significant effects from ionic core repulsion and variations arising from two distinct models used to describe the electron-core potential.

This paper presents a cosmological investigation of the Dirac-Born-Infeld (DBI) dRGT massive gravity theory, a novel extension of the standard de Rham-Gabadadze-Tolley framework. Within this model, a DBI scalar field is coupled to the graviton. We derive the cosmological background equations and identify self-accelerating solutions characterized by an effective cosmological constant. Furthermore, we analyze tensor perturbations to determine the dispersion relation for gravitational waves within a Friedmann-Lema\^itre-Robertson-Walker universe. Finally, we examine vector and scalar perturbations to establish the stability criteria of the theory.

Underwater imagery suffers from color distortion and contrast loss due to the selective attenuation of light. The severity of this degradation is influenced by water conditions, the distance between the object and the camera, and the depth of the scene. Filtering techniques aim to either restore or enhance the visual appearance of submerged objects. Restoration approaches address the actual physical degradation, while enhancement methods focus on improving perceived quality or optimizing computer vision performance. Given the rising interest in filtering strategies, including learning-based solutions, and the challenges they present, a comprehensive review of current state-of-the-art methods is necessary. This paper examines the design principles of these filters and revisits the oceanographic fundamentals essential for understanding degradation causes. It also analyzes image formation models and restoration outcomes across different water types. Additionally, we present enhancement methods tailored to specific tasks, categorize datasets for neural network training and evaluation, and discuss assessment strategies, including subjective tests and quantitative metrics. To complement this survey, we provide an online platform (https://puiqe.eecs.qmul.ac.uk/) that hosts leading underwater filtering methods and enables comparative analysis.

Wireless backhaul networks offer a promising solution for urban 5G deployments, facilitating future ultra-dense small cell architectures to satisfy growing user needs. However, the optimal planning and management of these 5G backhaul systems remain complex challenges. This paper introduces strategies for the optimal placement of gateways and wireless backhaul routing designed to maximize cost efficiency. Generally, gateway deployment and routing adjustments occur across different temporal scales. Specifically, gateway quantity and location are optimized over the long term, while wireless backhaul routes are optimized over the short term to account for time-varying channel conditions. Numerical results demonstrate that optimizing both gateways and routes significantly enhances cost efficiency. Furthermore, the proposed optimization algorithm outperforms conventional methods, including the widely used Shortest Path (SP) and Bellman-Ford (BF) algorithms, in terms of cost efficiency within 5G wireless backhaul networks.

Online microblogging platforms, increasingly utilized for information sharing, have emerged as a promising approach for profiling multimedia content by offering users a socialized perspective on such material. This paper introduces a microblogging profiling framework designed to socially demonstrate television programs. The study faces two primary challenges: first, since most TV shows originate offline, establishing a link between these programs and online microblogging services is essential; second, microblog content is inherently noisy for video profiling, necessitating the strategic retrieval of the most relevant information. To overcome these obstacles, we propose MAP, a microblogging-assisted profiling framework, which makes three key contributions: (i) a joint user and content retrieval scheme that leverages both actors and topics to identify related microblogs; (ii) a social-aware profiling strategy that analyzes videos based on their content, the social relationships among microblog users, and their propagation within the social network; and (iii) an analysis of real-world TV show profiling conducted using this framework.

We introduce Godot Reinforcement Learning (RL) Agents, an open-source framework for building environments and agents within the Godot Game Engine. This interface facilitates the design and training of agent behaviors in complex 2D and 3D settings using diverse on-policy and off-policy Deep RL algorithms. By offering a standard Gym interface alongside wrappers for Ray RLlib and Stable Baselines, the system grants users access to more than 20 state-of-the-art on-policy, off-policy, and multi-agent RL methods. Serving as a versatile tool for researchers and game designers, it supports the creation of environments featuring discrete, continuous, and mixed action spaces. The framework demonstrates strong performance, achieving 12,000 interactions per second on a high-end laptop when parallelized across four CPU cores. An overview video can be viewed here: https://youtu.be/g1MlZSFqIj4

We present fastcoref, a Python library designed for rapid, precise, and user-friendly English coreference resolution. Available via pip, the package offers two operational modes: an accurate mode utilizing the LingMess architecture to achieve state-of-the-art performance, and F-coref, a significantly faster model that is the primary focus of this study. F-coref can process 2,800 OntoNotes documents in just 25 seconds on a V100 GPU, compared to 6 minutes for the LingMess model and 12 minutes for the popular AllenNLP coreference model, while maintaining only a slight reduction in accuracy. This efficiency is attained through distilling a compact model from LingMess and implementing efficient batching via a technique we term "leftover batching." The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/shon-otmazgin/fastcoref.

Explaining cooperative behavior within biological and social systems remains a significant scientific challenge that has driven intense research over recent decades. Numerous mechanisms have been suggested to account for the emergence and sustainability of cooperation, yet no single explanation exists because various scenarios are driven by distinct forces. This paper introduces a model examining situations where voluntary participation entails an access cost in addition to the inherent cost of cooperation. Our proposed Costly-Access Prisoner's Dilemma, a symmetric donation game featuring voluntary and costly engagement, disrupts the equilibrium between non-participants and active participants found in the standard Voluntary Prisoner's Dilemma. Mean-field analysis indicates that in well-mixed populations, the system inevitably evolves toward total abstention. Conversely, numerical simulations of structured populations reveal alternating dynamics among mono-strategic, multi-stable, and coexistence phases, contingent on the return parameter. These outcomes are comprehensively accounted for by a theoretical examination of strategic motifs, with transitions occurring as the stability of these motifs shifts.

By analyzing an open string that exhibits both rotational and pulsating dynamics, we examine the intrinsic frequency of a photon. Specifically, we compute the zero-point fluctuation of this string, which is expressed as the sum of the quantum mechanical ground state energy in its vibrational mode and the classical energy in its rotational mode. Our results indicate that the photon's intrinsic frequency is $\omega_{\gamma}=9.00\times 10^{23}~{\rm sec}^{-1}$, a value comparable to those of baryons such as the nucleon and delta baryon. Furthermore, within a phenomenological stringy photon framework, we determine the photon's size to be $\langle r^{2}\rangle^{1/2}(\rm photon)=0.17~{\rm fm}$.

This study examines the dynamical evolution of quantum coherence in a displaced squeezed thermal state interacting with an external bath. By employing a Fano-Anderson Hamiltonian to represent the environment and solving the quantum Langevin equation, we derive the Green's functions necessary to compute the expectation values of quadrature operators and subsequently construct the covariance matrix. Quantum coherence is quantified using a relative entropy-based measure. The single-mode squeezed thermal state is analyzed across Ohmic, sub-Ohmic, and super-Ohmic regimes for various mean photon numbers. Our results indicate that under weak system-environment coupling, coherence decays monotonically, reflecting Markovian behavior. Conversely, strong coupling yields an initial Markovian phase that transitions into non-Markovian dynamics over time, driven by environmental back action. Furthermore, we investigate the long-time steady-state dynamics in both low and high temperature limits, observing consistent qualitative behavior; however, quantitative differences arise because thermal decoherence reduces coherence levels in the high-temperature regime.

This study presents a novel exact solution to the governing equations of geophysical fluid dynamics for an inviscid, incompressible fluid with a general density profile under forcing influences. These forcing terms are essential for modeling realistic, observation-based oceanic flows. By utilizing spherical coordinates, we avoid resorting to geometric simplifications, such as $f$-plane or $\beta$-plane approximations. The resulting explicit solution describes a steady, purely azimuthal stratified flow with a free surface; the integration of forcing terms and the Earth's spherical geometry renders this model particularly suitable for analyzing the Antarctic Circumpolar Current. Furthermore, using functional analytical methods, we demonstrate that the free surface deformation is uniquely and implicitly determined by the pressure at the surface. Finally, we establish relationships between the monotonicity of surface pressure and surface distortion that align with physical expectations.

Let $G$ denote a locally compact group equipped with its group algebra $L^1(G)$, and let $N$ be a closed normal subgroup of $G$. Given a continuous character $\xi:N\to\mathbb{T}$, we define $L_\xi^1(G,N)$ as the $L^1$-space comprising all $\xi$-covariant functions on $G$. We have established that $L^1_\xi(G,N)$ is isometrically isomorphic to a quotient of $L^1(G)$, and it has been further demonstrated that the dual space $L^1_\xi(G,N)^*$ is isometrically isomorphic to $L^\infty_\xi(G,N)$.

Extending the research of Fayad and Nekovár, we demonstrate that a specific component of the étale cohomology for certain abelian-type Shimura varieties is semisimple, provided that the corresponding automorphic Galois representations exist and possess favorable properties. Our proof integrates an abstract semisimplicity criterion established by Fayad and Nekovár with the Eichler-Shimura relations.

Logic locking serves as a hardware security mechanism designed to protect intellectual property (IP) from threats within the IC supply chain, particularly those originating from untrusted fabrication facilities. This approach embeds extra locking circuitry into an integrated circuit (IC) that triggers malfunctioning behavior when an incorrect key is supplied; the magnitude of this malfunction defines the technique's effectiveness. "SAT attacks" offer a robust mathematical method for deducing the correct key in locked circuits. To achieve high resistance against SAT attacks, many traditional logic locking methods fail to introduce enough errors, as seen in SARLock and Anti-SAT, where only a minimal number of input minterms result in output errors. The state-of-the-art Stripped Functionality Logic Locking (SFLL) technique introduced a compromise between SAT resilience and effectiveness. This paper demonstrates that such a trade-off is inherent to all logic locking methods. To achieve high effectiveness without sacrificing SAT resilience, we introduce a new scheme called Strong Anti-SAT (SAS). Addressing the prevalence of removal-based attacks alongside SAT attacks, we further propose Robust SAS (RSAS), which maintains the same level of SAT resilience and effectiveness as SAS while offering protection against removal attacks. SAS and RSAS offer three key improvements over current techniques: (1) their SAT resilience remains intact even as effectiveness increases; (2) unlike previous work limited to circuit-level impacts, we integrate SAS-locked modules into a processor to demonstrate significant application-level effects; and (3) experimental results indicate that SAS and RSAS provide superior SAT resilience compared to SFLL while maintaining comparable effectiveness.
We demonstrate that for a general canonical curve, the linear syzygy spaces are generated entirely by syzygies of minimal rank.

We present a novel extended Heisenberg model that incorporates orbital-dependent spins and the retarded effects of spin torque. This framework is directly derived from dynamical linear response functions concerning transversal spin fluctuations. Unlike the standard Heisenberg model, our approach enables the investigation of previously inaccessible phenomena. Specifically, it allows for the description of relaxation effects arising from Landau damping due to Stoner excitations, as well as Fermi surface nesting effects. Furthermore, we explore the potential of this extended model by analyzing high-resolution plots of the spin susceptibility in iron (Fe).

We introduce data structures designed to handle intersection queries in four-dimensional space involving segments, triangles, and tetrahedra. Our research focuses on three specific challenges: (i) preprocessing $n$ tetrahedra in $\reals^4$ to answer segment-tetrahedron intersection queries; (ii) preprocessing $n$ triangles in $\reals^4$ to support triangle-triangle intersection queries; and (iii) preprocessing $n$ segments in $\reals^4$ to facilitate tetrahedron-segment intersection queries. For each case, the goal is to detect, count, or report all intersections. To our knowledge, these problems have not been previously investigated. Regarding problem (i), we initially propose a standard approach where, for a storage parameter $s$ such that $n \le s \le n^6$, the data structure requires $O^*(s)$ storage and expected preprocessing time, answering queries in $O^*(n/s^{1/6})$ time (with $O^*(\cdot)$ suppressing subpolynomial factors). Using comparable reasoning, we achieve identical asymptotic bounds for problems (ii) and (iii). We subsequently refine the solution for problem (i) by introducing a more complex data structure that utilizes $O^*(n^2)$ storage and expected preprocessing, enabling segment-tetrahedron intersection queries to be resolved in $O^*(n^{1/2})$ time.

This paper initiates an investigation into the Fermat equation within real biquadratic fields, using $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3})$ as an initial case study. To improve the established asymptotic bound for this specific field, we identify torsion primes of degree 8 by applying prior research by Derickx, Kamienny, Stein, and Stoll. Furthermore, we address smaller prime exponents through the analysis of modular parametrisation, while examining specific cases with lower integer exponents by studying particular hyperelliptic curves.

This paper introduces the concept of Mannheim partner curves within a three-dimensional Lie group G equipped with a bi-invariant metric. The primary finding, presented as Theorem 3.3, establishes that a curve {\alpha} possessing the Frenet apparatus {T,N,B,{\kappa},{\tau}} in G qualifies as a Mannheim partner curve if and only if the condition {\lambda}{\kappa}(1+H2)=1 holds, where {\lambda} is a constant and H represents the harmonic curvature function of {\alpha}.

Quantum Hall-superconductor hybrid systems offer promising avenues for inherently fault-tolerant quantum computation. Inspired by recent experimental successes in combining these phases, we analyze transport phenomena across a proximitized integer quantum Hall edge, with a specific focus on the role of superconducting vortices. Through an examination of downstream conductance, we uncover regimes where sub-gap vortex states facilitate Andreev processes that remain suppressed in the absence of vortices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that at finite temperatures and with a high density of vortices, the downstream conductance can average to zero, suggesting the superconductor mimics the behavior of a normal contact. These findings underscore the necessity of accounting for vortices when utilizing transport measurements to probe superconducting correlations in quantum Hall-superconductor composites.

The objective of Question Answering over Knowledge Graphs (KGQA) is to retrieve answers to natural language queries from a knowledge graph. Current KGQA methods often utilize a Neural Machine Translation (NMT) strategy, converting natural language questions into structured query languages. However, NMT faces significant challenges with out-of-vocabulary terms, where unseen words in a question hinder translation; this is especially critical given the millions of entities in large knowledge graphs. Instead, we propose a KGQA framework that offloads entity processing to Entity Linking (EL) systems. In this approach, NMT generates a query template containing placeholders, which are subsequently populated by entities identified during the EL phase. A slot-filling mechanism determines the appropriate entity for each placeholder. Experiments conducted on Wikidata demonstrate that our method surpasses pure NMT performance: although the approach still relies heavily on having encountered similar query templates during training, it significantly reduces errors associated with entities.

Smartphone users frequently execute security-sensitive applications alongside untrusted and potentially harmful software on the same device, a situation that demands reliance on hardware and system software to effectively sandbox malicious code—a trust that is frequently misplaced. Our objective is to reduce both the quantity and intricacy of hardware and software elements that users must trust to resist adversarial attacks. We propose a multi-domain hardware architecture featuring statically partitioned, physically isolated trust domains. To facilitate this, we introduce a limited set of simple, formally verified hardware components that allow programs to obtain provably exclusive and simultaneous access to computation and I/O resources temporarily. To oversee this hardware, we developed OctopOS, an operating system built from mutually distrustful subsystems. We implemented a prototype of this system on a CPU-FPGA board, demonstrating that it incurs minimal hardware overhead compared to contemporary System-on-Chip (SoC) designs. For security-critical applications, our machine significantly lowers the required trust compared to standard Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) while maintaining satisfactory performance. For standard applications, performance remains comparable to that of legacy systems.

We introduce a non-perturbative, *ab initio* method for calculating the electrical conductivity of liquid metals. Unlike conventional empirical approaches relying on the Kubo-Greenwood formula, our strategy, which combines the Kubo formula with electron-phonon coupling (EPC) theory, rigorously incorporates the interaction between electrons and moving ions. We demonstrate that at high temperatures, conductivity is governed by the EPC parameter $\lambda_{\mathrm{tr}}$, a value that can be determined non-perturbatively through the correlation of electron scattering matrices induced by ions, which are computable via molecular dynamics simulations. Implemented using density-functional theory and pseudopotential methods, this *ab initio* framework was applied to liquid sodium, yielding results that align well with experimental data. The method is both efficient and grounded in rigorous theory, making it suitable for studying general metallic liquid systems.

Scatterplots represent one of the most prevalent methods for data visualization. Effective scatterplots enhance data comprehension by utilizing visual perception to heighten awareness during specific visual analytic activities. Design elements within scatterplots, including graphical encodings and data attributes, can significantly influence the quality of decision-making for low-level tasks such as clustering. Consequently, developing frameworks that account for both the perception of visual encodings and the specific task at hand allows for the optimization of visualizations to maximize their effectiveness. This paper introduces an automated tool designed to optimize scatterplot design factors to highlight the most prominent cluster structures. Our methodology employs a merge tree data structure to detect clusters and refine the selection of subsampling algorithms, sampling rates, marker dimensions, and marker opacity for generating scatterplot images. We validate our approach through user and case studies demonstrating its ability to efficiently produce high-quality scatterplot designs from a vast parameter space.

Bipolar Disorder is a chronic psychiatric condition marked by pathological mood fluctuations that severely disrupt emotional regulation. Effective care for these dynamic and debilitating states relies heavily on clinical mood monitoring. While frequent, detailed observation enhances clinical sensitivity to detect shifts in mood, it often demands expensive and scarce resources. Since speech patterns alter during both manic and depressive episodes, automated analysis of speech signals offers a viable method for tracking mood changes. Nevertheless, predicting mood states from speech is difficult because speech is influenced by numerous other factors. We propose that incorporating emotion as an intermediate step can enhance mood state prediction. This paper outlines key developments in this pipeline, featuring (1) the PRIORI Emotion Dataset, a novel "in the wild" collection of conversational speech from everyday smartphone usage; (2) baseline models for recognizing activation and valence emotions on this dataset (achieving Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.71 and 0.41, respectively); and (3) a strong correlation between predicted emotions and actual mood states in individuals with bipolar disorder. These findings provide evidence and a functional baseline for utilizing emotion as a meta-feature to monitor mood states.

Training Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) at scale on graphs with billions of vertices and edges using minibatch sampling presents a significant hurdle: strong scaling leads to reduced compute efficiency, increased communication overhead, and potential performance degradation. To overcome this, DistGNN-MB introduces a new Historical Embedding Cache alongside compute-communication overlap techniques. Evaluated on a 32-node (64-socket) cluster featuring third-generation Intel Xeon Scalable Processors (36 cores per socket), DistGNN-MB successfully converged 3-layer GraphSAGE and GAT models on the OGBN-Papers100M dataset within 2 and 4.9 seconds per epoch, respectively, utilizing all 32 compute nodes. At this scale, DistGNN-MB achieved a 5.2x speedup over the popular DistDGL for GraphSAGE training. Furthermore, as compute nodes increased from 2 to 32, DistGNN-MB demonstrated a 10x speedup for GraphSAGE and a 17.2x speedup for GAT.

We develop a relativistic quantum mechanics (RQM) framework for a massive photon that does not rely on quantum field theory or the massive Proca model. This approach yields a novel theoretical solution allowing the massive photon to possess either positive or negative energy states. Specifically, we predict the existence of an "anti-photon" associated with the negative energy solution, analogous to the positron in Dirac's RQM for electrons. We suggest that anti-photons might manifest as intense gamma-ray flares during bursts. Within this RQM, we establish a positive definite probability density and a nontrivial diagonal Hamiltonian, while also addressing the case of a massless photon. Furthermore, we verify that both the relativistic equation of motion for the massive photon and its corresponding probability continuity equation maintain covariance under Lorentz transformations.

Little Higgs models, often viewed as a specific type of composite Higgs framework, account for the observed 125 GeV Higgs boson as a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson arising from spontaneously broken global symmetry. A collective symmetry breaking mechanism elevates the ultraviolet scale of these theories to 10 TeV or beyond. To eliminate tree-level conflicts with electroweak precision measurements, T-parity is implemented as a discrete symmetry. Although LHC Run 1 results indicated that electroweak precision observables imposed tighter constraints than both Higgs data and direct searches, a comprehensive re-analysis of all available 13 TeV LHC Run 2 data demonstrates that direct searches now provide the stronger limits. This presentation will detail the updated exclusion bounds for the LHT model and offer a perspective on the upcoming high-luminosity LHC phase.

Inverse propensity weighting (IPW) is a widely used technique for estimating treatment effects using observational data, yet its validity depends on the untestable and often unrealistic assumption that every confounder has been measured. This paper presents a robust sensitivity analysis for IPW that determines the range of treatment effects consistent with a specific degree of unobserved confounding. The derived range converges to the tightest possible interval (given the stated assumptions) guaranteed to include the true treatment effect. Our approach refines the influential sensitivity analysis proposed by Zhao, Small, and Bhattacharya (2019), which we demonstrate produces overly wide bounds even in the asymptotic limit. This methodology relies on novel partial identification results derived from Tan (2006)'s marginal sensitivity model.

Astrophysical black holes (BHs) are characterized solely by their mass and spin, yet generating rapidly rotating ones is exceptionally challenging because progenitor stars typically shed most of their angular momentum before collapse. While tight binaries with low-mass companions can produce high-spin BHs via tidal interactions, systems with massive companions cannot, as the latter are too large for such close orbits. The recent observation of rapidly spinning BHs paired with extremely massive stars contradicts standard stellar-formation models. Existing theoretical frameworks that minimize core-envelope coupling and stellar winds fail to align with both observations and theory, and they also inadequately address the system's energetics. Since BH spin cannot arise from stellar collapse itself, and mechanisms relying on orbital spin from explosion fallback or accepted mass-transfer channels either conflict with data or require timescales exceeding stellar lifetimes, these alternatives are generally rejected. Instead, this work demonstrates that fast mass-transfer mechanisms—predicted to eventually merge the BH and star—can effectively spin up BHs. Furthermore, it proposes a method to prevent these mergers and circumvent the primary drawbacks of other models, thereby naturally accounting for the observed phenomena. These findings carry potentially paradigm-shifting implications for high-energy black hole astrophysics.

In complex, distributed systems where dependencies shift as the system evolves, executing events can be modeled in various ways, including through Context-Dependent Event structures, which share conceptual roots with Petri nets. This paper proposes a specific type of Petri net that corresponds to Context-Dependent Event structures, thereby imparting an operational perspective to their dependencies. While Petri nets typically represent dependencies operationally via tokens generated by one activity and consumed by another, this work shifts the focus to contextual arcs. These arcs characterize the history of events to effectively describe the interdependencies among various activities.

Rochberg's coboundary theorem establishes criteria for the solvability of the equation $(I-T)y = x$, where $T$ represents a unilateral shift on a Hilbert space, $I$ denotes the identity operator, and $x$ is a specific vector. These criteria are formulated using a Wold-type decomposition associated with $T$ and the growth behavior of $T$'s iterates applied to $x$. This paper revisits Rochberg's theorem to demonstrate the following: if $T$ is an isometry on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ and $x \in \mathcal{H}$ satisfies the condition $\sum_{k=0}^\infty k \| T^{*k} x \| < \infty$, then $x$ lies in the range of $(I-T)$ if and only if $\|\sum_{k= 0}^n T^k x \| = o(\sqrt{n})$. Furthermore, when $T$ is only a contraction, $x$ qualifies as a coboundary provided an additional assumption holds. The work also presents applications regarding $L^2$-solutions to the functional equation $f(x)-f(2x) = F(x)$, originally examined by Fortet and Kac.

We examine a Deligne-Mumford stack $X$, defined as the quotient of an affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}A$ by a finite group $G$'s action, and demonstrate that the Balmer spectrum of the tensor triangulated category of perfect complexes on $X$ is homeomorphic to the space of homogeneous prime ideals within the group cohomology ring $H^*(G,A)$.

Silicon spin qubits are distinguished by their extended coherence times, compatibility with industrial manufacturing processes, and the potential for integrating classical control electronics. To enable truly scalable architectures, a coherent mid-range connection capable of transporting electrons between qubit registers has been proposed to address signal fan-out challenges. This study presents a blueprint for a $\approx 10\,\mu$m long structure, termed a "spin qubit shuttle," which connects gate arrays into a limited number of sets. Controlling these sets requires only a few voltage lines, and the count of these sets—and consequently the necessary control signals—remains independent of the link's length. Two operational modes for this shuttle are examined: a "qubit conveyor," involving a laterally moving potential minimum, and a "bucket brigade," where electrons traverse tunnel-coupled quantum dots via adiabatic passage. Considering realistic Si/SiGe devices with potential disorder from charged defects at the Si/SiO$_2$ interface and typical charge noise, the conveyor approach appears more promising. Focusing on transfer fidelity in conveyor mode, we analyze motional narrowing, the interaction between orbital and valley excitations and relaxation given $g$-factors dependent on orbital and valley states, and the impact of spin-hotspots. We determine that a transfer fidelity of 99.9% is achievable in Si/SiGe at speeds around 10 m/s, provided average valley splitting and its inhomogeneity remain within realistic limits. Operating at a low global magnetic field of approximately 20 mT and engineering materials for higher valley splitting are favorable strategies for attaining high transfer fidelities.

A network consists of numerous communities, defined as groups of nodes and edges characterized by stronger internal relationships and distinct, sometimes overlapping, properties. Detecting these communities is vital because they function as local units that capture interactions within a network. Communities manifest in diverse forms, spanning biological origins to those driven by technology. In the realm of technology-induced communities, social media platforms like Twitter and Facebook link vast numbers of diverse users, creating a highly connected and dynamic environment. While numerous algorithms exist for identifying socially cohesive groups on Twitter, the challenges of mining and analyzing them persist. This study introduces a novel detection method utilizing a scalable framework to uncover related communities. We propose a multilevel clustering technique (MCT) that integrates structural and textual data to identify local communities, termed "microcosms." Experimental results on benchmark models and datasets validate the approach's effectiveness. This research adds a new perspective to the detection of cohesive communities in social networks, offering greater clarity on how low-level communities evolve and behave on Twitter. Practically, identifying these groups can enhance recommendation systems and provide other significant benefits.

This study identifies H$\alpha$ emission and stellar continuum extending roughly 30 physical kpc from H$\alpha$-emitting galaxies at $z=0.4$, noting directional H$\alpha$ patterns in their outer regions. Utilizing narrow-band selected H$\alpha$ emitters at $z=0.4$ from the Hayashi et al. (2020) emission-line catalog—which relies on Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program's Deep and Ultradeep layers—researchers analyzed deep narrow- and broad-band imagery of 8,625 emitters covering 16.8 deg$^2$. This data enabled the creation of deep composite emission-line and continuum images. The resulting stacked images reveal diffuse H$\alpha$ emission (sensitivity down to $\sim5\times10^{-20}$ erg~s$^{-1}$cm$^{-2}$arcsec$^{-2}$) and stellar continuum (sensitivity down to $\sim5\times10^{-22}$ erg~s$^{-1}$cm$^{-2}$A$^{-1}$arcsec$^{-2}$) that stretch beyond 10 kpc in galaxies with stellar masses exceeding $10^9$ M$_\odot$, with some portions likely stemming from stellar halos. These radial profiles align broadly. Furthermore, the study finds an H$\alpha$ emission dependence on position angle, observing higher equivalent widths along the minor axis toward galaxy disks. While this H$\alpha$ directionality might indicate biconical outflows, additional hydrodynamic simulations are urgently needed to determine the precise origin.

This study details the automated identification of 11 transients, including seven potential supernovae and four active galactic nuclei candidates, within the Zwicky Transient Facility's fourth data release (ZTF DR4). All detected events occurred in 2018 and were missing from existing public catalogs; notably, three of them did not appear in the ZTF alert stream. Our detection methodology utilizes 41 physically motivated features derived from actual light curves alongside four simulated models (SN Ia, SN II, TDE, and SLSN-I). These inputs feed into a k-D tree algorithm to identify the 15 nearest neighbors. Following pre-processing and selection criteria, our dataset comprised approximately one million objects. We visually examined the 105 closest neighbors from seven of our brightest and best-sampled simulations, which included 89 distinct ZTF DR4 sources. These findings highlight the effectiveness of combining domain expertise with automated learning algorithms, a core principle of the SNAD team. Furthermore, they confirm that the ZTF DR4 serves as an ideal environment for testing data mining techniques designed to handle future astronomical data.

Regression serves as a pivotal task in machine learning with extensive applications across various domains. Traditionally, regression problems are addressed by minimizing mean square error (MSE) or its regularized forms, which rely on prior knowledge of the models. Recently, Yi et al. introduced a supervised learning framework based on mutual information, incorporating label entropy regularization that operates without such prior assumptions. When adapted for classification tasks and optimized using stochastic gradient descent (SGD), this method outperformed standard cross-entropy loss and its variants. However, the authors omitted a theoretical convergence analysis for the SGD algorithm in their formulation, and extending the framework to regression remains challenging due to the potentially infinite support of labels. This paper explores regression within the mutual information-based supervised learning framework. We demonstrate that MSE minimization is equivalent to a conditional entropy learning problem and propose a mutual information formulation for regression using reparameterization techniques. Furthermore, we provide a convergence analysis of the SGD algorithm for our proposed method. Finally, we examine a multi-output regression data model to derive a lower bound on generalization performance expressed through the mutual information of the underlying data distribution. Our findings suggest that high dimensionality can be beneficial rather than detrimental, provided it is managed by a specific threshold. We anticipate that this work will lay a solid foundation for future research on mutual information-based regression.

Following decades of extensive digitization, an immense volume of historical documents and their corresponding machine-readable texts is now accessible. Although this advancement significantly improves preservation and accessibility, it also creates new possibilities for content mining. The primary challenge now is developing technologies to efficiently search, retrieve, and explore this "big data of the past." Within semantic indexing, recognizing and classifying named entities is highly sought after by humanities scholars. However, named entity recognition (NER) systems face significant difficulties when dealing with the diverse, historical, and noisy nature of these inputs. This survey outlines the specific challenges historical documents present to NER, catalogs existing resources, reviews the main approaches used to date, and highlights key priorities for future advancements.

Thurston's hyperbolization theorem for Haken manifolds, combined with normal surface theory, provides an algorithm to determine if a compact orientable 3-manifold with a toroidal boundary admits a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric on its interior. A conjecture by Gabai, Meyerhoff, and Milley can be reduced to a computation utilizing this algorithm.

We investigate the holomorphic symplectic geometry of the smooth part of the space of holomorphic sections within a twistor space that admits a rotating circle action. This twistor space features a meromorphic connection originally constructed by Hitchin. We provide an interpretation of Hitchin's connection through the lens of the Atiyah--Ward transform applied to the associated hyperholomorphic line bundle. It is demonstrated that the residue of this meromorphic connection functions as a moment map for the induced circle action, and we analyze its critical points. Particular focus is placed on the case of Deligne--Hitchin moduli spaces.

In large-scale networks, adversaries can easily introduce false data into communication links, prompting this paper to propose a novel security defense strategy focused on attack detection scheduling. Unlike existing methods, the proposed scheduling strategy ensures the security of a node's local state estimation by detecting information from only half of its neighboring nodes. The problem of selecting which sensors to detect is formulated as a combinatorial optimization task that is NP-hard. To address this, the objective function is transformed into a submodular function, leading to a proposed attack detection scheduling algorithm based on sequential submodular maximization. This algorithm integrates an expert problem to more effectively handle dynamic attack strategies, operating in polynomial time with a guaranteed theoretical lower bound on the optimization rate. Furthermore, the algorithm guarantees overall network security under two distinct insecure conditions, analyzed through the lens of augmented estimation error. Finally, numerical simulations of an industrial continuous stirred tank reactor demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Robot assistants are increasingly serving as advanced technological aids for daily living. To effectively support users within home settings, these robots must possess adaptable mobility to safely traverse cluttered areas. This paper presents a novel method for person-following assistance and surveillance. Our strategy utilizes an omnidirectional robot platform to separate the calculation of linear and angular velocities, enabling navigation in domestic spaces without losing sight of the user. While linear speed is controlled by a standard Dynamic Window Approach (DWA) local planner, a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) agent is trained to generate optimized angular velocity commands, ensuring the robot maintains the correct orientation toward the person. We tested this navigation system on a physical omnidirectional robot across multiple indoor environments, showing that our approach offers significant advantages over traditional differential steering following methods.

We investigate how spatial locality influences the evolution of random quantum systems under Markovian noise. Specifically, we analyze a model where both the system Hamiltonian and its noise couplings are random matrices with entries decaying as power laws of distance, characterized by distinct exponents $\alpha_H$ and $\alpha_L$. Although the steady state remains featureless regardless of parameters, the convergence rate to this state displays three distinct phases governed by $\alpha_H$ and $\alpha_L$. These include a regime with asymptotically exponential relaxation driven by a spectral gap in the Lindblad superoperator, alongside two gapless phases featuring subexponential decay, differentiated by how the gap scales with system size. Perturbative analysis reveals that phase boundaries in the $(\alpha_H, \alpha_L)$ plane vary between weak and strong dissipation regimes, implying noise-strength-dependent phase transitions. However, we identify nonperturbative effects that eliminate these transitions in the thermodynamic limit.

This study presents a dual-critic reinforcement learning (RL) framework designed to solve frame-level bit allocation issues in HEVC/H.265, aiming to minimize Group of Pictures (GOP) distortion within a rate limit. While earlier RL approaches handle this constrained optimization by maximizing a single, often ad hoc reward function combining distortion and rate metrics—which may fail to generalize across different video sequences and coding conditions—this work adapts the deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) algorithm to utilize two critics. One critic predicts the distortion reward, updating the agent primarily when the rate constraint is met, while the other predicts the rate reward, prioritizing the bit budget if the agent exceeds it. Experimental evaluations on standard datasets demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms both the x265 bit allocation scheme and single-critic baselines in rate-distortion performance, while maintaining precise rate control.

This study theoretically examines ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) modulation within bilayers composed of $d$-wave superconductors (SC) and ferromagnetic insulators (FI).
