Based on the D-brane locations within the internal space, supersymmetry may be broken at the string scale on the branes or solely at the massive level. A key innovation of this construction is the absence of NS-NS disk tadpoles without inducing open-string instabilities. The one-loop potential, which varies with D-brane positions, reaches its minimum when supersymmetry is maximally broken and realized nonlinearly. Furthermore, the orientifold projection and the effective field theory analysis indicate soft supersymmetry breaking within the closed-string sector. These models allow for the decoupling of the gravitino mass from the scalar potential value while preventing brane instabilities.

The Standard Model (SM) of elementary particle physics fails to account for the observed matter-antimatter asymmetry. To address this, A. Sakharov proposed that new sources of $\mathcal{CP}$-violating effects are necessary. Electric Dipole Moments (EDMs) of subatomic particles could serve as such a source, as their existence would imply a violation of both $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{P}$ symmetries. By utilizing polarized beams within storage rings, researchers can measure the EDMs of charged particles by monitoring how the EDM affects spin dynamics. The Cooler Synchrotron (COSY) at Forschungszentrum J\"ulich is uniquely suited for this purpose, as it delivers polarized protons and deuterons with momenta reaching 3.7 GeV/c. This capability makes COSY the ideal platform for the JEDI Collaboration (J\"ulich Electric Dipole moment Investigations) to conduct the inaugural direct measurement of the deuteron EDM. This document outlines recent progress in EDM research conducted at COSY.

A collaborative filtering recommender system anticipates user preferences by identifying shared characteristics between users and items. This inference is implemented using a Bayesian double feature allocation model, which operates on random pairs of subsets. Specifically, an Indian buffet process (IBP) connects users and items to features, where each feature represents a corresponding subset of users and items. By training on feature-specific rating effects, the system predicts ratings. We demonstrate the model's posterior inference and its ability to predict preferences for unseen items relative to previously rated ones using MovieLens data. To handle the large scale of users and items typical in such applications, the implementation includes a novel semi-consensus Monte Carlo method. This approach enables parallel posterior sampling across multiple user shards while maintaining shared global parameters related to items across these shards.

Given an automorphic Galois representation modulo $p$, denoted $\bar\rho$, it is a natural inquiry whether automorphic points are Zariski dense within the deformation space of $\bar\rho$. This work establishes new findings addressing this question specifically for unitary groups that are split and unramified at $p$. When $\bar\rho$ corresponds to an automorphic form for a unitary group contributing to coherent cohomology, we demonstrate that the "infinite fern"—defined as the image of a suitable Eigenvariety within the polarised deformation space of $\bar\rho$—is Zariski dense within a non-empty collection of irreducible components. These results extend prior work by Gouvêa-Mazur regarding $GL_2/\mathbb Q$, Chenevier concerning $U(3)$, and the recent contributions of Hellmann-Margerin-Schraen. Our approach introduces novelty through the application of the Breuil-Hellmann-Schraen local model to manage tangent spaces in local deformation rings, combined with a geometric strategy on the Eigenvariety, originally developed by Bellaïche-Chenevier and Taïbi, to isolate points possessing an enormous image. At these specific points, we leverage a recent theorem by Newton-Thorne to regulate the vanishing of a Selmer group. Consequently, our framework does not require the standard "Taylor-Wiles" hypothesis on $\bar\rho$, allowing $\bar\rho$ to be irreducible. Furthermore, if the Taylor-Wiles hypothesis on $\bar\rho$ and an additional condition at $p$ are satisfied, Allen's result ensures Zariski density throughout the entire space.

Venusian clouds contain a convective zone between approximately 50 and 60 km that facilitates the mixing of heat, momentum, and chemical constituents. While observations and numerical simulations have elucidated the complexity of this region, its specific influence on chemistry remains unclear. In this study, we employ a three-dimensional convection-resolving model incorporating passive tracers to simulate SO$_2$ and H$_2$O across two latitudinal scenarios. These tracers are relaxed toward measured vertical profiles using a timescale that spans multiple orders of magnitude. We quantify vertical mixing, finding it to be robust when the relaxation timescale is significantly shorter than the convective timescale, roughly 4 hours. Additionally, we estimate the spatial and temporal variability of tracers driven by convection, revealing horizontal structures on the scale of several kilometers. At the Equator, the model resolves a convective layer at the cloud top (70 km), a feature supported by certain observations, marking the first time the impact of such turbulence on chemical species is accounted for. Derived from resolved convective plumes, the vertical eddy diffusion aligns with previous in-situ measurements but exceeds values used in one-dimensional chemistry models by several orders of magnitude. Comparisons with observations indicate some correlation in spatial and temporal variability, suggesting that the convective layer does influence chemical species.

This study investigates visual explanations within deep metric learning and their practical applications. Although metric learning has recently gained significant traction as a critical task for representation learning, its interpretability has been less explored compared to classification. To address this, we introduce an intuitive approach that identifies the primary contributors to the overall similarity between two images by decomposing final activations. Rather than merely displaying individual activation maps, our method generates point-to-point activation intensities between image pairs, thereby revealing relationships across different regions. We demonstrate that this framework is directly applicable to a wide variety of metric learning tasks and offers valuable insights into model behavior. Additionally, experimental results validate its effectiveness in two specific domains: cross-view pattern discovery and interactive retrieval. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/Jeff-Zilence/Explain_Metric_Learning}.

We develop a nonconforming virtual element method (ncVEM) utilizing approximation spaces augmented with specific singular functions. This enriched ncVEM is specifically designed to approximate solutions to elliptic problems exhibiting singularities caused by domain geometry. Unlike traditional extended Galerkin approaches that enrich local spaces with singular functions using a partition of unity, our method avoids this technique entirely. Instead, it relies on the unique structure of nonconforming virtual element spaces. We provide a theoretical analysis of the method and validate it through multiple numerical experiments. Additionally, we introduce an orthonormalization procedure that significantly reduces the ill-conditioning of the resulting system.

The recent observation of current-induced orthogonal reorientation, or orthogonal switching, in metallic Mn$_2$Au and CuMnAs has facilitated the potential for ultrafast antiferromagnet (AFM) writing. However, phenomenological theory suggests that the critical field required for SOT switching with ultrashort pulses scales inversely with pulse duration, which constrains the effectiveness of such rapid stimuli. We investigate whether adjusting the operating temperature can lower this critical field, thereby enabling orthogonal switching under ultrashort pulse conditions. By extending prior theoretical models to include finite temperature effects, we demonstrate a strong temperature dependence of the critical field for orthogonal switching and analyze how this dependence varies with pulse duration. Specifically, while the anisotropy field governs the temperature dependence for long pulses, the characteristic AFM frequency dominates for ultrashort pulses. Furthermore, we derive an analytical expression that bridges the critical field limits for both short and long pulse durations.

This study presents a gcd-pair within $\mathbb{Z}_n$, defined as an unordered pair $\{[a]_n, [b]_n\}$ of elements in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ where $0\leq a,b < n$ and the greatest common divisor $\gcd(a,b)$ is a divisor of $n$. The work examines the characteristics of these gcd-pairs and their corresponding graph structures. Additionally, it derives a formula for counting gcd-pairs in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ and its subsets, and includes algorithms designed to identify, count, and verify such pairs.

Although neural metrics demonstrate strong alignment with human assessments in evaluating machine translation, we must identify—and preferably eliminate—biases that assign high scores to poor translations before optimizing for them. Our experiments indicate that sample-based Minimum Bayes Risk decoding can effectively investigate and measure these flaws. Applying this approach to COMET for English-German and German-English pairs reveals that the models lack sufficient sensitivity to variations in numerical values and named entities. Additionally, we demonstrate that these biases are difficult to eradicate solely through training on extra synthetic data, and we provide our code and dataset to support further research.

This article outlines the assembly category evaluation conducted during the 13th iteration of the CASP community-wide experiment. For the second time, protein assemblies have been designated as a standalone assessment category. Compared to the previous edition, we observed a significant increase in participation, the release of a greater number of oligomeric targets, and a steady, albeit moderate, enhancement in prediction quality. Analysis of tertiary structure predictions reveals that disregarding the oligomeric state of targets impedes modeling success. Additionally, while certain contact prediction groups accurately identified homomeric interfacial contacts, it seems these insights were not utilized in assembly modeling. In this round, homology modeling supplemented by substantial human intervention appears to underpin the assembly prediction methodologies. Future progress should prioritize more integrated modeling frameworks where multiple subunits are inherently incorporated into the process, which would advance the entire field of structure prediction.

This research investigates risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) utilizing an entropic risk measure within episodic, non-stationary Markov decision processes (MDPs). In this setting, both reward functions and state transition kernels are unknown and permitted to change arbitrarily over time, subject to a constraint on their cumulative variations. When the variation budget is known beforehand, we introduce two restart-based algorithms—Restart-RSMB and Restart-RSQ—and derive their dynamic regrets. Building on these findings, we develop a meta-algorithm that eliminates the need for prior knowledge of the variation budget by adaptively detecting non-stationarity in exponential value functions. We subsequently establish a dynamic regret lower bound for non-stationary risk-sensitive RL to validate the near-optimality of our proposed methods. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that if the variation budget is known, risk control and non-stationarity handling can be designed independently, whereas the detection mechanism in the adaptive algorithm relies on the risk parameter. To our knowledge, this work provides the first non-asymptotic theoretical analysis for non-stationary risk-sensitive RL.

We determine the ground state of the deuteron by employing a variational neural network ansatz for the wave function in momentum space. This approach offers a versatile representation of both $S$ and $D$ states, achieving energy relative errors that fall within fractions of a percent of a full diagonalization benchmark. Our work advances this field in two key areas: first, by investigating novel architectures through increased network layers and varied inter-state connections; and second, by refining numerical uncertainty estimates by accounting for oscillations at the minimization's conclusion. Our results indicate that the optimal architecture is a simple, one-layer, state-independent network. In contrast, two-layer networks exhibit signs of overfitting in regions outside the fixed momentum basis used for calculations. Across all configurations, errors stemming from model oscillations near the true minimum exceed those arising from stochastic initialization. These findings are broadly applicable to other quantum mechanics contexts.

This study addresses the simultaneous scheduling and resource allocation for a stream of requests across a collection of computing units, modeling the system as a multi-queue architecture where each unit is a node. Drawing inspiration from communication network congestion control, we introduce an AIMD-like admission control policy that remains stable regardless of the number of nodes or specific AIMD parameters. This policy enables the creation of an event-driven discrete model activated by a locally detectable condition. Furthermore, we develop a decentralized resource allocation strategy using a straightforward nonlinear state feedback controller, which ensures global convergence to a bounded set within a finite timeframe. Finally, we link these characteristics to Quality of Service metrics by deriving a simple formula for local queuing time that aligns with Little's Law.

Organizations utilize Issue Tracking Systems (ITSs) to record project activities through individual units known as issues. This documentation approach fosters evolutionary refinement, allowing each issue to be enhanced independently, annotated, connected to others, and advanced through organizational workflows. While GitHub, GitLab, and Bugzilla are frequently studied, Jira—despite being widely used and rich in data—has not received comparable academic attention. This scarcity of research is likely due to the challenges in locating and accessing public Jira repositories. To address this, we introduce a dataset comprising 16 public Jira instances covering 1,822 projects. This collection contains 2.7 million issues, 32 million changes, 9 million comments, and 1 million issue links. We anticipate that this resource will facilitate extensive research into issue evolution, linking patterns, cross-project studies, and cross-tool analysis when integrated with established ITS datasets.

Quantum confinement refers to the discretization of energy levels that occurs when particle motion is restricted to dimensions smaller than their de Broglie wavelength. This phenomenon has significantly influenced various physics disciplines and enabled new technological advancements. In semiconductor physics, confining optically excited quasiparticles like excitons or trions typically relies on modulating material properties, a method hindered by the absence of *in situ* tunability and scalability in confining potentials. Consequently, achieving fully tunable quantum confinement for optical excitations remains a primary objective in quantum photonics. This study demonstrates electrically controlled quantum confinement of neutral excitons within a gate-defined monolayer p-i-n diode. Tight confinement in the narrow neutral region is achieved through a combination of a large in-plane dc Stark shift and a novel mechanism involving repulsive interactions between excitons and free charges. The quantization of exciton motion is evidenced by multiple discrete, spectrally narrow, and voltage-dependent optical resonances appearing below the free exciton resonance. Our findings highlight unique characteristics of these quantum confined excitons, such as an in-plane dipolar nature, one-dimensional center-of-mass confinement, and a dramatic increase in exciton size under magnetic fields. This approach offers a viable pathway to scalable arrays of identical single-photon sources, serving as essential components for strongly correlated photonic systems.

This paper outlines the CRNNs employed for Task 5 of the DCASE 2020 challenge, which centers on hierarchical multilabel urban sound tagging incorporating spatiotemporal context. The corresponding code can be accessed via our GitHub repository at https://github.com/multitel-ai/urban-sound-tagging.

This paper introduces TEScalib, a new extrinsic self-calibration method for LiDAR and stereo cameras that leverages geometric and photometric data from the surrounding environment. Designed for automated driving vehicles, this approach eliminates the need for calibration targets. Given the widespread use of LiDAR and stereo cameras for sensor fusion in autonomous vehicles, accurate extrinsic calibration is critical; however, existing methods are predominantly target-based and time-consuming. Furthermore, recent targetless approaches often suffer from inaccuracy or incompatibility with driving platforms. To overcome these limitations, TEScalib utilizes 3D mesh reconstruction-based point cloud registration to accurately and robustly estimate extrinsic parameters between the LiDAR and stereo camera. For stereo camera calibration, a photometric error function is constructed, incorporating LiDAR depth to transform key points between cameras. During operation, these two components are processed iteratively. Additionally, we propose an uncertainty analysis to assess the reliability of the estimated parameters. Evaluations on the KITTI dataset demonstrate that our TEScalib approach yields highly promising results.

This study presents a resource-efficient approach utilizing a single pump laser to facilitate frequency conversion via Bragg-scattering four-wave mixing within a photonic crystal fiber. We demonstrate the bidirectional conversion of coherent light between the Sr+ P1/2 - D3/2 emission line at 1092 nm and the telecommunication C band, achieving up-conversion and down-conversion efficiencies of 4.2% and 37%, respectively. Furthermore, we explore how this scheme can be effectively scaled to satisfy the temporal, spectral, and polarization stability demands of a hybrid light-matter quantum network.

Amidst increasing pressure to lower CO2 emissions, it is essential to determine the optimal design for membrane cascade separations that minimizes energy usage. However, this task is difficult because multiple feasible configurations often exist, varying in both cost and energy efficiency. This study introduces a Mixed Integer Non-linear Program (MINLP) capable of identifying the cascade architecture and operating parameters that reduce energy consumption for binary separations involving either liquids or gases. The model for individual membrane stages relies on an analytical solution derived from a system of differential and algebraic equations based on the crossflow model and solution-diffusion theory. Numerical results confirm that this single-stage model accurately replicates experimental data. Despite its accuracy, the model is non-convex, causing even advanced solvers to struggle in proving global optimality for the identified cascades and conditions. To address this, we develop specific cuts that improve relaxation quality and accelerate the convergence of branch-and-bound solvers. We demonstrate through various examples that these cuts enable solvers to reach a 5% optimality gap within a reasonable timeframe, a result unattainable with a simple formulation of the membrane model. Ultimately, this proposed optimization framework serves as a practical tool for researchers and practitioners aiming to design energy-efficient membrane cascades.

A permutation where every prefix contains no more descents than ascents is defined as a ballot permutation. This paper introduces a decomposition of ballot permutations that facilitates a bijection between them and permutations of odd order, thereby proving a set-valued extension of a conjecture by Spiro that utilizes peak values. Furthermore, this bijection maintains the neighbors of the largest element, which settles a refinement of Spiro's conjecture suggested by Wang and Zhang. The proposed decomposition extends to well-labelled positive paths, a category of generalized ballot permutations derived from polytope theory and previously enumerated by Bernardi, Duplantier, and Nadeau. Additionally, the study examines the enumeration of ballot permutations that avoid a single pattern of length 3 and identifies a relationship between 213-avoiding ballot permutations and Gessel walks.

We have derived new mass estimates and cumulative mass profiles for the Milky Way (MW), complete with Bayesian credible regions, by utilizing the Galactic Mass Estimator (GME) code alongside kinematic data from dwarf galaxies (DGs) sourced from various studies. The GME code employs a hierarchical Bayesian framework to concurrently determine the true positions and velocities of DGs, their velocity anisotropy, and the parameters governing the Galaxy's overall gravitational potential. This research integrates significant prior information derived from previous investigations and simulations. Specifically, the prior distributions for the physical model are guided by Eadie & Juric (2019), who utilized globular clusters, and by subhalo distributions from Ananke Gaia-like surveys within the Feedback In Realistic Environments-2 (Fire-2) cosmological simulations (Sanderson et al. 2020). Leveraging DGs located beyond 45 kpc, we report median and 95% credible interval estimates for $r_{200}$ as 212.8 kpc (range: 191.12–238.44 kpc) and for the total enclosed mass $M_{200}$ as $1.19 \times 10^{12}M_{\odot}$ (range: 0.87–1.68 $\times 10^{12}M_{\odot}$), adopting $\Delta_c=200$. Additionally, we provide median mass estimates at specific radii, such as $M(<50\text{ kpc})=0.52\times10^{12}M_{\odot}$ and $M(100\text{ kpc})=0.78\times10^{12}M_{\odot}$. These findings align with other recent studies utilizing GAIA DR2 and DGs but differ significantly from those of Eadie & Juric (2019). A sensitivity analysis was conducted to assess whether individual DGs or a more massive Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) of approximately $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ influence our mass estimates. Our results offer potential evidence suggesting that certain DGs are impacted by a massive LMC and are consequently not in equilibrium with the Milky Way.

This study introduces the concept of experiment precision, which quantifies the variance inherent in user ratings during subjective evaluations. While various measures exist to assess this precision, the literature currently lacks systematic analyses of these tools. Furthermore, within the field of Multimedia Quality Assessment (MQA), no systematic framework exists for comparing subjective experiments based on their precision. Consequently, this paper proposes a framework for evaluating subjective experiments in MQA using appropriate precision metrics. We introduce three distinct precision measures and three corresponding comparison methods, then systematically analyze their performance. This analysis involves both a simulation study—where we manipulate user rating variance and bias, with a specific focus on crowdsourcing QoE experiments known for higher variability—and an evaluation using data from four real-world Quality of Experience (QoE) subjective experiments. Our results demonstrate that the proposed measures and methods effectively capture experiment precision across both simulated and real-world scenarios. Notably, one measure successfully handles significantly biased responses. We believe this assessment framework will facilitate the comparison of different subjective experiment methodologies, aiding decisions on which approach yields more precise ratings and potentially informing future standardization efforts.

While neural models demonstrate robust performance on datasets like SNLI, they struggle with out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. This study establishes a few-shot learning framework to investigate how natural language explanations influence OOD generalization. By utilizing templates from the HANS dataset, we created templated natural language explanations for each template. Although these generated explanations achieved BLEU scores comparable to groundtruth versions, they did not enhance prediction accuracy. Furthermore, we observed that generated explanations frequently hallucinate details and omit critical elements necessary for indicating the correct label.

User-uploaded images on review platforms often provide an instant, concrete impression of a restaurant's character, making them valuable assets for creating intuitive search experiences on dining websites. This paper introduces a new method to deduce restaurant categories—such as ambiance, cuisine types, and occasion suitability—from these user-submitted photos. To achieve this, we assembled a unique dataset linking user photos with restaurant styles sourced from TripAdvisor. We then developed a deep multi-instance multi-label (MIML) learning framework to address the specific challenges of this classification task. Our approach utilizes a two-step bootstrap strategy to train a multi-label convolutional neural network (CNN). This CNN calculates confidence scores for various restaurant styles across all images associated with a specific venue. These scores subsequently train a dedicated binary classifier for each style tag. Once trained, the system profiles restaurant styles by analyzing their photos using the combined multi-label CNN and SVM models. Experimental results confirm that our crowdsourcing-based method effectively infers restaurant styles, provided there are enough user-uploaded images for the establishment.

This method transforms second-order partial differential equations (PDEs) into first-order PDEs, thereby simplifying the Initial Value Problem (IVP) or Boundary Value Problem (BVP) for most second-order differential equations. This reduction facilitates the most straightforward proofs regarding the existence and uniqueness of solutions for both PVI and BVP problems.

This study examines the Stark shift in Rydberg rubidium atoms using electromagnetically induced transparency to measure both direct current (dc) and 60~Hz alternating current (ac) voltages. Such a technique offers immediate utility for atom-based voltage metrology and the calibration of electrical instruments. We report experimental data across various atomic states, enabling voltage measurements from 0~V to 12~V. A Rydberg atom-based voltage standard could serve as an alternative calibration approach, offering advantages in size, weight, power consumption, and cost relative to the highly precise Josephson voltage standard. Furthermore, this research demonstrates how voltage measurements can be employed to calculate the atomic polarizability of Rydberg states. Ultimately, this technology would provide a complementary means for disseminating the voltage scale directly to end users.

Amplitude Estimation (AE) serves as a vital subroutine across numerous quantum algorithms, offering a quadratic speedup for tasks such as financial Monte Carlo simulations. Significant research has focused on developing efficient amplitude estimation techniques that avoid costly operations like the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT), a requirement particularly critical for Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. Recent approaches have minimized the necessary quantum operations, making them the most viable near-term candidates for AE. Although the precise circuit depth needed for a quantum advantage in AE-dependent applications is yet to be determined, it is essential to continuously benchmark the algorithm's performance and associated circuit costs on existing quantum hardware. In light of this, we extend previous findings on using Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) to approximate quantum state amplitudes and establish empirical upper limits on feasible circuit depths for AE on superconducting quantum computers. Our findings demonstrate that MLE, when applied to optimally compiled circuits, currently surpasses naive sampling for up to three Grover iterations with a circuit depth of 131, exceeding depths reported in other experiments. This functional benchmark represents one of several metrics that will be tracked against current quantum hardware to gauge progress toward achieving quantum advantage.

A partially ordered set (poset) can be viewed as a category containing at most one morphism between any two objects, with the additional constraint that for distinct objects $c$ and $c'$, at most one of the hom-sets $\text{Hom}(c,c')$ or $\text{Hom}(c',c)$ is nonempty. By retaining this latter condition but permitting multiple morphisms between objects, we obtain a generalized poset characterized by multiplicities on covering relations and potentially nontrivial automorphism groups; we refer to such a structure as an "updown category." This paper provides a rigorous definition of these categories, develops a corresponding theoretical framework, and offers a comprehensive examination of ten examples, including updown categories associated with integer partitions, integer compositions, planar rooted trees, and rooted trees.

Nash-Williams established that the edge set of an undirected graph $ G $ can be partitioned into cycles if and only if every cut contains either an even or infinite number of edges. Later, C. Thomassen provided a more straightforward proof of this result and proposed a directed counterpart conjecture: the edges of a digraph can be partitioned into directed cycles if and only if, for every subset of vertices, the number of incoming edges equals the number of outgoing edges. This paper aims to prove that conjecture.

We propose a general method for quasi-deforming the KdV equation by altering its associated Hamiltonian. Utilizing the standard Abelianization technique grounded in the intrinsic $sl(2)$ loop algebra, we derive an infinite set of anomalous conservation laws; these yield conserved charges provided the deformed solution exhibits definite space-time parity. Selecting the deformed Hamiltonian carefully results in an integrable system with scaled parameters and a hierarchy of deformed systems, some of which may be quasi-integrable. Specifically, one such deformed KdV system corresponds to the known quasi-NLS soliton in the established weak-coupling limit, while a generic scaling of the KdV amplitude ($u \to u^{1+\epsilon}$) also approaches quasi-integrability through an order-by-order expansion. Based on a comprehensive parity analysis of the deformed system, quasi-conservation requires these solutions to be parity-even, a condition likely satisfied by our analytical method. Furthermore, leveraging the proven quasi-integrability of the RLW and mRLW systems [Nucl. Phys. B 939 (2019) 49-94] as specific instances of this framework, exact solitons of the quasi-KdV system can be determined numerically.

This study investigates composition operators acting on Zen spaces, which are weighted Bergman spaces defined over the right half-plane and linked via the Laplace transform to weighted function spaces on the positive half-line. The work extends previous research by Kucik regarding norms and essential norms, builds upon Schroderus's findings on (essential) spectra, and advances the studies by Arvanitidis and the authors concerning semigroups of composition operators. These findings are demonstrated through an analysis of the Hardy--Bergman space, representing the intersection of the Hardy and Bergman Hilbert spaces on the half-plane.

The University of Rochester infrared detector group is collaborating with Teledyne Imaging Sensors to create HgCdTe detector arrays with a 15 $\mu m$ cutoff wavelength for upcoming space missions. To achieve this 15 $\mu m$ target, we first developed four arrays with a cutoff wavelength of approximately 13 $\mu m$. This intermediate step was designed to detect any unexpected issues arising from extending the cutoff wavelength beyond the well-characterized 10 $\mu m$ arrays used for the NEOCam mission. Characterization of these $\sim$13 $\mu m$ arrays at the University of Rochester enabled us to identify the primary dark current mechanisms that constrain HgCdTe array performance across various temperatures and bias levels as the cutoff wavelength increases. We present preliminary dark current and well depth measurements from a 15 $\mu m$ cutoff array, revealing that dark current values are two orders of magnitude lower at high reverse bias than previously anticipated based on our best prior structures.

The long-standing understanding of $\alpha$ cluster structures in nuclei, rooted in geometrical configurations, is further explored using the spatially localized Brink $\alpha$ cluster model within the generator coordinate method. This approach reveals an apparent duality between crystallinity and condensation, characterizing these structures as supersolids. To investigate the condensation component, a field-theoretical superfluid cluster model (SCM) is proposed, which rigorously incorporates the condensation order parameter by addressing the Nambu-Goldstone mode arising from the spontaneous breaking of global phase symmetry. Applying the SCM to $^{40}$Ca using ten $\alpha$ clusters—which was previously interpreted through a crystalline lens—successfully reproduces its structure, corroborating the dual nature of $\alpha$ clustering alongside earlier findings for $^{12}$C. The emergence of a low-energy $0^+$ state near the $\alpha$ threshold is interpreted as a manifestation of the Nambu-Goldstone zero mode (a soft mode) resulting from this condensation aspect, analogous to the Hoyle state in $^{12}$C. Ultimately, the coexistence of incompatible crystalline and coherent wave properties in $\alpha$ cluster structures is attributed to the Pauli principle, which drives the formation of clusters.

This review paper showcases our latest findings on nonlinear and nonlocal mathematical models derived from contemporary financial mathematics. Drawing upon four joint publications by J. Cruz, M. Grossinho, D. Sevcovic, and C. Udeani, along with sections of J. Cruz's doctoral thesis, we examine linear and nonlinear partial integro-differential equations (PIDEs) related to option pricing and portfolio selection. We analyzed the systematic connections between these PIDEs and option pricing theory within the Black–Scholes framework. Initially, we relaxed assumptions regarding liquid and complete markets, extending models of market illiquidity to scenarios where asset prices evolve according to a Lévy stochastic process with jumps. Subsequently, we formulated the corresponding PIDE for option pricing under appropriate conditions. Using the theory of abstract semilinear parabolic equations within Bessel potential spaces, we explored the qualitative properties of solutions to nonlocal linear and nonlinear PIDEs. Furthermore, we demonstrated the existence and uniqueness of solutions for a broad class of admissible Lévy measures satisfying specific growth conditions at infinity and near the origin, within a multidimensional setting.

Astrophysics encounters chirality, or handedness, through three distinct mechanisms. First, magnetic fields and vortex lines often exhibit helical structures with systematic twists that differ between the northern and southern hemispheres of stars or galaxies, driven by external influences. Second, chirality can originate at the microphysical level, ultimately tracing back to the parity-violating weak force. Third, it may arise spontaneously, a process that necessitates both an instability and nonlinear interactions; examples of this phenomenon appear in magnetohydrodynamics and astrobiology, where the establishment of homochirality among biomolecules likely occurred at life's origin. This review examines and compares all three modes of chirality generation.

Federated learning has been widely applied to supervised deep learning tasks, such as image classification and segmentation, particularly in human-in-the-loop scenarios like film post-production where it facilitates the efficient exchange of human artists' domain expertise. However, these applications often require safeguarding training data from leakage during gradient sharing due to intellectual property or privacy concerns. Although recent studies show that training data can be reconstructed from gradients in image-classification models when the architecture is known, the theoretical understanding of why these attacks succeed or fail remains incomplete. This paper investigates the root causes of such training data leakage. We frame data reconstruction as an iterative optimization problem solved layer by layer. The objective function for each layer is primarily driven by the layer's weights and gradients, along with the output reconstructed from the subsequent layer, and may also incorporate a "pull-back" constraint from the preceding layer. By solving this problem backward from the network's output through each layer, we can reconstruct the training data. This formulation allows us to attribute potential data leakage in deep networks to their specific architectures. Furthermore, we introduce a metric to evaluate the security level of deep learning models against gradient-based attacks on training data.

The oblique random survival forest (RSF) serves as an ensemble supervised learning technique designed for right-censored data. Unlike standard RSF, which relies on single predictors to split nodes, oblique RSF constructs branches using linear combinations of predictors, often yielding superior prediction accuracy. However, evaluating all possible linear combinations creates substantial computational costs that hinder scalability on large datasets, and these models remain difficult to interpret compared to axis-based alternatives. This study presents two contributions: a method to enhance computational efficiency and a technique to estimate individual predictor importance within oblique RSFs. To reduce computational overhead, we apply the Newton-Raphson scoring optimization method to the Cox partial likelihood function at every non-leaf node. Predictor importance is estimated by negating each coefficient associated with a predictor in the linear combinations and calculating the resulting drop in out-of-bag accuracy. Benchmarking indicates that our implementation is approximately 450 times faster than existing software while maintaining equivalent discrimination and achieving a better Brier score. Simulation results demonstrate that this "negation importance" approach more reliably distinguishes between relevant and irrelevant predictors than permutation importance, Shapley additive explanations, or previous analysis-of-variance-based methods. These methods are now available in the aorsf R package.

By employing a nearly product structure determined by a spray, we establish the necessary and sufficient criteria for a linear connection with zero torsion to be Riemannian; furthermore, we demonstrate that the semi-simplicity of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over $\mathbb{R}$ is equivalent to the derived ideal coinciding with the algebra itself and to the property that every derivation of the algebra is interior.

Using a curated dataset, we examine how the size of prominent machine learning systems has evolved. Between 1950 and 2018, language model sizes grew steadily across seven orders of magnitude; however, this trend accelerated significantly from 2018 to 2022, with an additional five orders of magnitude increase in just four years. In contrast, vision models expanded at a more consistent rate, achieving a total growth of seven orders of magnitude from 1950 to 2022.

Furthermore, we observe that since 2020, there has been a proliferation of language models under 20 billion parameters and those exceeding 70 billion parameters, while the 20–70 billion range remains notably empty. We term this phenomenon the "parameter gap." We outline key characteristics of this gap and suggest several hypotheses for its existence. Our preferred explanations are: (a) scaling beyond 20 billion parameters necessitates distinct parallelism strategies, rendering mid-sized models less cost-efficient, and (b) GPT-3's magnitude—being an order of size larger than prior language models—prompted researchers to focus primarily on even larger architectures to surpass it. Although these factors likely contribute to the gap, we acknowledge that we lack high confidence in their exclusivity, as other potentially more significant dynamics may also be at work.

Current research on certified robustness in machine learning has mainly concentrated on adversarial input perturbations constrained by a fixed attack budget for each data point. This paper introduces provable robustness guarantees regarding model accuracy under bounded Wasserstein shifts of the entire data distribution. We demonstrate that a straightforward procedure which randomizes inputs within a transformation space offers provable robustness against distributional shifts defined by that transformation. Our framework supports variable perturbation sizes specific to individual data points across the input distribution and encompasses fixed-sized perturbations as a special case. Consequently, our certificates provide guaranteed lower bounds on model performance for any shift—whether natural or adversarial—within a Wasserstein ball centered on the original distribution. We apply this approach to: (i) certify robustness against natural image transformations like color, hue, brightness, and saturation shifts; (ii) certify robustness against adversarial distributional shifts; and (iii) establish provable lower bounds (hardness results) on the performance of models trained on "unlearnable" datasets that have been poisoned to disrupt training.

We introduce a non-standard cosmological model driven by the duality symmetries of string theory, where the big bang singularity is substituted by a "big bounce" occurring at high yet finite curvature. This bouncing era is preceded by an extended period of cosmic evolution, potentially infinite, that originates from an initial state asymptotically near the string perturbative vacuum.

This manuscript examines high-impact science at the EIC, aiming to pinpoint segments of the program for QCD precision research that necessitate or significantly benefit from high luminosity and low center-of-mass energies. The identified scientific areas encompass: (1) Generalized Parton Distributions, 3D imaging, and mechanical nucleon properties; (2) nucleon mass and spin; (3) momentum dependence of the nucleon in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering; (4) exotic meson spectroscopy; (5) nuclear science highlights; (6) precision Lattice QCD studies in the EIC era; (7) far-forward particle detection; (8) radiative effects and corrections; (9) Artificial Intelligence; and (10) EIC interaction regions supporting high-impact science with discovery potential. This paper establishes the scientific foundation for this program and outlines the pathway to realizing the second EIC interaction region.

Existing online 3D dense reconstruction techniques often fail to effectively balance memory usage and surface fidelity, primarily because they rely on static geometric representations like TSDFs or surfels that lack scene prior information. This paper introduces DI-Fusion (Deep Implicit Fusion), which utilizes a new 3D representation called Probabilistic Local Implicit Voxels (PLIVoxs) for online reconstruction using standard RGB-D cameras. Our PLIVox encoding incorporates scene priors by modeling both local geometry and uncertainty through a deep neural network. Leveraging these deep priors, we achieve state-of-the-art accuracy in camera trajectory estimation and mapping quality, while also improving storage efficiency over prior online methods. The implementation can be accessed at https://www.github.com/huangjh-pub/di-fusion.

We introduce a categorical framework designed to model causal structures across a broad spectrum of process theories, encompassing both classical probabilistic systems and quantum mechanics. Distinct from previous approaches in categorical quantum mechanics, this theory utilizes objects that capture fine-grained causal dependencies between subsystems, offering a novel methodology for formulating and deducing properties of diverse causal structures. We demonstrate that this framework allows for the definition of process families compatible with any acyclic causal ordering. Specifically, it accommodates one-way signalling (semi-causal) processes, non-signalling processes, and quantum $n$-combs. Moreover, the framework is sufficiently versatile to include recent extensions of classical and quantum theories where processes exhibit fixed local causal orderings but permit indefinite global causal orderings. To illustrate this capability, we identify specific processes—including the quantum switch, process matrices proposed by Oreshkov, Costa, and Brukner, and a classical three-party scenario by Baumeler, Feix, and Wolf—as instances of a specific family termed $\textrm{SOC}_n$ within a suitable category of higher-order causal processes. Following the definition of these causal structures, we derive their operational behavior using straightforward, diagrammatic axioms.

The spectrum calculated for the most tightly focused portion of radiation emitted by a superluminally moving current sheet in the magnetosphere of a non-aligned neutron star yields a distribution function that independently accounts for the entire gamma-ray spectrum of the Crab pulsar. This represents the first instance where the full range of this spectrum, spanning 10² to 10⁶ MeV, is both described and explained by a single distribution function and a unified emission mechanism.

In the framework of general relativity, traversable wormholes and bubble universes represent two facets of a single underlying concept. This paper unifies the examination, presentation, and derivation of a Minkowski-Minkowski traversable wormhole and a Minkowski-Minkowski closed bubble universe. Specifically, a static Minkowski-Minkowski closed universe (bubble universe) is constructed by merging two 3-dimensional flat spheres along a thin spherical shell of matter, known as a domain wall. Conversely, a static Minkowski-Minkowski open universe, functioning as a traversable wormhole, arises from joining two 3-dimensional regions that are the complements of flat spheres along a thin spherical throat. These constructions demonstrate that Minkowski-Minkowski bubble universes and wormholes are complementary. Furthermore, these spacetimes exhibit notable similarities to two established static models: the Minkowski-Minkowski static closed universe mirrors the Einstein universe, a static, homogeneously dust-filled spherical cosmos with a cosmological constant; while the Minkowski-Minkowski static open universe resembles the Friedmann static universe, a static, homogeneously dust-filled hyperbolic space with negative energy density and a negative cosmological constant, featuring two disjoint branes often regarded as a failed wormhole. This parallel suggests that the Einstein and Friedmann universes also share a dual conceptual nature. A linear stability analysis is conducted for all these spacetimes, revealing that the complementarity between bubble universes and traversable wormholes, observed in these static configurations, extends to dynamical spacetimes, indicating its generality. Ultimately, the study posits that bubble universes and traversable wormholes originate from the same concept, implying that the existence of one necessitates the existence of the other.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a variational quantum method designed to find sub-optimal solutions for combinatorial optimization problems. It is widely expected that QAOA could demonstrate practical quantum advantages on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices using circuits of shallow depth. Since QAOA relies on calculating expectation values of the problem Hamiltonian, a critical practical inquiry is whether an efficient classical algorithm exists to compute quantum mean values for general shallow circuits. In this work, we introduce a novel classical algorithm based on graph decomposition that achieves linear scaling with the number of qubits for most shallow QAOA circuits, with the exception of complete graph cases. Numerical evaluations on Max-cut, graph coloring, and Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model problems demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by orders of magnitude. These findings are significant not only for investigating quantum advantages via QAOA but also for benchmarking NISQ processors.

This work integrates the Perdew-Zunger self-interaction correction (PZSIC) with approximate density functional theory (DFT), the DFT+U Hubbard correction, and Rung 3.5 functionals under the Adiabatic Projection framework. By altering the Kohn-Sham reference system to include electron self-interaction in specific states, the method recovers these three approaches: selecting localized orbitals yields PZSIC, choosing localized atomic states produces DFT+U, and picking states at every spatial point results in Rung 3.5. Typically, Hubbard U parameters correspond to scaled versions of PZSIC, while a Rung 3.5 adaptation of DFT+U successfully induces a band gap in the homogeneous electron gas.

This paper introduces a four-parameter distribution family that includes the K-distribution as a special case. Derived as a mixture model combining a three-parameter reflected Gamma distribution as the parent and a two-parameter Gamma distribution as the prior, the family's properties—such as its probability density function, cumulative distribution function, moments, and cumulants—are thoroughly examined. Named the symmetric K-distribution (SKD) due to its structural resemblance to the K-distribution and inherent symmetry, the study also explores its standard form, which frequently serves as a sufficient model. Additionally, the work presents an order statistics analysis and derives the distributions for the product and ratio of two independent and identically distributed SKD random variables. Furthermore, a generalized version of the family capable of accommodating non-zero skewness is investigated. Both the SKD and the resulting skew-SKD are demonstrated to accurately model complex dynamics in machine learning, Bayesian analysis, and other domains using simplified, high-precision expressions.

We introduce a microscopic framework describing plasmon excitations in graphene/${\alpha}$-RuCl${_3}$ heterostructures. Using a Kondo-Kitaev model incorporating diverse interactions, we demonstrate the emergence of a heavy Fermi liquid characterized by flat bands; in this state, itinerant graphene electrons effectively hybridize with the fractionalized fermions of the Kitaev quantum spin liquid. Our analysis reveals new correlated plasmon bands arising from the interaction between these flat bands and many-body effects, and we show that our theoretical approach aligns with existing experimental observations on these heterostructures. Furthermore, we forecast novel plasmon branches extending beyond the long-wavelength regime and explore the implications for investigating correlation effects in other flat band systems.

High-precision asteroseismic data from space missions like NASA's Kepler on solar-type stars now enable detailed investigations of stellar interiors. These capabilities allow researchers to constrain core properties—such as size, chemical composition, and physical processes—thereby refining the accuracy of estimated stellar ages. We utilized the binary system 16 Cyg A and B as benchmark objects to introduce a novel methodology for filtering stellar models generated through forward modeling. This approach isolates models that most accurately represent the stellar cores by comparing specific observed frequency ratios against those predicted by the viable models. Our results demonstrate that this technique effectively narrows down the core hydrogen mass fraction, thereby determining the stars' precise evolutionary stages and ages. Specifically, the derived core hydrogen mass fractions for 16 Cyg A and B range from [0.01 - 0.06] and [0.12 - 0.19], respectively. Given that the stars are coeval, their ages and metal mass fractions are constrained to the intervals [6.4 - 7.4] Gyr and [0.023 - 0.026]. Furthermore, our findings indicate that assuming a single helium-to-heavy element enrichment ratio ($\Delta Y/\Delta Z$) during forward modeling of the 16 Cyg binary can yield acceptable models that fail to simultaneously match the observed frequency ratios. This suggests that relying on a fixed $\Delta Y/\Delta Z$ value may be insufficient for accurately determining helium content in individual stellar studies.

MnBi$_2$Te$_4$, recognized as the first intrinsic antiferromagnetic (AFM) topological insulator (TI), offers a unique platform for exploring emergent phenomena resulting from the synergy of magnetism and band topology. Through a comprehensive investigation of (Mn$_{1-x}$Pb$_x$)Bi$_2$Te$_4$ single crystals ($0\leq x \leq 0.82$) utilizing x-ray diffraction, electrical transport, magnetometry, neutron scattering, chemical analysis, pressure studies, and first-principles calculations, we elucidate how magnetic dilution influences both magnetism and band topology. As the Pb concentration $x$ increases, both lattice parameters $a$ and $c$ expand linearly by approximately 2%. All samples exhibit a paramagnetic-to-A-type antiferromagnetic transition, with the Néel temperature dropping linearly from 24 K at $x=0$ to 2 K at $x=0.82$. Neutron refinement for the $x=0.37$ sample determines an ordered moment of 4.3(1)$\mu_B$/Mn at 4.85 K and confirms that Mn$_{\rm{Bi}}$ antisite defects are negligible within experimental error. Isothermal magnetization data indicate a slight reduction in interlayer plane-plane antiferromagnetic exchange interaction and a monotonic decline in magnetic anisotropy, attributed to the dilution of magnetic ions and the enlargement of the unit cell. Under external pressure at $x=0.37$, the interlayer antiferromagnetic coupling strengthens, raising the Néel temperature by 1.4 K/GPa and the saturation field by 1.8 T/GPa. Additionally, first-principles calculations show that band inversion occurs at the $\Gamma$ point for MnBi$_2$Te$_4$ and the $Z$ point for PbBi$_2$Te$_4$, with gapless points emerging at $x=0.44$ and $x=0.66$, implying potential topological phase transitions induced by doping.

This paper attempts a pedagogical overview of experimental findings regarding the spin-dependent structure of nucleons, both past and present, before the Electron-Ion Collider comes online. Following an introduction, it details results from fixed-target facilities at SLAC, Fermilab, Jefferson Lab, CERN, and DESY, as well as data from RHIC's collider experiments. The discussion begins with the nucleon's longitudinal spin structure, proceeds to generalized parton distributions (GPDs) that map the proton in transverse position space, and concludes with transverse proton and parton spin along with transverse parton momenta (TMDs) and their spin-orbit correlations, all supported by numerous recent studies. GPDs and TMDs offer complementary approaches to mapping the multi-dimensional structure of the nucleon.

This letter investigates dynamic game optimal control under imperfect state observations and proposes an iterative approach to determine a local Nash equilibrium. The method integrates a backward recursion akin to minimax differential dynamic programming with a forward recursion similar to a risk-sensitive Kalman smoother, linked by a coupling equation that ties the control law to the state estimates. Ultimately, this algorithm functions as a Newton step yet maintains linear complexity relative to the time horizon. To ensure convergence, we introduce a merit function alongside a line search procedure. The derived controller addresses uncertainty by planning against worst-case disturbances. Additionally, the algorithm's low computational burden renders it a viable candidate for high-frequency output-feedback model predictive control on complex systems. Numerical simulations on realistic robotic scenarios demonstrate the risk-sensitive characteristics of the resulting controller.

Grain boundary (GB) energy significantly dictates the properties and growth behavior of polycrystalline metals. We demonstrate that GB energy, when normalized by bulk cohesive energy, depends solely on four geometric characteristics. By applying machine learning to a comprehensive dataset of 361 small $\Sigma$ ($\Sigma < 10$) GBs from over 50 metals, we created a model capable of predicting grain boundary energies with a mean absolute error of 0.13 J m$^{-2}$. Crucially, this universal model can be extrapolated to high $\Sigma$ GBs without compromising accuracy. These findings underscore the necessity of incorporating fundamental scaling physics and domain expertise to build interpretable and extrapolatable machine learning models for materials science.

This study introduces a Deep neural network-assisted Particle Filter (DePF) framework designed to solve the joint synchronization and localization challenge for Mobile Users (MUs) within ultra-dense networks. The DePF method utilizes an asymmetric timestamp exchange protocol between MUs and Access Points (APs), which traditionally yields data regarding clock offset and skew. However, this exchange also inherently reveals the propagation delay, allowing for distance estimation. Furthermore, to determine the angle of arrival of incoming synchronization packets, the approach employs a multiple signal classification algorithm driven by the Channel Impulse Response (CIR) of these packets; the CIR is additionally used to assess link conditions, specifically distinguishing between Line-of-Sight (LoS) and Non-LoS scenarios. To achieve joint synchronization and localization, DePF leverages particle Gaussian mixtures, enabling a hybrid fusion of the gathered information through both particle-based and parametric Bayesian Recursive Filtering (BRF) techniques to simultaneously estimate MU positions and clock parameters. Simulation outcomes confirm the proposed algorithm's superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods, particularly those based on Extended Kalman Filters and linearized BRF. Specifically, relying solely on timestamp exchanges and CIRs, the method achieves absolute position and clock offset estimation errors under 1 meter and 2 nanoseconds, respectively, in 90% of test cases.

This paper introduces novel copulas grounded in perturbation theory to elucidate the \emph{symmetrization} process for asymmetric copulas. We also outline specific properties of the resulting \emph{symmetrized} copulas and investigate families of copulas defined by a predetermined symmetrized form. Furthermore, we analyze the topological structure of the set containing all symmetric copulas, presenting both established and newly discovered characteristics.

This study investigates phonon properties and electron-phonon coupling in thin NbTiN films, materials widely utilized in superconducting applications. The examined films, with thicknesses under 10 nm, exhibit disorder regarding electron transport, characterized by an Ioffe-Regel parameter of $k_F l_e = 2.5-3.0$ (where $k_F$ is the Fermi wave vector and $l_e$ is the electron mean free path), and strong inelastic electron-phonon interaction, indicated by $q_T l_e \ll 1$ ($q_T$ being the thermal phonon wave vector). Utilizing magnetoconductance and photoresponse methods, we calculated the inelastic electron-phonon scattering rate $1/\tau_{e-ph}$ and established sound velocities and phonon heat capacities. Between 12 and 20 K, the scattering rate follows a temperature dependence of $1/\tau_{e-ph}\propto T^{3.45\pm0.05}$, extrapolating to roughly 16 ps at 10 K. When comparing these films to other superconducting device materials like polycrystalline granular NbN and amorphous WSi, we observed a consistent reduction in sound velocity of approximately 50% relative to bulk crystalline counterparts. However, the resulting increase in phonon heat capacities falls short of Debye model predictions. We attribute these observations to the films' reduced dimensionality and specific morphology.

Grimsley et al. (Nat. Commun. 10, 3007) recently introduced the Adaptive Derivative-Assembled Pseudo-Trotter ansatz Variational Quantum Eigensolver (ADAPT-VQE), an adaptive variational algorithm requiring $O(N^8)$ measurements. This work proposes an efficient adaptive variational quantum solver for the Schrödinger equation that combines ADAPT-VQE with reduced density matrix reconstruction, thereby reducing the measurement scaling to $O(N^4)$. Due to its low circuit complexity and diminished measurement overhead, this enhanced algorithm is well-suited for simulating chemical systems on near-term noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware. Numerical benchmarks on small molecules confirm that the method accurately reproduces ground-state potential energy curves. Furthermore, by integrating the variational quantum deflation approach, the algorithm has been extended to excited states, achieving accuracy comparable to ground-state simulations.

This paper investigates a class of pseudo-differential operators called time-frequency localization operators on $\Z^n$, which are determined by a symbol $\varsigma$ and two window functions, $g_1$ and $g_2$. We first define the short-time Fourier transform on $ \Z^n \times \T^n $ and modulation spaces on $\Z^n$, outlining their fundamental properties. Subsequently, employing modulation spaces on $\Z^n \times \T^n$ as suitable symbol classes, we examine the boundedness and compactness of these localization operators within modulation spaces on $\Z^n$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these operators belong to the Schatten--von Neumann class. Additionally, we establish the connection between Landau--Pollak--Slepian type operators and localization operators on $\Z^n$. Finally, under appropriate conditions on the symbols, we prove that the localization operators function as paracommutators, paraproducts, and Fourier multipliers.

Ghost imaging is a fascinating phenomenon where an image is reconstructed from photons that never interacted with the object. Conventionally, this effect relies on initially correlated but spatially separated photons—one interacting with the target and the other forming the image—and has been demonstrated across various physical contexts, including both classical and quantum regimes. To date, every recorded instance of ghost imaging has produced an image with the same contrast as the object, meaning bright areas in the object appear bright in the image and dark areas appear dark. In this study, we demonstrate ghost imaging in a novel system using photons that have never interacted. By employing entanglement swapping between independent pairs of spatially entangled photons, we establish positional correlations between two initially independent photons. Due to an anti-symmetric projection inherent in the entanglement swapping process, the resulting image exhibits reversed contrast compared to the object; where the object is bright, the image is dark, and vice versa. These findings underscore the critical role of state projection in ghost imaging and offer a potential route for teleporting images across quantum networks.

The stability of the npm dependency ecosystem is vital, as numerous projects and web applications depend heavily on package functionalities, particularly those with extensive user bases. Historically, the removal or updates of specific npm packages have triggered widespread disruptions and downtime across the internet. This study aims to monitor the network's resilience over time to determine if its structural robustness is improving. We demonstrate that the network remains vulnerable to targeted attacks, where security flaws in a small number of critical nodes can impact a significant portion of the system. However, because these pivotal packages are typically supported by rigorous communities with high standards, the situation is not alarming; it is instead a natural outcome of the network's power-law distribution. Current trends show a decrease in the average number of dependencies and a reduced influence of key nodes on the rest of the network, thereby enhancing resilience and establishing a positive trajectory for development. Additionally, we observe that communities naturally form around the most significant packages, though these groupings do not strictly align with standard modularity definitions. Finally, we offer guidelines for package development designed to bolster network robustness and minimize the risk of introducing security vulnerabilities.

Road networks constitute a fundamental pillar of national infrastructure, enabling the flow of people, commodities, and concepts, thereby driving economic and cultural interactions domestically and internationally. Accurate, current mapping of road locations and conditions is critical for high-stakes applications such as land-use planning and wilderness preservation. This task poses a significant hurdle in developing nations, characterized by inadequate documentation and a projected surge in road construction over the coming decades. This paper introduces a novel crowdsourced methodology for evaluating road quality and examines the primary obstacles and prospects involved in adapting deep learning techniques across different domains.

Simulating convection-dominated two-phase flows with high density ratios presents significant difficulties, particularly in resolving the thin shear layers at interfaces. To address this, we introduce a sharp discretization approach for the two-velocity formulation of the two-phase Navier-Stokes equations. This method enables the modeling of shear layers by permitting velocity discontinuities tangential to the interface, rather than requiring their explicit resolution. This paper specifically examines the transport of mass and momentum under such discontinuous conditions. We extend the dimensionally unsplit geometric Volume of Fluid (VOF) method to handle interface advection within the two-velocity framework. We derive sufficient conditions for constructing donor regions that guarantee the boundedness of volume fractions in unsplit advection schemes. Furthermore, we propose interpolating mass fluxes from the geometric VOF method to advect the staggered momentum field, achieving semi-discrete energy conservation. Since dividing momentum by mass to derive velocity can be ill-defined in nearly empty control volumes, our flux interpolant is carefully designed to ensure this division remains well-defined without introducing unnecessary dissipation. In addition to the proposed two-velocity model, we detail an exactly conservative implementation (conserving mass per phase and total linear momentum) of the standard one-velocity formulation for comparative purposes. Finally, we validate these discretization methods using classical, time-reversible flow fields, where advection is currently uncoupled from the Navier-Stokes solver, which will be integrated in future work.

The concept of quantum curves was first introduced within the physics community. This work establishes a mathematical framework specifically for quantum curves linked to Hitchin spectral curves. In this setting, a quantum curve is defined as a Rees $\mathcal{D}$-module on a smooth projective algebraic curve, where its semi-classical limit yields the Hitchin spectral curve of a Higgs bundle. We present a quantization method for Hitchin spectral curves by explicitly constructing one-parameter deformation families of opers. Additionally, we propose a variation of the Eynard–Orantin and Mirzakhani topological recursion tailored for singular Hitchin spectral curves. We demonstrate that a partial differential equation (PDE) formulation of topological recursion facilitates all-order WKB analysis for the Rees $\mathcal{D}$-modules, which represent the quantization of Hitchin spectral curves associated with meromorphic $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$-Higgs bundles. Topological recursion can be viewed as a quantization process for Hitchin spectral curves. We prove that these two distinct quantization approaches—constructing families of opers and employing PDE-based topological recursion—coincide for both holomorphic and meromorphic $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$-Higgs bundles. Classic examples, such as the Airy differential equation, illustrate how quantum curves connect Higgs bundles, opers, Gaiotto's conjecture, and quantum invariants like Gromov–Witten invariants.

This study introduces a stochastic framework to forecast the spectral signatures of proton-transfer events, applying it to infrared spectra derived from *ab initio* molecular-dynamics simulations of an isolated H$_5$O$_2{}^{+}$ cation. By fixing the distance between oxygen atoms, the system functions as a tunable model for proton-transfer processes featuring adjustable barrier heights. The analysis identifies and analytically predicts three distinct spectral components at different frequencies: quasi-harmonic vibrations around the most probable configuration, which can be addressed via normal-mode analysis; the contribution from transfer paths as the proton crosses the barrier; and a low-frequency shoulder resulting from the stochastic distribution of transfer waiting times. While the latter two components reflect proton-transfer kinetics and remain undetected by standard normal-mode analysis, the frequency of the transfer-waiting component decreases exponentially with increasing barrier height, consistent with reaction kinetic theory, whereas the transfer-path component shows minimal sensitivity to barrier height variations.

We detail a rapid transient classification algorithm central to the kilonova (KN) science module within the Fink broker, presenting results derived from both simulated catalogs and actual ZTF alert stream data. Noiseless, uniformly sampled simulations were utilized to establish a principal component (PC) basis, with light curves from a more realistic ZTF simulation expressed as linear combinations of these components. These coefficients served as features for training a random forest classifier, applied separately to long (>30 days) and medium (<30 days) light curves; the latter mirrored the conditions of the ZTF alert stream. Analysis of long light curves yielded a precision of 73.87% and a recall of 82.19%, while the medium baseline analysis achieved 69.30% precision and 69.74% recall, validating the precision stability even with only 30 days of data. In both scenarios, dwarf flares and Type Ia supernovae emerged as the primary contaminants. The finalized model has been deployed in the Fink broker to distribute fast transients tagged as \texttt{KN\_candidates} to the astronomical community, particularly via the GRANDMA collaboration. We demonstrated that features tailored to capture diverse light curve behaviors contain sufficient information to distinguish between fast (KN-like) and slow (non-KN-like) evolving events. This module constitutes a vital component of the Fink broker team's broader infrastructure chain for multi-messenger astronomy, currently being established in anticipation of data from the Vera Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time.

This study examines multi-particle systems governed by linear deterministic Hamiltonian dynamics. While these systems possess a continuum of invariant tori and corresponding invariant measures alongside the Liouville measure, we demonstrate that subjecting a single particle to a random linear transformation (specifically, a velocity flip) at stochastic intervals ensures convergence to the Liouville measure from any initial state. Establishing this proof required investigating non-linear transformations defined on the energy surface.

This paper introduces RiemannianFlow, a deep generative model enabling robots to acquire complex and stable skills on Riemannian manifolds. Riemannian data in robotics, such as stiffness (symmetric positive definite matrices) and orientation (unit quaternions), differs from Euclidean data because its dimensions are linked by geometric constraints that must be respected during learning. By employing distance-preserving mappings, our method transfers data between the original manifold and the tangent space, effectively managing these constraints. This approach extends existing frameworks to learn stable skills from Riemannian data while ensuring result stability. Experimental results on a dataset of manifold motions demonstrate RiemannianFlow's capacity to learn diverse data patterns and maintain model stability. Additionally, we evaluated the model's robustness across various hyperparameter combinations; while stability remained consistent regardless of these settings, an optimal configuration improved accuracy by up to 27.6%. Finally, we validated RiemannianFlow's effectiveness in a real-world peg-in-hole task, generating stable and consistent position and orientation trajectories from diverse initial robot poses.

It is hypothesized that a "modular" architecture within artificial neural networks facilitates learning, compositionality, and generalization, yet defining and measuring modularity remains unresolved. We frame the detection of functional modules as the identification of clusters comprising units with similar functions, prompting the inquiry into what constitutes functional similarity. We examine two primary methodological families: those relying on unit responses to structured input variations ("upstream") and those based on how hidden unit activation changes influence outputs ("downstream"). Through an empirical study, we quantify the modularity of hidden layer representations in simple, fully connected feedforward networks across various hyperparameters. For each model, we calculate pairwise associations between hidden units using diverse upstream and downstream metrics, then cluster them by optimizing a "modularity score" with established network science tools. Our findings reveal two unexpected outcomes: first, dropout significantly enhances modularity, whereas other weight regularization techniques yield only modest improvements. Second, while upstream and downstream methods generally agree on the existence of clusters, they show minimal consensus on specific cluster assignments across the two families. This discrepancy holds significant implications for representation learning, suggesting that discovering modular representations aligned with input structure (such as disentanglement) is a distinct objective from those aligned with output structure (such as compositionality).

Addressing multi-label recognition (MLR) for images under low-label conditions remains a difficult yet highly relevant challenge. While recent approaches attempt to bridge textual and visual spaces to mitigate scarce image labels, they often suffer from accuracy drops due to the lack of sufficient MLR annotations. Our method leverages the robust alignment of visual and textual features pre-trained on millions of auxiliary image-text pairs and introduces Dual Context Optimization (DualCoOp), a unified framework designed for both partial-label and zero-shot MLR. By incorporating class names as positive and negative contexts within linguistic prompts, DualCoOp achieves rapid adaptation to multi-label tasks with limited data or even unseen categories, imposing minimal learnable overhead on the underlying vision-language model. Experimental results on standard benchmarks across two demanding low-label scenarios confirm that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

We introduce designs for 'mirror' pulses tailored for large-momentum-transfer atom interferometers, ensuring high fidelity even as the wavepacket momentum difference grows. Developed via optimal control methods to match the evolving bi-modal momentum distribution, these bi-selective pulses enable larger interferometer areas and enhanced inertial measurement sensitivity without necessitating high Rabi frequencies or prolonged frequency chirps. Simulations based on an experimentally validated model demonstrate the application of these pulse designs to large-momentum-transfer atom interferometry using stimulated Raman transitions in a laser-cooled sample of $^{85}$Rb at 1 $\mu$K. After the wavepackets separate by 42 photon recoil momenta, our pulses sustain a fringe contrast of 90%, compared to less than 10% for both adiabatic rapid passage and conventional $\pi$ pulses. Additionally, we illustrate how these pulses can be modified to mitigate detrimental off-resonant excitation, a limitation affecting other broadband pulse schemes.

Deep learning relies on globally optimizing non-convex objective functions characterized by numerous local minima, a challenge also prevalent in physical simulations. This issue can be addressed using Langevin dynamics combined with Simulated Annealing, a proven technique for minimizing many-particle potentials, offering valuable perspectives for stochastic optimization in machine learning. Our analysis reveals that discretizing the Langevin equation yields a coordinate update rule identical to the Momentum optimization algorithm. A key finding is that gradually reducing the momentum coefficient from near unity to zero mimics the physical process of Simulated Annealing or slow cooling. Leveraging this insight, we introduce CoolMomentum, a new stochastic optimization method. Empirical results on optimizing ResNet-20 for CIFAR-10 and EfficientNet-B0 for ImageNet demonstrate that CoolMomentum achieves high accuracy.

Effective decision-making requires adaptively connecting past experiences and contextual details to new scenarios. While standard deep reinforcement learning (RL) primarily relies on gradient descent to embed decision-making information into network weights, we propose an alternative method where agents perform large-scale, context-aware database lookups to assist their parametric calculations. This enables agents to learn end-to-end how to leverage pertinent information for their outputs. Furthermore, agents can incorporate new data without retraining by merely expanding the retrieval dataset. We evaluate this strategy in offline RL for 9x9 Go, a complex game where the expansive state space favors generalization over direct experience matching. By employing rapid approximate nearest-neighbor techniques to access relevant data from tens of millions of expert demonstrations, we achieve a notable improvement in both prediction accuracy and gameplay performance compared to using demonstrations solely as training trajectories. This offers strong evidence for the benefits of large-scale retrieval in offline RL agents.
