The Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO) employs 20,000 tons of liquid scintillator (LS) for neutrino detection, where the presence of radioactive impurities can compromise experimental outcomes. To mitigate radioactive metal ions within the LS, JUNO plans to implement counter-current water extraction. This article investigates key variables influencing the final extraction efficiency, including the partition coefficient and its determinants, optimal mass transfer droplet size, flow rate ratios, theoretical stages, and operational modes (whether LS serves as the continuous or dispersed phase). We have constructed both a laboratory-scale counter-current extraction prototype and a pilot plant at Daya Bay. Beyond analyzing these critical factors, we have also accumulated valuable engineering insights that are worth sharing.

Drawing inspiration from subspace coding, this paper introduces the concepts of subspace-metric codes and subset-metric codes, which serve as coordinate-position independent pseudometrics well-suited for folded codes. We establish half-Singleton upper bounds for linear variants of both subspace-metric and subset-metric codes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that subspace and subset distances act as natural lower bounds for insdel distances, thereby enabling the estimation of insertion-deletion error-correcting capabilities. These new code types allow for the direct construction of explicit, well-structured insertion-deletion codes. Specifically, $k$-deletion correcting codes with rates approaching 1 can be derived from subspace codes. Finally, by analyzing the subset distances of folded codes constructed from evaluation codes of linear mappings, we show they possess high subset distances, confirming their status as explicit and effective insertion-deletion codes.

The Floquet time crystal, known for breaking discrete time-translation symmetry, represents a fascinating phenomenon within non-equilibrium systems. Gaining insight into the rigidity and robustness of discrete time crystal (DTC) phases in many-body contexts is essential, and identifying a precisely solvable model can facilitate this understanding. In this work, we introduce and analyze a solvable spin chain model by utilizing the Jordan-Wigner transformation to map it onto a Floquet superconductor. The phase diagrams of these Floquet topological systems are defined by topological invariants, which indicate the presence of anomalous edge states. These edge states can generate the sub-harmonic oscillation—a hallmark signal of the DTC—and are safeguarded by topological protection. Furthermore, we assess the robustness of the DTC by introducing both symmetry-preserving and symmetry-breaking perturbations. Our findings regarding topologically protected DTCs offer profound insights that may extend to other interacting or dissipative systems.

The application of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism of General Relativity is essential for characterizing exact solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review aims to present the fundamental concepts and computational procedures regarding these bivectors, specifically by transforming the complex self-dual electromagnetic field from an orthonormal Minkowski basis into a complex null tetrad basis. Additionally, within this framework, the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the Newman-Penrose formalism are derived.

This paper introduces a collection of Python tools designed for forecasting using time series data. The content originates from a four-week course the author has instructed for seven years to students in operations research, management science, analytics, and statistics within one-year MSc programs. While primarily tailored for these groups, the material is easily adaptable for other audiences, such as executive management or undergraduate students. No prior Python expertise is necessary to utilize this resource. However, proficiency in standard statistical forecasting methods—including exponential smoothing, ARIMA, and regression-based techniques—is assumed, as these are essential for delivering the course. To support those interested in teaching similar courses or gaining familiarity with the underlying mathematics and tools, access to relevant data, code, and lecture notes is provided via github.com/abzemkoho/forecasting.

Leveraging Natural Language Processing (NLP) to identify rare diseases within clinical notes presents significant hurdles, primarily stemming from limited case data for machine learning and the requirement for expert annotation. To address this, we introduce a methodology combining ontologies with weak supervision. The framework operates in two stages: first, a Text-to-UMLS step that maps textual mentions to concepts in the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) using a named entity linker like SemEHR, enhanced by weak supervision derived from tailored rules and BERT-based contextual embeddings; second, a UMLS-to-ORDO step that aligns UMLS concepts with rare diseases in the Orphanet Rare Disease Ontology (ORDO). Validated using MIMIC-III US intensive care discharge summaries, our findings demonstrate that weak supervision substantially improves the Text-to-UMLS process without necessitating any annotated data from domain specialists. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the complete pipeline can successfully uncover rare disease instances that are largely absent from manual ICD codes recorded during hospital admissions.

While optimal control problems for dynamical systems can be modeled using variational calculus, solving them for complex systems often proves analytically and computationally impossible. This Letter introduces a versatile neural ordinary-differential-equation control (NODEC) framework featuring implicit energy regularization, which generates neural-network-based control signals capable of guiding dynamical systems to a target state within a specified timeframe. We demonstrate that NODEC can learn control signals that closely match those derived from traditional optimal control frameworks regarding both control energy and deviation from the desired target. Our findings indicate that NODEC is effective at solving a broad spectrum of control and optimization challenges, including those that are analytically intractable.
This piece offers a concise introduction and summary of the theoretical foundations supporting the experiments detailed in the remainder of this review.

Mobile microscopy is an emerging discipline born from the convergence of optical microscopy with the expanding computational power, versatility, and reach of mobile devices. Although the concept of integrating a microscope, advanced computer vision algorithms, and a mobile platform has been frequently explored, existing solutions still necessitate a skilled operator to manage specimen digitization. This paper proposes a solution to overcome this limitation by introducing a "smart" mobile microscope designed for the automatic capture of the most significant visual data from specimens. We achieve this by unifying automated microscope configuration with established techniques—including auto-focusing, in-focus filtering, and focus-stacking—which have been refined and optimized within a mobile, cross-platform library.

This paper establishes the convergence of the two-species Vlasov-Poisson-Boltzmann (VPB) system to the two-fluid incompressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier-Poisson (NSFP) system incorporating Ohm's law, specifically within the framework of classical solutions. By addressing strong interspecies interactions, we derive uniform estimates with respect to the Knudsen number $\varepsilon$ for solutions to the two-species VPB system near equilibrium. Consequently, we demonstrate that as $\varepsilon$ approaches 0, the system converges to the two-fluid incompressible NSFP.

Although supermassive black hole masses have been recorded throughout cosmic history, robust spin measurements exist for only a handful of them. By expanding and refining the current Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) into the next-generation version (ngEHT), researchers will be able to capture multifrequency, polarimetric movies at event horizon scales, thereby imposing new constraints on space-time and accretion dynamics. By integrating these data, the ngEHT is expected to determine the masses and spins of tens of supermassive black holes. This white paper examines current spin measurements and outlines numerous proposed techniques for the ngEHT to assess the spins of target black holes. Notably, spins derived from the ngEHT would constitute a unique, unbiased sample of sources, distinct from existing collections that favor high accretion rates. This new dataset promises to yield fresh insights into accretion processes, feedback mechanisms, and the cosmic assembly of supermassive black holes.

Ulam posed the question of whether every connected Lie group admits a representation on a countable structure, a result already established for linear groups. This paper demonstrates that the answer is affirmative for the first class of non-linear groups, specifically nilpotent ones. Additional context is provided to highlight the significance of nilpotent groups in addressing Ulam's problem.

This study investigates the topological phases of a dimerized square lattice under an external magnetic field. The dimerization of hopping amplitudes can open bulk energy gaps within the Hofstadter spectrum at specific fractional fillings, leading to diverse topological states. Specifically, we demonstrate that at $\frac{1}{2}$-filling, a topological quadrupole insulator phase emerges in certain parameter regimes across all magnetic flux values; this phase features a quantized quadrupole moment of $\frac{e}{2}$ and corner-localized mid-gap states. At $\frac{1}{4}$ filling, the system supports either obstructed atomic limit or Chern insulator phases. For configurations gapped at fillings below $\frac{1}{4}$, the system exhibits Chern insulator phases with non-zero Chern numbers. Throughout the phase diagram, the model displays both bulk-obstructed and boundary-obstructed topological phase transitions.

Network modeling has established itself as a highly effective instrument across various interdisciplinary fields, such as biology, sociology, and transportation, to analyze complex real-world systems. Concurrently, cellular automata (CA) have been widely studied over recent decades as a formalism for investigating patterns within the dynamic spatio-temporal behaviors of these systems through local rules. Certain research has applied cellular automata to examine network dynamics, a concept referred to as network automata (NA). Recently, NA has demonstrated efficacy in network classification by utilizing time-evolution patterns (TEP) for feature extraction. However, prior studies relied on TEPs consisting of binary values, which fail to capture detailed information about the analyzed networks. Consequently, this paper introduces alternative information sources as descriptors for classification tasks, termed density time-evolution pattern (D-TEP) and state density time-evolution pattern (SD-TEP). We investigate the density of active neighbors for each node—a continuous metric—and derive feature vectors from histograms of these TEPs. Our findings indicate a substantial improvement over previous studies across five synthetic and seven real-world network databases. Furthermore, our proposed method not only offers a robust approach for network pattern recognition but also exhibits significant potential for applications involving other data types, such as images.

As digital data volumes and social networking platforms expand, the role of social media science in guiding corporate decisions regarding product features and customer service has become increasingly vital. Specifically, platforms like Twitter, where users freely share experiences on virtually any topic, can significantly influence the reputations and offerings of both companies and tourist destinations. Although literature has explored text mining tools for extracting value from Twitter through trend detection and sentiment analysis, the accuracy of these models heavily depends on using domain-specific data. This paper outlines a \textit{DataOps / MLOps} pipeline applied to a tourism-focused Twitter dataset to understand tourist motivations and interests. The insights derived from this analysis can be leveraged by the travel and hospitality sectors to create data-driven strategic services, while also enabling travelers to access relevant information about their destinations.

Public goods games on undirected networks typically possess pure Nash equilibria that are straightforward to identify. Conversely, we demonstrate that for directed networks, a wide variety of public goods games present computationally intractable equilibrium challenges: determining the existence of pure Nash equilibria is NP-hard, while locating mixed Nash equilibria is PPAD-hard. We introduce general utility public goods games, establishing a complexity dichotomy for pure equilibria and proving PPAD-completeness for mixed Nash equilibria. Notably, even in the divisible goods variant where existence is guaranteed, finding an equilibrium remains PPAD-complete. However, we show that if the treewidth of the directed network is suitably bounded, polynomial-time algorithms become feasible.

The statement $\mathsf{MM}^{++}(\kappa)$ asserts that the forcing axiom $\mathsf{MM}^{++}$ applies exclusively to stationary set preserving posets with cardinality no greater than $\kappa$. We provide a comprehensive exposition of Asper\`o and Schindler's demonstration that $\mathsf{MM}^{++}(\kappa)$, combined with the existence of a proper class of Woodin cardinals, entails Woodin's axiom $(*)$ under the conditions that $\Diamond_\kappa$ holds and $\kappa > \aleph_2$. Our approach leverages the concept of a consistency property, specifically reformulating Asper\`o and Schindler's forcing method as a particular case of the "consistency property" employed by Makkai, Keisler, Mansfield, and others in their research on infinitary logics. Additionally, we have restructured the sequence in which the proof's components are presented. Apart from these modifications, our account remains substantially faithful to the original proof by Asper\`o and Schindler.

This study presents the first practical assessment of the structural rounding framework for approximation algorithms. The approach involves transforming an instance into a well-structured class, efficiently solving the modified version, and then "lifting" the resulting partial solution to generate an approximation for the original input. Focusing on the Vertex Cover problem, we edit instances into bipartite graphs, where an exact polynomial-time solution exists. Beyond the naive lifting method outlined by Demaine et al., we propose a range of novel lifting strategies and evaluate their performance on a large dataset of synthetic graphs. Our results demonstrate that structural rounding substantially surpasses standard 2-approximations in this context, with simpler lifting techniques proving highly competitive against more complex methods. All implementations are released as an open-source Python package, ensuring full reproducibility of the experiments.

Current cosmological studies utilizing large-scale structure and weak lensing data, commonly known as 3$\times$2pt, have historically required discarding significant signal-to-noise from small scales due to difficulties in accurately modeling non-linearities and baryonic effects. Galaxy-galaxy lensing, which measures the position-shear correlation between lens and source galaxies as one of the three two-point correlation functions in these analyses, is typically estimated via mean tangential shear. However, tangential shear measurements at a specific angular scale $\theta$ or physical scale $R$ inherently incorporate information from all smaller scales, necessitating scale cuts in real data that are far more restrictive than the point where theoretical uncertainties become an issue. Recently, several independent initiatives have sought to address the non-locality inherent in galaxy-galaxy lensing signals. This study compares various methods, including the Y transformation (Park et al. 2021), the point-mass marginalization approach (MacCrann et al. 2020), and the Annular Differential Surface Density statistic (Baldauf et al. 2010). The comparison is conducted at the level of cosmological constraints using noiseless simulations of combined galaxy clustering and galaxy-galaxy lensing. We find that all estimators perform equivalently in a setup resembling the Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) Year 1, as each effectively projects out the mode responsible for the non-local nature of the measurements, identified here as $1/R^2$. Finally, we apply these estimators to DES Y3 data, confirming that they all yield consistent results.

Image super-resolution (SR) is a rapidly evolving domain where new architectures frequently capture attention. However, the majority of SR models rely on outdated training methodologies. This study re-examines the widely used RCAN model to investigate how various training configurations impact SR performance. Surprisingly, or perhaps predictably, we demonstrate that RCAN can match or surpass nearly all CNN-based SR architectures released after its introduction on standard benchmarks, provided a suitable training strategy is employed alongside minimal architectural modifications. Furthermore, despite RCAN being a substantial architecture comprising over four hundred convolutional layers, our key finding is that underfitting remains the primary constraint on model capability rather than overfitting. We present supporting evidence indicating that extending training iterations significantly enhances performance, whereas applying regularization techniques typically degrades predictions. We refer to this streamlined version of RCAN as RCAN-it and advise practitioners to adopt it as a baseline for future studies. The code is accessible at https://github.com/zudi-lin/rcan-it.

This study utilizes statistical learning methods on an observational Quantified-Self (QS) dataset to construct a descriptive model of sleep quality. Data spanning 472 days, gathered via an Oura ring, was integrated with lifestyle, environmental, and psychological metrics. The paper tackles specific hurdles inherent in n-of-1 QS projects—such as data heterogeneity, missing entries, high dimensionality, dynamic feedback loops, and human bias—by implementing an end-to-end pipeline that yields robust descriptive models. Sleep quality was chosen as the target because of its high noise levels and numerous weakly influential factors, making it a rigorous test case for generalizing approaches to other n-of-1 QS endeavors. The research details techniques for feature engineering across diverse data classes, frequencies, and schemas, including event logs, weather, and geo-spatial information. Comprehensive statistical analyses are provided for outliers, normality, (auto)correlation, stationarity, and missing data, alongside a proposed hierarchical clustering method to identify correlated feature groups. To address missing data, the study employs a blend of knowledge-based and statistical strategies, including multiple multivariate imputation algorithms. Additionally, "Markov unfolding" is introduced to transform time series data into independent observations while retaining historical context. The resulting model was analyzed through internal $\beta$-parameters and the SHAP framework, which together identified the 16 most predictive features. This demonstrates that observational QS studies can significantly reduce the feature set required for designing subsequent interventional studies.

Our educational framework consists of sequential curricula, such as the progression in mathematics from addition to multiplication and eventually integration. Establishing a curriculum for either humans or machines shares the fundamental objective of optimizing knowledge transfer from initial to subsequent tasks while reducing the forgetting of earlier concepts. In this study, we comprehensively examined how curricula impact existing continual learning algorithms within a class-incremental setting, where models must acquire classes sequentially from a continuous data stream. Our findings reveal that across various class orderings, curricula significantly affect information retention, an effect driven by more than just stochasticity. As a key step toward automated curriculum design, we introduced a method that designs and ranks effective curricula based on inter-class feature similarities. Comparisons between these predicted curricula and empirically successful ones demonstrated substantial alignment. To aid curriculum designers, we performed human psychophysics experiments and established a new benchmark for continual learning in object recognition to evaluate the convergence of effective curricula between humans and machines. Surprisingly, our automated designer successfully identified an optimal set of curricula that also facilitates human learning. While curriculum design involves numerous factors, including timely feedback and multi-modal learning, this research represents the first effort to establish a standard framework for the community to address the challenge of enabling continuous learning for both humans and machines.

The feedback vertex set problem is among the most extensively researched parameterized problems, with various generalizations focusing on vertex deletions to produce graphs nearly acyclic. This paper presents a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm for removing at most $k$ vertices to form an $r$-pseudoforest, defined as a graph where at most $r$ edges can be removed from each component to yield a forest. While Philip et al. originally introduced this problem and provided an $O^*(c_{r}^{k})$ algorithm where the base $c_r$ grows double exponentially with $r$, our approach achieves a runtime of $O^*((10k)^{k})$, which remains independent of $r$.

Most network analysis algorithms are tailored for single-relational networks, where every edge shares the same type—such as exclusively representing friendship, kinship, or collaboration. Conversely, multi-relational networks utilize a heterogeneous set of edge labels within a single structure to capture diverse relationship types. Although this approach offers greater expressiveness, there is a pressing need for a general framework to adapt the abundance of single-relational algorithms for use in multi-relational contexts. Merely running a single-relational algorithm on a multi-relational network while disregarding edge labels is inadequate. This article introduces an algebraic method for mapping multi-relational networks into single-relational formats, thus enabling their analysis using established single-relational algorithms.

Conduits formed by the buoyancy-driven interaction of two miscible Stokes fluids with a significant viscosity difference display complex nonlinear wave behaviors, yet the fundamental dispersion characteristics of this medium remain poorly understood. This study employs a pump to introduce a time-periodic flow, thereby generating both small and large amplitude periodic traveling waves along the interface. By treating this setup as a wavemaker, the researchers measured the linear and nonlinear dispersion relations alongside the corresponding wave profiles. These experimental results align well with predictions from a fully nonlinear, long-wave model known as the conduit equation, as well as the analytically derived linear dispersion relation for two-Stokes flow. A critical frequency was identified, representing the threshold separating propagating waves from those that are non-propagating and spatially decaying. Quantitative agreement was found between the measured wave profiles and wavenumber-frequency dispersion relations and the solutions of the conduit equation. Notably, the experimentally observed critical frequency was higher than that predicted by the conduit equation; this discrepancy is attributed to the inclusion of a weak recirculating flow within the full two-Stokes model, a phenomenon confirmed during the experiment. When the boundary conditions matched the temporal profile of a nonlinear periodic traveling wave solution from the conduit equation, both weakly and strongly nonlinear cnoidal-type waves were observed, showing quantitative consistency with the conduit's nonlinear dispersion relation and wave profiles. Ultimately, this wavemaker configuration serves as a crucial foundation for future experimental studies of broader boundary value problems in nonlinear wave dynamics within viscous fluid conduits.

Large annotated datasets have been crucial for the success of deep learning, yet annotating medical images remains difficult due to the need for specialized expertise and significant funding. Specifically, labeling various cell types in histopathology faces high inter- and intra-rater variability caused by the inherent ambiguity of the task, a factor whose relationship with model performance has been largely overlooked. This study investigates the variability in cell annotations across 120 board-certified pathologists and its impact on deep learning model performance. We introduce a method to quantify this variability and demonstrate that filtering out annotators with low consistency reveals a trade-off between data volume and quality. Our findings indicate that simply expanding dataset size by accepting higher inter-rater variability does not guarantee improved cell detection models. Conversely, prioritizing lower inter-rater variability, even at the cost of a smaller dataset, leads to superior performance. Models trained on data with reduced inter-labeler variability consistently outperform those trained on data with higher variability, suggesting that careful annotator evaluation can address fundamental budget constraints in histopathology.

While stable relationships are well-documented, the temporal dynamics of transient relationships, which form a significant portion of communication networks, remain poorly understood. Existing research indicates that emotional intensity in these ties fades gradually until dissolution. However, analysis of mobile phone data from the US, UK, and Italy reveals that communication volume between individuals and their contacts remains remarkably stable for most of a transient relationship's lifespan. Contacts maintained for longer durations receive more calls, and the total relationship duration can be predicted based on call volume within the first few weeks of interaction. Typically, these relationships begin with an initial spike in communication frequency, stabilize into a steady state, and then end abruptly. This pattern holds true across all three nations, regardless of the life stages of the participants. These findings support the theory that people initially interact frequently with new contacts to assess their potential as lasting ties before settling into a contact frequency that aligns with the contact's value according to the "Seven Pillars of Friendship."

This paper examines countably infinite two-player stochastic games with reachability goals, offering a comprehensive analysis of the memory demands for $\varepsilon$-optimal and optimal strategies. These findings hinge on the dimensions of the players' action spaces and the necessity for strategies to be uniform (state-independent). The primary finding indicates that if the Minimizer possesses infinite action sets, infinite memory is required for Maximizer to achieve $\varepsilon$-optimality or optimality. This lower bound remains valid even under stringent constraints; notably, in infinitely branching turn-based reachability games, a step counter combined with finite private memory remains insufficient for the Maximizer, even when almost-sure winning strategies exist. Concerning uniformity, we demonstrate that positional, uniformly $\varepsilon$-optimal strategies for the Maximizer may not exist, regardless of whether action sets are finite or the game is finitely branching. Conversely, in games with finite action sets, a uniformly $\varepsilon$-optimal Maximizer strategy utilizing only a single bit of public memory is guaranteed to exist.

This study reports measurements of both inclusive and differential fiducial cross sections for the Higgs boson within the $\tau$ lepton decay channel. The differential cross sections are determined as functions of the Higgs boson's transverse momentum, jet multiplicity, and the transverse momentum of the leading jet, provided one exists. Utilizing proton-proton collision data acquired by the CMS detector at the LHC with a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV and an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$, this analysis presents the first-ever differential measurements of the Higgs boson cross section in the two $\tau$ lepton final state. Furthermore, in scenarios involving high jet multiplicity or a Lorentz-boosted Higgs boson, these results represent a substantial enhancement compared to measurements conducted in other final states.

This study examines the interplay between the solar wind helium-to-hydrogen abundance ratio ($A_\mathrm{He}$), solar wind velocity ($v_\mathrm{SW}$), and sunspot number (SSN) across solar cycles 23 and 24. Representing the first complete 22-year Hale cycle recorded by the Wind spacecraft, this dataset spans a full solar dynamo cycle with two polarity reversals. Although prior research has confirmed a robust correlation between $A_\mathrm{He}$ and SSN, we demonstrate that the phase delay between these two variables increases monotonically with $v_\mathrm{SW}$. When accounting for this velocity-dependent lag, $A_\mathrm{He}$ stabilizes to a consistent value for any given SSN, regardless of the solar wind speed or whether the cycle is rising or falling. We conclude that this lag arises from the mechanism responsible for reducing $A_\mathrm{He}$ in slow wind relative to fast wind during the solar wind formation process.

Achieving efficient nonlinearity compensation is essential for overcoming capacity limits in fiber-optic communication systems. While past research generally favored fewer steps in designing practical compensation schemes, this paper challenges that notion by demonstrating that carefully engineered multi-step approaches can yield superior performance-to-complexity ratios compared to their simpler counterparts. We focus on learned digital backpropagation (LDBP), a method that reinterprets the linear stages of the split-step algorithm as general linear functions akin to weight matrices in deep neural networks. Our primary contribution is an experimental validation of LDBP in a 25 Gbaud single-channel optical transmission system. We demonstrate the successful integration of LDBP into a coherent receiver's digital signal processing chain and its effective training despite various hardware impairments. Our findings indicate that LDBP, even with limited complexity, outperforms standard digital backpropagation by employing very short, jointly optimized finite-impulse response filters per step. Furthermore, this work reviews recent LDBP extensions and discusses promising directions for future research.

Local moments facilitate local regression by calculating statistical metrics like sums, averages, and standard deviations, as well as approximating probability distributions. This discussion addresses scenarios involving massive I/O arrays of size n where the goal is to compute the first N local moments (for a constant N). Without precomputation, this process demands O(n) time. We present a series of increasingly advanced algorithms that leverage precomputation and extra buffer memory to accelerate query responses. Simpler methods divide the I/O array into sequential segments known as bins; these are versatile enough to handle both local-moment and algebraic queries (such as MAX, AVERAGE, and SUM). Utilizing N buffers of size √n reduces the time complexity to O(√n). A more refined strategy employs hierarchical buffering, achieving logarithmic time complexity (O(b log_b n)) with N hierarchical buffers of size n/b. Furthermore, Overlapped Bin Buffering demonstrates that a single buffer suffices, similar to wavelet-based approaches, while requiring significantly less storage. These techniques find applications in multidimensional and statistical databases dealing with large datasets, interactive image processing, and visualization.

The advent of deep shotgun sequencing and the analysis of genomes, transcriptomes, amplified single-cell genomes, and metagenomes have facilitated the study of diverse organisms and ecosystems. Nevertheless, short-read datasets suffer from sampling variability, and modern sequencers exhibit high error rates, creating significant computational hurdles for data interpretation. These obstacles have spurred the creation of new mapping tools and *de novo* assemblers, which are continually tested by rising sequencing throughput. This paper introduces digital normalization, a single-pass computational algorithm that standardizes coverage in shotgun sequencing data. By reducing sampling variation, eliminating redundant information, and removing most errors, digital normalization significantly shrinks dataset sizes and lowers the memory and time demands for *de novo* assembly, all while maintaining the integrity of the resulting contigs. We demonstrate the application of digital normalization to microbial genomic data, amplified single-cell genomic data, and transcriptomic data. Our implementation is freely available for use and modification.

Introducing a longitudinal field into the quantum critical transverse-field Ising chain generates a quantum integrable model in the scaling limit, featuring massive excitations governed by the exceptional $E_{8}$ Lie algebra. Leveraging the analytical form factors of this quantum $E_{8}$ integrable system, we conduct a systematic investigation of the spin dynamic structure factor for the perturbed Ising chain, covering particle channels with total energies up to $5m_1$ (where $m_1$ denotes the mass of the lightest $E_{8}$ particle). Beyond substantial single-particle contributions to the dynamic spectrum, every two-particle channel comprising distinct masses reveals an edge singularity at the total mass threshold, decaying inversely with the square root of energy; this behavior stems from the singularity in the two-particle density of states at the threshold. However, this singularity vanishes for particles of equal mass due to a cancellation mechanism inherent in the form factor structure. Consequently, the dynamic structure factor manifests a series of bumping peaks within the continuum region, exhibiting distinct singular characteristics that offer robust guidance for the material implementation of the quantum $E_{8}$ model.

A 3-graph $\mathcal{F}$ is termed \emph{$U(s, 2s+1)$} if the union of any $s$ edges $e_1,...,e_s\in E(\mathcal{F})$ contains at most $2s+1$ vertices. In 2020, Frankl and Kupavskii conjectured that for any 3-graph $\mathcal{F}$ on $n$ vertices satisfying the $U(s, 2s+1)$ condition, the number of edges $e(\mathcal{F})$ is bounded by $\max\left\{{n-1\choose 2}, (n-s-1){s+1\choose 2}+{s+1\choose 3}, {2s+1\choose 3}\right\}$. This paper establishes the validity of Frankl and Kupavskii's conjecture.

We establish the Frenkel-Gaitsgory localization conjecture, which characterizes regular Kac-Moody representations at critical level through eigensheaves on the affine Grassmannian, by employing categorical Moy-Prasad theory. This builds upon earlier contributions by the same authors.

We construct solitary wave solutions within a $1+1$ dimensional massless scalar ($\phi$) field theory utilizing a specifically designed potential $V(\phi)$. The equation governing perturbations around these solitary waves features an effective potential composed of a simple harmonic well in a specific region and a constant value outside it. This structure enables us to guarantee the stability of the solitary wave via the presence of bound states within the well, which are identified using semi-analytical techniques. Stability is further verified by searching for quasi-normal modes (QNMs) under purely outgoing boundary conditions. We present and discuss in detail the time-domain profiles of the perturbations alongside the parametric evolution of the QNM values. As anticipated, our analysis of the quasi-normal modes reveals a damped oscillatory temporal behavior (ringdown) in the fluctuations.

Machine reading comprehension (MRC) serves as a valuable benchmark for assessing machine natural language understanding, particularly within the NLP community where numerous datasets across various languages have driven its popularity. Despite this, MRC research remains underexplored in specific domains, such as religious literature. The Qur'an QA 2022 shared task aims to address this deficiency by advancing state-of-the-art question answering and reading comprehension specifically for the Qur'an. This paper outlines the DTW team's participation in the task. Their methodology leverages transfer learning to utilize existing Arabic MRC data, with further performance enhancements achieved through diverse ensemble learning strategies. Ultimately, their approach yielded a partial Reciprocal Rank (pRR) score of 0.49 on the test set, demonstrating strong efficacy in the task.

This research examines top quark production at hadron colliders within the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) framework. We conduct a tree-level analysis that incorporates all relevant dimension-six operators across various orders of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and Electroweak (EW) couplings. Our findings reveal instances where formally subleading terms yield substantial contributions, offering potential sensitivity to a wide range of operators. We present both inclusive and differential predictions for the LHC and a prospective 100 TeV proton-proton circular collider. By estimating operator sensitivities and executing a simplified chi-square fit to constrain SMEFT Wilson coefficients, we evaluate the necessity of incorporating subleading terms and differential data for limiting new physics effects. Furthermore, we calculate SMEFT predictions involving the double insertion of dimension-six operators and investigate how specific higher-order terms in the EFT expansion may enhance sensitivity.

This tutorial offers a comprehensive introduction to Bayesian data assimilation, catering to practitioners who need to interpret algorithms and results, as well as researchers conducting theoretical studies on new schemes. It covers the rich historical context of geophysical data assimilation and its contemporary trends. To serve educational goals, the discussion centers on a simplified scenario involving a 'perfect' model. While some high-level mathematical derivations are presented to highlight core concepts regarding different estimators, the primary emphasis is on building intuition; readers seeking more rigorous and detailed treatments should consult the cited references. By examining various widely adopted assimilation schemes, the tutorial underscores that Bayesian analysis offers a unified framework for the estimation problem, enabling diverse solution formulations that address operational challenges within the geosciences.

Knowledge-based visual question answering (VQA) is a vision-language challenge where an agent must answer image-related queries using external knowledge not visible in the image. This task is more difficult than standard VQA and represents a crucial step toward developing a general VQA system. While most current knowledge-based VQA approaches treat image and knowledge data similarly, they overlook the fact that knowledge bases provide complete triplet information, whereas extracted image data may be incomplete due to missing or erroneous object relations. This paper introduces DMMGR, a novel model featuring dynamic knowledge memory-enhanced multi-step graph reasoning. It conducts explicit reasoning over a key-value knowledge memory module and implicit reasoning over a spatial-aware image graph. Specifically, the memory module learns dynamic knowledge representations and produces knowledge-aware question representations at each reasoning step, which subsequently guide a graph attention operator on the spatial-aware image graph. Our model achieves new state-of-the-art accuracy on the KRVQR and FVQA datasets, and ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component.

The recently identified fully charmed tetraquark candidate, $X(6900)$, has been examined using effective-range expansion, compositeness relations, width saturation, and coupled multichannel dynamical methods. Incorporating constraints from heavy-quark spin symmetry, we constructed coupled-channel amplitudes involving the $J/\psi J/\psi$, $\chi_{c0}\chi_{c0}$, and $\chi_{c1}\chi_{c1}$ states to match experimental di-$J/\psi$ event distributions near 6.9 GeV. Additionally, a second dynamical two-channel amplitude combining $J/\psi J/\psi$ and $\psi(3770) J/\psi$ was evaluated to describe the same data. All three theoretical frameworks yield consistent results, indicating that two-meson components are not dominant within the $X(6900)$. The resonance poles in the complex energy plane derived from our refined coupled-channel analysis align with existing experimental findings. Furthermore, the amplitudes reveal an additional pole representing a narrow, molecular-origin resonance, $X(6825)$, located below the $\chi_{c0}\chi_{c0}$ threshold. We also provide predictions for the line shapes of the $\chi_{c0}\chi_{c0}$ and $\chi_{c1}\chi_{c1}$ channels, offering valuable guidance for future experimental investigations.

Set disjointness with a disjointness promise is a highly utilized problem in communication complexity applications. It involves $k$ players holding subsets $S^1, \ldots, S^k$ from $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$, with the guarantee that either the sets are pairwise disjoint, or there exists a single element $j$ present in all sets while the rest remain disjoint. Solving this problem with constant probability in the blackboard model requires $\Omega(n/k)$ total communication. However, for many practical uses, a variant called the ``mostly'' set disjointness problem suffices: instead of requiring the unique element $j$ to be in all sets, it only needs to appear in at least half of them, with the remaining sets being pairwise disjoint. This modification yields a more straightforward proof of an $\Omega(n/k)$ randomized total communication lower bound, bypassing the need for Hellinger distance and Poincare inequalities. Leveraging this result, we establish several new findings in data streams:

*   **$\ell_2$-Heavy Hitters:** In the insertion-only model, any $O(1)$-pass streaming algorithm to detect the existence of an $\eps$-$\ell_2$-heavy hitter must use $\min(\frac{1}{\eps^2}\log \frac{\eps^2n}{\delta}, \frac{1}{\eps}n^{1/2})$ bits of memory, which is optimal up to a $\log n$ factor. For deterministic algorithms with constant $\eps$, this establishes an $\Omega(n^{1/2})$ lower bound, surpassing the previous $\Omega(\log n)$ limit. Additionally, we derive lower bounds for Zipfian distributions.
*   **$\ell_p$-Estimation ($p > 2$):** We demonstrate that in the insertion-only model, outputting an $O(1)$-approximation with probability $1-\delta$ requires $\Omega(n^{1-2/p} \log(1/\delta))$ bits using an $O(1)$-pass algorithm. This bound is optimal, improving upon the prior best lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1-2/p} + \log(1/\delta))$.

This study examines a confirmatory, two-stage adaptive method for evaluating average bioequivalence, offering insights into its theoretical underpinnings. The approach utilizes Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) to determine overall conclusions regarding the two conventional null hypotheses associated with average bioequivalence. These tests function as combination tests for each hypothesis individually, utilizing the respective pair of stagewise p-values. Key characteristics of this procedure include an integrated futility stopping rule, the capacity for sample size reassessment, and the capability to evaluate average bioequivalence across multiple endpoints simultaneously while maintaining control over the familywise error rate. To support final trial inference, we also derive overall confidence intervals that align with the decisions made for each one-sided hypothesis, accompanied by theoretical justification for their validity. The method's performance was evaluated through simulations within the context of designing a study to compare two administration methods for a biologic treatment of atopic dermatitis.

This study addresses the bandit problem involving the selection of $K$ arms from $N$ available options at each time step, where the reward may be a non-linear function of the selected arms' individual rewards. Directly applying standard multi-armed bandit algorithms is challenging due to the large action space of $\binom{N}{K}$ possible combinations. While existing combinatorial bandit research typically assumes linear feedback to simplify the problem, this paper establishes a lower bound for top-$K$ subset selection under bandit feedback with potentially correlated rewards. We introduce a new algorithm for this combinatorial setting that operates without individual arm feedback or the assumption of linearity, effectively handling correlated arm rewards. Named aDaptive Accept RejecT (DART), our method sequentially identifies high-performing arms and discards poor ones using confidence bounds. DART is computationally efficient, requiring storage linear in $N$, and achieves a regret bound of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(K\sqrt{KNT})$ over a time horizon $T$, matching the bandit feedback lower bound up to a $\sqrt{\log{2NT}}$ factor. When applied to cross-selling optimization and maximizing mean individual rewards, the algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, DART demonstrates significant superiority over existing approaches in both linear and non-linear joint reward scenarios.

**Background:** Ongoing debates persist concerning whether the ICSE Technical Research track admits an excessive volume of certain contribution types while underrepresenting others.  
**Questions:** Do the contributions accepted by ICSE align effectively with the priorities necessary to advance software engineering?  
**Method:** The study involved qualitative evaluation and extensive quotation-based reporting of 26 interviews conducted with senior members of the ICSE community.  
**Results:** Approximately 75% of respondents expressed general dissatisfaction with ICSE's alignment. Two recurring grievances specifically highlighted a) the inclusion of numerous low-relevance submissions and b) the scarcity of several high-relevance contribution types within the program.

The Spallation Neutron Source (SNS) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory serves as a pulsed neutron source, generating an intense flux of pulsed neutrinos through stopped-pion decay as a secondary effect. The COHERENT collaboration leverages this facility to study coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering and related phenomena using various detectors. This research details our Geant4 simulation of neutrino generation at the SNS and the resulting flux calculations that guide COHERENT experiments. Based on validation with existing low-energy pion production data, we estimate the uncertainty in these calculations to be approximately 10%.

This paper presents $\Delta$-MILP, an advanced variant of the mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) framework designed to address NASA's Deep Space Network (DSN) scheduling challenges. Building upon our prior MILP framework (DOI:10.1109/ACCESS.2021.3064928), this work retains its foundational formulations and strengths while introducing new constraints to enhance schedule feasibility. These additions include segmenting larger tracks into shorter intervals and eliminating track overlaps across different antennas. Furthermore, $\Delta$-MILP employs a heuristic to balance mission satisfaction, enabling the prioritization of specific missions during critical scenarios such as emergencies and landings. Numerical evaluations confirm that $\Delta$-MILP achieves 100% constraint satisfaction and generates equitable schedules for missions, outperforming state-of-the-art methods during the most oversubscribed weeks in 2016 and 2018.

Nickel and Kiela (2017) introduced a novel technique for embedding tree nodes within the Poincare ball, proposing that these hyperbolic embeddings significantly outperform Euclidean ones, particularly for large, hierarchically structured graphs such as the WordNet nouns hypernymy tree, especially when operating in low dimensions. In this study, we replicate their experiments regarding the embedding and reconstruction of the WordNet nouns hypernymy graph. Contrary to their findings, we demonstrate that Euclidean embeddings can represent this tree with equal or better efficacy than Poincare embeddings, provided they are allowed at least 50 dimensions. While this does not undermine the value of their work, which remains impressive in very low-dimensional contexts, our objective is to offer a revised and more precise comparison between Euclidean and hyperbolic embeddings, considering the substantial impact of their original research.

Unlike extractive methods, abstractive summarization synthesizes various segments of the source text, which can lead to the generation of fabricated facts. Our initial investigation indicates that nearly 30% of outputs from a leading neural summarization system are affected by this issue. While prior abstractive approaches have primarily targeted improvements in informativeness, we contend that faithfulness is equally critical for practical systems. To prevent the creation of false information, we utilize open information extraction and dependency parsing to derive factual descriptions directly from the source. We then introduce a dual-attention sequence-to-sequence framework that conditions generation on both the original text and these extracted facts. Experiments on the Gigaword dataset show that our model significantly reduces fake summaries by 80%. Furthermore, these fact descriptions notably enhance informativeness, as they often effectively condense the source text's meaning.

We examine the reliability of various methods for calculating jet and hadron spectra across different collision energies. This analysis is crucial for identifying energy loss during the upcoming oxygen-oxygen (OO) run at the LHC, where no dedicated proton-proton (pp) reference run is scheduled. To address this, we calculate the ratio of hadron and jet spectra between different pp energies using perturbative QCD to establish a reference, or alternatively, interpolate from measured data at nearby energies. We assess the precision of both approaches for the spectra ratio pertinent to the OO run, finding that central values align with 4% accuracy for hadrons and 2% accuracy for jets. Finally, we recommend measuring the ratio of OO to pp spectra at varying collision energies, a strategy that distinctly separates experimental measurements from theoretical calculations.

This article investigates shape fitting, $\epsilon$-coresets, and total sensitivity, with a specific focus on $(j,k)$-projective clustering tasks such as $k$-median/$k$-means, $k$-line clustering, $j$-subspace approximation, and the integer variant of $(j,k)$-projective clustering. By deriving upper bounds for total sensitivity, we construct corresponding $\epsilon$-coresets. Employing a dimension-reduction approach, we significantly streamline previous findings regarding total sensitivity for $k$-median/$k$-means clustering and generate positively-weighted $\epsilon$-coresets for multiple $(j,k)$-projective clustering variants. Additionally, we generalize prior results on $\epsilon$-coresets for the integer $(j,k)$-projective clustering problem from fixed to high dimensions.

In 2009, Keller and Yang provided a categorification of quiver mutation by characterizing it through equivalences of derived categories. This methodology relied on Ginzburg's Calabi-Yau algebras and the mutation of quivers with potential developed by Derksen, Weyman, and Zelevinsky. Recently, Matthew Pressland extended the mutation framework from quivers with potential to ice quivers with potential. This paper demonstrates that Pressland's rule induces derived equivalences between the corresponding relative Ginzburg algebras. These algebras represent specific instances of Yeung's deformed relative Calabi-Yau completions, which emerge within the theory of relative Calabi-Yau structures pioneered by Toën and Brav-Dyckerhoff. We present examples drawn from the research of Baur, King, and Marsh concerning dimer models and the cluster categories of Grassmannians. Furthermore, we offer a categorification of mutation at frozen vertices, as observed in recent studies by Fraser, Sherman, and Bennett on positroid cluster structures.

This paper introduces a novel method for calculating generalisation performance, predicated on the known distribution of risks, $\rho(r)$, within a learning scenario. Using this, the expected error of a machine employing empirical risk minimisation is derived for both classification and regression tasks. A pivotal factor in assessing generalisation is the power-law behaviour of $\rho(r)$ near its minimum, termed "attunement." The study computes $\rho(r)$ for all Boolean functions and for the perceptron across two distinct settings. The analysis begins with a simplified model assuming loss independence, followed by a more precise evaluation that incorporates chance correlations in the training data, resulting in adjustments to the typical observed behaviour.

It is generally accepted that left-hand circularly polarized microwaves fail to efficiently generate spin waves (SWs) in ferromagnets because of angular momentum conservation constraints. However, this study demonstrates that left-hand microwaves can indeed drive nonreciprocal SWs when there is a significant ellipticity mismatch between the microwave field and the precessing magnetization. We predict a critical frequency above which left-hand microwaves cannot excite SWs; away from this threshold, the SW amplitude shows a strong sensitivity to the ellipticity of the left-hand microwaves, a behavior sharply contrasting with that driven by right-hand microwaves. By adjusting the microwave frequency, we achieve switchable non-reciprocity in a single-layer ferromagnet. To explain these results, we propose a mode-dependent mutual demagnetizing factor. This research enhances our comprehension of photon-magnon conversion and facilitates the development of diode-like components in nano-scaled magnonics.

Managing data and digital assets presents several challenges, particularly the necessity to comply with legal standards regarding personal data protection and copyright. Software platform providers can leverage usage control technologies to responsibly manage these assets and grant owners greater oversight. To better evaluate the potential of different usage control proposals, we categorize the relevant requirements, compare major frameworks against these criteria, and pinpoint current challenges and opportunities to inform future research directions.

This study characterizes stationary fronts and dark solitons arising from counterpropagating waves in micro-ring and fiber resonators featuring two input fields, normal dispersion, and nonlocal coupling. Unlike systems with local coupling, the existence and stability of these features rely on a precise balance of the areas offset from homogeneous solutions. When scanning one cavity detuning, stable solutions emerge as plateaus separated by two fronts in one counter-propagating field, while the other remains homogeneous. These two-front plateau solutions correspond one-to-one with solutions of the Lugiato-Lefever equation at the unique Maxwell point. By defining effective detunings for fixed input powers where fronts appear, we derive expressions for both the Maxwell point and the distance between stable fronts as functions of detunings and input powers for both fields, showing strong agreement with numerical simulations. For specific detuning values, we identify multi-stable states comprising plateaus with fronts, oscillating homogeneous states, and non-oscillating homogeneous states of the counter-propagating fields. Furthermore, the robustness and parameter ranges of these unusual dynamical states, which coexist with stable non-homogeneous front solutions, are detailed.

Self-supervised techniques have become a highly promising approach for representation learning recently, primarily because they reduce reliance on labeled datasets, which are both scarce and costly to obtain. In the audio domain, contrastive methods are widely used for self-supervision; these typically generate a learning signal by ensuring model invariance to input transformations. However, such methods often necessitate mechanisms like negative sampling or specific regularization to avoid collapsing into trivial solutions. This work proposes an alternative approach that leverages equivariance rather than invariance as a self-supervision signal to learn audio tempo representations from unlabeled data. We introduce a straightforward loss function that prevents network collapse during training without the need for regularization or negative sampling. Experimental results demonstrate that meaningful representations for tempo estimation can be learned solely through equivariant self-supervision, achieving performance on par with supervised methods across multiple benchmarks. Additionally, our method requires only moderate computational resources, making it accessible to a broad research community.

The stabilizer formalism has undeniably been the most effective framework for generating quantum error-correcting codes with robust error-correction capabilities. This paper examines strong automorphism groups within stabilizer codes, first introducing the corresponding concept from classical coding theory. We also explore two relaxed definitions: the weak automorphism group and the Clifford-twisted automorphism group, supported by numerous examples that illustrate the interconnections among these group types. Specifically, we present a $[[10,0,4]]$ stabilizer code to demonstrate a potential link between Clifford-twisted automorphism groups and the Mathieu groups. Furthermore, we establish nonexistence theorems for stabilizer codes possessing highly transitive strong or weak automorphism groups, which hints at an inverse correlation between a code's error-correcting strength and the transitivity of its automorphism groups.

This work derives a Maximum Likelihood recursive state estimator designed for non-linear and non-Gaussian state-space models. By integrating a particle filter to approximate conditional densities with the Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm for iterative maximum likelihood estimation, the approach facilitates algorithms for filtering, prediction, and smoothing. The convergence properties of these methods, inherited from EM, are theoretically proven and validated through two examples. It is demonstrated that, utilizing randomized reinitialization—a capability enabled by the algorithm's simplicity—the methods successfully converge to the Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE) for multimodal, truncated, skewed, and disjoint-support densities.

This paper demonstrates that the sequential products introduced by Liu and Shen and Wu in [J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. {\bf 42}, 185206 (2009), J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. {\bf 42}, 345203 (2009)] are merely unitarily equivalent to the sequential product defined as $A\circ B=A^{\frac{1}{2}}BA^{\frac{1}{2}}$.

Machine learning models are now ubiquitous across various industries, executing diverse tasks. However, as the volume of deployed models grows, monitoring them to ensure appropriate behavior becomes increasingly challenging. Furthermore, emerging regulations for high-risk ML systems that impact human lives mandate a verifiable link between models and their training data. Existing monitoring solutions often function as add-ons to ML libraries, offering provenance and experiment tracking that can suffer from inconsistencies and skew between tracked objects and their metadata. This paper presents Tribuo, a Java-based ML library that unifies model training, inference, strong type-safety, runtime validation, and automatic provenance recording within a cohesive framework. Tribuo automatically captures the complete data processing pipeline, including training algorithms, hyperparameters, and data transformation steps, for all models and evaluations. This provenance is embedded within the model object and can be persisted independently using standard markup formats. The library supports numerous popular algorithms for classification, regression, clustering, multi-label classification, and anomaly detection, while also providing interfaces for XGBoost, TensorFlow, and ONNX Runtime. The source code is hosted at https://github.com/oracle/tribuo under the Apache 2.0 license, with additional documentation and tutorials available at https://tribuo.org.

The minimum-cost $k$-edge-connected spanning subgraph ($k$-ECSS) problem extends and intensifies the extensively researched minimum-cost spanning tree (MST) problem. Although the distributed round complexity for MST is well-established, the $k$-ECSS problem remains largely unresolved, particularly when $k \geq 3$. This paper introduces the first distributed algorithm capable of computing a sublinear-time approximation for $k$-ECSS across general values of $k$. Specifically, we propose a randomized distributed algorithm that, within $\tilde{O}(k(D+k\sqrt{n}))$ rounds, generates a $k$-edge-connected spanning subgraph with a cost no more than an $O(\log n\log k)$ factor above the optimal. In these expressions, $n$ represents the vertex count and $D$ the graph's diameter. For any $k$ that is a polynomial in $\log n$, this runtime is nearly optimal, closely approaching the $\tilde{\Omega}(D+\sqrt{n/k})$ lower bound. Notably, our method achieves sublinear round complexity for $k \geq 3$, a scenario significantly more difficult than the well-understood cases of $k=1$ (MST) and $k=2$. Our approach reduces the $k$-ECSS problem to $k$ set cover instances, progressively enhancing the connectivity of the subgraph. To address each set cover instance, we integrate new insights into minimum cut structures with graph sketching techniques. A pivotal component of our algorithm is a new structural lemma that enables the decentralized compression of information regarding all minimum cuts into a concise representation. We anticipate that this succinct representation could prove useful in other computational contexts or for solving different problems.

This paper presents a neural texture learning framework for 6D object pose estimation, utilizing synthetic data alongside a limited set of unlabelled real images. Our primary contribution is an innovative learning scheme that overcomes the limitations of prior approaches, specifically the heavy reliance on co-modalities or additional refinement steps previously required to generate training signals for convergence. We decompose this scheme into two distinct sub-optimization tasks: learning realistic object textures from real image collections and estimating pose from pixel-perfect synthetic data. By merging these capabilities, we can synthesize photorealistic novel views to supervise the pose estimator with precise geometric information. To mitigate pose noise and segmentation errors inherent during the texture learning phase, we introduce a surfel-based adversarial training loss combined with texture regularization derived from synthetic data. Our results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms recent state-of-the-art methods lacking ground-truth pose annotations and shows marked improvements in generalization to unseen scenes. Notably, our scheme substantially enhances the performance of adopted pose estimators, even when they are initialized with considerably inferior results.

This study presents an image-based approach to predicting the effective heat conductivity of highly heterogeneous microstructured materials. The synthetic materials examined exhibit variations in inclusion morphology, orientation, volume fraction, and topology. Effective property prediction relies solely on image data, with a primary focus on the two-point spatial correlation function. The methodology employs both unsupervised and supervised machine learning techniques. Initially, snapshot proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) analyzes extensive sets of random microstructures, compressing their significant characteristics into a low-dimensional feature vector. To handle the associated data volume and computational demands, three distinct incremental snapshot POD methods are introduced. Subsequently, feed-forward neural networks utilize the derived feature vectors to forecast the effective material properties. Numerical examples demonstrate the incremental basis identification process and the prediction accuracy of the proposed approach. A Python implementation of the surrogate model is provided free of charge.

This dissertation investigates the behavior of quantum annealing (QA) and its applications within an open system framework. We provide both analytical derivations and numerical strategies for effective parallel simulation techniques tailored to the time-dependent open dynamics of QA devices. Our analysis covers the weak-coupling regime with respect to an environment, as well as scenarios involving $1/f$ noise. Furthermore, the stochastic time-dependent quantum trajectories method is applied to examine weak measurements and feedback error correction in QA. We then concentrate on open system descriptions of reverse annealing (RA), a promising QA variant, demonstrating that RA can leverage interactions between the annealer and its environment to gain advantages through various simulation tools.

Causal inference techniques are extensively utilized across economics, policy, and medicine, primarily to estimate treatment effects for decision-making. Existing approaches typically rely on binary yes-or-no decisions regarding a single outcome dimension, failing to account for treatment policies with varying intensities or the complexity of matching specific treatments to subjects. We introduce a parametrizable model that defines treatment effectiveness, expanding the scope to include continuous policy treatment functions and matching likelihoods across multiple intensities and complexities. By decomposing treatment effect functions into distinct effectiveness factors, we establish a framework for modeling a rich spectrum of actions using causal inference. Leveraging deep learning, we optimize a holistic metric space rather than predicting single-dimensional counterfactuals, utilizing a population-wide effectiveness measure to significantly enhance overall model performance. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithms; when employing generic continuous space treatments and a matching architecture, we achieve a 41% improvement over prior art in cost-effectiveness and a 68% improvement over similar methods in average treatment effect. These algorithms capture nuanced variations within the treatment space, streamline optimization techniques, and enable a wide array of applications.

This work presents an initial exploration of the dynamical behavior of Schröder's method, a well-established iterative technique for solving nonlinear equations, specifically within the complex plane. Utilizing topological conjugations, we characterize the basins of attraction for Schröder's method when applied to polynomials featuring two roots with varying multiplicities. We demonstrate that these basins take the form of half-planes or circles, contingent upon the root multiplicities. The study concludes with a graphical comparison of the basins of attraction between Schröder's method and Newton's method applied to specific polynomials.

Key: Schröder's method; basin of attraction; nonlinear equation.

We present a new family of postquantum Br\`{e}gman relative entropies constructed through nonlinear embeddings into reflexive Banach spaces, utilizing specific instances such as reflexive noncommutative Orlicz spaces over semi-finite W*-algebras, nonassociative L$_p$ spaces over semi-finite JBW-algebras, and noncommutative L$_p$ spaces over general W*-algebras. This framework enables the formulation of geometric categories for nonlinear postquantum inference theory, extending Chencov's foundational approach to statistical inference, where objects are represented as nonlinear images of closed convex sets and morphisms correspond to constrained maximizations of Br\`{e}gman relative entropies. We further expand this into a broader framework for nonlinear convex operational theories by incorporating a wider set of morphisms defined by Br\`{e}gman nonexpansive operations, which constitute a robust family of Mielnik's nonlinear transmitters. Finally, we apply this structure to derive various nonlinear postquantum resource theories characterized by this specific class of operations.

The random phase approximation (RPA) frequently provides highly accurate correlation energy estimates for condensed matter systems; nevertheless, efforts to enhance its precision continue, prompting an investigation into the significance of single excitations within prototypical solid-state materials. This study begins by deriving the RPA through the adiabatic connection formalism and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, distinguishing itself from standard approaches by permitting the density to vary during the coupling constant integration, a method that aligns closely with conventional perturbation theory. We re-derive the standard single excitations of G\"orling-Levy perturbation theory, underscore the similarity between our formulation and the renormalized singles proposed by Ren and colleagues, and propose a novel approximation for singles utilizing the density matrix within the RPA framework. Furthermore, we examine the physical significance of these single excitations alongside illustrative cases of weakly bonded systems—such as rare gas solids (Ne, Ar, Xe), ice, water adsorption on NaCl, and solid benzene—as well as their impact on covalently and metallically bonded materials.

We provide an explicit description of the second cohomology of a regular semisimple Hessenberg variety using generators and relations derived from GKM theory. Under Tymoczko's dot action, this cohomology forms a module over the symmetric group $\mathfrak{S}_n$. Leveraging our explicit formulation, we derive a formula for the isomorphism class of the second cohomology as an $\mathfrak{S}_n$-module. Although this formula differs in appearance from those established by Chow or Cho-Hong-Lee, it is mathematically equivalent to them. Additionally, we explore generalizations of this result to higher degrees.

We investigate the momentum dependence of static magnetic susceptibility $\chi(q)$ in the paramagnetic phase of Heisenberg magnets and its connection to critical behavior within the nonlinear sigma model (NLSM) for arbitrary dimensions $2<d<4$. Employing the first-order $1/N$ expansion, where $N$ denotes the number of spin components, we derive $\chi(q)\propto[q^{2}+\xi^{-2}(1+f(q\xi ))]^{-1+\eta /2}$. In this expression, $\xi$ represents the correlation length, $q$ is the momentum relative to the magnetic wave vector, and the universal scaling function $f(x)$ characterizes the deviation from standard Landau-Ginzburg momentum dependence. Consistent with prior studies for large $x$, we find $f(x\gg 1)\simeq (2B_{4}/N)x^{4-d}$, noting that the absolute value of the coefficient $B_4$ grows with $d$ when $d>5/2$. Utilizing the NLSM, we calculate the contribution of the "anomalous" term $\xi^{-2}f(q\xi )$ to the critical exponent $
u$ and compare it with the contribution arising from the non-analytical dependence linked to the critical exponent $\eta$; the resulting values for $
u$ and $\eta$ align with previous research. For the range $3\leq d<4$, we determine that the former contribution is dominant, fully dictating the $1/N$ correction to the critical exponent $
u$ as $d$ approaches 4.

Machine learning techniques were utilized to re-analyze data from multiple passive seismic experiments conducted in Finland. We constructed datasets representing various stages of the receiver function method and applied a fundamental machine learning algorithm, specifically the $k$-nearest neighbors algorithm, to process them uniformly. This approach yielded two primary findings: a Moho depth map for the region and the identification of a near-surface layer with low $S$-wave velocity across three distinct areas in the northern, southern, and central parts of the study region. While the low $S$-wave velocities in the northern and southern zones correspond to existing geological structures, the anomaly in the central area is attributed to extensive water-saturated cracks within the upper 1–5 km. Structural analysis of this central zone indicates that the resulting macrofracturing was likely caused by the effects of the last deglaciation.

We examine the almost sure convergence of the stochastic differential equation $dX_t=\alpha_t d t + \beta_t d W_t$ given a $C^2$-Lyapunov function $F:\mathbb R^d \to \mathbb R$. Specifically, we demonstrate that provided the process remains local, $(F(X_t))$ converges almost surely along with $\nabla F(X_t)\to 0$ when $|\beta_t|=\mathcal O( t^{-\beta})$ for some $\beta>1/2$. Furthermore, if $F$ satisfies the Lojasiewicz condition, the process itself converges almost surely under the condition $|\beta_t|=\mathcal O(t^{-\beta})$ with $\beta>1$. These conditions are proven to be optimal, as evidenced by a divergent counterexample where $|\beta_t|$ scales as $t^{-1}$.

Global warming is expected to significantly affect ocean ecosystems, making fish behavior a crucial indicator of these environmental shifts. Consequently, automatically recognizing key fish behaviors in video footage is an essential tool for marine researchers studying climate change impacts. We introduce a dataset featuring startle responses from sablefish (*Anoplopoma fimbria*) captured in underwater videos and explore deep learning (DL) approaches for detecting these behaviors. Our proposed system utilizes DL frameworks to detect fish instances, generates trajectory tracks, extracts novel behavior-specific features, and applies Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to identify startle events in sablefish. We evaluate the system's performance by benchmarking it against a state-of-the-art DL-based video event detector.

This study derives several possibilistic versions of the laws of large numbers, which differ from previous findings yet represent natural extensions of their probabilistic counterparts. These results rely on the possibility measure alongside "maxitive" definitions for both possibility expectation and variance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that within this framework, the weak law of large numbers entails the strong law.

We update the predicted future evolution of a specific class of scalar-tensor theories called kinetic gravity braiding models. While it is established that these theories can drive the universe toward a future de Sitter state if their Lagrangian remains invariant under constant scalar field shifts, this is not their sole possible outcome, as demonstrated in this letter. We show that these shift-symmetric models can also lead to future cosmic singularities marked by diverging energy density. Furthermore, we provide a concrete example illustrating a scenario where a big rip singularity represents the exclusive future fate of the cosmos.

We present a new semi-supervised video segmentation method built upon an efficient video representation termed "super-trajectory." Each super-trajectory aggregates multiple compact trajectories that share consistent motion, similar visual characteristics, and close spatiotemporal proximity. Trajectories are generated via a probabilistic model that robustly and naturally manages occlusions and drifts. To ensure reliable trajectory grouping, we employ a modified density peaks clustering algorithm capable of capturing rich spatiotemporal relationships during the clustering phase. This proposed video representation is sufficiently discriminative to accurately transfer initial annotations from the first frame to subsequent frames. Comprehensive experiments on demanding benchmarks show that our approach effectively distinguishes target objects from complex backgrounds and successfully reidentifies them even after prolonged occlusions.

We extend the concept of stochastic resonance to the nonadiabatic regime by modeling a double-well potential as a combination of two quadratic potentials. By employing a singular perturbation technique, we derive an approximate analytical solution for the probability density function, which smoothly bridges local solutions within boundary layers near the two minima and those in the region between them. Numerical simulations validate the accuracy of this analytical approach. Unrestricted by the adiabatic limit, this method enables the prediction of escape rates between stable basins for systems subjected to more intricate periodic forcing.

This paper constructs a family of holomorphic functions, $\beta_\lambda(s)$, that solve the asymptotic tetration equation. Every function in this family, $\beta_\lambda$, adheres to the functional equation $\beta_\lambda(s+1) = \frac{e^{\beta_\lambda(s)}}{e^{-\lambda s} + 1}$, which asymptotically approaches $\log \beta_\lambda(s+1) = \beta_\lambda (s) + \mathcal{O}(e^{-\lambda s})$ as $\Re(\lambda s) \to \infty$. This collection of asymptotic solutions serves as the foundation for building a holomorphic function $\text{tet}_\beta(s)$ defined on $\mathbb{C}/(-\infty,-2]$ that maps to $\mathbb{C}$. This resulting function satisfies $\text{tet}_\beta(s+1) = e^{\text{tet}_\beta(s)}$ and establishes a bijection from the interval $(-2,\infty)$ to $\mathbb{R}$.

Distributed machine learning (DML) across time-varying networks holds promise for emerging decentralized applications like autonomous driving and drone fleets. However, standard DML systems relying on weighted arithmetic mean aggregation often suffer from high model loss, reduced accuracy, and sluggish convergence in dynamic network environments. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces a novel non-linear class of aggregation functions designed for efficient DML over time-varying networks. Departing from the linear aggregation of neighbor models typical in existing research, our approach employs a weighted power-mean (WPM) function to combine local models. Optimization is subsequently performed using mirror descent, defined via Bregman divergence, ensuring convergence to optimality. We rigorously analyze the properties of the WPM and provide formal proofs of our aggregation mechanism's convergence.
