Additionally, the locally monochromatic and locally constant field approximations are formulated and validated against comprehensive quantum electrodynamic calculations.

Open World Object Detection (OWOD) represents a demanding new computer vision task that connects traditional object detection benchmarks with real-world scenarios. Unlike standard detection, OWOD requires algorithms to identify and classify both known objects and novel, unknown ones, with the latter capable of incremental learning. In conventional object detection, proposals not overlapping with labeled objects are automatically treated as background; consequently, direct application of these methods to OWOD fails because unknown objects are misclassified as background. The core difficulty lies in the lack of supervision needed to distinguish between unknown objects and background proposals. While previous OWOD approaches have tried to address this through pseudo-labeling, performance on unknown object detection remains suboptimal. This work proposes a solution using probabilistic and generative models. We introduce a novel probabilistic framework for objectness estimation that alternates between estimating probability distributions and maximizing the objectness likelihood of known objects within an embedded feature space, thereby enabling the estimation of objectness probabilities for various proposals. The resulting PROB system, a transformer-based open-world detector, integrates this framework into traditional detection models to adapt them for open-world conditions. Extensive experiments on OWOD benchmarks demonstrate that PROB surpasses all current methods, achieving approximately double the unknown object recall and a 10% improvement in mean Average Precision (mAP) for known objects. The source code will be released upon publication at https://github.com/orrzohar/PROB.

We examine long-term average or "ergodic" optimal control problems featuring a specific structure where control acts in all directions, and the associated costs are proportional to the squared norm of the control field relative to the metric defined by the noise. The long-term stochastic dynamics on the manifold are fully described by the steady-state density $\rho$ and the steady-state current density $J$. Consequently, these control problems can be recast as variational problems defined over $\rho$ and $J$. We analyze several optimization scenarios: one where both $\rho$ and $J$ are unconstrained, one where $\rho$ is held fixed, and one where $J$ is fixed. These scenarios result in distinct operator problems: linear partial differential equations (PDEs) for the first two cases and a nonlinear PDE for the third. These findings are derived via a variational principle employing infinite-dimensional Lagrange multipliers. Furthermore, if the initial dynamics are reversible, we demonstrate that the optimally controlled diffusion is also symmetrizable. Specifically, when the optimally controlled process is constrained to be reversible, it yields a linear eigenvalue problem for the square root of the density process.

This letter investigates point-to-point wireless communication between a transmitter (Tx) and a receiver (Rx), enhanced jointly by an active intelligent reflecting surface (AIRS) and a passive IRS (PIRS). We analyze two practical deployment configurations: Tx$\rightarrow$PIRS$\rightarrow$AIRS$\rightarrow$Rx (TPAR) and Tx$\rightarrow$AIRS$\rightarrow$PIRS$\rightarrow$Rx (TAPR). Under line-of-sight channel assumptions, we derive achievable rates by optimizing AIRS placement while keeping the PIRS location fixed. Our findings indicate that when PIRS element counts or AIRS amplification power are limited, the AIRS should be positioned closer to the Rx in both schemes; under these optimized conditions, TAPR outperforms TPAR. Simulation results confirm our analysis, demonstrating significant performance improvements from jointly optimizing AIRS/PIRS deployment compared to a baseline double-PIRS system, given identical power and IRS element constraints.

Sediment transport across an erodible bed is investigated using particle-resolved simulations employing a hybrid parallel strategy. To address load imbalance issues inherent in traditional domain decomposition methods when dealing with highly uneven particle distributions, the parallel framework originally designed for point particle simulations by Darmana et al. (2006) has been adapted and integrated into particle-resolved approaches. A new memory optimization technique is introduced to minimize the memory footprint of this hybrid method when handling spherical particles of uniform size. The proposed hybrid parallel scheme demonstrates excellent scalability and high parallel efficiency, even in demanding scenarios involving over a million spherical particles. The code's accuracy is verified through multiple benchmark cases, yielding results that align well with existing experimental and computational data. Additionally, simulations of turbulent flow over an erodible sediment bed are conducted. A novel extraction method is developed to differentiate between saltating and rolling particles, capturing impact and rebound details from particle-bed interactions. Probability distribution functions (PDFs) for key saltation parameters—including velocity, angle, and spanwise angular velocity of impact and rebound events—are analyzed. Furthermore, splash functions characterizing particle-mobile bed interactions in turbulent flow are established; these are rarely examined in experiments and offer significant value for modeling complex particle-bed dynamics within such flows.

Stance detection involves determining an author's attitude toward a specific target, a task that becomes difficult when the model lacks contextual knowledge about that target. This study demonstrates how integrating Wikipedia background knowledge can improve stance detection performance. We present WS-BERT, a model designed to incorporate this knowledge directly into stance encoding. Extensive evaluations across three benchmark datasets—covering social media discussions and online debates—show that our approach significantly surpasses state-of-the-art methods in target-specific, cross-target, and zero/few-shot stance detection scenarios.

This paper investigates recent advancements in dynamic view synthesis (DVS) from monocular video. While current methods yield impressive results, we identify a gap between real-world capture procedures and standard experimental protocols, revealing that existing setups inadvertently leak multi-view signals during training. To quantify the extent of multi-view information in input sequences based on relative camera-scene motion, we introduce Effective Multi-View Factors (EMFs). Furthermore, we propose two new evaluation metrics—co-visibility masked image metrics and correspondence accuracy—that resolve limitations in current protocols. We also present a novel iPhone dataset featuring a wider variety of real-life deformation sequences. Under our proposed protocol, state-of-the-art methods exhibit a 1-2 dB reduction in masked PSNR without multi-view cues and a 4-5 dB drop when handling complex motion. The code and dataset are available at https://hangg7.com/dycheck.

Contemporary unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly equipped with sophisticated capabilities to execute machine learning applications, which involve computationally demanding tasks like matrix multiplications. Given these computational limitations, UAVs often offload tasks to edge servers. To address straggler issues, coded distributed computing (CDC) can be employed for offloading. This paper introduces an Optimal Task Allocation Scheme (OTAS) utilizing Stochastic Integer Programming, aimed at minimizing energy consumption during the offloading process. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that, despite uncertainties in task completion, the proposed method effectively reduces energy usage within the UAV network.

The Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) represents the most ambitious radio telescope project conceived to date, offering the potential for groundbreaking research into the Sun, corona, and heliosphere while addressing numerous unresolved questions within these fields. Its capacity to explore vast, previously inaccessible regions of phase space also suggests significant discovery potential. The Indian community focused on solar and heliospheric physics has been actively preparing to capitalize on this scientific opportunity, with a major component of their efforts dedicated to securing a leading role in developing science with SKAO precursor instruments. This article provides a brief overview of the current progress across various aspects of this initiative and outlines our future objectives.

A partial affirmative response to Baker's inquiry regarding the boundedness of Fatou components for transcendental entire functions is provided. Furthermore, we have tackled Wang's question concerning Fejér gaps and extended certain findings related to functions possessing Fabry gaps and exhibiting infinite order.

Time-resolved investigations into electron dynamics, particularly those requiring high statistics or signal-to-noise ratios like coincidence spectroscopy and studies of large molecules in chemistry and biology, rely heavily on high-repetition-rate attosecond pulse sources. While pump-probe configurations using such lasers are feasible, only a limited number of these systems have been successfully demonstrated. This study reports the generation of a 100-kHz attosecond pulse train (APT) by shaping the driving laser into an annular beam, achieving the highest on-target energy to date (51 pJ/shot, originating from 269 pJ at generation) among temporally characterized high-repetition-rate systems (>10 kHz). By minimizing losses from harmonic filtering and reflections, an unprecedented 19% transmission rate from the generation point to the target was attained. Furthermore, the probe beam was also shaped into an annular profile, utilizing a specialized holey mirror to combine with the APT and minimize transmission losses. Both experimental and theoretical analyses confirm the benefits of employing annular beams for generating attosecond pulses with high-average-power lasers, alongside a detailed examination of how nonlinear propagation within the generation medium influences this approach.

This paper introduces a novel approach for estimating and characterizing spatial variations across dies or wafers. Leveraging recent advancements in matrix completion, this technique allows for accurate estimation of spatial variation using a minimal set of randomly selected sampling points. Furthermore, the method is highly adaptable, capable of extending to mixed spatial data alongside structure or device type information.

We present a straightforward, adaptable, and affordable system designed to automate the majority of existing kinematic mounts. This solution integrates 3D-printed parts, an Arduino board, stepper motors, and basic electronics. The developed system can independently and simultaneously manage up to ten stepper motors via serial port commands, making it ideal for applications requiring periodic optical realignment with flat mirrors.

This paper investigates the design principles and performance limits of rateless codes operating over fading channels. By employing the diversity-multiplexing tradeoff (DMT) framework to evaluate system performance across all feasible transmission rates, the analysis demonstrates that these rateless codes should adhere to the design principles of approximately universal codes for parallel MIMO channels, where each sub-channel functions as a distinct MIMO link. Specifically, for single-input single-output (SISO) channels, it is shown that existing permutation codes of unit length designed for parallel channels with rate LR can be directly converted into rateless codes of length L supporting multiple rate levels (R, 2R, ..., LR), thereby achieving the theoretical DMT performance limit.

Multi-component T2-mapping via gradient and spin-echo (GraSE) acquisition has become the standard approach for myelin water imaging at 3T. While higher magnetic field strengths offer potential signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvements, they present challenges related to specific absorption rate limits and shortened T2 times. This study explores in vivo compartmental T2 times and examines both the benefits and obstacles of multi-component T2-mapping at 7T. We collected 3D multi-echo GraSE data from seven healthy adults at 7T, with three participants also scanned at 3T. To address stimulated echoes caused by B1+ inhomogeneities, we employed the extended phase graph (EPG) algorithm. Using the calculated T2 distributions, we identified distinct water pools and evaluated the signal and fit-to-noise characteristics of the estimations. We compared short T2 fractions and intermediate water pool properties between 3T and 7T. Flip angle mapping validated that the EPG method accurately characterized the larger inhomogeneity present at 7T. Multi-component T2 analysis revealed shorter T2 times at 7T compared to 3T. Although fit-to-noise and SNR ratios were improved at 7T, these metrics relied on B1 homogeneity. By lowering the minimum T2 threshold to 8 ms and adjusting the separation threshold for water compartments to 20 ms, the short T2 fractions at 7T aligned with 3T data. Short T2 fractions in myelin-dense white matter were reduced at 7T relative to 3T but increased in iron-rich regions. Due to the accelerated T2 relaxation at 7T, adjusting compartment boundaries was necessary. While reducing echo spacing would better capture fast-decaying signals, it would exacerbate peripheral nerve stimulation. This study utilized a multi-echo 3D-GraSE sequence to characterize multi-exponential T2 decay at 7T and adapted T2 parameters to assess the short T2 fraction. Ultimately, the 7T multi-component T2-maps showed strong agreement with 3T data.

During active epidemics, particularly those involving novel pathogens, available data is often fragmented and sparse, further complicated by external variables such as climatic conditions and the readiness of healthcare systems. Nevertheless, by applying certain universality assumptions, we demonstrated that a probabilistic Polya urn scheme can be used to model pandemics and derive strategic insights. Within this framework, we derived both the distribution of infected individuals and an asymptotic estimate of the incidence rate, confirming that observed data aligns with a general underlying process across various scales. Leveraging European confirmed case and diagnostic test data for COVID-19, we conducted a comprehensive comparative analysis across European nations and between Europe and Italy at the regional level, covering both major infection waves. Our global incidence rate estimates align with prior research; however, this metric also serves as a critical proxy for obtaining an unbiased estimate of the true incidence rate, encompassing both symptomatic and asymptomatic cases.

The Hubble Space Telescope captured six images of IRC+10216 across three epochs—2001, 2011, and 2016—which are compared within the rest frame of the central carbon star. Leveraging Gaia Data Release 2, precise astrometry was attained; the star's position in each epoch was calculated using its established proper motion to define this rest frame. In 2016, a compact, red brightness peak was observed at the stellar location. Comparing color maps from 2011 and 2016 indicates that the reddest feature moved with the star, suggesting it represents dusty material surrounding the star. A relatively red ambient region forms an $\Omega$-shaped distribution, aligning well with a dusty disk previously inferred from near-infrared polarization data. On a larger scale, analyzing the differential proper motion of multiple ring-like structures in the star's rest frame yields an average transverse wind expansion velocity of approximately 12.5 km s$^{-1}$ ($d$/123 pc), where $d$ denotes the distance to IRC+10216. A three-dimensional geometry is inferred by comparing these findings with line-of-sight wind velocities derived from the half-widths of submillimeter emission lines of abundant molecules. Furthermore, uneven brightness variations across different searchlight beams and the anisotropic distribution of the extended halo are re-examined in the context of stellar light passing through a porous envelope, with postulated longer-term variations occurring over a period of less than 10 years.

We address the challenge of learning stabilizer states under noise within the Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) framework for quantum states introduced by Aaronson (2007). While Rocchetto (2018) recently provided an algorithm for the noiseless scenario, the noisy variant remained unresolved. Drawing inspiration from noise-tolerance strategies in classical learning theory, we propose the Statistical Query (SQ) model for PAC-learning quantum states and demonstrate that algorithms within this model are robust against typical noise types, such as classification and depolarizing noise. Furthermore, we establish an exponential lower bound for learning stabilizer states in the SQ model. Additionally, we show that, even beyond the SQ framework, learning noisy stabilizer states is generally as difficult as the classical Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) problem. These findings characterize the problem of learning stabilizer states as the quantum counterpart to classical parity learning: tractable without noise but appearing intractable even with simple noise models.

This paper introduces NNCF, a novel framework designed for neural network compression with fine-tuning. By integrating recent advancements in compression techniques—specifically sparsity, quantization, and binarization—NNCF generates hardware-optimized models capable of efficient execution on general-purpose processors (CPU, GPU) and specialized deep learning accelerators. Our results demonstrate that these methods effectively accelerate inference across a diverse array of models without compromising original accuracy. The framework offers flexibility, functioning either within provided training datasets or as a standalone package that integrates seamlessly into existing training pipelines with minimal code modifications. Currently, a PyTorch implementation of NNCF is accessible as part of the OpenVINO Training Extensions at https://github.com/openvinotoolkit/nncf.

We utilized the COSMOS2020 catalogue to determine the stellar-to-halo mass relation (SHMR) for central and satellite galaxies across redshifts from $z=0.2$ to $z=5.5$. Based on precise photometric redshifts, we measured the near-infrared selected two-point angular correlation and stellar mass functions within ten redshift bins, fitting the data using an HOD-based model. At each redshift, we calculated the stellar-to-halo mass ratio ($M_*/M_h$), revealing a strong dependence on halo mass that peaks at $M_h^{\rm peak} \sim 10^{12}\, M_{\odot}$. These findings align with the hypothesis that the peak of star-formation efficiency shifts toward more massive halos at higher redshifts. Additionally, we analyzed the satellite fraction as a function of stellar mass and redshift, observing that the satellite fraction declines at higher redshifts for all stellar mass thresholds and is higher for low-mass satellites at any given redshift. The contribution of satellites to the total stellar mass budget surpasses that of centrals in halos with masses exceeding $M_h > 10^{13} \, M_{\odot}$, yet remains below the peak, suggesting that quenching mechanisms in massive halos suppress star-formation efficiency. Finally, we compared our results with three hydrodynamical simulations: Horizon-AGN, Illustris-TNG-100, and EAGLE. The most notable discrepancy occurs at the high-mass end, where simulations generally predict a higher satellite contribution to the stellar mass budget than observed. Combined with the finding that simulations yield a higher satellite fraction, this indicates that feedback mechanisms in group- and cluster-scale halos are less efficient at quenching satellite mass assembly in simulations, or that quenching occurs significantly later in the simulated timelines.

Analysis of 44 TESS observations from Sector 1 identified 19 new roAp stars, 103 stars with non-peculiar characteristics but roAp-like frequencies, and 617 $\delta$~Scuti stars exhibiting independent frequencies typical of roAp stars. A broader review of all chemically peculiar stars monitored by TESS revealed 199 Ap stars pulsating as either $\delta$~Sct or $\gamma$~Dor variables. The proportion of pulsating Ap stars matches that of pulsating chemically normal stars. No clear distinction exists between chemically peculiar $\delta$~Sct stars and roAp stars regarding frequency or radial order; indeed, all previous characteristics used to differentiate roAp stars from $\delta$~Sct stars have vanished. Consequently, there is no basis to assume that the high frequencies observed in roAp stars arise from a different mechanism than those in chemically normal stars. While chemically peculiar stars are significantly more prone to high-frequency pulsation, the term "roAp" should be abandoned, as all such stars are simply normal $\delta$~Scuti stars.

We present a Bayesian framework designed to forecast continuous or binary outcomes from data exhibiting a multi-way (multidimensional tensor) structure collected across multiple sources. Using molecular data from various 'omics sources, measured at multiple developmental time points to predict early-life iron deficiency (ID) in a rhesus monkey model as a motivating case, our approach employs a linear model with low-rank coefficient structures to capture multi-way dependencies. Additionally, we model coefficient variance separately for each source to infer their relative contributions. Conjugate priors enable an efficient Gibbs sampling algorithm for posterior inference, applicable to both continuous outcomes with normal errors and binary outcomes with a probit link. Simulation results indicate that the model performs as anticipated regarding misclassification rates and the correlation between estimated and true coefficients, showing significant performance improvements by integrating multi-way structure and moderate gains by accounting for varying signal sizes across sources. Furthermore, the model successfully provides robust classification of ID monkeys in our primary application. R code implementing this software is accessible at https://github.com/BiostatsKim/BayesMSMW.

Weakly-supervised learning (WSL) has been introduced to mitigate the trade-off between annotation expenses and model efficacy by utilizing sparsely-grained supervision (such as point, box, or scribble data), achieving notable success, especially in image segmentation. Nevertheless, this remains a formidable challenge, particularly when labeled samples are scarce. Furthermore, most current WSL segmentation approaches are tailored for star-convex shapes, which differ significantly from curvilinear structures like blood vessels and nerves. This paper presents YoloCurvSeg, a new framework for segmenting curvilinear structures with sparse annotations, leveraging image synthesis. The system employs a background generator that creates realistic images by inpainting dilated skeletons, which are then merged with randomly synthesized curves produced by a Space Colonization Algorithm-based foreground generator. A multilayer patch-wise contrastive learning synthesizer integrates these elements to generate a synthetic dataset comprising images and curve segmentation labels, requiring only one or a few noisy skeleton annotations. A segmenter is subsequently trained using this synthetic data alongside potentially unlabeled data. Evaluated on four public datasets (OCTA500, CORN, DRIVE, and CHASEDB1), YoloCurvSeg demonstrates substantial improvements over state-of-the-art WSL methods. Remarkably, using merely one noisy skeleton annotation (representing 0.14%, 0.03%, 1.40%, and 0.65% of full annotations respectively), it attains over 97% of fully-supervised performance on each dataset. The code and datasets will be made available at https://github.com/llmir/YoloCurvSeg.

High-statistics Belle data concerning the $\gamma\gamma\to\pi^+\pi^-$ and $\gamma\gamma\to\pi^0\pi^0$ processes have been analyzed together, revealing the primary dynamical mechanisms for energies under 1.5 GeV. The study demonstrates that the direct coupling constants of the $\sigma(600)$ and $f_0(980)$ resonances to a $\gamma\gamma$ pair are minimal. Furthermore, the $\sigma(600)\to\gamma\gamma$ and $f_0(980)\to\gamma\gamma$ decays are identified as four-quark transitions, driven mainly by $\pi^+\pi^-$ and $K^+K^-$ loop mechanisms, respectively. The significance of chiral shielding for the $\sigma(600)$ resonance is highlighted. Estimates for the widths of these decays, averaged over their respective mass distributions, along with the $f_2(1270)\to\gamma\gamma$ width, yield $(\Gamma_{f_0\to\gamma\gamma})_{\pi\pi}\approx 0.19$ keV, $(\Gamma_{\sigma \to\gamma\gamma})_{\pi\pi}\approx 0.45$ keV, and $\Gamma_{f_2\to\gamma\gamma}(m^2_{f_2})\approx 3.8$ keV.

Social scientists can more easily analyze human behavior by examining interactions on social media, where conversations often form tree-like structures known as threads. By studying structural attributes like depth, width, and size, researchers can infer user discussion patterns and conversation dynamics. This paper investigates the architecture of online discussions on Reddit by evaluating both global and local discussion-tree properties. Global features relate to the broader community or subreddit context, while local features pertain to the specific post. Using a dataset comprising approximately 250,000 posts and several million comments from a single year, we conducted statistical analyses to disentangle the relative contributions of these feature types to structural patterns. Our findings reveal that both local and global characteristics account for significant structural variation, with local features collectively explaining more variance than global ones. Nevertheless, the impact of individual features varies considerably; certain global attributes, such as topic, age, popularity, and subreddit content redundancy, also play a vital role in shaping discussion tree properties.

Speech segmentation, the process of dividing lengthy audio into smaller units, is crucial for speech translation (ST). Widely used Voice Activity Detection (VAD) tools, such as WebRTC VAD, typically depend on pause-based segmentation. However, pauses do not always align with sentence boundaries, and sentences are often linked by extremely brief pauses that VAD systems struggle to identify. This study introduces a segmentation approach utilizing a binary classification model trained on a segmented bilingual speech corpus. Additionally, we propose a hybrid strategy that integrates this new method with traditional VAD. Experimental findings indicate that the proposed method outperforms conventional techniques in both cascade and end-to-end ST systems, while the hybrid approach further enhances translation quality.

This study establishes the lower limits for orbital periods of hydrogen-rich objects with masses spanning from Saturn's to that of the Sun ($1 \, M_{\odot}$), with a specific focus on gas giants and brown dwarfs within the $0.0003 - 0.074 \, M_\odot$ range. We provide analytic fitting equations for the minimum period ($P_{\rm min}$) based on both the object's mass and its mean density, assuming the host star's density is high enough to avoid imposing further constraints, a condition typically met by white dwarfs. Part of this research aims to differentiate brown dwarfs from planets orbiting white dwarfs via transit, without relying on near-infrared or radial velocity data. Specifically, orbital periods of roughly 100 minutes or less are highly indicative of brown dwarfs, with an overall minimum period across the full mass range estimated at approximately 37 minutes.

Weather forecast data is poised to play an increasingly vital role in managing future energy systems. This study presents an augmented state space model featuring linear dynamics, designed to integrate forecast information that updates dynamically as the underlying state evolves. We employ the martingale model for forecast evolution (MMFE) to ensure the necessary consistency in how forecasts and state variables develop together. Furthermore, this formulation produces jointly Markovian dynamics that result in computationally feasible Markov decision processes (MDPs). To our knowledge, this work is the first to impose MMFE consistency requirements within an MDP framework without sacrificing computational tractability.

We investigate the Leray transform $\bf{L}$ acting on a family $M_\gamma$ of unbounded hypersurfaces within two complex dimensions. For a broad class of measures, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for the $L^2$-boundedness of $\bf{L}$ and provide an exact spectral characterization of $\bf{L}^*\bf{L}$. These results determine both the norm and the high-frequency norm of $\bf{L}$, with the latter resolving an open conjecture by affirmatively linking the essential norm of $\bf{L}$ to a projective invariant defined on bounded hypersurfaces. Furthermore, we demonstrate that $\bf{L}$ serves as a crucial link between projective geometric and function-theoretic concepts of duality. Our findings enable the construction of projectively invariant Hardy spaces on $M_\gamma$ and reveal that their duals correspond to invariant Hardy spaces on the dual hypersurfaces.

We describe new relationships between the Riemann, Ricci, and Einstein tensors that are necessary for a geometry to support Killing-Yano tensors. Utilizing these relations, we define novel conserved currents associated with such tensors. Focusing on a specific current derived from the Einstein tensor, we examine the associated conserved charges and their implications for matter interacting with gravity. Additionally, we determine the geometric conditions required for a background to admit asymptotic conserved charges for the current proposed by Kastor and Traschen, highlighting further properties of this current. Notably, we demonstrate that this current vanishes when constructed from rank $(D-1)$ Killing-Yano tensors in $D$ dimensions.

This work investigates high-dimensional sparse linear regression within a distributed framework, addressing both computational and communication limitations. We examine a star-shaped network where multiple machines, each possessing noisy observations from a linear model sharing an unknown sparse $d$-dimensional coefficient vector $\theta$, are linked to a central fusion center via brief message exchanges. The fusion center aims to estimate both $\theta$ and its support while minimizing computational and communication costs at each node. We analyze distributed algorithms rooted in Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP), theoretically demonstrating their capacity to precisely recover the support of $\theta$. Our proofs show that under specific conditions, these distributed OMP methods can successfully identify the support even at low signal-to-noise ratios where individual machines fail to do so, achieving this with total communication costs sublinear in $d$. Furthermore, simulations confirm that these algorithms perform comparably to, and in certain instances surpass, more complex and computationally demanding techniques.

The existence of spin$^c$ structures on every compact oriented 4-manifold, a result established by Hirzebruch and Hopf, is traditionally proven through methods that lack directness and clarity. This paper presents a more straightforward and geometrically intuitive alternative proof based on twistor spaces. Following an application of these concepts to illuminate diverse facets of four-dimensional geometry, the article demonstrates how similar principles extend the understanding of spin and spin$^c$ structures to arbitrary dimensions.

Over recent years, the transformer architecture and its variants have achieved remarkable success across numerous machine learning tasks. This success stems fundamentally from the ability to process long sequences and incorporate context-dependent weights via the attention mechanism. We posit that these features are ideally suited for a Meta-Reinforcement Learning (Meta-RL) algorithm. Specifically, a Meta-RL agent must infer tasks from sequences of trajectories and employ a rapid adaptation strategy to adjust its policy for new tasks, a capability effectively realized through the self-attention mechanism. In this work, we introduce TrMRL (Transformers for Meta-Reinforcement Learning), a Meta-RL agent that emulates the memory reinstatement process using the transformer architecture. By linking recent past experiences in working memory, the model recursively constructs episodic memory through transformer layers. We demonstrate that self-attention generates a consensus representation at each layer that minimizes Bayes Risk, thereby supplying meaningful features for determining optimal actions. Experiments conducted in high-dimensional continuous control environments involving locomotion and dexterous manipulation reveal that TrMRL achieves comparable or superior asymptotic performance, sample efficiency, and out-of-distribution generalization relative to baseline methods.

This paper investigates the semiclassical properties of scattering data for a non-self-adjoint Dirac operator featuring a rapidly oscillating potential that is complex analytic near the real axis. While we present some rigorous and broadly applicable results, a full and concrete understanding demands an exploration of the WKB geometry within specific instances. To perform these detailed calculations, we utilize a particular case previously analyzed numerically by Bronski and Miller over two decades ago, relying extensively on their numerical findings. Predominantly through the exact WKB method, we deliver a complete, rigorous, and uniform semiclassical analysis of the Bohr-Sommerfeld condition governing eigenvalue locations across unions of analytic arcs, alongside the corresponding norming constants. Conversely, regarding the reflection coefficient and eigenvalues near zero in the spectral plane, we apply an established theory developed in detail by Olver. Our study is driven by the necessity to comprehend the semiclassical dynamics of the focusing cubic NLS equation with initial data $A\exp\{iS/\epsilon\}$, leveraging the well-known insight by Zakharov and Shabat that inverse scattering theory allows the NLS equation to be solved via the spectral analysis of the Dirac operator.

This study employs both analytical and numerical techniques to investigate the scattering of Dirac fermions against topological solitons within the $(2+1)$-dimensional nonlinear $O(3)$ $\sigma$-model. We derive general expressions for fermion scattering and establish the symmetry characteristics of the partial scattering amplitudes and $S$-matrix components. Utilizing the Born approximation, we analytically calculate the scattering amplitudes, differential and total cross-sections for fermion-soliton interactions, examining their symmetry properties and asymptotic behavior. Furthermore, numerical methods are applied to determine the momentum dependence of the first few partial $S$-matrix elements, with key features of these dependencies analyzed and discussed.

This paper introduces an inverse preconditioner designed for the numerical resolution of an elliptic Laplace problem within a global circulation ocean model. By employing an inverse preconditioning technique, we achieve efficient computation of the elliptic kernel using the Conjugate Gradient (CG) method. We demonstrate the relationship between the solver's performance and convergence rate with respect to discretized grid resolution and the Laplace coefficients of the oceanic model. Finally, we outline a straightforward GPU implementation of the solver utilizing scientific computing libraries and evaluate its performance.

We explore catalysis within the context of elementary thermal operations, leveraging their distinct benefits to clarify catalytic dynamics. As a foundation, we develop novel technical instruments that enhance the computability of state transition rules for these operations, specifically delivering a complete characterization for qutrit systems. By combining these tools with numerical methods, we demonstrate that employing even a single qubit catalyst substantially expands the range of accessible state transitions for a qutrit system, effectively bridging the gap between elementary and generic thermal operations. Furthermore, we break down catalytic transitions into time-resolved evolutions to monitor nonequilibrium free energy exchanges. Our findings confirm the presence of simple and practical catalytic advantages in thermodynamics and offer a method for analyzing the underlying mechanisms of catalytic processes.

Particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) is a prevalent method for capturing time-resolved, three-dimensional velocity and pressure fields in fluid dynamics, yet it suffers from significant errors due to inaccurate particle localization and tracking, particularly when using single-camera defocusing, plenoptic imaging, or digital in-line holography (DIH). To mitigate this, we introduced stochastic particle advection velocimetry (SPAV), a statistical framework that enhances PTV accuracy. SPAV relies on an explicit particle advection model that forecasts particle trajectories based on estimated velocity fields, incorporating non-ideal factors such as drag on inertial particles. We derived and approximated a statistical loss function that evaluates discrepancies between tracked and advected positions while accommodating arbitrary localization and tracking uncertainties. Our implementation utilizes a physics-informed neural network that jointly minimizes the SPAV loss, a Navier-Stokes physics constraint, and relevant wall boundary conditions. Validated on both simulated and experimental DIH-PTV data for laminar and turbulent flows, our statistical approach substantially outperforms conventional methods, achieving nearly a 50% average error reduction. Additionally, the proposed framework is easily adaptable to other data assimilation strategies, including state observers, Kalman filters, and adjoint-variational techniques.

The Evryscope is a telescope array engineered to expand optical astronomy's parameter space by simultaneously monitoring vast sky regions for short-duration events. Comprising a 22-camera array with 780 MPix, an 8150 sq. deg. field of view, 13" pixel sampling, and a sensitivity of Mg=16 in 2-minute dark-sky exposures, the system covers 18,400 sq. deg. nightly with high-cadence imaging. It is specifically built to identify rare phenomena requiring all-sky surveillance, such as transiting exoplanets orbiting exotic stars (e.g., white dwarfs and hot subdwarfs), diverse stellar activity within the Milky Way, nearby supernovae, and transients like gamma-ray bursts and electromagnetic counterparts to gravitational waves. Averaging 5,000 images per night—each containing roughly 300,000 sources—the system has captured over 3.0 million images, generating 250TB of raw data. This has resulted in a light curve database for 9.3 million targets, averaging 32,600 epochs per target through 2018. This paper details the Evryscope's hardware and performance, offering insights on telescope and electronics design, precision polar alignment procedures for similar systems, robotic operations, and safety optimization. We evaluate on-sky performance, analyze data pipelines, and showcase variable star and eclipsing binary discoveries. Additionally, we highlight new findings of rare objects, including two hot subdwarf eclipsing binaries with late M-dwarf companions (HW Vir systems), two white dwarf/hot subdwarf short-period binaries, and four hot subdwarf reflection binaries. The paper concludes with an update on transit surveys, M-dwarf flare monitoring, and transient detection efforts.

With the growing adoption of low-carbon transportation, particularly electric vehicles (EVs), eco-driving has become a focal point. Unlike traditional internal combustion engine vehicles that lack regenerative braking, this study introduces a genetic algorithm (GA)-driven eco-driving strategy tailored for EVs to leverage this capability. The method employs a GA to identify the optimal or near-optimal set of variables within an EV's driving cycle. The process begins by creating an initial population of chromosomes, each encoding the relevant variables. Through iterative generations involving crossover, mutation, and elitist selection, the algorithm evolves a driving cycle that minimizes energy consumption. Validated through two case studies, the results demonstrate the method's effectiveness in calculating minimum energy driving cycles.

Using $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing analysis, we introduce a new approach to derive the physical solutions for the hadronic properties of the $Y(4230)$ resonance from experimental data. While previous studies have reported multiple solutions for the decays $Y(4230) \to \eta J/\psi$ and $Y(4230) \to \eta' J/\psi$, our method yields a single, unique solution for $Y(4230) \to \eta' J/\psi$. Furthermore, assuming the $Y(4230)$ contains no $s\bar{s}$ component, we favor two solutions for $Y(4230) \to \eta J/\psi$ out of the three originally reported.

A foundational set of features defines the core of thermodynamic descriptions, emerging from large-deviation properties within systems characterized by hierarchical timescales, yet remaining independent of conservation laws or microscopic reversibility in the underlying substrate. The primary elements include the relationship between macrostates and large-deviation entropy, alongside the partitioning of irreversibility contributions among interacting subsystems, which establishes the basis for the concept of heat in both classical and stochastic thermodynamics. A natural decomposition is identified into relative entropy and housekeeping entropy rate; these define, respectively, the \textit{intensive} thermodynamics of a system and an \textit{extensive} thermodynamic vector that situates the system within its context. Both components rely on the Hartley information of the system's instantaneous stationary state, representing information regarding the joint impact of system processes on their contribution to irreversibility. Specific results are derived for stochastic Chemical Reaction Networks, including a Legendre duality for the housekeeping entropy rate that fully characterizes irreversible processes on equal footing with those at the detailed-balance limit. This work aims to foster the development of intrinsic thermodynamic descriptions for rule-based systems and living states, avoiding reductive explanations based solely on heat flows.

Camouflage serves as a vital survival strategy across various species, with common tactics including background matching and disruptive coloration to obscure body outlines [35]. Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) focuses on segmenting objects that blend into their surroundings. Current COD models rely on binary ground truth to identify these objects but fail to quantify the degree of their camouflage. This paper re-examines the task, proposing that explicitly modeling the conspicuousness of camouflaged objects relative to their specific backgrounds can deepen our understanding of animal camouflage and evolution while offering insights for designing advanced camouflage methods. We observe that certain specific regions of these objects are primarily responsible for their detectability by predators. Leveraging this insight, we introduce Rank-Net, the first ranking-based COD network capable of simultaneously localizing, segmenting, and ranking camouflaged objects. The localization component identifies discriminative regions that render the objects noticeable, the segmentation component delineates the full extent of the objects, and the ranking component assesses their relative detectability. Additionally, we provide a large-scale COD testing set to evaluate model generalization. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, resulting in a more interpretable COD framework.

In condensed matter physics, the spin-orbit (SO) interaction can be characterized by a non-Abelian potential, commonly referred to as a color field in high-energy physics. This analysis demonstrates that the magnetic component of this color field necessarily induces diamagnetic color currents, which correspond exactly to the equilibrium spin currents recognized in condensed matter theory. Consequently, these dissipationless spin currents emerge as a universal feature of systems exhibiting SO interaction. Specifically, in semiconductors characterized by linear SO coupling, the spin currents are connected to the effective non-Abelian field through the Yang-Mills magnetostatics equation.

The real Fourier-Mukai transform maps a section of a torus fibration to a connection defined on the total space of the dual torus fibration. Utilizing this approach, Leung, Yau, and Zaslow formulated deformed Hermitian Yang-Mills (dHYM) connections for Kähler manifolds, while Lee and Leung established deformed Donaldson-Thomas (dDT) connections for $G_2$- and ${\rm Spin}(7)$-manifolds. In this work, we propose an alternative definition of a dDT connection for manifolds with a ${\rm Spin}(7)$-structure, arguing that it is more suitable through a meticulous recomputation of the real Fourier-Mukai transform. Furthermore, we present evidence indicating that our proposed definition aligns with dDT connections on $G_2$-manifolds and dHYM connections on Calabi-Yau 4-manifolds. Another key contribution of this paper is that it lays the groundwork for subsequent research; specifically, based on the computations presented here, we advance the theories regarding deformations of dDT connections for ${\rm Spin}(7)$-structured manifolds and the "mirror" of the volume functional, known as the Dirac-Born-Infeld (DBI) action in physics.

Federated learning seeks to develop a global model that performs effectively on client devices with minimal cross-client communication, while Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) expands this framework to address data heterogeneity by training personalized models. A primary difficulty in this context is achieving effective learning across clients despite each possessing unique, often scarce data. We introduce pFedGP, a PFL solution grounded in Gaussian processes (GPs) enhanced by deep kernel learning. GPs are highly expressive and perform robustly in low-data scenarios due to their Bayesian foundations; however, their application to PFL presents several hurdles. Specifically, GP performance relies heavily on a high-quality kernel function, and learning such a kernel typically demands a substantial training set. To overcome this, we propose a shared kernel function learned across all clients via a neural network, paired with a personalized GP classifier for each client. Additionally, we extend pFedGP by incorporating inducing points through two novel methods: one to enhance generalization in low-data regimes and another to reduce computational overhead. We derive a PAC-Bayes generalization bound for novel clients, demonstrating empirically that it provides non-vacuous guarantees. Extensive experiments on standard PFL benchmarks using CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CINIC-10, as well as a new setup involving input noise, reveal that pFedGP delivers well-calibrated predictions, significantly outperforming baseline methods with accuracy gains of up to 21%.

Transformers are now integral to modern architectures for diverse applications, including natural language processing and computer vision. This study introduces Gransformer, an algorithm designed for graph generation leveraging Transformer principles. We adapt a basic autoregressive Transformer encoder to effectively utilize existing graph structures via efficient modifications. Specifically, the attention mechanism is adjusted to account for the existence or non-existence of edges between node pairs. Additionally, we incorporate a graph-derived familiarity metric applicable to both attention and positional encoding; this metric relies on message passing algorithms to encapsulate structural graph data. Notably, this familiarity measure is autoregressive, enabling the model to compute required conditional probabilities within a single forward pass. In the output layer, a masked autoencoder is employed for density estimation to efficiently model the sequential generation of interdependent edges. Furthermore, utilizing BFS node orderings, we propose a technique to prevent the creation of isolated nodes disconnected from preceding ones. We assess this approach on two real-world datasets, benchmarking it against other state-of-the-art autoregressive graph generation techniques. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our method performs comparably to these benchmarks, including recurrent models and graph convolutional networks.

We conduct an in-depth examination of stimulated parametric down-conversion (PDC) to explore the influence of spatiotemporal degrees of freedom, yielding insights valuable for PDC-driven metrology. By employing a Wigner functional framework, we derive the resulting down-converted state as a Bogoliubov-transformed input state, expressed through Bogoliubov kernel functions. This framework is then applied to analyze coherent state seeding in stimulated PDC, alongside the calculation of the background arising from spontaneous PDC.

Bhargava, along with the first author, established a functorial Galois closure operation for finite-rank ring extensions, extending prior work by Grothendieck and Katz–Mazur. This paper utilizes Galois closures to define a novel infinite series of irreducible components within Hilbert schemes of points. We demonstrate that these components are elementary, as they parametrize algebras supported at a single point.

This study investigates quantum unitary dynamics within the driven tight-binding chain (TBC) framework, where these dynamics are periodically interrupted by random stochastic resets that simulate non-unitary effects from environmental interactions. The model features a quantum particle hopping between nearest-neighbor sites on a one-dimensional lattice while subjected to a time-periodic external driving field. We assume these resets occur at exponentially distributed random times. By employing the stochastic Liouville equation, we obtain exact expressions for the probability of finding the particle at specific sites at a given time, averaged over various dynamical realizations. Our results demonstrate a significant localization effect of the TBC particle on the lattice sites over long durations. In contrast, without stochastic resets, the system exhibits delocalization, meaning the particle lacks a time-independent probability distribution even at long times, leading to unbounded growth in the mean-squared displacement from its initial position. While localization in the bare model can only be achieved by fine-tuning the ratio of field strength to frequency to match a zero of the zeroth-order Bessel function of the first kind, we show that stochastic resets provide a far simpler mechanism to induce such localization.

This study examines the Clarkson-McLeod solutions to the fourth Painlev\'e equation, which exhibit asymptotic behavior proportional to $\kappa D_{\alpha-\frac{1}{2}}^2(\sqrt{2}x)$ as $x$ approaches $+\infty$, with $\kappa$ representing an arbitrary real constant and $D_{\alpha-\frac{1}{2}}(x)$ denoting the parabolic cylinder function. By applying the Deift-Zhou nonlinear steepest descent method, we derive the singular asymptotics of these solutions as $x\to-\infty$ under the condition $\kappa (\kappa -\kappa ^*)>0$, where $\kappa ^*$ is a specific real constant. Furthermore, we explicitly calculate the associated connection formulas. These results confirm and broaden the conjecture by Clarkson and McLeod, demonstrating that for parameters satisfying $\kappa >\kappa ^*>0$, the solutions possess infinitely many simple poles located on the negative real axis.

Prompt learning represents a novel approach within Natural Language Processing (NLP) that has demonstrated remarkable effectiveness across various language tasks, performing well in full, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios on standard datasets. Notably, recent findings indicate that large, frozen pre-trained language models (PLMs) utilizing prompt learning can surpass smaller models that undergo fine-tuning. However, similar to other NLP trends, even the most advanced PLMs like GPT-3 struggle with specialized domains, such as medical texts, where the standard practice for achieving state-of-the-art results still involves pre-training and fine-tuning on downstream tasks. Relying on fine-tuned large PLMs poses significant challenges in clinical environments, which often lack GPU resources, making resource-efficient training methods for domain-specific models essential. This study examined the potential of prompt learning for clinically relevant decision-making tasks, directly comparing it against traditional fine-tuning approaches. The results partially align with existing literature, showing that prompt learning can match or exceed the performance of fine-tuning while using significantly fewer trainable parameters and less training data. Consequently, we argue that prompt learning offers a computationally efficient alternative to fine-tuning increasingly massive PLMs, particularly suited for clinical settings. Reproducible code for the experiments described in this work is available at: https://github.com/NtaylorOX/Public_Clinical_Prompt.
This paper investigates the quantum wave packet within the context of the Schrödinger equation under continuous quantum measurement conditions.

Consider the Schrödinger operator $L = -\Delta + V$ acting on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$, where the non-negative potential $V$ belongs to the reverse Hölder class $B_q$ for some $q \geq n$. Let $\text{BMO}_L(\mathbb{R}^n)$ represent the space of functions of bounded mean oscillation associated with $L$. This paper demonstrates that a function $f \in \text{BMO}_L(\mathbb{R}^n)$ serves as the trace of the solution to $L'u = -u_{tt} + Lu = 0$ with initial condition $u(x,0) = f(x)$, provided that $u$ satisfies a Carleson condition. Conversely, this Carleson condition characterizes precisely those $L$-harmonic functions whose traces lie within $\text{BMO}_L(\mathbb{R}^n)$. These findings extend the analogous characterization established by Fabes, Johnson, and Neri for the classical BMO space defined by John and Nirenberg.

This study investigates partial information near-optimal control for systems described by forward-backward stochastic differential equations with observation noise, assuming a convex control domain. Utilizing Ekeland's variational principle alongside fundamental estimates for state and adjoint processes, we derive necessary conditions for $\varepsilon$-near-optimal controls in a local framework, achieving an error order of precisely $\varepsilon^{1/2}$. Furthermore, given additional convexity requirements on the Hamiltonian, we demonstrate that an $\varepsilon$-maximum condition, expressed as an integral form of the Hamiltonian, serves as a sufficient criterion for near-optimality.

This paper presents a search-driven method for creating new levels in bullet hell games, action genres defined by the necessity of evading massive quantities of projectiles. Levels are encoded using a domain-specific language, explored via a novel adaptation of the Map-Elites algorithm that integrates a feasible-infeasible strategy for handling constraints. Level fitness is assessed through simulation, employing an agent guided by best-first search. This agent's performance can be adjusted across two axes—strategy and dexterity—enabling the discovery of level configurations demanding specific blends of these skills. To our knowledge, this work introduces the first generator for this specific game genre and features multiple algorithmic advancements.

This study examines how current density varies with phase difference within SIS'IS-type layered superconducting structures. To facilitate the calculations, quasiclassical equations for Green's functions in the *t*-representation are formulated, treating the order parameter as a piecewise constant function. The analysis covers the general case without limiting the transparency of the dielectric layer or the thickness of the intermediate layer. The results yield a novel analytical expression for the current-phase relation, which can recover various previously established results in specific limiting cases.

Recent studies utilizing the spin wave approximation to examine the quantum characteristics of an antiferromagnet have characterized eigenstates as two-mode squeezed sublattice states, revealing significant sublattice entanglement within uniform squeezed vacuums and one-magnon configurations. This work extends that analysis by investigating the squeezing behavior across all sublattice Fock states throughout the magnetic Brillouin zone. We calculate the complete statistics for sublattice magnon numbers at wave vector $\vec k$ within the ground state, demonstrating that magnons are generated in pairs with opposing wavevectors, thereby entangling both modes. Using the Duan-Giedke-Cirac-Zoller inequality to quantify entanglement, we prove its violation across all modes, noting that the entanglement magnitude diminishes toward the Brillouin zone boundaries. By linking this entanglement to measurable correlations between the N\'eel and magnetization vector components, we enable experimental verification of the squeezed vacuum's quantum nature. Furthermore, the distinct $\vec k$-space distribution of probabilities indicates that the squeezed vacuum possesses a nonuniform profile, a feature exposed through $\vec k$-dependent correlators of the magnetization and N\'eel vectors.

Action-adventure games present various obstacles, with enemies being the most prevalent. These adversaries aim to impede player advancement by depleting health points, employing unique tactics specific to their type. This paper presents an enhanced evolutionary method for procedurally generating enemies, focusing on optimizing enemy difficulty. Our approach advances enemy generation research by integrating a MAP-Elites population, which ensures diversity in generated enemies without compromising quality. Computational experiments demonstrated that the method successfully evolved most MAP-Elites individuals in under a second for the majority of cases. Furthermore, we conducted trials with players testing an action-adventure prototype featuring our generated enemies. The results indicated that players enjoyed most levels, and we successfully created enemies perceived as easy, medium, or difficult.

The NA61/SHINE experiment operates as a fixed-target facility with broad acceptance at the CERN SPS. This contribution outlines the latest findings from the strong interactions program and announces updates regarding the detector upgrade scheduled for future data collection. The program involves a two-dimensional scan covering beam momenta ranging from 13A to 150A/158A GeV/c (corresponding to \sqrt{s_{NN}} from 5.1 to 17.3 GeV) and various system sizes, including p + p, Be + Be, Ar + Sc, and Xe + La collisions. The research aims to identify the second-order critical end-point in the temperature versus baryo-chemical potential phase diagram and investigate the onset of deconfinement previously observed by the NA49 experiment at the CERN SPS. The presented results cover K/{\pi} multiplicity ratios across different energies and system sizes, the production of singly and multi-strange hadrons in p + p reactions, multiplicity and net-charge fluctuations analyzed through higher-order moments in p + p, Be + Be, and Ar + Sc collisions, proton and charged hadron intermittency in Ar + Sc and Pb + Pb reactions, HBT measurements in Ar + Sc, and collective electromagnetic effects within Ar + Sc collisions.

This study introduces three metrics designed to quantify the distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability of online signature templates. The distinctiveness metric is calculated using a collection of enrolled signature samples alongside a statistical model of random signatures. The complexity metric is derived from the same set of enrolled samples, while the repeatability metric is determined from a validation set for a given template. These metrics serve as indicators for evaluating the system's ability to reject both random and skilled forgeries, as well as the users' capability to provide accepted genuine signatures. The efficacy and applicability of these measures are validated through experiments conducted on three online signature datasets and one keystroke dynamics dataset, utilizing various verification algorithms.

This article presents a novel, general definition of fractional derivatives and integrals that relies on an unspecified kernel. Utilizing these definitions, we derive fundamental properties for both fractional integrals and derivatives, including the Product Rule, Quotient Rule, Chain Rule, Rolle's Theorem, and the Mean Value Theorem. Additionally, several illustrative examples are provided.

Research into localizing mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks (WSNs) remains a significant and active field. This paper introduces a new RSSI-based localization algorithm designed for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) WSNs. We develop and implement a novel range-based approach specifically to reduce cross-technology interference in shared frequency bands, with the objective of minimizing the mean square error. The hardware implementation aligns with ideal simulation results (assuming no interference), achieving a localization accuracy of under 0.5 meters.

As globalization intensifies, geographic literacy becomes essential. This paper introduces a collaborative two-player game designed to enhance users' skills in locating countries on a world map. We examine two versions of this game: an initial web-based iteration featuring the remote-controlled agent Nellie, and a subsequent face-to-face version adapted for the Furhat robot Neil, leveraging insights from extensive online data collection. Our analysis reveals that participants found the game highly engaging and reported acquiring enduring knowledge about world geography.

A primary challenge in rarefied gas dynamics research is obtaining steady-state solutions to the Boltzmann equation efficiently. While conventional iteration schemes converge rapidly for highly rarefied systems (large Knudsen numbers), they require hundreds of thousands of iterations for near-continuum flows (small Knudsen numbers), often resulting in solutions compromised by accumulated errors and significant numerical dissipation. Although recent implicit unified gas kinetic schemes (UGKS) and their variants, grounded in gas kinetic models, have improved efficiency in near-continuum regimes, they still demand more iterations than those required for highly rarefied flows. This paper introduces a general synthetic iteration scheme (GSIS) capable of achieving steady-state solutions for general rarefied gas flows within dozens of iterations across any Knudsen number. Since GSIS is independent of specific kinetic models or collision operators, it can be readily extended to rapidly converge solutions for mixture flows and chemically reacting flows. These two key advantages are also anticipated to accelerate the slow convergence observed in direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) and its low-variance variants when simulating near-continuum flows.

Automated train scheduling continues to pose a significant challenge for contemporary railway systems, with the underlying Vehicle Rescheduling Problem (VRSP) remaining a central focus of Operations Research for decades. Conventional methods rely on intricate simulators that make testing diverse innovative solutions time-consuming and computationally expensive. To address this, we present "Flatland," a two-dimensional simplified grid environment designed to accelerate experimentation. Beyond reducing the complexity of full physical simulations, Flatland offers an accessible interface for evaluating novel VRSP approaches, including Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Imitation Learning (IL). To explore the capabilities of Machine Learning within this framework, we conducted an initial series of RL and IL experiments and established a public Benchmark at NeurIPS 2020 to foster a broad research community. Our findings indicate that while ML shows promise for solving the VRSP on Flatland, several critical areas require further investigation. Ultimately, Flatland has emerged as a robust and valuable platform for studying VRSP in railway networks, providing a solid foundation for future research and benchmark participants. Collectively, these initiatives hold the potential to significantly influence the development of future mobility systems.

This paper aims to classify two types of almost Kenmotsu manifolds that admit Ricci-Yamabe solitons. It is demonstrated that a $(k,\mu)'$-almost Kenmotsu manifold supporting a Ricci-Yamabe or gradient Ricci-Yamabe soliton is locally isometric to the Riemannian product $\mathbb{H}^{n+1}(-4) \times \mathbb{R}^n$. In the latter scenario, the potential vector field is pointwise collinear with the Reeb vector field. Furthermore, it is established that a $(k,\mu)$-almost Kenmotsu manifold admitting a specific Ricci-Yamabe soliton satisfying the curvature condition $Q \cdot P = 0$ is locally isometric to the hyperbolic space $\mathbb{H}^{2n+1}(-1)$, while the existence of the curvature property $Q \cdot R = 0$ is proven to be impossible.

We present a deep learning approach designed to deduce the non-linear velocity field from the dark matter density distribution. This method employs a "U-net" style convolutional neural network, comprising 15 convolutional layers and 2 deconvolutional layers, which transforms a 3D density field of $32^3$ voxels into 3D velocity or momentum fields of $20^3$ voxels. By analyzing dark matter simulations with a resolution of $2 {h^{-1}}{\rm Mpc}$, we demonstrate that the network effectively predicts the non-linearity, complexity, and vorticity of these fields, as well as their power spectra regarding value, divergence, and vorticity. The model achieves prediction accuracy up to $k\simeq1.4$ $h{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$, with relative errors between 1% and $\lesssim$10%. Comparative analysis indicates that neural networks offer a significant advantage over perturbation theory in reconstructing velocity and momentum fields.

Vertical federated learning (VFL) has gained significant interest for facilitating privacy-preserving cross-silo data collaboration. Although existing VFL research predominantly targets linear and tree-based models, neural networks remain underexplored. This paper examines SplitNN, a prominent VFL neural framework, and highlights the inherent trade-off between data security and model performance. SplitNN operates by exchanging gradients and transformed data; however, training on transformed data rather than raw data causes a loss of low-level feature information, thereby reducing model performance. Conversely, attempting to improve performance by aggregating at lower layers (which preserves more raw features) exposes the data to inference attacks. To resolve this conflict, we introduce Security Forward Aggregation (SFA), a novel VFL protocol that modifies data aggregation methods and employs removable masks to safeguard raw data. Experimental results demonstrate that networks utilizing SFA successfully achieve both high model performance and robust data security.

Ultra-cold atoms serve as excellent platforms for interferometry due to their macroscopic matter-wave characteristics, which yield extended coherent lengths and durations, thereby enabling high-precision and highly sensitive measurements. This review summarizes our work aimed at enhancing interferometer performance. We introduce a shortcut protocol for controlling ultra-cold atoms within an optical lattice; unlike conventional approaches, this method accelerates manipulation by up to three orders of magnitude. Utilizing this technique, we built a matter-wave Ramsey interferometer for trapped motional quantum states and extended its coherence time by an order of magnitude through an echo strategy. Additionally, we explored resolution enhancement via a multimode scheme. Implementing a noise-resilient multi-component interferometer demonstrated that increasing the number of paths sharpens time-domain interference fringes, doubling the resolution compared to a standard double-path two-mode system. The aforementioned shortcut method also facilitated improved momentum resolution, achieving atomic momentum patterns narrower than 0.6 $\hbar k_L$. To identify and mitigate systematic errors, we applied principal component analysis (PCA), which reduced detection noise to nearly the $1/\sqrt{2}$ level of photon-shot noise, allowing for the separation, identification, and elimination of specific noise sources. Finally, based on our research into ultra-cold atoms for precision metrology, we propose a method to accurately measure local gravitational acceleration over a few-centimeter range.

Meta reinforcement learning (Meta-RL) distills experience from diverse tasks into a meta-policy capable of achieving near-optimal performance on new, related tasks after minimal adaptation. A primary obstacle to applying Meta-RL in real-world scenarios is the prevalence of sparse reward functions, which merely signal partial or full task completion. This work addresses scenarios where offline data, potentially generated by sub-optimal agents, is available for each task. We introduce Enhanced Meta-RL using Demonstrations (EMRLD), a framework that leverages this data to provide training guidance even when it is sub-optimal. EMRLD integrates reinforcement learning with supervised learning on offline data to produce a meta-policy exhibiting monotonic performance gains. Additionally, we propose EMRLD-WS, a warm-start variant optimized for efficiency with sub-optimal demonstrations. Empirical results demonstrate that our EMRLD algorithms significantly surpass existing methods across various sparse reward environments, including mobile robot applications.

Although soft robotic hands offer significant potential for diverse grasping tasks, designing and fabricating them is often constrained by difficulties in sensing and reconstructing the robot's pose. This study introduces a new method for 3D pose reconstruction to analyze the grasping movements of a bidirectional soft robotic hand using experimental video data. By employing an imaging system with a single camera and multiple mirrors, images were captured from top, front, back, left, and right perspectives. Deep learning techniques were utilized to extract coordinate and orientation data for the soft fingers: a Faster R-CNN model identified fingertip locations, while a U-Net model determined the lateral boundaries of the fingers. Leveraging kinematic principles, databases corresponding to these coordinates and orientations were created. The reconstructed 3D poses demonstrated high accuracy and satisfactory performance. Furthermore, the efficacy coefficient method was applied to compare the soft robot hand with the human hand, analyzing the contributions of finger bending angles and inter-finger distances. The findings indicate that the soft robotic hand achieves human-like motion during both single-direction and bidirectional grasping.

This paper explores the hypothesis that geo-tagged tweets can reveal how individuals interact with their surroundings, aiming to support urban and city planning. By leveraging Twitter activity signatures, the study employs supervised learning to identify spatial land uses within cities. The methodology applies this technique to data from three Australian cities: Brisbane, Melbourne, and Sydney. The analytical findings were validated against zoning data supplied by the respective city councils, demonstrating a strong alignment between the predicted land uses and the official zoning classifications. These results indicate that geo-tagged tweets possess distinctive features valuable for land use identification.

This study demonstrates that spherically symmetric black hole (BH) solutions derived from the linear charged field equation of Rastall gravity remain independent of the Rastall parameter, aligning with existing literature. In contrast, applying Rastall's field equations to a specific nonlinear electrodynamics (NED) source yields a new spherically symmetric BH solution that explicitly incorporates the Rastall parameter. This parameter emerges primarily because the trace of the NED source does not vanish, unlike in the linear case. The resulting spacetime corresponds to Anti-de-Sitter Reissner-Nordström geometry, where the Rastall parameter is effectively absorbed into the cosmological constant. In the general relativity limit, where the Rastall parameter approaches zero, this solution reduces to the standard Reissner-Nordström metric. To further analyze this black hole, we investigate its stability through geodesic deviation to establish stability criteria. Additionally, we examine its thermodynamic properties, revealing that it is stable, whereas the linear charged case exhibits a second-order phase transition. Finally, we confirm the validity of the first law of thermodynamics for this solution.

Community platforms like Reddit, Yahoo! Answers, and Quora enable users to pose open-ended inquiries to a broad audience, with responses proving valuable for individuals and communities regarding topics such as health, sports, and finance. Amidst the recent COVID-19 crisis, these platforms saw a surge of over 2,000 user questions concerning various disease-related aspects. Considering the pandemic's widespread impact, this study investigates methods to enhance the ranking of user-generated answers specifically for COVID-19 queries. We specifically examine the potential of integrating external technical side information, such as CDC guidelines or WHO FAQs, to improve answer ranking. Our findings indicate that relying solely on question-answer similarity is inadequate, and current models fail to effectively leverage external side information. Instead, we demonstrate the efficacy of attention-based neural models capable of directly utilizing side information from technical documents or verified sources, including research publications and the WHO website. By incorporating a temperature mechanism, these models can selectively assess the relevance of side information to a specific user question during the ranking process.

This paper introduces a Boolean Linear Programming approach for preemptive single-machine scheduling characterized by uniform processing times, flexible release dates, and variable weights aimed at minimizing total weighted completion time. Typically, the Linear Programming relaxation yields an integral optimal solution that can be directly transformed into an optimal schedule. For instances resulting in fractional solutions, we offer two heuristic methods; frequently, these heuristics achieve objective values matching the lower bounds established by the relaxation. When the heuristic upper bounds diverge from the lower bounds, we integrate them into a Branch and Bound framework to guarantee an optimal solution. Extensive computational testing demonstrates that this algorithm significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

The Horizon-10T collaboration \cite{Beisembaev:2016cyg,2017EPJWC.14514001B,Beznosko:2019cI,2019EPJWC.20806002B,Beisembaev:2019nzd} has reported the detection of Multi-Modal Events (MMEs) characterized by multiple peaks indicative of a clustering origin, which cannot be adequately explained by conventional cosmic rays (CR). We hypothesize that these MMEs originate from dark matter annihilation within the axion quark nugget (AQN) framework, a model initially developed to account for the observed parity between dark and visible matter densities ($\Omega_{\rm DM}\sim \Omega_{\rm visible}$) without adjustable parameters. This hypothesis is supported by showing that the AQN annihilation emission in the atmosphere aligns well with the observed MME properties, including their frequency, intensity, spatial distribution, duration, clustering behavior, and other characteristics. We outline several distinct features of AQN events that differentiate them from standard CR air showers; the presence or absence of these features in future observations could validate or refute our proposal.

Contrastive learning has recently experienced a revival within self-supervised representation learning for deep models. This paper reveals that current contrastive approaches for self-supervised video recognition primarily address inter-variance while overlooking the intra-variance present within clips of the same video. Consequently, we introduce a method to learn dual representations for each clip: (\romannumeral 1) encoding intra-variance via a shuffle-rank pretext task, and (\romannumeral 2) encoding inter-variance through a temporally coherent contrastive loss. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach is crucial for balancing both types of variance, yielding consistent performance improvements across various backbones and contrastive frameworks. When integrated with SimCLR and pretrained on Kinetics-400, our method achieves downstream classification accuracies of $\textbf{82.0\%}$ on UCF101 and $\textbf{51.2\%}$ on HMDB51, along with a video retrieval accuracy of $\textbf{46.1\%}$ on UCF101, surpassing both pretext-task and contrastive learning baselines. The source code is accessible at \href{https://github.com/lzhangbj/DualVar}{https://github.com/lzhangbj/DualVar}.

Numerous new commercial services operate by sharing or pooling resources to lower expenses, with delivery, mobility, and transport-as-a-service models becoming widespread standards that fulfill live, on-demand customer requests. Despite their prevalence, many such challenges are classified as NP-hard, making accurate modeling and resolution difficult. This study examines the Ride Pooling Problem (RPP), a specific routing scenario where multiple customers seek on-demand pickups and drop-offs from a shared fleet. The core combinatorial optimization task involves efficiently grouping these requests using a limited number of vehicles, similar to operating a small-scale, flexible bus route. To address this, we develop a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) formulation and present efficient methods for solving the RPP via metaheuristics, with a specific focus on emerging quantum optimization algorithms.

We introduce a sample of 19 radio-luminous supernovae (SNe), exhibiting flux densities between $L_{\nu}{\sim}10^{26}-10^{29}\,\rm{erg\,s^{-1}Hz^{-1}}$ during the initial phase of the Very Large Array Sky Survey (VLASS) at 2–4 GHz.
