This group comprises one long Gamma-Ray Burst, SN 2017iuk/GRB171205A, alongside 18 core-collapse SNe observed approximately 1 to 60 years post-explosion. No thermonuclear explosions displayed significant radio emission, and core-collapse events with spectroscopic classifications at the time of detonation were predominantly hydrogen-poor (79%). We analyze these results within the framework of radio emission generated by forward shock interactions with the circumstellar medium (CSM). Our findings suggest deviations from the standard single wind-like density profile ($\rho_{\rm{CSM}}\propto r^{-2}$) anticipated around massive stars and/or from a spherical Newtonian shock model. Plausible explanations include shock interaction with a detached, dense CSM shell created by a high mass-loss rate ($\dot M \sim (10^{-4}-10^{-1})$ M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, assuming a wind velocity of $1000\,\rm{km\,s^{-1}}$), emission from an off-axis relativistic jet intersecting our line of sight, or the rise of a newly formed pulsar-wind nebula. The relativistic SN 2012ap, detected 5.7 and 8.5 years after explosion with $L_{\nu}{\sim}10^{28}$ erg s$^{-1}$ Hz$^{-1}$, may represent the first identification of an off-axis jet+cocoon system in a massive star; however, no VLASS-SNe with archival data align with our modeled off-axis jet light curves. Upcoming multi-wavelength observations will be necessary to differentiate between these scenarios. The VLASS source catalogs utilized for cross-matching are accessible publicly at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4895112.

This study examines the behavior of gas and dust near pressure bumps within a protoplanetary disc (PPD) influenced by Vertical Shear Instability (VSI) turbulence. We conducted global 2D axisymmetric and 3D simulations across varying dust-to-gas ratios (Z), particle Stokes numbers ($\tau$), and pressure bump amplitudes (A), incorporating dust feedback mechanisms. For the first time, our global 3D simulations reveal the accumulation of dust within long-lived vortices generated by the VSI. In the absence of a pressure bump, with Z $\approx$ 0.01 and $\tau$ $\approx$ 0.01, these vortices achieve dust-to-gas density ratios just below unity in the mid-plane; however, such vortices are largely absent when Z > 0.05. When a pressure bump is present and Z $\approx$ 0.01 with $\tau$ $\approx$ 0.01, a dusty vortex forms with ratios several times unity, potentially triggering the SI before shearing into a turbulent dust ring. At Z $\approx$ 0.03, this occurs for $\tau$ $\approx$ 0.005, producing a weaker, short-lived vortex, whereas larger $\tau$ values result only in a turbulent dust ring. For Z > 0.03, the dust ring becomes increasingly axisymmetric with higher $\tau$, reaching d/g ratios of approximately 1 when $\tau$ > 0.005. Additionally, for Z > 0.03, the vertical mass flow profile is significantly altered by dust: gas moves inward near the mid-plane and outward at greater heights, reversing the pattern seen in simulations with low or zero dust content. Viscous $\alpha$-values decrease moderately from 0.001 to 0.0001 as Z increases from 0 to 0.05. Our findings suggest that the VSI can actively contribute to planetesimal formation via vortex creation for realistic Z and $\tau$ values and may explain the variable presence or absence of asymmetries in observed PPD dust rings based on Z.

Research on neural activity in behaving animals often seeks to identify interpretable, low-dimensional structures within large-scale population recordings. One method used for this purpose is demixed principal component analysis (dPCA), a supervised linear technique designed to isolate components tied to specific experimental parameters. In this work, I present kernel dPCA (kdPCA), a nonlinear extension of dPCA achieved by applying kernel least-squares regression to the demixing process. Using simulated neural populations with known low-dimensional activity, I compare the components recovered by dPCA and kdPCA. These simulations reveal that neural nonlinearities, such as stimulus-dependent gain and rotation, can hinder the linear demixing of activity into parameter-specific components. Nevertheless, kdPCA successfully recovers interpretable components in these scenarios. Finally, I apply kdPCA to two real-world datasets of neural populations recorded during perceptual decision-making tasks.

This study theoretically examines the optimal operation of an optical key distribution (OKD) link, which utilizes fine intensity modulation of an optical signal sent through an attenuating channel to a direct detection receiver. By employing appropriate digital postprocessing, users can generate a secret key that remains unknown to an unauthorized party passively intercepting a portion of the signal missed by the legitimate receiver. Security is guaranteed by the shot noise inherent in any eavesdropper's attempt to detect the intercepted signal. The analysis demonstrates that the amount of key material generated depends on the ratio between the legitimate recipient's and the eavesdropper's detection capabilities, including the noise contributions from their respective detectors. A simple proportional relationship is derived for the strong eavesdropping scenario, and closed-form expressions are provided for the optimal binary intensity modulation depth and the discrimination thresholds required for hard-decoded direct detection. These findings significantly streamline the design of practical OKD systems, particularly those operating under varying external conditions such as fluctuating atmospheric absorption in free-space optical links.

We have assessed the centrality dependence of chemical freeze-out parameters using yield data for $\pi^\pm$, $K^\pm$, $p$, and $\bar{p}$ at mid-rapidity across collision energies from the LHC, RHIC-BES, and RHIC experiments. Our analysis utilized a simple hadron resonance gas model and a parameterization scheme based on QCD conserved charges ($B, Q, S$). The model incorporates temperature, three chemical potentials ($T, \mu_B, \mu_Q, \mu_S$), and a strangeness under-saturation factor ($\gamma_S$) to account for partial equilibration in the strange sector. Our results indicate that the freeze-out temperature remains relatively constant with varying centrality, while chemical potentials and $\gamma_S$ exhibit significant centrality dependence. Notably, strange hadrons deviate from full chemical equilibrium at freeze-out during peripheral collisions, a discrepancy that becomes more pronounced at lower RHIC-BES energies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this departure from equilibrium diminishes in central collisions, suggesting that strange particle equilibration occurs once a threshold number of participants is reached in $A$-$A$ collisions.

We examine perturbative four-point amplitudes within the most basic string theory models featuring T-fold backgrounds, specifically those exhibiting N=6 supersymmetry in four dimensions. These models consist of two theories constructed as asymmetric orbifolds of orders 2 and 3, respectively. Our analysis demonstrates that both the perturbative spectrum and the one-loop four-point amplitudes remain invariant under an arithmetic symplectic group defined over Hurwitz (and respectively Eisenstein) quaternions. We identify the supersymmetry-imposed constraints on low-energy effective couplings, conjecture the theory's U-duality group, and propose that the non-perturbative completion of the six-derivative coupling corresponds to a rank-one theta series. Furthermore, we explore the non-perturbative spectrum of BPS states based on our findings.

Recent breakthroughs in optical magnetometry have established record-breaking sensitivity across both macroscopic and nanoscopic scales, facilitating numerous applications through high bandwidth and room-temperature operation. In contrast, microscale optical magnetometers have historically been limited to sensitivities approximately five orders of magnitude inferior to current state-of-the-art performance. This study presents, for the first time, an ambient optical micro-magnetometer capable of picoTesla-level sensitivity, representing a leap forward of over three orders of magnitude compared to prior achievements. Distinct from other ultra-sensitive optical magnetometers, this device functions at Earth's magnetic field strength, delivers tens of MHz bandwidth, and features an integrated, fiber-coupled design. With a spatial resolution of 60 micrometers and minimal optical power requirements in the microWatt range, these distinctive attributes enable diverse applications, including cryogen-free and microfluidic magnetic resonance imaging, as well as the electromagnetic interference-free study of spin physics in condensed matter systems like semiconductors and ultracold atom clouds.

While deep learning has proven effective at modeling intricate facial details using high-quality imagery, accurately recognizing faces in uncontrolled, real-world environments remains a significant challenge. In unconstrained settings, factors like lighting, pose, and occlusion introduce variations that distort the deep feature space, causing direct feature-to-label associations to yield suboptimal results. Consequently, a preliminary analysis of the feature space is essential before attempting recognition. This paper proposes a joint clustering and classification framework that learns face associations progressively from easy to difficult instances. The approach utilizes hierarchical clustering, where early iterations maintain high reliability. The underlying principle is that trustworthy clustering outcomes reveal the feature space's distribution, thereby guiding subsequent classification steps. Experimental results across face verification, identification, and rank-order search tasks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves performance that is either superior to or competitive with current state-of-the-art techniques.

The weak-gravity bound, previously identified in asymptotically safe gravity-matter systems as a cap on gravitational fluctuation strength, is investigated in this study for the first time within multi-gauge field configurations. We examine whether a system containing 12 gauge fields, analogous to the Standard Model, adheres to this bound and if the gravitational fixed point can circumvent it. Additionally, we assess the robustness of both current and prior findings by analyzing their sensitivity to the gravitational gauge parameter. Beyond theoretical implications, the weak-gravity bound carries significant phenomenological weight, serving as a cornerstone for a mechanism that restricts spacetime dimensionality to four or five dimensions. This paper reinforces evidence for such a mechanism, thereby enhancing the predictive capacity of the asymptotic safety paradigm to derive spacetime geometric parameters from first principles, potentially explaining the universe's four-dimensional nature.

PointGoal Navigation is an embodied task where agents must reach a designated location within an unseen environment. Although Wijmans et al. demonstrated that this task is solvable, their approach is computationally expensive, demanding 2.5 billion frames and 180 GPU-days. This study introduces a method to markedly enhance both sample and time efficiency for learning PointNav by incorporating self-supervised auxiliary tasks, such as predicting actions between egocentric views or distances along a trajectory. We observe that simply stacking multiple auxiliary tasks boosts sample efficiency but yields diminishing returns beyond a certain threshold. To address this, we employ attention mechanisms to integrate representations derived from individual auxiliary tasks. Our top-performing agent achieves the same performance level as the previous state-of-the-art, DD-PPO, in 5.5 fewer frames (reaching that benchmark at 40M frames), while also surpassing DD-PPO's performance at 40M frames by 0.16 SPL. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/joel99/habitat-pointnav-aux.

While the classical method for counting lattice points in a triangle applies when the lattice is $\mathbf{Z}^2$ and the vertices possess integer coordinates, we investigate the scenario where the lattice is substituted with $(2 \mathbf{Z})^2$. We provide an explicit formula expressing the count of such points within a triangle using Hardy sums. Furthermore, we offer a second geometric interpretation of these sums as signed intersection numbers with a specific oriented network of geodesics. Leveraging this geometric perspective, we establish a generalized reciprocity law for Hardy sums through an elementary proof.

This article examines a random access protocol for indoor Internet of Things (IoT) systems utilizing optical wireless communication (OWC). We analyze a Slotted ALOHA (SA) approach where multiple OWC IoT devices compete to transmit data to a central receiver. For any active user selected at random within a slot, we assess the decoding reliability of their data packet by deriving signal-to-noise-and-interference-ratio (SINR) statistics and calculating the probability that the SINR falls below a specific threshold. Situated within an indoor OWC uplink environment and using a standard channel model, we explore the trade-offs between reliability and system parameters, such as cell area and transmitter semi-angle. These findings offer critical insights for designing SA-based random access solutions in typical indoor OWC cells.

Peer review serves as a prevalent strategy for student engagement, a pedagogical approach proven to enhance educational results, yet empirical data regarding its use in visualization courses remains scarce. Beyond fostering engagement, this method offers varied feedback and strengthens recently acquired concepts by requiring students to critically evaluate their peers' work. This study examines the implementation and application of peer review within two visualization courses offered by different colleges at the University of South Florida. We further analyze student projects and peer review comments using sentiment analysis to derive actionable insights for visualization instructors, covering areas such as content focus, engagement levels across diverse student groups, concept mastery, temporal course trends, and the efficacy of expert intervention. Ultimately, we offer recommendations for adapting peer review mechanisms in other visualization contexts to boost student engagement and deepen instructors' comprehension of the peer review process.

We demonstrate that, given a specific non-cancellation condition, the attenuated Radon transform uniquely recovers a piecewise constant attenuation coefficient $a$ and a piecewise $C^2$ source density $f$ featuring jumps across real analytic boundaries that may include corners. Additionally, we examine numerical cases where this non-cancellation condition is violated, revealing that unique reconstruction of multi-bang $a$ and $f$ remains seemingly feasible, even though current theoretical frameworks do not yet account for this phenomenon.

Characterizing laser-accelerated ion bunches presents significant challenges, necessitating the creation of specialized beam diagnostics. Specifically, the brief, high-intensity particle bunches characterized by wide energy distributions and accompanying strong electromagnetic pulses (EMPs) exceed the capabilities of standard monitoring technologies. Recently, an ionoacoustic method—measuring acoustic waves generated by energy deposition in water—has been refined into the Ion-Bunch Energy Acoustic Tracing (I-BEAT) system [https://doi.org/10.1118/1.4905047]\cite{haffa_i-beat:_2019}. I-BEAT enables cost-effective, EMP-resistant online detection of individual proton bunches. By utilizing a simple water phantom with a single ultrasound transducer aligned with the ion beam, the system can reconstruct the intricate energy spectra typical of manipulated laser-accelerated ions. To capture lateral bunch characteristics, additional transducers can be incorporated, such as those placed perpendicular to the beam axis. This established configuration was adapted for deployment immediately behind the laser target and validated at the PHELIX laser facility at GSI, successfully demonstrating its ability to retrieve broad proton spectral data despite harsh near-source conditions. While future enhancements, particularly expanding the dynamic range, are necessary, I-BEAT shows great potential to become a dedicated online diagnostic tool for developing and optimizing high-repetition-rate laser-driven ion sources.

Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) is a prevalent technique for investigating the development and degeneration of brain white matter. However, conventional DTI estimation approaches rely on a substantial number of high-quality measurements, necessitating lengthy scan times that pose significant challenges for specific patient groups, such as neonates. We introduce a novel method capable of accurately estimating the diffusion tensor using only six diffusion-weighted measurements. This is achieved by training the model to leverage relationships between diffusion signals and tensors in adjacent voxels. Built upon transformer networks, which currently represent the leading technology for modeling sequential signal relationships, our architecture comprises two distinct networks. The first network estimates the diffusion tensor based on diffusion signals within a local voxel neighborhood. The second network refines these estimations by learning correlations between diffusion signals and the tensors predicted by the first network across neighboring voxels. Experimental results across three datasets demonstrate that our proposed method yields highly accurate diffusion tensor estimations, outperforming three competing methods. Specifically, estimations derived from our method using just six measurements match the quality of standard methods requiring 30 to 88 measurements. Consequently, this approach offers the potential for reduced scan times and more reliable white matter assessment, particularly for non-cooperative patients like infants and neonates.

Battery energy storage serves as a critical element within microgrids, where maintaining optimal battery operating temperatures is vital; excessive heat typically elevates losses, shortens lifespan, and poses fire risks. Consequently, effectively managing the thermal profile of battery modules and packs during operation is indispensable. To address this, a two-layer optimal control and operation framework is introduced for microgrids incorporating energy storage. The first layer establishes an optimal control model to determine a policy that minimizes control efforts—specifically fan speed and battery current magnitude—to meet a target temperature distribution across the modules. The second layer involves the microgrid operator conducting an optimal power flow to identify the ideal temperature distribution reference for the first layer and the associated battery operating current, thereby minimizing the overall system's operational costs. This hierarchical approach provides significant computational advantages, facilitating the large-scale integration of battery systems. A case study validates the proposed two-layer model by demonstrating its performance.

Background Foreground Separation (BFS) is a prevalent computer vision task involving the isolation of moving foreground elements from a static scene background. This process is typically executed using consumer-grade cameras, favored for their affordability, high resolution, and ease of human interpretation. However, both the cameras and the BFS algorithms used to analyze their data often encounter shared limitations caused by lighting fluctuations, reflective surfaces, and occlusions. To address these issues, integrating an additional sensor modality can enhance robustness. This paper investigates how a cost-effective radar system can complement the widely used Robust PCA method for BFS. By applying the emerging algorithm unrolling technique, we achieve real-time computation, feedforward inference, and superior generalization compared to conventional deep learning approaches. Evaluation on the RaDICaL dataset demonstrates both quantitative gains from incorporating radar data and qualitative evidence of improved robustness against typical failure modes found in image-only methods.

Virasoro conformal blocks serve as universal components within correlation functions of two-dimensional conformal field theories (2d CFTs) possessing Virasoro symmetry. It is recognized that in the classical regime—characterized by a large central charge and large external and intermediate conformal weights with fixed ratios—Virasoro blocks exponentiate into functions termed Zamolodchikov's classical blocks. These special functions possess profound mathematical and physical significance, finding applications across diverse fields such as uniformization, monodromy problems, black hole physics, quantum gravity, entanglement, quantum chaos, holography, N=2 gauge theory, and quantum integrable systems (QIS). In this paper, leveraging established connections between the power series and integral representations of (quantum) Virasoro blocks, we introduce new finite closed-form expressions for specific multi-point classical Virasoro blocks on the sphere. Specifically, by merging the classical limit of Virasoro block expansions with the saddle-point asymptotics of Dotsenko-Fateev (DF) integrals, we establish a relationship between classical Virasoro blocks and the critical value of the "Dotsenko-Fateev matrix model action." This action is the "DF action" evaluated at a solution to the saddle-point equations, which manifest as Bethe equations for certain QIS, namely Gaudin spin models. Our primary motivation for this research stems from the connection to integrable models.

Distributionally robust optimization utilizes multiple probability measures within its framework, which can be aggregated to form a risk functional. This equivalence establishes risk functionals as a core component of distributionally robust stochastic programming. Multistage programming, however, necessitates conditional versions of these functionals to evaluate future risks following partial realizations and prior decisions. This paper presents a method for constructing the conditional counterpart of a risk functional by transferring its intrinsic properties to its conditional forms. The resulting conditional risk functionals differ from the nested analogues of the original law-invariant risk measure. Furthermore, it is shown that the initial measure and its nested decomposition are applicable within a distributionally robust multistage context.

This study examines a straightforward mathematical framework designed to investigate the emergence and regulation of radicalization. The model divides the population into two distinct groups: a "core" subpopulation and a "sensitive" subpopulation, whose lifestyles may be partially incompatible. When conflict arises, core agents remain rigidly opposed to the issue, whereas sensitive agents must choose between coexisting peacefully with the core group or opposing them. While Galam and Javarone (2016) previously addressed this modeling approach using constant pairwise couplings, this work extends the analysis to a more general scenario featuring time-dependent transition rates, specifically to evaluate how such temporal variations influence the model's critical behavior. Both analytical and numerical findings indicate that, under certain conditions, the nonequilibrium active-absorbing phase transition can be suppressed. This suppression manifests as the elimination of the absorbing phase, resulting in the complete disappearance of radical agents from the population in stationary states.

We introduce a concept of VC-dimension tailored for subsets of groups, defining the dimension of a set $A$ based on the VC-dimension of the family $\{ (xA) \cap A : x \in A\cdot A^{-1} \}$. Our findings demonstrate that for a finite subset $A$ within an abelian group, bounded VC-dimension ensures that the convolution $1_A*1_{-A}$ exhibits Bohr uniform continuity, with quantitatively significant strength. This result extends and refines a specific formulation of the stable arithmetic regularity lemma by Terry and Wolf. Notably, it directly validates the Polynomial Bogolyubov--Ruzsa Conjecture—a robust variant of the Polynomial Freiman--Ruzsa Conjecture—for sets characterized by bounded VC-dimension. Additionally, we establish several findings applicable to non-abelian contexts. Fundamentally, this work provides a structure theorem for translation-closed set systems possessing bounded (classical) VC-dimension: specifically, if a family of subsets in an abelian group is both VC-bounded and closed under translation, then every member can be described simply using Bohr sets, modulo a minor error.

We examine a spherical particle levitating above a liquid bath due to the Leidenfrost effect, sustained by an insulating vapour film—formed by either the bath or the sphere—that counteracts the particle's weight. Utilizing a reduced model grounded in lubrication-type approximations, we apply matched asymptotics to characterize the vapour film's shape, assuming the sphere is small compared to the capillary length (low Bond number) and that the densities of the sphere and bath are similar. Our analysis reveals that this regime consists of two formally infinite sequences of distinguished limits converging at an accumulation point, governed by the ratio of a small intrinsic evaporation number to the Bond number. These sequences uncover a complex evolution of film morphology as sphere size increases: beginning with a neck-bubble structure typical of Leidenfrost drops on flat solid surfaces and progressing toward a uniform-film configuration resembling that of a large liquid drop floating above a liquid bath.

Rear-actuated ("pullers") and front-actuated ("pushers") microswimmers exhibit distinct collective behaviors in fluid suspensions. While puller suspensions remain stable, pusher suspensions develop a hydrodynamic instability above a specific density threshold, resulting in active turbulence. This study employs kinetic theory and extensive particle-resolved simulations to analyze the collective dynamics of a binary mixture containing both types. We establish and validate an instability criterion demonstrating that the critical density required for active turbulence increases with the fraction of pullers ($\chi$) and vanishes entirely when $\chi \geq 0.5$. Furthermore, both analytical and numerical analyses reveal that the two-point hydrodynamic correlations in a 1:1 pusher-puller mixture match those of a suspension of noninteracting swimmers. Notably, our numerical findings indicate that the full probability distribution of fluid velocity fluctuations in this 1:1 mixture collapses onto that of a noninteracting system at the same density, where swimmer-swimmer correlations are absent. Consequently, our results suggest that fluid velocity fluctuations in 1:1 pusher-puller mixtures are identical to those of the corresponding noninteracting suspension across all densities, representing a surprising cancellation effect with no equivalent in equilibrium long-range interacting systems.

Assume $\widetilde{\mathbb R}$ is an o-minimal expansion of the real field where restricted power functions are definable. We demonstrate that if $\widehat{\mathbb R}$ is both an expansion and a reduct of the expansion $\widetilde{\mathbb R}^{\mathbb R}$ (which includes all real power functions), and provided that $\widetilde{\mathbb R}$ and $\widehat{\mathbb R}$ share the same field of exponents, then they define identical sets. This result represents a polynomially bounded analogue of a longstanding conjecture by van den Dries and Miller.
This paper establishes a theorem demonstrating that every sufficiently large odd number can be expressed as the sum of three nearly equal Piatetski-Shapiro primes.

DRAM-based main memory serves as a critical component in almost all computing systems. A primary strategy to mitigate the memory bottleneck is processing-in-memory (PiM), which relocates computation closer to memory. Recent PiM approaches offer a promising path to enhance performance and energy efficiency in current and future architectures without incurring additional DRAM hardware costs. This work introduces PiDRAM, the first flexible, end-to-end, and open-source framework designed to facilitate system integration studies and the evaluation of practical PiM techniques using actual DRAM chips. A prototype of PiDRAM was developed on an FPGA-based platform (Xilinx ZC706) running an open-source RISC-V system (Rocket Chip). To showcase the framework's flexibility and usability, two PiM techniques were implemented: (1) RowClone, an in-DRAM mechanism for copying and initialization utilizing command sequences from ComputeDRAM, and (2) D-RaNGe, an in-DRAM true random number generator leveraging DRAM activation-latency failures. End-to-end evaluation of RowClone demonstrated up to 14.6X speedup for copy operations and 12.6X speedup for initialization tasks compared to conventional CPU-based methods (memcpy and calloc). The D-RaNGe implementation achieves high-throughput true random number generation at 8.30 Mb/s. Based on the Verilog and C++ foundations provided by PiDRAM, the total implementation effort for RowClone was 198 lines of Verilog and 565 lines of C++, while D-RaNGe required 190 lines of Verilog and 78 lines of C++. The PiDRAM framework is available as open source on GitHub at https://github.com/CMU-SAFARI/PiDRAM.

This work investigates separability conditions for continuous variable states by employing entanglement witnesses constructed from Gaussian operators. We recast the validity of a Gaussian witness as a problem concerning Bosonic Gaussian channels. Consequently, leveraging the properties of these channels, we determine that the maximal expectations for two-mode and certain four-mode Gaussian operators over product pure states are realized by vacuum states (or coherent and squeezed states). Furthermore, we establish necessary and sufficient separability criteria applicable not only to Gaussian quantum states but also to non-Gaussian states generated by adding or subtracting photons from Gaussian states. These criteria can be explicitly formulated using either the covariance matrix of the underlying Gaussian state or that of the Gaussian kernel associated with the non-Gaussian state, thereby facilitating the precise identification of non-Gaussian entanglement.

The STAR Collaboration presents measurements of back-to-back azimuthal correlations for di-$\pi^0$ particles produced at forward pseudorapidity ($2.6<\eta<4.0$) in $p+p$, $p+\mathrm{Al}$, and $p+\mathrm{Au}$ collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon-nucleon pair of 200 GeV. A distinct suppression of away-side correlated yields is evident in $p+\mathrm{Au}$ collisions and, for the first time, in $p+\mathrm{Al}$ collisions when compared to $p+p$ data. The greater suppression observed in $p+\mathrm{Au}$ relative to $p+\mathrm{Al}$ demonstrates a dependence on the mass number $A$ consistent with the saturation scale ($Q_s^2$). Furthermore, the suppression of back-to-back pairs as a function of event activity and transverse momentum indicates the presence of non-linear gluon dynamics driven by high parton densities.

We have developed hypersequent calculus proof systems for the theories of Riesz spaces and modal Riesz spaces, establishing their soundness, completeness, and cut elimination. Leveraging these results, we provide entirely syntactic proofs for several significant findings regarding both theories. A primary achievement is demonstrating that the theory of modal Riesz spaces is decidable. This research holds relevance for the study of logics governing probabilistic programs, as modal Riesz spaces serve as the algebraic semantics for the Riesz modal logic that underpins the probabilistic mu-calculus.

Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) policies are susceptible to unauthorized replication attacks, where adversaries use imitation learning to reconstruct target policies based on observed behavior. To counter this, we introduce Constrained Randomization of Policy (CRoP), a mitigation strategy that triggers random execution of sub-optimal actions while adhering to specific performance loss constraints. This paper provides a parametric analysis of CRoP, investigates its optimality, and derives theoretical bounds regarding the adversarial budget and expected loss. Additionally, we present experimental results evaluating CRoP in Atari environments under adversarial imitation, which confirm the method's effectiveness and practical viability in defending against policy replication attacks.

The CMS collaboration presents updated preliminary findings based on complete datasets from 2011 and 2012 regarding the analysis of a Higgs-like boson at 125 GeV. Combining 5.1$fb^{-1}$ of 7 TeV data and 19.6$fb^{-1}$ of 8 TeV data, the study observes a signal strength of $0.78^{+0.28}_{-0.26}$ relative to Standard Model predictions for a particle with a mass of $125.4\pm0.8$ GeV. This resonance exhibits a significance of $3.2\sigma$ compared to a background-only hypothesis. Additionally, a cut-based cross-check analysis yields a signal strength of $1.11^{+0.32}_{-0.30}$ times the Standard Model expectations, with a significance of $3.9\sigma$ at a mass of 124.5 GeV.

Investigating interacting many-body systems in quantum simulators, such as quantum gas microscopes, has seen significant advancement through the analysis of higher-order correlation functions. Experimental data on mixed spin-charge correlations in the 2D Hubbard model have previously illuminated the equilibrium characteristics of magnetic polarons and distinguished between coherent and incoherent dynamic regimes. This study theoretically extends such methodologies to systems employing pinning potentials to restrict the mobility of a single dopant within the Mott insulating phase of the 2D Hubbard model. Our findings indicate that pinning a dopant drastically alters its magnetic dressing: while third-order connected spin correlations diminish for a mobile hole, they intensify near an immobile one. Regarding fifth-order correlation functions, the bare values exhibit opposite signs between mobile and fully pinned dopants, whereas the connected components remain comparable across both scenarios. We further examine how thermal fluctuations suppress these higher-order correlators, showing they remain detectable at temperatures approaching the spin-exchange energy $J$. Finally, we explore the broader implications of these results for comprehending the interaction between spin and charge in doped Mott insulators.

Utilizing Non-Reductive Geometric Invariant Theory, one can quotient the unstable HKKN strata within a moduli problem defined by Geometric Invariant Theory to build "moduli spaces of unstable objects," thereby broadening standard moduli classifications. Following a comprehensive, self-contained explanation of this procedure, the approach is applied to generate moduli spaces for specific unstable coherent sheaves of HN length 2 on a projective scheme, termed $\tau$-stable sheaves. This work generalizes an earlier finding by Brambila-Paz and Mata-Guti\'{e}rrez concerning rank two vector bundles on a curve.

Contemporary mobile applications often struggle to balance runtime customization and efficiency with context awareness, despite context-oriented programming (COP) offering a path to enhanced context sensitivity. However, COP's primary construct, the "layer," lacks inherent customizability. We introduce novel persistent contextual values designed specifically for mobile development. These values automatically adjust to the current context and enable access without performance overhead. Their specifications and stored values are managed within key-value configuration files, allowing developers to easily tailor contextual values for any specific scenario by simply modifying these files. Additionally, our approach generates code from these specifications to streamline development. Our implementation, named Elektra, supports multiple programming languages, including C++ and Java. Benchmarking compares thread and application-level layer activations, while a case study involving a web server on a mobile embedded device demonstrates minimal performance overhead, even under frequent context switching.

Driven by practical needs in DNA storage, flash memory, and magnetic recording, this study examines perfect burst-correcting codes designed for the limited-magnitude error channel. These codes are defined as lattices that tile the integer grid using a corresponding error ball. We introduce two families of such perfect codes capable of correcting a single burst of length $2$ under $(1,0)$-limited-magnitude errors, covering both cyclic and non-cyclic burst scenarios. Additionally, we propose a general construction method that relies on the existence of a primitive element within a finite field possessing specific attributes. We subsequently demonstrate that such primitive elements exist across various parameter regimes, thereby establishing the existence of infinitely many perfect burst-correcting codes.

This study establishes lower bounds for the size of Clifford circuits used to measure commuting families of Pauli operators. These bounds rely on the relationship between two graphs: the Tanner graph representing the measured Pauli operators and the connectivity graph depicting the qubit links necessary for circuit implementation. Specifically, for local-expander quantum codes—promising candidates for low-overhead quantum error correction—we demonstrate that any syndrome extraction circuit utilizing local Clifford gates within a 2D square patch of $N$ qubits must have a depth of at least $\Omega(n/\sqrt{N})$, where $n$ denotes the code length. Subsequently, we introduce two families of quantum circuits that achieve this bound. First, we develop 2D local syndrome extraction circuits for quantum LDPC codes with bounded depth, employing only $O(n^2)$ ancilla qubits. Second, we design 2D local syndrome extraction circuits for hypergraph product codes that utilize $O(n)$ ancilla qubits and achieve a depth of $O(\sqrt{n})$. Furthermore, circuit noise simulations compare the performance of hypergraph product codes using this final family of 2D syndrome extraction circuits against those using fully connected qubits. While fully connected implementations exhibit a threshold near $10^{-3}$, the 2D local implementation shows no threshold even at simulated error rates as low as $10^{-6}$. This indicates that quantum LDPC codes are likely impractical on 2D local quantum hardware. We believe our proof technique holds independent interest and may be applicable elsewhere. Our circuit size lower bounds are derived by combining a lower bound on the correlations between two subsets of qubits with an upper bound on the correlations introduced by individual circuit gates.

Recommendation systems based on user-item graphs have progressed from relying solely on single identifiers or interaction histories to leveraging higher-order neighbors, a shift that enabled the success of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) like PinSage and LightGCN. However, we contend that these models face two key drawbacks: (1) high-degree nodes disproportionately influence representation learning, which harms the recommendation quality of low-degree (long-tail) items; and (2) the neighborhood aggregation mechanism amplifies the impact of observed edges, making representations susceptible to noisy interactions. To address these issues, this work investigates self-supervised learning on user-item graphs to enhance the accuracy and robustness of GCNs. Our approach augments the traditional supervised recommendation task with an auxiliary self-supervised objective that strengthens node representations through self-discrimination. Specifically, we create multiple views of a node to maximize the agreement between different views of the same node relative to those of other nodes. We introduce three operators—node dropout, edge dropout, and random walks—to generate these views by altering the graph structure in distinct ways. We designate this novel learning framework as \textit{Self-supervised Graph Learning} (SGL) and apply it to the state-of-the-art LightGCN model. Theoretical analysis reveals that SGL can automatically mine hard negatives, while empirical evaluations on three benchmark datasets confirm its effectiveness in boosting recommendation accuracy, particularly for long-tail items, and increasing robustness against interaction noise. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/wujcan/SGL}.

We introduce a straightforward model describing a domain wall within a thin-film ferromagnet. This domain wall is conceptualized as a nonreciprocal string, where transverse waves travel at varying speeds depending on their direction. The model relies on three parameters: mass density, tension, and a gyroscopic constant that measures the degree of nonreciprocity. We examine the distinctive dynamics of such a nonreciprocal string within a finite geometry, finding that it aligns closely with numerical simulations of ferromagnetic domain wall motion in a strip of uniform width.

The mystery of how the million-degree corona persists above the cooler photosphere remains an unsolved challenge in astrophysics. Investigating the quiescent corona, which exists independently of the solar cycle's phase, may offer valuable clues to solving this puzzle. However, because these regions are spatially unresolved, the characteristics of heating mechanisms can only be derived statistically. This study introduces a two-step inversion framework, adapting the machine learning approach of Upendran & Tripathi (2021a) to the empirical impulsive heating model by Pauluhn & Solanki (2007), and applies it to disk-integrated flux data from the quiet corona obtained by the X-ray solar monitor (XSM) on Chandrayaan-2. Utilizing three energy bands (1–1.3 keV, 1.3–2.3 keV, and 1–2.3 keV), we estimated the frequency, duration, amplitudes, and amplitude distribution of typical impulsive events. Our findings indicate that these events occur at a rate of approximately 25 per minute with a mean lifetime of about 10 minutes. They follow a power-law distribution with a slope $\alpha \leq 2.0$. The typical energy amplitudes range from $10^{21}$ to $10^{24}$ ergs, exhibiting a radiative loss of roughly $\approx 10^3$ erg cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ within the 1–2.3 keV band. These results impose additional constraints on the properties of sub-pixel impulsive events required to sustain the quiet solar corona.

EBLM J0113+31 is a moderately luminous (V=10.1), metal-poor ([Fe/H]$\approx-0.3$) G0V star hosting a significantly fainter M dwarf companion in a wide, eccentric orbit with a period of 14.3 days. By combining near-infrared spectroscopy from the SPIRou instrument—which measured the M dwarf's orbital semi-amplitude—with high-precision eclipse and transit photometry from CHEOPS and TESS, we determined the system's geometry. Integrating these new findings with prior observations yields model-independent mass and radius values of $M_1 = 1.029 \pm 0.025 M_{\odot}$, $M_2 = 0.197 \pm 0.003 M_{\odot}$, $R_1 = 1.417 \pm 0.014 R_{\odot}$, and $R_2 = 0.215 \pm 0.002 R_{\odot}$. Utilizing the primary star's radius and the Gaia EDR3 parallax, we calculated its angular diameter as $\theta = 0.0745 \pm 0.0007$ mas. After correcting for extinction and the negligible flux contribution from the M dwarf (<0.2%), the apparent bolometric flux is ${\mathcal F}_{\oplus,0} = (2.62\pm 0.05)\times10^{-9}$ erg.cm$^{-2}$.s$^{-1}$, resulting in an effective temperature for the G0V star of $T_{\rm eff,1} = 6124{\rm\,K} \pm 40{\rm \,K\,(rnd.)} \pm 10 {\rm \,K\,(sys.)}$. EBLM J0113+31 serves as an ideal benchmark for validating stellar parameters derived from large-scale spectroscopic surveys and asteroseismology via PLATO. The methodologies employed here can be extended to numerous other eclipsing binaries to establish a broader network of such reference stars.

This paper investigates thermo-electric transport within interacting two-dimensional Dirac-type systems by employing a phenomenological Boltzmann framework. We examine a configuration capable of supporting electrons, holes, and collective modes. The initial section focuses on electron-hole hydrodynamics, a model widely used in graphene research, and analyzes its transport characteristics. Subsequently, we introduce a new form of hydrodynamics where the fluid comprises electrons, holes, and plasmons, with a specific emphasis on its thermo-electric properties. These findings can also be extended to fluids consisting of electrons and phonons. Additionally, a companion technical paper provides a rigorous derivation of the Boltzmann equations and the associated conservation laws.

This study presents observations of gamma-ray emissions within the 100 TeV range originating from the Cygnus region of our Galaxy. Two sources are significantly detected, corresponding to the directions of the Cygnus OB1 and OB2 associations. Based on positional alignment, one source is linked to the pulsar PSR J2032+4127, while the other is primarily associated with the pulsar wind nebula G75.2+0.1, whose central pulsar has drifted away from its birthplace near the centroid of the gamma-ray emission. These findings are expected to encourage further investigation into particle acceleration mechanisms at these gamma-ray sources.

This paper demonstrates the existence of a strongly universal cellular automaton within the dodecagrid, the {5,3,4} tessellation of hyperbolic 3D space, utilizing only four states. Unlike the five-state, rotation-invariant automaton described in arXiv:2104.01561, the automaton presented here lacks full rotation invariance. Consequently, this work does not represent an improvement over arXiv:2104.01561; rather, the reduction to four states is achieved by relaxing the strict requirement of rotation invariance. This relaxation remains partial: the rules remain invariant under rotations of the dodecahedron that preserve the structure globally and maintain a pair of opposite faces. Given that there are twenty-five such rotations, the reduction to four states is deemed significant despite the necessary compromise on invariance.

The trend of decarbonization through electrification necessitates substantial grid investments, prompting a need for revised tariff structures that effectively incentivize peak load reduction. However, the price signals conveyed by these tariffs may become distorted when combined with spot prices, which constitute a major portion of total consumer bills. This study investigates potential conflicts between grid tariff signals and spot prices. By employing a generic demand response model within a cost-minimizing linear program to simulate peak load reductions, the authors compare four distinct tariff designs using metered data from 3,608 consumers in Oslo, Norway. The findings indicate that novel tariff designs achieve peak load reductions ranging from 1% to 4%, with lower reduction rates observed when consumers are also exposed to electricity spot prices.

This research examines the contact process on random graphs characterized by low infection rates, $\lambda$. While it is established that survival time on random $d$-regular graphs remains $O(\log n)$ below the critical threshold $\lambda_c$, the dynamics differ significantly on Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi graphs $\mathcal G(n,d/n)$, where rare high-degree nodes enable substantially prolonged survival. We demonstrate that survival duration is dictated by high-density local configurations; specifically, we identify a contiguous sequence of high-degree vertices sustaining infection for a duration of $n^{\lambda^{2+o(1)}}$. To derive a corresponding upper bound, we propose a modified contact process that disregards infections failing to propagate further, thereby facilitating a sharper recursive analysis on branching process trees representing the graph's local-weak limit. Furthermore, our approach extends to random graphs with specified degree distributions possessing exponential moments.

This volume explores a broad spectrum of problems where stochastic processes, stochastic calculus, large deviation theory, group representation theory, and quantum statistics are applied across diverse domains including dynamical systems, electromagnetics, statistical signal processing, quantum information theory, quantum neural networks, quantum filtering, quantum electrodynamics, quantum general relativity, string theory, biology, and both classical and quantum fluid dynamics. The problem selection draws from courses the author has delivered to undergraduate and postgraduate students in electronics and communication engineering. Furthermore, stochastic process theory is utilized to address system identification challenges based on time series models, leading to the derivation of recursive parameter estimation methods for both time and order, followed by a statistical performance analysis.

For a spectrally negative Lévy process $X$, let $g_t$ denote the last moment $X$ remains below zero prior to time $t \geq 0$. Employing a perturbation technique for Lévy processes, we establish an Itô formula and determine the infinitesimal generator for the three-dimensional process $\{(g_t, t, X_t), t \geq 0\}$. Furthermore, defining $U_t := t - g_t$ as the duration of the current positive excursion, we derive a comprehensive formula to compute functionals of the entire path of $(U, X) = \{(U_t, X_t), t \geq 0\}$ based on the positive and negative excursions of $X$. As a corollary, we obtain the joint Laplace transform of $(U_{\mathbf{e}_q}, X_{\mathbf{e}_q})$, where $\mathbf{e}_q$ represents an independent exponential time, along with the $q$-potential measure for the process $(U, X)$. Additionally, leveraging these findings, we solve a general optimal stopping problem dependent on $(U, X)$, including applications related to corporate bankruptcy. Finally, we demonstrate a connection between the optimal prediction of $g_{\infty}$ and optimal stopping problems formulated in terms of $(U, X)$, consistent with the approach by Baurdoux and Pedraza (2020).

In the context of upmixing stereo audio to multichannel for music, a primary objective is to determine the directional placement of instrument sources within the rendered output. This paper introduces a modified variational autoencoder designed to learn a latent space that represents spatial imagery in multichannel music. By disentangling spatial images from the underlying musical content, the model ensures that its latent variables remain invariant to the specific audio track. During inference, these latent variables are utilized to control source panning. We demonstrate two application scenarios: transferring spatial images across different songs and performing blind panning driven by the generative model. Through both objective and subjective evaluations, we empirically validate that the model successfully isolates spatial imagery from music content and enables interactive, transfer-based panning.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) hold great promise for next-generation 6G wireless networks. However, the large number of elements typically required leads to significant overhead in channel estimation and notable power consumption. Consequently, enhancing system capacity while restricting the number of RIS elements is critical. Departing from conventional regular RIS architectures where elements are placed on a uniform grid, this paper introduces an irregular RIS structure. The core concept involves distributing a fixed set of RIS elements across an expanded surface in an irregular pattern, thereby offering additional spatial degrees of freedom compared to regular configurations. This approach boosts received signal power, ultimately increasing system capacity. We formulate a joint optimization problem to simultaneously determine the RIS topology and precoding strategy for maximizing capacity in irregular RIS-aided systems. To address this, we propose a low-complexity algorithm that alternately optimizes the topology and precoding. Specifically, a tabu search-based method is employed to design the irregular topology, while a neighbor extraction-based cross-entropy method is utilized for precoding optimization. Simulation results confirm that, under constraints on the number of RIS elements, the proposed irregular RIS architecture significantly improves system capacity.

Traditional approaches typically aggregate frame-level visual features over time using methods like LSTM, Fisher Vectors, or NetVLAD to generate robust video-level representations. In this work, we propose a learnable aggregation technique designed primarily to preserve short-term temporal structures between frame-level features and their spatial interdependencies within the representation. Additionally, the method is highly adaptable to scenarios with very limited training data. We evaluate our approach on a real-fake expression prediction dataset to demonstrate its superiority. On the official MAP evaluation of the test dataset, our method achieves a 65% score, matching the best reported result in the Chalearn Challenge with only a single misclassified decision (66.7%). Finally, we believe this method can be extended to other tasks, such as action or event recognition, in the future.

Polyethylene Naphthalate (PEN) plastic scintillator has emerged as a promising candidate for self-vetoing structural materials in low-background physics experiments. Radio-pure PEN scintillating components were fabricated via injection compression molding and are intended to serve as active mounts for Germanium detectors within the \legend-$200$ neutrinoless double beta decay experiment. This paper details the measurement of the optical properties of these components, reporting on the emission spectrum, time constant, attenuation, bulk absorption length, light output, and light yield. Furthermore, the surfaces of the PEN components were characterized, including an assessment of surface roughness. The light output of the completed \legend-$200$ detector holders was also measured and reported. Based on these findings, the self-vetoing efficiency of the holders was estimated.

This study introduces an Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC) framework utilizing in-band Full Duplex (FD) radios. The setup features a massive Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) base station employing hybrid Analog and Digital (A/D) beamforming to serve multiple DownLink (DL) users while concurrently estimating the Direction of Arrival (DoA) and range of randomly located radar targets using identical signaling waveforms. Leveraging a recently developed reduced-complexity FD hybrid A/D beamforming architecture, we propose a unified protocol for DL data transmission and radar target tracking. Furthermore, we present an optimization framework designed for the joint configuration of massive A/D beamformers and the Self-Interference (SI) cancellation unit, aiming to simultaneously enhance radar tracking precision and DL communication performance. Simulation results at millimeter-wave frequencies, based on 5G NR wideband waveforms, demonstrate the system's superior radar tracking accuracy and its ability to achieve higher sum rates compared to benchmark methods.

This study evaluates the classical approximation of the waterfall phase transition in hybrid inflation using an effective field theory (EFT) framework. By integrating out the waterfall field fluctuations up to the one-loop order of the perturbative expansion, we observe that, under slow-roll conditions immediately following the waterfall's onset, the backreaction of these fluctuations on the system's evolution can become dominant. Such dominance completely invalidates the classical approximation. Consequently, we establish the specific constraint required to ensure the EFT remains valid.

This research investigates the relative roles of dynamical and explicit chiral symmetry breaking within QCD models utilizing the quark-gap equation, varying frequently used ans\"atze for the dressed interaction and quark-gluon vertex. While explicit symmetry breaking is characterized by a constituent-quark sigma term, the combined impact of both breaking mechanisms is captured by a Euclidean constituent-mass solution. The analysis extends to a quark-gluon vertex surpassing the Abelian approximation, incorporating numerical gluon and ghost dressing functions derived from lattice QCD. Results indicate that the ratio of the sigma term to the Euclidean mass remains largely invariant across different nonperturbative interaction and vertex models for current-quark masses ranging from $m_{u,d}(\mu)$ to $m_b(\mu)$. Specifically, equal contributions from explicit and dynamical chiral symmetry breaking arise at $m(\mu) \approx 400$~MeV; however, when employing lattice propagators for massive gap equation solutions, this threshold drops to approximately 200~MeV.

Programmable packet-processing hardware, including switches and network interface cards, is rapidly gaining mainstream adoption. These systems are configured using domain-specific languages like P4, where compilers translate high-level programs into machine instructions tailored for specific targets. As networks increasingly rely on such programmable devices, ensuring the reliability of these compilers becomes paramount.

This paper addresses the challenge of identifying compiler bugs within the P4-16 framework for packet processing. We present domain-specific techniques designed to trigger both abnormal terminations (crash bugs) and miscompilations (semantic bugs) in compilers. These methods were applied to three platforms: (1) the open-source P4 compiler (P4C) infrastructure, which acts as a common foundation for various back ends; (2) the P4 back end for the reference software switch; and (3) the P4 back end for the Barefoot Tofino switch.

Over an eight-month period across these three platforms, our tool, Gauntlet, identified 96 distinct new bugs, comprising 62 crashes and 34 semantic errors, all of which were verified by the respective compiler developers. Of these, 54 bugs (31 crashes and 23 semantic) have been resolved, while the remainder have been assigned to developers. Additionally, our findings prompted six updates to the P4 specification. We have open-sourced Gauntlet at p4gauntlet.github.io, and it is now integrated into P4C's continuous integration pipeline.

Adversarial machine learning research has demonstrated that injecting even a small number of poisoned data points into training sets can severely degrade model performance. Although the impact of such attacks on model accuracy has been extensively examined, their influence on other performance metrics remains largely unexplored. This study presents an optimization framework designed to target algorithmic fairness through poisoning attacks, specifically developing a gradient-based method to induce classification disparities across different demographic groups. Our empirical results confirm the effectiveness of this attack in both white-box scenarios, where the attacker possesses full access to the target model, and black-box scenarios, where the attack is optimized against a surrogate model and transferred to the target. We argue that these findings establish a foundation for defining a new class of adversarial attacks focused on algorithmic fairness across various contexts, and that understanding these vulnerabilities is essential for developing more robust algorithms and countermeasures in the future.

This study details a modeling effort spanning over two decades of the solar wind-magnetosphere-ionosphere system, utilizing version 5 of the Grand Unified Magnetosphere-Ionosphere Coupling Simulation (GUMICS-5). Input data consist of 16-second resolution magnetic field measurements and 1-minute plasma data from the Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE) satellite, covering the period from 1998 to 2020. The modeled timeframe is segmented into 28-hour simulations with a 4-hour overlap. The magnetospheric grid achieves a maximum resolution of 0.5 Earth radii (Re) within approximately 15 Re of Earth, with resolution diminishing at greater distances. In the ionosphere, resolution peaks at roughly 100 km poleward of ±58° magnetic latitude, decreasing toward the equator. Compared to GUMICS-4, GUMICS-5 features a parallelized magnetosphere implemented via the Message Passing Interface and incorporates various enhancements, such as reduced numerical diffusion.

Simulation outputs are compared against multiple empirical models and geomagnetic indices derived from ground-based magnetic field observations. GUMICS-5 successfully reproduces observed solar cycle variations in magnetopause stand-off distance and magnetospheric lobe field strength; however, consistency regarding plasma sheet pressure and ionospheric cross-polar cap potential is less pronounced. Geomagnetic index comparisons yield superior results for the Kp index relative to the AE index. The complete simulation data, including full ionospheric files and size-optimized magnetospheric files, are accessible at https://doi.org/10.23729/ca1da110-2d4e-45c4-8876-57210fbb0b0d, while the data used to generate the figures can be found at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6641258. These extensive results offer a potential foundation for developing combined physics-based and black-box approaches for real-time near-Earth space forecasting or serving as input for other physics-based models of the inner magnetosphere, upper, and middle atmospheres.

This study utilizes a sample of $z=0$ slow rotator (SR) galaxies visually identified within the EAGLE hydrodynamical simulations to investigate how galaxy mergers influence their formation, characterize their intrinsic properties, and examine the link between quenching and kinematic transformation. SRs experiencing major or minor mergers (with mass ratios $\ge 0.3$ and $0.1-0.3$, respectively) exhibit higher triaxiality parameters and ex-situ stellar fractions compared to "no-merger" SRs, which formed without mergers or underwent only very minor ones. No-merger SRs are notably more compact, possess lower black hole-to-stellar mass ratios, and quench later than other SRs, thereby leaving distinct marks on their $z=0$ chemical composition. For most SRs, quenching driven by active galactic nuclei feedback occurs before kinematic transformation, except for satellite SRs where these processes happen simultaneously. However, in approximately 50% of these satellites, satellite-satellite mergers determine their SR status, while environmental factors (such as tidal fields and interactions with the central galaxy) account for the transformation in the remainder. By categorizing SRs into kinematic sub-classes, we observe that flat SRs favor major mergers, round SRs prefer minor or very minor mergers, and prolate SRs favor gas-poor mergers. Both flat and prolate SRs are more prevalent among satellites in massive halos ($>10^{13.6}\,\rm M_{\odot}$) and central galaxies with high stellar masses ($M_{\star} > 10^{10.5}\, \rm M_{\odot}$). While EAGLE galaxies broadly align with observed kinematic properties, discrepancies exist, such as inverted stellar age and velocity dispersion profiles, which we discuss alongside potential solutions in future simulations.

We present REDO, a class-agnostic framework designed to reconstruct dynamic objects from RGBD or calibrated video inputs. Unlike previous approaches, our formulation offers a more realistic but challenging scenario for three key reasons: first, objects may be partially occluded or obscured by camera limitations, yet we aim to recover their full shape; second, the framework accommodates various dynamics, including rigid and non-rigid motions as well as articulation; and third, it reconstructs diverse object categories using a single unified system. To overcome these hurdles, we propose two innovative modules: a canonical 4D implicit function that aligns with pixels and aggregates temporal visual information, and a 4D transformation module that captures object dynamics to facilitate temporal propagation and aggregation. We evaluate REDO's performance through extensive experiments on synthetic datasets (SAIL-VOS 3D and DeformingThings4D++) and real-world data (3DPW), demonstrating that it surpasses state-of-the-art dynamic reconstruction methods by a significant margin. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each proposed component.

Identifying traffic accidents automatically has become a critical area of research for modern traffic monitoring. With many city intersections now utilizing surveillance cameras linked to traffic management systems, computer vision offers a promising solution for automating accident detection. This paper introduces a novel, efficient framework designed for accident detection at intersections within traffic surveillance contexts. The system operates through three hierarchical stages: first, accurate and efficient object detection using the advanced YOLOv4 algorithm; second, object tracking via a Kalman filter integrated with the Hungarian algorithm for association; and third, accident identification through trajectory conflict analysis. A custom cost function is employed during the tracking phase to handle challenges such as occlusion, overlapping objects, and shape variations. Trajectories are evaluated based on velocity, angle, and distance to identify various conflicts, including those between vehicles, vehicles and pedestrians, and vehicles and bicycles. Tests on real-world traffic video data demonstrate the method's viability for real-time surveillance, successfully detecting near-accidents and actual collisions at urban intersections with high detection rates and minimal false alarms. Furthermore, the framework's robustness was assessed using diverse video sequences from YouTube featuring varying lighting conditions. The dataset is publicly accessible at: http://github.com/hadi-ghnd/AccidentDetection.

Broad-area vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers (VCSELs) operating in solitary continuous-wave mode exhibit rich nonlinear and chaotic behaviors driven by the interplay of multiple lasing modes. A thorough examination of their polarization states, spectral outputs, near-field patterns, and temporal evolution reveals a sequence of bifurcations accompanied by fluctuations at the birefringence splitting frequency and other components. These bifurcations align with transitions in transverse modes and/or polarization states, highlighting the critical role of both spatial and polarization degrees of freedom in mode competition. Consequently, the intrinsic nonlinear dynamics of broad-area VCSELs are substantially more intricate than those of single-spatial-mode VCSELs.

By integrating nitrogen enrichment into our existing, empirically calibrated multi-zone galactic chemical evolution framework, we establish empirical limits on nitrogen nucleosynthetic yields. Our approach utilizes a metallicity-independent ("primary") nitrogen yield from massive stars alongside a metallicity-dependent ("secondary") yield from AGB stars. In this model, galactic radial zones initially evolve with rising [O/H] at a constant [N/O], before shifting upward in [N/O] due to secondary nitrogen production. Around $t\approx5$ Gyr, the system reaches an equilibrium [N/O]-[O/H] relation that mirrors the radial oxygen gradient. We achieve strong alignment with observed [N/O]-[O/H] trends in extra-galactic systems by assuming an IMF-averaged massive star yield of $y_\text{N}^\text{CC}=3.6\times10^{-4}$—consistent with rapidly rotating progenitor predictions—and a fractional AGB yield that scales linearly with mass and metallicity: $y_\text{N}^\text{AGB}=(9\times10^{-4})(M_*/M_\odot)(Z_*/Z_\odot)$. This framework successfully replicates the [N/O]-[O/H] relation seen in APOGEE Milky Way stars, as well as stellar [N/O] and [O/Fe] trends with age, albeit imperfectly. While the metallicity-dependent yield primarily dictates the gas-phase [N/O]-[O/H] relation, the AGB time-delay is essential for matching APOGEE data on stellar age and [O/Fe]. Introducing approximately 40% oscillations in the star formation rate allows the model to reproduce the scatter in external galaxy gas-phase [N/O] versus [O/H] observed by MaNGA. Furthermore, we evaluate models using published AGB yields, finding that for all considered cases, simple stellar populations release half their nitrogen within roughly 250 Myr.

While the composition of any two nontrivial classical knots results in a satellite knot—and is therefore non-hyperbolic according to Thurston's work—this paper investigates the composition of virtual knots. These virtual knots extend classical knot theory by generalizing knots in $S^3$ to knots embedded in $S \times I$, where $S$ represents a closed orientable surface. Our findings reveal that virtual knots exhibit distinct behavior under composition; specifically, the composition of two hyperbolic virtual knots remains hyperbolic. Furthermore, we derive robust lower bounds for the volume of such compositions based on the properties of the constituent knots.

Multilingualism denotes advanced proficiency in two or more languages across both spoken and written communication, frequently leading to code-mixing, where speakers interleave multiple languages within a single utterance. This paper examines the current landscape of NLP research, including its limitations and potential pitfalls, specifically regarding five real-world applications aimed at social good: crisis management, healthcare, political campaigning, fake news detection, and hate speech mitigation in multilingual contexts. Furthermore, we propose futuristic datasets, models, and tools designed to significantly propel advancements in multilingual NLP for societal benefit. As a representative case study, we analyze English-Hindi code-mixing, extending these insights to other language pairs.

We outline the $p$-divisibility transposition concerning the Fourier coefficients of Siegel modular forms, thereby extending Wilton's findings on the $p$-divisibility properties of the Ramanujan $\tau$-function.

During a phase of intense $\gamma$-ray flaring in BL Lacertae, we coordinated follow-up observations using Swift, NICER, and NuSTAR. Swift-XRT monitored the source from August 11 to October 16, 2020, revealing a variability amplitude of 65, with flux ranging from $1.0 \times 10^{-11}$ to $65.3 \times 10^{-11}$ erg cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. Notably, on October 6, 2020, Swift-XRT captured the source at its historical peak X-ray flux. The data indicates a "softer-when-brighter" behavior, implying enhanced synchrotron emission in the X-ray band during this bright state. Both Swift-XRT and NICER detected rapid soft X-ray variability, with minimum timescales of 60 and 240 seconds, and doubling timescales of 274 and 1008 seconds, respectively, pointing to very compact emission regions ($1.1 \times 10^{14}$ and $4.0 \times 10^{14}$ cm). NuSTAR observed a minimum variability timescale of approximately 5.5 ks in the hard X-ray band. We present the first simultaneous NICER and NuSTAR observations of BL Lacertae during October 11–12, 2020. The combined spectra are well-described by a broken power law with distinct photon indices of 2.10 below and 1.60 above an energy break at $\sim$ 2.7 keV, indicating two separate emission components (synchrotron and inverse Compton) across the broad X-ray spectrum. Allowing the total hydrogen column density to vary freely yielded an estimate of $N_{H,tot} = (2.58 \pm 0.09) \times 10^{21}$ cm$^{-2}$.

Platinum (Pt) is extensively utilized in spintronics for spin-charge conversion, leveraging its substantial intrinsic spin-orbit interaction. The weak-antilocalization effect, which generates magnetoconductance within the quantum interference regime, serves as a potent method for extracting microscopic details regarding spin-orbit interactions and coherence phase-breaking scattering processes among itinerant electrons. To investigate various scattering mechanisms, we conducted a magnetoconductance analysis on Pt thin films exhibiting multi-band (multi-channel) conduction. A comprehensive examination of the quantum interference-driven weak-antilocalization effect indicates the presence of strong (weak) inter-band scattering between similar (different) orbitals. We observed that coherence phase-breaking lengths ($l_{\phi}$) and their temperature dependencies vary significantly between these two conducting bands. These findings align with theoretical predictions suggesting three Fermi sheets composed of one $s$ and two $d$ orbital characters. Consequently, this study offers evidence for two independent, non-similar conducting channels, anisotropic spin-orbit interaction, and electron-electron ($e$-$e$) correlation within Pt thin films.
We present an overview of recent advancements in investigating the K-stability of Fano varieties through an algebro-geometric lens.

This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of non-trivial solutions for non-homogeneous $p(x)$-Laplacian equations featuring non-polynomial growth operators, within the context of variable exponent Sobolev spaces on Riemannian manifolds, employing the Mountain Pass Theorem.

When action potentials travel through cardiac tissue and encounter local irregularities, they can trigger reflected waves. These waves are often linked to the initiation of cardiac arrhythmias; although their precise generation mechanisms remain unclear, their presence is connected to one-dimensional (1D) spiral waves. Consequently, analyzing the existence and stability of 1D spirals is vital for assessing the probability of these unwanted reflected pulses. Mathematically, we examine these phenomena by modeling the 1D spiral as a time-periodic, antisymmetric source defect. By employing both direct numerical simulations and continuation methods, we explore the existence and stability of 1D spiral waves within a qualitative ionic model to evaluate how system parameters influence the tendency for reflections. Our findings validate and expand upon a prior hypothesis that the 1D spiral represents an unstable periodic orbit arising from a global reorganization of heteroclinic orbits, while also pinpointing specific parameters and physiological processes that either encourage or inhibit reflective behavior.

Driven by privacy concerns, multi-party gradient tree boosting has gained significant traction among machine learning researchers and practitioners. However, existing research on vertically partitioned datasets remains scarce; current approaches often lack scalability or suffer from information leakage. To address these issues, this work introduces SSXGB, a scalable and secure multi-party gradient tree boosting framework designed for vertically partitioned data with partially outsourced computations. Security is ensured through an additive homomorphic encryption (HE) scheme, upon which we design two sub-protocols to execute the non-linear operations inherent to gradient tree boosting. Furthermore, we develop secure training and prediction algorithms within the SSXGB framework, accompanied by theoretical analyses of security and communication costs. Finally, the framework's performance is validated through experiments using two real-world datasets.

Tissue-level semantic segmentation is a critical component of computational pathology. While fully-supervised models have demonstrated exceptional performance using dense pixel-level annotations, acquiring such labels for giga-pixel whole slide images is prohibitively costly and time-intensive. This study addresses this challenge by achieving tissue semantic segmentation on histopathology images using solely patch-level classification labels, thereby significantly reducing annotation efforts. We introduce a two-stage framework comprising a classification phase and a segmentation phase. In the classification stage, a CAM-based model generates pseudo masks from patch-level labels, while the segmentation stage employs our proposed Multi-Layer Pseudo-Supervision to perform tissue segmentation. Several novel techniques are implemented to bridge the information gap between pixel-level and patch-level annotations. Additionally, we present a new weakly-supervised semantic segmentation (WSSS) dataset for lung adenocarcinoma, named LUAD-HistoSeg. Extensive experiments conducted on two datasets demonstrate that our model surpasses two state-of-the-art WSSS methods. Notably, our approach yields results comparable to fully-supervised models, with only a roughly 2% difference in MIoU and FwIoU metrics. Compared to manual labeling, our method drastically reduces annotation time from hours to minutes. The source code is accessible at: \url{https://github.com/ChuHan89/WSSS-Tissue}.

We characterize $Q_K$ spaces, Besov spaces, and analytic Morrey spaces by employing the Cauchy-Riemann operator to define them through pseudoanalytic extensions of primitive functions. Furthermore, these findings extend to several well-known classical Banach spaces, including the Bloch space, $BMOA$, and the Dirichlet space.

Leptons, quarks, and weak bosons are proposed to be composite particles formed from new underlying constituents. This framework predicts the existence of an isosinglet weak boson, designated as the X particle, with an estimated mass of approximately 400 GeV and a decay width of roughly 20 GeV.

In recent years, approximately 30 extragalactic fast X-ray transients (FXRTs) have been identified, primarily within Chandra and XMM-Newton datasets. Their origins remain uncertain, with suggested causes ranging from double neutron star mergers and tidal disruption events involving intermediate-mass black holes and white dwarfs to supernova shock breakouts. Distinguishing definitively among these three leading scenarios necessitates a deeper understanding of FXRT energetics, environments, and host characteristics. This study reports optical observations of XRT 000519 using the Very Large Telescope and Gran Telescopio Canarias, aimed at locating potential host galaxies. In $g_s$, $r_s$, and $R$-band imaging, we identified an extended source to the North-West of the $\sim$ $1^{\prime\prime}$ (68% confidence) error circle associated with the X-ray position of XRT 000519, measuring a Kron magnitude of $g_s=$26.29$\pm$0.09 (AB). We analyze the association between XRT 000519 and this probable host across various distances, concluding that if they are linked, a supernova shock breakout scenario is unlikely. Conversely, no host galaxy was detected near XRT 110103 down to a limiting magnitude of $R>25.8$.

In prior work, we showed that the stable and unstable equilibrium configurations of prismatic Coulomb-actuated Euler-Bernoulli micro-beams with clamped ends can be effectively simulated by integrating finite element analysis (FEM) with continuation methods. These simulations were validated through experiments that combined direct optical observation with modal analysis of Euler-Bernoulli eigenmodes.
