Neutrinoless double beta decay is regarded as a potent method for resolving unresolved questions within the neutrino sector of particle physics, including extensions beyond the Standard Model. Following the conclusion of Phase I in 2013, the GERDA apparatus was upgraded to initiate Phase II. This phase targets a sensitivity to the $0\nu\beta\beta$ half-life exceeding $10^{26}$ years over a three-year data-taking period, utilizing roughly 35 kg of $^{enr}$Ge with a background index near $10^{-3}$ cts/(keV$\cdot$kg$\cdot$yr). A key enhancement involves liquid argon scintillation light readout to reject events that deposit energy only partially in both the germanium and the surrounding liquid argon. This paper outlines the anticipated objectives of Phase II, details the associated upgrades, and highlights selected features from the 2015 commissioning and 2016 calibration runs, while also reviewing the primary accomplishments of Phase I.

A Chain of Evolution Algebras (CEA) is defined as an uncountable, time-dependent collection of evolution algebras over the real number field, where the matrix of structural constants adheres to the Kolmogorov-Chapman equation. This paper examines three specific CEAs consisting of three-dimensional real evolution algebras that rely on multiple non-zero functions defined over time. For each chain, we provide a complete classification of the algebras up to isomorphism based on the time parameter, and we identify specific functions that guarantee the corresponding CEA encompasses every possible three-dimensional evolution algebra.

Event information extraction systems face significant challenges in text annotation due to its high cost, difficulty, and susceptibility to errors. This study explores the viability of incorporating coarse-grained data, such as document or sentence-level labels, which are much easier to acquire, rather than expanding the volume of fully annotated documents. Our approach employs a multi-task model that combines the primary token classification objective with two auxiliary binary classification tasks for documents and sentences. Through extensive experiments under various data integration scenarios, we demonstrate that while adding coarse-grained data enhances both performance and robustness, meaningful improvements can also be achieved simply by including negative documents containing no event information.

Graph sparsification aims to reduce data size while maintaining a graph structure that remains similar to the original. Current approaches primarily rely on sampling, which often incurs high computational costs and lacks the flexibility required for diverse reduction goals. We introduce SparRL, the first general and effective reinforcement learning framework dedicated to graph sparsification. SparRL offers easy adaptability to various reduction objectives and ensures computational complexity that is independent of graph size. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that SparRL surpasses all existing sparsification methods in generating high-quality graphs across a wide range of objectives.

The Pauli Exclusion Principle manifests when fermions occupy the ground state of a two-dimensional harmonic oscillator trap at extremely low temperatures, leading to the formation of Pauli crystals through their non-interaction. This study provides a statistical mechanical framework for understanding the principles behind these Pauli crystals by computing key parameters—such as energy and radius—of the ultra-cold, non-interacting fermion arrangement. By addressing the problem from two distinct perspectives, namely fermion degeneracy and harmonic oscillator treatment, and subsequently unifying these approaches, the work offers a more comprehensive and robust description of the various characteristics of Pauli crystals.

Following the methodology introduced in [16], we investigate stochastic differential equations with distribution-dependent coefficients driven by a continuous process, without imposing constraints on the process's law. We establish multiple criteria ensuring the existence and uniqueness of solutions that extend beyond the traditional globally Lipschitz framework. Specifically, we demonstrate the well-posedness of the equation and the almost sure convergence of the corresponding particle system for drifts that satisfy conditions such as Osgood-continuity, monotonicity, local Lipschitz properties, or Sobolev differentiability.

A computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation framework designed for fluid-flow prediction has been developed using the Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) platform. The TPU architecture, characterized by accelerated dense matrix multiplication, extensive high-bandwidth memory, and rapid inter-chip connectivity, makes it ideal for high-performance scientific computing. This CFD framework addresses the variable-density Navier-Stokes equations via a low-Mach approximation, with governing equations discretized using a finite-difference method on a collocated structured mesh. The system employs TensorFlow's graph-based programming paradigm. Numerical and analytical studies evaluate the framework's accuracy and performance, with specific attention to the impact of TPU-native single-precision floating-point arithmetic. The algorithm and implementation are validated through canonical 2D and 3D Taylor-Green vortex simulations. To demonstrate capability in simulating turbulent flows, tests were performed on two configurations: decaying homogeneous isotropic turbulence and a turbulent planar jet, both yielding statistical results that align well with reference solutions. Performance analysis reveals linear weak scaling and superlinear strong scaling, achieving optimal results across a full TPU v3 pod comprising 2048 cores.

This study investigates the commutation relations of light-ray operators within conformal field theories. We first construct the algebra of such operators derived from higher spin currents in free CFTs, deriving explicit formulas for the associated structure constants. These algebras exhibit a striking resemblance to the generalized Zamolodchikov's $W_\infty$ algebra found in two-dimensional conformal field theories. Subsequently, we calculate the commutator of generalized energy flow operators in generic, interacting CFTs where $d>2$. Our results indicate that this commutator is contributed to by the energy flow operator itself, as well as by light-ray operators constructed from scalar primary operators with dimension $\Delta \leq d-2$ that appear in the operator product expansion of two stress-energy tensors. Furthermore, the commutators of the light-ray operators discussed herein generate CFT sum rules that extend superconvergence relations and align naturally with dispersive sum rules, both of which have been the subject of recent research.

Dipolar Bose-Einstein condensates, supported by quantum fluctuations, can create self-bound, liquid-like droplets even in regimes where mean-field theory predicts instability. Although the standard Bogoliubov theory suggests dynamical instability due to imaginary phonon energies in the long-wavelength limit—a problem also identified in binary quantum droplets that is resolved by higher-order fluctuations—this study employs the Beliaev formalism to analyze dipolar quantum droplets. We demonstrate that quantum fluctuations enhance phonon stability and derive an anisotropic sound velocity suitable for experimental verification.

The emergence of x-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) has facilitated novel experimental studies of matter subjected to extreme conditions through intense x-ray interactions. These interactions occur on femtosecond timescales, generating transient high-energy-density plasmas where electrons and ions often deviate significantly from local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE). Modeling these systems remains difficult due to the disparate thermalization rates between electrons and ions, as well as the enormous complexity of atomic configurations needed to describe the resulting highly-ionized plasmas. This study utilizes CCFLY, a non-LTE Fokker-Planck collisional-radiative code, to examine the evolution of high-energy-density systems. Specifically, we apply CCFLY to analyze the dynamical evolution of an XFEL-driven solid-density plasma, investigating its relaxation toward LTE over femtosecond intervals with respect to charge state distributions, electron density, and temperature.

In 2019, the global community confronted a health emergency caused by the newly emerged coronavirus, COVID-19. Approximately 196 nations were impacted, with the highest active case counts recorded in the USA, Italy, China, Spain, Iran, and France. Significant challenges persist within medical and healthcare sectors regarding the delayed detection of the virus. Consequently, numerous artificial intelligence systems have been developed to automatically identify COVID-19 through chest X-rays. This article examines various detection approaches and the associated hurdles. Developing an automated detection system is crucial to prevent viral transmission via contact. Several deep learning architectures, including ResNet, Inception, and GoogLeNet, have been deployed for this purpose. However, while these methods effectively identify pneumonia, it remains difficult to distinguish whether the condition stems from COVID-19 or from other bacterial or fungal infections.

Rotating spheroidal stars are prevalent throughout the universe, making their study highly significant. Since Newton's era, numerous astronomers and physicists have examined the gravitational characteristics of these stars by utilizing moment equations derived from Eulerian hydrodynamic equations. This paper investigates the scattering of Dirac spinors, with a specific focus on the scenario involving rotating Maclaurin spheroids. The study begins by presenting the metric for a rotating ellipsoidal star, formulates the Dirac equation within this metric, and subsequently derives the scattering solution. This process establishes a relationship between the differential scattering cross-section ($\sigma$) and the stellar matter density ($\mu$). The findings indicate that the sensitivity of $\sigma$ to variations in $\mu$ is directly proportional to the density itself. Given the weak gravitational field and constant mass density assumptions, the results are considered reasonable. These findings are applicable to white dwarfs, main-sequence stars, red giants, and supergiants, provided their gravitational fields are sufficiently weak to allow for Newtonian approximations and the fluid is treated as incompressible. It is important to note that the star's matter density is treated as an average value, and the star is not assumed to be compact; consequently, these results cannot be applied to neutron stars or black holes. Specifically, the results are well-suited for white dwarfs, which typically exhibit average densities ranging from $10^{5}$ to $10^{6}$ g cm$^{-3}$, corresponding to masses between $0.21$ and $0.61 M_{\bigodot}$ and radii between $6000$ and $10000$ km.

Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models rely on realistic inflow boundary conditions (BCs) to accurately simulate blood flow and investigate the pathophysiology of ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms (ATAA). Due to the scarcity of in vivo velocity data, researchers often rely on idealized BCs; however, this study addresses that gap by creating and characterizing a comprehensive dataset of synthetic 4D aortic velocity profiles for CFD applications. Velocity fields were extracted from 4D flow MRI scans of 30 ATAA patients, ensuring spatial alignment and interpolating data to a common reference frame. Extensive analysis of the clinical cohort's velocity profiles was conducted using spatial and temporal flow morphology descriptors. Principal component analysis (PCA) was then utilized to construct a statistical shape model (SSM) of these 4D profiles, resulting in the generation of 437 synthetic cases with realistic properties. Validation against clinical data revealed that the synthetic profiles matched the clinical population in key morphological parameters. While the average profile qualitatively appeared parabolic, it quantitatively captured complex flow patterns that idealized models fail to replicate. Significant statistical correlations were identified between PCA modes of variation and flow descriptors. Ultimately, this research established a data-driven generative model for 4D aortic velocity profiles suitable for computational hemodynamic studies, accompanied by software capable of mapping any generated profile to the inlet plane of a virtual subject based on its coordinate set.

As commercial interest in blockchain expands, permissioned systems have gained significant focus. However, current BFT consensus protocols underpinning these systems suffer from poor scalability or restricted throughput. Most algorithms demand that a single process collect and verify votes from all others before broadcasting results, creating an inherent scalability bottleneck. While some approaches mitigate this by employing aggregation trees to gather and validate votes, they currently provide limited throughput and degrade rapidly when faults occur. This paper introduces \thesystem, the first BFT communication abstraction that structures participants into a tree for scalable vote aggregation and ensures protocol termination within an optimal number of reconfigurations ($f+1$) even during faulty runs. We precisely identify which aggregation trees enable optimal reconfiguration and demonstrate that, unlike prior protocols, \thesystem scales effectively with large process counts and exceeds HotStuff's throughput by up to 38x when utilizing these configurations.

Neutrino oscillations are described within the Standard Model under the assumption that a neutrino consists of left-handed and right-handed massless fermions, with the process occurring through the four-component Higgs field as an intermediate state.

In time-division-duplexing (TDD) massive MIMO systems, channel reciprocity is utilized to mitigate excessive pilot training and feedback overhead. However, practical imperfections in this reciprocity, primarily stemming from radio-frequency mismatches among base station antennas, can substantially degrade system performance and act as a limiting factor. To address these issues, we propose and evaluate two novel calibration schemes for TDD-based massive multi-user MIMO systems: relative calibration and inverse calibration. Notably, the designed inverse calibration accounts for the combined impact of channel reciprocity errors and channel estimation errors. Furthermore, we derive closed-form expressions for the ergodic sum rate under maximum ratio transmission, considering this compound error effect. Our findings demonstrate that the inverse calibration scheme surpasses traditional relative calibration in performance. Additionally, the proposed analytical results are validated through simulation.

Reservoir computers (RCs) represent a simplified recurrent neural network architecture that has proven effective in predicting spatiotemporally chaotic dynamical systems. A key advantage of RCs is their ability to replicate intrinsic dynamical quantities necessary for integration into numerical forecasting workflows, such as the ensemble Kalman filter, which addresses sparse and noisy data in numerical weather prediction. This study examines the architectural and design parameters required to create a top-tier RC across various characteristic dynamical systems, demonstrating how these choices facilitate scaling to larger models via localization. Our analysis highlights the critical role of large-scale parameter optimization and emphasizes the significance of incorporating input bias into RC design, a factor that substantially influences forecast accuracy. Testing reveals that employing a nonlinear readout operator does not impact forecast duration or stability. Additionally, we investigate the effects of reservoir dimension, spinup duration, training data volume, normalization, noise, and the RC time step. Although a universally accepted benchmark for mean forecast time across different models is not currently established in the literature, our results show a more than twofold increase in mean forecast time compared to the best-performing RC model by Vlachas et al. (2020) for the 40-dimensional Lorenz 1996 dynamics, achieved with a smaller reservoir size.

Two signed graphs are defined as switching isomorphic if one is isomorphic to a switching equivalent of the other. To calculate the number of switching non-isomorphic signed graphs on a given graph, we develop a method utilizing the action of its automorphism group. Applying this approach, we classify all switching non-isomorphic signed graphs derived from the complete graph K5 and the generalized Petersen graph GP(7; 2), while also deriving results concerning the automorphism groups of the resulting signed graphs.

Doubly heavy tetraquark states represent the most promising candidates for tightly bound exotic configurations. This study provides a systematic analysis of the mass spectra for $S$-wave doubly heavy tetraquarks ($QQ\bar{q}\bar{q}$, where $q=u, d, s$ and $Q=c, b$) possessing quantum numbers $J^P=0^+$, $1^+$, and $2^+$, utilizing the improved chromomagnetic interaction (ICMI) model. The ICMI model parameters are derived by fitting conventional hadron spectra and subsequently applied to predict tetraquark masses. For heavy quarks, parameter uncertainties are determined by comparing masses of doubly and triply heavy baryons against results from lattice QCD, QCD sum rules, and potential models. The analysis reveals several compact, stable bound states within both the doubly charmed and doubly bottomed tetraquark systems. Notably, the predicted mass for the $cc\bar u\bar d$ state aligns with recent measurements reported by the LHCb collaboration.

This study details the detection of transit timing variations (TTVs) in WASP-161b through the integration of TESS data with archival observations. Analysis reveals that the TESS transit midpoints deviate from previously published ephemerides by approximately 67 minutes in January 2019 and 203 minutes in January 2021. While the archival light curve from SSO-Europa (January 2018) aligns with the published ephemeris under a constant period model, its transit midpoint shows a significant 6.62-minute discrepancy (at 4.40 $\sigma$) relative to predictions based on TESS timings and a constant orbital period. These TTVs are best described by a quadratic function, indicating a constant rate of period change. The derived period derivative is $\dot{P} = -1.16\times10^{-7}\pm2.25\times10^{-8}$ days per day (equivalent to $-3.65$ seconds per year), based on combined SSO-Europa and TESS data. Although scenarios such as period decay and apsidal precession could theoretically account for these variations, they introduce inconsistencies. To resolve the underlying mechanism, CHEOPS observations of two transits in January 2022 have been secured, with an expected timing deviation of roughly 5 minutes relative to the constant-period prediction from SSO-Europa and TESS.

Fog computing represents a vital paradigm for time-sensitive Internet of Things (IoT) applications, offering faster processing outcomes and reduced network traffic by handling data near the user edge. However, the highly dynamic nature of the Fog environment, combined with the battery-powered status of most devices, creates a high risk of application failure, which can delay results. Conversely, rerunning failed applications on other devices often violates time-sensitivity constraints. Therefore, ensuring energy-efficient application execution is critical yet challenging due to the environment's dynamism. The goal is to schedule applications to prevent failures caused by energy shortages. This paper introduces a multiple linear regression-based resource allocation mechanism designed to run applications in an energy-aware fashion within Fog computing, thereby minimizing energy-constraint-induced failures. Existing solutions often neglect energy-aware execution in the context of Fog's dynamism. Consequently, we propose a sustainable, energy-aware framework and algorithm that addresses these objectives. Our analysis reveals that balancing energy-efficient allocation with application execution time has a minimal negative impact on the system. Comparative studies against existing approaches demonstrate that our method reduces delay and processing time by 20% and 17%, respectively, while decreasing Service Level Agreement (SLA) violations by 57%.

This paper aims to foster understanding and computational expertise regarding time-varying matrix problems and Zeroing Neural Networks (ZNN) in Western contexts. Although ZNNs were developed in China around 2001 specifically for time-varying matrix issues, the majority of subsequent advancements and ongoing research still originate from China. These methods have become fundamental for resolving discretized, sensor-driven time-varying matrix problems in real-time, finding extensive application in robotics, control theory, and engineering. ZNNs are the preferred approach for numerous time-varying matrix challenges that demand efficient, accurate, and predictive real-time computations. A typical discretized ZNN algorithm requires seven distinct steps for initialization. The development of these algorithms begins with a model and its corresponding error equation, under the constraint that the error function must decrease exponentially. This error differential equation is combined with a convergent look-ahead finite difference formula to generate a unique multi-step solver capable of reliably predicting the system's future state based on current and historical data. MATLAB implementations of discretized ZNN matrix algorithms generally involve solving one linear equation and performing one recursion of existing data per time step. This architecture makes discretized ZNN algorithms highly competitive with adaptive ordinary differential equation (ODE) initial value path-following or homotopy methods, offering distinct characteristics and applicability compared to multi-step ODE solvers that lack predictive capabilities by design. Furthermore, discretized ZNN methods for time-varying matrices can address problems derived from sensor data with constant sampling intervals or from functional equations.

This letter derives the cumulative distribution function (CDF) for the $k$th contact distance (CD) and nearest neighbor distance (NND) within the $n$-dimensional Matérn cluster process (MCP). We introduce a novel method utilizing the probability generating function (PGF) of the random variable representing the point count in a ball of arbitrary radius to obtain its probability mass function (PMF). This approach is versatile and applicable to any point process with a known probability generating functional (PGFL). Furthermore, we validate our findings through numerical simulations and offer analytical insights. Finally, we examine two applications—macro-diversity in cellular networks and caching in device-to-device (D2D) networks—to evaluate the performance impact of clustering.

Constraining theories beyond the Standard Model typically requires navigating vast, multi-dimensional parameter spaces to verify observable predictions against experimental limits and theoretical restrictions. This process is often time-consuming and computationally demanding, particularly when severe constraints result in extremely low efficiency for random sampling. To address this challenge, we employed Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning algorithms designed for Black-Box optimization. By analyzing the cMSSM and pMSSM parameter spaces under Higgs mass and Dark Matter Relic Density constraints, we evaluated both sampling efficiency and parameter space coverage. Our results demonstrate that this methodology achieves orders-of-magnitude improvements in sampling efficiency while maintaining reasonable coverage of the parameter space.

The impact of fission fragment structures on their production yields is investigated using a statistical framework, incorporating excitation energies and level density parameters for fragments at specific temperatures derived from the temperature-dependent relativistic mean field (TRMF) formalism. For comparative analysis, calculations are also performed using the finite range droplet model. The study reveals that structural effects significantly influence yields at temperatures between 1 and 2 MeV. Furthermore, at 3 MeV, the fragments adopt spherical shapes, causing the distribution peaks to align with close or near-close shell nuclei.

Determining the optical spectrum of single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) is crucial for advancing opto-electronic devices and sensors across various applications. Although real SWCNTs are finite structures, most existing research relies on infinite models; however, their spectra differ significantly. This study calculates the optical spectra of finite (3,3) and (5,5) SWCNTs as a function of length. For (3,3) nanotubes, the absorption spectra—computed for light polarized both parallel and perpendicular to the tube axis—align well with experimental data. Notably, our findings suggest that the lowest energy peak observed in experiments for parallel polarization arises from a surface-plasmon resonance due to the finite size of the SWCNTs, rather than from other chiralities as previously theorized. We further investigate this surface-plasmon resonance using the Aharonov-Bohm effect. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that the surface-plasmon resonance in finite SWCNTs can be effectively modeled using a one-dimensional infinite well.

Elliptic partial differential equations (PDEs) are prevalent across various computational sciences, including biophysics, engineering, geophysics, and computational fluid dynamics. Solving these equations presents significant challenges due to their global characteristics and often ill-conditioned operators. This overview examines standard discretization techniques for elliptic PDEs—such as finite difference, finite volume, finite element, and spectral methods—along with the resulting linear systems. Furthermore, it surveys both traditional and contemporary approaches to resolving these linear systems, covering direct methods, hierarchical techniques, splitting strategies, and Krylov subspace methods. The discussion concludes by highlighting applications that stand to gain from rapid and efficient elliptic PDE solvers, specifically projection methods for incompressible Navier-Stokes equations and shallow water wave equations incorporating dispersive corrections.

Saddle point approximations, which are vital across many physical domains, necessitate the analytic continuation of canonically conjugate quantities into the complex plane within quantum mechanics. A critical step in applying this method involves calculating the phase correction due to caustics, which relies on determinantal prefactors. A widely used approach that employs the total accumulated phase of half a determinant's inverse frequently results in sign errors. This issue stems from the determinants vanishing at complex times as they cross the real time axis. While deforming the complex time contour to circumvent these zeros can rectify the sign discrepancies, a more practical solution is presented: this method connects the saddles to their corresponding real trajectories, thereby eliminating the need to locate the complex time zeros of the determinants.

We demonstrate the non-existence of bounded-degree expanders with non-negative Ollivier-Ricci curvature, resolving a longstanding open question originally proposed by Naor and Milman and highlighted by Ollivier in 2010. This result holds true even when permitting a diminishing fraction of edges with large degrees, large eigenvalues, or negative curvature. To achieve this, we analyze Benjamini-Schramm limits directly, utilizing the entropic definition of the Liouville property on stationary random graphs to prove that non-negative curvature and spectral expansion are fundamentally incompatible at infinity. We subsequently extend this finding to finite graphs using local weak convergence. Furthermore, this methodology addresses the Bacry-Emery curvature condition CD$(0,\infty)$, confirming a recent conjecture by Cushing, Liu, and Peyerimhoff (2019).

Thorne's research on tidal stabilization of fully relativistic neutron stars demonstrated that the expression for tidal heating in the relativistic regime matches that of non-relativistic Newtonian theory. He further emphasized that this tidal heating is independent of the specific localization of gravitational energy, rendering the expression unambiguous. Subsequently, Favata computed tidal heating using various classical gravitational pseudotensors, including M$\o$ller's, finding that they all yielded the same Newtonian value. However, upon re-evaluating the calculation with the M$\o$ller pseudotensor, we confirm it produces the correct result provided the mass $M$ remains constant. In contrast, Favata treated $M$ as time-dependent, an approach that is invalid because it violates the harmonic gauge condition he employed. Additionally, we extend the analysis of the M$\o$ller pseudotensor to black hole scenarios, thereby exploring contexts beyond Newtonian physics.
Category Theory offers a precise definition of internal structure, enabling us to concentrate on a specific kind of relationship between context and structure.

The ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) is a celebrated data assimilation technique, particularly valued for its application to high-dimensional problems through the update of an ensemble of particles using sample mean and covariance matrices. This chapter introduces the recent adaptation of the EnKF to inverse problems, termed Ensemble Kalman Inversion (EKI). EKI functions as a black-box optimizer for parameter estimation in PDE-constrained inverse problems. We provide a comprehensive review of the EKI methodology, highlighting emerging research directions and supporting them with numerical experiments across various geoscience and numerical weather prediction models.

Reversible debuggers enable programmers to more rapidly identify the origins of faults in concurrent systems by executing programs backward from the point of failure to locate the underlying causes. These tools are grounded in the well-established theory of causal-consistent reversibility, which mandates that an action can only be undone once all its consequences have been reversed. This approach enhances debugging efficiency by minimizing the number of states that must be examined during backward execution. However, existing research on causal-consistent reversibility has not yet addressed time, a critical factor in practical applications. This work investigates the relationship between reversibility and time within concurrent systems using process algebra. Specifically, we utilize the Temporal Process Language (TPL) by Hennessy and Regan—a recognized extension of CCS featuring discrete time and a timeout operator—to define revTPL, a reversible variant of TPL. We demonstrate that revTPL adheres to the properties required for a causal-consistent reversible calculus, and alternatively, we show that it can be viewed as an extension of reversible CCS that incorporates time.

The fracture of aluminum alloys containing precipitates typically involves two concurrent mechanisms: the ductile failure of the aluminum-rich matrix and the brittle failure of the precipitates. This study develops a coupled crystal plasticity-phase field model to examine how precipitate morphology and size distribution influence damage evolution in such alloys, specifically addressing mixed ductile-brittle failure modes. A thermodynamically consistent framework governing elastic and plastic work dissipation within the fracture process zone is employed to define the constitutive behaviors for both ductile and brittle damage. Representative Volume Elements (RVEs) featuring various particle morphologies and orientations were created and subjected to uniaxial loading to evaluate the damage resistance of distinct microstructures. Simulations using critical energy release rate ($G_c$) values for the aluminum matrix ranging from 4 to 8 Jm$^{-2}$ for single crystals and 10 to 16 Jm$^{-2}$ for polycrystals indicate a shift in failure modes from particle debonding to cracking, followed by ductile matrix failure. This transition in particle failure mechanisms due to increased $G_c$ was observed in both single and polycrystalline microstructures. Regarding particle debonding, microstructures containing circular or ellipsoidal particles (with the major axis perpendicular to the loading direction) exhibited superior ductility and fracture work compared to other configurations. Conversely, in cases of particle cracking, microstructures with ellipsoidal particles aligned parallel to the loading axis demonstrated the highest ductility and fracture work. These simulations qualitatively replicate experimentally observed particle failure mechanisms—specifically cracking and debonding—for two matrix alloy classes (commercially pure and 2xxx alloys) reinforced with ceramic particles.

Using both combinatorial and analytic techniques, this paper establishes an exact formula for the $2m$-th power mean value of generalized quadratic Gauss sums, where $m\geq 2$. This result confirms a conjecture proposed by He and Zhang in their work published in the Bulletin of the Korean Mathematical Society in 2011.

The proliferation of varied mobile applications, including augmented reality, severely restricts user experience due to limited device computational power and finite battery life. Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) and wireless power transfer offer viable solutions to these constraints; however, both are vulnerable to propagation delays and signal loss. Capitalizing on the potential for short-range line-of-sight communication provided by Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), this study investigates a UAV-enabled wireless-powered MEC framework. The research formulates a power minimization problem under constraints regarding computation bits and energy harvesting causality. Given the non-convex nature of this problem, an efficient solution is developed using an alternative optimization approach based on sequential convex optimization. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed design outperforms benchmark schemes and that the algorithm achieves rapid convergence.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) typically involves training and assessing a vast number of architectures. Recent predictor-based NAS methods aim to reduce these computational burdens by sampling architecture-performance pairs and training a proxy accuracy model. However, with limited samples, these predictors struggle to accurately identify top-tier architectures due to the challenges of modeling the massive search space. This paper addresses a fundamental question: if the ultimate goal is to discover the best architecture, is it necessary to model the entire search space effectively? We propose a paradigm shift from using a single, strong predictor to cover the whole space, to progressively fitting a search path toward a high-performance sub-space using a series of weaker predictors. A defining characteristic of these weak predictors is that their probability of selecting superior architectures increases over time. Consequently, we sample only a few high-performing architectures guided by the previously trained predictor to estimate an improved, subsequent weak predictor. This straightforward framework, named WeakNAS, employs a coarse-to-fine iterative process to gradually refine the ranking of the search space. Extensive experiments show that WeakNAS requires fewer samples to locate top-performance architectures on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201 compared to state-of-the-art (SOTA) predictor-based NAS methods. Specifically, WeakNAS outperforms all existing methods significantly, needing at least 7.5 times fewer samples to find the global optimum on NAS-Bench-101. Additionally, WeakNAS can integrate existing ideas to further enhance performance and achieves a new SOTA accuracy of 81.3% in the ImageNet MobileNet Search Space. The code is accessible at https://github.com/VITA-Group/WeakNAS.

This paper reports initial findings from an implicit large eddy simulation of the MTU T161 low-pressure turbine, conducted at a Reynolds number of 90,000 and a Mach number of 0.6 (both referenced to isentropic exit conditions) using a high-order discontinuous Galerkin approach. The primary objective is to verify the numerical configuration against existing experimental data. We detail the procedures for establishing realistic inflow boundary conditions, specifically concerning end-wall boundary layer thickness and free-stream turbulence intensity, by customizing the input distributions of Reynolds stresses and turbulent length scales to match a Fourier series-based synthetic turbulence generator. Results indicate excellent agreement with measurements for both blade loading and total pressure losses at midspan. After briefly examining secondary flow structures generated by the interaction between the incoming boundary layer and the turbine blades, we demonstrate that the simulation successfully replicates the loss distribution behind the blade across the entire channel height.

We re-examine parallel-innermost term rewriting as a framework for parallel computation involving inductive data structures, introducing a corresponding runtime complexity measure that depends on the size of the initial term. We introduce automatic methods to determine both upper and lower bounds on parallel rewriting complexity, allowing for the direct application of established sequential complexity techniques. The method's applicability and precision are illustrated by the minimal effort required to extend the program analysis tool AProVE, alongside experiments using various benchmarks from existing literature.

Models proposing highly inhomogeneous baryosynthesis suggest that the asymmetric baryonic universe could contain macroscopic antimatter domains, potentially evolving into globular clusters of antimatter stars within our Galaxy. Assuming that the evolutionary trajectory of such a cluster mirrors that of a standard stellar cluster due to the matter-antimatter symmetry, these objects could serve as sources of antihelium nuclei in galactic cosmic rays. This framework enables predictions regarding expected cosmic antinuclei fluxes by leveraging known properties of matter-based globular clusters. Furthermore, we have calculated the minimum energy required for antinuclei to penetrate from an antimatter globular cluster located in the galactic halo into the galactic disk, utilizing simulations of particle dynamics within the Galaxy's large-scale magnetic field structure. Finally, we have determined the specific magnetic cutoff magnitude for the globular cluster M4.

A primary difficulty in quantum physics involves efficiently forecasting the out-of-equilibrium dynamics of observables within many-body systems. This issue is particularly relevant in adiabatic quantum computing, where optimizing computational speed depends critically on determining the structure of the Hamiltonian's instantaneous gap. Motivated by this, our study investigates the capacity of deep learning to map the parameters defining a problem Hamiltonian to the complete trajectory of the gap during an adiabatic sweep, testing various network architectures. We identify that a key constraint on learnability is the input size, specifically how the number of Hamiltonian parameters grows with system size. Our results indicate that Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks can successfully predict the gap when the parameter space scales linearly with the system size. Notably, integrating this LSTM architecture with a convolutional neural network to address spatial correlations enables the prediction of gap evolution for system sizes exceeding those encountered during training. This approach offers a substantial speedup over current exact and approximate algorithms for gap calculation.

We introduce the concept of a positive integer $n$ being $k$-layered, defined as a number whose divisors can be partitioned into $k$ sets of equal sum, and begin a systematic investigation of this class. Specifically, we present algorithms to identify even $k$-layered numbers $n$ such that $2^{\alpha}n$ remains $k$-layered for all positive integers $\alpha$. Additionally, we determine the smallest $k$-layered number for $1 \leq k \leq 8$. The study further examines the conditions under which $n!$ is $3$-layered or $4$-layered and classifies all $4$-layered numbers of the form $n=p^{\alpha}q^{\beta}rt$, where $\alpha \geq 1$, $1 \leq \beta \leq 3$, and $p, q, r, t$ are distinct primes. Furthermore, we discuss additional findings regarding the relationship between these numbers and $k$-multiperfect, near-perfect, and superabundant numbers. Finally, we establish upper bounds for the differences between consecutive $k$-layered numbers for $1 \leq k \leq 5$, and derive another upper bound for these differences based on the smallest $k$-layered number.

We introduce a novel, straightforward, and effective approach that combines lesion priors with a 3D U-Net to enhance brain tumor segmentation. Initially, ground-truth lesion data from multiple patients are used to generate heatmaps representing various lesion types. These heatmaps form a volume-of-interest (VOI) map, encapsulating prior knowledge about brain tumors. This VOI map is then fused with multimodal MR images and fed into the 3D U-Net for segmentation tasks. Evaluated on a public benchmark dataset, our proposed feature fusion technique outperforms baseline methods and demonstrates competitive results against state-of-the-art approaches.

By drawing parallels to Ra\~{n}ada-Hopf fields, we develop a set of knot solutions for the gravitoelectromagnetic (GEM) equations within the linearized gravity framework in a vacuum. For these solutions, we provide the dual metric tensors associated with the bi-metric geometry of the gravitational vacuum featuring knot perturbations, calculate the geodesic equation based on two complex parameters defining the GEM knots, and finally compute the Landau--Lifshitz pseudo-tensor along with a scalar invariant specific to these GEM knots.

This paper introduces DeltaZ, a centimeter-scale, low-cost delta-style robot designed for robust performance and diverse capabilities. Leveraging current technology, DeltaZ can be 3D-printed from both soft and rigid materials, facilitating easy assembly and maintenance while reducing barriers to entry. The robot's functionality arises from its three translational degrees of freedom and a closed-form kinematic solution, which renders manipulation tasks more intuitive than those with other manipulators. Additionally, its affordability offers a chance to democratize robotic manipulators for research environments. The authors also outline its potential as a reinforcement learning benchmark. Open-source 3D-printable designs and code are publicly accessible.

Phase contrast transmission electron microscopy (TEM) serves as a potent technique for visualizing the local atomic architecture of materials. Its high dose efficiency has made it a staple in investigating defect structures within two-dimensional materials, such as monolayer graphene. Nevertheless, phase contrast imaging often yields complex nonlinear contrast, even in weakly-scattering specimens, which hinders the creation of fully-automated analysis pipelines using traditional image processing methods. A primary challenge in automating the analysis of extensive graphene regions lies in segmenting the target structure from extraneous features like surface contaminants. This study evaluates a conventional Bragg filtering approach against a deep learning framework utilizing the U-Net architecture. Our findings demonstrate that the deep learning method offers greater versatility, practical simplicity, and superior accuracy and robustness compared to the traditional algorithm. Furthermore, we supply adaptable source code for all reported results and explore the prospective applications of deep learning in fully-automated TEM image analysis.

Scientific extreme summarization (TLDR) focuses on generating ultra-short summaries of research papers. Previous attempts to build TLDR datasets for science have struggled to scale due to the need for extensive human annotation and specialized domain knowledge. This paper introduces a straightforward yet effective method to automatically derive TLDRs from citation texts. Leveraging this approach, we have developed a new benchmark called CiteSum, which requires no human annotation and is approximately 30 times larger than the prior human-curated SciTLDR dataset. We provide a thorough analysis of CiteSum, exploring its data characteristics and setting robust baselines. Furthermore, we demonstrate the dataset's utility by adapting models pre-trained on CiteSum (named CITES) to new tasks and domains with minimal supervision. In scientific extreme summarization, CITES surpasses most fully-supervised methods on SciTLDR without fine-tuning and achieves state-of-the-art results using only 128 examples. For news extreme summarization, CITES yields significant improvements on XSum compared to its base model, including a +7.2 ROUGE-1 zero-shot gain and state-of-the-art few-shot performance. Additionally, in news headline generation, CITES outperforms other unsupervised and zero-shot methods on the Gigaword dataset. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/morningmoni/CiteSum.

We report simultaneous broad-band radio observations of the abnormal emission mode from PSR B1859+07 conducted with the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST). This pulsar exhibits unique emission behaviors, characterized by occasional shifts to an earlier rotational phase and mode changes at the normal phase. Our datasets confirm all three emission modes: the B (burst) and Q (quiet) modes associated with non-shift pulses, and an emission shift mode displaying a quasi-periodicity of 155 pulses. Additionally, we identify a novel type of emission shift event where emission occurs at the normal phase during the event. A detailed analysis of the polarisation properties reveals that all three modes share similar polarisation angle (PA) curves, suggesting that the emission from all three modes originates from the same height.

Numerous theories, grounded in computational concepts alongside neuroscientific and psychological data, have been developed to elucidate how consciousness arises within the central nervous system. While these frameworks identify fundamental mechanisms underlying consciousness, they only partially address how these mechanisms serve functional and adaptive purposes. Recently, emerging cognitive and neuroscientific models have attempted to bridge this gap by associating consciousness with goal-directed behavior, the critical cognitive capability that enables mammals to adapt flexibly to challenging environments. This paper introduces the Representation Internal-Manipulation (RIM) theory, which integrates core elements of existing consciousness theories with the components and functions of goal-directed behavior, positing that consciousness plays a central role in the goal-directed manipulation of internal representations. This process depends on four specific computational operations that facilitate the flexible internal adaptation of all key aspects of goal-directed computation, ranging from object representations to goals, actions, and plans. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of "manipulation agency," which connects the sense of agency to the internal manipulation of representations. Consequently, we propose that the subjective experience of consciousness corresponds to the human ability to generate and control a vividly perceived and felt simulated internal reality, utilizing the same perceptual and emotional mechanisms employed when interacting with the external world.

The Swiss State Secretariat for Migration has recently initiated a pilot program utilizing machine learning to assign refugee resettlement placements, a method capable of markedly boosting refugee employment rates in Switzerland. However, the current proposal overlooks family preferences. This paper extends that prior work by introducing two matching mechanisms that incorporate families' location preferences. The first mechanism is strategyproof, whereas the second is not but yields greater family welfare. Crucially, both mechanisms are parameterized, allowing placement officers to precisely balance family welfare against overall employment success. Preliminary simulations using synthetic data indicate that both mechanisms can substantially enhance family welfare with only a minimal reduction in the overall employment rate of refugees.

We created a grain growth model grounded in the minimization of surface energy relative to volume energy and the surrounding environment. By analyzing the well-established FePt L1$_\text{0}$ system, we identified the physical mechanisms governing the morphology and dimensions of FePt grains. Our findings indicate that preferred growth occurs along symmetry planes dictated by fundamental crystal structures and optimized through surface energy reduction. This developed model enables the prediction of grain growth and shape based on atomic number and composition. Consequently, manipulating grain boundaries and surfaces allows for the control of magnetic grain morphology.

Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) have demonstrated remarkable success across numerous generation tasks. By simulating the reverse of a gradual diffusion process that transforms data into a Gaussian distribution, generating samples in DDPMs involves iteratively removing noise from randomly sampled Gaussian inputs. However, practical applications of DDPMs typically require hundreds to thousands of denoising steps to produce high-quality samples from Gaussian noise, resulting in severely limited inference efficiency. This work introduces a principled acceleration approach called Early-Stopped DDPM (ES-DDPM). The core concept involves terminating the diffusion process early, considering only the initial diffusing steps and initiating the reverse denoising phase from a non-Gaussian distribution. By integrating a powerful pre-trained generative model, such as a GAN or VAE, ES-DDPM enables efficient sampling from this target non-Gaussian distribution by diffusing samples derived from the pre-trained model. Consequently, the necessary number of denoising steps is drastically reduced. Simultaneously, the sample quality of ES-DDPM improves significantly, surpassing both standard DDPMs and the utilized pre-trained generative models. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CelebA, ImageNet, LSUN-Bedroom, and LSUN-Cat datasets demonstrate that ES-DDPM achieves substantial acceleration and performance gains over representative baseline methods. Furthermore, ES-DDPM exhibits several desirable characteristics, including orthogonality to existing acceleration techniques and the simultaneous capability to provide both global semantic and local pixel-level control in image generation.

This paper presents a novel nonlinear reconstruction operator designed for two-dimensional triangular domains composed of equilateral triangles. We concentrate on defining the operator locally, drawing inspiration from fundamental characteristics of the harmonic mean of three positive values. Furthermore, we establish several theorems concerning the operator's approximation capabilities and conduct numerical experiments that demonstrate the effective suppression of Gibbs phenomena.
We demonstrate that all words are strongly concise within the class of compact $R$-analytic groups.

We report the discovery of a luminous, nearby Sun-like star ($G = 13.8$; $d = 480$ pc) orbiting a dark companion. The Gaia mission's astrometric orbital solution identified this system as a black hole candidate, a finding supported by refined radial velocity measurements and spectroscopy that excluded significant light from additional stars. Joint modeling of astrometry and radial velocities constrains the companion's mass to $M_2 = 9.62 \pm 0.18\,M_{\odot}$. While the spectroscopic orbit alone establishes a minimum mass of $M_2 > 5\,M_{\odot}$, a $5\,M_{\odot}$ star at this distance would be 500 times more luminous than the entire system. These constraints remain robust regardless of the primary star's mass, which is a slowly rotating G dwarf ($T_{\rm eff}=5850\,\rm K$, $\log g = 4.5$, $M=0.93\,M_{\odot}$) with near-solar metallicity ($\rm [Fe/H] = -0.2$) and standard abundances. No plausible astrophysical scenario explains the orbit without invoking a black hole. With an orbital period of $P_{\rm orb}=185.6$ days, this system has the longest period known for any stellar-mass black hole binary. Its modest eccentricity ($e=0.45$), high metallicity, and thin-disk Galactic trajectory suggest formation within the Milky Way disk with a minimal natal kick. The formation mechanism remains uncertain; common envelope evolution requires extreme, likely unphysical assumptions to produce such a wide orbit, whereas triple systems or dynamical assembly in open clusters offer more promising explanations. This object is the nearest known black hole, being three times closer than the previous record holder, implying a substantial population of dormant black holes in binaries. Future Gaia data releases are expected to reveal dozens of similar systems.

Out-of-Domain (OOD) detection is a crucial element of task-oriented dialog systems, designed to determine if an input query lies outside the set of predefined supported intents. Prior softmax-based detection methods have been shown to exhibit excessive confidence when encountering OOD samples. This paper investigates the source of this overconfidence, attributing it to distribution uncertainty arising from a mismatch between training and test distributions, which hinders the model's ability to make confident predictions and results in anomalous softmax scores. To address this, we introduce a Bayesian OOD detection framework that leverages Monte-Carlo Dropout to calibrate distribution uncertainty. Our approach is flexible and can be easily integrated into existing softmax-based baselines, achieving a 33.33% increase in OOD F1 scores while incurring only a 0.41% rise in inference time compared to MSP. Additional analyses confirm the efficacy of Bayesian learning for OOD detection.

Although online social media provides a venue for marginalized voices to be heard, it simultaneously facilitates the dissemination of hate speech. Typically originating in fringe groups, this harmful content often leaks into mainstream platforms. This study quantifies the impact of joining fringe hate groups by measuring the increase in hate speech propagated to the broader social network. Utilizing Reddit data, we examine the effects of participating in a specific type of echo chamber—a digital community of like-minded individuals displaying hateful behavior. We analyze members' usage of hate speech outside their specific community before and after becoming active participants. Employing Interrupted Time Series (ITS) analysis as a causal inference tool, we assess the "spillover effect," where hateful language from within a group spreads outward, using out-of-community hate word usage as a proxy for learned hate. The research investigates four distinct Reddit sub-communities addressing racism, misogyny, and fat-shaming. Across all three categories, we observed an increase in hate speech outside the originating communities, indicating that joining these groups leads to a wider spread of hate throughout the platform. Furthermore, users were found to retain this newly acquired hateful speech for months after their initial membership. These findings demonstrate that harmful speech does not remain isolated within the community. Consequently, our results offer new evidence of the detrimental impact of echo chambers and suggest the potential benefits of moderating them to curb the adoption of hateful language.

We present a natural filtration on the simplicial homology of a finite simplicial complex $X$ derived from vertex bi-colourings. This approach generates two dual homology theories that extend standard simplicial homology and bear a close resemblance to discrete Morse matchings on $X$. We provide an explicit formula for the associated graded object of these homologies when $X$ represents the matching complex of the Tait graph of a plane graph $G$, expressed via subgraphs linked to specific matchings on the dual of $G$. Subsequently, utilizing one of these homologies for graphs, we define a conjecturally optimal dissimilarity pseudometric, establishing various results and performing several computations for it. Furthermore, by arranging the horizontal homologies of a simplicial complex within the poset of its colourings, we construct a triply graded homology theory termed "uberhomology." Although not a homotopy invariant, this theory captures both combinatorial and topological data about $X$; for instance, we demonstrate that "uberhomology vanishes in the lowest degree for subdivisions but aligns with the fundamental class in the top degree for homology manifolds. We calculate "uberhomology across multiple example classes and infinite families, verifying properties such as its well-behaved nature under coning and suspension in extremal degrees. Focusing on simple graphs, we establish a detection result. Finally, we define singly-graded homologies for graphs by specializing "uberhomology to specific bi-degrees, offering computations and leveraging computer-aided analysis to formulate conjectures.

The widespread implementation of AI technologies has been obstructed by insufficient interpretability, yet both the core concept of interpretability and its practical application remain ambiguous. This study introduces interpretability concepts grounded in approximation theory. We initially apply this approximation-based interpretation to a fully connected neural network and subsequently suggest using Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) as universal interpreters to elucidate arbitrary black-box models. Comprehensive experiments validate the efficacy of our proposed approach.

Egocentric network structures mirror the equilibrium individuals strike between the necessity for intense, close bonds and a variety of weaker connections. This structure is measurable through "social signatures," which map how communication efforts are distributed among network members (alters). Analyses of call data reveal that individuals primarily interact with a select few close contacts, maintaining these distinct patterns over time. To determine if these findings apply to other communication methods, this study compares social signatures derived from call and text message data, while also introducing a method to create composite signatures using both channels. The results show that signatures across all formats exhibit stable, individual-specific differences that endure despite changes in specific network members. Furthermore, call, text, and mixed signatures are remarkably similar both across the general population and among specific individuals. This consistency is notable given that channel selection seems alter-specific without a broad pattern, and networks formed from calls and texts only partially overlap in terms of who is included. Ultimately, these findings confirm that individuals differ in how they allocate communication effort within their personal networks, and this variation remains consistent over time and across different communication platforms.

The paper examines certain invariant tensors within two specific Naveira classes of Riemannian product manifolds, which are associated with natural connections—linear connections that maintain both the Riemannian metric and the product structure.

The LHCb experiment conducted a search for the rare decays $B^0_s\to e^+e^-$ and $B^0\to e^+e^-$ utilizing proton-proton collision data acquired at center-of-mass energies of $7$, $8$, and $13\,\text{TeV}$, with integrated luminosities of $1$, $2$, and $2\,\text{fb}^{-1}$, respectively. No significant signal was detected. Under the assumption that $B^0\to e^+e^-$ does not occur, an upper bound of $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to e^+e^-)<9.4\,(11.2)\times10^{-9}$ was established at $90\,(95)\,\%$ confidence level. Conversely, if $B^0_s\to e^+e^-$ is excluded, a limit of $\mathcal{B}(B^0\to e^+e^-)<2.5\,(3.0)\times10^{-9}$ was derived at $90\,(95)\,\%$ confidence level. These newly determined upper limits represent an improvement of more than an order of magnitude compared to prior measurements.

This brief note outlines the deformations of quantum field theories and defines the action of the pro-algebraic group $U^*$, as utilized by Connes and Marcolli, on finite QFTs generated via the Epstein-Glaser renormalization framework.

Monads are ubiquitous in computer science and can be composed via Beck's distributive laws; however, identifying these laws is often arduous and prone to errors. While existing literature offers general guidelines for constructing such laws, no methods have previously existed to prove their non-existence. This work introduces three families of theorems designed to demonstrate when no distributive law exists between two monads. The first family broadly generalizes a counterexample attributed to Plotkin, subsuming all prior known no-go results for specific monad pairs while yielding numerous new findings. The second and third families are entirely original, addressing diverse practical scenarios. These results resolve the open question regarding whether the list monad distributes over itself, uncover a previously unnoticed error in the literature, and validate a conjecture by Beck from his initial paper on the subject. Furthermore, we define conditions under which a distributive law between two monads can exist in at most one form, thereby proving the uniqueness of several established distributive laws.

The advent of nanoindentation technology, which supports higher oscillation frequencies, enables the observation of complete resonant behavior. In this work, we present a proposed mathematical framework to analyze the measured dynamic compliance of a system, thereby revealing the viscoelastic properties of the test samples.

This manuscript seeks to establish a lower bound for the modulus of the Dirichlet eta function along vertical lines defined by $\Re(s)=\alpha$. To achieve this, we employ a method utilizing two-dimensional principal component analysis that aligns with the complex plane's dimensionality, grounded in a parametric ellipsoidal structure. The resulting lower bound, valid for all $s \in \mathbb{C}$ where $\Re(s) \in ]1/2,1[$, is given by $|\eta(s)| \geq \text{Min}\left(1- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2^{\alpha}},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2^\alpha}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)$, with $\eta$ denoting the Dirichlet eta function. This bound relates to the Riemann hypothesis by ensuring $|\eta(s)| >0$ for every point in the strip $\Re(s) \in ]1/2,1[$. Furthermore, an elementary proof of the Riemann hypothesis is presented by reformulating the problem as a system of biquadratic equations and examining their solutions.

Generally, a system's topological property is a static characteristic, such as the topological edge state detected through local density of states measurements. In this study, we introduce a system where topological features emerge exclusively through dynamic processes. Specifically, we investigate a nonlinear dynamical topological phase transition revealed by the quench dynamics of a Cooper-pair box array linked by capacitors. Governed by coupled nonlinear differential equations arising from the Josephson effect, this system appears trivial under static conditions. However, wave propagation triggered by the quench dynamics uncovers a complex topological phase diagram dependent on the input strength.

This work presents a self-contained quantum mechanical derivation of the Wigner-Wilkins [W-W] neutron/nucleus scattering kernel, a fundamental element of neutron thermalization theory. Although a quantum derivation exists in the literature, we argue that it lacks rigor due to its excessive generality. In contrast, our approach follows a complete path utilizing the Fermi pseudopotential and the first-order term of a time-dependent Born approximation series. Every step of our calculation is fully explicit, including a final integration that is only briefly mentioned in existing literature. Most significantly, we demonstrate that the resulting quantum-mechanical W-W kernel is identical, down to the last detail, to its classical counterpart; this classical formulation is grounded not merely in historical precedence but in classical Newtonian mechanics.

Denoising diffusion probabilistic models and score matching have demonstrated significant efficacy in generative tasks. Although these methods have been adapted for discrete graph generation, they have traditionally depended on continuous Gaussian perturbations. In this study, we propose employing discrete noise within the forward Markov process to guarantee that the graph structure remains discrete at every intermediate stage. Experimental evaluations across four datasets and various architectures reveal that our discrete noising approach yields superior sample quality, evidenced by a 1.5-fold reduction in average MMDs. Additionally, the sampling procedure is accelerated by 30 times, reducing the required denoising steps from 1000 to just 32.

Recent research into deep-learning methods for small defect segmentation reveals that models trained in specific environments are often constrained by fixed contexts. During training, networks inevitably encode background features from the training data before identifying defects, leading to poor performance during inference when the context shifts; addressing this requires retraining for every new scenario, which hinders practical use in robotics where environments are constantly changing. To overcome this, rather than training networks context-specifically and hoping for generalization, we propose training them using pure simulation to avoid misleading them with limited real-world contexts. This paper introduces SSDS, a network capable of distinguishing small defects between images irrespective of context, enabling a "train once, use everywhere" approach. The architecture incorporates a small defect detection layer that leverages the pose sensitivity of phase correlation, followed by an outlier masking layer. Trained on randomly generated simulated data featuring simple shapes, SSDS demonstrates strong generalization to real-world scenarios. Validation on collected real-world data confirms that even when trained in cost-effective simulations, SSDS can successfully detect small defects in real environments, highlighting its effectiveness and potential for practical application.

We present a blow-up construction applied to a smooth manifold along the singular leaves of an arbitrary Stefan-Sussmann singular foliation, alongside a corresponding construction for the holonomy groupoid defined by Androulidakis and Skandalis. This approach yields a locally compact, locally Hausdorff groupoid that serves as a desingularization of the singular foliation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this resulting structure retains certain smooth properties.

To scale deep bidirectional representation learning for natural language, Lite BERT (ALBERT) was introduced. However, due to the absence of pretrained ALBERT models for Korean, researchers typically rely on multilingual models or revert to other BERT-based architectures. This paper presents KoreALBERT, a monolingual ALBERT model pretrained specifically for Korean language understanding. We propose a novel training objective, Word Order Prediction (WOP), which complements the existing Masked Language Modeling (MLM) and Sentence Order Prediction (SOP) tasks within the same architecture and shared parameters. Despite having significantly fewer model parameters—making training faster—our pretrained KoreALBERT surpasses its BERT counterpart across six different Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks. Aligning with empirical findings for English by Lan et al., KoreALBERT demonstrates improved performance on downstream tasks involving multi-sentence encoding in Korean. To foster further research and application development in Korean NLP, the pretrained KoreALBERT model is publicly available.

Let $I$ and $J$ be monomial ideals within a polynomial algebra over a field, where $I$ strictly contains $J$, and the algebra is generated in degrees at least $d$ and $d+1$, respectively. This paper investigates the conditions under which the Stanley Conjecture applies to the quotient $I/J$, leveraging recent findings from \cite{IKM} regarding polarization.

The structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of bulk CoTiO$_3$ ilmenite are investigated using density functional theory (DFT) with both generalized gradient approximation (GGA) and Hubbard-corrected methods. Our results identify the G-type antiferromagnetic (G-AFM) configuration—characterized by antiferromagnetically coupled ferromagnetic $ab$ planes—as the system's ground state, aligning with experimental data. Additionally, cobalt titanates exhibit two critical temperatures associated with the disruption of inter- and intra-layer magnetic ordering, implying that individual planes retain ferromagnetism even above the Néel temperature. Inclusion of spin-orbit coupling reveals out-of-plane magnetic anisotropy, which can be shifted to in-plane anisotropy through minor electron doping, roughly equivalent to 2.5% Ti substitution for Co, matching experimental predictions. Consequently, we offer a disorder-dependent analysis of magnetic anisotropy in bulk $\text{CoTiO}_3$, a factor essential for determining its magnon properties, including topological features.

The evaluation of the Wigner function for quantum states within the entangled state representation is introduced, serving as the foundation for a novel method to derive the time evolution formula of the Wigner function during laser processes. The application of this formula to calculate the time evolution of photon number is also presented, with a specific discussion on the scenario where the initial state is a photon-added coherent state.

Although extensive research has utilized RGB-D data for salient object detection, significant challenges remain due to semantic gaps across different feature levels, causing salient cues in RGB images to manifest at various scales and resolutions. While similar salient patterns exist in cross-modal depth images and across multiple scales, the integration of cross-modal fusion and multi-scale refinement remains an unresolved issue in RGB-D salient object detection. To address this, we propose a top-down and bottom-up iterative refinement architecture to harness multi-scale features, alongside an attention-based fusion module (ABF) designed to capture cross-modal correlations. Extensive experiments conducted on seven public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

Ultrasound imaging is a vital routine procedure for breast cancer diagnosis, valued for being non-invasive, radiation-free, and cost-effective. Nevertheless, its diagnostic precision remains constrained by inherent limitations, making accurate identification via breast ultrasound images (BUS) a significant challenge. Although numerous learning-based computer-aided diagnostic approaches have been developed, most depend on pre-defined Regions of Interest (ROIs) for lesion classification. While conventional backbones like VGG16 and ResNet50 can deliver strong results without ROIs, they lack interpretability, which hinders their clinical adoption. To address this, we introduce a novel ROI-free model for BUS-based breast cancer diagnosis that ensures interpretable feature representations. By exploiting anatomical prior knowledge regarding the distinct spatial relationships between tissue layers in malignant versus benign tumors, we developed a HoVer-Transformer. This architecture utilizes HoVer-Trans blocks to capture both inter- and intra-layer spatial information horizontally and vertically. Additionally, we have established and released the GDPH&SYSUCC open dataset for BUS cancer diagnosis. The model was rigorously evaluated across three datasets against four CNN-based and two vision transformer models using five-fold cross-validation, achieving state-of-the-art classification accuracy alongside superior interpretability. Furthermore, when provided with a single BUS image, our model outperformed two experienced sonographers in diagnosing breast cancer.

We introduce a variant of iterated belief revision tailored for resource-constrained environments, such as mobile autonomous robots. This approach utilizes a memory architecture termed the {\em universal memory architecture} (UMA), which stores an epistemic state as a system of default rules akin to those developed by Pearl and Goldszmidt and Pearl (specifically systems $Z$ and $Z^+$). A duality exists between the category of UMA representations and their corresponding model spaces, an extension of the Sageev-Roller duality linking discrete poc sets and discrete median algebras. This relationship creates a bidirectional mapping between inference and geometry, yielding substantial computational efficiencies at the expense of representation quality, which can be measured via topological invariants. Furthermore, this framework facilitates comparisons among various model spaces, enabling the analysis of relative deficiencies. This paper outlines the formalism of UMA, evaluates the complexity of its maintenance and inference operations, and offers learning guarantees for UMA-based learners. Additionally, we provide simulation results demonstrating the approach's viability and conclude with a discussion of the strengths, limitations, and future development potential of UMA-based learners.

This study examines H-like ions situated within astrophysical plasmas characterized by dense, strongly coupled, and weakly coupled regimes. It explores how variations in the confinement radius ($r_c$) influence temperature fluctuations. By applying two independent, generalized scaling frameworks, the study analyzes how the plasma screening constant ($\lambda$) and ionic charge ($Z$) affect these systems. Several novel relations are established to link the original Hamiltonian with two scaled versions. Specifically, within exponential cosine screened Coulomb potential (ECSCP) and weakly coupled plasma (WCP) environments, these scaling laws yield a linear relationship between the critical screening constant ($\lambda^{(c)}$) and $Z$; their ratio defines a state-dependent threshold beyond which specific states disappear. Shannon entropy is utilized to assess plasma impacts on the ion. As $\lambda$ increases, the accumulation of surrounding opposite charge grows, thereby reducing the number of bound states, although a higher ionic charge $Z$ can mitigate this effect. The interplay between plasma charge density ($n_e$) and temperature in both WCP and ECSCP scenarios is further investigated, alongside the derivation of a recently proposed virial-like theorem. Additionally, multipole oscillator strengths ($k=1-4$) and polarizabilities for $1s$ and $2s$ states are analyzed. As a supplementary contribution, analytical closed-form expressions for $f^{(k)}$ and $\alpha^{(k)}$ ($k=1-4$) involving $1s$ and $2s$ states are derived for free H-like ions.

The Ariel mission aims to analyze the chemical and thermal characteristics of the atmospheres of approximately one thousand transiting exoplanets. Observing such a vast sample will deepen our comprehension of planetary and atmospheric formation during their early stages, offering a representative overview of exoplanetary chemistry and linking it directly to the nature and chemical environment of their host stars. Consequently, accurately and precisely determining the fundamental properties of these host stars is crucial for Ariel to construct a comprehensive picture of the underlying physics of these systems. This paper outlines a structured methodology for characterizing Ariel target stars that prioritizes homogeneity and coherence across a large set of stellar parameters. We detail the ongoing studies and benchmark analyses designed to establish robust stellar fundamental parameters, elemental abundances, activity indices, and stellar ages. Specifically, we present findings on the homogeneous estimation of activity indices S and log(R'HK), along with preliminary data for the elemental abundances of Na, Al, Mg, Si, C, and N. Furthermore, we examine how variations in a planetary spectrum, as measured by Ariel, correlate with uncertainties in the stellar effective temperature. Finally, we describe our observational campaign aimed at precisely and homogeneously characterizing all Ariel stars to facilitate the meaningful selection of final targets prior to the mission launch.

Composite materials featuring a soft polymer matrix and stiff, high-aspect-ratio particles experience a mechanical strength transition when the inclusion density exceeds a critical limit. Known as rheological percolation, this phenomenon typically occurs at a density higher than that required for conductivity percolation. Conductivity percolation results from contact percolation, where conducting particles form a connected network spanning the material. In contrast, rheological percolation lacks a complete theoretical framework. We hypothesize that it stems from rigidity percolation, defined as the formation of a spanning rigid network within the inclusions. To investigate this, we modeled composites as random isotropic dispersions of soft-core rods and analyzed their rigidity percolation. Extending prior two-dimensional findings, we created an algorithm that approximates spanning rigid components by iteratively identifying and compressing provably rigid motifs, effectively decomposing large rigid structures into smaller rigid assemblies. Applying this method to random rod systems, we estimated the rigidity percolation threshold and examined its relationship with rod aspect ratio. Our results indicate that this transition point, similar to contact percolation, scales inversely with the average rod excluded volume (which depends on aspect ratio). However, unlike contact percolation, this scaling holds true for relatively low aspect ratios. Furthermore, the critical rod contact number remains constant for aspect ratios above a certain low threshold and falls below the predictions of Maxwell's isostatic condition.

For finite point configurations $P_1, \dots, P_n \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, we define $\mathbf{m}_{\mathbb{R}^d}(P_1, \dots, P_n)$ as the maximum density of a subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ that avoids containing any congruent copy of the $P_i$.
