While experiments by Wang et al. have challenged the necessity of platform rotation in the Sagnac effect, recent theories attribute the phenomenon to the relative motion between the light-path-defining reflectors and the observer. In this work, we introduce a thought experiment on the linear Sagnac effect and re-examine a previously proposed scenario to demonstrate that the effect does not stem from frame rotation disrupting clock synchronization nor from relative motion between the source and observer. Instead, we argue that the Sagnac effect arises solely from the observer's asymmetric position relative to the light paths. This conclusion is corroborated by analyzing a gedanken experiment involving rotation.

When the economy is conceptualized as a quantum circuit, every microscale process functions as a quantum gate between agents. The global state of the economy is determined by optimizing the circuit's overall sustainability, utilizing geodesics derived from initial approximations. A related but distinct methodology is employed for both the economy as a closed system and as an open system. Calculations may be partially explicit, particularly when reality is modeled in a simplified manner. Furthermore, the circuit can be optimized by minimizing its complexity; while this shares a somewhat similar formalism, it generally follows different paths.

Although semi-supervised learning has garnered significant interest within computer vision for image analysis, its application in time series remains underexplored. This study examines the transferability of cutting-edge deep semi-supervised models from image to time series classification tasks. We address essential model adaptations, specifically focusing on suitable backbone architectures and customized data augmentation techniques. Leveraging these modifications, we assess the viability of deep semi-supervised learning for time series classification by testing our approaches on extensive public datasets with varying degrees of labeled data. Our evaluation employs a rigorous, realistic framework featuring a unified reimplementation of all considered algorithms, a gap previously absent in the field. Our findings reveal that these transferred models achieve substantial performance improvements over robust supervised, semi-supervised, and self-supervised baselines, particularly in data-scarce scenarios.

This letter examines a tightly coupled Lidar-Inertial Odometry and Mapping (LIOM) framework capable of integrating multiple lidars with complementary fields of view (FOV). Specifically, we introduce a time-synchronization mechanism that merges features from distinct lidars into a unified point cloud, which subsequently aids in building a local map and calculating feature-map matching (FMM) coefficients. These coefficients, combined with IMU preintegration data, form a factor graph optimized to estimate the sliding window trajectory. Additionally, we propose a key-frame-based map management approach to marginalize specific poses and point clouds within the sliding window, thereby expanding a global map used to reconstruct the local map in subsequent stages. The integration of multi-lidar complementary FOV and the global map ensures low drift and robust localization, even in scenarios where single-lidar systems fail or perform poorly. To achieve real-time performance, our implementation utilizes multi-threading to significantly reduce computation time. We validate the system's effectiveness through experiments on public aerial vehicle datasets.

This study introduces a memory-efficient symbol level precoding (SLP) framework built upon a deep neural network (DNN) featuring realistic finite precision weights. Specifically, we develop an unsupervised deep learning-based SLP model (SLP-DNet) and derive its quantized variant, SLP-SQDNet, using stochastic quantization (SQ). By quantizing a scalable fraction of the DNN weights, this approach achieves a flexible tradeoff between performance and memory usage, examining both binary and ternary quantization schemes. Experimental results indicate that while the SLP-DNet delivers near-optimal performance, its SQ-quantized versions reduce model size by 3.46x and 2.64x for binary and ternary configurations, respectively. Furthermore, the proposed method decreases computational complexity by 20x relative to SLP optimization-based approaches and by 10x compared to the SLP-DNet.

This study examines the isotopy problem concerning Taniguchi semifields, providing a full characterization of the conditions under which two such semifields are isotopic. Additionally, we establish precise upper and lower limits for the count of non-isotopic Taniguchi semifields, demonstrating that for a size of $p^{2m}$, there are approximately $p^{m+s}$ distinct non-isotopic instances, where $s$ denotes the largest divisor of $m$ such that $2s \neq m$. These findings confirm that the family of Taniguchi semifields represents the largest known family of semifields with odd order on an asymptotic scale. The proofs rely on a specialized technique involving group theory, which leverages the presence of specific large subgroups within the autotopism group of a semifield to determine isotopy.

The objective of anomaly detection is to distinguish anomalous instances from normal ones. This study operates under the assumption that only a limited set of anomalies, covering just a few specific types, are available during training, meaning most anomaly categories remain entirely absent from the dataset. To effectively utilize this incomplete anomalous knowledge, we propose learning a probability distribution that models normal samples while ensuring low density assignments for the observed anomalies. To achieve this, we develop an anomaly-aware generative adversarial network (GAN). Unlike standard GANs that focus solely on modeling normal data, our approach explicitly prevents the assignment of probabilities to collected anomalous samples. Furthermore, to support the calculation of detection metrics such as reconstruction error, the proposed GAN is designed as a bidirectional architecture with an encoder attached to the generator. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our method effectively leverages incomplete anomalous information, resulting in significant performance improvements over existing techniques.
We demonstrate that the $(2,1)$-cable of the figure-eight knot is not smoothly slice by establishing that its branched double cover does not bound any equivariant homology ball.

This study calculates the impact of the Earth-Moon system on the free-fall trajectories of LISA test masses. We demonstrate that the periodic gravitational attraction from the Earth-Moon system creates a resonance at a fundamental frequency of 1 yr^-1, alongside a series of periodic perturbations occurring at integer harmonics of the synodic month (9.92 × 10^-7 Hz). By evaluating the influence of these perturbations—up to the sixth harmonic—on the relative motion between test mass pairs, we find displacements ranging from 10 pm to 3 mm for the sixth and second harmonics, respectively. When comparing these effects against the LISA sensitivity curve extrapolated to 10^-6 Hz, we conclude that several Earth-Moon harmonics are detectable within the Doppler data gathered by the LISA mission. This indicates that the gravitational near field of the Earth-Moon system could serve as an absolute calibration standard for LISA's sensitivity at very low frequencies.

This study examines optimal liability-driven portfolios across a range of fat-tailed and extremal risk measures, focusing on fixed cashflow liabilities for pension funds and insurers, as well as liabilities from derivatives portfolios like delta-one or options books under stochastic volatility. In the extremal limit, we derive a novel tail risk metric called Extreme Deviation (XD), which exhibits significantly greater sensitivity to extreme returns than CVaR. The resulting optimal portfolios maximize return per unit of XD, with weights composed of a liability hedging component and a risk-seeking component aimed at generating positive risk-adjusted returns. We analyze these allocations both qualitatively and quantitatively across various limiting scenarios.

While artists routinely create soap bubbles several meters long, this study generates soap films up to two meters in height by pulling a horizontal fishing line through a soapy solution at speeds between 20 cm/s and 250 cm/s. We analyze the thickness distribution of the film's central region, which acts similarly to a rubber band under tension. Our findings indicate that this profile aligns well with a static model describing a homogeneous elastic film stretched by gravity, resulting in an exponential thickness distribution where the characteristic length scale arises from the balance between gravitational forces and surface elasticity. The model's prefactor is determined by the film's geometry and area, influenced by the fishing line's motion as well as the continuous extraction of foam from the lateral menisci. These lateral regions are thicker than the center and gradually encroach upon the film. Ultimately, our proposed model effectively captures the complex interaction between gravity, film elasticity, and extraction processes, yielding predictions that closely match our experimental observations.

The mechanical characteristics of two-dimensional (2D) materials are crucial for diverse applications such as flexible electronics, composite materials, and van der Waals systems. However, significant debates persist in the literature regarding specific properties; for instance, theoretical predictions for the bending rigidity, $\kappa(T)$, of graphene at 0 K range widely from 0.8 to 10 eV, with some models suggesting temperature dependence that contradicts others. This work introduces the first systematic experimental investigation into the temperature dependence of graphene's bending rigidity. By extracting $\kappa$ values from the ZA-phonon dispersion relation obtained via helium atom scattering, we demonstrate that $\kappa(T)$ increases as sample temperature rises. A linear regression analysis over the temperature interval of 120 K to 480 K yields the relation $\kappa (T) = (1.1 \pm 0.1)[\textrm{eV}] + (0.0013 \pm 0.0001)[\textrm{eV/K}] \times T$.

Circadian rhythms are approximately 24-hour cycles that govern physical, mental, and behavioral changes in all living organisms, regulating the sleep-wake pattern. In livestock management, wearable accelerometers are commonly employed to capture animal motion, allowing for the estimation of activity types. This study utilizes accelerometer data collected from the necks of newborn calves over an eight-week period to analyze their overall movement. By employing a sliding 7-day window across the logged data, we calculate the intensity of 24-hour periodicity at successive intervals as the calves age, serving as a metric for individual calf welfare. Our findings indicate that the intensities of these daily rhythms in a herd of 19 calves fluctuate in synchrony. These results demonstrate that processing and visualizing movement data in this manner allows for the detection of external factors influencing herd welfare, revealing insights that are not apparent when analyzing movement data in isolation.

We address the challenge of sequentially manipulating deformable objects with robotic tools. Prior research demonstrates that differentiable physics simulators, which supply environmental state gradients, accelerate trajectory optimization by orders of magnitude compared to model-free reinforcement learning for such tasks. Nevertheless, gradient-based optimization typically relies on full simulator state access and is limited to short-horizon, single-skill tasks due to local optima. To overcome these limitations, we introduce DiffSkill, a novel framework that leverages differentiable physics simulators for skill abstraction to tackle long-horizon deformable object manipulation from sensory inputs. Specifically, we first derive short-horizon skills for individual tools via a gradient-based optimizer utilizing full state data within the differentiable simulator. Subsequently, we train a neural skill abstractor on demonstration trajectories that accepts RGBD images as input. Finally, we plan long-horizon tasks by identifying intermediate goals through skill selection and execution. Our results demonstrate the superiority of DiffSkill over previous reinforcement learning algorithms and trajectory optimizers on a new set of sequential deformable object manipulation tasks.

This work introduces a tagging algorithm designed to identify jets significantly displaced from the proton-proton (pp) interaction point within the CMS detector at the LHC. Such displaced jets are indicative of long-lived particle (LLP) decays, a phenomenon predicted by various theoretical extensions of the standard model. The proposed tagger functions as a multiclass classifier utilizing a deep neural network, with parameters tuned to the LLP's proper decay length ($\mathrm{c}\tau_0$). A new labeling scheme has been developed to reliably tag LLP-originated jets for supervised training. The neural network was trained using both simulated events and pp collision data collected by the CMS detector at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. To enhance the simulation's accuracy in modeling jet class probability distributions observed in real data, domain adaptation via backward propagation was implemented. The tagger's efficacy is illustrated through a search for long-lived gluinos, a signature of split supersymmetric models. It achieves a rejection factor of 10,000 for standard model jets while maintaining an LLP tagging efficiency between 30% and 80% for gluinos with decay lengths ranging from 1 mm to 10 m. Additionally, the expected coverage of the split supersymmetry parameter space is detailed.

Let $b$ be an integer greater than $1$. Every set of nonnegative integers can be represented in base $b$ using a language formed by the alphabet $\{0, 1, \dots, b - 1\}$. A set is defined as $b$-recognisable if its representation is a regular language. While it is established that ultimately periodic sets are $b$-recognisable for any base $b$, Cobham's theorem indicates that no other sets share this property across all bases. This paper addresses the decision problem of determining whether a given $b$-recognisable set $S$—specified by a finite automaton over $\{0, 1, \dots, b - 1\}$—is periodic. Although Honkala proved this problem is decidable in 1986, Leroux introduced a quadratic algorithm in 2005 by adopting the least significant digit first (LSDF) convention to solve a broader problem. Adopting the same LSDF convention, we provide a structural characterization of minimal automata accepting periodic sets and demonstrate that verifying this structure can be done in linear time. Consequently, we establish an $O(b \log(n))$ procedure to decide if an automaton with $n$ states recognizes an ultimately periodic set of nonnegative integers.

Spatio-temporal forecasting is widely utilized for analyzing wireless, traffic, and financial networks. However, many traditional statistical models struggle to capture the inherent complexity and high non-linearity found in time-series data. Although recent deep learning advancements enable superior modeling of spatial and temporal dependencies, most existing approaches prioritize accurate point forecasts at the expense of characterizing prediction uncertainty. This study treats time-series data as random realizations from a nonlinear state-space model and aims to perform Bayesian inference on hidden states for probabilistic forecasting. We employ particle flow to approximate the posterior distribution of these states, leveraging its proven effectiveness in complex, high-dimensional environments. Extensive experiments across various real-world time-series datasets indicate that our method offers a more robust characterization of uncertainty while achieving accuracy comparable to leading point-forecasting techniques.

While the propagation of Galactic cosmic rays within the solar system is well established, this phenomenon remains poorly understood in M dwarf systems. Accurately quantifying the cosmic ray flux reaching exoplanets is crucial for assessing their relevance to life. This study calculates such fluxes for the AU Mic and Prox Cen systems using a one-dimensional transport model. Our findings indicate that for Prox Cen b, as well as AU Mic b and c, the Galactic cosmic ray flux is significantly suppressed, falling below levels observed at Earth. Notably, this is the first time particle drift effects—caused by gradients and curvatures in the stellar magnetic field—have been included in models for a star other than the Sun. For Prox Cen, incorporating particle drift results in less suppression of the cosmic ray flux compared to models where it is omitted. In the case of AU Mic, we examined two wind scenarios with varying stellar mass-loss rates; while particle drift also reduces suppression in these models, the effect is only significant under the high mass-loss rate condition. Regardless of the wind scenario, both cases for AU Mic lead to strong suppression of Galactic cosmic rays. Ultimately, precise modeling of stellar winds is essential for determining cosmic ray fluxes at exoplanets, and these results will aid in interpreting future atmospheric observations and models.

GPU technology has rapidly evolved in both performance and scale, enabling researchers in HPC and AI/ML to accelerate scientific breakthroughs. Nevertheless, this progress often results in suboptimal resource utilization, as many GPU-intensive workloads fail to fully leverage available hardware, thereby necessitating GPU multi-tenancy solutions. We introduce MISO, a method that leverages the Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) feature on recent NVIDIA datacenter GPUs (such as A100 and H100) to dynamically allocate GPU resources for co-located tasks. MISO's core approach utilizes the lightweight and adaptable Multi-Process Service (MPS) capability to forecast optimal MIG partition configurations for various jobs, avoiding the overhead associated with implementing these partitions during the exploration phase. By enhancing resource efficiency, MISO reduces average job completion times by 49% compared to unpartitioned setups and by 16% relative to optimal static partitioning schemes.

This article employs an operational formulation of the Choi-Jamio\l{}kowski isomorphism to investigate a quantum mechanical framework where the state is not fundamental. I first contextualize this project within generalized probabilistic theories, arguing that such a framework allows for conclusions regarding the intratheoretic causal structure of quantum mechanics that remain independent of any specific ontological view. Subsequently, I present an operational formulation of the Choi-Jamio\l{}kowski isomorphism and demonstrate that in any operational theory exhibiting this isomorphism, various features typically attributed to the quantum state can instead be derived from constraints on non-local correlations. This indicates that postulating states as the bearers of these properties is unnecessary, as they can be understood as consequences of a fundamental equivalence between multipartite and temporal correlations.

Antiferromagnets are increasingly valued in both fundamental physics and technology due to their unique traits, including resilience against perturbative fields and ultrafast dynamics. Recent discoveries demonstrate that in antiferromagnets possessing parity-time symmetry, the Néel vector can be toggled via current-induced staggered spin-orbit torque, while nonsymmorphic symmetry facilitates the manipulation of Dirac fermions. Despite these advances, the real-time evolution of magnetic and electronic structures remains poorly understood. In this study, we introduce a theoretical framework for ultrafast dynamics in antiferromagnetic Dirac semimetals, revealing that terahertz-pulse-induced Néel spin-orbit torque, alongside torques from magnetic anisotropies, can rotate the Néel vector within picoseconds. This reorientation is coupled with fluctuations in the mass of Dirac fermions and can be monitored in real time through magneto-optical phenomena. Consequently, our findings establish a theoretical foundation for next-generation ultrafast antiferromagnetic spintronics that integrates topological material properties.

Although graphene inherently exhibits weak spin-orbit interaction (SOI), this review demonstrates that the proximity effect significantly amplifies SOI when graphene is placed atop transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs). We analyze the symmetry of these induced interactions and compare how different TMD substrates vary in their ability to generate strong SOI in graphene. These enhanced SOIs facilitate novel physical phenomena, such as robust supercurrents that persist even under magnetic fields on the scale of teslas.

This study examines the simultaneous impact of photo-induced topological phase transitions and the magnetic-field-induced quantum Hall effect on the Casimir force between two parallel sheets of staggered 2D graphene-family materials. We demonstrate that the interaction between these phenomena allows for on-demand switching of the force between attractive and repulsive states while maintaining its quantized nature. Furthermore, we show that doping these 2D materials below their first Landau level enables the investigation of photoinduced topology within the Casimir force, avoiding the complexities associated with circularly polarized lasers. Finally, we illustrate that the magnetic field exerts a significant influence on the thermal Casimir effect in dissipationless materials; the quantized energy levels result in strong repulsion that remains measurable even at room temperature.

We define a set of extended operators within the cohomology associated with a pair of twisted Schur supercharges in 4d N=2 superconformal field theories (SCFTs). Derived from local Schur operators via a topological descent procedure, these extended operators manifest as world volume integrals of specific super-descendants of the Schur operators. Their world volumes span directions transverse to a spatial plane in Minkowski spacetime, and their correlation functions depend meromorphically solely on the intersection points with this plane. This construction expands the vertex operator algebra originally defined by Schur operators. To demonstrate this enlarged algebra, we calculate certain extended operator product expansions within the free hypermultiplet SCFT.

We are developing a method to optimize mirror prescriptions for wide-field X-ray telescopes, encompassing polynomial coefficients, relative displacements between mirror shells, and—given four focal plane detectors—their axial placement and tilt. Our approach aims to decrease the number of Monte-Carlo ray traces needed to explore the multi-dimensional design space and simplify the process of identifying optimal parameters. Treating higher-order polynomial terms as minor perturbations to a base Wolter I design, we first utilize Monte-Carlo ray tracing results to construct trial analytic functions representing spatial resolution on an arbitrary focal surface for a single Wolter I shell. Next, we establish a notation and toolset for Monte-Carlo ray tracing of polynomial mirror prescriptions that keeps polynomial coefficients symbolic. Theoretically, for a defined set of underlying Wolter I optical parameters, a single set of Monte-Carlo ray traces can determine the polynomial coefficients by solving a large system of linear equations involving these symbolic variables. We outline the current progress of this development.

Global news events are distributed across diverse channels, each guided by unique reporting criteria. While the abundance of these outlets theoretically guarantees a range of perspectives, emerging data suggests that increasing media ownership consolidation may undermine this expectation. This insight drives research into how ownership structures shape the global media environment and affect viewer coverage. Specifically, the selection of reported events serves as a key indicator of the broader news ecosystem's high-level structure. Nevertheless, current methodologies offer only a static snapshot of a fundamentally dynamic system, resulting in suboptimal statistical models and limiting our comprehensive understanding of the media landscape.

This study introduces a dynamic embedding technique designed to learn the decision-making processes of individual news sources regarding event selection, while simultaneously facilitating the systematic identification of large-scale shifts within the media landscape over extended periods. Through an experiment analyzing over 580 million real-world event mentions, we demonstrate that our approach surpasses static embedding methods in predictive accuracy. We highlight the method's utility for news monitoring and investigative journalism by revealing significant programming changes driven by mergers, acquisitions, policy shifts, or network-wide content diffusion. These results provide evidence of pronounced content convergence trends within major broadcasting groups, exerting influence on the news ecosystem amid growing media ownership concentration.

Experimental evidence indicates that small droplets bouncing on a vibrated liquid bath can traverse the surface by interacting with their self-generated wave field. This phenomenon occurs on a life-size scale in gunwale bobbing, where a person standing on a canoe's gunwales propels the vessel by rhythmically oscillating their legs. The canoe advances by riding the resulting wave field. Following an initial transient phase, the vessel reaches a steady cruising speed determined by an equilibrium between the thrust produced by pushing against the wave field's surface gradients and the drag forces arising from both profile and wave resistance. By combining Havelock's (1919) linear wave theory for steady cruising with Helmholtz's theory for an oscillating source, we demonstrate that this force balance is sustainable. We determine the optimal parameters required to maximize canoe velocity and compare these theoretical predictions with accelerometer data collected from a participant performing gunwale bobbing. Finally, we examine the parallels and distinctions between gunwale bobbing and hydrodynamic quantum analogues, alongside potential applications in competitive sports.

Given the rapid growth of interdisciplinary science driven by materials informatics and other elements, there is an urgent need for a structured approach to articulate knowledge and enhance communication across diverse scientific disciplines. While function decomposition trees offer a suitable representation, domain experts often struggle to construct them. Consequently, this study identifies the common challenges faced by novices in creating these trees and introduces a novel function decomposition method grounded in a causality-first perspective to address these issues. By deriving the causality-first decomposition tree from workflows organized by processing sequence, the research also developed software capable of automatically converting data using these tree features. The proposed method was successfully applied to materials informatics to validate its utility in systematically representing expert knowledge.

The ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider has measured charged-particle fragmentation functions for jets that are azimuthally balanced with a high-transverse-momentum, prompt, isolated photon, utilizing $25$ pb$^{-1}$ of $pp$ and $0.49$ nb$^{-1}$ of Pb+Pb collision data collected at $5.02$ TeV per nucleon pair. These results are contrasted with Monte Carlo generator predictions and measurements of inclusively selected jets. In $pp$ collisions, the fragmentation function in photon-tagged events differs from that in inclusive jet events, a discrepancy attributed to the varying fragmentation of light quarks versus gluons. Ratios of fragmentation functions in Pb+Pb events relative to those in $pp$ events are employed to investigate the parton color-charge dependence of jet quenching within the hot medium. While fragmentation functions in relatively peripheral collisions show similar modification patterns for both photon-tagged and inclusive jets, photon-tagged jets in central Pb+Pb events exhibit larger modifications than their inclusive counterparts.

This study offers a thorough and integrated numerical investigation into nonlinear systems of parabolic variational inequalities (PVIs) under Dirichlet boundary conditions. The analysis facilitates the proof of the existence of an exact solution for the model and demonstrates the convergence of both the approximate solution and its gradient. These findings hold validity across various conforming and non-conforming numerical schemes.

Leaderboards are a fundamental component of contemporary applied machine learning research, organizing entries into a linear hierarchy where the highest-scoring model is designated as the "state of the art" (SOTA). Driven by rapid advancements in information retrieval, especially through neural models, the top-ranked entry on these leaderboards is frequently replaced and hailed as an improvement. However, such claims rarely undergo significance testing. Focusing on the MS MARCO document ranking leaderboard, we investigate how to determine if a new run is statistically superior to the current SOTA. This inquiry arises within the context of recent debates in information retrieval regarding scale types, specifically questioning whether standard significance tests are mathematically valid. Acknowledging these methodological risks, our study introduces an evaluation framework that treats specific outcomes as distinct rather than aggregating them into a single metric. Our empirical analysis of MS MARCO SOTA runs reveals nuances regarding what constitutes a "significantly better" performance, insights that remain hidden under the current official metric (MRR@100).

We provide a qualitative explanation of the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam (FPU) recurrence analog within a one-dimensional focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLSE). This recurrence arises from the nonlinear evolution of modulation instability. Known exact localized soliton solutions, which describe propagation against a modulationally unstable condensate background, demonstrate that the system returns to the condensate state following soliton interaction. After the solitons depart, the condensate locally regains its original amplitude and form, though with a shifted phase, constituting the NLSE analog of FPU recurrence. Leveraging the integrability of the NLSE, we show that this recurrence applies not only to condensates but also to more general solutions, specifically cnoidal waves. These solutions are spatially periodic and can be viewed as a solitonic lattice; this lattice simplifies to isolated solitons when the distance between them is large and transforms into a condensate under conditions of dense soliton packing. While cnoidal waves are also modulationally unstable due to soliton overlap, this instability does not induce recurrence at the linear stage. Instead, recurrence occurs at the nonlinear stage of the modulation instability. This nonlinear characteristic is practically significant, particularly for fiber communication systems that utilize solitons as information carriers.

Traditionally, complex flow simulations are executed on high-performance computing (HPC) clusters. However, due to the scarcity of HPC resources and the steep learning curve associated with traditional supercomputing infrastructure, there is growing interest in deploying flow simulation software on cloud platforms. This study demonstrates how a sophisticated computational framework capable of assessing COVID-19 transmission risks across various indoor classroom settings can be abstracted and deployed on cloud services. Access to such cloud-based, personalized planning tools empowers educational and medical institutions, public sector entities (such as courthouses, police stations, and airports), and other organizations to comprehensively evaluate in-person interaction scenarios for transmission risks. The simulation framework was deployed on the Azure cloud infrastructure, leveraging the Dendro-kT mesh generation tool and PETSc solvers, with cloud abstraction provided by RocketML. We compared the performance of these cloud machines against the state-of-the-art HPC system, TACC Frontera. Our findings indicate that cloud-based HPC resources represent a viable strategy, enabling a diverse range of end-users to rapidly and efficiently deploy simulation software.

This paper introduces a novel family of minimum divergence estimators grounded in Bregman divergence, with the widely used density power divergence (DPD) identified as a specific subset of this framework. We define and investigate a new subclass termed the exponentially weighted divergence (EWD). Similar to the minimum DPD estimator, the minimum EWD estimator qualifies as an M-estimator; this classification facilitates the analysis of its asymptotic behavior and robustness. We evaluate the performance of both estimator classes using simulations and real-world data. Furthermore, we develop an estimation procedure applicable to both independent, homogeneous, and non-homogeneous data. The study also addresses general parametric hypothesis testing based on Bregman divergences, deriving the asymptotic null distribution of the proposed test statistic and examining its performance on real data. Ultimately, the inference procedures derived from the new EWD divergence demonstrate competitiveness or superior performance compared to those based on DPD.

Although the impact of the environment is unavoidable, it is frequently overlooked in research concerning the electronic transport characteristics of nanoscale systems. This environment-mediated interaction is typically modeled as a parity-time symmetric non-Hermitian system featuring a balanced distribution of gain and loss. It is well-established that, in addition to conventional junction currents, a bias-driven circular current can arise within loop geometries, contingent upon the specific junction configuration. This circulating current generates a robust magnetic field, potentially reaching magnitudes of several Tesla. The inquiry arises as to how these parameters respond when the system couples with its surroundings, specifically whether a detrimental effect occurs. To investigate these questions, we examine a two-terminal ring structure where the junction arrangement is modeled using a tight-binding approach. All transport metrics are calculated via the standard Green's function formalism grounded in the Landauer-Büttiker formalism.

We have computed the binding energies of $\Upsilon$ and $\eta_b$ nuclear states across a range of nuclei, disregarding any width-related effects. The necessary inputs for these calculations, specifically the medium-modified masses of $B$ and $B^*$ mesons along with nuclear density distributions, were derived using the quark-meson coupling (QMC) model. Within the local density approximation, the attractive potentials experienced by $\Upsilon$ and $\eta_b$ mesons in nuclei were determined from the corresponding mass shifts in nuclear matter. These potentials arise from in-medium enhancements of $B\overline{B}$ and $BB^*$ loops in the mesons' self-energies. Following a thorough analysis, our findings indicate that both $\Upsilon$ and $\eta_b$ mesons are expected to form bound states with all the nuclei examined.

For an inaccessible cardinal $\kappa$, given a cofinal function $h \in {}^\kappa\kappa$, we examine the dominating $h$-localisation number, defined as the minimal size of a set of $h$-slaloms that dominates all $\kappa$-reals and localizes them. Previous work in arXiv:1611.08140 established that these localisation numbers can vary consistently depending on the choice of $h$, specifically contrasting the identity function with the power function. In this work, we construct a family of $\kappa$ many such functions $h$ alongside their respective localisation numbers. By employing a ${\leq}\kappa$-supported product of forcing that preserves cofinality, we demonstrate that any simultaneous assignment of these localisation numbers to cardinals exceeding $\kappa$ is consistent, thereby resolving an open problem posed in arXiv:1611.08140.

The families $\mathcal F_0,\ldots,\mathcal F_s$, each consisting of $k$-element subsets of $[n]:=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$, are defined as cross-union if no selection of $F_i \in \mathcal F_i$ for each $i$ satisfies $F_0\cup\ldots\cup F_s=[n]$. A generalization of the famous Erd\H{o}s--Ko--Rado theorem, established by Frankl and Tokushige, asserts that when $n\le (s+1)k$, the geometric mean of the sizes $|\mathcal F_i|$ does not exceed $\binom{n-1}{k}$. Frankl hypothesized that this bound also applies to the arithmetic mean, provided certain mild conditions are met. We confirm Frankl's conjecture in a robust manner by demonstrating that the arithmetic mean is uniquely maximized (up to isomorphism) by the standard configuration where $\mathcal F_0=\ldots=\mathcal F_s=\binom{[n-1]}{k}$.

Pattern-forming systems far from equilibrium are widespread across nature, ranging from driven quantum materials and living organisms to atmospheric and interstellar gases. However, identifying universal features of their dynamics and statistics presents significant theoretical and practical hurdles because these systems lack energy and momentum conservation laws. In this work, we explore the statistical properties of representative nonequilibrium systems where intrinsic length-scale selection restricts dynamics to a mean energy hypersurface. Using spectral analysis of field modes and scaling reasoning, we establish a universal distribution for kinetic field observables in such systems. We validate these predictions through experimental data on Faraday surface waves and simulations of quantum chaos and active turbulence. Our findings suggest that transport and pattern dynamics in driven physical and biological matter can frequently be modeled using monochromatic random fields, offering a route toward a unified statistical field theory for nonequilibrium systems with length-scale selection.

We introduce a new neural radiance model designed for self-supervised training to achieve novel-view synthesis in dynamic, unstructured environments. Our fully trainable algorithm rapidly learns intricate real-world static scenes in seconds and dynamic scenes involving both rigid and non-rigid movements in minutes. By distinguishing between static and motion-centric pixels, we generate high-quality representations from sparse image sets. Through comprehensive qualitative and quantitative assessments on established benchmarks, we achieve state-of-the-art results on the demanding NVIDIA Dynamic Scenes Dataset. Furthermore, we validate our model's performance on difficult real-world datasets, including Cholec80 and SurgicalActions160.

Beyond mastering long-range natural language interactions, transformers have become the industry standard for numerous vision tasks due to their power and scalability. Particularly in cross-modal domains bridging text and images, vector quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) are commonly employed to convert raw RGB images into sequences of feature vectors. To more effectively exploit the relationship between visual and textual data, we introduce L-Verse, a new architecture combining a feature-augmented variational autoencoder (AugVAE) with a bidirectional auto-regressive transformer (BiART) for both image-to-text and text-to-image generation. Our AugVAE achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction results on the ImageNet1K validation set and demonstrates robustness when handling unseen real-world images. Unlike other models, BiART uniquely distinguishes between an image (or text) serving as a conditional reference versus a generation target. L-Verse can perform image-to-text or text-to-image generation directly without requiring any fine-tuning or additional object detection frameworks. Quantitative and qualitative experiments on the MS-COCO Captions dataset reveal that L-Verse outperforms previous methods in both generation directions. Furthermore, we evaluate the scalability of the L-Verse architecture on Conceptual Captions, presenting initial findings on bidirectional vision-language representation learning across general domains.

Ultra-relativistic cosmic rays (CRs) constantly bombard Earth. Those reaching energies up to a few PeV (10$^{15}$ eV), a point in the spectrum called the "knee," are thought to originate from within our Galaxy, implying the existence of one or more active PeVatrons. However, directly detecting PeV protons from their sources is impossible because Galactic magnetic fields deflect them. Instead, $\gamma$-rays in the hundred TeV range, generated by the decay of $\pi^0$ mesons formed when PeV CRs collide with surrounding gas, offer conclusive proof of proton acceleration to these energies. This study reports the discovery by the High Altitude Water Cherenkov (HAWC) observatory of the $\gamma$-ray source HAWC~J1825-134, which exhibits an energy spectrum extending beyond 200 TeV without any observed break or cutoff. This source aligns with a giant molecular cloud characterized by an ambient gas density as high as 700 protons/cm$^3$. Although the specific nature of this extreme accelerator is still uncertain, it is likely that CRs accelerated to several PeV and interacting with the ambient gas are responsible for the observed radiation.

Recent investigations into dense laser-driven atomic gases [G. Ferioli et al., arXiv:2207.10361 (2022)] have successfully created a many-body system that, in the thermodynamic limit, manifests as a boundary time crystal. This unique state of matter is maintained by the interplay between coherent driving and collective dissipation. The referenced experiment theoretically permits the acquisition of in situ data regarding the system's nonequilibrium dynamics through the observation of the output light field. We demonstrate that both the photon count signal and the homodyne current enable the identification and characterization of critical behavior at the time-crystal phase transition. At the transition point, the emission signal dynamics exhibit slow drifts interspersed with abrupt, strong fluctuations. The mean interval between these fluctuation events displays a power-law scaling with respect to system size, a peculiar dynamic whose origin is elucidated by a simple non-linear phase model. Furthermore, we establish that the time-integrated homodyne current functions as an effective dynamical order parameter. From this standpoint, the time crystal can be conceptualized as a state of matter characterized by the coexistence of distinct oscillation patterns.

Over recent decades, global efforts have focused on creating realistic space weather forecasting tools to predict solar and interplanetary conditions. Consequently, specific metrics have been developed to evaluate these tools, which are essential for validating models, comparing different approaches, and tracking performance improvements over time. This study introduces Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) as a novel method to assess model performance, specifically for quantifying discrepancies between observed and modeled solar wind time series. We outline the method's benefits and limitations, demonstrating its application to WIND observations and EUHFORIA predictions at Earth. DTW operates by warping time sequences to align them with minimal cost through dynamic programming. It offers two evaluation modes: first, calculating a Sequence Similarity Factor (SSF) to quantify forecast quality against ideal and non-ideal scenarios; second, measuring time and amplitude differences between optimally matched points in the two sequences. Consequently, DTW functions as a hybrid metric that bridges continuous measurements, such as correlation coefficients, and point-by-point comparisons. This promising technique provides a comprehensive evaluation portrait for assessing solar wind profiles.

Cold dark matter is modeled as a gas of massive particles that collide, interact gravitationally, and exchange energy quanta. A novel nonrelativistic quantum framework for this model is introduced, derived from a recently identified equation for a free, spinless, and uncharged particle. This theory details the quantum interactions of these particles, defines the necessary characteristic wavelength for energy quanta, imposes limits on the mass of dark matter particles, and forecasts a detectable gravitational wave background linked to dark matter halos.

Bloch's theorem serves as the cornerstone of topological band theory, an approach that has shaped a significant era in quantum materials research. Nevertheless, this theorem fails in the presence of a perpendicular magnetic field, complicating the investigation of topological systems under strong flux. Moiré materials have recently rendered this challenge experimentally pertinent, prompting the present study to address its resolution. We develop gauge-invariant irreducible representations of the magnetic translation group at $2\pi$ flux within infinite boundary conditions, thereby deriving analytical expressions involving the Siegel theta function for the magnetic Bloch Hamiltonian, non-Abelian Wilson loops, and many-body form factors. To demonstrate our framework, we apply it to a simple square lattice model and the Bistritzer-MacDonald Hamiltonian for twisted bilayer graphene, revealing reentrant ground states at $2\pi$ flux driven by Coulomb interactions.

The spectral statistics of chaotic 4-regular quantum graphs are analyzed in this work by examining their periodic orbits, bypassing the semiclassical limit traditionally required in Gutzwiller and related trace formulae. We determine the variance of the $n$-th coefficient of the characteristic polynomial based on the counts of distinct primitive periodic orbits with $n$ bonds that lack self-intersections, as well as the counts of orbits with specific self-intersection patterns formed by two sections of a pseudo-orbit intersecting at a single vertex. Through this analysis, we identify the underlying mechanism linking semiclassical findings to the total number of orbits, independent of their structural details.

This note demonstrates that the expected value of the separating systole for a random surface of genus $g$ with respect to Weil-Petersson volume scales as $2\log g$ in the limit as $g$ approaches infinity. This finding stands in stark contrast to the behavior of the expected value of the non-separating systole, which, according to results by Mirzakhani and Petri, remains independent of the genus.

Spin-mechanical hybrid systems are extensively utilized in quantum information processing, yet their inherently weak interactions present a significant hurdle in achieving strong or ultra-strong coupling regimes. We introduce a protocol that markedly boosts spin-mechanical coupling by pairing a diamond spin vacancy with a levitated micromagnet. By employing a driving electrical current to modulate the micromagnet's mechanical motion, we induce a two-phonon drive that exponentially amplifies both spin-phonon and phonon-mediated spin-spin coupling strengths. Additionally, this approach enables the generation of high-fidelity Schrödinger cat states and an unconventional, high-fidelity two-qubit geometric phase gate characterized by faster operation speeds. Consequently, this protocol offers a promising platform for quantum information processing involving NV spins coupled to levitated micromagnets.

The envelope theory serves as a technique for calculating approximate eigensolutions of quantum $N$-body Hamiltonians possessing a broad structure across $D$ dimensions. Key benefits of this approach include its straightforward implementation and the treatment of $N$ as just another Hamiltonian parameter, enabling calculations for systems of any magnitude. While reliable solutions are typically not highly precise, accuracy can be enhanced for systems with identical particles in dimensions $D \ge 2$ by integrating the envelope theory with an $N$-body extension of the dominantly orbital state method. This improvement is also demonstrated for systems comprising identical particles alongside a distinct one. The efficacy of this refined procedure has been validated across various systems.

English Natural Language Understanding (NLU) systems have reached high levels of performance, surpassing humans on benchmarks such as GLUE and SuperGLUE; however, these evaluations rely exclusively on Standard American English (SAE), causing other dialects to be neglected within the NLP field. This oversight results in biased and inequitable NLU systems that cater only to specific speaker groups. To investigate existing disparities and promote the development of more dialect-aware NLU models, we present the VernAcular Language Understanding Evaluation (VALUE) benchmark, a challenging adaptation of GLUE generated using lexical and morphosyntactic transformation rules. In this initial release (V.1), we establish rules for 11 African American Vernacular English (AAVE) features and engage fluent AAVE speakers to verify each transformation's linguistic acceptability through participatory design. Experimental results indicate that incorporating these dialectal features can significantly reduce model performance. For access to the transformation code and both synthetic and gold-standard dialectal GLUE benchmarks, please visit https://github.com/SALT-NLP/value.

The analytic deep prior (ADP) approach was recently developed to provide a theoretical framework for deep image prior (DIP) methods utilizing specific network architectures. In this work, we demonstrate that ADP is fundamentally equivalent to classical variational Ivanov methods used for solving ill-posed inverse problems. Furthermore, we introduce a novel variant that integrates an early-stopping strategy within the ADP model. For both versions, we establish how standard regularization properties—including existence, stability, and convergence—can be achieved under widely accepted assumptions.

We provide cosmological limits on the sum of neutrino masses as a function of their lifetime, within a model where neutrinos decay into dark radiation once they become non-relativistic. Our analysis shows that in this regime, data from the cosmic microwave background (CMB), baryonic acoustic oscillations (BAO), and uncalibrated supernova luminosity distances (from the Pantheon catalog) constrain the sum of neutrino masses to $\sum m_\nu < 0.42$ eV at 95% confidence level. Although this bound represents a substantial improvement over Planck 2015 limits for the same scenario, it remains a significant relaxation compared to constraints derived for stable neutrinos. We demonstrate that the majority of this improvement stems from more precise low-$\ell$ polarization measurements in Planck 2018, which tighten constraints on $\tau_{\rm reio}$ (and consequently on $A_s$), thereby breaking the degeneracy caused by the impact of large neutrino masses on the CMB power spectrum amplitude.

We introduce a new framework in which Dirac neutrinos emerge despite the presence of lepton-number violating Majorana mass terms. This model operates within the Randall-Sundrum scenario featuring bulk right-handed neutrinos, incorporating both Majorana and Dirac bulk mass terms. We demonstrate that massless zero-mode solutions arise when the bulk Dirac mass is vanishing; under this condition, the resulting effective 4D neutrino mass is predominantly of Dirac nature, rendering Majorana contributions negligible. This setup bears a striking resemblance to models utilizing flat extra dimensions. We analyze neutrino phenomenology by simultaneously fitting charged lepton and neutrino masses. Using a single Higgs doublet localized on the IR brane proves highly constrained, as it necessitates unnaturally large Yukawa couplings to accommodate charged lepton masses. Consequently, we propose a straightforward extension involving two Higgs doublets, which allows for an adequate fit of the lepton mass spectrum.

This study details hyperfine-resolved laser spectroscopy of the A$^2\Pi \leftarrow$ X$^2\Sigma^+$ transition in MgF, a process pertinent to laser cooling applications. We successfully recorded 25 rotational transitions with an absolute precision exceeding 20 MHz, identified 56 hyperfine lines, and calculated precise structural parameters for the A$^2\Pi$ state regarding rotation, fine structure, and hyperfine splitting. The radiative lifetime of this excited state was found to be 7.2(3) ns, aligning well with *ab initio* theoretical predictions. Additionally, we documented the transition isotope shift between bosonic MgF isotopologues and compared these findings against values predicted by the Born-Oppenheimer approximation. By applying electric fields up to 10.6 kV cm$^{-1}$, we measured the Stark effect on specific rotational lines of the transition, yielding permanent electric dipole moments of $\mu_X=$2.88(20) D for the ground X$^2\Sigma^+$ state and $\mu_A=$3.20(22) D for the first excited A$^2\Pi$ state of $^{24}$MgF. Based on these results, we highlight potential losses in the optical cycling transition caused by electric field-induced parity mixing in the excited state; consequently, to scatter $10^4$ photons, the electric field must be maintained below 1 V cm$^{-1}$.

We investigate the extended Bogomolny equations with gauge group $SU(2)$ defined on $\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^+$, subject to generalized Nahm pole boundary conditions and a nilpotent Higgs field. By establishing a Kobayashi-Hitchin correspondence that links these equations to specific holomorphic data, we achieve a complete classification of all solutions.

Various blockchain types have been deployed across different domains, yet their relative independence often results in isolated data silos. To address this, cross-chain interaction mechanisms have been introduced to link disparate blockchains; however, existing solutions frequently compromise the security of the original chains. These methods either rely on insecure third-party intermediaries or less secure techniques, leading to either a "security downgrade" where cross-chain security falls below that of the source blockchains, or the "blockchain invisible" issue where interactions occur even if the paired blockchain does not exist. This paper first introduces a system interaction model to analyze potential security vulnerabilities. Based on these findings, we propose the CIFuV method, which verifies paired blockchain data using the latter's consensus algorithm. This approach ensures that cross-chain interaction maintains security parity with the paired blockchain. Finally, we evaluate security challenges during system interactions and assess the feasibility of implementing the CIFuV model on public blockchains.

Precise and rapid evaluation of resection margins is a critical component of a dermatopathologist's daily workflow. This study presents a deep learning approach designed to aid pathologists by highlighting critical areas within Whole Slide Images (WSI) that are likely to contain pathological features, specifically focusing on Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) detection via semantic segmentation using UNet-based models. The research utilized a dataset of 650 WSIs comprising 3,443 tissue sections, with two clinical dermatopathologists manually annotating tumor locations on 100 images to create ground truth. The remaining data served for model validation and testing. We evaluated two distinct encoders for the UNet's initial stage and implemented two training strategies: deep supervision and a linear combination of decoder outputs, providing insights into the decoder's behavior under each condition. The top-performing model demonstrated over 96% accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity on the test set.

Fock states serve as the foundational quantum states for bosonic fields, providing a critical framework for analyzing their quantum behavior. As eigenstates of both energy and particle number, they possess a precisely defined count of quanta, making them the most accurate representation of the particle-like properties of fields. These characteristics render them highly valuable for applications in metrology, quantum simulation, and information processing. However, generating Fock states remains a significant challenge, particularly in optics, where deterministically creating states with more than one photon—or at macroscopic scales—is exceptionally difficult. This difficulty stems from a scarcity of mechanisms capable of producing large Fock states and the negative impact of linear dissipation.

In this work, we propose a novel phenomenon in nonlinear boson physics resulting from the interaction between dissipation and Kerr nonlinearity. In this effect, a nonlinear resonance becomes dissipationless only when it contains a specific number of quanta (such as photons), while remaining lossy otherwise. This loss, driven by nonlinear interference, gives rise to new quantum statistical phenomena. Notably, it induces spontaneous condensation of intensity noise, which could facilitate the creation of large Fock states and light with extreme photon-number squeezing. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this effect impacts new optoelectronic device classes, such as lasers, which can stabilize ultra-low-noise states by balancing gain against the newly introduced nonlinear loss. We illustrate these concepts with examples of realizable systems: one scenario shows how nonlinear dissipation could produce optical Fock states with $n=1000$, while another demonstrates how standard laser architectures could generate macroscopic light ($>10^{12}$ photons) with approximately 95% less noise than the standard quantum limit.

Attention mechanisms are fundamental to natural language processing, particularly in recurrent neural networks. Recent scholarship has increasingly questioned whether intermediate representations from these modules can elucidate a model's reasoning and reveal its decision-making logic. While a recent study by Jain and Wallace (2019) argues that "Attention is not Explanation," we contest several of their foundational assumptions. We maintain that their conclusion relies heavily on a specific definition of explanation and that valid testing requires a rigorous experimental design incorporating all model components. To address this, we introduce four alternative evaluation methods: a uniform-weights baseline, variance calibration across multiple random seeds, a diagnostic framework utilizing frozen pretrained weights, and an end-to-end adversarial attention training protocol. These approaches facilitate meaningful interpretation of attention in RNNs. Our findings demonstrate that even when robust adversarial distributions are identified, they fail the simple diagnostic test, suggesting that prior research does not invalidate the utility of attention mechanisms for explainability.

This paper introduces SolidStateDetectors.jl, an open-source software package designed to compute electric fields and simulate charge carrier drifts along with resulting pulses in solid-state detectors. The tool supports full 3D calculations and can leverage detector symmetries, allowing for the analysis of surrounding environmental effects. Developed in the performance-oriented and user-friendly language Julia, the package enables efficient, parallel execution of 3D field computations and drift simulations. Although applicable to various semiconductor devices, the focus is specifically on germanium detectors, with verification demonstrated using an n-type segmented point-contact germanium detector. The authors also outline planned features for upcoming releases.

As genome sequencing technologies advance, researchers can construct increasingly accurate reference genomes, thereby enhancing the sensitivity of read mapping and subsequent analyses like variant calling. This heightened sensitivity is essential for a deeper comprehension of genome donors, such as their health profiles. Consequently, read sets from sequenced samples should ideally align with the most recent reference genome that best represents the relevant population. However, the exponential growth in genomic data renders the complete re-mapping of every read set to an updated reference prohibitively costly. While various tools aim to accelerate the process of transferring read data from one reference to another, they face a critical limitation: if a read aligns to a region in the old reference that lacks sufficient similarity in the new reference, the read cannot be remapped. Due to this flaw, current state-of-the-art remapping tools result in the loss of a substantial portion of annotations. To overcome this significant constraint, we introduce AirLift, a rapid and comprehensive method for remapping alignments across different genome versions. Compared to the standard approach of full re-mapping, AirLift reduces the execution time required to transfer read sets between two reference versions by up to 27.4 times. Validation against GATK confirms that AirLift maintains high accuracy in detecting ground truth SNP and INDEL variants.

We employ the horizontal lift path integral formulation of the vielbein bundle alongside the holonomy map from gauge theory to concisely characterize parallel transport and geodesic equations on a manifold. This approach is initially demonstrated through a review of Schwarzschild geometry within the framework of general relativity. We subsequently adopt the Newton-Cartan formulation of the Schwarzschild metric established in prior literature and re-examine the system for both torsional and non-torsional geometries. The analysis investigates specific transport curves, including circular timeless loops, circular geodesic loops, radial geodesic loops, and stationary loops. After comparing the results across these three geometries and summarizing their key distinctions, we discuss the underlying mechanisms. Notably, our findings reveal a "performance tradeoff" between torsional and non-torsional Newton-Cartan theories: the torsional variant produces more precise equations of motion, while the non-torsional version accurately simulates relativistic dilation and contraction effects.

We have discovered a novel category of vulnerabilities within differential privacy implementations, specifically stemming from the mismatch between finite-precision arithmetic (using integers or floats) and idealized arithmetic over real numbers or integers when calculating basic statistics like sums. This discrepancy causes the actual sensitivity of these statistics—measuring how much a single individual's data influences the outcome—to be significantly higher than anticipated. As a result, virtually all existing differential privacy libraries fail to add sufficient noise to satisfy differential privacy guarantees, leaving them susceptible to realistic attacks capable of extracting individual-level data from private query systems. Beyond identifying these flaws, we also propose several remedies that adjust or restrict how sums are computed to restore idealized or near-idealized sensitivity bounds.

Solving variational problems and other scientific machine learning tasks using neural networks has been hindered by issues of inconsistency and the inability to precisely integrate expressions containing neural network structures. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a new neural network architecture that merges a polynomial mixture-of-experts framework with free knot $B_1$-spline basis functions. Essentially, this design executes piecewise polynomial approximation across each cell of a trainable partition of unity. The architecture supports both $h$- and $p$-refinement for regression tasks, achieving convergence rates predicted by approximation theory, thereby ensuring consistency in variational problem solving. Furthermore, the network, its moments, and its partial derivatives can all be integrated exactly, eliminating the need for sampling or quadrature and facilitating error-free computation of variational forms. We validate the efficacy of our network through various regression and variational problems, highlighting its consistency and exact integrability.

For Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) to achieve agility, it must be compatible with DevOps, which serves as the technical foundation of Agile practices. This paper outlines our experiences in implementing and applying the BB8 architecture, which enables the reuse of Eclipse-based MDE toolkits within an integrated workflow system. We detail the application of this architecture within the GitLab DevOps environment and discuss emerging areas for future research resulting from our implementation.
This paper demonstrates that the functor of idempotent probability measures, when operating within the category of compacta and their continuous mappings, is perfectly metrizable.

This paper investigates specific problems within unitary ensembles, focusing on the probability of finding a gap symmetric around zero, defined as $(-a,a)$, in both the Gaussian unitary ensemble (GUE) and the Jacobi unitary ensemble (JUE), with the latter restricted to $\alpha=\beta$. By leveraging the even parity of the weight, we map the gap problem to determining the product of the smallest eigenvalue distributions for the Laguerre unitary ensemble (LUE) with parameters $\alpha=-1/2$ and $\alpha=1/2$, alongside the shifted JUE with weights $x^{1/2}(1-x)^{\beta}$ and $x^{-1/2}(1-x)^{\beta}$. The $\sigma$ function, representing the derivative of the logarithm of the smallest eigenvalue distributions for finite-$n$ LUE or JUE, adheres to the Jimbo-Miwa-Okamoto $\sigma$ form of Painlevé $P_{V}$ and $P_{VI}$. Notably, in the shifted Jacobi case involving the weight $x^{\alpha}(1-x)^{\beta}$, the $\beta$ parameter does not appear in the resulting equation. Furthermore, we derive asymptotic expansions for the smallest eigenvalue distributions of the LUE and JUE under appropriate double scalings and determine the constants within the asymptotic expansions of the gap probabilities, which are expressed using the Barnes $G$-function evaluated at specific points.

This study examines the metric power-law $f(R)\sim R^n$-gravity model for a four-dimensional metric tensor defined by two coordinates. We derive exact analytical vacuum solutions across various values of $n$. These solutions encompass both non-stationary configurations characterized by travelling waves and stationary ones, including those dependent on a single radial variable.

Although LiDAR mapping is crucial for self-driving cars and mobile robotics, it presents significant challenges. To address this global point cloud registration issue, DeepMapping transforms complex map estimation into a self-supervised training process for simple deep networks. While DeepMapping achieves broad convergence on small datasets, it fails to yield satisfactory results on large-scale datasets containing thousands of frames. This limitation stems from a lack of loop closures and precise cross-frame point correspondences, as well as the slow convergence of its global localization network. We introduce DeepMapping2, which incorporates two new techniques to resolve these problems: (1) organizing training batches according to map topology derived from loop closing, and (2) a self-supervised local-to-global point consistency loss that utilizes pairwise registration. Experiments and ablation studies on public datasets (KITTI, NCLT, and Nebula) validate the effectiveness of our approach, and our code will be made available.

This paper presents a classical radiation reaction model for electron betatron oscillations within a plasma wakefield accelerator. It determines the peak energy an electron can attain due to longitudinal radiation reaction and analyzes damping caused by both longitudinal and transverse effects. Theoretical and numerical results are compared, showing strong agreement. The paper also examines the conditions under which quantum radiation becomes significant. Ultimately, this model holds importance for the design of future plasma-based super accelerators or colliders.

A weighted simplicial complex is defined as a simplicial complex where vertices are assigned specific values known as weights. This paper focuses on such complexes equipped with weights taking values in $\mathbb{R}^2$. The study investigates the concepts of weighted homology and weighted analytic torsion within the context of these structures.

The CP2K software suite, often likened to the swiss army knife of atomistic simulations, is introduced with a particular focus on ab-initio molecular dynamics utilizing the second-generation Car-Parrinello approach. Following an overview of ongoing and upcoming development initiatives for massively parallel, low-scaling post-Hartree-Fock and eigenvalue solvers, the text presents innovative strategies to leverage future low-precision hardware architectures. The primary objective is to integrate the submatrix method with approximate computing principles to meet the demands of the impending exascale era.

Histopathology images are gigapixel in scale and contain information across various resolutions. Obtaining annotations for these images demands specialized pathologists, resulting in high costs and significant time investment. Self-training mitigates these annotation limitations by leveraging both labeled and unlabeled data, thereby decreasing the number of pathologist annotations needed. This study investigates teacher-student self-training architectures for Non-alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH) using clinical histopathology datasets with sparse annotations. The models are assessed on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution test sets under conditions of clinical data shift. Results indicate that through self-training, the optimal student model statistically surpasses the teacher, achieving a 3% absolute improvement in macro F1 score. Furthermore, this best-performing student model reaches performance levels comparable to a fully supervised model trained with double the number of annotations.

Quantum spin liquids represent a rare state characterized by intense many-body entanglement, offering promising prospects for future quantum computing. This research presents muon spin relaxation ($\mu^+$SR) data obtained from a newly synthesized high-pressure material, Hollandite K$_{2}$V$_8$O$_{16}$. In this quasi-one-dimensional system, charge ordering at $T_{\rm MIT}\approx160$~K isolates half of the vanadium chains, creating model-like Heisenberg spin-1/2 chains. Zero-field $\mu^+$SR measurements reveal an exponential relaxation profile persisting down to $T=100$~mK, confirming the lack of long-range magnetic order. Furthermore, the relaxation rate remains constant below $T_{\rm QSL}\approx2$~K, and longitudinal field experiments indicate a highly dynamic ground state. These findings constitute the first verification of quantum spin liquid (QSL) behavior in the Hollandite family, stabilized by charge ordering. Additionally, strong local electron correlations and a one-dimensional Fermi surface suggest this QSL acts as a gapless Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid (TLL), uniquely observed in a stoichiometric compound under zero magnetic field and ambient pressure.

We demonstrate the existence and symmetry properties of every minimizer for a constrained variational problem that utilizes the fractional gradient. This mathematical framework is intrinsically linked to certain fractional kinetic equations.

We establish a theoretical framework for gapped domain walls separating topologically ordered systems in two spatial dimensions. Our analysis reveals a novel superselection sector, termed the "parton sector," which partitions the established superselection sectors residing on these domain walls. Furthermore, we investigate composite superselection sectors constructed from these parton sectors. We present a systematic approach to defining such sectors, along with their fusion spaces and fusion rules, by deriving nontrivial identities that connect their quantum dimensions and fusion multiplicities. Additionally, we propose a set of axioms concerning the ground state entanglement entropy in systems capable of hosting gapped domain walls, extending the bulk axioms introduced in [B. Shi, K. Kato, and I. H. Kim, Ann. Phys. 418, 168164 (2020)]. Mirroring our bulk analysis, we derive these primary findings by scrutinizing the self-consistency relations of an entity known as the information convex set. As a practical application, we define an analog of topological entanglement entropy specifically for gapped domain walls and obtain its precise analytical expression.

Probabilistic context-free grammars have historically served as generative models within machine learning and symbolic regression, where they produce algebraic expressions. We treat these expressions as equivalence classes of strings generated by a grammar and investigate the challenge of determining the probability of deriving a specific expression under a given grammar, demonstrating that this problem is generally undecidable. However, we introduce specific grammars tailored for generating linear, polynomial, and rational expressions, for which probability calculation algorithms are feasible. For these particular cases, we develop methods to compute exact probabilities as well as efficient approximations with arbitrary precision.

Within boundary conformal field theory, we establish a sum rule connecting the two- and three-point functions of the displacement operator. In the specific case of a three-dimensional boundary within a four-dimensional conformal field theory, this rule links the two distinct boundary contributions to the trace anomaly of the stress tensor. We validate this sum rule across various free theories and a weakly interacting scenario, where a bulk free scalar field couples marginally to a generalized free field residing on the boundary.

A large built-in electric field along the growth axis renders excitons in wide GaN/(Al,Ga)N quantum wells spatially indirect even without external bias. High densities of these indirect excitons can be gathered in electrostatic traps created within the quantum well plane by depositing a thin metal layer on the heterostructure's surface. Through combined spatially-resolved photoluminescence and photo-induced current measurements, we show that an external electric bias can regulate the exciton density within the trap by modifying the trap depth. Specifically, a negative bias deepens the trapping potential but fails to increase exciton accumulation because the lateral electric field at the electrode edges triggers exciton dissociation. This carrier loss manifests as higher photo-current and diminished photoluminescence intensity. Conversely, a positive bias eliminates the electrode-induced trapping potential, allowing excitons to escape the trap and resume free propagation in the plane, a phenomenon confirmed by spatially-resolved photoluminescence.
Building on [Pan21], we introduce and investigate a functor that maps equivariant sheaves on $\mathbb{P}^1$ to automorphic sheaves on modular curves.

This study addresses the challenge of estimating causation probabilities in scenarios where both treatments and outcomes are non-binary. While Tian and Pearl previously established sharp bounds for the probability of necessity and sufficiency (PNS), probability of sufficiency (PS), and probability of necessity (PN) based on experimental and observational data, our work extends this by deriving theoretical bounds for all causation probability types applicable to multivalued treatments and effects. Additionally, we present illustrative examples demonstrating how these bounds inform practical decision-making and employ simulation studies to assess the informativeness of the bounds across various data configurations.

Graphs serve as a fundamental tool for modeling data relationships, supporting graph machine learning (ML) across diverse fields, from molecular drug discovery to social network recommendations. However, standard graph ML methods often demand extensive labeled data to perform well, a requirement that is frequently unmet in real-world settings where labeled data for emerging concepts is scarce. Although meta-learning has been employed for few-shot graph tasks, most existing approaches assume that data from seen classes is perfectly labeled, causing them to fail when faced with weakly-labeled data containing significant noise. Consequently, this paper addresses the novel challenge of weakly-supervised graph meta-learning to enhance model robustness and knowledge transfer. We introduce Graph Hallucination Networks (Meta-GHN), a new framework built upon robustness-enhanced episodic training. Meta-GHN is designed to hallucinate clean node representations from noisy, weakly-labeled inputs and extract highly transferable meta-knowledge, facilitating rapid adaptation to unseen tasks with limited labels. Extensive experiments confirm that Meta-GHN outperforms current graph meta-learning methods in weakly-supervised few-shot node classification.

Leveraging digitally recorded and quantified neurological exam data is crucial for healthcare systems to enhance care delivery—both in-person and through telehealth—amidst an increasing shortage of neurologists. However, existing digital biomarker pipelines are often limited to specific exam components or targeted conditions. This paper introduces Digitized Neurological Examination (DNE), an accessible, vision-based solution utilizing smartphones or tablets to broaden biomarker recording capabilities and clinical applications. The DNE software enables healthcare providers and individuals at home to video-record instructed neurological tests, such as finger tapping, finger-to-finger movements, forearm rolls, and stand-up-and-walk tasks. Its modular architecture allows for the integration of additional tests. By extracting 2D/3D human body poses from recordings, DNE quantifies kinematic and spatio-temporal features that are clinically significant, allowing clinicians to document and monitor movement changes over time. The system includes a web server and user interface for viewing recordings and visualizing features. Evaluated on a dataset of 21 subjects featuring both normal and simulated impaired movements, DNE demonstrated overall accuracy through various machine learning models, achieving over 90% accuracy for upper-limb tests and 80% for stand-up and walk tests.

We provide a proof of Pixton's generalized Faber-Zagier relations within the tautological Chow ring of $\overline M_{g,n}$. Our approach closely mirrors the method employed by Pandharipande, Pixton, and Zvonkine to establish the same result in cohomology. Central to our argument is the Givental-Teleman classification of semisimple cohomological field theories.
