Additionally, as a difficult case study, we learn a Lorenz analogue from a single scalar extracted from video footage of a chaotic waterwheel experiment. This proposed framework integrates deep learning to identify effective coordinates with the Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) for interpretable modeling. Consequently, we demonstrate that it is feasible to simultaneously learn both a closed-form model and its corresponding coordinate system for partially observed dynamics.

Although XSD binary floating-point datatypes are frequently employed for precise numeric values within RDF, their application in knowledge representation often degrades data quality and raises the likelihood of erroneous processing outcomes compared to the XSD decimal datatype. This analysis argues that the XSD decimal datatype is generally more appropriate for representing numeric values in RDF. Furthermore, an examination of datatype usage within a subset of the December 2020 Web Data Commons dataset—which includes over 19 billion literals from real-world web data—confirms the practical significance of this issue, revealing that 29% to 68% of binary floating-point values are distorted by the datatype.

Our findings indicate that Migdal-Eliashberg theory ceases to be valid once the electron-phonon coupling $\lambda$ exceeds a finite critical value $\lambda_c$, a limit that holds true irrespective of the specific model Hamiltonian used. This critical threshold $\lambda_c$ falls roughly between 3.0 and 3.7. For coupling strengths greater than $\lambda_c$, a novel phase emerges that breaks lattice translational symmetry; depending on crystal symmetry and filling fraction, this phase manifests as either an insulator or a Fermi liquid. A defining characteristic of this state is a gap or a significant depression in the fermionic density of states near the Fermi level. We demonstrate the theory's failure from within the Migdal-Eliashberg framework by showing that the specific heat of the normal state becomes negative for $\lambda \ge 3.7$ and that quasiparticle lifetimes vanish in the strong-coupling limit. At any fixed $\lambda > \lambda_c$, the transition to this new phase occurs at a temperature higher than the superconducting transition temperature. Furthermore, varying $\lambda$ across $\lambda_c$ at a constant temperature induces a first-order phase transition between the new phase and the superconducting state. To address the regime beyond the validity of Migdal-Eliashberg theory, we propose a new "lattice-fermionic theory of superfluidity." This framework connects the Migdal-Eliashberg approach with strong-coupling physics, reducing to the former at small $\lambda$ while accurately describing the new phase and related phenomena for $\lambda > \lambda_c$.

This study investigates various space complexity metrics for two types of stack automata variants: non-erasing stack automata and checking stack automata. These metrics define the minimal stack size needed to recognize every word in the language (weak measure), the maximal stack size consumed during any accepting computation for an accepted word (accept measure), and the maximal stack size used across all possible computations (strong measure). The paper offers a thorough characterization of the accept and strong space complexity for checking stack automata, demonstrating that exactly one of three scenarios applies: the complexity is constant, grows linearly with input length, or is unbounded by any function of the input length (with decidability established for determining which case holds). Conversely, this trichotomy does not apply to non-erasing stack automata; the authors present an example where space complexity increases proportionally to the square root of the input length. Additionally, the work examines complexity bounds for machines accepting specific languages and addresses the decidability of space complexity properties.

This study examines sparse sample covariance matrices defined as $\frac1{np_n}\mathbf X\mathbf X^*$, where $\mathbf X$ represents an $n\times m$ sparse matrix with a sparsity parameter $p_n$. We establish the local Marchenko--Pastur law within a specific complex domain, provided that $np_n>\log^{\beta}n$ for some $\beta>0$ and a $(4+\delta)$-moment condition holds for $\delta>0$.

Introducing heavy neutral leptons, specifically right-handed neutrinos, into the Standard Model offers one of the most compelling explanations for observed neutrino masses and flavor mixing. The mixing between active and sterile neutral leptons alters charged and neutral currents, generating new signatures detectable by future collider experiments. This paper investigates the potential for discovering very heavy right-handed neutrinos at upcoming facilities such as the Large Hadron electron Collider (LHeC) and the linear collider. We examine production mechanisms through both $t$- and $s$-channel processes, focusing on decays into semi-leptonic final states. Particular attention is given to scenarios where the gauge boson resulting from heavy neutrino decay is highly boosted, forming a fat-jet. Finally, we compare our findings on sterile neutrino constraints with limits established by previous experiments.

We provide a normal form for pseudo-Einstein contact forms and utilize it to construct intrinsic CR normal coordinates parameterized by the CR geometry structure group. This proof relies on Jerison and Lee's construction of parabolic normal coordinates.
The $f$-invariant represents a concept of entropy associated with probability-measure-preserving actions of free groups, and we demonstrate that it remains unchanged under bounded orbit-equivalence.

High-energy neutrinos are anticipated to originate from interactions involving accelerated particles at their production sites; consequently, investigating correlations between the arrival directions of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) and high-energy neutrinos is of significant interest. This study presents the outcomes of a search for such correlations between UHECR events recorded by the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array, and high-energy neutrino candidates detected by IceCube and ANTARES. We conducted a cross-correlation analysis by scanning the angular separation between the arrival directions of these particles. Comparing our findings against null hypotheses assuming isotropic distributions for either neutrinos or UHECRs yielded post-trial p-values on the order of $\sim 10^{-2}$.

This study introduces dynamic equations governing two-dimensional closed surfaces and provides analytical solutions for simplified scenarios. We derive the equations for surface normal motions through two distinct methods. The analysis of normal-direction motion equations reveals that any homogeneous, two-dimensional closed surface with constant surface energy density assumes a constant mean curvature configuration upon reaching equilibrium with its surroundings. To illustrate this, we apply the framework to examine the equilibrium geometries of micelles, clarifying their tendency to form spherical, lamellar, and cylindrical structures. Furthermore, we demonstrate that theoretical calculations for the optimal micellar radius align closely with both all-atom simulations and experimental data.

The type-III seesaw mechanism offers a natural and straightforward explanation for the extremely small masses of neutrinos. Unlike high-energy seesaw theories, which typically introduce a greater number of effective parameters than those observable in low-energy neutrino phenomenology, the Casas-Ibarra parametrisation allows the information lost by integrating out heavy fermions to be encoded within an arbitrary complex orthogonal matrix. The CMS collaboration has previously searched for triplet fermions within the type-III seesaw model, assuming a single generation that decays democratically into Standard Model leptons. We reinterpret this CMS search within a realistic framework featuring two or three generations of triplet fermions and aim to understand the consequences of the aforementioned matrix on the $95\%$ CL lower bound for triplet fermion masses. Furthermore, we examine the phenomenological implications of this matrix regarding charged lepton flavour violation and displaced decays of triplet fermions at colliders.

This study details simulation outcomes for the July 14, 2000 "Bastille Day" solar proton event. Utilizing the Energetic Particle Radiation Environment Model (EPREM) and the CORona-HELiosphere (CORHEL) suite within the SPE Threat Assessment Tool (STAT) framework, we modeled proton acceleration to GeV levels caused by a coronal mass ejection (CME) traversing the low solar corona, subsequently comparing these results with GOES-08 data. The coupled simulations tracked particle acceleration from 1 to 20 $R_\odot$ before transitioning to modeling only particle transport. The model successfully replicated the event's peak fluxes, timing, and spatial distribution of energetic particles. While peak fluxes and initial hourly variations aligned well with observations, the simulated CME exited the inner simulation boundary after a few hours. Consequently, the model accurately captures low-coronal acceleration processes and identifies the primary acceleration sites near the Sun. Integral flux envelope plots from multiple simulated observers near Earth further refined the comparison to observations, enhancing the potential for predicting solar particle events. Broken-power-law fits to fluence spectra aligned with diffusive acceleration theory in the low-energy range, whereas high-energy fits revealed acceleration rate variability mirroring that observed in solar-cycle 23 GLEs. We also discuss improvements for STAT predictions, such as applying corrected GOES energy bins and calculating fits to the seed spectrum. Ultimately, this paper establishes a predictive tool for simulating low-coronal SEP acceleration.

The differential entropy rate is a key metric for characterizing continuous-valued stochastic processes. While the convergence rates of many properties in Long-Range Dependent (LRD) processes are slower than intuition derived from conventional models like Markov processes suggests, it remains an open question whether this holds true for the entropy rate. This paper investigates the differential entropy rate of processes whose autocorrelation functions decay according to a power law. We demonstrate that despite sharing similar autocorrelation and spectral density functions, Fractional Gaussian Noise and ARFIMA(0,d,0) exhibit distinct entropic characteristics, especially under negative correlation parameterizations. Furthermore, we establish an equivalence between mutual information (between past and future) and differential excess entropy for stationary Gaussian processes, identifying the finiteness of this quantity as the threshold separating short-range from long-range dependence. Finally, we analyze the convergence of conditional entropy to the differential entropy rate, finding that for short-range dependence the rate is $O(n^{-1})$, whereas for LRD processes the convergence is slower and contingent upon the Hurst parameter.

This study reports a search for high-mass hadronic resonances decaying into a parton and a Lorentz-boosted resonance, which subsequently decays into two partons. Utilizing data from proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV recorded by the CMS detector at the LHC (an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$), the boosted resonance is identified as a single wide jet exhibiting substructure indicative of a two-body decay, while the high-mass resonance is treated as a dijet system. By leveraging jet substructure details and the kinematic characteristics of cascade decays, the analysis distinguishes the signal from the dominant quantum chromodynamics multijet background. The dijet mass spectrum is examined for signs of new high-mass resonances and aligns with standard model background predictions. These findings are interpreted within a warped extra dimension framework, where the high-mass resonance corresponds to a Kaluza-Klein gluon, the boosted resonance to a radion, and the final-state partons are all gluons. Production cross-section limits are established as a function of the masses of the Kaluza-Klein gluon and radion. At a 95% confidence level, these limits rule out models featuring Kaluza-Klein gluon masses between 2.0 and 4.3 TeV and radion masses between 0.20 and 0.74 TeV. Through the exploration of this novel experimental signature, the observed limits on the Kaluza-Klein gluon mass are extended by approximately 1 TeV relative to prior searches.

Isothermal compressibility ($\kappa_{\rm T}$) serves as a crucial thermodynamic metric that reveals how a system diverges from ideal fluid behavior. In this study, we present the first estimation of $\kappa_{\rm T}$ for QCD matter generated in high-energy hadronic and nuclear collisions, utilizing the color string percolation model (CSPM). Our analysis examines variations in $\kappa_{\rm T}$ relative to final-state charged particle multiplicity and initial percolation temperature across diverse collision systems. Determining the initial percolation temperature for various collision scenarios and energies enhances our comprehension of the system's early evolution phase. By comparing CSPM-derived $\kappa_{\rm T}$ values with those of standard fluids, we suggest that matter produced in heavy-ion collisions represents the {\it closest perfect fluid} identified in nature. This finding aligns with the established observation of a minimal shear viscosity to entropy density ratio in the potential quark-gluon plasma (QGP) medium created during heavy-ion experiments. Furthermore, a threshold pseudorapidity density of charged particles, $\langle dN_{\rm ch}/d\eta \rangle \geq 20$, is identified in final-state event multiplicities; exceeding this value at LHC energies warrants the investigation of possible QGP formation.

Domain adaptation techniques aim to transfer knowledge from a source domain to an unseen target domain. Currently, the leading unsupervised methods for subjective text classification utilize both labeled source data and unlabeled target data. This paper introduces a novel approach for single-task text classification that relies on a simple yet effective strategy of diversity-based generalization. Unlike existing methods, our approach does not require unlabeled target data while achieving performance comparable to the state-of-the-art. Diversity acts as a mechanism to enhance generalization and mitigate domain shift by compelling the model to avoid over-reliance on identical features. We apply this concept to the most interpretable component of neural networks: the attention layer. To foster sufficient diversity, we developed a multi-head attention model incorporating a constraint that ensures each head learns distinct patterns. We further extended this model by implementing tri-training and establishing an additional diversity constraint between the attention heads of the tri-trained classifiers. Extensive evaluations on the standard Amazon reviews benchmark and a newly created Crisis events dataset demonstrate that our fully unsupervised method performs on par with competing baselines that utilize unlabeled target data. Our findings indicate that machine learning architectures prioritizing diversity achieve superior generalization, suggesting a promising direction for future research into creating universally applicable learning models that function without labeled target data.

Post-translational modifications (PTMs) occur after protein translation and play critical roles in various cellular functions, including DNA repair, cell signaling, and apoptosis. Succinylation, a recently identified PTM, alters the charge of lysine residues from $-1$ to $+1$. Because experimental identification of succinylation sites via mass spectrometry is highly labor-intensive, researchers increasingly rely on computational approaches leveraging machine learning. This study introduces a deep learning model designed to predict these succinylation sites. When evaluated against current state-of-the-art deep learning models and conventional machine learning methods, the proposed architecture demonstrates a favorable balance between computational efficiency and classification accuracy.

We demonstrate the local-in-time existence of classical solutions for the vacuum free boundary problem associated with the viscous Saint-Venant system for shallow waters, a system rigorously derived by Gerbeau-Perthame from the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with a moving free surface. Our solutions, representing height and velocity, remain smooth up to the moving boundary, even though the height exhibits a singularity related to the distance from the vacuum interface. The proof relies on novel higher-order weighted energy functionals and corresponding estimates designed to handle the degeneracy near the moving vacuum boundary.

This study explores techniques for extracting speaker details from personalized speaker-adapted neural network acoustic models (AMs) used in automatic speech recognition (ASR). This issue is particularly critical within federated learning frameworks for ASR, where a global model is trained on a server using updates from numerous clients. We introduce a method to analyze information within neural network AMs by employing a neural network footprint on an Indicator dataset. Leveraging this approach, we constructed two attack models designed to deduce speaker identities from updated personalized models without requiring access to the original users' speech recordings. Experimental results on the TED-LIUM 3 corpus confirm that these methods are highly effective, achieving equal error rates (EER) of 1-2%.

Human culture depends on innovation, defined as the continuous exploration of combining existing elements to generate new ones. This process is not isolated but relies on collective search and accumulation. While reinforcement learning (RL) typically assumes that fully-connected groups are optimal for innovation, human studies indicate that hierarchical innovation is more effectively achieved through dynamic social networks. In these dynamic environments, individuals oscillate between solitary or small-group innovation and sharing results with the broader community. To our knowledge, the impact of social network structure on innovation has not been systematically investigated within RL frameworks. This study employs a multi-level problem setting (WordCraft) with three distinct innovation tasks to test the hypothesis that social network structures influence the performance of distributed RL algorithms. We systematically designed networks of Deep Q-Networks (DQNs) sharing experiences from replay buffers across varying topologies (fully-connected, small-world, dynamic, and ring) and introduced behavioral and mnemonic metrics to extend the traditional reward-centric evaluation of RL. Comparing innovation levels across different tasks and network structures reveals that: first, consistent with human findings, dynamic structures facilitate the highest innovation in tasks characterized by deceptive elements and large search spaces; second, experience sharing is less beneficial when a single clear path to innovation exists; and third, the proposed metrics offer crucial insights into the success of different network structures by analyzing experience diversity at both individual and group levels.

The Silicon Vertex Detector (SVD), composed of four double-sided silicon strip sensor layers, serves as one of the two vertex sub-detectors for Belle II at the SuperKEKB collider in KEK, Japan. Since data collection began in 2019, the SVD has proven reliable and highly efficient, even under the extreme beam backgrounds generated by the collider's record-breaking instantaneous luminosity. To achieve optimal track reconstruction—including efficient pattern recognition and fitting—while accurately propagating position uncertainties to track parameters, it is essential to precisely determine the resolution of cluster position measurements. This discussion will cover several methods for estimating this position resolution directly from data.

Hop-by-hop flow control mechanisms are prevalent across various environments, ranging from data centers to on-chip wormhole-routing architectures. Network Calculus (NC), an algebraic framework representing traffic and service guarantees as curves in a Cartesian plane, provides a method to calculate worst-case end-to-end delays in these networks. By employing transformation operations like min-plus convolution, NC models how traffic profiles evolve as they traverse network nodes. This approach enables the modeling of flow-controlled systems, allowing for the computation of an end-to-end service curve that defines the minimum guaranteed service for a flow passing through a sequence of flow-controlled nodes. Although the algebraic expression for this curve is concise, its practical computation is often intractable due to the rapid explosion of data structures, rendering operations unfeasibly complex even for networks with merely three hops. This paper introduces computational and algebraic strategies to address this challenge. We demonstrate that existing methods, such as reducing to compact domains, are unsuitable for this specific scenario. Instead, we propose a suite of solutions designed to curb the expansion of data representation space and to implement computationally efficient algorithms for min-plus convolution. Our approach yields significant performance improvements, enabling the analysis of previously infeasible case studies, and delivers exact results without relying on any approximations.

Publicly traded firms must file periodic reports using word-level eXtensive Business Reporting Language (XBRL) tags, a process that is manually tedious and expensive. Consequently, we frame XBRL tagging as a novel entity extraction task within the financial sector and introduce FiNER-139, a dataset comprising 1.1 million sentences annotated with gold-standard XBRL tags. Distinct from standard entity extraction resources, FiNER-139 features an expansive label set of 139 entity types. The majority of annotated tokens are numeric, where the appropriate tag relies heavily on contextual cues rather than the token's intrinsic properties. We demonstrate that fragmenting numeric expressions into subwords degrades BERT's performance, whereas word-level BILSTMs yield superior results. To enhance BERT, we propose two straightforward yet effective strategies that substitute numeric expressions with pseudo-tokens capturing both original token shapes and numerical magnitudes. Additionally, we evaluate FIN-BERT, a pre-existing financial domain BERT variant, and release our own SEC-BERT, pre-trained on financial filings, which achieves the best performance. Finally, through data and error analysis, we pinpoint potential limitations to guide future research on XBRL tagging.

Recent years have seen a significant focus on accelerated degradation testing to accurately assess the reliability properties of systems intended to function effectively over years or even decades. In this context, degradation data collected under specific stress levels are extrapolated using suitable statistical models to estimate lifetime quantiles under normal operating conditions. This paper introduces optimal experimental designs for repeated measures accelerated degradation tests involving competing failure modes, which correspond to multiple response components. It is assumed that observation time points are predetermined and fixed. Marginal degradation paths are modeled using linear mixed effects models, and the optimal design is derived by minimizing the asymptotic variance of the estimator for a specific quantile of the failure time distribution under normal use conditions. Numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the robustness of the proposed designs and to compare their efficiency against standard experimental designs.

Unit commitment (UC) serves as a critical resource for transmission system operators to determine cost-effective and feasible generation schedules and dispatch instructions. Constraint screening has gained significant interest due to its potential to eliminate inactive or redundant constraints within the UC framework, thereby accelerating the resolution of large-scale optimization problems. While standard screening methods optimize over load and generation variables to identify binding line flow limits, they often remain conservative, leaving a substantial number of constraints for the UC solution. This paper introduces a novel machine learning (ML) model that forecasts the most economical costs based on load inputs. By connecting the cost implications of UC decisions with optimization-based screening, this ML approach enables the exclusion of a higher proportion of operational constraints. We validate the method's effectiveness in both sample-aware and sample-agnostic contexts, demonstrating that the proposed scheme significantly reduces computation time across various UC problem configurations.

Cells maintain homeostasis through intricate biochemical mechanisms known as signaling pathways, typically visualized as networks where proteins serve as nodes and their interactions as edges. Accurately mapping these pathways is essential for comprehending cellular-level diseases and treatments. Because disease states can alter these pathways, deriving them from specific patient or condition data holds significant value. While various methods exist for this inference, our work builds on previous research that frames the task as estimating Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) using phosphoproteomic time-series data. Employing a Bayesian framework, we utilize Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to determine a posterior distribution of potential DBN structures. Our main contributions include (i) a new proposal distribution designed to efficiently sample sparse graphs and (ii) the removal of standard restrictive modeling constraints. We have implemented this approach, titled Sparse Signaling Pathway Sampling, in Julia using the Gen probabilistic programming language. This methodology enables the construction of robust statistical models; the resulting code is modular, readable, and extensible. Specifically, Gen allows us to tailor the inference process for biological networks and achieve efficient sampling. We assessed our algorithm on both simulated datasets and the HPN-DREAM pathway reconstruction challenge, benchmarking it against multiple baseline techniques. Our findings highlight the immense promise of probabilistic programming, particularly Gen, for inferring biological networks. The full codebase is available at https://github.com/gitter-lab/ssps.

This study introduces a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) based deep learning framework for Child Activity Recognition (CAR), addressing the fact that previous research in this field has relied predominantly on CNNs and LSTMs despite the superior capabilities of GCNs. To our knowledge, this is the first application of a GCN model specifically within the CAR domain. To mitigate challenges associated with limited publicly available datasets for child actions, we employed several learning strategies, including feature extraction, fine-tuning, and curriculum learning, to enhance model performance. Motivated by conflicting views on transfer learning in CAR, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of transfer learning and investigated its negative effects, an area previously unexplored in this context. Our primary contribution is the development of an ST-GCN based CAR model that achieved approximately 50% accuracy on vanilla implementations despite the small dataset size. By integrating feature extraction and fine-tuning, accuracy improved by 20% to 30%, reaching a peak of 82.24%. Additionally, empirical results on activity datasets demonstrate that carefully selecting pre-trained models via curriculum learning can further boost accuracy. Finally, we offer preliminary insights into the impact of frame rate on CAR model accuracy, suggesting a promising direction for future research.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents frequently struggle to generalize to unseen variations within the state space encountered during training. This challenge is particularly acute in image-based RL, where minor changes, such as a shift in background color, alter numerous pixels and drastically disrupt the agent's latent image representation, often causing the learned policy to fail. To foster more robust representations, we propose TEmporal Disentanglement (TED), a self-supervised auxiliary task that leverages the sequential nature of RL observations to create disentangled image representations. Empirical results demonstrate that RL algorithms incorporating TED as an auxiliary task adapt more rapidly to environmental variable changes during continued training compared to current state-of-the-art representation learning methods. Furthermore, because TED enforces a disentangled representation structure, policies trained with it exhibit superior generalization to unseen values of both task-irrelevant variables (e.g., background color) and task-relevant variables that influence the optimal policy (e.g., goal positions).

In 2018, the Micro-X mission became the inaugural program to deploy Transition-Edge Sensors with SQUID readouts into space, aiming to capture a high-resolution, spatially resolved X-ray spectrum of the Cassiopeia A Supernova Remnant. Although a rocket pointing error prevented the instrument from observing its target, the mission successfully validated the system's flight performance. While the detectors recorded X-rays from an onboard calibration source, their operational time was constrained by sensitivity to external magnetic fields. Despite this limitation, detector responses remained consistent between ground-based and flight operations. This paper outlines the initial flight performance and details the upgrades prepared for a reflight, including enhancing SQUIDs to reduce magnetic susceptibility, synchronizing digital electronics clocks to minimize beat frequencies, and replacing cryostat-to-rocket mounts to strengthen mechanical integrity. Given that the flight performance matched ground-level results, achieving laboratory goals is now viewed as a reliable predictor of future mission success.

Code modifications are executed differently across mobile and non-mobile environments. While previous studies have examined specific platform differences, there remains a gap in understanding how code evolution varies across these distinct software platforms. This paper presents a study investigating the frequency of changes and the co-evolution of source code, build, and test modifications in both mobile and non-mobile contexts. We constructed regression models to identify factors influencing change frequency and utilized the Apriori algorithm to detect frequently co-occurring change types. Our results indicate that non-mobile repositories exhibit a higher volume of monthly commits; furthermore, our regression analysis suggests that the mobile nature of a project significantly reduces commit frequency even when controlling for confounding variables like code size. Additionally, we observed that developers rarely modify source code files simultaneously with build or test files. We argue that these findings offer developers valuable insights into platform-specific practices, enabling them to adopt strategies from successful software systems.

Multi-site spectroscopic observations from three locations enabled the identification of frequencies and pulsational modes for the $\gamma$ Doradus star HD 12901. Six frequencies within the 1-2 c/d range were detected, with their identifications corroborated by various line-profile measurement techniques and prior photometric data. Five of these frequencies possessed adequate signal-to-noise ratios for mode identification; notably, all five exhibited similar three-bump standard deviation profiles that were well-fitted by $(l,m)=(1,1)$ modes, yielding reduced chi-squared values below 18. Consequently, we suggest that HD 12901 is an ideal candidate for testing models of non-radially pulsating $\gamma$ Doradus stars, given the presence of multiple $(1,1)$ modes.

This study presents tests of lepton universality in the decays $B^0\to K^0_S \ell^+ \ell^-$ and $B^+\to K^{*+} \ell^+ \ell^-$, where $\ell$ represents either an electron or a muon. Differential branching fractions for $B^0\to K^0_S e^+ e^-$ and $B^+\to K^{*+} e^+ e^-$ are measured across various intervals of the dilepton invariant mass squared. Utilizing proton-proton collision data from the LHCb experiment with an integrated luminosity of $9\, \mathrm{fb}^{-1}$, the findings align with both the Standard Model and prior lepton universality tests in analogous decay channels. Furthermore, this work reports the initial observation of $B^0 \to K^0_S e^+ e^-$ and $B^+ \to K^{*+} e^+ e^-$ decays.

Rationale refers to a subset of input features that best justifies or underpins the predictions made by machine learning models. Identifying these rationales has enhanced the interpretability and generalization capabilities of neural networks when processing vision and language data. In graph-based applications, such as predicting properties for molecules and polymers, pinpointing representative subgraph structures known as graph rationales is critical for optimizing graph neural network performance. However, current methods relying on graph pooling or distribution interventions struggle due to a scarcity of examples needed to learn optimal graph rationales. To address this, we introduce a novel augmentation technique called environment replacement, which automatically generates virtual data instances to bolster rationale identification. We further propose an efficient framework that conducts rationale-environment separation and representation learning on both real and augmented data within latent spaces, thereby circumventing the high complexity associated with explicit graph decoding and encoding. Experimental results across seven molecular and four polymer datasets, compared against recent techniques, validate the effectiveness and efficiency of this proposed augmentation-driven graph rationalization framework.

Neural networks are increasingly deployed across various contexts to forecast wind direction and speed, critical variables for estimating wind farm power potential. However, their utility is often constrained because traditional neural networks cannot quantify uncertainty. This study explores Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs), where weights, biases, and outputs are modeled as distributions instead of fixed point estimates. This approach enables the assessment of both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, yielding well-calibrated predictions for wind speed and power. Specifically, we apply BNNs to offshore wind resource forecasting for renewable energy. Our analysis utilizes data from the FINO1 research platform in the North Sea, employing oceanic metrics such as water temperature and current direction as predictors. The probabilistic forecasts generated by the BNN significantly enhance the results, particularly by indicating the network's reliability when predicting out-of-sample data. Leveraging this capability, we determine that the accuracy and uncertainty of our wind speed and direction predictions remain stable despite the construction of the nearby Alpha Ventus wind farm. Consequently, networks trained on pre-construction ocean data can effectively predict wind field characteristics from ocean data even after the wind farm is operational.

Shifting toward renewable energy sources presents significant challenges for grid stability and operation, where secondary control plays a vital role in restoring the system to its reference state after disturbances. Insufficient estimation of required control capacity can necessitate emergency actions like load shedding, highlighting the need to understand the underlying risks and drivers of control activation. This study develops an explainable machine learning model to analyze secondary control power activation in Germany. By training gradient-boosted trees, we achieve an accurate depiction of when control is triggered. Furthermore, utilizing SHapely Additive exPlanation (SHAP) values, we examine how external factors—including the generation mix, forecasting inaccuracies, and electricity market data—influence control activation. This analysis identifies the specific drivers behind elevated reserve requirements in the German power system. Our transparent methodology, which leverages open data and enhances the interpretability of machine learning models, creates new pathways for scientific discovery.

In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), where agents operate with partial observations, effectively utilizing local information is paramount. Over extended observation periods, agents can cultivate \textit{awareness} regarding their teammates to mitigate partial observability challenges. However, existing MARL approaches typically fail to harness this type of local information. To solve this issue, we introduce a new framework called multi-agent \textit{Local INformation Decomposition for Awareness of teammates} (LINDA), enabling agents to decompose local data and construct awareness for each teammate. We conceptualize awareness as stochastic random variables and employ representation learning to guarantee the quality of these awareness representations by maximizing the mutual information between them and the actual trajectories of the corresponding agents. LINDA is algorithm-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated into various MARL methods. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework successfully extracts informative awareness from local partial observations, enhancing collaboration and significantly boosting learning performance, particularly on difficult tasks.

Attention mechanisms currently lead the field in explaining deep models, generating input probability distributions widely interpreted as indicators of feature importance. However, this paper identifies a critical flaw in these explanations: their inability to accurately determine the polarity of a feature's impact. This limitation can be misleading, as high attention weights do not always signify faithful contributions to predictions; instead, such features may exert suppressing effects. In light of this discovery, we re-evaluate the explainability of existing attention-based techniques, including Attentio$\odot$Gradient and LRP-based methods. We introduce a practical diagnostic approach, termed the faithfulness violation test, to assess the consistency between explanation weights and the actual direction of feature impact. Extensive experiments reveal that most tested explanation methods are unexpectedly compromised by faithfulness violations, a problem particularly prevalent in raw attention mechanisms. Furthermore, empirical analyses of the factors driving these violations offer valuable insights for selecting appropriate explanation strategies in attention models.

This study investigates the exclusive decay channels of the Higgs boson into $B_c B_c$ and $B_c^\ast B_c^\ast$ pairs. The hard components of the decay amplitudes are calculated using perturbative Standard Model methods, including one-loop corrections, while the soft fusion of heavy quarks into quarkonium is modeled within a relativistic quark framework.

Can the genesis of novel computational concepts be elucidated through computation itself? Is it viable to characterize the discovery of new algorithmic methods using solely mathematical principles? This research represents the inaugural attempt to examine this type of inquiry from the perspective of the endeavor required to devise a new algorithm for a specific problem. We establish program reachability as a probability function where the input is a measure of energetic cost, specifically algorithmic entropy, associated with the problem.

This paper investigates the emergence of limit cycle bifurcations within an epidemic framework featuring two distinct categories of aware individuals. While most transition rates remain constant, the alerting decay rate for the most aware group and the creation rate for the less aware group vary non-linearly based on disease prevalence. To analyze the ODE model, we compute limit cycles and assess their stability using the Poincaré map, and we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of an endemic equilibrium. These conditions highlight a specific relationship between disease transmissibility and awareness transmission. Additionally, stochastic simulations with a minimal rate of imported cases are employed to validate the bistability scenarios—specifically the coexistence of an endemic equilibrium and a limit cycle—observed in the ODE solutions.

We establish a Bonnesen-type inequality for the real projective plane, extending Pu's systolic inequality to metrics with positive curvature. The remainder term in this inequality, which mirrors the structure of Bonnesen's original result, depends on a suitably normalized function of R minus r, where R and r denote the circumradius and inradius of the Weyl-Lewy Euclidean embedding of the orientable double cover. This work utilizes John ellipsoids associated with a convex body and applies Pogorelov's rigidity theorem.

We investigate the XXX spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ Heisenberg chain on a circle with an arbitrary twist. By employing the modified algebraic Bethe ansatz, we characterize the model's spectral problem and examine the scalar product between the Bethe vector and its dual. This approach yields modified Slavnov and Gaudin-Korepin formulas for the system, offering the first instance of such formulas for quantum integrable models lacking ${\rm U}(1)$ symmetry that are defined by an inhomogenous Baxter T-Q equation.

This study reports Ultraviolet-photoemission (UPS) data, complemented by specific-heat, thermal-expansion, resistivity, and magnetic-moment measurements, for the magnetic shape-memory alloy Ni$_2$MnGa across the temperature interval $100K < T < 250K$. All experimental techniques consistently identify distinct signatures of the premartensitic transition ($T_\mathrm{PM}\sim 247K$) and the martensitic transition ($T_\mathrm{M} \sim 196K$). Temperature-dependent UPS reveals a pronounced depletion of states, known as a pseudogap, at $T_\mathrm{PM}$ situated 0.3eV beneath the Fermi energy. First-principles electronic structure calculations indicate that the peak observed at 0.3eV in UPS spectra for temperatures above $T_\mathrm{PM}$ arises from Ni-d minority-spin electrons. Below $T_\mathrm{M}$, this peak vanishes, leading to an increased density of states near 0.8eV. This enhancement corresponds to Ni-d and Mn-d contributions to the majority-spin density of states and is associated with substantial Fermi surface reconstruction.

This study analyzes the pitch angle distribution function (PADF) in nearby galaxies and derives the resulting black hole mass function (BHMF) using the established link between pitch angle and black hole mass. Our dataset includes 74 spiral galaxies from the Carnegie-Irvine Galaxy Survey with absolute $B$-band magnitudes $\mathfrak{M}_{B}>-19.12$ mag and luminosity distances $D_{\mathrm{L}} \leq 25.4$ Mpc, extending a prior complementary sample of 140 more luminous ($\mathfrak{M}_{B}\leq-19.12$ mag) late-type galaxies. Surprisingly, the PADFs of these two groups are not significantly different, a finding with potential significance for spiral galaxy formation theories. Our results reveal a clear bimodal distribution in pitch angles separating Sa-Sc and Scd-Sm types, with Sa-Sc galaxies exhibiting tighter spiral arms on average. Crucially, we identify a distinct bifurcation in the BHMF: Sa-Sc galaxies typically host "supermassive" black holes ($M_{\bullet}\gtrsim10^6\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$), while Scd-Sm galaxies contain "less-than-supermassive" black holes ($M_{\bullet}\lesssim10^6\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$). We anticipate that the latter population will yield valuable discoveries of elusive intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs), providing the precise benchmarks needed for future gravitational wave detector generations.

This study introduces the inaugural streaming algorithms for multitasking scheduling across parallel machines with shared processing. Our proposed streaming approximation schemes can deliver an approximate optimal makespan within a single pass; however, if jobs are accessible in two passes, the algorithm can construct a schedule with that approximate value. Beyond offering a big data algorithmic solution for this specific problem, this work also sheds light on designing streaming algorithms for other scheduling challenges.

The threat of adversarial attacks against unprotected Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) operating in public spaces is escalating. While integrating AI, particularly Deep Learning (DL), to control and guide UAVs enhances performance, it introduces safety concerns regarding vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks that can confuse agents and increase collision risks. This paper introduces a novel method leveraging the explainability of DL techniques to create an efficient detector that safeguards these DL frameworks and the UAVs employing them from potential threats. The agent utilizes a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) scheme for guidance and planning, specifically a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) with Prioritised Experience Replay (PER), which incorporates Artificial Potential Fields (APF) to accelerate training and improve obstacle avoidance. Adversarial attacks were simulated using the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Basic Iterative Method (BIM), which reduced obstacle course completion rates from 80% to 35%. A realistic synthetic environment designed for UAV explainable DRL planning and guidance, complete with obstacles and adversarial scenarios, was constructed. Two detectors were proposed: the first employs a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) achieving 80% detection accuracy, while the second utilizes a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, attaining 91% accuracy with significantly faster computation times compared to the CNN-based approach.

This work introduces a novel formalism for expressing and manipulating diversity metrics of qualitative variables within a Hilbert space. The inherent abstraction of this space naturally accommodates the equivalence of qualitative variables, enabling the representation of binary responses to categories and establishing a new criterion for selecting diversity measures based on their robustness against uncertainty. The full utility of this Hilbert space formulation becomes evident when tackling the common data analysis challenge of category reduction. By integrating strategies from mathematical and physical statistics—specifically the concept of partial trace—the proposed formalism resolves this issue, demonstrating that proper normalization of diversity measures is essential for interpreting results sensibly during category reduction. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the straightforward measurement of diversity and execution of category reduction in scenarios involving the selection of simultaneous categories.

Controlling non-equilibrium open quantum systems is a difficult yet essential challenge for advancing current quantum information technologies. We present a general, model-free framework utilizing Reinforcement Learning to discover out-of-equilibrium thermodynamic cycles that achieve Pareto-optimal balances between power and efficiency for quantum heat engines and refrigerators. Unlike traditional approaches, this method requires no prior knowledge of the quantum thermal machine, its system model, or its quantum state; it relies solely on observing heat fluxes, making it suitable for both simulations and experimental setups. We validated our approach by identifying Pareto-optimal power-efficiency trade-offs in two distinct systems: an experimentally realistic refrigerator using a superconducting qubit, where we uncovered non-intuitive control sequences that mitigate quantum friction and surpass previously proposed cycles; and a heat engine based on a quantum harmonic oscillator, where we identified cycles with complex structures that exceed the performance of the optimized Otto cycle.

This report introduces an automated system for classifying diseases in dermoscopic images, leveraging deep learning through transfer learning applied to VGG16 and GoogLeNet architectures. Our approach prioritizes preprocessing techniques, specifically image augmentation and color normalization. The system's performance was assessed on Task 3 (Lesion Diagnosis) of the ISIC 2018 challenge, which focuses on skin lesion analysis for melanoma detection.

This paper establishes that for indefinite quadratic programming problems with linear constraints, any sequence produced by the Proximal DC decomposition algorithm $R$-linearly converges to a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker point, assuming a solution exists. Furthermore, it demonstrates that sequences generated by the DC algorithm converge to a locally unique solution when initial points are selected from an appropriately chosen neighborhood. To address these implicitly defined iterative sequences, the study employs local error bounds for affine variational inequalities alongside novel techniques. The paper presents numerical results, analyzes the impact of the decomposition parameter, and compares the Proximal DC decomposition algorithm with the Projection DC decomposition algorithm. These findings complement a significant recent study by Le Thi, Huynh, and Pham Dinh (J. Optim. Theory Appl. 179 (2018), 103-126).

This paper introduces an open-source Python framework designed for managing datasets in music processing, with the primary goals of enhancing research reproducibility and evaluating the generalization capabilities of machine learning models. The system automates the retrieval and setup of frequently used multimodal music datasets. It offers a Python API that allows users to access these datasets via Boolean set operations on specific attributes, such as intersections and unions of composers and instruments. The framework is engineered to simplify the integration of new datasets and their corresponding ground-truth annotations, enabling users to construct, transform, and extend custom collections that can be distributed using a compliant format to leverage the API. All code and annotations are released under appropriate open licenses.

Let $E_N$ represent the coarse moduli space of smooth elliptic surfaces defined over $\mathbb{P}^1$ possessing a fundamental invariant $N$. For all $N \geq 2$, we calculate the Chow ring $A^*(E_N)$. It is noteworthy that for each such $N$, the ring $A^*(E_N)$ exhibits Gorenstein properties with a socle located in codimension 16, a result that is unexpected given the dimension of $E_N$ is $10N-2$. Leveraging this finding, we demonstrate that the highest possible dimension of a complete subvariety within $E_N$ is 16. Specifically, when $N=2$, the associated elliptic surfaces correspond to K3 surfaces polarized by the hyperbolic lattice $U$. Furthermore, we establish that the generators of $A^*(E_2)$ consist of tautological classes on the moduli space $\mathcal{F}_{U}$ of $U$-polarized K3 surfaces, thereby offering support for a conjecture by Oprea and Pandharipande concerning the tautological rings of moduli spaces of lattice-polarized K3 surfaces.

Ensuring safety is critical when applying reinforcement learning (RL) to real-world scenarios, making chance constraints an effective approach for enhancing safety amidst uncertainty. However, current chance-constrained RL techniques, such as penalty and Lagrangian methods, often suffer from periodic oscillations or result in policies that are either overly conservative or unsafe. To overcome these limitations, we introduce the Separated Proportional-Integral Lagrangian (SPIL) algorithm. By analyzing the constrained policy optimization process through a feedback control lens—treating the penalty weight as the control input and the safe probability as the output—we model the penalty method as a proportional controller and the Lagrangian method as an integral controller. This framework allows us to unify these approaches into a proportional-integral Lagrangian method that combines their advantages, utilizing an integral separation technique to constrain the integral value within a reasonable range. Furthermore, we employ a model-based calculation for the gradient of safe probability to accelerate training. Our method demonstrates reduced oscillations and conservatism in a car-following simulation and proves its practicality in a real-world mobile robot navigation task, where the robot successfully evades a moving obstacle exhibiting highly uncertain or aggressive behavior.

We contend that Stoner magnetism in bands characterized by Berry curvature is deeply shaped by the chiral interplay between Berry's orbital magnetization and spin chirality density. The primary mechanism involves carriers traversing a spin texture perceiving it as a pseudo-magnetic field source, which couples to their orbital dynamics via a chiral Aharonov-Bohm effect. This interaction promotes chiral spin configurations, such as skyrmions—topologically protected entities with particle-like characteristics that stabilize in the ground state. By lowering the threshold for Stoner instability, this chiral coupling makes chiral spin-ordered phases easily achievable under realistic conditions. We demonstrate this phenomenon using a graphene multilayer model where magnetization and pseudo-magnetic fields vary across valleys, though the findings extend to general Stoner magnets.

This study investigates the emergence of superconductivity in rhombohedral trilayer graphene driven exclusively by long-range Coulomb repulsion. This repulsion-induced phase contrasts sharply with those observed in twisted bilayer and trilayer graphenes, where the unique momentum-space geometry of Bloch wavefunctions creates an effective electron-electron attraction. Consequently, twisted systems typically exhibit less modulated order parameters and spin-singlet pairing. In contrast, rhombohedral trilayer graphene displays spin-triplet superconductivity with critical temperatures reaching up to 0.15 K. These temperatures are highly sensitive to electron filling and peak at points where the density of states diverges. Furthermore, the order parameter exhibits substantial modulation within each valley pocket of the Fermi surface.

Simulating the Hubbard model is considered a primary candidate for the initial practical applications of fault-tolerant quantum computing. A recent investigation into quantum algorithms for early Hubbard model simulations [Kivlichan \textit{et al.} Quantum 4 296 (2019)] demonstrated that the most efficient resource utilization was achieved through split-operator Trotterization paired with the fast-fermionic Fourier transform (FFFT) on $L \times L$ lattices where $L=2^k$. For lattices where $L \neq 2^k$, Givens rotations serve as an alternative to FFFT but incur significantly higher resource costs. We introduce a novel analytical method for bounding simulation errors arising from Trotterization, yielding substantially tighter constraints for the split-operator FFFT approach and resulting in a sixteen-fold improvement in error bounds. Additionally, we propose plaquette Trotterization, which functions across lattices of any size, and apply our refined error analysis to demonstrate competitive resource requirements. In the context of a phase estimation task, we show that plaquette Trotterization decreases the count of non-Clifford gates by a factor ranging from $5.5\times$ to $9\times$ (dependent on the parameter regime) compared to previous best estimates for $8 \times 8$ and $16 \times 16$ lattices, with even greater reductions for other lattice sizes not conforming to $L=2^k$. Ultimately, we identify a potentially viable application for fault-tolerant quantum computers utilizing approximately one million Toffoli gates.

Although goal-conditioned reinforcement learning grants agents diverse capabilities, it frequently falters on tasks demanding extended temporal reasoning. To address this, we introduce a method that integrates imagined subgoals into policy learning to master complex objectives. These subgoals are forecasted by a dedicated high-level policy, trained concurrently with the primary policy and its critic. Utilizing the value function as a reachability indicator, this high-level policy anticipates intermediate states en route to the final goal. Unlike traditional approaches, the agent does not need to explicitly reach these subgoals; instead, they inform a prior policy that is embedded within a KL-constrained policy iteration framework to accelerate and stabilize learning. While these imagined subgoals guide the training process, they are excluded during inference, where only the final policy is executed. Our approach is validated on intricate robotic navigation and manipulation scenarios, demonstrating significant performance gains over current state-of-the-art methods.

We introduce a link lattice complex for plumbed links, extending the work of Ozsv\'ath, Stipsicz, and Szab\'o, as well as Gorsky and N\'emethi. We demonstrate that for any plumbed link within a rational homology 3-sphere, this link lattice complex is homotopy equivalent to the link Floer complex as an $A_\infty$-module. Furthermore, we establish that the link Floer complex of a plumbed L-space link serves as a free resolution of its homology. Consequently, we provide an algorithm to calculate the link Floer complexes of plumbed L-space links, including algebraic links, directly from their multivariable Alexander polynomials.

For a considerable period, it has been recognized that the standard inference drawn from the observed near-flatness of the large-scale Universe—specifically, the cosmological "flatness problem," which serves as a primary motivation for positing an ultra-short inflationary expansion in the early Universe—is fundamentally flawed. This contribution reinforces earlier findings demonstrating the absence of such a cosmological flatness problem that inflation could resolve. It achieves this by clarifying prevalent misconceptions and elaborating on specific arguments with greater detail.

Although Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) excel at producing high-quality images, they are often hindered by inefficiency stemming from high computational costs and excessive memory consumption. While recent attempts to compress GANs have yielded smaller generators, these methods typically compromise image quality or rely on lengthy search procedures. This study addresses these limitations by employing a teacher network that defines a search space for efficient architectures and facilitates knowledge distillation. First, we refine the search space for generative models by incorporating inception-based residual blocks into the generators. Second, to meet specific computational targets, we introduce a one-step pruning algorithm that derives a student architecture from the teacher, significantly lowering search overhead. This approach eliminates the need for L1 sparsity regularization and its associated hyperparameters, thereby streamlining the training process. Finally, we propose distilling knowledge by maximizing feature similarity between the teacher and student using a metric called Global Kernel Alignment (GKA). Our resulting compressed networks maintain image fidelity (measured by FID and mIoU) comparable to or superior to the original models while drastically reducing computational costs, such as MACs. The code is available at https://github.com/snap-research/CAT.

Inspired by the need for question generation in conversational news recommendation systems, we introduce a model designed to create question-answer (QA) pairs featuring self-contained, summary-focused questions and length-limited, article-summarizing responses. We start by assembling a novel dataset comprising news articles with titles formatted as questions, paired with summaries of varying lengths. This dataset trains a QA pair generation model that simultaneously produces concise yet sufficient summaries as answers alongside their corresponding questions. Furthermore, we apply a differentiable reward function to reinforce the generation process, addressing exposure bias, a prevalent issue in natural language generation. Evaluations through both automatic metrics and human assessment confirm that these QA pairs effectively capture the core essence of the articles and maintain high answer accuracy.

This study provides a spectral and temporal analysis of {\it Swift}/XRT and {\it NuSTAR} data collected from GRS 1716--249 during its 2016--2017 outburst. Following a 23-year quiescent period since its last major eruption in 1993, this low-mass X-ray binary experienced an exceptional outburst. Observations were conducted over two epochs in April 2017, specifically on the 7th and 10th. Joint spectral fitting across the 0.5–79.0 keV range reveals a spectrum dominated by relatively cold, weak disk blackbody emission and thermal Comptonization, alongside a relativistically broadened fluorescent iron K$\alpha$ line. A distinct Compton hump was identified near 30 keV, and an excess feature of approximately 1.3 keV was also detected. Adopting a lamp-post corona geometry, the inner disk radius was constrained to $11.92^{+8.62}_{-11.92}$ R$_{ISCO}$ (an upper limit) for the first epoch and $10.39^{+9.51}_{-3.02}$ R$_{ISCO}$ for the second epoch, where R$_{ISCO}$ denotes the radius of the innermost stable circular orbit. Furthermore, a significant ($\sim5\sigma$) type-C quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) at $1.20\pm0.04$ Hz was detected for the first time in GRS 1716--249; this frequency drifted to $1.55\pm0.04$ Hz ($\sim6\sigma$) by the conclusion of the second observation. The derived spectral and temporal characteristics demonstrate a positive correlation between the QPO frequency and the photon index.

We provide an explicit formula for the Waring rank of any binary binomial form with complex coefficients. Several examples are presented to demonstrate this result, and we compare the Waring rank against the real Waring rank for these forms.

This study reports on the degradation of signal output in plastic scintillator tiles within the hadron endcap (HE) calorimeter of the CMS detector caused by radiation damage. The tiles were subjected to particles from proton-proton collisions at the CERN LHC, operating at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV and an integrated luminosity of 50 fb$^{-1}$. These measurements utilize HE readout channels equipped with silicon photomultipliers and synthesize data from multiple origins, including a laser calibration system, a movable radioactive source, and hadrons and muons generated during pp collisions. The discussion also encompasses findings from various irradiation experiments utilizing $^{60}$Co sources. The observed damage is analyzed as a function of dose rate, revealing that within the measured range, a constant dose results in greater damage when the dose rate is lower.

Video generation presents a fascinating challenge within the field of computer vision, finding widespread use in data augmentation, motion special effects, and AR/VR applications. Driven by advancements in deep learning, numerous deep generative models have emerged to address this task. These models enable the utilization of vast amounts of unlabeled online images and videos by learning deep feature representations in an unsupervised fashion, and they are capable of producing diverse image types that hold significant value for visual applications. However, video generation remains notably more difficult than image generation because it requires modeling not only object appearances but also their temporal dynamics. This work proposes decomposing every video frame into content and pose components. We begin by extracting pose information from videos using a pre-trained human pose detection model, then employ a generative model to synthesize the video by integrating the content code and pose code.
We present the infinite dihedral group as an automaton group, gathering fundamental results and providing comprehensive, detailed proofs for every assertion.

Silicon pixel detectors form the foundation of both the existing and upcoming upgrades to the ATLAS experiment at the LHC. Due to their immediate placement near the interaction point, these sensors will endure exceptionally high levels of radiation throughout their operational life. The current detector has already suffered non-ionizing radiation damage exceeding $10^{15}$ 1 MeV ${n}_{eq}/{cm}^2$, whereas the detector designed for the high-luminosity LHC must withstand fluence levels an order of magnitude greater. This paper introduces a digitization model that accounts for radiation-induced effects on pixel sensors. The model is thoroughly detailed, and its predictions regarding charge collection efficiency and the Lorez angle are contrasted with collision data gathered from 2015 to 2017 (up to $10^{15}$ 1 MeV ${n}_{eq}/{cm}^2$).

This study focuses on modeling and numerically simulating speciation processes. Specifically, under conditions where speciation events occur within an ecosystem, we aim to construct the requisite modeling and simulation tools, ensuring a robust mathematical foundation that forms the basis of our framework, particularly in the paper's first half. The second half introduces a multi-scale framework for eco-evolutionary modeling, distinguishing between species-level and individual/population-level scales. Consequently, interacting species are described at the species level, whereas branching events require a population-level description. Our multi-scale approach couples these models by detecting speciation events in advance and resolving them at the population scale until branching concludes. Since the population model is defined as a partial differential equation (PDE), we first prove well-posedness in a time-discrete setting and then derive a posteriori error estimates, providing fully computable upper bounds on energy-type errors. These estimates remain valid for general smooth distributions, which aids in detecting speciation events. Finally, various numerical experiments validate the practical effectiveness of our framework.

Recognizing and drawing analogies is frequently employed as a benchmark for human intelligence, with Bongard problems serving as a specific instance of such a test. It has been hypothesized that the capacity to quickly form new abstractions is essential for solving these analogical tasks. Constructing a program that generates a given image represents one form of abstraction, a capability demonstrated by the Dreamcoder project. This paper offers a preliminary investigation into whether programs synthesized by Dreamcoder can facilitate analogical reasoning to address specific Bongard problems. Our approach involves using Dreamcoder to identify programs that produce the images within a Bongard problem, which are then represented as sequences of state transitions. These transitions are automatically annotated with positional data and encoded as logical facts in Prolog. Subsequently, we apply inductive logic programming (ILP) to derive an interpretable theory for the abstract concept underlying each Bongard problem instance. Experiments conducted on synthetically generated Bongard problems involving concepts like 'above/below' and 'clockwise/counterclockwise' indicate that our end-to-end system is capable of solving these tasks. Furthermore, we analyze the significance and completeness of each component of our methodology, identifying current limitations and suggesting avenues for improvement in both our specific formulation and Dreamcoder-like program synthesis systems generally.

The Cascaded lattice-Boltzmann method (Cascaded-LBM) utilizes a novel category of collision operators designed to enhance numerical stability. Unlike standard single or multiple relaxation time approaches, it executes the relaxation process based on central moments—defined as hydrodynamic fluid velocity-shifted moments—applied sequentially at varying relaxation rates. This study introduces and derives source terms for Cascaded-LBM to capture the influence of external and internal forces on fluid dynamics. This is accomplished by aligning the discrete representation of source or forcing terms with their continuous central moment forms. Various continuous central moment formulations for sources are examined, including one derived from a local Maxwellian. Consequently, the resulting forcing terms are inherently Galilean invariant. The specific expressions for these source terms, dependent on force and macroscopic velocity fields, are fully determined by the central moment method and the orthogonal properties of the moment basis. Compared to existing forcing schemes, the proposed approach incorporates higher-order terms in velocity space. Furthermore, the method effectively generalizes both local equilibrium and source terms within the standard lattice frame, with these generalizations contingent upon the ratios of relaxation times for moments of different orders. Chapman-Enskog multiscale expansion analysis confirms that the Cascaded-LBM with these forcing terms remains consistent with the Navier-Stokes equations. Finally, computational tests on canonical problems featuring diverse force types validate the method's accuracy.

This paper presents a conceptual framework called The Golden Circle, which maps the roles and interactions of actors across individual, organizational, and societal levels within the content moderation ecosystem. Emphasizing harm reduction and context-aware moderation, it contends that the machine learning community must develop multimodal solutions, align their efforts with organizational values and objectives, and remain responsive to shifting social contexts embedded in their sociotechnical systems. This approach integrates sociological and technical perspectives to address the why, how, and what of content moderation.

Absolute model companionship (AMC) represents a rigorous strengthening of model companionship, defined as follows: Given a theory $T$, the notation $T_{\exists\vee\forall}$ refers to the logical consequences of $T$ that are boolean combinations of universal sentences. A theory $T^*$ is the AMC of $T$ if it is model complete and satisfies $T_{\exists\vee\forall} = T^*_{\exists\vee\forall}$. This concept is employed to investigate the continuum problem and to measure the expressive capacity of forcing. We demonstrate that a definable version of $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$ is the sole solution to the continuum problem compatible with the AMC of a "partial Morleyization" of the $\in$-theory $\mathsf{ZFC}$ augmented by the existence of "many" supercompact cardinals. Furthermore, assuming large cardinals, we show that forcibility overlaps with consistency for any mathematical problem $\psi$ expressible as a $\Pi_2$-sentence in a substantial fragment of third-order arithmetic; examples of such problems include the Continuum Hypothesis ($\mathsf{CH}$), the Suslin hypothesis, and the Whitehead conjecture regarding free groups.

Partial Morleyizations can be defined as follows: Let $\mathsf{Form}_{\tau}$ be the collection of first-order $\tau$-formulae. For a subset $A \subseteq \mathsf{Form}_\tau$, the language $\tau_A$ expands $\tau$ by introducing atomic relation symbols $R_\phi$ for every formula $\phi \in A$, and $T_{\tau,A}$ is the $\tau_A$-theory stating that each $\phi(\vec{x}) \in A$ is logically equivalent to its corresponding atomic formula $R_\phi(\vec{x})$. Consequently, for a $\tau$-theory $T$, the theory $T + T_{\tau,A}$ constitutes the partial Morleyization of $T$ induced by $A$.

Finally, we characterize a robust form of Woodin's axiom $(*)$ as the claim that the first-order theory of $H_{\aleph_2}$, when formalized in a specific natural signature, is model complete.

To generate high-resolution depth maps, several existing learning-based multi-view stereo techniques construct a cost volume pyramid using a coarse-to-fine strategy. These methods rely on fixed depth range hypotheses to create cascaded plane sweep volumes; however, assigning identical ranges to every pixel is suboptimal because depth prediction uncertainties vary spatially. In contrast, we introduce a Dynamic Depth Range Network (DDR-Net) that determines depth range hypotheses adaptively. This is achieved through a Range Estimation Module (REM) trained to learn the uncertainties of hypotheses from earlier stages. Our DDR-Net begins by creating an initial depth map at the coarsest resolution across the full depth spectrum. Subsequently, the REM uses the probability distribution of this initial map to dynamically calculate depth range hypotheses for subsequent stages. Furthermore, we propose a new loss strategy that leverages these learned dynamic ranges to refine depth maps, ensuring that the ground truth value of each pixel remains within the hypothesized range for the next iteration. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches on the DTU benchmark and yields comparable results on the Tanks and Temples benchmark. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Tangshengku/DDR-Net.

This paper introduces general-purpose preconditioners for regularized augmented systems derived from optimization problems, including their associated normal equations. We examine positive definite preconditioners appropriate for CG and MINRES methods. Our approach involves "sparsifications" designed to prevent the eigenvalues of the preconditioned matrix from becoming complex. Particular focus is placed on systems resulting from the application of regularized interior point methods to linear and nonlinear convex programming problems.

We demonstrate that bicircular matroids possess only a finite set of excluded minors. Our proof relies on representing matroids through biased graphs and the recently defined class of quasi-graphic matroids. We establish that any excluded minor $N$ with a rank of ten or greater must be quasi-graphic. Furthermore, several smaller excluded minors are also quasi-graphic; by utilizing biased-graphic representations, we show that such an $N$ necessarily contains one of these smaller minors. Finally, we derive an upper bound on the number of elements in an excluded minor relative to its rank, thereby confirming the result.
The PBW theorem and universal enveloping algebras of braided m-Lie algebras are derived using combinatorics on words.

We compute the charge balance function for the bulk quark system prior to hadronization, as well as for the directly produced and final hadron systems in high-energy heavy ion collisions. Using the covariance coefficient to quantify the correlation strength between quark and anti-quark momenta when produced as pairs, we determine the parameter by matching hadronic results to existing data. By comparing hadronic outcomes with those of the bulk quark system, we investigate the impacts of hadronization and decay contributions. Our findings indicate that while hadronization through the quark combination mechanism slightly broadens the charge balance function widths, it maintains key characteristics such as longitudinal boost invariance and scaling properties in rapidity space. Although resonance decays exert a more substantial influence on the balance function width, they similarly fail to disrupt these boost invariance and scaling properties. Additionally, we present the balance functions in the azimuthal direction.

A primary obstacle in natural language generation (NLG) is effectively managing named entities, which frequently trigger grammatical errors involving incorrect prepositions, articles, or inflections. These mistakes are often overlooked during evaluation if one relies on small, randomly selected argument sets or translates from linguistically simpler languages like English to complex ones like Russian. Nevertheless, achieving broad grammatical precision is vital for certain applications, as native speakers may perceive entity-related errors as jarring, silly, or even offensive. To facilitate the development of more linguistically diverse NLG datasets, we introduce the Corpus of Linguistically Significant Entities (CLSE), which features annotations by linguistic experts. Spanning 34 languages and 74 semantic types, this corpus supports diverse applications ranging from airline ticketing to video games. As a demonstration of CLSE's utility, we created an augmented version of the Schema-Guided Dialog Dataset, termed SGD-CLSE. By leveraging CLSE entities and a limited set of human translations, we established a linguistically representative NLG evaluation benchmark across three languages: French (high-resource), Marathi (low-resource), and Russian (highly inflected). We further established quality baselines for neural, template-based, and hybrid NLG systems, analyzing the respective strengths and limitations of each approach.

X-ray ptychography imaging at synchrotron sources such as the Advanced Photon Source (APS) requires managing instrument hardware to capture diffraction patterns from overlapping coherent spots on extended samples, alongside handling data storage, reconstructing images, and providing visualization and feedback. Beyond this complex workflow, ptychography instruments can generate several terabytes of data per second, necessitating real-time processing. Consequently, there is a critical need for a high-performance, robust, and user-friendly software package for ptychographic data analysis. This paper introduces a software framework offering visualization, workflow control, and data reconstruction capabilities. To accelerate computation and handle large datasets, the reconstruction module utilizes the ePIE, DM, and LSQML algorithms implemented with CUDA-C on GPUs.

GitHub Copilot, which has recently become a prominent topic in both academic research and industry practice, is trained on billions of lines of publicly available code. While its intended purpose is to assist developers in creating secure and efficient code through advanced intelligence, it has sparked ethical and security concerns among practitioners and researchers. Key questions include whether copyleft-licensed code should be freely utilized for training and if insecure code should be included in the training dataset at all. These issues significantly impact Copilot and similar products that rely on deep learning models to extract knowledge from vast amounts of open-source code, a trend that is accelerating with the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence. To address these challenges, we propose the development of robust mechanisms to safeguard open-source code from exploitation by such models. In this work, we design and implement CoProtector, a prototype that employs data poisoning techniques to fortify source code repositories against these threats.
