The branching fraction ratio relative to the $\Lambda_b\rightarrow\psi(2S)p K^{-}$ decay mode—where the $\psi(2S)$ meson is reconstructed in the $J/\psi \pi^+\pi^-$ final state—is determined to be: \begin{equation*}
\frac{\Lambda_b^0\to\chi_{c1}(3872)pK^-}{\Lambda_b\to\psi(2S)p K^-} \times
\frac{\mathcal{B}(\chi_{c1} \to J/\psi \pi^+\pi^-)}{\mathcal{B}(\psi(2S)\to
J/\psi \pi^+\pi^-)} = \left(5.4 \pm 1.1 \pm 0.2\right)\times 10^{-2}\,,
\end{equation*} with the first uncertainty representing statistical error and the second representing systematic error.

This study introduces (3+1)D dynamical simulations of asymmetric nuclear collisions conducted at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). By integrating a dynamical initial state model with (3+1)D viscous relativistic hydrodynamics, we investigate the rapidity dependence of anisotropic flow within the RHIC small system scan at a center-of-mass energy of 200 GeV. Parameters are calibrated to accurately model central $^3$He+Au collisions, allowing for extrapolations to d+Au and p+Au systems. Our findings indicate that roughly 50% of the $v_3(p_T)$ discrepancy observed between the STAR and PHENIX Collaborations can be attributed to the utilization of reference flow vectors drawn from distinct rapidity regions. These results highlight the critical role of longitudinal flow decorrelation in anisotropic flow measurements for asymmetric nuclear collisions and underscore the necessity of (3+1)D simulations. Additionally, we provide data regarding the beam energy dependence of particle spectra and anisotropic flow in d+Au collisions.

Over the last few years, tiny machine learning (tinyML) has gained prominence, targeting the deployment of machine learning models on embedded AI processors that feature severely limited memory and computational resources. Low-precision quantization stands as a vital model compression strategy, significantly lowering both memory usage and the computational expenses associated with inference. This study concentrates on post-training quantization (PTQ) algorithms capable of reducing model precision to below 8-bit using minimal calibration datasets, evaluating them across various tinyML applications. To ensure a fair assessment, we constructed a simulated quantization framework to test recent PTQ methods. Additionally, we deconstructed these algorithms into their core components and reassembled them into a universal PTQ pipeline. Through an ablation study of different component alternatives within this pipeline, we identified critical design decisions for low-precision quantization. We anticipate that this research will offer valuable insights and guide future investigations into low-precision quantization techniques.

This study introduces a forecasting framework for telecommunications network rollout planning that leverages both data and machine learning. Accurately estimating milestone completion times is vital for this planning process, as precise predictions facilitate improved crew allocation and the optimization of material and logistics costs. To address the challenge of building a model from historical milestone data that integrates domain expertise, manages noise, and remains interpretable for project managers, the authors propose partition-based regression models. These models embed data-driven statistical techniques within specific partitions. Benchmarking results indicate that this approach achieves performance comparable to or superior to the best existing alternative based on Gradient Boosting, while utilizing a fraction of its complexity. Furthermore, the experiments confirm the method's effectiveness for both short-term and long-term forecasting. Ultimately, this approach is versatile and applicable to any scenario involving time-series regression with noisy, attributed data.

We demonstrate that the subspace $c_0$, consisting of sequences converging to zero, lacks a complement within the space $ac_0$ of sequences that almost converge to zero. Subsequently, we apply this identical methodology to the inclusion chain $c_0 \subset A_0 \subset \ell_\infty$.

Accurate precision tests of CKM unitarity within the Standard Model necessitate a systematic handling of strong and electromagnetic corrections in semi-leptonic decays. These electromagnetic effects demand the renormalization of a semileptonic four-fermion operator. This study computes the $\mathcal{O}(\alpha\alpha_s)$ perturbative conversion factors between the $\bar{\rm MS}$ scheme and various momentum-space subtraction schemes, including those applicable to lattice calculations. We examine schemes defined by MOM and SMOM kinematics, highlighting the critical role of the projector selection for each. The standard projector used for MOM kinematics in previous literature induces QCD corrections to the conversion factor that persist even when $\alpha=0$, creating an artificial dependence on the lattice matching scale that only vanishes upon summing all orders of perturbation theory. This issue stems from the violation of a Ward identity valid in the $\alpha=0$ limit. We demonstrate how to resolve this through careful projector choices and prove that the Wilson coefficients in these improved schemes are devoid of pure QCD contributions. Consequently, the resulting Wilson coefficients and operator matrix elements exhibit significantly reduced scale dependence. Our preference for the $\bar{\rm MS}$ scheme over the conventional $W$-mass scheme is driven by its greater tractability at higher orders and its ability to allow a clear separation of scales, unlike the latter. Leveraging this advantage, we derive renormalization-group-improved leading-log and next-to-leading-log strong corrections for electromagnetic contributions and investigate the dependence on the lattice matching scale induced by QED.

This paper investigates the numerical characteristics of supersolvable resolutions within line arrangements. We establish upper bounds for the extension to supersolvability numbers associated with specific extreme line arrangements in $\mathbb{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{C}}$, demonstrating that these values cannot be deduced solely from the arrangement's intersection lattice.

This study employed evolutionary algorithms coupled with first-principles calculations to globally search for crystal structures of ternary Mg-Sc-H hydrides (Mg$_x$Sc$_y$H$_z$) within the high-pressure range of 100 to 200 GPa. Utilizing these results, we constructed the thermodynamic convex hull and pressure-dependent phase diagram for compositions where $z/(x+y) < 4$. Four thermodynamically stable compounds with elevated hydrogen content were identified: $R\bar{3}m$-MgScH$_{6}$, $C2/m$-Mg$_{2}$ScH$_{10}$, $Immm$-MgSc$_{2}$H$_{9}$, and $Pm\bar{3}m$-Mg(ScH$_{4}$)$_{3}$. Their superconducting transition temperatures were estimated using the McMillan-Allen-Dynes formula integrated with first-principles phonon calculations. All four compounds exhibit superconductivity, with $R\bar{3}m$-MgScH$_{6}$ predicted to possess the highest critical temperature ($T_{c}$) of 23.34 K at 200 GPa.

Study Analysis Group 21 (SAG21) of the Exoplanet Exploration Program Analysis Group (ExoPAG) was established to investigate how stellar contamination impacts space-based transmission spectroscopy, a technique used to analyze exoplanet atmospheres by tracking the wavelength-dependent changes in a planet's radius during its transit across a star. Because this method depends on an accurate comprehension of the obscured star's spectrum, it faces challenges since stars are not uniform or static; rather, they possess evolving photospheres and chromospheres characterized by irregularities such as spots, faculae, and plages. To address current needs and optimize transit observations using existing NASA assets like HST and JWST, SAG21 assembled an interdisciplinary consortium of over 100 scientists, including theorists and observers from heliophysics, stellar astrophysics, planetary science, and exoplanet atmosphere research. The group's analysis yielded 14 key findings organized into three Science Themes: (1) utilizing the Sun as the primary benchmark for calibrating knowledge of stellar heterogeneities; (2) expanding this understanding through the study of stellar heterogeneities on stars beyond our Sun; and (3) integrating data gathered from both the Sun and other stars into transit study methodologies.

A primary obstacle for blockchain technology is interoperability, given that these systems are typically built as isolated units. Designing interoperability solutions for privacy-centric blockchains is especially difficult because they must harmonize with the underlying chain's unique privacy mechanisms to verify claims about specific transactions without compromising obfuscation. Consequently, users are often compelled to sacrifice privacy, such as by utilizing centralized exchanges, to transfer assets between different chains. This paper introduces ZCLAIM, a trustless framework for cross-chain asset migration grounded in the Zcash privacy protocol. ZCLAIM connects a smart-contract-enabled issuing chain with a Sapling implementation of Zcash to enable private cross-chain transfers. We demonstrate that a tokenized representation can be established through a series of collateralized intermediaries, ensuring that no third party learns or requires knowledge of the total transaction amount.

Code-switching refers to the practice of utilizing two or more languages within a single message, a trend that has become increasingly prevalent in social media communications. This linguistic mixing poses significant challenges for sentiment analysis tasks. This study employs a standard convolutional neural network to determine the sentiment of tweets containing a mixture of Spanish and English. Our straightforward method attained an F1-score of 0.71 on the competition's test set. Furthermore, we evaluate the capabilities of our top-performing model and conduct error analysis to highlight key obstacles in classifying sentiment within code-switching contexts.

This article explores coprimeness characteristics within one- and two-dimensional discrete equations that decompose into multiple polynomial factors. Following an initial experiment with a simple equation, we concentrate on higher-power extensions of the Somos-4 equation and the (1-dimensional) discrete Toda equation. Our earlier findings established that these equations possess both irreducibility and coprimeness when the right-hand side is non-factorizable. In this paper, we demonstrate that the coprimeness property remains valid for all these equations even when the right-hand side is factorizable, though the irreducibility property no longer holds.

Synapses are essential for cognition, learning, and memory, primarily by transforming pre-synaptic voltage spikes into post-synaptic currents and scaling input signals. Although various brain-inspired architectures have been developed to mimic biological synapse behavior, creating flexible, biocompatible circuits with biologically realistic time constants and adjustable gain remains a significant challenge. This study presents a physically flexible organic log-domain integrator circuit designed to overcome these limitations. Fabricated from electrically active organic materials, the circuit ensures flexibility and biocompatibility while maintaining time constants crucial for encoding spatiotemporal patterns and neural learning codes. Employing a 10 nF synaptic capacitor, the device achieved time constants of 126 ms before bending and 221 ms during bending. The research characterizes the circuit's performance both prior to and during flexion, subsequently investigating how weighting voltage, synaptic capacitance, and pre-synaptic signal disparity influence the time constant.

Researchers and practitioners are increasingly turning to machine learning for data modeling and inference. Unlike statistical methods, machine learning imposes fewer explicit assumptions regarding data structures, such as linearity; however, its parameters often remain difficult to connect to the underlying data-generating process. To understand these modeled relationships, practitioners frequently employ partial dependence (PD) plots and permutation feature importance (PFI). Despite their utility, PD and PFI currently lack a theoretical framework linking them to the data-generating process. This work formalizes PD and PFI as statistical estimators of ground truth targets derived from that process. We demonstrate that estimates from these methods deviate from the ground truth due to statistical biases, model variance, and Monte Carlo approximation errors. To address model variance in PD and PFI estimation, we introduce learner-PD and learner-PFI methods based on model refitting, alongside proposed estimators for corrected variance and confidence intervals.

Variational Gaussian process (GP) approximations have emerged as a standard approach for efficient GP inference, yet they necessitate user selection of variational features to enhance performance. Current literature offers diverse and non-generalizable choices for these features. We introduce a framework that treats GPs as elements within a Banach space, providing a unified perspective. This approach elucidates the relationships among existing features and establishes a link between kernel ridge regression and variational GP approximations.

This paper introduces the first and third cohomology groups for Leibniz triple systems, with applications to extension theory and $1$-parameter formal deformation theory. We examine the central extension theory for these systems, demonstrating a one-to-one correspondence between equivalence classes of central extensions and the third cohomology group. Furthermore, we analyze $T^*$-extensions of Leibniz triple systems, proving that under suitable conditions, every even-dimensional quadratic Leibniz triple system $(\mathfrak{L},B)$ is isomorphic to a $T^*$-extension. We also provide necessary and sufficient conditions for a quadratic Leibniz triple system to possess a symplectic form. Finally, we develop the $1$-parameter formal deformation theory for Leibniz triple systems, establishing that it is controlled by these cohomology groups.

Fractional derivatives and time delays serve as crucial instruments for modeling memory characteristics within natural systems. This study focuses on the stability analysis of a fractional-order delay differential equation given by $ D^\alpha x(t)=\delta x(t-\tau)-\epsilon x(t-\tau)^3-px(t)^2+q x(t) $. We derive the linearization of this system near its equilibrium points and establish corresponding linearized stability criteria. To evaluate the stability of these points, we formulate specific constraints on the parameters $\delta$, $\epsilon$, $p$, $q$, and $\tau$. Despite the involvement of five distinct parameters, we successfully map the stable region within the $q\delta-$plane for any positive values of $\epsilon$ and $p$, thereby offering a comprehensive stability analysis. Additionally, we examine chaotic behavior in the proposed model, which demonstrates chaos across a broad spectrum of delay parameters.

Employing a microscopic-macroscopic approach that combines a deformed Woods-Saxon single-particle potential with a Yukawa-plus-exponential macroscopic energy term, we computed static fission barriers ($B_f$) for 1305 heavy and superheavy nuclei ($98 \leq Z \leq 126$), covering even-even, odd-even, even-odd, and odd-odd configurations. For odd and odd-odd nuclei, adiabatic potential energy surfaces were derived by minimizing configurations with one blocked neutron and/or proton ranging from the 10th level below to the 10th above the Fermi level. Model parameters, previously optimized by fitting even-even heavy nuclear masses, remained constant. Saddle points were identified using the "Imaginary Water Flow" method on a fundamental five-dimensional deformation grid that accounts for triaxiality, while two auxiliary grids were employed to investigate mass asymmetry and hexadecapole non-axiality effects. Ground states were determined through energy minimization across configurations and deformations. Our results indicate that non-axiality substantially alters both the first and second fission barriers in numerous nuclei. Furthermore, the mass-asymmetry effect, recognized for reducing second fission barriers in actinides, manifests at less deformed saddles in over 100 of the heaviest nuclei. This occurs in saddles where triaxiality is negligible, implying a decoupling between mass-asymmetry and triaxiality effects. We also examined how pairing interaction strength influences the staggering of $B_f$ for odd and even particle numbers. Finally, our findings are compared with other theoretical fission barrier calculations and existing experimental data.

This study examines the origins of intracluster light (ICL) and brightest cluster galaxies (BCG) in clusters at $z=0$ through multi-resolution cosmological N-body simulations employing the "Galaxy Replacement Technique" (GRT). We analyze how the formation pathways of the ICL and BCG vary with distance from the cluster center and the dynamical state of the clusters at $z=0$. By tracing ICL and BCG stars backward in time, we identify the stellar components present when they initially accreted into the clusters. Our results indicate that progenitors in the cluster center arrived earlier and possessed a higher total mass ratio relative to the cluster compared to those in the outer regions, creating a negative radial gradient in both infall time and mass ratio. While the stellar mass of progenitors does not exhibit a consistent radial gradient across all clusters, massive galaxies ($M_{\rm{gal}} > 10^{10}~M_{\odot}~h^{-1}$) remain the primary formation channel for the ICL and BCG in all clusters except the most relaxed one. In dynamically unrelaxed clusters, we observe that ICL and BCG progenitors accrete more recently and with greater mass and mass ratios. Additionally, we find that pre-processed diffuse material from massive galaxies and group-mass halos contributes significantly to the ICL in the outer regions of unrelaxed clusters.

For a $k$-graph $H$, its complete blow-up, denoted $\hat{H}$, is constructed by substituting every vertex $v \in V(H)$ with a non-empty vertex class $A_v$ and adding all possible edges between any $k$ classes that correspond to an edge in $H$. For a subgraph $G \subseteq \hat{H}$ and an edge $e \in E(H)$, the density $d_e(G)$ is defined as the fraction of edges existing in $G$ between the vertex classes associated with $e$. The density Turán problem for $H$ seeks to find the minimal threshold $d_{crit}(H)$ such that if every edge $e \in E(H)$ satisfies $d_e(G) > d_{crit}(H)$, then $G$ must contain a transversal copy of $H$—a subgraph isomorphic to $H$ that intersects each vertex class of $\hat{H}$ exactly once. This work provides upper bounds for this hypergraph density Turán problem, extending results previously established for graphs by Csikvári and Nagy (2012), albeit utilizing a distinct approach based on entropy compression.

Inspired by the weighted Hurwitz product acting on sequences within an algebra, we construct a collection of monoidal structures on the category of Joyal species. Additionally, we propose a set of tensor products suitable for charades. Our approach starts by identifying weighted derivational algebras and weighted Rota-Baxter algebras as specific instances of monoids and semigroups, respectively, under a shared monoidal structure defined on the category of graphs within a monoidal additive category. Furthermore, we demonstrate the lifting of weighted derivations to the categorical level.

This study examines the structural and dynamic characteristics of water through a series of molecular dynamics simulations conducted between 213 K and 360 K using the SPC/E model. Isobaric-isothermal simulations at 1 bar were executed with the GROMACS software package, involving 1185 water molecules. Structural analysis relied on oxygen-oxygen radial distribution functions, order parameters, and hydrogen bond distribution functions, while dynamic behavior was assessed via history-dependent bond correlation functions and the non-Gaussian parameter $\alpha_2(t)$ associated with the mean square displacement of water molecules. Results indicate that as temperature decreases, both translational ($\tau$) and orientational ($Q$) order parameters exhibit a linear correlation and increase, reflecting enhanced structural order. Although the probability of forming four hydrogen bonds and the $Q$ parameter show a reciprocal relationship with temperature, hydrogen bond distribution analysis provides a more reliable description of changes in water's structure and dynamics. Consequently, below 293 K—where a four-hydrogen-bond structure predominates—the system experiences an intensified caging effect and the emergence of long-lived hydrogen bonds.

It is beneficial for machines to operate computers like humans do, enabling them to assist with daily activities. This approach allows for the utilization of large-scale expert demonstrations and human judgments regarding interactive behavior, both of which have significantly contributed to recent AI advancements. In this study, we explore computer control via keyboard and mouse, where objectives are defined using natural language. Rather than relying on manually designed curricula or specialized action spaces, we propose a scalable methodology grounded in reinforcement learning enhanced by behavioral priors derived from real human-computer interactions. Our method achieves state-of-the-art and human-level performance across all tasks in the MiniWob++ benchmark, a rigorous suite of computer control challenges, and exhibits strong evidence of transferability across tasks. These findings underscore the value of a unified human-agent interface for training machines to use computers. Collectively, our results indicate a pathway to achieving general computer control competency comparable to human abilities, extending beyond the MiniWob++ benchmark.

We introduce a balance relation between uncertainty and complementarity, establishing quantitative links among non-locality, complementarity, and uncertainty. Formulated independently of any specific theory, this relation asserts that for sequential measurements, the disturbance-based complementarity of the first measurement cannot exceed its uncertainty. Quantum theory adheres to this balance, allowing the derivation of the Tsirelson bound with only a negligible assumption. In the basic Bell scenario, we demonstrate that the Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt inequality bound for a general non-local theory can be expressed as a function of the theory's specific balance strength. Applying this framework, we calculate the balance strength and non-local bound for the Popescu-Rohrlich box. These findings illuminate the quantitative interconnections among the three fundamental concepts of uncertainty, complementarity, and non-locality.

End-to-end simulations are essential for analyzing high-sensitivity CMB experiments, offering unmatched capabilities for propagating systematic errors with high fidelity. This paper tackles a critical aspect of these simulations: how to define inputs based on sky models and instrument parameters. These inputs can either be constrained realizations derived from actual data or random realizations independent of the data; we label these approaches as Bayesian and frequentist simulations, respectively. We demonstrate that these two methods yield distinct correlation structures. Specifically, frequentist simulations incorporate cosmic variance but omit realization-specific correlations arising from non-linear degeneracies, whereas Bayesian simulations do not. Consequently, the two approaches quantify fundamentally different uncertainties and serve complementary scientific purposes, although this distinction is not absolute. Prior to BeyondPlanck, most pipelines relied on a hybrid mix of constrained and random inputs for all applications, often without clear statistical justification. BeyondPlanck introduces the first end-to-end CMB simulation framework capable of generating both simulation types, bringing this issue to the forefront. While Bayesian BeyondPlanck simulations and their applications are detailed in companion papers, this paper focuses on a key use case for frequentist simulations: code validation. We generate a set of 1-year LFI 30 GHz frequentist simulations with known inputs to validate the core low-level BeyondPlanck algorithms, including gain estimation, correlated noise estimation, and mapmaking.

This systematic investigation examines the anisotropy of the superconducting (SC) and normal states in Fe$_{1+y}$Te$_{0.6}$Se$_{0.4}$ single crystals containing varying concentrations of excess iron ($y$ = 0, 0.07, and 0.14). The superconducting anisotropy, $\gamma_{H}$, was determined by measuring upper critical fields exceeding 50 T under magnetic fields aligned parallel to both the $ab$ plane and the $c$ axis. Conversely, the normal-state anisotropy, $\gamma_{\rho}$, was derived from resistivity measurements where current flowed along the $ab$ plane ($\rho_{ab}$) and the $c$ axis ($\rho_c$). To ensure precise and consistent measurements of $\rho_{ab}$ and $\rho_c$ within the same specimen region, eliminating variations between different pieces, we employed a novel technique utilizing a micro-fabricated bridge featuring an additional neck along the $c$ axis. While $\gamma_{H}$ drops from a value dependent on the excess Fe content at $T_{\rm{c}}$ to a common value of approximately 1 at 2 K, the differing $\gamma_{H}$ values at $T_{\rm{c}}$ (roughly 1.5 for $y$ = 0 and 2.5 for $y$ = 0.14) indicate that the effective mass anisotropy $m_c^*/m_{ab}^*$ rises from about 2.25 to 6.25 as excess Fe increases. This near-isotropic behavior of $\gamma_{H}$ at low temperatures is attributed to a strong spin paramagnetic effect when $H\parallel ab$. In contrast, $\gamma_{\rho}$ exhibits significantly higher values, ranging from approximately 17 ($y$ = 0) to 50 ($y$ = 0.14), just above $T_{\rm{c}}$. By combining the findings for $\gamma_{H}$ and $\gamma_{\rho}$ near $T_{\rm{c}}$, we conclude that the discrepancy between the anisotropies in the SC and normal states stems from a large anisotropy in the scattering time, $\tau_{ab}/\tau_c \sim$ 7.8, which remains independent of the excess Fe concentration.

This study generalizes Hochman and Shmerkin's projection theorem to product measures derived from Mandelbrot cascades acting on ergodic measures, as visualized through canonical mappings of one-dimensional iterated function systems lacking separation constraints. As a result, we broaden the scope of Furstenberg's sumset theorem to include images of subshifts within symbolic spaces and Mandelbrot percolations defined on invariant sets.
We examine several widely accepted approximations for radiative transfer equations in climatology by employing both theoretical and numerical reasoning.

This research investigates the three-dimensional (3D) fully compressible magnetohydrodynamic system within a general bounded domain, subject to slip boundary conditions for velocity, adiabatic conditions for temperature, and perfect conduction for the magnetic field. For regular initial data characterized by small energy but potentially large oscillations, the study establishes the global existence of both classical and weak solutions, along with an exponential decay rate for the initial-boundary-value problem. Notably, these classical solutions permit the density and temperature to vanish initially. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that if initial vacuum conditions exist (even at a single point), the oscillation of the density in classical solutions will grow unboundedly at an exponential rate. To address the challenges posed by slip boundary conditions, new observations and essential estimates are derived.

As autonomous systems and humans increasingly share physical spaces, robots are collaborating more closely with people to compensate for each other's limitations. These cooperative interactions are becoming ever more sophisticated, making the ability to reason not only about a human's center of gravity but also their granular motion a critical prerequisite for effective human-robot interaction. However, many existing algorithms overlook the multimodal nature of human movement or fail to account for uncertainty in motion predictions. We introduce Motron, a multimodal, probabilistic, graph-structured model that leverages probabilistic methods to capture human multimodality while also generating deterministic maximum-likelihood motions along with confidence scores for each mode. Designed for tight integration within the robotic planning, control, and interaction loop, our model produces physically feasible human motions with high computational efficiency. We validate Motron's performance on several challenging real-world motion forecasting datasets, demonstrating that it surpasses a wide range of generative and variational methods. Furthermore, it achieves state-of-the-art single-output motion prediction when needed, all while consuming significantly less computational power than current state-of-the-art algorithms.

In July 1995, D-Lib Magazine launched as an open-access, HTML-only online publication, becoming the central hub for the nascent digital library research community. By 2017, the magazine ceased operations, partly due to the maturation of the field it supported and the growing competition from eprints, institutional repositories, conferences, social media, and online journals—the very ecosystem D-Lib had helped cultivate. As veteran members of the digital library community and prolific contributors to the magazine, we look back on its history and the evolution of the digital library field, using its inaugural issue as a guiding reference. That first edition featured three articles detailing the Dublin Core Metadata Element Set, a status report on the NSF/DARPA/NASA-funded Digital Library Initiative (DLI), and a summary of the Kahn-Wilensky Framework (KWF), which introduced Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs) and other foundational concepts. Over its 23-year run, D-Lib Magazine described numerous technologies that have exerted a profound and lasting influence on both digital library and general web communities.

We enhance McMullen's construction of knot sequences in $S^3$ that satisfy the Chebotarev law through two distinct approaches. First, we generalize his theorem to apply to pseudo-Anosov flows that allow for a finite set of 1-pronged singular orbits. Second, we utilize rational Fried surgeries to generate a wide variety of pseudo-Anosov flows. These techniques notably demonstrate that modular knots surrounding the missing trefoil in $S^3$ adhere to the Chebotarev law, thereby establishing an equidistribution theorem for the Rademacher symbol.

A set of subsets $A$ is defined as an antichain when no distinct pair $x,y \in A$ satisfies $x \subset y$, and it is termed a distance-$r$ code if the Hamming distance between any two distinct elements is at least $r$. In this work, we demonstrate that for any $A \subset 2^{[n]}$ which is simultaneously an antichain and a distance-$(2r+1)$ code, the size of $A$ satisfies $|A| = O_r(2^n n^{-r-1/2})$. This finding, optimal up to the constant factor, offers a purely combinatorial enhancement to several results in Littlewood–Offord theory; notably, it provides a concise combinatorial derivation of H\'alasz's theorem, contrasting with earlier proofs that relied entirely on Fourier analysis.

Holography utilizes the interference of light fields to systematically reconstruct wavefronts. While classical techniques have proven highly effective in fields ranging from microscopy to manufacturing and basic science, applying them to single photons presents significant technical challenges. Recent advances have shown that the spatial structure of a single photon can be retrieved by using a well-characterized reference photon, leveraging the non-classical Hong-Ou-Mandel interference at a beam splitter. This study introduces a novel method to record a single-photon hologram without directly detecting the photons and, crucially, without requiring a known companion reference photon. Our approach relies on quantum interference between two-photon probability amplitudes within a nonlinear interferometer. Similar to classical holography, this technique enables the full retrieval of a photon's "shape," including its amplitude and phase, even though the photon itself remains undetected.

Scattering amplitudes, which encode the characteristics of resonances and excited states near decay thresholds, can be derived from single- and multiparticle correlators within finite volumes. Recent lattice calculations have finally achieved the necessary precision to study these correlators reliably. The distillation method offers a substantial advancement by streamlining quark contractions and facilitating the expansion of the operator basis for interpolators. We provide preliminary findings on charmonium bound states and resonances using Nf=2+1 CLS ensembles. Our long-term objective is to elucidate the properties of X resonances that defy conventional quark-antiquark meson models. By tuning various parameters of the distillation method and the charm quark mass, we have obtained the masses of ground and excited states in the 0++ and 1-- channels as an initial result.

Most scientific literature is distributed in PDF format, creating significant accessibility barriers for blind and low vision (BLV) readers. To quantify this issue, we evaluated the accessibility of 11,397 PDFs published between 2010 and 2019 across diverse disciplines, revealing that merely 2.4% met our established accessibility standards. To mitigate these challenges, we developed SciA11y, a system utilizing machine learning to extract content from scientific PDFs and convert it into accessible HTML enriched with new navigational features for screen reader users. Internal evaluations show that 87% of the HTML outputs generated by SciA11y are free of readability issues or contain only minor ones. Through a qualitative user study, we identified the specific needs of BLV researchers and determined how well SciA11y addresses them, resulting in five design recommendations for future accessible scientific reading systems. User feedback was overwhelmingly positive; all participants indicated a high likelihood of future usage, with some suggesting the system could become their primary workflow. Ultimately, SciA11y has successfully generated HTML versions for over 12 million papers, with an open-access subset of 1.5 million papers available for browsing at https://scia11y.org/.

Transfer learning is an established approach in 2D computer vision that maximizes performance on small datasets by utilizing vast amounts of existing data, a strategy particularly valuable given the high costs associated with acquiring and annotating data. Although annotation remains expensive in 3D, transfer learning methods have only recently been explored in this domain, with unsupervised pre-training being the preferred method due to the scarcity of large, annotated datasets. This study addresses real-time 3D semantic segmentation of sparse outdoor LiDAR scans, which are increasingly common but suffer from inconsistent labeling standards across different datasets. We introduce an intermediate-level labeling scheme known as "coarse labels," which enables the utilization of all available data without requiring manual annotation. This approach expands dataset size while simplifying the segmentation task. Based on this, we propose a novel pre-training method called Coarse Label Pre-training (COLA). Through a comprehensive analysis across various datasets and architectures, we demonstrate that COLA significantly boosts performance, particularly in scenarios where fine-tuning is constrained by limited data.

We report on the formation rates and collisional stability of lithium Feshbach molecules within an ultracold three-component system comprising two resonantly interacting fermionic $^6$Li spin states and bosonic $^{174}$Yb. Despite the presence of a substantial ytterbium environment, we detect molecule lifetimes exceeding 100 ms and determine the system's reaction rate coefficients. Our findings demonstrate robust collisional stability within the unitary regime, thereby enabling novel investigations and probes of strongly interacting quantum gases in contact with a bath species.

We present a quantification of the uniqueness of Gibbs measures for topologically mixing countable Markov shifts with locally H\"older continuous potentials, along with corollaries regarding the convergence rate when approximated by finite subsystems.

During the pandemic, highly transmissible and pathogenic new COVID-19 variants, such as Delta and Omicron, have emerged globally, leading to significant mortality. Early prediction of potential variants, particularly their spike proteins, based on mutated SARS-CoV-2 RNA sequences is crucial for timely prevention and treatment. This study introduces DeepQuantum, a tool that integrates quantum and quantum-inspired algorithms with deep learning to predict spike protein structural variations in epidemic strains. This hybrid quantum-classical model achieves, for the first time, quantum-inspired blur convolution analogous to classical depthwise convolution and successfully implements quantum progressive training using quantum circuits, ensuring the model serves as the quantum counterpart to the renowned style-based GAN. Results indicate that the fidelity of randomly generated spike protein variations exceeds 96% for Delta and 94% for Omicron. Furthermore, the training loss curve demonstrates greater stability and superior convergence with multiple loss functions compared to classical algorithms. Ultimately, the evidence strongly supports that quantum-inspired algorithms effectively enhance classical deep learning, enabling hybrid models to accurately predict mutant strains.

We have recently released a deep learning investigation into the efficacy of encoder-decoder networks for segmenting the 2D CAMUS ultrasound dataset. This abstract introduces an expanded evaluation framework that incorporates anatomical assessment, addressing the limitation of conventional geometric and clinical metrics in cardiac segmentation, which often fail to verify the anatomical validity of predicted structures. The comprehensive study offers fresh insights into the comparative ranking of various models.

This study investigates a diffuse interface model known as the Navier-Stokes/Cahn-Hilliard system, which typically characterizes the dynamics of immiscible two-phase flows featuring a diffusing interface. For the periodic boundary value problem of this system defined on the torus $\mathbb{T}^3$, we demonstrate the existence of a unique global strong solution in the vicinity of the phase separation state. This result implies that phenomena such as vacuum formation, shock waves, mass concentration, interface collisions, and rupture do not develop within a finite time. Additionally, we analyze the long-term behavior of these global strong solutions, specifically showing that the phase field converges algebraically toward the phase separation state.

We derive a precise one-component equation governing the probability amplitude of a time-dependent target state and apply it to restructure quantum dynamics and control for both isolated and open systems. By utilizing this equation, we demonstrate the induction of an unforeseen, leakage-free time-dependent trajectory and identify the key quantity responsible for decoherence suppression. Furthermore, our control protocol, grounded in a nonperturbative leakage elimination operator, offers a unified framework that links subtle yet significant concepts in quantum control, including dynamical decoupling, the quantum Zeno effect, and adiabatic passage. The resulting one-component equation is poised to deliver substantial benefits to both quantum mechanics and control theory.

Transformer-based language models (LMs) keep improving their performance on NLP benchmarks, including those testing human-like "commonsense" reasoning. To better gauge the extent of these linguistic reasoning capabilities, researchers are increasingly applying psychometric tools. However, the reverse question remains: can LMs effectively predict the psychometric properties of test items when administered to humans? To answer this, we collected responses from both numerous human participants and various LMs (including transformer and non-transformer models) on a comprehensive diagnostic test of linguistic competence. We then calculated standard psychometric properties for each item separately based on human and LM responses to assess how well these predictions aligned. Our findings reveal that transformer-based LMs consistently predict psychometric properties accurately in some categories but poorly in others, offering new insights into the fundamental similarities and differences between human and LM reasoning.

Code comments are vital for understanding, developing, and maintaining software. However, due to inconsistent standards and their unstructured or semi-structured format, developers—particularly novices—often struggle to determine the appropriate conventions or tools for documentation. Consequently, they frequently turn to external online platforms for guidance. This study examines discussions regarding code comments on sites like Stack Overflow and Quora to illuminate the nature of developers' inquiries. By applying Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), we identified emerging topics, followed by a manual analysis of a statistically significant sample to construct a taxonomy of these questions. Our findings reveal that on Stack Overflow, nearly 40% of questions pertain to writing or processing comments within documentation tools, while about 20% address the capabilities and limitations of tools for automatically enriching comments. In contrast, Quora users predominantly seek background information (35%) or opinions (16%) on commenting practices. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that (i) coding style guidelines often omit specific aspects of comments, such as how to include certain types of information; (ii) developers require assistance in mastering syntax and formatting conventions for various comment types; and (iii) there is a strong interest in automated strategies for comment management, such as detecting poor-quality comments or verifying style consistency, yet current tool support remains insufficient.

This study verifies a smoothed variant of a recent conjecture regarding the variance of the k-fold divisor function within arithmetic progressions modulo individual composite numbers, albeit within a limited range. Unlike the earlier work by Rodgers and Soundararajan, our approach eliminates the need for averaging across moduli. We adapt a method developed by S. Lester, who previously addressed the variance of the k-fold divisor function in short intervals within the same range. Our proof relies on a smoothed Voronoi summation formula modified by multiplicative characters. Employing Dirichlet characters enables us to broaden the applicable range compared to the prior findings of Kowalski and Ricotta, who utilized additive characters. Furthermore, the smoothing technique allows for an unconditional treatment of all k values. This outcome is intimately connected to the moments of Dirichlet L-functions.

We examine the strong solution of the 2D Navier-Stokes equations within a torus under additive noise, employing a fully implicit temporal scheme combined with a spatial finite element method. We establish that the convergence rate of these schemes is $\eta\in[0,1/2)$ with respect to time and 1 in space, where the coefficient $\eta$ corresponds to the time regularity of the solution in $\LL^2$. Our approach is founded on the existence of finite exponential moments for both the exact solution and its discrete approximation. The core of our methodology involves applying a discrete Gronwall lemma for error estimation without requiring any localization.

We introduce the development of a multi-resolution photoemission spectroscopy (MRPES) system designed to investigate quantum materials across energy, momentum, spatial, and temporal domains. This flexible apparatus consolidates three distinct light sources into a single photoemission platform, enabling seamless transitions between conventional angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), time-resolved ARPES (trARPES), and micron-scale spatially resolved ARPES ($\mu$ARPES). It offers a unique all-in-one solution achieving an energy resolution below 4 meV, a temporal resolution under 35 fs, and a spatial resolution of approximately 10 $\mu$m. Notably, this setup attains the fastest time resolution among trARPES systems utilizing solid-state nonlinear crystals for frequency upconversion. Additionally, the MRPES is coupled with a shadow-mask-assisted molecular beam epitaxy system, converting traditional photoemission spectroscopy into a tool for quantum device characterization. We validate the capabilities of this new quantum material testbed through experiments on FeSe/SrTiO$_3$ thin films and MnBi$_4$Te$_7$ magnetic topological insulators.

The family of ZrSiS-type 111 materials, known for hosting various topological fermionic phases, has attracted significant experimental and theoretical attention. Within this group, the LnSbTe subfamily (where Ln represents lanthanide elements) has recently emerged as a focal point of interest; the strong correlation effects and magnetism driven by the 4f electrons of lanthanides offer a crucial platform for investigating the interplay between topology, magnetism, and correlation. This paper presents a systematic investigation of the electronic structure of SmSbTe—a member of the LnSbTe subfamily—combining angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy with first-principles calculations, alongside transport and magnetic measurements. Our experimental findings confirm the existence of multiple Dirac nodes that form nodal lines along the G-X and Z-R directions in the bulk Brillouin zone, a result consistent with theoretical predictions. Additionally, we observed a surface Dirac-like state originating from the square net plane of Sb atoms at the X point of the surface Brillouin zone. Overall, this study establishes SmSbTe as a promising candidate for elucidating the topological electronic structure within the LnSbTe material family.

The propagation of COVID-19 has been extensively studied, underscoring the need for robust epidemic models. In this work, we present a new framework utilizing a latent Hawkes process enhanced with temporal covariates to simulate infection dynamics. Distinct from existing approaches, our method models reported cases through a probability distribution governed by the latent Hawkes process. By employing this process, we can identify the specific source of infection for each individual. To infer latent infections, the reproduction number, and forecast upcoming cases, we develop a Kernel Density Particle Filter (KDPF). The algorithm's computational cost scales with the number of infections, thereby enabling the use of particle filter techniques like the KDPF. We validate the proposed method using both synthetic data and reported COVID-19 cases from various UK local authorities, comparing its performance against alternative models.

Detecting mitosis remains a significant challenge in computational pathology due to its resemblance to non-mitotic structures and the scarcity of publicly available datasets. While deep learning algorithms show promise in this domain, they struggle when applied to pathology images with high cellular density and diverse characteristics. This paper presents an optimized UV-Net architecture designed to capture mitotic details at high resolution by preserving key features. To enhance generalization across different conditions, stain normalization techniques are employed. Using this network, an F1 score of 0.6721 was achieved.

This study integrates the isothermal Jeans model with adiabatic halo contraction to create a streamlined semi-analytic framework for calculating the density profiles of self-interacting dark-matter (SIDM) haloes influenced by resident galaxies. The model aligns closely with cosmological SIDM simulations throughout the core formation phase and until the beginning of gravothermal core collapse. Our analysis reveals that SIDM halo responses to baryons exhibit greater diversity than cold dark matter (CDM) responses and are highly sensitive to galaxy size, providing a crucial connection to the structural variety observed in bright dwarf galaxies. The computational efficiency of this approach enables complex analyses difficult to perform numerically: (1) we quantify SIDM halo responses across a fine grid of baryonic properties, specifically the baryon-to-total-mass ratio ($M_{\rm b}/M_{\rm vir}$) and galaxy compactness ($r_{1/2}/R_{\rm vir}$); (2) we demonstrate with high statistical confidence that SIDM profiles in typical Milky-Way-like systems resemble their CDM counterparts; and (3) we map the gravothermal core-collapse regime within the $M_{\rm b}/M_{\rm vir}$-$r_{1/2}/R_{\rm vir}$ plane for fixed cross-sections and halo concentrations. Furthermore, comparing the isothermal Jeans model to the more complex gravothermal fluid model shows that the former produces faster core formation and better matches cosmological simulations. We attribute this discrepancy to whether the target CDM halo serves as a boundary condition or an initial condition for gravothermal evolution, offering insights for future refinements of the fluid model. The associated modeling programs are publicly accessible at https://github.com/JiangFangzhou/SIDM.

This work investigates the positivity of complete intersections formed by nef classes. Initially, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for complete intersection classes to possess the hard Lefschetz property on a compact complex torus, or equivalently, in the linear setting. Consequently, this yields novel types of cohomology classes that exhibit either the Hodge-Riemann or hard Lefschetz property on any compact Kähler manifold. Furthermore, we provide a full characterization of when these complete intersection classes are non-vanishing on an arbitrary compact Kähler manifold. Both characterizations rely on the numerical dimensions of specific partial sums of the given nef classes. As a notable secondary result, we demonstrate that numerical dimension induces a loopless polymatroid structure on any finite collection of nef classes.

Current heat engines function as dissipative open systems, which precludes their fully coherent operation. We suggest overturning this traditional thermodynamic framework with a novel approach: treating heat machines as nonlinear, coherent, closed systems consisting of a limited number of field modes. In this model, nonlinear interactions convert thermal-state inputs into non-thermal outputs characterized by controlled quantum fluctuations and the ability to perform work within a specific mode. This revised paradigm effectively unites quantum coherent and thermodynamic descriptions.

This work investigates the statistical mechanics and dynamical relaxation of modulationally unstable one-dimensional quantum droplets governed by a modified Gross-Pitaevskii equation. To derive the classical partition function, we employ a semi-analytical transfer integral operator (TIO) method. This approach forecasts a distribution of wave function amplitudes and generates two-point correlation functions, offering insights into the emergent dynamics of these droplets. We compare the TIO outcomes with probability distributions derived from long-time modulationally unstable dynamics and the equilibrium characteristics of a tailored Langevin dynamics. Our findings reveal that the instability triggers the spontaneous creation of quantum droplets, which undergo multiple collisions before coalescing at extended evolution times. Results from both methodologies align closely, except in the special low-temperature limit where droplets widen. In this specific regime, the distribution develops a distinct bimodal shape, revealing a discrepancy between the TIO solution and the Langevin dynamics.

We introduce a new non-randomized anytime orienteering algorithm designed to identify k-optimal objectives that maximize rewards within budget limits on a specialized graph. This graph models a real-world scenario equivalent to locating the k most optimal goal states in an orienteering problem.

For a smooth compact Riemannian manifold $A$, the isoperimetric inequality guarantees a constant ${\bf c}(A) > 0$ such that any $(k+1)$-dimensional integral current $S_0$ in $A$ admits an integral current $S$ in $A$ satisfying $\partial S = \partial S_0$ and ${\bf M}(S) \leq {\bf c}(A){\bf M}(\partial S)^{(k+1)/k}$. While this inequality remains valid for any compact Lipschitz neighborhood retract $A$, it can fail if $A$ includes even a single polynomial singularity. However, by substituting the exponent $(k+1)/k$ with $1$, we establish that the linear bound ${\bf M}(S) \leq {\bf c}(A){\bf M}(\partial S)$ holds for any compact algebraic, semi-algebraic, or subanalytic set $A$. This linear inequality applies not only to integral currents (with $\boldsymbol{Z}$ coefficients) but also to normal currents (with $\boldsymbol{R}$ coefficients) and, more broadly, to normal flat chains with coefficients in any complete normed abelian group. Furthermore, a relative version holds for subanalytic pairs $B \subset A$, with implications for the variational and metric characteristics of subanalytic sets.
We outline multiple demonstrations of the Fary–Milnor theorem.

This study explores testing Weakly Interacting Massive Particle (WIMP) dark matter (DM) models by employing a basic phenomenological framework that incorporates an interaction term between dark energy (DE) and WIMP DM, defined as $Q = 3\gamma_{DM} H\rho_{DM}$. Generally, the coupling strength $\gamma_{DE}$ is negligible due to the weak interaction between DE and WIMP DM, allowing the impact of $\gamma_{DE}$ on the evolution of $Y$ (related to DM energy density) to be disregarded. Furthermore, our numerical results indicate that $x_f \approx 20$, corresponding to the DM freeze-out temperature, remains consistent with the non-interacting scenario. Regarding DM relic density, it is enhanced by a factor of $\frac{2-3\gamma_{DM}}{2}[{2\pi g_* m_{DM}^3}/{(45 s_0 x_f^3})]^{\gamma_{DM}}$, offering a novel method to constrain WIMP DM models. We specifically examine the case where WIMP DM is a scalar. Cosmological data from (SGL+SNe+Hz) and (CMB+BAO+SNe) yield $\gamma_{DM}=0.134^{+0.17}_{-0.069}$ and $\gamma_{DM}=-0.0008\pm0.0016$, respectively. When integrating constraints from direct and indirect DM detection experiments along with relic density limits, we find that the allowed parameter space for the scalar DM model is entirely ruled out by the former dataset but expands under the latter. This discrepancy between the two observational sets presents a near-paradoxical outcome. Consequently, we anticipate tighter constraints on WIMP DM models as more precise cosmological observations accumulate in the near future.

This study investigates multipath-based positioning and tracking within off-body channels. Drawing on channel measurements from an indoor setting, it analyzes the impact of the human body on positioning and tracking capabilities. The research highlights how radio signal bandwidth affects the human body-induced field of view (FOV) and the quantity of multipath components (MPCs) identified and estimated by a deterministic maximum likelihood (ML) algorithm. A novel positioning and tracking algorithm is introduced that links estimated MPC parameters to floor plan features while utilizing a human body-dependent FOV function. This proposed method delivers precise position estimates even in multipath-prone off-body radio channels, though signal bandwidth is identified as a constraining factor.

We examine a finite one-dimensional chain of quantum rotors coupled to thermal baths at varying temperatures. When rotor interactions are rendered chiral, the system functions as an autonomous thermal motor, transforming heat flows into significant rotational currents. This dynamic behavior is particularly pronounced within a specific range of Hamiltonian parameters where the ground state, in the thermodynamic limit, undergoes a quantum phase transition. These optimal operating points are characterized by extensive quantum coherence and multipartite correlations within the system's state. Consequently, this indicates that the most efficient operating regime for such a quantum autonomous motor corresponds to a state of maximal quantumness.

We develop a novel Chandrasekhar transformation for Kerr spacetime based on an alternative tortoise coordinate, enabling precise analysis of the Teukolsky equation across arbitrary frequencies. Furthermore, we provide an interpretation of this transformation through the framework of quantum Seiberg-Witten geometry.

Conversational agents represent systems equipped with conversational interfaces that enable spoken language interaction. Although these systems are increasingly common and favored across numerous contexts and by many users, their automated testing infrastructure lags behind that of traditional software, hindering efficient and effective development. Implementing an automated testing framework for conversational systems could enhance their quality by aiding developers in creating, running, and sustaining test cases. This paper presents our work-in-progress framework, implemented in Python, and explores key research challenges in building such tools for conversational agents. Specifically, we highlight difficulties related to defining expected behaviors, referred to as test oracles, and performing semantic comparisons of utterances.

This report presents our straightforward two-stage "detect-then-match" approach for video instance segmentation. The initial stage generates numerous instance mask proposals by performing segmentation on individual frames, while the subsequent stage utilizes optical flow to match these masks across frames. We show that high-quality mask proposals render a simple matching mechanism sufficient for tracking tasks. Furthermore, our method secured first place in the UVO 2021 Video-based Open-World Segmentation Challenge.

While most idealized investigations into stratified shear instabilities assume the shear and buoyancy interfaces align, this study examines the impact of asymmetry on their development. By combining linear stability theory with direct numerical simulations, we demonstrate that asymmetric shear instabilities display characteristics of both Holmboe and Kelvin-Helmholtz (KH) modes, leading to a framework for classifying them. Furthermore, these asymmetric instabilities generate asymmetric mixing with traits of both overturning and scouring flows, which tends to realign the shear and buoyancy interfaces. In simulations of KH instability that are not perfectly symmetric, we note a collapse in the gradient Richardson number ($Ri_g$) distribution, indicating that asymmetry diminishes the parameter sensitivity of KH-driven mixing events. Consequently, the reliance of turbulent dynamics on fine-scale details of shear and stratification carries significant implications for interpreting oceanographic data.

This work introduces a compilation pipeline for creating CNN inference accelerators on FPGAs. The process converts a static model into OpenCL kernels using the TVM compiler and then employs the Intel OpenCL SDK to generate FPGA bitstreams. We enhance the quality of the resulting hardware by applying optimizations to the base OpenCL kernels produced by TVM; these improvements boost parallelism and concurrency, lower memory access latency, and conserve on-chip resources. By automating these optimizations within TVM, we evaluated the approach by generating accelerators for LeNet-5, MobileNetV1, and ResNet-34 on an Intel Stratix~10SX. Our results demonstrate that the optimized accelerators achieve up to an 846X performance gain over base versions. Furthermore, they outperform TensorFlow on CPU by up to 4.57X and single-threaded TVM by 3.83X, reaching only 0.34X of the performance of TVM running with 56 threads. Additionally, our optimized kernels surpass those from a comparable high-level synthesis approach in terms of functionality and flexibility, though they fall short of hand-optimized designs. Consequently, we position this method as a valuable solution for pre-production settings, offering enhanced performance and rapid prototyping capabilities that leverage FPGA advantages without requiring specialized hardware design skills.

Voice classification holds significant value in the digital age, where identifying singers among the vast array of available tracks is crucial for music information retrieval and property indexing. This paper introduces a novel approach to identifying singer names by analyzing Vietnamese popular music. Our methodology utilizes vocal segment detection and singing voice separation as pre-processing stages to isolate the singer's voice from the mixed audio. To construct the classifier, we developed a neural network architecture that utilizes Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs) as input features extracted from the isolated vocals. To validate our approach, we evaluated the model using a dataset comprising 300 Vietnamese songs featuring 18 renowned artists. By employing 5-fold stratified cross-validation, we achieved an accuracy of 92.84%, surpassing other methods tested on the same dataset.

The fitness landscape, defined as a mapping from genotype to fitness, dictates the biological evolution of populations. Since these landscapes are contingent upon environmental conditions, the dynamics of evolution in shifting environments remain poorly understood. This study examines a specific model of bacterial antibiotic resistance evolution, treating antibiotic concentration as an environmental variable and incorporating fitness trade-offs between adaptation to low and high concentrations. Assuming evolutionary dynamics follow fitness gradients, the system's behavior under slowly varying antibiotic levels mirrors the athermal dynamics of disordered physical systems subjected to external drives. Leveraging this analogy, we demonstrate that the model can be characterized as a system of interacting hysteretic elements. Consistent with driven disordered systems, adaptive evolution under cycling antibiotic concentrations exhibits hysteresis loops and memory effects. We derive analytical results for quasistatic concentration variations and conduct numerical simulations to analyze how these phenomena change under discrete-step driving protocols. Ultimately, our approach offers a general framework for investigating evolutionary dynamics motifs in biological systems facing environmental changes.

The fundamental and applied potential of nematic and columnar phases in lyotropic chromonic liquid crystals (LCLCs) has been extensively researched within material science and medical diagnostics. These phases consist of self-assembled disc-shaped molecules linked by noncovalent interactions, resulting in properties that are highly sensitive to temperature and concentration. However, there remains a gap in understanding microscale behaviors of confined LCLCs, particularly regarding how confinement geometry and surface characteristics influence them. This study reports the development of time-dependent textures in static disodium chromoglycate (DSCG) solutions housed within PDMS-based microfluidic devices. Utilizing soft lithography, surface characterization, and polarized optical imaging, we generated and analyzed these confinement-induced textures, revealing that herringbone and spherulite patterns emerge over time due to a spontaneous transition from the nematic (N) phase to the columnar M-phase. This transition propagates from the LCLC-PDMS interface into the bulk material. By adjusting the confinement geometry, anchoring conditions, and initial DSCG concentration, we systematically controlled the temporal dynamics of this N-to-M phase transition and the resulting textural behavior. Because static molecular states define the initial conditions for liquid crystal flows, the observed time-dependent boundary and bulk dynamics suggest that local surface-mediated processes are crucial for understanding LCLC flows and their associated transport properties.

We present two straightforward theorems regarding squeezing generated by bilinear spin-spin interactions that maintain spin parity—a category encompassing most quantum spin models currently realized by advanced quantum simulators. Specifically, we demonstrate that squeezing represents the initial manifestation of quantum correlations arising from: 1) equilibrium processes, where spin-spin interactions are adiabatically activated from a factorized state aligned with an external, arbitrary field; and 2) non-equilibrium dynamics, where the identical state evolves unitarily under the interacting Hamiltonian.

Predicting the fundamental band gaps of crystalline solid-state systems using only density functional theory has long been a significant challenge. We introduce a straightforward and cost-effective approach that overcomes this by non-empirically optimizing the parameters of a screened range-separated hybrid functional. This optimization relies on enforcing an ansatz that extends the ionization potential theorem to the removal of an electron from an occupied state described by a localized Wannier function within a moderately sized supercell calculation. When benchmarked against experimental data for a diverse set of materials—ranging from narrow-gap semiconductors to wide-gap insulators with fundamental band gaps between 0.2 and 14.2 eV—the method demonstrates quantitative accuracy across the entire spectrum, achieving a mean absolute error of approximately 0.1 eV and a maximum error of about 0.2 eV.

Recent experimental upper limits on the branching ratios for lepton flavor violating (LFV) decays of the 125 GeV Higgs boson, specifically $h\rightarrow e\mu$, $h\rightarrow e\tau$, and $h\rightarrow \mu\tau$, have been published by the ATLAS and CMS Collaborations. This study primarily examines these LFV Higgs decays within the framework of the minimal supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model incorporating local $\emph{B-L}$ gauge symmetry. Furthermore, we incorporate constraints derived from LFV rare processes such as $\mu\rightarrow e\gamma$, $\tau\rightarrow e\gamma$, $\tau\rightarrow \mu\gamma$, and the muon $(g-2)$ to evaluate the numerical outcomes.

Detecting driver drowsiness through video or image analysis is a critical component of modern driver safety. The application of deep learning, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) within computer vision, has yielded significant results in this field, driven by rapid technological advancements over recent decades. Key indicators of drowsiness include excessive eye closure or blinking, yawning, head nodding, and facial occlusion. This study evaluates four distinct CNN architectures on the YawDD dataset to assess drowsiness levels based on yawning frequency, accounting for specific poses and occlusion variations. Preliminary computational findings indicate that the proposed Ensemble Convolutional Neural Network (ECNN) surpasses traditional CNN methods, achieving an F1 score of 0.935. In comparison, the other three CNN models (CNN1, CNN2, and CNN3) attained F1 scores of 0.92, 0.90, and 0.912, respectively.

A method is introduced for solving the Fokker-Planck equation under conditions of constant diffusion and time-dependent drift, utilizing the analogy between this equation and the non-stationary Schrödinger equation. The approach extends supersymmetric quantum mechanics by directly applying the Darboux transformation to the non-stationary Schrödinger equation, which allows a solution to a Fokker-Planck equation to generate a solution for its Darboux partner. When drift coefficients meet shape invariance criteria, this yields a supersymmetric hierarchy of Fokker-Planck equations where solutions are interconnected via the Darboux transformation.

Although numerous nanophotonic structures have been proposed to enhance light trapping and coupling in thin crystalline silicon solar cells, assessing their effectiveness at the module level under realistic irradiation is crucial. This study evaluates the annual energy output of thin heterojunction (HJT) solar modules equipped with optimized titanium dioxide (TiO$_2$) nanodisk square arrays for light trapping and anti-reflection on both front and rear interfaces. Our numerical analysis indicates that as crystalline silicon (c-Si) wafer thickness decreases, the relative annual energy yield can increase by up to 11.0 %$_\text{rel}$ for mono-facial and 43.0 %$_\text{rel}$ for bifacial modules compared to reference HJT modules featuring only flat optimized anti-reflective coatings.

Sorting is a foundational and extensively researched problem that is critical to database systems, as pre-sorting relations significantly accelerates query processing. Merge sort is particularly popular in this domain. In modern data centers, data resides on storage servers while computation occurs on separate compute servers, necessitating data transfer over the network. This transmission creates an opportunity to leverage programmable switches for partial sorting, thereby speeding up the final sort performed by the server. Since packets must pass through the switch regardless, this optimization is feasible, despite the switches' restricted and non-intuitive programming models, which make implementation challenging. We developed a novel partial sorting algorithm tailored to these switch constraints to expedite the server-side merge sort. By exploiting the switch's built-in parallelism, we divide data into sequential ranges; the server then sorts each range independently before concatenating them into a single sorted stream. This approach reduces the workload for the server, as it only needs to sort smaller, already partially sorted sections, resulting in a more virtual-memory-friendly access pattern. Our evaluation across various data stream compositions and switch configurations demonstrates that our method improves sorting runtime by 20% to 75% compared to sorting the original stream without this optimization.

Inspired by various online matching platforms, we examine demand and supply units distributed independently and identically within the $[0,1]^d$ space, where every demand unit must be paired with a supply unit. The objective is to minimize the expected average distance between these matched pairs, referred to as the "cost." We model dynamic arrivals for one or both unit types with uncertain future locations and analyze how the achievable cost scales with system size (the number of supply units) relative to the dimension $d$. Our theoretical achievability results are supported by specific matching algorithms. Across all scenarios, we demonstrate that the platform can achieve a cost nearly identical to that attainable if future arrival locations were known in advance. Moreover, in every case except one, a cost nearly as low as the expected distance to the nearest neighboring supply unit is achievable, meaning the matching constraint does not inflate the cost. The single exception occurs when only demand arrivals are dynamic and $d=1$; in this specific instance, having excess supply significantly lowers the cost.

The matrix game, synonymous with the two-person zero-sum game, stands as a prominent model within game theory, supported by established principles like the von Neumann minimax theorem. Despite this, existing literature has largely overlooked the connection between eigenvalues and eigenvectors and the inherent properties of matrix games. This paper identifies such relationships for specific matrices and attempts to generalize these findings to broader matrix classes.

Photon-graviton conversion in magnetic fields is typically analyzed at the tree level, though one-loop corrections involving scalars and spinors have also been derived. Unlike the tree-level process, the one-loop amplitude exhibits dependence on photon polarization, resulting in dichroism. However, prior calculations neglected a specific tadpole contribution that was long assumed to vanish in QED but was shown in 2016 by H. Gies and one of the authors to be non-negligible. This study computes that previously omitted diagram in closed form and demonstrates that it does not contribute to dichroism.

This study details the interaction between two mechanisms that inject background electrons into a plasma bubble evolving behind an intense laser pulse: one driven by the bubble's overall expansion and the other by its periodic undulations. These mechanisms operate concurrently when a shock-like, steepened front forms as the pulse propagates through the plasma. The undulations along the propagation path can either suppress or enhance electron injection caused by expansion. We demonstrate that Carrier Envelope Phase (CEP) controlled undulations of the plasma bubble, induced by self-steepening of the laser pulse, create a distinctive electron injector termed the Expanding Phase controlled Undulating Bubble (EPUB). The longitudinal structure of the electron bunch generated by the EPUB can be manipulated via laser polarization and power, yielding electron beams with high charge (multiple nano-Coulombs), high current (tens of kilo-Amperes), and ultra-short temporal structures (femtosecond scale). Furthermore, the production of high-energy betatron radiation with polarization and CEP-controlled energy spectra and angular distributions is analyzed as a promising application of EPUB-generated beams.

We present a scanning superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) microscope installed in a cryogen-free dilution refrigerator, achieving a base temperature of at least 30 mK at the sample stage. To ensure optimal thermal anchoring, the microscope is rigidly attached to the mixing chamber plate. Its housing is designed to fit within the bore of a superconducting vector magnet and supports a high density of wires connecting the sensor to the sample. By integrating vibration isolation within the cryostat with a rigid microscope structure, we minimize relative motion between the SQUID and the sample. This enables imaging with micrometer resolution across a 150 $\mu$m range while maintaining the sample stage at base temperature. As a demonstration of the system's performance, we provide simultaneous images of the static magnetic field, magnetic susceptibility, and magnetic fields generated by currents flowing above a superconducting micrometer-scale device.

Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has proven effective for learning heuristics to tackle complex combinatorial optimization problems using policy networks, yielding promising results. Current research predominantly targets vehicle routing problems due to their balanced complexity. While state-of-the-art methods utilize reinforcement learning to create policies that function as pseudo-solvers with good performance in certain scenarios, they often converge prematurely to suboptimal solutions within the vast search spaces typical of these problems. To address this, we propose Entropy Regularised Reinforcement Learning (ERRL), a method that enhances exploration by generating more stochastic policies, thereby improving optimization outcomes. Empirically, ERRL's low variance ensures fast and stable RL training. Additionally, we integrate local search operators during the testing phase, which significantly boosts solution quality and complements ERRL. Qualitative analysis of vehicle routing problems indicates that higher policy entropy smooths the optimization landscape, facilitating easier optimization. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that our model performs comparably to existing state-of-the-art variants. Specifically, our experiments show that the model achieves state-of-the-art performance on various Vehicle Routing Problem variants, including the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), Multiple Routing with Fixed Fleet Problems (MRPFF), and the Travelling Salesman Problem.

We derive an AdS$_2$ solution within Type IIA supergravity preserving 4 Poincaré supersymmetries by applying non-Abelian T-duality with respect to a freely acting SL(2,$\mathbf{R}$) isometry on the AdS$_3\times$S$^3\times$CY$_2$ background of Type IIB. This operation specifically targets the AdS$_3$ factor. The resulting dual background belongs to the family of AdS$_2\times$S^3\times$CY$_2$ solutions in massive Type IIA identified in [1]. Furthermore, we introduce and analyze a quiver quantum mechanics dual to this configuration, which we interpret as modeling the backreaction of the baryon vertex arising from a D4-D8 brane intersection.

Observations reveal that the star formation rate (SFR) within nuclear rings fluctuates significantly over time and often displays asymmetry rather than uniformity. To investigate the drivers behind these temporal and spatial variations, we conducted semi-global hydrodynamic simulations of nuclear rings under conditions of time-dependent and/or asymmetric mass inflow. While the ring's radius ($600\,{\rm pc}$) and orbital period ($18\,{\rm Myr}$) remained roughly constant, these controlled inflow variations induced corresponding changes in star formation. Our results demonstrate that both mass inflow rates and supernova feedback influence the ring SFR. Specifically, an oscillating inflow rate with an amplitude of 2 and a period $\Delta \tau_\text{in} \gtrsim 50\,{\rm Myr}$ generates quasi-periodic, large-amplitude SFR variations (by a factor of $\gtrsim 5$). The time-varying interstellar medium (ISM) weight and midplane pressure closely track one another, maintaining instantaneous vertical equilibrium. The observed time-varying depletion time aligns with self-regulation theory predictions when accounting for the time lag between star formation and supernova feedback. Supernova feedback accounts for only minor SFR fluctuations (a factor of $\sim 2$) on timescales less than $40\,{\rm Myr}$. Furthermore, inflow asymmetry does not inherently cause asymmetric star formation; lopsided star formation occurs only if the inflow from a single dust lane suddenly increases dramatically, triggering a transient phase of asymmetry.

Meta-learning seeks to develop algorithms that can rapidly adapt to new tasks even when training data is scarce, with one-shot learning serving as a particularly challenging benchmark. In this low-data setting, algorithms often struggle with uncertainty due to limited samples, leading to overfitting. This issue can be mitigated by supplying the model with additional information, a goal efficiently achieved through multi-task learning.
