Responisbly reported to the GSMA (CVD-2021-0045), the SPARROW covert channel scheme utilizes the downlink power of LTE/5G base stations to broadcast Contention Resolution Identity (CRI) from anonymous devices in accordance with 3GPP standards. Consequently, SPARROW-enabled devices can secretly relay short messages over long distances, posing a potential threat to critical infrastructure. Additionally, SPARROW schemes could complement existing solutions for long-range machine-to-machine (M2M) applications. This study examines the security versus performance trade-offs inherent in CRI-based contention resolution mechanisms and proposes a rigorously engineered method to randomly obfuscate CRI broadcasts in future 5G/6G standards. Numerical results demonstrate that, compared to reducing CRI length, the proposed method provides significant protection against SPARROW exploitation while minimizing the impact on random-access performance.

Recent years have seen growing interest in multi-task learning for video understanding. This paper introduces a generalized framework that integrates both auxiliary tasks, which the model must master, and adversarial tasks, which it should fail to perform well on. We utilize Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA) as a data-driven method to classify tasks into these categories. Our proposed Adversarial Multi-Task Neural Networks (AMT) penalizes specific adversarial tasks—identified by NCA as scene recognition within the Holistic Video Understanding (HVU) dataset—to enhance action recognition. This challenges the conventional belief that multi-task learning should always optimize performance across all tasks. Concurrently, AMT preserves the generalization benefits of multi-task learning, extending existing methods by using object recognition as an auxiliary task to support action recognition. We establish two difficult Scene-Invariant test splits of the HVU dataset, evaluating the model on action-scene co-occurrences absent during training. Our results demonstrate a ~3% accuracy improvement, showing that the model learns to focus on action features rather than relying on correlations with scene features.

This work re-examines the "counterfactual quantum communication" proposed by Salih et al. [1], where observer "Bob" allegedly transmits a single bit to "Alice" without any physical particle traversing the space between them. We demonstrate that this information transfer is mediated by a locally conserved, massless current of modular angular momentum ($L_z \text{ mod } 2\hbar$). By integrating the flux of this current from Bob to Alice, we find it equals one of the two possible eigenvalues of $L_z \text{ mod } 2\hbar$ (either 0 or $\hbar$), thereby exactly accounting for the transmitted bit. While we previously derived this outcome using weak values of $L_z \text{ mod } 2\hbar$ [2], the current analysis proceeds without relying on weak values.

While the basics of Brownian motion have been well-established since the early 1900s, recent research has primarily addressed anomalous diffusion by adjusting drag coefficients, a focus that highlights long-term dynamics. However, new findings reveal that secondary modes also exist at short and intermediate times in fluids containing anisotropic particles. This study investigates the dynamics of a specific group of nearly-hard n-gons through molecular dynamics simulations, identifying a unique caging phenomenon exclusive to anisotropic systems. We demonstrate that this caging effect manifests in the mean squared displacement of n-gons at intermediate volume fractions. Furthermore, we formulate an extended Langevin theory that directly links translational and rotational motion based on relative anisotropy across different n-gons, successfully predicting the observed caging. By extending this framework to include secondary, off-phase cross-correlations between particles, we can also forecast both the translational and rotational relaxation times of the system.

We examine the projective, irreducible plane curves defined over an algebraic closure $K$ of a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ that remain invariant under seven specific nonsporadic, maximal subgroups $G$ of $\mathrm{PGL}(3,q)$. For each subgroup, we calculate the minimum degree $d(G)$ of such invariant curves, classify all curves of this minimal degree, and identify the first gap $\varepsilon(G)$ in the sequence of possible degrees. Our results indicate that, except when the curves are uniquely fixed by $G$, the curves of degree $d(G)$ form a pencil specific to each subgroup. Furthermore, we highlight distinct geometric properties of these minimal-degree curves, including Frobenius nonclassicality and atypical distributions of $\mathbb{F}_{q^i}$-rational points. While the full automorphism group of such invariant curves is typically linear (contained within $\mathrm{PGL}(3,K)$), we demonstrate that exceptions exist where a curve possesses a large linear automorphism group, yet its complete automorphism group is nonlinear.

Research in Europe indicates that approximately 56% of all public transport trips are taken by bus. A primary driver influencing this usage rate and the overall demand for public transit is service quality, which has seen a decline in user satisfaction. End-users evaluate quality through multiple lenses, such as information availability, including access to transit details and service specifics. This paper proposes an innovative methodology leveraging data mining and machine learning to generate data that was previously inaccessible. Specifically, by analyzing GPS traces, the study reconstructs a complete public transport network graph. The approach was validated using a real-world dataset from the bus system in L'Aquila, Italy. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed method and its framework are both effective and efficient, rendering them ready for deployment.

In Lionel Levine's hat challenge involving $t$ players, each participant wears a stack of hats—potentially infinite in number—where every hat's color (black or white) is assigned independently at random. Players may coordinate strategies beforehand but cannot communicate once the colors are revealed. Each player observes all hats except those on their own head and must simultaneously attempt to select a black hat from their stack. Success is defined only if every player correctly picks a black hat. While Levine conjectured that the probability of total success approaches zero as the number of players increases, we demonstrate that this probability strictly decreases as $t$ grows. Furthermore, we establish connections to graph theory, specifically examining the relationship between the size of the largest independent set in a graph versus its random induced subgraphs, as well as bounding the size of vertex sets that intersect every maximum independent set.

Charged particles undergoing acceleration release both electromagnetic and gravitational radiation. Classical analysis revealed that the energy spectrum of electromagnetic radiation emitted by an electron within a monochromatic plane wave is proportional to its gravitational counterpart. Furthermore, quantum mechanical studies demonstrated that at the tree level, the amplitudes for graviton photoproduction and Compton scattering are proportional to one another. In this work, we integrate strong-field quantum electrodynamics with quantum gravity to show that the amplitude of nonlinear graviton photoproduction in an arbitrary plane wave remains proportional to the amplitude of nonlinear Compton scattering. Additionally, by defining classical amplitudes, we establish that this proportionality stems from the semiclassical character of the electron's motion in a plane wave and the conservation of energy and momentum, resulting in an identical proportionality constant across both classical and quantum regimes. These findings strengthen the connection between gravity and electromagnetism, extending it to nonlinear and quantum domains.

Monitoring ultrafast phenomena arising from light-matter interactions is frequently difficult. In molecular contexts, electronic coherence established initially is rapidly damped by slow nuclear rearrangements occurring on a femtosecond scale, rendering real-time observation of electron dynamics within molecules exceptionally challenging. This study presents an extension of the theoretical framework for attosecond transient absorption spectroscopy (ATAS) to molecular systems, fully incorporating coupled electron-nuclear dynamics within the initially generated wave packet. We apply this approach to investigate the oscillations of positive charge generated following outer-valence ionization of propiolic acid. Leveraging element-specific core-to-valence transitions driven by X-ray radiation, we demonstrate that ATAS offers the resolution necessary to track electron density dynamics with atomic spatial precision.

Ensuring fairness is a core necessity for building reliable, human-centric Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems. Nevertheless, deep neural networks (DNNs) frequently generate biased predictions when trained on data sourced from diverse sub-populations characterized by varying attributes such as race, gender, or age. This issue often stems from the data itself, where bias is inadvertently encoded alongside relevant features like class and semantic information. To address this, we propose employing sketching techniques that filter out detrimental bias while preserving essential semantic details required for accurate classification. Furthermore, we introduce a specialized fair loss function to enhance model equity. Extensive experiments conducted on both general and medical datasets demonstrate that our image-to-sketching approach significantly improves fairness and delivers competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Painlevé metrics represent a class of Riemannian metrics that extend the well-established separable metrics of Stäckel. While Stäckel metrics rely on the complete orthogonal separation of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation into ordinary differential equations, Painlevé metrics achieve additive separation of variables through groups of independent variables. This paper aims to extend the extensive analysis conducted for Stäckel metrics regarding the relationship between variable separation in the Hamilton-Jacobi and Helmholtz equations, as well as the links between quadratic first integrals of the geodesic flow and symmetry operators of the Laplace-Beltrami operator. Consequently, we derive the generalization of the Robertson separability conditions for the Helmholtz equation—previously known for Stäckel metrics—expressed via the vanishing of the off-block diagonal components of the Ricci tensor, thereby generalizing Eisenhart's formulation for Stäckel metrics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that when these generalized Robertson conditions hold, there exist $r < n$ linearly independent, mutually commuting second-order differential operators that commute with the Laplace-Beltrami operator. These operators possess block-separable solutions of the Helmholtz equation as formal eigenfunctions, with separation constants serving as eigenvalues. Finally, we investigate conformal deformations compatible with the block-variable separation of the Helmholtz equation for Painlevé metrics, yielding solutions that are $R$-separable in blocks, and conclude with a discussion of open questions and future perspectives.

Algorithmic Gaussianization describes a phenomenon where randomized sketching or sampling methods generate compact representations of large datasets that mimic the robust performance traits of sub-Gaussian random designs, a potent statistical model. Although this effect has previously been examined only for limited tasks, specific metrics, or via computationally intensive approaches, we introduce an efficient algorithmic framework based on averaging to achieve data Gaussianization. We prove that it is possible to construct data sketches nearly indistinguishable from sub-Gaussian designs using total variation distance. Specifically, by utilizing Leverage Score Sparsified (LESS) embeddings, we demonstrate the ability to create an $n \times d$ sketch from an $N \times d$ matrix $A$ (where $n \ll N$) in $O(\text{nnz}(A)\log N + nd^2)$ time, with $\text{nnz}(A)$ denoting the count of non-zero entries. Consequently, rigorous statistical guarantees and precise asymptotics established for estimators derived from sub-Gaussian designs—such as those for least squares and Lasso regression, covariance estimation, and low-rank approximation—can be readily adapted to this sketching framework. We validate this approach with a novel approximation guarantee for sketched least squares and additional examples.

We establish a combinatorial formula for alternating descent polynomials in types A and B. By integrating this with Josuat-Verg\`es' combinatorial interpretation of Hoffman's derivative polynomials for tangent and secant functions, we derive a unified combinatorial proof of the two Ma-Yeh formulae that connect these polynomial families.

Deep learning has emerged as the gold standard for segmenting medical imaging data, yet the inherent variability and heterogeneity of real-world clinical datasets remain a significant challenge. To address this, we propose an approach that explicitly captures and leverages such variations, building upon our prior work to enhance the clinical acceptance of (semi-)automatic segmentation tools. Unlike conventional neural networks that generate a single segmentation, our method utilizes a Multi-Path U-Net architecture capable of producing multiple segmentation variants, each reflecting different variations present in the dataset. In this framework, distinct network paths are trained on disjoint data subsets; however, since the specific variations in the data are often unknown beforehand, these subsets are automatically identified using an evolutionary optimization algorithm to find the optimal data partitioning. This strategy allows each network path to specialize on more homogeneous data, thereby achieving superior segmentation quality. In practice, medical experts are presented with a range of automatically generated segmentations to select the most appropriate one. Experimental results on a real-world clinical dataset of CT scans for prostate segmentation demonstrate that our approach improves Dice and surface Dice coefficients by several percentage points compared to training all network paths on the entire dataset. Notably, the most significant gains occur in the upper prostate region, which is historically known to exhibit the highest inter-observer segmentation variability.

This study extends the research previously conducted by the second author alongside P. Daskalopoulos and J.L. V\'{a}zquez. Their prior work established the Yamabe flow linked to fractional curvature and demonstrated the existence of mild (semi-group) solutions. The current paper advances this line of inquiry by proving convergence of the flow for a specific set of data within a broader framework. Our methodology draws upon the simplified approach presented in M. Struwe's book.

We conducted magnetization measurements and time-of-flight neutron powder diffraction on pulverized YCrO$_3$ single crystals to investigate its magnetism at high temperatures (300–980 K) and crystal structure across a range of 321–1200 K. The temperature-dependent inverse magnetic susceptibility follows a piecewise linear trend across five regimes, allowing us to fit a Curie-Weiss law and determine the frustration factor $f$. These fits suggest the formation of magnetic polarons between 300 and 540 K alongside significant magnetic frustration. By incorporating a parameter $\eta$ representing the degree of spin interactions into the Brillouin function, we successfully modeled the magnetization's dependence on applied magnetic fields. No structural phase transitions were detected between 321 and 1200 K. The average thermal expansions of the lattice parameters (\emph{a}, \emph{b}, \emph{c}, and \emph{V}) align well with Gr$\ddot{\textrm{u}}$neisen approximations, except for an anomaly near 900 K that suggests an isosymmetric structural phase transition. These expansions exhibit anisotropy along the \emph{a}, \emph{b}, and \emph{c} axes, with incompressibility following the order $K^a_0 > K^c_0 > K^b_0$. Notably, at 321 K, the local distortion sizes satisfy $\Delta$(O2) $\approx$ 1.96$\Delta$(O1) $\approx$ 4.32$\Delta$(Y) $\approx$ 293.89$\Delta$(Cr). Analysis of refined Y-O and Cr-O bond lengths reveals the local distortion environments and modes for Y, Cr, O1, and O2 ions. Specifically, Y and O2 ions show distinct atomic displacements and charge subduction, potentially offering insights into the dielectric properties of YCrO$_3$. Furthermore, comparing Kramers Mn$^{3+}$ with non-Kramers Cr$^{3+}$ ions indicates that whether an ion is Kramers or non-Kramers significantly influences local distortion size but does not alter the detailed distortion mode.

Few-shot learning seeks to identify new categories based on a minimal number of labeled examples. Despite recent advancements, most current approaches rely on averaging operations to compute prototypes, which restricts their performance due to sensitivity to outlier samples. This paper introduces a straightforward yet powerful framework for few-shot classification that utilizes an episodic prototype generator module to produce high-quality prototypes from limited support data. These generated prototypes are designed to align closely with specific target prototypes while remaining robust against outliers. Comprehensive experiments confirm the efficacy of this module, yielding significant improvements over baseline models and competitive results against prior methods on the \textit{mini}ImageNet, \textit{tiered}ImageNet, and cross-domain (\textit{mini}ImageNet $\rightarrow$ CUB-200-2011) benchmarks.

We employ a function field adaptation of the Hardy-Littlewood circle method to investigate the set of free rational curves on any smooth projective hypersurface of sufficiently low degree. This approach serves a dual purpose: it establishes an upper bound for the dimension of the singular locus within the moduli space of rational curves on these hypersurfaces, and it provides insight into Peyre's reformulation of the Batyrev-Manin conjecture, which frames the problem using slopes relative to the tangent bundle.

The widespread presence of multicellular life is partly attributed to the capacity to build intricate structures, where the arrangement of cells within these formations represents a core biophysical challenge that dictates functional capabilities. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding how cellular packing geometries emerge and how they respond to stochastic noise during development, particularly when distinct developmental programs are missing. In this study, we analyze the statistical properties of cellular neighborhoods in two distinct multicellular eukaryotes: laboratory-evolved "snowflake" yeast and the green alga *Volvox carteri*. Our findings reveal that, despite substantial variations in cellular organization, the free volume surrounding individual cells in both species aligns closely with a modified gamma distribution, matching maximum entropy predictions previously established for granular materials. This "entropic" packing mechanism provides a level of predictability amidst noise, enabling parent-offspring consistency even without developmental regulation. Combined with simulations of various growth forms, these results indicate that gamma-distributed cell neighborhood sizes constitute a universal characteristic of multicellularity, stemming from conserved principles of cellular packing.

In the context of keyword search within data graphs, a solution is defined as a non-redundant subtree encompassing all query keywords. A straightforward method for generating all such solutions by increasing height involves extending Dijkstra's algorithm to enumerate all acyclic paths based on weight. To address this, the "freezing" technique is introduced to ensure that non-shortest paths are generated only when strictly necessary for forming answers. This leads to the GTF algorithm for subtree generation, which is complex and relies on a sophisticated correctness proof. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that GTF surpasses current systems, including those that sacrifice completeness for efficiency. Specifically, GTF exhibits scalability and maintains high performance on large data graphs, even when numerous answers are required.

This study employed density functional theory to examine how the electronic structures of single-walled molybdenum disulfide nanotubes (MoS$_2$ NTs) vary with diameter. Our results indicate that the band gap region is highly dependent on the nanotube size: armchair MoS$_2$ NTs function as indirect gap semiconductors for diameters up to roughly 5.0 nm, whereas those with larger diameters behave as direct gap semiconductors, with band edges situated near $k = 2\pi/3$. Consequently, large-diameter MoS$_2$ NTs are expected to display photoluminescence characteristics similar to 2D monolayer MoS$_2$. This transition from an indirect to a direct band gap is attributed to the upward shift of the valence band peak at the $\Gamma$ point in smaller diameter nanotubes, a phenomenon driven by the tensile strain inherent to their tubular geometry.

Recent years have seen extensive research into pattern formation within evolving, time-dependent domains, recognizing that domain growth enhances pattern robustness and selection while offering more realistic models for developmental biology. While previous studies largely focused on domains evolving according to prescribed time functions, this work addresses the highly relevant scenario of concentration-dependent dynamics. We investigate such domain evolution in reaction-diffusion systems to uncover fundamental characteristics of these complex models. By proposing a general framework for one-dimensional domain evolution and extending it to $N$-dimensional manifolds under mild constitutive assumptions—rather than constructing a full tissue-mechanical model—we explore these dynamics. In one dimension, we apply linear stability analysis around homogeneous equilibria, although this approach has limited utility for understanding complex patterns in rapid growth regimes. Numerical simulations across one- and two-dimensional planar geometries reveal diverse dynamical behaviors and several novel phenomena, particularly near critical bifurcation boundaries such as peak-splitting instabilities. We demonstrate that for sufficiently rapid growth and contraction, concentration-dependence significantly alters the system's nonlinear dynamics, both qualitatively and quantitatively. Furthermore, we distinguish key differences between one-dimensional evolution and higher-dimensional models, clarify the limitations of linear analysis in higher dimensions, and emphasize the necessity of careful constitutive choices when defining domain evolution in those contexts. Finally, we identify significant questions regarding the modeling and analysis of biological systems, noting that while certain mathematical problems are tractable in one dimension, they become substantially more challenging in higher dimensions.

For certain corporations and government bodies, leveraging digital footprints of societal frameworks and human behavior has become a standard practice, yet the individual and collective utilization of this data remains in its early stages. This paper offers a concise overview of an initiative aimed at fostering civic empowerment through practical experiments in data gathering and distribution. The scope extends from analyzing the flow of social structures to utilizing complex networks and natural language processing for resource suggestions, as well as implementing linked data and ontological frameworks to organize social and participatory systems.

Keywords: complex networks, natural language processing, linked data, social participation, anthropological physics

This work investigates Thompson Sampling algorithms for stochastic multi-armed bandits within a batched framework, aiming to minimize regret over a sequence of arm selections by limiting the number of policy updates (batches). We introduce two distinct algorithms and validate their performance through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of these methods, deriving nearly tight regret-batch tradeoffs specifically for the two-armed scenario.

A planar pure braid is defined by $n$ descending smooth arcs, where each arc links a point on a horizontal line $\ell_{1}$ to a point directly beneath it on a horizontal line $\ell_{2}$. While arcs may intersect, triple intersections are forbidden. The collection $\Gamma_{n}$ of all such planar pure braids on $n$ strands forms a group under a natural stacking operation. We demonstrate that $\Gamma_{n}$ is invariably a diagram group, as defined by Guba and Sapir. This result implies several consequences, including the biautomaticity and bi-orderability of these groups. Furthermore, every group $\Gamma_{n}$ acts properly and cocompactly on a CAT(0) cubical complex. (This updated version rectifies a typographical error and notes its overlap with prior work by Genevois.)

Unlike traditional machine learning (ML) training in data centers, federated learning (FL) develops ML models across local datasets residing on resource-limited, heterogeneous edge devices. While existing FL algorithms typically strive to create a single global model for all participants, this approach often fails to benefit every device due to data heterogeneity. Recently, Hanzely and Richt\'{a}rik (2020) introduced a novel formulation for personalized FL that balances the traditional global model with individual local models trained on private data. They developed the Loopless Gradient Descent (L2GD) algorithm to address this, demonstrating that it offers superior communication complexity guarantees in scenarios demanding higher personalization. This paper enhances the L2GD algorithm with a bidirectional compression mechanism to further alleviate the communication bottleneck between local devices and the server. Distinct from other compression methods in FL, our compressed L2GD employs a probabilistic communication protocol rather than a fixed schedule. Furthermore, our approach retains a convergence rate comparable to vanilla SGD without compression. To empirically assess the algorithm's efficiency, we conducted diverse numerical experiments on both convex and non-convex problems utilizing various compression techniques.

Online Continual Learning (OCL) seeks to allow models to continuously acquire new knowledge from non-stationary data streams while retaining previously learned information, all within the constraints of limited system resources and computational budgets. The primary hurdle in this domain is "catastrophic forgetting," defined as the failure to retain past knowledge when learning new tasks. Focusing specifically on class-incremental OCL for classification, recent advancements have utilized contrastive learning to create more generalized feature representations, achieving state-of-the-art results yet still failing to completely eliminate catastrophic forgetting. This paper adopts a similar contrastive learning strategy but introduces a semantically distinct augmentation technique. By employing strong augmentation to generate additional samples that are treated as semantically different from their original classes (effectively simulating out-of-distribution data), the proposed method helps alleviate forgetting and enhance model stability. Furthermore, the model design integrates the standard classification mechanism—specifically a softmax classifier and cross-entropy loss—to leverage label information and accelerate convergence. Crucially, it incorporates a sampling strategy to counteract the model's natural bias toward favoring recently learned classes. Extensive experiments on the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Mini-Imagenet datasets demonstrate that this approach outperforms various baseline methods.

Ensuring the safety of automated driving systems necessitates accounting for uncertainties in environmental perception. This study reviews existing literature on how perception testing is integrated into safety assurance processes. Specifically, we examine verification and validation testing at the interface between perception and planning, organizing our analysis around three dimensions: test criteria and metrics, test scenarios, and reference data. The reviewed literature also encompasses related safety standards, benchmarking of safety-independent perception algorithms, and sensor modeling. Our findings indicate that achieving safety-aware perception testing remains an unresolved challenge, as current solutions have not sufficiently addressed the complexities and interdependencies among these three testing axes.

A framework for projective quantum logic based on relative states is constructed, highlighting the critical role of information exchange between a system and its surroundings. The necessity of tracking the system's historical evolution is underscored, revealing that while conjunctions of observations involving conjugate variables can be consistently defined, they are inherently non-commutative. This analysis demonstrates that the Birkhoff and von Neumann approach to quantum logic cannot adequately handle such conjunctions. Although the proposed scheme generally lacks distributivity, the resulting discrepancy is directly linked to interference effects that vanish when information flows from the system to the environment. Furthermore, it is argued that projection probabilities should be mapped onto an orthocomplemented ternary logic, within which the law of the excluded middle remains valid.

I. E. Segal explored the natural extension of Von Neumann entropy to arbitrary semifinite von Neumann algebras. This study connects that entropy to relative entropy, demonstrating that for an inclusion of von Neumann factors, the entropy increase is limited by the logarithm of the Jones index. This bound is proven to be optimal when the factors are infinite-dimensional.

This article examines a real scalar field theory, demonstrating that under a Bogoliubov transformation in the infinite volume or thermodynamic limit, the resulting Hamiltonian loses its invariance under the U(1) symmetry that previously characterized it. This loss of symmetry was verified by analyzing correlation functions under the U(1) group action. Furthermore, by defining field operators linked to particle production, we showed that their correlation functions similarly fail to exhibit U(1) invariance, a direct consequence of the transformed Hamiltonian's non-invariance. Given that Bogoliubov transformations in curved spacetime are mathematically equivalent to coordinate transformations, and considering Einstein's equivalence principle equates coordinate changes to the presence of gravity, these findings confirm that gravity induces particle production. Additionally, the study reveals that particle production does not occur from the vacuum state but can arise from other many-particle states; specifically, the vacuum state is not an eigenvector of the Hamiltonian in the transformed Fock space and does not remain invariant under time evolution.

A century ago, Noether's theorem was established, demonstrating that local gauge variations of gauge-invariant actions are identically conserved (or more precisely, that such variations vanish). However, its geometric converse—whether every identically conserved local symmetric tensor arises as a variation of some coordinate-invariant action—remains an unsolved problem. This paper surveys the current state of this question and examines our specific efforts toward a solution, which include a notable improvement. For notational convenience, the detailed analysis is primarily conducted in $D=2$ dimensions, though the discussion also extends to generic $D$.

This study introduces a new variant of the off-policy natural actor-critic algorithm utilizing linear function approximation, achieving a sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3})$ that surpasses all existing convergence bounds for such methods. To mitigate divergence caused by the "deadly triad" in off-policy policy evaluation with function approximation, we propose a critic based on an $n$-step TD-learning algorithm with an appropriately selected $n$. We provide finite-sample convergence bounds for this critic under both constant and diminishing step sizes, findings that hold independent value. Additionally, we develop a natural policy gradient variant under function approximation that achieves an improved convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ over $T$ iterations. By integrating the finite-sample error bounds of both the actor and the critic, we derive the overall $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3})$ sample complexity. Notably, our bounds rely solely on the assumption that the behavior policy adequately explores all states and actions, representing a significantly weaker requirement than those found in related literature.

This study examines a network of agents whose decision-making frameworks are grounded in a previously proposed quantum decision theory. Choices are made by assessing the utility and attractiveness of alternatives alongside available information, which together determine the probability of selecting a specific option. The interplay of these three factors results in a multimodal selection process. Agents communicate through two channels: direct information exchange and collectively generated societal information. This shared information field acts to smooth temporal fluctuations in choice probabilities, potentially eliminating sharp variations entirely. For agents with short-term memory, probabilities often oscillate strongly toward their limiting values; under certain conditions, these oscillations persist indefinitely, symbolizing perpetual hesitation. Activating the collective information field reduces oscillation amplitudes and can stop endless fluctuations, compelling probabilities to converge on stable limits. The analysis also describes the dynamic disjunction effect.

Reinforcement learning stands as a leading strategy for automated game play, enabling agents to evaluate state utilities and select optimal actions within unfamiliar environments. This study applies reinforcement learning techniques to Flappy Bird, specifically implementing SARSA and Q-Learning enhanced with modifications including an $\epsilon$-greedy policy, discretization, and backward updates. Our results demonstrate that both SARSA and Q-Learning surpass the baseline performance, consistently achieving scores exceeding 1400, with a peak in-game score of 2069.

Although gradient descent and backpropagation have facilitated remarkable achievements for neural networks in numerous real-world scenarios, the training process remains often slow and demanding. We introduce Zeroth-Order Relaxed Backpropagation (ZORB), a straightforward yet accelerated training method. Rather than computing gradients, ZORB propagates information using the pseudoinverse of targets. This algorithm aims to significantly shorten the training duration for deep neural networks without compromising performance. To demonstrate this efficiency gain, we trained an 11-layer feed-forward network on the MNIST dataset, finding that ZORB converged 300 times faster than Adam while maintaining a similar error rate, all without requiring hyperparameter tuning. Furthermore, we extended ZORB to convolutional neural networks, applying it to subsets of the CIFAR-10 dataset. Experimental results across standard classification and regression benchmarks highlight ZORB's superiority over conventional backpropagation using gradient descent.

This English translation presents Anders Wiman's 1927 classical work, "Über die Anwendung der Tschirnhausen Transformation auf die Reduktion algebraischer Gleichungen," which was originally published in the extraordinary edition of *Nova Acta Regiae Societatis Scientiarum Upsaliensis* that same year. In this paper, Wiman argues that a general polynomial of degree nine can be solved using a single algebraic function of four variables along with accessory irrationalities of degree no greater than five. However, his reasoning relies on the assumption that certain intersections in affine space are generic, without providing proof for this claim.

The study presents measurements for the coherence factor $R_{K3\pi}$, the average strong-phase difference $\delta^{K3\pi}_D$, and the mean amplitude ratio $r_D^{K3\pi}$ associated with the decay $D \to K^-\pi^+\pi^+\pi^-$. These parameters serve as crucial inputs for determining the unitarity triangle angle $\gamma$ in $B^- \to DK^-$ decays, where the $D$ meson represents a superposition of $D^0$ and $\bar{D}{}^0$ states decaying to the same final state. The findings stem from a combined fit of observables derived from a re-analysis of the CLEO-c $\psi(3770)$ dataset and measurements from a $D^0\bar{D}^0$ mixing investigation conducted by the LHCb collaboration.

With the rising popularity of WiFi, airtime contention has become a growing issue. While network policy enforcement offers a potential solution, it is difficult to implement because WiFi protocols lack support for usage policies, and ensuring network-wide coordination is generally unfeasible. However, prior research has demonstrated that an access point can influence connected devices by adjusting its transmission scheduling, thereby achieving airtime fairness. This study extends that mechanism to effectively enforce airtime usage policies across WiFi networks. Building on our previous airtime fairness research, we developed PoliFi, a system designed for policy enforcement. Our evaluation indicates that PoliFi enables the expression of various useful policies, such as prioritizing specific devices, balancing device groups across different logical networks or slices, and restricting device groups for guest networks or low-priority services. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these capabilities can enhance the performance of real-world DASH video streaming applications.

This paper examines the optimization landscape of the log-likelihood function and the convergence properties of the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm within latent Gaussian tree models, where leaf nodes are observable and internal nodes are latent. We demonstrate that the population log-likelihood possesses a unique non-trivial stationary point which corresponds to its global maximum, and we prove that the EM algorithm is guaranteed to converge to this point in scenarios involving a single latent variable. Our findings regarding the log-likelihood landscape in general latent tree models reinforce the widespread practical application of maximum likelihood methods in this domain. Furthermore, our results on EM convergence extend existing research aimed at establishing global convergence guarantees for this widely used algorithm. We establish the uniqueness of the non-trivial stationary point by showing that a specific system of polynomial equations derived from the EM updates admits only one non-trivial solution. Additionally, we derive the global convergence of the EM algorithm by demonstrating that all trivial fixed points function as higher-order saddle points.

While likelihood serves as an effective training loss, it is a suboptimal objective for guiding open-ended generation from language models (LMs). Current generation methods struggle because they must steer clear of unlikely strings that are incoherent and highly probable ones that are short and repetitive. We introduce contrastive decoding (CD), a more dependable search strategy that calculates the difference in likelihood between a large LM (the expert, such as OPT-13b) and a smaller LM (the amateur, such as OPT-125m). CD is based on the observation that errors common in smaller models are even more frequent in them, and this discrepancy precisely identifies preferred texts. This approach requires no additional training and yields higher-quality output than decoding from the larger LM alone. Furthermore, CD generalizes across different model architectures (including OPT and GPT2) and significantly surpasses four other strong decoding algorithms in both automated and human evaluations.

Networks serve as a versatile abstraction applicable across numerous scientific disciplines. Models that elucidate their structure and growth mechanisms enable a more systematic analysis and comprehension of various phenomena. However, constructing such models is frequently difficult and demands insights that often defy intuition. Currently, no general methodology exists to derive improved models. We have introduced an approach that automatically identifies realistic decentralized network growth models from empirical data by utilizing a machine learning technique inspired by natural selection, alongside a unified formalism that represents these models as computer programs. Because this method is entirely general and relies on no pre-existing models, it can be applied directly to any network. To empirically validate our approach, we systematically rediscovered predefined growth laws governing several canonical network generation models as well as plausible laws for diverse real-world networks. Furthermore, we identified programs simple enough to facilitate a genuine understanding of the proposed mechanisms, specifically for a simple brain network and a social network.

Estimating and testing the covariance matrix in high-dimensional settings presents significant challenges because traditional multivariate asymptotic theory becomes invalid when the dimension is large or grows alongside the sample size. Consequently, standard likelihood-based tests for covariance matrices exhibit poor performance under these conditions. Current high-dimensional testing methods often suffer from high computational costs or fail to adequately control type I error rates. This paper introduces CRAMP, a novel testing procedure that utilizes random projections to evaluate hypotheses concerning one or more covariance matrices. By randomly projecting high-dimensional data into lower-dimensional subspaces, CRAMP mitigates the curse of dimensionality, thereby enabling the application of conventional multivariate tests. The study includes an extensive simulation comparing CRAMP with asymptotic-based high-dimensional tests and demonstrates the method's utility through applications to two gene expression datasets.

This paper introduces a novel method for addressing beam squint in wideband terahertz (THz) hybrid massive MIMO systems by jointly optimizing phase shifter (PS) and true-time delay (TTD) parameters, subject to specific per-TTD device delay constraints. Unlike previous methods that assume unbounded time delays, this approach strictly adheres to the limited delay range of practical TTD devices. Rather than focusing solely on TTD design, the proposed technique simultaneously optimizes both TTD and PS values to effectively manage these real-world limitations. Simulation results demonstrate the performance advantages of this new method in compensating for beam squint. Furthermore, analysis and simulations reveal that this approach generalizes earlier TTD-based precoding strategies.

We introduce a new learning framework based on neural mean-field (NMF) dynamics designed for inference and estimation tasks within heterogeneous diffusion networks. By utilizing the Mori-Zwanzig formalism, our approach derives an exact evolution equation for individual node infection probabilities, transforming this into a delay differential equation where the memory integral is approximated by learnable time convolution operators. Utilizing direct information diffusion cascade data, the framework simultaneously learns both the diffusion network's structure and the progression of node infection probabilities. We also establish connections between parameter learning and optimal control, resulting in a rigorous and practical algorithm for training NMF. Furthermore, we demonstrate that projected gradient descent can effectively solve the difficult influence maximization problem, with gradients calculated rapidly by integrating the NMF forward in time only once per iteration. Comprehensive empirical evaluations indicate that our method is versatile, robust against variations in underlying diffusion network models, and significantly surpasses existing approaches in both accuracy and efficiency on synthetic and real-world datasets.

Current state-of-the-art convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for vision tasks are characterized by their large size and extensive weight counts, making their training highly demanding in terms of computational power and memory. While significant research has focused on pruning or compressing these models to lower inference costs, relatively little attention has been paid to optimizing training expenses. This work specifically targets the acceleration of training through PruneTrain, a cost-effective mechanism that progressively diminishes training costs as the process unfolds. PruneTrain employs a structured group-lasso regularization technique to guide optimization toward both high accuracy and minimal weight magnitudes; these small weights are subsequently eliminated by periodically reconfiguring the network into a more compact architecture. By integrating this structured-pruning strategy with novel reconfiguration methods, the resulting pruned model remains efficiently executable on GPU accelerators. In summary, PruneTrain reduces the end-to-end training time for ResNet50 on ImageNet by 39%, achieving a 40% decrease in FLOPs, a 37% reduction in memory accesses for bandwidth-constrained layers, and a 55% cut in inter-accelerator communication.

This study presents Voronoi Progressive Widening (VPW), extending both Voronoi optimistic optimization (VOO) and action progressive widening to partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). By effectively balancing local and global action searches, VPW enables tree search algorithms to manage continuous or hybrid action spaces efficiently. The authors introduce two VPW-based algorithms and evaluate them through both theoretical analysis and simulations. Voronoi Optimistic Weighted Sparse Sampling (VOWSS) serves as a theoretical foundation for VPW-based online solvers, marking the first algorithm to provide global convergence guarantees for continuous state, action, and observation POMDPs. Additionally, Voronoi Optimistic Monte Carlo Planning with Observation Weighting (VOMCPOW) is presented as a versatile and efficient method that surpasses current state-of-the-art POMDP algorithms across multiple simulation benchmarks.

Stream monitoring plays a critical role in various data-driven domains, including financial tracking, security, anomaly detection, and load balancing. Among these metrics, quantiles are especially valuable as they often reflect user utility; for instance, high tail latency in video streams degrades perceived quality even when average and median latencies remain low. This study addresses the challenge of approximating per-item quantiles, where stream elements consist of (ID, latency) pairs, and the goal is to monitor latency quantiles for each unique ID.

While existing quantile sketches are typically designed for single-number streams (such as latency alone), allocating a separate sketch for every ID is often memory-prohibitive. Instead, this work focuses on tracking quantiles for heavy hitters—frequently occurring items that are of particular importance—without prior knowledge of which items they will be.

We begin by introducing a straightforward sampling algorithm to serve as a baseline. Subsequently, we propose an algorithm that integrates a quantile sketch into each entry of a heavy hitter mechanism, achieving comparable space complexity while offering a deterministic error guarantee. Finally, we introduce SQUAD, a method that merges sampling and sketching techniques to enhance asymptotic space efficiency. Intuitively, SQUAD employs a background sampling process to capture latency patterns for items before assigning them a sketch, thereby reducing the number of required samples and sketches. Our proposed solutions are rigorously analyzed, and extensive simulations demonstrate the superiority of our approach.

A quantum spin liquid (QSL) featuring a spinon Fermi surface represents an exotic insulator characterized by neutral Fermi surfaces existing within the energy gap. When subjected to an external magnetic field, these neutral Fermi surfaces undergo Landau quantization via an induced emergent gauge magnetic field, forming Landau levels (LLs). This study calculates the electronic density of states (DOS) for such a QSL under an orbital magnetic field. Our findings reveal that LLs originating from the neutral Fermi surfaces produce distinct steps at the boundaries of the upper and lower Hubbard bands. When weak gauge binding effects from gauge field fluctuations are incorporated, these steps evolve into band edge resonance peaks. Crucially, each step and its corresponding resonance peak map directly to a specific LL from the neutral Fermi surfaces, identifying these features as unique signatures of the Landau quantization of in-gap neutral Fermi surfaces.

We further investigate the strong gauge binding regime, where band edge resonance peaks shift into the Mott gap, transforming into genuine in-gap bound states. In this regime, we solve for the bound state LL spectrum. For bound states exhibiting a Mexican hat-like band dispersion, the energy envelope required to excite a state from the bound state LL decreases quadratically with increasing magnetic field. This quadratic reduction aligns with the expectation that magnetic fields localize states and energetically favor the formation of in-gap bound states. Finally, we relate our theoretical results to experimental electronic DOS spectra observed in layered 1T-TaS$_2$, suggesting that a QSL with a quasi-bound state in the upper Hubbard band could reproduce the experimentally measured DOS profiles.

We investigate systems featuring an Adler-Bell-Jackiw anomaly through the lens of non-invertible symmetry. We introduce a novel type of non-invertible charge defect, where a local current operator situated on the defect plays a crucial role. These charge defects are characterized by elements of a continuous $U(1)$ group. Leveraging this framework, we demonstrate an analogue of Goldstone's theorem applicable to such non-invertible symmetries and discuss potential implications for string theory.

First theorized by Einstein in 1916 as minute spacetime ripples within his general theory of relativity, gravitational waves remain undetected from rapidly rotating neutron stars that possess non-axisymmetric shapes. Although these objects represent a potential astrophysical source, known as continuous waves, their faint signals are likely obscured by the instrumental noise of LIGO and Virgo detectors, creating a major hurdle for data analysis. To assist researchers in this field, the OctApps library offers a collection of functions developed in Octave specifically designed to facilitate searches for continuous gravitational waves.

More than two and a half decades ago, two studies examining low-energy pion-nucleon ($\pi N$) data (specifically for pion laboratory kinetic energies $T \leq 100$ MeV) identified a deviation in the extracted scattering amplitudes from the triangle identity. This identity is satisfied by the amplitudes for the elastic reactions $\pi^\pm p \to \pi^\pm p$ and the charge-exchange reaction $\pi^- p \to \pi^0 n$ only if isospin invariance holds within the hadronic component of the $\pi N$ interaction. Such a discrepancy suggests that at least one of three underlying assumptions is flawed: the correct absolute normalization of most low-energy $\pi N$ datasets, the insignificance of residual corrections intended to eliminate electromagnetic (EM) effects from measurements, or the validity of isospin invariance in the hadronic interaction. Given the inconsistencies among various methods used to remove trivial EM effects at the $\pi N$ threshold ($T = 0$ MeV), it is necessary to reevaluate the probability of lingering EM influences in the extracted scattering amplitudes from the scattering region (above threshold). Consequently, this work underscores the critical need for developing a unified framework to determine reliable EM corrections applicable both at the threshold and in the scattering region, which could resolve the established low-energy discrepancy.

Scalar leptoquarks (LQs) have garnered significant recent interest due to their potential to resolve flavor anomalies in $R(D^{(*)})$ and $b \rightarrow s \ell^+ \ell^-$ transitions, as well as the anomalous muon magnetic moment. This work establishes a foundation for automated studies by detailing the full Lagrangian and associated Feynman rules for scalar leptoquarks. Specifically, we examine the five representations $\Phi_1, \Phi_{\tilde1}, \Phi_2, \Phi_{\tilde2}$, and $\Phi_3$, incorporating their triple and quartic self-interactions alongside couplings to Standard Model fermions, gauge bosons, and the Higgs. The computations were carried out using FeynRules, and all corresponding model files are accessible online at https://gitlab.com/lucschnell/SLQrules.

We present simulations of active Brownian particles designed to investigate how particle shape affects clustering and dynamics. These particles consist of four disk-like components connected by springs, with their relative dimensions adjustable to smoothly transition between concave and convex geometries. We demonstrate that even pairs of these composite particles can display collective motion that alters the effective Peclet number. Furthermore, we explore how variations in particle geometry can elucidate the phase behavior of systems containing many such particles.

Geometric quantum gates are inherently resilient to noise because of the global characteristics of their evolution trajectories. While recently introduced nonadiabatic noncyclic geometric quantum computation (NNGQC) operates more rapidly than traditional nonadiabatic geometric quantum computation (NGQC), it retains the robustness typical of geometric operations. In this study, we experimentally realized NNGQC using a single trapped ultracold $^{40}$Ca$^{+}$ ion to validate its speed and noise resistance. By executing unitary operations under imperfect conditions, we demonstrated the superiority of NNGQC over both conventional NGQC gates and standard dynamical evolution through measured fidelities obtained via quantum process tomography. These findings offer the first proof that accelerated quantum information processing is feasible even with limited systematic errors and in non-ideal environments.

Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) has gained significant research interest due to its capacity to mitigate data sparsity in recommender systems. Nevertheless, conventional single-target or dual-target CDR approaches are limited by two key issues: the unrealistic assumption that at least one domain is data-rich and an over-reliance on domain-invariant preferences. These limitations are problematic in real-world scenarios where sparsity is pervasive and can hinder effective user preference learning. To address these challenges, we introduce the Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) model, designed for multi-target cross-domain tasks. Unlike traditional methods, MSDCR acknowledges that all relevant domains may be sparse and aims to enhance recommendation quality across each domain simultaneously. We develop a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to boost domain-specific aspect preferences within a target domain by leveraging complementary aspects from others; the MDSN preserves domain uniqueness via adversarial training, while GAPE adaptively determines complementarity. Additionally, we propose a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture domain-invariant aspect preferences. By integrating these enhanced domain-specific and domain-invariant preferences, MSDCR achieves a holistic understanding of user preferences even in sparse domains. Extensive experiments on real datasets confirm that MSDCR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art single-domain and cross-domain recommendation models.

We examine a flat FLRW framework within $f(R,T)$-gravity, incorporating quadratic terms of the scalar curvature $R$ alongside a linear term of the stress-energy tensor trace $T$. This model demonstrates late-time cosmic behavior characterized by accelerated expansion culminating in a Big Rip. By parametrizing the scale factor $a(t)$, we construct a scenario originating from a point-like singularity, defined by zero volume, infinite energy density, and infinite temperature. Currently, the model exhibits accelerated expansion, transitioning into $\Lambda$CDM-like behavior in the far future. Furthermore, it aligns with quintessence dark energy in the present epoch while remaining consistent with standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology at late times.

Most convex optimization tasks can be modeled using conic extended formulations that rely on auxiliary variables and constraints, utilizing only the limited set of standard cones supported by sophisticated solvers like MOSEK 9. However, these extended forms are frequently far larger and more intricate than equivalent conic natural formulations, which can leverage a wider variety of "exotic" cones. We classify a cone as exotic if it is a proper cone for which we can develop tractable logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier oracles for either the cone or its dual. This paper presents Hypatia, a highly configurable, open-source conic primal-dual interior point solver featuring a generic interface for exotic cones. Written in Julia and accessible via JuMP, Hypatia currently supports approximately two dozen predefined useful cones, including several variants. We define specific exotic cones within Hypatia and analyze methods for constructing equivalent representations using standard cones for constraints involving these exotic cones. For problems across various applications, we propose natural formulations utilizing these exotic cones, demonstrating that they are both simpler and lower-dimensional than their equivalent extended counterparts. Our computational results highlight the potential benefits—particularly regarding solve time and memory efficiency—of addressing natural formulations with Hypatia compared to solving extended formulations with either Hypatia or MOSEK 9.

This study calculates the temperature-dependent thermal rate constant for the reaction Cl($^2$P) + CH$_4$ $\rightarrow$ CH$_3$ + HCl using a Gaussian Process machine learning (ML) method to train on and forecast rate constants across an extensive temperature range. Building on methodologies from two prior reports, we utilized a training set comprising roughly 40 reaction/potential surface combinations, where each combination generated a database of rate constants at approximately eight temperatures. For this specific application, we trained on the full dataset and then predicted the temperature dependence of the target reaction using a "split" dataset strategy. This approach applies corrections at both low and high temperatures to account for tunneling and recrossing phenomena. The findings represent an improvement over recent RPMD calculations relative to accurate quantum benchmarks, utilizing the same high-level ab initio potential energy surface. The results indicate that tunneling at low temperatures and recrossing at high temperatures significantly influence the rate constants. Notably, recrossing effects—which TST and even advanced tunneling corrections fail to capture—are evident in experiments above approximately 600 K. The ML model successfully describes these effects; at 600 K, the ML results converge with RPMD results (which inherently describe recrossing), and both approaches align closely with experimental data at the highest measured temperatures.

To address the growing computational demands of emerging workloads, scalable design paradigms integrate multiple Deep Neural Network (DNN) accelerators into large multi-accelerator systems, primarily targeting data centers with diverse workloads in vision, language, and recommendation tasks. Due to the vast cross-coupled design space, existing approaches have independently investigated hardware configuration and mapping strategies; however, neglecting their interdependence can result in sub-optimal performance when workloads fluctuate. Furthermore, although data center accelerators involve multiple objectives, most prior works aggregate these into a single mono-objective, which fails when objectives conflict, as optimizing one often degrades another. This paper introduces MOHaM, a multi-objective hardware-mapping co-optimization framework for multi-tenant DNN accelerators. Given an application model and a library of heterogeneous, parameterized, and reconfigurable sub-accelerator templates, MOHaM generates a Pareto-optimal set of multi-accelerator systems, each with an optimal schedule, to minimize overall system latency, energy, and area. Evaluated against diverse workload scenarios using state-of-the-art sub-accelerators, the resulting Pareto-optimal set of competitive designs allows for selecting the most suitable configuration based on specific requirements.

The Haldane-Shastry spin chain, a long-range model, possesses numerous notable characteristics, such as Yangian symmetry and, for spin 1/2, explicit highest-weight eigenvectors described by Jack polynomials (specifically their zonal spherical variant). These attributes originate from the spin-Calogero-Sutherland model, which simplifies to the Haldane-Shastry model under a specific "freezing" limit. This study clarifies certain aspects previously absent from the literature, presenting two primary findings. First, we demonstrate that applying the freezing limit to the fermionic spin-Calogero-Sutherland model naturally yields the structure of explicit Haldane-Shastry wave functions. Second, we provide a proof supporting the assertion by Bernard, Gaudin, Haldane, and Pasquier that the Yangian highest-weight eigenvectors of the $\mathfrak{sl}_r$ Haldane-Shastry spin chain are derived from freezing $\mathfrak{sl}_{r-1}$ spin-Calogero-Sutherland eigenvectors at the zonal spherical point $\alpha^\star = 1/2$.

Multi-fidelity Monte Carlo techniques utilize low-fidelity and surrogate models to reduce variance, enabling feasible uncertainty quantification even when high-fidelity numerical simulations are computationally prohibitive. This study introduces a context-aware multi-fidelity Monte Carlo approach that optimally balances the expenses of training low-fidelity models against those of Monte Carlo sampling. The method extends earlier context-aware bi-fidelity frameworks to accommodate hierarchies of multiple models and broader categories of low-fidelity approximations. During the training of low-fidelity models, the proposed strategy incorporates the specific context of their application—namely, variance reduction in Monte Carlo estimation—to identify optimal trade-offs between training and sampling costs that minimize the upper bounds of mean-squared errors within fixed computational budgets. This stands in sharp contrast to conventional surrogate modeling and model reduction techniques, which primarily aim to closely approximate high-fidelity outputs and often neglect the downstream context in which these models are deployed. The proposed method is applicable to diverse hierarchies of low-fidelity models, including sparse-grid and deep-network architectures. Numerical experiments using the \textsc{Gene} gyrokinetic simulation code demonstrate speedups of up to two orders of magnitude compared to standard estimators when quantifying uncertainties in small-scale plasma fluctuations within fusion reactors. This efficiency translates to a runtime decrease from 72 days to approximately four hours on a single node of the Texas Advanced Computing Center's Lonestar6 supercomputer.

The likelihood ratio statistic, which typically follows an asymptotic $\chi^2$ distribution at regular model points, is frequently employed for hypothesis testing. However, at model singularities and boundaries, this asymptotic distribution may deviate from $\chi^2$, a limitation noted in recent research by Drton. Simulations reveal that relying on a $\chi^2$ distribution in these regions can result in poor performance, causing tests to be either overly conservative or anti-conservative. This paper introduces a novel distribution tailored for hypothesis testing near singularities and boundaries, which asymptotically aligns with the distribution of the likelihood ratio statistic. Using two example trinomial models from evolutionary tree inference, we demonstrate that the proposed distributions outperform the standard $\chi^2$.

This paper introduces EGDB, a novel dataset comprising transcriptions of electric guitar performances derived from 240 tablatures played with varying tones. We evaluate two established piano transcription models alongside a newly developed multi-loss Transformer on this dataset. Our assessment, which includes a separate set of real-world recordings, highlights the impact of timbre on guitar sheet transcription accuracy, the benefits of employing multiple losses within Transformer architectures, and the remaining potential for advancement in this field.

Evolutionary game theory serves as a robust framework for investigating the self-organization of collective behaviors through frequency-dependent fitness. It reveals that a strategy's stability is influenced not just by payoffs from individual interactions, but also by population size. This study examines $2\times2$ games in well-mixed finite populations by evaluating the fixation probabilities of single mutants across varying population sizes. We demonstrate that 21 out of the 24 possible games result in fixation functions that decrease monotonically, mirroring scenarios with fixed fitness. Conversely, 12 specific games—encompassing coordination, anti-coordination, and dominance types—exhibit increasing regions in their fixation functions. Counter-intuitively, this indicates that single-mutant strategies often gain an advantage in larger populations. While fixation functions that rise from a global minimum to a positive asymptote are widespread, they may have been obscured by the weak selection limit. We derive sufficient conditions for observing increasing fixation in small populations and identify three distinct mechanisms for this phenomenon. Finally, we characterize fixation functions with increasing regions bounded by extremes under intermediate population sizes, linking their occurrence to transitions between different global extreme configurations.

Breiman's Random Forest (RF) functions as an implicit kernel generator, where the resulting proximity matrix acts as a data-driven RF kernel. While this kernel perspective has facilitated theoretical analyses of RF's statistical properties, the practical applications of the connection between kernels and RF have not been extensively or systematically explored. This work investigates the relationship between kernel methods and RF, specifically examining the performance and characteristics of data-driven RF kernels when employed by regularized linear models. A comprehensive simulation study involving continuous, binary, and survival targets demonstrates that for continuous and survival problems, RF kernels are competitive with standard RF in high-dimensional settings with numerous noisy features; for binary targets, both methods perform comparably. Since the RF kernel asymptotically approaches the Laplace kernel, the latter was also included in the evaluation. Across most simulation scenarios, both RF and RF kernels outperformed the Laplace kernel, although the Laplace kernel remained competitive in specific cases, highlighting its potential utility. Additionally, results from real-world datasets covering regression, classification, and survival are presented to demonstrate practical applications. Finally, the study discusses further extensions of RF kernels regarding interpretable prototype and landmarking methods for classification, regression, and survival, and outlines future research directions involving kernels derived from Bayesian counterparts of RF.

We derive the self-consistent harmonic approximation for the $2D$ XY model featuring non-local interactions. The resulting equation governing the variational couplings is valid for any spin-spin coupling form and in any dimension. We then specialize this analysis to power-law couplings that decay with distance $r$ as $\propto 1/r^{2+\sigma}$ to examine the robustness of the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition at finite $\sigma$, given that it occurs in the short-range limit $\sigma \to \infty$. By proposing an ansatz for the functional form of the variational couplings, we demonstrate that the BKT mechanism persists for any $\sigma > 2$. This study establishes an upper bound for the lower critical threshold $\sigma^\ast = 2$, indicating that the traditional BKT transition remains viable despite long-range couplings whenever $\sigma$ exceeds this value.

Weighted finite-state machines serve as a cornerstone for natural language processing systems, proving their durability from their initial application in 1990s noisy channel models to contemporary neurally parameterized conditional random fields. This study investigates the calculation of higher-order derivatives concerning the normalization constant within these machines. We introduce a novel, general algorithm for computing derivatives of any order, a capability absent from previous literature. Specifically for second-order derivatives, our method achieves optimal time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(A^2 N^4)$, where $A$ denotes alphabet size and $N$ represents the number of states, outperforming earlier algorithms in speed. Furthermore, this approach enables a substantially faster computation of second-order expectations, including covariance matrices and gradients of first-order expectations.

Emergent axion electrodynamics within magneto-electric media promises new methods for manipulating and sensing material characteristics using electromagnetic fields. Although this topic has been extensively researched for more than ten years, its theoretical framework has largely been restricted to static conditions. This work presents a theory of axion electrodynamics applicable across a broad frequency range. We establish a precise definition of the optical axion magneto-electric coupling by linking it to optical surface Hall conductivity and outline methods for computing it in lattice models. Utilizing these derived formulas, we demonstrate that axion electrodynamics can generate a pronounced Kerr effect in thin-film antiferromagnets at wavelengths long enough to obscure the spatial variations of magnetism. We also determine the specific wavelength threshold beyond which this Kerr effect diminishes. This theoretical framework is especially pertinent to materials such as MnBi$_2$Te$_4$, a topological antiferromagnet where our findings indicate that the axion contribution dominates the magneto-electric response even at optical frequencies.

Galaxy clusters and the interstellar medium are thought to host magnetic fields generated by small-scale dynamos. During the dynamo's kinematic phase, a Kazantsev spectrum emerges, peaking at the resistive scale; this spectrum is only marginally shallower than the Saffman spectrum, which characterizes random, causally linked magnetic fields, while causally disconnected fields exhibit the steeper Batchelor spectrum. This study demonstrates that all three spectral types coexist within the small-scale dynamo. Specifically, during the kinematic stage, the Batchelor spectrum dominates scales larger than the turbulence's energy-carrying scale, whereas the Kazantsev spectrum appears on smaller scales within the inertial range, even when the magnetic Prandtl number equals unity. Upon saturation, the dynamo develops a Saffman spectrum on large scales, indicating the emergence of long-range correlations. At high magnetic Prandtl numbers, synthetic synchrotron emission maps of parity-even E polarization reveal elongated structures. Furthermore, a notable excess of E polarization over parity-odd B polarization is observed at subresistive scales, contrasted by a deficiency at larger scales. These results contradict observations of Galactic microwave foreground emission, which are linked to larger scales and show an E polarization excess. Additionally, E and B polarizations may display significant non-Gaussianity and skewness during the kinematic regime, whereas dust emission polarization remains nearly Gaussian with a much weaker E polarization excess.

We define a mapping between a dynamic programming formalism for hypergraphs and the calculation of semiring-based provenance in Datalog programs. This translation enables a novel approach to computing provenance for particular semiring classes. Through both theoretical and practical optimizations, we developed an efficient implementation using \textsc{Souffl\'e}, a leading Datalog interpreter. Experiments on real-world data indicate that this method is highly efficient in practical scenarios, rivaling our earlier specialized solutions for provenance in annotated graph databases. Furthermore, the performance overhead relative to standard Datalog evaluation remains modest in many relevant cases.

Historically, data poisoning in reinforcement learning has concentrated on degrading overall performance, with targeted attacks succeeding through perturbations that manipulate the victim's policy and rewards. In contrast, we present a stealthy poisoning attack that induces agent misbehavior exclusively at designated target states. This is achieved by making minimal modifications to a small subset of training observations, without requiring control over the policy or reward signals. Our approach adapts a recent gradient alignment technique specifically for reinforcement learning. We validate this method and demonstrate its effectiveness across two Atari games of differing difficulty levels.

Partial least squares regression (PLSR) is a prevalent statistical technique for uncovering linear relationships among latent factors derived from independent and dependent variables. However, conventional solution methods typically operate within Euclidean space and are prone to converging on local minima. To address this, we introduce a novel approach called PLSR via optimization on the bi-Grassmann manifold (PLSRbiGr). This method utilizes a three-factor SVD-type decomposition of the cross-covariance matrix defined on the bi-Grassmann manifold, transforming the orthogonally constrained optimization task into an unconstrained one. Furthermore, it integrates Riemannian preconditioning through matrix scaling to adjust the Riemannian metric during each iteration. The efficacy of PLSRbiGr is confirmed through extensive experiments on decoding EEG signals for motor imagery (MI) and steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) tasks. Results indicate that PLSRbiGr surpasses competing algorithms in various EEG decoding scenarios, thereby significantly enhancing the learning capabilities for small sample datasets.

In relativistic quantum field theory, particles with half-integer spin are required to follow Fermi-Dirac statistics, necessitating that their quantum operators anticommute at spacelike separations, unlike commuting physical observables. We demonstrate that Fermi-Dirac spin $1/2$ operators can emerge from a fully commuting field theory composed of spin 0 and 1 constituents arranged into directed strings and loops. This construction reproduces massive Dirac dynamics in the presence of background fields. Although such an underlying description may violate relativistic invariance, it features no manifest long-range interactions and maintains rotation symmetry. Furthermore, we establish that under specific model constraints, a well-defined and stable ground state—a Fermi sea—exists, preventing the conversion of fermions into bosons.

It is nearly always simpler to locate a model that is both accurate and complex than one that is accurate and simple. Discovering optimal, sparse, and accurate models across various structures—such as linear models with integer coefficients, decision sets, rule lists, and decision trees—is typically NP-hard. Since we often cannot determine if searching for a simpler alternative is worthwhile, we frequently avoid such efforts. This study addresses a critical practical inquiry: can we prove or predict the existence of accurate-yet-simple models before explicitly searching for them? We hypothesize that a key reason simple-yet-accurate models often exist is the large size of the Rashomon set, defined as the collection of models with nearly equal accuracy within a specific function class. A large Rashomon set implies the presence of many accurate models, increasing the likelihood that a simple one exists among them. In this work, we formally introduce the Rashomon ratio as a novel metric for assessing simplicity in a learning problem, based on a function class and dataset. Distinct from standard statistical learning theory complexity measures, the Rashomon ratio calculates the proportion of the hypothesis space occupied by accurate models. Studying this ratio offers a straightforward method to anticipate whether simpler models might exist for a given problem, specifically by observing whether diverse machine learning methods achieve comparable performance on the data. Consequently, the Rashomon ratio serves as a powerful instrument for understanding the conditions under which accurate-yet-simple models can be found. If our hypothesis holds—that many real-world datasets possess large Rashomon sets—the implications are profound: it suggests that simple or interpretable models can frequently be employed for high-stakes decisions without sacrificing accuracy.

Scientific models must yield verifiable predictions to hold value. Within opinion dynamics, which examines how individuals interact and exchange views, numerous theoretical frameworks exist, including the Martins model. This model stands out because it employs a parameter that is more amenable to experimental control. Consequently, this paper presents an experiment designed to validate the Martins model and advance experimental methodologies in opinion dynamics through our innovative approach.

We introduce a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian framework to characterize type III and IV Weyl fermions. The Hamiltonian's spectrum exhibits a distinct form of anisotropy, where its hermiticity varies significantly with direction in momentum space: the spectrum remains real along certain directions but becomes complex along others. This behavior results in non-trivial adiabatic evolution and fractional Chern numbers.
