Notably, they significantly advance previous quantum ridge regression results, offering polynomial improvements in condition number handling and exponential gains in accuracy. The approach relies on approximate block-encodings of input matrices and robust QSVT for linear algebra tasks. Specifically, we present a variable-time matrix inversion algorithm based on QSVT that substitutes gapped phase estimation with quantum eigenvalue discrimination, thereby reducing the ancilla qubit requirements compared to earlier methods. Due to the flexibility of the block-encoding framework, these algorithms support diverse input models and represent enhanced, generalized versions of existing standard quantum least squares procedures.

The Hirsch index ($h$) is a widely used metric for assessing citation inequality among individual researchers. When plotting the citation count ($n_c$) against the rank of papers ($n_p$), ordered from most to least cited, $h$ represents the largest integer where $n_p$ equals $n_c$ at the fixed point of the non-linear citation function. This same index applies to avalanche or cluster size distributions ($n_s$) in elastic fiber bundle and percolation models, where $h$ corresponds to $s$. Another inequality measure, the Kolkata index ($k$), indicates that a fraction $k$ of citations is concentrated in $(1-k)$ of the papers, with $k=0.80$ reflecting Pareto's 80-20 law. Our findings demonstrate that near critical thresholds—such as the bundle failure stress ($\sigma_c$), percolation probability ($p_c$), or the critical Kolkata index ($k_c$)—the Hirsch index exhibits Widom-Stauffer-like scaling. Specifically, the relationship $h/[\sqrt{N}/\log N] = f(\sqrt{N}[\sigma_c -\sigma]^\alpha)$ holds for fiber systems of size $N$, while $h/[\sqrt{N}/\log N]=f(\sqrt{N}|p_c -p|^\alpha)$ applies to lattice sites, and $h/[\sqrt{N_c}/\log N_c]=f(\sqrt{N_c}|k_c -k|^\alpha)$ applies to citation counts $N_c$, all governed by an asymptotic scaling function $f$ and exponent $\alpha$. Furthermore, we show that identifying the number of parliament members or national assembly seats ($N_m$) as the $h$-index for countries with population $N$ yields a fit to the scaling relation $N_m \sim \sqrt N / \log N$, thereby resolving a significant recent debate.

The use of minimally invasive surgery (MIS) has surged in recent years, driven by its advantages, including reduced bleeding, minimal scarring, fewer post-operative complications, and faster recovery. Despite these benefits, MIS presents challenges such as a limited field of view, a cramped operating space, and an indirect visual perspective, which can result in instrument collisions that endanger tissues or organs. To mitigate these risks and enhance both the accuracy and success rates of surgical procedures, real-time monitoring of surgical tools using endoscopic video feeds is essential. This paper investigates, analyzes, and evaluates enhancements made to the YOLOv5 object detector specifically for identifying surgical instruments. The study involved annotating a novel endoscopic dataset, conducting performance-based ablation studies, and examining the effects of modifying the YOLOv5 model's backbone, neck, and anchor configurations. Furthermore, the proposed method was benchmarked against four state-of-the-art detectors (YOLOv7, YOLOR, Scaled-YOLOv4, and YOLOv3-SPP). Experimental results on the new endoscope dataset demonstrated that our refined model outperformed all baseline models, including the original YOLOv5. The only exception was YOLOv3-SPP, which matched our model's mean Average Precision (mAP) at 98.3% and exhibited comparable inference speed.

Recent research has established the Motivation Dynamics framework, which employs bifurcations to represent decision-making processes within autonomous mobile agents. This study explores the multi-agent adaptation of that framework, demonstrating its capacity to encode enduring rendezvous behaviors among multiple agents. We provide an analytical characterization of the bifurcation properties of this extended system and offer numerical evidence indicating complex recurrent dynamics that suggest the presence of a strange attractor.

We contend that within general renormalizable field theories, topological angles can acquire an additive beta function beginning at no earlier than the two-loop level. This leading-order expression is uniquely fixed by a single model-independent coefficient. We identify the relevant divergent diagrams and examine several independent techniques for deriving the beta function using dimensional regularization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the unique characteristics of topological angles impose non-trivial constraints on the anomalous dimensions of CP-violating operators and analyze the implications of a non-zero beta function for Weyl consistency conditions, concluding with some phenomenological insights.

Current research in real-time strategy (RTS) game artificial intelligence frequently employs multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL) algorithms, with the StarCraft II environment serving as the primary benchmark due to its global recognition. This study introduces a MADRL approach grounded in the distributed QMIX algorithm. To further optimize efficiency, we integrate state categorization to substantially lower computational complexity, while utilizing self-attention mechanisms to map agent relationships as graphs. These components form the proposed Categorized State Graph Attention Policy (CSGA-policy). Performance evaluations within the StarCraft II simulation environment demonstrate that the CSGA-policy performs effectively across diverse scenarios.

This study examines the transition from noise-limited to dense interference-limited conditions in fifth-generation (5G) small cell networks (SCNs), accounting for both line-of-sight (LoS) and non-line-of-sight (NLoS) transmissions. Four distinct performance regimes are identified based on base station (BS) density: the noise-limited, signal-dominated, interference-dominated, and interference-limited regimes. To characterize these regimes, we introduce a unified framework for analyzing future 5G networks over generalized shadowing and fading channels. This framework evaluates user association strategies based on either the strongest instantaneous received power (SIRP) or the strongest average received power (SARP), incorporating both NLoS/LoS transmissions and a multi-slope path loss model. Simulation results demonstrate that as BS density increases, network performance is successively and individually dominated by noise, the desired signal, and interference, respectively. Consequently, these findings provide new insights into the design and management of SCNs across urban and rural environments with varying BS deployment densities.

We construct a model featuring a quantum field trapped in a cavity bounded by a movable wall whose position is quantized. This framework provides a complete account of the dynamics for both the field and the wall, contingent upon the system's initial state. The model incorporates mutual reactions and back-reactions between the field and the wall, alongside external driving forces acting on both. It precisely replicates the dynamical Casimir effect—stimulation of resonant cavity modes by periodic mirror motion—as well as standard radiation pressure effects on the quantized wall (optomechanics). Furthermore, the model captures the interplay between these two phenomena. Ultimately, the evolution of the radiation force reveals the interaction between the static and dynamical Casimir effects.

This study investigates the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn$_3$, CmSn$_3$, and the solid solution Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ (where $x$ equals 0.25, 0.5, and 0.75) using the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method combined with the generalized gradient approximation plus $U$. The bulk materials, which crystallize in an AuCu$_3$-type structure, are analyzed to determine their ground-state properties. The calculated results for GdSn$_3$ align well with established experimental and theoretical data. Findings indicate that both CmSn$_3$ and GdSn$_3$ exhibit metallic behavior with their most stable magnetic configurations being the anti-ferromagnetic type A (AFM-A). Additionally, the magnetic moment diminishes as the concentration of Cm increases within the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ series. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that these compounds share several common properties, suggesting their potential utility in spintronic applications.

An investigation into CP violation within $D^0 \rightarrow K^{-} K^{+}$ and $D^0 \rightarrow \pi^{-} \pi^{+}$ decays utilizes $pp$ collision data with an integrated luminosity of $3~fb^{-1}$ gathered by the LHCb detector at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. The charm meson's flavor is determined via the pion charge in $D^{*+}\rightarrow D^0\pi^+$ and $D^{*-}\rightarrow \bar{D^0}\pi^{-}$ decays. The difference between the CP asymmetries, defined as $\Delta A_{CP} \equiv A_{CP}(K^{-} K^{+}) - A_{CP}(\pi^{-} \pi^{+})$, is measured to be $\left( -0.10 \pm 0.08(stat) \pm 0.03(syst) \right) \%$. This result represents the most accurate time-integrated CP asymmetry measurement in the charm sector achieved by a single experiment.

The \texttt{NumericalCertification} package provides tools for verifying numerical approximations of solutions to systems of polynomial equations. It employs Smale's $\alpha$-theory and the Krawczyk method to certify regular solutions, while utilizing soft verification through the iterative deflation method for singular solutions. The package's capabilities are illustrated through its integration with existing numerical solvers in \texttt{Macaulay2}.

This paper extends the notion of realised covariation to stochastic processes taking values in a Hilbert space. Specifically, utilizing high-frequency functional data, we develop an estimator for the trace-class operator-valued integrated volatility process associated with general mild solutions of stochastic evolution equations in Hilbert spaces, as defined by Da Prato and Zabczyk (2014). We establish a weak law of large numbers for this estimator, demonstrating that convergence occurs uniformly on compacts in probability under the Hilbert-Schmidt norm. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the requisite conditions on the volatility process hold true for the majority of standard stochastic volatility models within Hilbert spaces.

Over the past several decades, uncertainty quantification (UQ) techniques have been extensively employed to guarantee the robustness of engineering designs. This chapter outlines recent advancements in widely used UQ methods within the engineering sector. Specifically, it examines two prominent meta-modeling approaches suitable for such applications: the Polynomial Chaos Method and Gaussian Processes. Additionally, these UQ methods are applied to a supersonic nozzle test case subject to multiple uncertainties. For deterministic solutions, the open-source computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solver SU2 is utilized, while the UQ frameworks are developed in Matlab and integrated with SU2 to perform uncertainty and sensitivity analyses. The findings are reported in terms of the mean and standard deviation of the resulting output quantities.

This study treats deceptive April Fools' Day (AFD) news articles as a valuable supplement for existing deception detection datasets. Given that such collections possess verified ground truth and are straightforward to create across different languages, we present a corpus comprising diachronic AFD and standard articles sourced from Greek newspapers and news sites. Additionally, we develop an extensive linguistic feature set to analyze and compare deception cues against the sole currently available English AFD collection. In line with current research trends, we also examine the individualism/collectivism dimension regarding deception within these two datasets. Finally, we construct classifiers by evaluating various monolingual and crosslingual configurations. The findings demonstrate that AFD datasets are beneficial for deception detection research and align with conclusions drawn from other studies in the field.

Building upon recent findings by Andrews and Merca regarding the count of even parts in partitions of n into distinct parts, denoted as a(n), this paper utilizes generating functions to extend these results. Specifically, it addresses the number of parts divisible by k in partitions of n where every part's multiplicity is strictly less than k, represented by ak(n). The study offers a combinatorial proof by adapting Glaisher's bijection and derives generating functions for this new sequence family. These functions are then employed to confirm generalized recurrence relations involving pentagonal, triangular, and square powers.

Establishing significant connections among the price fluctuations of financial assets is a critical yet difficult challenge across various financial sectors. Despite recent advancements in machine learning and deep learning that have primarily concentrated on price forecasting, research into modeling asset correlations has not kept pace. To bridge this gap, drawing inspiration from recent breakthroughs in natural language processing, we introduce a neural architecture designed to train stock embeddings. This model leverages historical return dynamics to capture the subtle interdependencies between financial assets. We provide a comprehensive overview of our methodology and explore its potential applications within finance. Additionally, we present evaluation results that highlight the approach's effectiveness compared to key benchmarks across two real-world financial analytics tasks.

For the last hundred years, Einstein's general relativity has remained our most sophisticated framework for understanding gravitation and its related phenomena. Despite this, cosmology continues to face numerous unresolved puzzles regarding the universe's large-scale nature and historical evolution. Recently, researchers have proposed and investigated various modified theories of gravity to address these issues, including a concept known as action-dependent gravity. The mathematical foundation of this theory is profound and extends beyond standard relativity; it relies on contact geometry, a branch of mathematics that governs the dynamics of dissipative systems, analogous to how symplectic geometry supports conservative Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics. This article leverages recent advancements in contact geometry to successfully derive the field equations for an action-dependent gravity theory through the direct variation of a modified Einstein-Hilbert action.

Clustering has garnered significant interest within Statistics and Machine Learning for creating statistical models and autonomous algorithms that extract insights from raw data to facilitate exploratory analysis. However, numerous existing techniques are limited to clustering sampled univariate vectors by relying solely on average values across the entire period. Consequently, these methods fail to fully capture the underlying data distribution and other features, particularly when dealing with structured time series. This study introduces a model-based clustering approach grounded in quantile regression, enabling the clustering of bivariate time series at various quantile levels. By modeling within-cluster density with an asymmetric Laplace distribution, the method accounts for asymmetries in the data distribution. The technique's performance is assessed via a simulation study, followed by its application to cluster time series derived from Glob-colour satellite data regarding trophic status indices. This application aims to evaluate temporal dynamics and identify homogeneous regions with similar trophic status within the Gulf of Gabes.

This paper examines stability concepts for generalized linear differential equations (GLDEs). We introduce and revisit multiple stability definitions, offering a full characterization based on the upper bounds and asymptotic behavior of the transition matrix. Furthermore, we apply these stability findings to linear periodic systems and linear impulsive differential equations. Finally, we demonstrate that the established notions of uniform asymptotic stability and variational asymptotic stability are equivalent to the global uniform exponential stability defined herein.

We derive connections between geometric quantum discord and entanglement measures derived from optimal witness operators. Specifically, we demonstrate a relationship between negativity and geometric discord defined via the Hilbert-Schmidt norm, which diverges slightly from a prior conjecture [Phys. Rev. A 84, 052110 (2011)]. Furthermore, we establish that reformulating geometric discord using the trace norm yields superior bounds. Our findings are substantiated through numerical illustrations.

By leveraging quantum superposition to enhance parallel processing capabilities, quantum computers promise to surpass classical systems with exponential scaling improvements. The concept of "quantum advantage" signifies the threshold where artificially controlled quantum systems can solve classically intractable problems on an unprecedented scale, even without error correction or established practical applications. Boson sampling, involving the quantum evolution of multiple photons across multimode photonic networks and its variations, has long been viewed as a leading candidate to achieve this milestone. However, existing photonic architectures face scaling limitations regarding both photon counts and circuit modes. To address this, we introduce a novel variant called timestamp memboson sampling, which utilizes single-photon timestamp data as a free resource, theoretically allowing the problem's scale to extend infinitely. We experimentally validated this approach on a self-looped photonic chip inspired by memristors, achieving multi-photon detection across 750,000 modes (a Hilbert space of up to $10^{254}$) with up to 56-fold registration. This work demonstrates an integrated, cost-effective pathway to entering the "quantum advantage" regime in photonic systems far exceeding previous limits, offering a scalable and controllable platform for quantum information processing.

Predicting and mitigating disruptions is crucial for developing sustainable tokamak reactors, a field where machine learning has emerged as an essential tool. This study evaluates and compares multiple machine learning models, with a specific emphasis on their portability—the ease of applying them to data from new devices. The research employs support vector machines (SVM), two-tiered SVMs, random forests, gradient-boosted trees, and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks. Findings indicate that among standard models, SVM performance was marginally superior, whereas gradient-boosted trees performed the poorest. However, portable variants of all models exhibited reduced performance, with random forests achieving the highest accuracy in this category. Additionally, the results suggest that disruptions can be detected up to 600 milliseconds prior to occurrence. Computational analysis reveals that all models execute in under 1 millisecond, providing ample time for effective disruption mitigation.

Building on prior knowledge of quantum field theory and the "Tensor Track" methodology (detailed in series I through VI), we outline recent advances in quantum gravity over the past two years. We then detail two algorithms inspired by Random Tensor Theory within the quantum gravity framework. The first focuses on detecting and recovering a signal embedded in random tensor noise, offering new theoretical guarantees for broader scenarios, including tensors with varying dimensions. The second, SMPI, is more ambitious but less rigorous; it aims to significantly enhance Tensor Principal Component Analysis performance, though it currently lacks complete theoretical proofs. Finally, we sketch various applications relevant to information theory and artificial intelligence, accompanied by their respective bibliographies.

In extensive air shower experiments, key muon parameters—such as the number crossing a detector at a specific location, along with their arrival time, direction, and energy—are derived from a fundamental three-dimensional distribution associated with the shower's hadronic core. These muons originate high in the atmosphere through the decay of mesons within the hadronic cascade. The production depth, energy, and transverse momentum distributions of these muons suffice to completely predict the muon component of air showers under any observational scenario. For the first time, air-shower simulations utilizing state-of-the-art hadronic interaction models have comprehensively analyzed these production distributions as functions of zenith angle, primary mass, and the specific interaction model, rigorously evaluating their universality.

This paper demonstrates that the global solution to the surface anisotropic two-dimensional quasi-geostrophic equation, featuring fractional horizontal dissipation and vertical thermal diffusion as established by the author in [2], remains uniformly bounded in Sobolev spaces over time.

This work describes deformed $N=Z$ nuclei using a formalism based on $\alpha$-like quartets. These quartets are variably constructed through proper intrinsic states, with multiple types of intrinsic states introduced to generate distinct quartet sets for each nucleus. Energy spectra are derived via configuration-interaction calculations within spaces defined by these quartets. The methodology was applied to $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si in the $sd$ shell, as well as to $^{48}$Cr in the $pf$ shell, successfully reproducing low-lying spectra in all instances. A notable feature of this approach is the strong correlation observed between the different quartet sets employed and the emergence of well-defined band-like structures in the studied systems' spectra.

Within the Color Glass Condensate framework, we investigate the charged hadron pseudo-rapidity distributions in both pp and pA collisions at the LHC, utilizing the UGD function derived from the GBW model. A $\chi^{2}$ analysis of CMS data from pp collisions at $\sqrt{s}=0.9,~2.36,$ and $7$ TeV yields a normalization factor, demonstrating strong agreement between the theoretical predictions and experimental observations. Subsequently, by incorporating the effects of nucleon hard parton distributions on participant numbers via a Glauber Monte Carlo approach, we provide predictive multiplicity distributions for p+Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s}=4.4$ TeV.

This study examines integrability conditions derived from general irrotational fluid-flow principles applied to a universe dominated by cosmic dark fluids, specifically under particular assumptions regarding spacetime shear. The analysis focuses heavily on linearized perturbations within quasi-Newtonian and anti-Newtonian spacetimes, aiming to derive and discuss the criteria required for the consistent existence and evolution of these spacetimes when modeled by Chaplygin gas.

Let $\mathbb{Z}_p$ denote the ring of integers modulo a prime $p$, where $p-1$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$. This work investigates constacyclic codes over the chain rings $\mathcal{R}=\frac{\mathbb{Z}_p[u]}{\langle u^2\rangle}$ and $\mathcal{S}=\frac{\mathbb{Z}_p[u]}{\langle u^3\rangle}$. Additionally, we examine additive constacyclic codes over $\mathcal{R}\mathcal{S}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathcal{R}\mathcal{S}$ by employing generator polynomials defined over $\mathcal{R}$ and $\mathcal{S}$, respectively. By introducing Gray maps on $\mathcal{R}$, $\mathcal{S}$, and $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathcal{R}\mathcal{S}$, we derive properties regarding the Gray images of additive codes. Subsequently, we establish weight enumeration formulas and MacWilliams identities for additive codes over $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathcal{R}\mathcal{S}$. Finally, leveraging the derived codes, we construct quantum codes via the CSS method.

This study investigates quasidefinite sesquilinear forms applied to Laurent polynomials within the complex plane, along with the associated CMV biorthogonal Laurent polynomial families. The research covers bivariate linear functionals, which include extensive classes of orthogonality such as Sobolev and discrete Sobolev types. Two distinct Christoffel transformations for these functionals are examined: multiplication by a Laurent polynomial or by the complex conjugate of one. Additionally, the Geronimus transformation is analyzed through two perturbation methods—division by a Laurent polynomial or division by its complex conjugate—with the inclusion of corresponding masses (linear functionals supported at the zeros of the perturbing polynomial) in each scenario. Connection formulas for CMV biorthogonal Laurent polynomials, their norms, and Christoffel-Darboux kernels are provided for all four transformation cases. For the Geronimus transformation, connection formulas regarding second kind functions and mixed Christoffel-Darboux kernels are also detailed for both perturbation cases. Specifically for prepared Laurent polynomials, defined as $L(z)=L_nz^n+\cdots+L_{-n}z^{-n}$ where $L_nL_{-n}\neq 0$, these formulas yield quasideterminantal (quotient of determinants) Christoffel expressions for all four transformations. These expressions represent an arbitrary degree perturbed biorthogonal Laurent polynomial as a combination of $2n$ unperturbed biorthogonal Laurent polynomials, their second kind functions, and their respective Christoffel-Darboux kernels and mixed variants. Finally, the unique characteristics of the unit circle case are explored in greater depth.

This study examines several states, including the $D^*_{s0}(2317)$, $D_{s1}(2460)$, $D^*_{0}(2300)$, and $D_{1}(2430)$, which cannot be adequately described as simple quark-antiquark pairs. According to theoretical predictions from unitarized chiral perturbation theory, these states likely arise from Goldstone-Boson--$D$-meson scattering. We provide results from an $SU(3)$ flavor-symmetric lattice QCD simulation conducted at large pion masses, indicating the existence of a $\pi D$ bound state within the flavor-sextet representation. Such a state is impossible for quark-antiquark configurations but emerges naturally from multiquark structures. Additionally, we observe repulsion in the [15] representation, confirming the interaction pattern predicted for Goldstone bosons and $D$ mesons. These findings imply that these states may possess a hadronic molecular structure.

Molecular graph representation learning (GRL) has recently gained significant traction for molecular property prediction (MPP), with existing research highlighting the critical role of 3D geometric data in enhancing model performance. However, the high cost and time required to generate accurate 3D structures hinder the widespread adoption of GRL. A promising approach involves using 3D-to-2D knowledge distillation to train models on 3D data while allowing inference on 2D inputs alone. Despite this, two major challenges persist: the substantial difference between 3D and 2D perspectives, and the instability and inconsistency of atomic gradient magnitudes caused by varying molecular sizes. To overcome these issues, we introduce a novel distillation framework comprising both global molecular and local atomic distillation components. We also offer theoretical insights to effectively coordinate atomic and molecular information, thereby mitigating the impact of variable molecular sizes on atomic distillation. Experiments on two prominent datasets show that our method outperforms existing approaches. Notably, on the PCQM4Mv2 dataset—often regarded as the "ImageNet" of graph machine learning—our model achieved a 6.9% improvement over the best prior work. Additionally, we secured fourth place in the OGB-LSC 2022 Graph Regression Task with a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.0734 on the test-challenge set. The code will be made publicly available shortly.

Medical diagnoses can profoundly alter an individual's life; consequently, gathering comprehensive evidence to ensure diagnostic certainty is always recommended. However, Brugada Syndrome (BrS), a rare hereditary cardiac condition, presents a unique challenge: it relies on a single diagnostic criterion, specifically a characteristic pattern on an Electrocardiogram (ECG). This treatise investigates whether machine learning techniques can enhance the identification of BrS-positive cases and refine the diagnostic workflow. We propose a pipeline that ingests scanned ECG images, converting them into digital time-voltage data through various processing stages. Subsequently, we introduce a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) classifier trained on this extracted data to facilitate diagnosis. This pipeline differentiates among three primary types of ECG images and reconstructs signals for each recorded lead. Although the digitization process preserves features and quality, certain issues remain unresolved (Part I). Despite these limitations, the program's results are viable for further computational analysis using the proposed classifier, which validates the concept and serves as a potential architectural framework for future studies (Part II). As components of a unified yet conceptually distinct process, the thesis is structured in two parts. Ultimately, this work aims to establish a new foundation for computational research regarding BrS and its diagnosis.

Biased associations have long hindered the creation of classifiers for identifying toxic language, compromising both fairness and accuracy. To address this, we examine recently introduced debiasing techniques for text classification datasets and models within the context of toxicity detection, with a specific focus on lexical elements (such as slurs and identity mentions) and dialectal markers, particularly African American English. Our comprehensive experiments reveal that current debiasing methods are insufficient in preventing biased behavior in existing toxicity detectors. Consequently, we propose an automatic, dialect-aware data correction method as a proof-of-concept. Although this approach utilizes synthetic labels, it successfully reduces dialectal associations with toxicity. Ultimately, our findings indicate that debiasing a model trained on biased toxic language data is less effective than simply relabeling the data to eliminate existing biases.

Numerous methods have been developed to rapidly detect and mitigate malware-induced network attacks, such as massive denial-of-service incidents; however, significant damage often occurs within the first few minutes before identification and containment. Consequently, there is a critical need for an early warning system capable of forecasting attacks prior to their manifestation, thereby allowing potential attackers to be blocked preemptively. Yet, automated blocking measures can inadvertently disrupt legitimate activities on targeted hosts. To mitigate this user inconvenience, it is essential to predict not only the occurrence of attacks but also their timing. This ensures that only the most severe threats trigger immediate auto-blocking, while less urgent ones are subject to manual investigation. To achieve this, we analyzed the typical infection trajectory of contemporary malware, modeling it as a Markov chain trained on actual malicious traffic. This approach enables the identification of behaviors most likely to precipitate attacks, successfully predicting 98% of real-world spamming and port-scanning incidents before they happen. Furthermore, by employing a Semi-Markov chain model, we can forecast the specific timing of impending attacks—a novel capability that accurately predicts the onset of 97% of real-world malware assaults. Our research marks a significant and timely advancement toward flexible threat response frameworks that minimize disruption to legitimate users.

This study demonstrates that three cavity fields can become entangled when they are tuned to resonance with an ensemble of dressed three-level atoms. We derive the master equation for the three cavity modes using atomic dressed states and characterize the inseparability of the output modes via a sufficient criterion introduced by van Loock and Furusawa. The underlying physical mechanism is attributed to atomic coherence effects, which generate quantum correlations within the field dynamics.

Leveraging the gravitational wave (GW) dispersion relation established in [1], we examine whether superfluidity (SF)—characterized by high density and dissipationless behavior—can cause GW reflection within neutron stars. Based on this framework, we propose an experimental strategy to detect SF in neutron stars through GW observations. We analyze two binary configurations: neutron star-black hole pairs and binary neutron star systems, assuming a weak gravitational field. Our findings reveal that GW reflection induces significant modulations in the total signal, manifesting as amplitude and phase variations distinct from the standard sine wave. We further demonstrate that these modulations could be detected by the Cosmic Explorer and Einstein Telescope at distances up to $100\,\mbox{Mpc}$. Identifying such signals would provide evidence for the existence of superfluidity in neutron stars and confirm the phenomenon of GW reflection induced by exotic superfluid dynamics.

This paper investigates geometric invariant theory within the context of algebraic spaces and constructs the moduli spaces of $\mathcal{H}$-semistable sheaves on projective Deligne-Mumford stacks defined over algebraic spaces $S$. We demonstrate that this resulting moduli space is projective over $S$ in its capacity as an algebraic space.

Hyperspectral imaging leverages high-quality spectral signals to identify minute spectral variations, enabling the differentiation of similar materials and offering a distinct advantage for anomaly detection. This capability allows for the effective isolation of anomalous pixels from heterogeneous backgrounds. Because materials exhibit consistent characteristics across both spatial and spectral dimensions, integrating these two information sources significantly boosts detection efficacy. This paper introduces a Spectro-Spatial Fusion Anomaly Detection (SSFAD) method tailored for hyperspectral imagery. Initially, original spectral signals are projected into a local linear background space defined by high-confidence median and mean values; within this domain, saliency weighting and feature enhancement strategies generate an initial detection map. Subsequently, to exploit the similarity information of the local background surrounding each test pixel, a novel detector is developed to extract spatial features from patch images based on local similarity. Finally, anomalies are identified by adaptively fusing the spectral and spatial detection maps. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed method outperforms traditional approaches in terms of detection accuracy.

Block-based motion modeling, which divides frames into fixed-size blocks for independent motion compensation, is a staple in video coding but often results in inefficiency because these rigid blocks rarely align with object contours. While hierarchical block partitioning was introduced to mitigate this, the surge in motion vectors limits its effectiveness. Recently, image segmentation using cuboidal partitioning has emerged as a promising alternative. These variable-sized rectangular segments are not only compatible with standard block-based coding techniques but also align closely with object boundaries by adhering to a homogeneity constraint that minimizes the sum of squared errors (SSE). This paper explores the application of cuboids for motion modeling in contrast to the fixed blocks used in scalable video coding. Specifically, we generate a motion-compensated current frame by leveraging cuboidal partitioning data from an anchor frame within a group-of-pictures (GOP). This predicted frame serves as the base layer, while the current frame is encoded as an enhancement layer using the scalable HEVC encoder. Experimental findings demonstrate bitrate reductions of 6.71% to 10.90% on 4K video sequences.

Pen and paper puzzles such as Sudoku, Futoshiki, and Skyscrapers remain extremely popular, yet modern AI systems find them trivial to solve. A key divergence lies in methodology: while most AI approaches rely heavily on backtracking, humans strive to minimize its use. Consequently, current AI solutions often fail to generate reasoning explanations that resonate with human solvers. To address this, we introduce Demystify, a tool that utilizes a high-level constraint programming language and Minimal Unsatisfiable Subsets (MUSes) to generate human-readable descriptions of solving steps. We have enhanced existing MUS-based solving techniques, enabling the resolution of significantly more complex puzzles with higher-quality explanations. By comparing Demystify's outputs against documented manual solving strategies for various puzzles, we demonstrate the tool's effectiveness and generality, showing that it can identify many of the same logical explanations found in human practice.

This study explores tensor network embeddings, defined as random matrices ($S$) possessing a tensor network architecture. These embeddings facilitate dimensionality reduction for tensor network structured inputs $x$ and speed up tasks like tensor decomposition and kernel regression. While prior research has created embeddings tailored to specific input structures to ensure efficient $Sx$ computation, we offer a systematic framework for designing Gaussian random tensor embeddings. Our approach ensures low sketch sizes (row dimensions of $S$) and minimal computational costs for inputs with broader tensor network structures.

We examine general tensor network embeddings reducible to sequential sketching matrices, establishing a sufficient condition to measure their accuracy. Using embeddings meeting this condition with sketch sizes smaller than any input dimension, we derive lower bounds for sketching asymptotic costs. Furthermore, we present an efficient algorithm for sketching input data using these embeddings, where the sketch size scales linearly with the number of input sketching dimensions. Assuming classical dense matrix multiplication for tensor contractions, this algorithm achieves an asymptotic cost within an $O(\sqrt{m})$ factor of the derived lower bound, with $m$ representing the sketch size. Additionally, when every dimension requiring sketching belongs to a tensor in the input, the algorithm attains the optimal asymptotic cost.

Finally, we apply this sketching analysis to inexact tensor decomposition optimization. We introduce a sketching algorithm for CP decomposition that is asymptotically faster than current methods in several regimes and demonstrate the optimality of an existing algorithm for tensor train rounding.

For a group $G$, the power graph $\mathcal{P}(G)$ is defined by taking the elements of $G$ as vertices and connecting two vertices $x$ and $y$ with an edge if the cyclic subgroup generated by one is contained within the cyclic subgroup generated by the other. Since the identity element is adjacent to every other vertex, the power graph of any group is inherently connected. Let $\kappa(G)$ denote the count of spanning trees within the power graph of a finite group $G$. This paper investigates properties of $\mathcal{P}(G)$ for finite groups, identifies certain divisors of $\kappa(G)$, and demonstrates that the simple group $A_6\cong L_2(9)$ is uniquely characterized by the tree-number of its power graph among all finite simple groups.

We demonstrate that the standard computational pipeline in probabilistic programming systems (PPSs) often proves inefficient for estimating expectations, prompting the introduction of expectation programming. In this approach, the backend inference engine is designed to directly estimate expected return values rather than approximating conditional distributions. Although this distinction is nuanced, it enables significant performance gains over traditional PPS pipelines by customizing computations to the specific expectation of interest. We implement a concrete version of this concept, called Expectation Programming in Turing (EPT), by extending the Turing PPS to facilitate automatic target-aware inference. Theoretically, we establish the statistical validity of EPT, and empirically, we demonstrate that it delivers substantial practical improvements.

In this study, we determine the total chromatic number for various Cayley graphs, including those derived from the symmetric group, alternating group, and dihedral group under specific generating sets, as well as other regular graphs.

We present a theoretical analysis of $L_2(D, \mu)$-approximation error for $n$ function samples $f : D\to\mathbb C$ drawn at random points according to a measure $\nu$. We demonstrate that the weighted least squares method, utilizing finite-dimensional function spaces $V_m$ with dimension $m < \infty$, achieves stability and optimality up to a constant factor when provided with exact samples and logarithmic oversampling. Additionally, for noisy data, our bounds characterize the bias-variance trade-off as a function of the approximation space dimension $m$. These results hold with high probability. As an illustration, we examine functions on the $d$-dimensional cube using uniform random samples, analyzing polynomials, half-period cosines, and a bounded orthonormal basis for the non-periodic Sobolev space $H_{\text{mix}}^2$. By resolving numerical challenges associated with this $H_{\text{mix}}^2$ basis, we introduce a novel stable approximation method exhibiting quadratic error decay. Numerical experiments confirm the practical applicability of our findings.

We demonstrate that within a four-dimensional conformal Haag-Kastler net, the massless particle spectrum arises from a free field subnet. Specifically, when this massless spectrum is scalar, the free field subnet separates as a tensor product component.

This section examines predictions from the bilepton model, an extension of the standard model where the gauge group shifts from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3) \times U(1)$ and fermion families are arranged non-sequentially, with the third family differing from the first two. To satisfy the requirements for triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom, the model necessitates exactly three families. The anticipated new physics comprises bileptons and three heavy quarks, ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. While QCD will bind these heavy quarks with light quarks and among themselves to create baryons and mesons, these composite particles will remain undetectable at the LHC but could be observed at a hypothetical 100 TeV proton-proton collider, unlike the bileptons.

Although crucial for refining Galactic chemical evolution models and identifying progenitor channels for Type Ia supernovae, the nova rate within the Milky Way remains poorly constrained. Previous estimates, ranging from approximately 10 to 300 per year, relied on extrapolating data from a few luminous optical novae or rates in nearby galaxies, both of which involve contentious assumptions. Consequently, the actual discovery rate of optical novae lags significantly behind these predictions at only about 5 to 10 per year, even with modern all-sky optical time-domain surveys. This study introduces a systematic catalog of 12 spectroscopically confirmed Galactic novae identified during the initial 17 months of the Palomar Gattini-IR (PGIR) survey, a wide-field near-infrared time-domain initiative. By observing in the $J$-band ($\approx1.2$ $\mu$m), which minimizes dust extinction effects, the PGIR sample reveals an extinction distribution heavily skewed toward high obscuration, with over 50% of events hidden by $A_V\gtrsim5$ mag. Leveraging current models of Galactic mass and dust distribution, we demonstrate that the observed extinction pattern aligns with theoretical expectations, whereas it starkly contradicts findings from prior optical searches (with a null hypothesis probability $< 0.01\%$). This discrepancy indicates that previous optical efforts have systematically overlooked a substantial population of heavily obscured novae. We conducted the first quantitative simulation of a $3\pi$ time-domain survey using PGIR to calculate the Galactic nova rate, yielding a result of $\approx 46.0^{+12.5}_{-12.4}$ yr$^{-1}$. These findings indicate that comprehensive all-sky near-infrared time-domain surveys are ideally suited to reveal the true extent of the Galactic nova population.

This paper presents the Local Logo Generative Adversarial Network (LL-GAN), a framework for logo generation that leverages regional features extracted by Faster R-CNN. We validate the effectiveness of this method by training it on a compact, style-diverse dataset of authentic heavy metal logos to create novel designs. LL-GAN surpasses state-of-the-art models, including StyleGAN2 and Self-Attention GAN, achieving an Inception Score of 5.29 and a Frechet Inception Distance of 223.94.

This study investigates thin runback water films on iced aircraft surfaces, driven by gas flow, pressure gradients, and gravity. To describe this flow, a three-dimensional film flow model is developed using the Finite Volume Method (FVM) combined with lubrication theory. The model stores depth-averaged velocity in Cartesian coordinates to eliminate the need for metric tensors. Governing equations are discretized within the first layer of structured grid cells designated for film flow. Validation is achieved by comparing numerical results with experimental data for ice shapes on NACA 0012 airfoils and GLC-305 swept wings, demonstrating strong agreement for both rime and glaze ice conditions. Overall, the model exhibits significant potential for accurately simulating ice accretion across various icing scenarios. Additionally, this approach avoids analytic metric terms and can be readily coupled with existing finite volume solvers utilizing logically Cartesian meshes.

Animals can either adapt their behavior rapidly after a single event or learn gradually over thousands of trials. This overview examines tasks characterized by these varying learning speeds and explores hypotheses regarding the distinct neural mechanisms involved. One theory suggests that fast learning depends on neural representations optimized for efficient Hebbian synaptic modification, which may be genetically encoded, creating a species-specific repertoire of rapid learning capabilities. Conversely, the necessary neural representations for learning might be developed through a slow, experience-driven process of unsupervised learning from the environment.

The standard gauge vector field model exhibits local conformal symmetry exclusively in four dimensions ($4d$). Unlike scalar and fermion fields, extending this conformal symmetry to arbitrary dimensions $d$ is unattainable, even within free theories. This study addresses how to bypass this limitation and develop four distinct conformal actions for vector fields. While one model corresponds to the previously established conformal theory of $n$-forms, the others represent novel constructions to our knowledge. Among these, some preserve gauge invariance, two utilize local actions incorporating auxiliary compensating scalar fields, and an extended variant of one model is on-shell equivalent to a final, non-analytic formulation based purely on the metric.

This study examines the vacuum expectation value of the current density for a charged scalar field within Rindler spacetime, where a subset of spatial dimensions is compactified into a torus. Assuming the field resides in the Fulling-Rindler vacuum state, the paper derives expressions for the Hadamard function and vacuum currents for arbitrary phase values in the periodicity conditions and for varying lengths of the compact dimensions. It is found that the current density along these compact dimensions behaves as a periodic function of the enclosed magnetic flux and becomes zero at the Rindler horizon. These findings are contrasted with currents in the Minkowski vacuum. Furthermore, the asymptotic behaviors of the vacuum currents near the horizon and at large distances are analyzed in the context of cylindrical black holes. In the near-horizon limit, the compact dimension lengths are fixed by the horizon radius, whereas at large distances, the geometry approximates a locally anti-de Sitter spacetime with toroidally compact dimensions, where the lengths are dictated by the negative cosmological constant.

Current graph neural networks (GNNs) predominantly depend on node embeddings that encode a node's identity, type, or content as a vector. Yet, many real-world applications, such as anonymized social networks, involve graphs with unattributed nodes. Previous GNN approaches either assign random labels to these nodes—introducing artifacts—or allocate a single embedding to all nodes, failing to differentiate between them. Moreover, when applied to unattributed node classification, existing GNNs exhibit an undesired equivariance property that renders them incapable of handling data with multiple potential outputs. This paper examines the limitations of current methods in node classification. Guided by this analysis, we introduce a generalized equivariance property and a Preferential Labeling technique that asymptotically satisfy the desired property. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach achieves high performance across various unattributed node classification tasks.

Cells have developed sophisticated mechanisms to investigate their surroundings and move through intricate settings. Whether facilitating metastatic dissemination, enabling locomotion within porous media, or allowing passage through tight constrictions—which are essential for linking isolated micro-regions in structured environments—escape remains a fundamental and vital element of cellular exploration. In this study, we utilize the model microalgae *Chlamydomonas reinhardtii* to integrate experimental and simulation approaches, creating a manageable realization of the classical Brownian narrow escape problem within active confined systems. Our findings diverge from predictions for standard Brownian particles or leaking chaotic billiards, demonstrating that interactions with the cell wall significantly alter escape rates and, under typical conditions, accelerate the dynamics of spread.

For a given stellar mass ($M_*$), massive satellite early-type galaxies (ETGs) in galaxy clusters exhibit, on average, larger effective radii ($R_{\rm e}$) at lower redshifts. We investigated this size evolution theoretically using the IllustrisTNG100 cosmological simulation. Our study focused on $75$ simulated satellite ETGs at $z=0$ with $M_* \ge 10^{10.4} M_{\odot}$ residing in the two most massive haloes ($\approx 10^{14.6} M_{\odot}$). By tracing the main progenitors of these clusters backward in time, we identified their satellite ETGs at $z>0$ using the same selection criteria applied at $z=0$. The $R_{\rm e}-M_*$ relation for these simulated cluster satellite ETGs, robustly measured up to $z=0.85$, evolves in a manner consistent with observed trends across the redshift range $0\lesssim z \lesssim 0.85$. In the simulation, the primary drivers of this evolution are the influx of new galaxies ("newcomers") into the clusters and the transformation of member galaxies located at large clustercentric distances ("suburbanites") at $z=0.85$, which become massive satellite ETGs by $z=0$. Although multiple physical processes influence the population of satellite ETGs within this redshift interval, the stellar mass function's shape for simulated cluster ETGs remains largely unchanged between $z=0.85$ and $z=0$, aligning with observational data.

The classical Monte Carlo method is employed to investigate the ground state properties and phase transitions within a spin-pseudospin model representing a two-dimensional Ising magnet characterized by competing charge and spin interactions. This competition induces system frustration and ground state degeneracy. The analysis reveals that within the frustration region, ground state degeneracy persists with non-zero probabilities for the formation of two distinct ordered states. Through histogram analysis of the Monte Carlo data, the nature of the phase transitions is determined; specifically, near the frustration point, first-order phase transitions are identified as a function of the ratio between spin ($s = 1/2$) and pseudospin ($S = 1$) interactions.

Reconstructing charged particle trajectories from detector hits in collider experiments, such as those at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), presents a computationally demanding combinatorial challenge. The projected ten-fold increase in luminosity at the upgraded High Luminosity LHC will create a detector environment with significantly higher hit density. Since traditional track reconstruction methods scale worse than quadratically with density, accurately assigning hits to the correct particles will become a computational bottleneck, necessitating the exploration of alternative solutions. This paper introduces a quantum-enhanced machine learning approach utilizing a support vector machine (SVM) equipped with a quantum-estimated kernel to determine whether a triplet of hits belongs to the same particle track. When compared against a fully classical SVM, the quantum algorithm demonstrates improved accuracy, particularly in the innermost detector layers, which are critical for the initial seeding phase of track reconstruction.

Recent observations indicate that ultra-hot Jupiters (UHJs) frequently exhibit temperature inversions, characterized by rising temperatures at higher altitudes; however, the specific opacity sources driving this phenomenon remain largely unconstrained by observations. We employed the LBT/PEPSI instrument to observe the UHJ KELT-20 b in both transmission and emission to identify potential molecular drivers of these inversions. Our methodology was validated by confirming a prior detection of Fe I in emission at $15.1\sigma$; conversely, we failed to replicate previously published detections of Fe II, Cr I, or Si I. We attribute the non-detection of Si I to the absence of spectral lines within our bandpass, yet the failures to detect Fe II and Cr I are puzzling given our significantly higher signal-to-noise ratio compared to earlier studies. Searches for inversion agents TiO, VO, FeH, and CaH yielded no detections. Through injection-recovery testing, we established $4\sigma$ upper limits on their volume mixing ratios, reaching as low as $\sim1\times10^{-10}$ for TiO. For TiO, VO, and CaH, these limits fall well below predictions from equilibrium chemical models, whereas the limit for FeH is lower than expectations only under a super-Solar metallicity scenario. Consequently, we rule out TiO, VO, and CaH as the cause of the temperature inversion in KELT-20 b, while FeH is only disfavored if the planet possesses a high-metallicity atmosphere.

Clouds are pivotal to Earth's energy balance, yet predicting their future changes remains one of the most significant uncertainties in climate modeling. Traditional efforts to understand cloud feedbacks using satellite data have been limited by simplistic classification systems that rely on single-pixel data rather than spatial textures and structures. However, recent breakthroughs in computer vision now allow for the automated grouping of image patterns without human-defined labels, offering a fresh approach to cloud classification. This unsupervised learning technique facilitates the identification of previously unknown, climate-relevant cloud patterns and enables the efficient processing of massive datasets. This study presents the creation of the AI-driven Cloud Classification Atlas (AICCA), which utilizes 22 years of MODIS satellite observations covering 800 terabytes of global ocean data. By employing a rotation-invariant cloud clustering (RICC) method, we categorized these observations into 42 AI-derived cloud classes at a spatial resolution of approximately 100 km. As a case study, we applied AICCA to investigate recent findings of declining cloud cover in a key region of the subtropical stratocumulus deck, demonstrating that these changes are linked to pronounced trends in specific cloud classes.

The ability to embed multiple watermarks within a single carrier through various techniques has facilitated numerous innovative applications. This study introduces a new multiple watermarking algorithm inspired by spread transform dither modulation (STDM). This method allows for the simultaneous embedding of several watermarks into the same image region and transform domain, while ensuring that each watermark can be extracted independently and blindly by the detector without mutual interference. Additionally, to enhance the fidelity of the watermarked image, the characteristics of the dither modulation quantizer and the proposed embedding strategy are analyzed, leading to the development of two practical optimization techniques. Finally, to increase application versatility, an extended version of the algorithm is introduced, enabling the sequential embedding of different watermarks into an image at each circulation stage. Compared to earlier multiple watermarking methods, the proposed approach offers greater practical flexibility and demonstrates superior robustness against distortions caused by common operations such as random noise, JPEG compression, and volumetric scaling.

This note presents a comprehensive extension of a classical theorem by Marcel Riesz, specifically adapting it to a full space quadratic external field for the equilibrium measure on a ball using Riesz s-kernels. We focus on the case where $s=d-3$ in any dimension $d$, which includes the logarithmic kernel scenario in three dimensions. The resulting equilibrium measure for this full space external field problem is identified as a radial arcsine distribution confined to a ball with a specific radius. Consequently, we derive novel integral identities featuring special functions, including elliptic integrals and, more broadly, hypergeometric functions. These identities appear absent from current series and integral tables and are not currently detected by advanced mathematical software. Our proofs rely on several key components: the Euler-Lagrange variational characterization, the Funk-Hecke formula, the Weyl regularity lemma, the maximum principle, and distinct properties of hypergeometric functions.

This research introduces a methodology to quantify cyber attack vulnerabilities and their consequences using probabilistic graphical models within the connected and autonomous vehicles (CAV) framework for intelligent transportation systems. Vulnerabilities across various attack types and their resulting impacts are computed for intelligent signals and cooperative adaptive cruise control (CACC) based on specific performance metrics. Numerical examples illustrate these impacts through average intersection queue lengths, stop counts, mean speeds, and delays. In signalized networks, the presence or absence of redundant systems results in queue and delay increases of 3% and 4%, or 15% and 17%, respectively. For CACC applications, an average delay difference of 50% occurs when a small amount of speed data is perturbed, while inserting significantly altered speed characteristics by an attacker causes delay differences to exceed 100% of normal traffic conditions.

Given the significant societal and environmental consequences of wildfires, predicting these events using multi-modal sensing data has become a critical analytical tool for various stakeholders, including state governments and power utilities, to better understand fire dynamics and implement preventive strategies. An ideal algorithm must accurately forecast both the risk level and intensity of wildfires for specific locations in real time. This paper introduces a flexible spatio-temporal framework for wildfire prediction that leverages multi-modal time series data. First, we estimate real-time wildfire risk by incorporating historical events through discrete mutually exciting point process models. Subsequently, we establish a wildfire magnitude prediction set using a flexible, distribution-free time-series conformal prediction approach. Theoretically, we provide guarantees for the recovery of risk model parameters, as well as for the coverage and size of the conformal prediction sets. Extensive experiments using real wildfire data from California demonstrate the effectiveness, flexibility, and scalability of our proposed methods across large regions.

To address energy consumption in modern computing, two primary approaches are being explored: one utilizes artificial neural networks (ANNs) grounded in photonic technologies, while the other employs a distinct paradigm involving random networks of nonlinear nanoscale junctions formed by nanoparticle or nanowire assemblies for neuromorphic computing. These networks exhibit emergent complexity and collective behaviors analogous to biological neural systems, characterized by self-organization, redundancy, and non-linearity. Building on this foundation, we formalize a generalized perceptron model for a classification device composed of interacting units with nonlinearly dependent input weights. This proposed model, termed the "receptron," offers significant advantages over the traditional perceptron, such as the ability to solve non-linearly separable Boolean functions using a single device. The receptron model serves as the basis for an all-optical device that leverages the non-linearity of optical speckle fields generated by a solid scatterer. By encoding these speckle patterns, we successfully generated a wide range of target Boolean functions without relying on time-intensive machine learning algorithms. We demonstrate that by appropriately tuning model parameters, various function classes with differing multiplicities can be solved efficiently. Ultimately, the optical implementation of the receptron scheme paves the way for developing a new class of hardware-efficient optical devices for neuromorphic data processing.

The Internet of Things (IoT) has revolutionized daily life by enabling remote control of devices, transforming traditional cyber-physical systems and other sectors into intelligent environments. However, most IoT edge devices possess limited processing capabilities, making them vulnerable to exploitation for various network attacks. As the number of connected devices expands exponentially, so does the risk of emerging, unknown threats. Consequently, there is an urgent need for an intelligent security framework capable of identifying such dangers. This paper introduces an unsupervised ensemble learning model designed to detect novel or unknown attacks within IoT networks using unlabelled data. The system generates a labelled dataset to train a deep learning model for attack detection, while also implementing a feature selection mechanism to isolate the most critical data attributes. The study demonstrates that the proposed model, when trained on the generated labelled data, outperforms other approaches, including Deep Belief Networks (DBN), achieving a detection accuracy of 97.5% and a false alarm rate of 2.3%.

This research investigates the viability of achieving ultrastrong (USC) and deep-strong (DSC) light-matter coupling regimes, specifically at resonance, using a superconducting charge qubit, or Cooper-Pair box (CPB). We demonstrate that shunting this qubit with a high-impedance LC-circuit enables the maximal attainment of both USC and DSC regimes, surpassing the classical limit $|g|\leq \sqrt{\omega_q\omega_r}/2$ applicable to two harmonic systems with frequencies $\omega_q$ and $\omega_r$. Our fundamental model represents an enhanced quantum Rabi model featuring a displacement field operator that violates internal parity symmetry. Additionally, we examine a multipartite system where two CPBs are ultrastrongly coupled to a mediating oscillator, analyzing a quantum state transfer protocol between a pair of transmon qubits under local incoherent noise channels with realistic parameters. This study paves the way for exploring light-matter interactions beyond the quantum Rabi model at extreme coupling strengths, offering a novel component for applications in quantum computation and information processing.

We introduce TACTIC (Task-Aware Compression Through Intelligent Coding), a lossy compression model designed to optimize the rate-distortion-accuracy trade-off for specific tasks. By prioritizing information critical to downstream problems, the system sacrifices visual fidelity to achieve superior task performance at low bitrates. Compared to JPEG at equivalent bitrates, our method boosts ImageNet subset classification accuracy by 4.5%. Furthermore, we demonstrate the approach's versatility across other tasks, achieving a 3.4% accuracy and 4.9% mean IoU improvement over task-agnostic compression in semantic segmentation.

The analysis demonstrates that the Plebanski equation of symmetry admits an infinite set of solutions, which are provided in explicit form. This finding implies that series solutions for the Plebanski equation can be derived analytically. Furthermore, several specific classes of explicit solutions are presented.

Distinguishing galaxy morphologies is crucial for comprehending their physical characteristics and evolutionary paths. The rise of extensive surveys has accelerated the demand for automated classification methods. We trained and evaluated multiple convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures to categorize galaxies using a dataset of 14,034 visually classified SDSS images, employing both a 3-class (elliptical, lenticular, spiral) and a 4-class (including irregular/miscellaneous) schema. Our newly developed CNN architecture surpassed existing models in both classification schemes, achieving overall accuracies of 83% for the 3-class and 81% for the 4-class tasks. Additionally, we analyzed binary classifications between all four types, revealing that ellipticals and spirals are the easiest to distinguish (>98% accuracy), whereas spirals and irregulars present the greatest challenge (78% accuracy). An examination of misclassified samples suggests these errors may hold physical significance; for instance, lenticulars incorrectly labeled as ellipticals tend to be more massive. We also combined binary CNN classifiers for hierarchical classification, which yielded comparable 3-class accuracy (81%) to the direct CNN approach but significantly lower 4-class performance (65%). Finally, we validated our networks on a subset of Galaxy Zoo images, securing accuracies of 92%, 82%, and 77% for binary, 3-way, and 4-way classifications, respectively.

This work investigates the entanglement characteristics of hypergraph states across arbitrary finite dimensions. We calculate the multipartite entanglement for elementary qudit hypergraph states, specifically those defined by a single hyperedge of maximum cardinality. Our findings demonstrate that, similar to the qubit scenario, connected qudit hypergraph states in any dimension possess a lower bound for multipartite entanglement; this bound corresponds to the multipartite entanglement of an elementary hypergraph state with the same dimension, featuring a hyperedge size equal to the largest-cardinality hyperedge of the original state. Additionally, we identify notable distinctions in entanglement properties between systems of prime and non-prime dimensions.

This study introduces an interpretable, semiautomatic Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) framework designed for staging ocular pathologies—including diabetic, hypertensive, and other retinopathies—within the context of major systemic diseases. Unlike current deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models that often lack transparency regarding their decision-making basis despite high performance, this research proposes a clinician-in-the-loop workflow to enhance interpretability. This approach performs retinal vascular assessments on fundus images to generate quantifiable and descriptive parameters, which function as hyper-parameters to clarify AI decisions. The methodology adopts a federated AI strategy for healthcare, incorporating greater clinician input and interpretation. The underlying machine learning pipeline utilizes image processing techniques for baseline tasks such as optic disc detection, vessel segmentation, and the identification of arterioles and venules.

This paper investigates the structural properties and topological indices of a specific class of random spider trees (RSTs), including degree-based metrics like the Gini and Hoover indices, as well as generalized Zagreb indices and related measures. Using probabilistic techniques, we derive both exact and asymptotic distributions for the count of leaves. Furthermore, we connect this model to RSTs that develop through a preferential attachment mechanism.

This study introduces and investigates a novel collider signature for heavy neutral scalars, a feature common across various multi-Higgs model classes. Particularly pertinent to Large Hadron Collider (LHC) data, this signature is defined by a topology yielding two charged leptons and four jets derived from first and second generation quarks. Focusing on a Branco-Grimus-Lavoura (BGL) model—enhanced by an abelian U(1) flavour symmetry and including a right-handed neutrino sector—we examine how the kinematics of scalar fields can effectively distinguish the signal from major backgrounds. We further assess the discovery prospects for these new heavy scalars in upcoming LHC runs. Additionally, the proposed methodology offers a framework for evaluating the statistical significance of heavy scalar production at the LHC and future colliders within any multi-Higgs model context.

Isobar collisions, characterized by identical backgrounds but differing magnetic fields, offer a unique avenue to validate the chiral magnetic effect (CME) in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Nevertheless, the initial findings from the RHIC-STAR isobar experiment failed to detect a CME signal, instead revealing distinct background differences between $_{44}^{96}\textrm{Ru}+_{44}^{96}\textrm{Ru}$ and $_{40}^{96}\textrm{Zr}+_{40}^{96}\textrm{Zr}$ collisions. To address this, we analyzed eighteen configurations of Woods-Saxon parameters arising from various nuclear deformation and structural effects within a multiphase transport model. Our results indicate that seven of these scenarios can adequately replicate three reference ratios observed by the STAR experiment. When accounting for both halo-type neutron skin structures and CME-like charge separation, we demonstrate that CME observables ($\Delta\delta$, $\Delta\delta$ ratio, $\Delta\gamma$, and $\Delta\gamma$ ratio) struggle to distinguish between the presence or absence of the CME if its strength is weak in isobar collisions. This limitation arises because final-state interactions substantially diminish the initial CME signal, leading to non-linear sensitivities of these observables regarding CME strength. Consequently, more sensitive observables are necessary to detect potential small CME signals in isobar collisions.

Recent years have seen an explosive surge in data, much of which consists of video footage from security cameras, smartphones, and dash cams. Timely analysis of this data is crucial for emerging applications like real-time facial recognition and object detection. This study tackles real-time in-situ video analytics for dash cam footage by introducing EdgeDashAnalytics (EDA), an edge-based system that facilitates near real-time processing using a local network of mobile devices. Specifically, EDA simultaneously processes videos from two dash cams mounted on a moving vehicle using one or more mobile devices. One camera faces forward to capture the road ahead, while the other faces inward to monitor the driver. The forward-facing footage is analyzed to identify potential driving hazards, whereas the interior footage is used to detect driver distraction. EDA achieves near real-time analytics on resource-constrained, transient mobile devices through several optimizations that accept a tolerable accuracy trade-off. Implemented as an Android application, EDA was evaluated using two dash cams and various heterogeneous mobile devices with the BDD100K dash cam dataset (arXiv:1805.04687 [cs.CV]) and the DMD driver monitoring dataset (arXiv:2008.12085 [cs.CV]). Experimental results confirm the feasibility of real-time video analytics regarding turnaround time and energy consumption (battery usage) when utilizing mobile devices in motion.

This paper investigates the isoperimetric problem within Randers planes, defined as $(\mathbb{R}^2, F=\alpha+\beta)$, which represent minor distortions of the Euclidean plane $(\mathbb{R}^2, \alpha)$ via appropriate one-forms $\beta$. We demonstrate that circles centered at the origin attain the local maximum area for the isoperimetric problem relative to standard volume forms in Finsler geometry.

We investigate charmonium states by evaluating a phenomenological nonrelativistic potential and introducing a novel set of parameters. These parameters are determined exclusively using the lowest-lying S-wave charmonia, where spin-orbit and tensor interactions are negligible. Following this fitting process, we examine the entire fine structure of charmonium states, incorporating spin-orbit and tensor effects. The results indicate that a nonrelativistic potential model utilizing these phenomenologically defined parameters provides a robust approximation for describing charmonium states.

Evaluating the quality of web information is a highly relevant task with numerous applications, particularly in critical sectors such as medicine. We operate on the premise that the quality of medical web content is influenced by domain-specific characteristics. These include the use of specialized vocabulary (Domain Informativeness), the implementation of specific codes (such as those found in Wikipedia infoboxes), and the document type (e.g., historical versus technical). This paper proposes utilizing these specific domain features to enhance the evaluation of Wikipedia's medical articles. Specifically, we employ an "actionable" model whose content-related features enable the system to not only assess quality but also directly propose strategies for improvement. We utilize Natural Language Processing (NLP) and dictionary-based methods to extract biomedical concepts from texts. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated by classifying medical articles from the Wikipedia Medicine Portal, which were previously manually labeled by the Wiki Project team. Our experimental results confirm that incorporating domain-oriented features yields significant improvements over existing solutions, particularly for articles that other methods misclassify. Beyond their intrinsic interest, these findings highlight the need for further research into domain-specific features suitable for assessing web data quality.

Future surveys like the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) are expected to identify up to 10 million variable celestial objects nightly over a decade. This data will flow continuously to brokers that employ machine learning to filter the most significant events for diverse scientific goals. This study examines the advantages and limitations of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) for such classification tasks. Results indicate that BNNs serve as precise classifiers while offering a distinct benefit: they quantify classification uncertainty, a feature that can be leveraged to process the anticipated influx of data more effectively.

Representations of the type-A Hecke algebra exist on spaces of polynomials in anti-commuting variables. Previously, Luque and the author [S\'em. Lothar. Combin. 66 (2012), Art. B66b, 68 pages, arXiv:1106.0875] developed nonsymmetric Macdonald polynomials valued in arbitrary Hecke algebra modules. This paper merges these two concepts to define and investigate nonsymmetric Macdonald polynomials valued in anti-commuting polynomials, termed superpolynomials. The study begins by deriving the relevant modules, their orthogonal bases, and their properties. Within the standard Young tableau framework for representations, these modules align with hook tableaux. The exposition covers the specifics of Dunkl-Luque theory and this specific application. An inner product is defined on these polynomials, rendering the Macdonald polynomials mutually orthogonal, with their squared norms explicitly calculated. Leveraging methods from Baker and Forrester [Ann. Comb. 3 (1999), 159-170, arXiv:q-alg/9707001], symmetric Macdonald polynomials are constructed from the nonsymmetric foundation; here, "symmetric" refers to the Hecke algebra context rather than the classical group context. Concise formulas are provided for the squared norm of the minimal symmetric polynomial, along with formulas for anti-symmetric polynomials. Additionally, both symmetric and anti-symmetric polynomials exhibit factorization when evaluated at specific points.

Emerging privacy initiatives, notably the EU General Data Protection Regulation, have compelled Machine Learning (ML) to undergo rigorous privacy and security evaluations. Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized, privacy-centric training framework that enhances the security of ML models. However, the rapid industry adoption and security assessments of FL have uncovered numerous vulnerabilities jeopardizing its Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA). This study evaluates the CIA principles of FL by reviewing current state-of-the-art methods and developing a comprehensive threat model that accounts for attack surfaces, adversarial actors, their capabilities, and objectives. Furthermore, we introduce the inaugural unified taxonomy for FL attacks and defenses, along with promising avenues for future research.

Object detection frequently struggles with an abundance of ineffective proposals, making the selection of high-quality candidates a significant challenge. This paper introduces a semantic, class-specific method for re-ranking object proposals that consistently enhances recall performance, even when utilizing fewer proposals. The approach extracts features for each proposal—including semantic segmentation, stereo data, contextual cues, CNN-based objectness, and low-level signals—and scores them using class-specific weights learned via a Structured SVM. The proposed model offers two key advantages: it can be seamlessly integrated with existing proposal generators with minimal computational overhead, and it achieves a high recall rate under strict criteria even with a reduced number of proposals. Evaluations on the KITTI benchmark demonstrate that our method significantly boosts the recall performance of popular existing generators. Furthermore, experimental results in object detection show that even with only 1,500 proposals, our approach yields a higher average precision (AP) than baseline methods using 5,000 proposals.
