We explore how non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) algorithms can enhance parameter estimation within topic models. Although previous research has examined the relationship between NMF and topic models, no prior work has proposed utilizing this link to create new fitting algorithms. By bypassing the "sum-to-one" constraints inherent in topic model parameters, NMF offers an optimization framework with a simpler structure and greater computational efficiency. Leveraging recent improvements in NMF optimization, we demonstrate that solving the NMF problem first and subsequently recovering the topic model fit yields significantly superior results in reduced time compared to conventional topic model algorithms. While our primary focus is on maximum likelihood estimation, we also indicate that this method can benefit variational inference for topic models. Our approach is available in the R package fastTopics.

This article extends the Fourier transform to a broader class of functions, initially addressing power-law functions with both integer and half-integer exponents, and subsequently applying it to the commonly utilized quantum statistics functions, specifically the Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein distributions. These findings facilitate the straightforward derivation of an integral formula. Furthermore, generalized Fourier transforms are employed to define fractional derivatives for distributions (generalized functions) and to establish Fourier series for periodic functions.

This paper introduces a straightforward yet highly effective method for inducing "selective amnesia" in backdoored models, termed SEAM. Drawing inspiration from the long-standing challenge of catastrophic forgetting (CF) in continual learning, our approach involves retraining a deep neural network (DNN) on randomly labeled clean data. This process triggers CF, causing the model to abruptly forget both its primary functions and backdoor triggers. Subsequently, we restore the primary task by retraining the randomized model on correctly labeled clean data. We analyzed SEAM by framing the unlearning process as a continual learning problem and approximating the DNN with a Neural Tangent Kernel to quantify CF. Our analysis demonstrates that random labeling maximizes CF regarding unknown backdoors in the absence of triggers while retaining sufficient feature extraction capabilities for a rapid recovery of the primary task. We evaluated SEAM across image processing and natural language processing tasks, addressing both data contamination and training manipulation attacks on thousands of models from popular image datasets and the TrojAI competition. Experimental results indicate that SEAM significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art unlearning techniques. It achieves high fidelity—defined as the accuracy gap between the primary task and the backdoor—within minutes (approximately 30 times faster than training from scratch on the MNIST dataset), requiring only a minimal amount of clean data (0.1% of training data for TrojAI models).

The ALICE experiment is designed to investigate the quark-gluon plasma (QGP), a high-temperature and high-density state of matter where quarks and gluons exist in a deconfined condition. A key probe for studying this phase is quarkonium, consisting of bound pairs of charm-anticharm (charmonia) or bottom-antibottom (bottomonia) quarks. The formation of the QGP is anticipated to alter quarkonium production yields in a distinct manner, resulting from the interplay between medium-induced suppression and recombination or hadronization processes. To characterize the properties of the QGP in nucleus-nucleus collisions, it is crucial to measure quarkonium differential yields in proton-proton collisions, which serve as a baseline for examining production mechanisms and for analyzing cold nuclear matter effects in proton-nucleus collisions. This contribution presents the most recent ALICE detector results on quarkonium production in proton-proton collisions across various energy levels. Additionally, data on the nuclear modification factor and anisotropic flow in lead-lead collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 5.02$ TeV and in proton-lead collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 8.16$ TeV, covering both mid- and forward rapidity regions, are reported. All these measurements are evaluated against a range of theoretical predictions.

LeQua 2022 introduces a new laboratory dedicated to evaluating techniques for "learning to quantify" within textual datasets, specifically for training predictors that estimate the relative frequencies of target classes across collections of unlabeled documents. Although one might initially achieve these predictions by classifying all documents via a standard text classifier and subsequently counting the assigned class instances, a growing body of literature demonstrates that this approach is suboptimal and has proposed superior alternatives. The primary objective of this lab is to facilitate a comparative assessment of learning-to-quantify methods, covering both binary and single-label multiclass scenarios. For each scenario, the lab provides data in either ready-made vector format or raw document form.

This paper primarily examines the finite extensible nonlinear elastic (FENE) dumbbell model for dimensions $d \geq 2$ across the entire space. First, we demonstrate that the steady-state FENE model admits only the trivial solution under certain integrable conditions, thereby extending and encompassing classical results for stationary Navier-Stokes equations. Subsequently, we analyze the $L^2$ decay behavior of the co-rotation FENE model. Specifically, for $d \geq 3$, the velocity decay rate is $(1+t)^{-\frac{d}{4}}$, whereas for $d=2$, it is $\ln^{-k}{(e+t)}$ with $k \in \mathds{N}^{+}$. These findings substantially improve upon the recent work of Schonbek (\cite{Schonbek2}). Additionally, we investigate the decay characteristics of the general FENE model.

Hamming weights of sparse, lengthy binary vectors play a critical role in numerous scientific fields, especially in spiking neural networks, which are the focus of our study. To enhance the area efficiency and latency of FPGA implementations for these weights, we introduce a method inspired by synaptic transmission failure that leverages FPGA lookup tables to compress long input vectors. To assess this approach, we determine the count of `1`s in the compressed vectors using a straightforward linear adder. We categorize the compressors into shallow types, utilizing up to two levels of lookup tables, and deep types, employing more than two levels. Our results demonstrate that the proposed architecture achieves area and latency reductions of up to 82% and 35%, respectively, across various shallow compressor configurations. Furthermore, simulation data indicates that computing the Hamming weight of a 1024-bit vector within a spiking neural network using exclusively deep compressors maintains the network's chaotic behavior while having only a minor impact on learning performance.

This study addresses the Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) involving an agent operating within a unichain MDP environment. During each interaction, the agent receives a reward, alongside $K$ distinct cost functions. The objective is to maximize the long-term average reward while ensuring that all $K$ long-term average costs remain below specified thresholds. We introduce CMDP-PSRL, a posterior sampling-based algorithm designed to enable the agent to learn optimal policies for such CMDPs. For an MDP characterized by $S$ states, $A$ actions, and diameter $D$, we demonstrate that the CMDP-PSRL algorithm bounds the regret—the difference in accumulated rewards compared to an optimal policy—by $\Tilde{O}(poly(DSA)\sqrt{T})$. Additionally, we establish that the violation of any of the $K$ constraints is similarly bounded by $\Tilde{O}(poly(DSA)\sqrt{T})$. To our knowledge, this represents the first work to achieve a $\Tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret bound for ergodic MDPs subject to long-term average constraints.

We derive a precise moment comparison inequality relating any negative moment to the second moment for sums of independent uniform random variables, thereby generalizing Ball's cube slicing inequality.

This perspective outlines the pivotal function of membranes in shaping the conformation of Amyloid Precursor Proteins to generate the peptides associated with Alzheimer's disease. Additionally, it examines fundamental concepts of protein aggregation, specifically highlighting how the excited states of monomers may trigger the aggregation process.

To safeguard the environment and mitigate the scarcity of fossil fuels, renewable energy sources are increasingly adopted for power generation. However, the inherent uncertainties in electricity production render deterministic optimization inadequate for operational requirements. Consequently, numerous optimization techniques designed to handle uncertainty have emerged as effective solutions. This paper introduces three prominent methods: stochastic programming (SP), robust optimization (RO), and a novel approach called distributionally robust optimization (DRO), which builds upon the first two. We outline the fundamental framework and general procedure of each method using specific examples, with a particular focus on how they address uncertainty. Furthermore, we evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of these approaches and discuss potential directions for future research.

Collaborators typically anticipate returns exceeding the mere sum of their individual contributions, a concept central to the public goods game where contributions are amplified by a synergy factor, $r$, before distribution. While larger groups could theoretically benefit from higher synergy, this study introduces a model featuring varied group sizes where the synergy factor scales with group magnitude. We analyze scenarios where the increase in $r$ is linear, gradual, or abrupt, finding that cooperation levels remain superior to those in populations with a uniform $r$. In homogeneous settings, smaller groups tend to excel; however, this dynamic flips when synergy is tied to group size, favoring larger collectives and thereby benefiting the entire community. Furthermore, this qualitative pattern holds true for other heterogeneous network structures, such as scale-free interaction graphs.

This study focuses on a Fokker-Planck equation associated with a nonlinear noisy leaky integrate-and-fire model applied to biological neural networks characterized by synaptic weights and Hebbian learning. The equation incorporates a small parameter, $\varepsilon$, which distinguishes between the time scales of learning and reaction within the neural system. By taking the limit as $\varepsilon \to 0$, an asymptotic model is derived in which microscopic quasi-static states and macroscopic evolution equations are linked via the total firing rate. To address the equation's inherent flux-shift structure and multi-scale dynamics within a unified approach, we introduce a numerical scheme that ensures mass conservation, unconditional positivity preservation, and asymptotic preservation. We validate the scheme's properties through extensive numerical tests and conduct experiments to examine the model's learning capabilities and analyze solution behavior in excitatory neural networks.

Investigating the production of vector bosons alongside jets provides an ideal setting to validate various QCD predictions. Using CMS data from proton-proton collisions, researchers have analyzed both total and differential cross-sections for vector bosons produced in association with jets. The study involves measuring differential distributions across a wide spectrum of kinematic variables and comparing them against theoretical models. This talk will summarize these investigations, focusing on the associated production of vector bosons with both inclusive jets and jets arising from heavy-flavor quarks.

Biomedical research frequently generates multi-view data, such as genomic and proteomic profiles, with a key objective of identifying sample subgroups defined by specific variable sets. Biclustering is particularly effective for this task because it isolates variable groups that are relevant only to specific sample subsets. While numerous biclustering algorithms exist for single-view data to detect row-column clusters, methods capable of handling multiple views are scarce. Existing multi-view approaches often rely heavily on regularization parameters to identify these clusters, creating a significant burden for users and restricting their practical application. We adapt an established sparse singular value decomposition (SSVD) biclustering technique, originally designed for single-view data, to accommodate multi-view datasets. Our proposed method, integrative sparse singular value decomposition (iSSVD), employs stability selection to manage Type I error rates, calculates the likelihood of samples and variables belonging to a bicluster, identifies stable clusters, and yields interpretable row-column associations. Both simulation studies and real-world data analyses demonstrate that iSSVD surpasses several other single- and multi-view biclustering methods in detecting meaningful patterns. As a user-friendly and computationally efficient algorithm, iSSVD holds great promise for various disease subtyping applications.

Metallic components in plasmonics are currently hindered by unavoidable optical losses, which obstruct the deployment of most applications. This study demonstrates that Ohmic losses can be significantly diminished in specific layered metals, such as the transition metal dichalcogenide TaS$_2$, owing to an exceptionally low density of states for scattering in the near-IR region, a result of their unique electronic band structure. Leveraging this finding, we introduce a novel category of band structure-engineered van der Waals layered metals formed by hexagonal transition metal chalcogenide-halide layers, characterized by markedly reduced intrinsic losses. First-principles calculations confirm that this suppression of optical losses enhances the performance of thin-film waveguiding and transformation optics.

This paper investigates Johnson-Schechtman inequalities concerning noncommutative martingales. Specifically, we establish disjointification inequalities for noncommutative martingale difference sequences within any symmetric operator space $E(\mathcal{M})$ associated with a finite von Neumann algebra $\mathcal{M}$, without imposing restrictions on the Boyd indices of $E$. We demonstrate that Johnson-Schechtman inequalities hold for arbitrary martingale difference sequences; notably, unlike the classical scenario involving independent random variables or the noncommutative setting with freely independent variables, these inequalities are one-sided unless $E=L_2(0,1)$. As a consequence, we partially address a question posed by Randrianantoanina and Wu in \cite{NW}. Furthermore, we derive sharp $\Phi$-moment analogues for Orlicz functions exhibiting $p$-convexity and $q$-concavity under the conditions ($1 \leq p \leq 2$, $q=2$) and ($p=2$, $2< q < \infty$), a result that represents new progress even in the classical context. Finally, we extend and reinforce the noncommutative Burkholder-Gundy inequalities applicable to symmetric spaces and the $\Phi$-moment framework.

The boundary between LaAlO$_3$ and SrTiO$_3$ insulators hosts a two-dimensional electron liquid (2DEL), a high-mobility system displaying superconductivity, magnetic signs, and strong correlations. Although this prominent oxide heterostructure holds promise for electronics, the microscopic origins and properties of the 2DEL remain elusive. This uncertainty stems from the difficulty in probing the electronic structures of such buried nanoscale interfaces, exacerbated by variable oxygen vacancy concentrations and the coexistence of localized and delocalized charges. These complexities have hindered definitive tests of intrinsic electronic and orbital reconstruction at the interface. In this study, we surmount previous challenges by developing an interface analysis utilizing inherently sensitive resonant x-ray reflectometry. We identify a high charge density of 0.5 electrons per interfacial unit cell in samples exceeding the critical LaAlO$_3$ thickness and determine the depth profiles of both orbital and electronic reconstructions near the buried interface. Our findings indicate that most reconstruction phenomena are confined to within two unit cells of the interface and quantify the significant impact of oxygen vacancies on the electronic system. These results offer robust evidence for polarity-induced electronic reconstruction, effectively distinguishing its effects from those caused by oxygen vacancies.

In recent years, Evolutionary Strategies have been widely investigated for robotic policy search due to their simplicity compared to reinforcement learning algorithms. However, these methods are often criticized for being highly sample-inefficient. Conversely, Differentiable Robot Simulators (DRS) are gaining traction because they can identify effective policies using only a few trajectories, although their resulting gradients are not always suitable for first-order optimization. This study demonstrates how to integrate DRS gradients with Evolutionary Strategies. Preliminary findings indicate that this hybrid approach can reduce the sample complexity of Evolutionary Strategies by 3 to 5 times, achieving improvements in both simulated and real-world environments.

Current natural language processing models struggle with noisy data caused by typos, whereas humans effortlessly identify the intended words based on misspellings and contextual cues. Drawing inspiration from this human capability, we tackle the standalone spelling correction challenge—specifically correcting token spellings without adding or removing tokens—by leveraging both spelling cues and global context representations. We introduce a straightforward yet effective approach that treats misspelling detection and correction as a sequence labeling task through the fine-tuning of a pre-trained language model. This method surpasses the previous state-of-the-art by achieving a 12.8% absolute improvement in F0.5 score.

We explore photonic arrays composed of quantum emitters within optically linked microcavities as a means to generate entanglement. These systems provide significant tunability alongside the capability for site-specific optical excitation. We examine coherent pumping as a mechanism to drive transitions from vacuum to entangled target states, employing both time-dependent methods and a quantum bath engineering strategy to achieve steady-state entanglement. Furthermore, we present a numerical framework that extends the determination of excitation parameters to larger array configurations and various classes of entangled states. This research advances the potential of utilizing coupled cavity arrays as hardware platforms for emerging quantum-photonic applications in quantum computing and quantum machine learning.

The continuous gravitational interaction between the Milky Way (MW) and its most massive satellite, the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), significantly disturbs the distribution and kinematics of distant halo stars, globular clusters, and satellite galaxies, introducing biases into MW mass estimates derived from these tracers. We introduce a method to correct for these perturbations regardless of the assumed MW potential by calculating the past trajectories of both the LMC and the MW, then integrating the orbits of tracer objects backward in time until LMC influence becomes negligible. At this stage, an equilibrium approximation can be applied using standard dynamical modeling techniques. We incorporate this orbit-rewinding procedure into a mass estimation framework that simultaneously fits the potential and the distribution function of tracers, applying it to two datasets utilizing the latest Gaia EDR3 6d phase-space coordinates for globular clusters and satellite galaxies. Our results indicate that models with an LMC mass between (1-2)×10^11 Msun provide the best fit to the observed tracer distributions, yielding a MW mass within 100 kpc of (0.75±0.1)×10^12 Msun; ignoring the LMC perturbation would result in an overestimation of approximately 15%.

This paper introduces several BERT-based architectures tailored for Russian biomedical text mining, namely RuBioBERT and RuBioRoBERTa. These models undergo pre-training using a collection of freely accessible texts within the Russian biomedical field. Leveraging this pre-training, the models achieve state-of-the-art performance on RuMedBench, a Russian benchmark for medical language understanding that encompasses various tasks such as text classification, question answering, natural language inference, and named entity recognition.

We demonstrate that the ice surface possesses self-healing properties, where micrometer-deep scratches vanish spontaneously through relaxation within approximately one hour. By analyzing these dynamics and contrasting them with various mass transfer processes, we identify sublimation and subsequent condensation as the primary mechanisms driving this repair. The kinetics of this self-healing exhibit a pronounced temperature dependence, adhering to Arrhenius behavior with an activation energy of $\Delta E = 58.6 \pm 4.6$ kJ/mole. This finding supports the proposed sublimation model and contradicts alternative explanations such as surface diffusion, fluid flow, or evaporation-condensation occurring within a quasi-liquid layer.

Identifying arguments within online exchanges is essential for comprehending the emergence and resolution of conflicts. Participants frequently employ figurative devices like sarcasm, utilizing them either as persuasive tools or as vehicles for ad hominem attacks. To deepen our insight into sarcasm's influence on the landscape of disagreement, we introduce a comprehensive experimental framework based on a dataset annotated with both argumentative stances (agree/disagree) and sarcasm markers. Our approach leverages joint modeling strategies, specifically: (a) integrating discrete features effective for sarcasm detection into argumentative relation classification tasks (agree/disagree/none), and (b) employing multitask learning via deep learning structures, such as dual Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks with hierarchical attention and Transformer-based models, to simultaneously address sarcasm detection and argument classification. Our findings indicate that incorporating sarcasm modeling enhances the accuracy of argumentative relation classification across all experimental configurations.

Achieving a Quantum Internet necessitates pre-shared entanglement between quantum nodes; however, the generation and distribution of maximally-entangled states are intrinsically hindered by quantum decoherence. Traditionally, this decoherence is addressed through a sequential process of entanglement distillation followed by teleportation, which introduces significant latency. To overcome this bottleneck, we introduce a new quantum communication protocol that utilizes realistic, noisy pre-shared entanglement, thereby removing the sequential delays inherent in standard methods. Specifically, our approach functions as a direct communication scheme that enhances the quantum bit error ratio (QBER) of logical qubits even when relying on imperfect entanglement. Performance evaluations indicate that our proposed scheme delivers competitive QBER, yield, and goodput relative to current state-of-the-art solutions, while simultaneously reducing the number of required quantum gates.

This paper examines asymptotic regularization under convex constraints applied to nonlinear ill-posed problems. The proposed approach accommodates non-smooth penalty terms, such as L1-like and total variation-like functionals, which are crucial for capturing specific solution characteristics like sparsity and piecewise constancy. We establish convergence properties for these methods under specific conditions and introduce Runge-Kutta-type schemes to discretize initial value problems, thereby developing novel iterative regularization techniques.

This study introduces Video Transformer Network (VTN), a novel and efficient method for Human Action Recognition. By integrating recent breakthroughs in Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing, VTN enhances video comprehension capabilities. The framework enables the development of compact CNN architectures that deliver high accuracy and real-time performance using only a standard RGB camera and a general-purpose CPU. Additionally, we detail a knowledge distillation strategy that improves accuracy by consolidating insights from multiple models with diverse modalities into one unified model. Our comparative analysis against state-of-the-art techniques demonstrates that VTN matches the performance of most existing methods on prominent action recognition benchmarks. Using a modern inference framework, we evaluated the models' speed, revealing that VTN offers a superior speed/accuracy trade-off, achieving 56 FPS on a CPU. Both the trained models and the training code are publicly accessible.

This paper presents a novel theoretical framework for Optimal Transport (OT) by integrating the terminology and methods of Fully Probabilistic Design (FPD). While OT is the standard approach for comparing probability measures and has proven effective across diverse fields such as computer vision, computer graphics, and natural language processing, we contend that existing frameworks face two critical limitations: the difficulty of incorporating generic constraints and probabilistic knowledge, and the failure to address uncertainty in marginals, which hinders the creation of robust solutions. By reframing the OT problem as the optimal design of a probability density function subject to marginal constraints, we demonstrate that OT is a specific instance of the broader FPD framework. This new perspective enables the OT framework to handle probabilistic constraints and derive uncertainty quantifiers, resulting in an extended approach termed FPD-OT. The primary contribution of this work is establishing the theoretical link between OT and FPD, offering fresh insights for both disciplines. This foundation will support future applications of FPD-OT, particularly in managing complex knowledge constraints and designing robust solutions under conditions of marginal uncertainty.

We derive the velocity expression as a function of the radial coordinate $r$ by employing polynomial interpolation on experimental data of rotational velocities observed in the distant outer regions of galaxies. Specifically, we utilize a fifth-degree polynomial followed by cubic spline interpolation. This rotational velocity data informs the geometry of galactic halo regions within Einstein's general relativity framework. In this letter, we examine features of these halo regions considering two dark matter density profiles: the Navarro, Frenk \& White (NFW) model~\citep{Navarro1996} and the Universal Rotation Curve (URC)~\citep{Castignani2012}. We argue that the spacetime of the galactic halo exhibits characteristics necessary to support traversable wormholes.

Nanoscale hardness in polycrystalline metals, as a bulk mechanical property, relies heavily on microstructural characteristics driven by the complexities of polycrystallinity, specifically individual grain orientations and the properties of adjacent grains. We developed a graph neural network (GNN) model, treating each grain center as a node, to evaluate how well micromechanical responses of nano-indented low-carbon 310S stainless steel (alloyed with Ni and Cr) surfaces can be predicted using only surface polycrystallinity data captured via electron backscatter diffraction maps. With a grain size distribution spanning $1-100~\mu$m and a mean size of $18~\mu$m, the GNN was trained on nanomechanical load-displacement curves from nanoindentation tests. This model predicts nano-hardness at different depths using exclusively grain locations and orientations as inputs. Despite training on a limited dataset of approximately $10^2$ hardness measurements, the model achieved satisfactory performance. We investigated how model performance correlates with various structural and topological grain-level descriptors, including grain size and the number of nearest neighbors. Similar GNN frameworks could facilitate rapid, low-cost hardness estimations to guide detailed nanoindentation experiments, much like cartography tools aided world exploration.

Nanopublications offer a granular, provenance-aware approach to representing Linked Data, a method already proven effective for various scientific datasets. While our prior work established reliable and verifiable identifiers for both individual nanopublications and their collections, widespread adoption was likely impeded by the risk of a triple explosion caused by auxiliary structural details and repetitive provenance and metadata. This study demonstrates that such significant overhead vanishes when accounting for the version history of nanopublication datasets, computing incremental updates, and enabling users to access only the specific subsets they require. Consequently, the total size and overhead of evolving scientific datasets are minimized, allowing researchers to efficiently reference and retrieve typical analytical subsets with optimized precision, persistence, and reliability.

Recent years have seen deep-learning-based speech emotion recognition models surpass traditional machine learning approaches. While prior neural network architectures, including Multitask Learning, addressed variations in emotional expression caused by demographic and contextual factors, current models suffer from specific limitations: 1) their dependence on explicit domain definitions (such as gender or noise levels) and corresponding labels, and 2) the tendency to prioritize domain-invariant features despite the domain-specific nature of many emotional expressions. To address these issues, this study introduces the Nonparametric Hierarchical Neural Network (NHNN), a lightweight hierarchical model grounded in Bayesian nonparametric clustering. Unlike Multitask Learning methods, the NHNN operates without requiring domain or task labels. Experimental results demonstrate that NHNN models generally outperform similarly complex models and state-of-the-art baselines in both within-corpus and cross-corpus evaluations. Furthermore, clustering analysis reveals that the NHNN successfully learns group-specific features, effectively narrowing the performance gap between different groups.

Natural language processing (NLP) holds immense promise for advancing materials design, yet a comprehensive, integrated framework equipped with curated datasets and tools remains necessary. This study introduces the ChemNLP library and a complementary web application designed to analyze critical materials chemistry data. Leveraging a publicly available arXiv dataset spanning 34 years with approximately 1.8 million articles, we first examine publication trends, categorizations, and recurring phrases. Subsequently, we developed an interactive, user-friendly web app to retrieve articles based on specific chemical compounds. We further validate the framework's efficacy in accelerating the discovery of superconducting materials by analyzing overlaps between density functional theory and text-based databases. Additionally, we employed machine learning for clustering and classification tasks using article titles, achieving up to 81.2% accuracy. The ChemNLP resources are accessible at https://github.com/usnistgov/chemnlp and https://jarvis.nist.gov/jarvischemnlp.

We provide a complete characterization of circle homeomorphisms that possess a homeomorphic extension to the unit disk with a finite bi-Sobolev norm. This result yields a bi-conformal adaptation of the renowned Beurling-Ahlfors extension theorem as a special case. Additionally, we demonstrate that established extension methods, whether utilizing the harmonic or Beurling-Ahlfors operator, perform inadequately in degenerate contexts. Consequently, we offer an affirmative resolution to a query posed by Karafyllia and Ntalampekos.

We introduce a straightforward yet effective modification to discriminators, termed "measure-conditional discriminators," designed as a plug-and-play component for various GAN architectures. By incorporating generated distributions into the input, the discriminator's target optimum remains stationary, rendering it more robust than standard discriminators. Additionally, a variant of this measure-conditional discriminator can manage multiple target distributions or function as a surrogate for statistical distances like KL divergence, proving useful in transfer learning scenarios.

This study evaluates fully convolutional networks for simulating surface wave motion and interactions within complex open and closed geometries. Specifically, we examine a U-Net architecture to assess its generalization capabilities to geometric configurations absent during training. Our results demonstrate that a modified U-Net can accurately forecast liquid surface height distributions in curved and multi-faceted environments, even when trained exclusively on simple box and right-angled corner shapes. Additionally, we employ an independent 3D CNN for time-interpolation of the U-Net's outputs, enabling the generation of simulations with finer temporal resolution than the original training time-step.

Connecting ion qubits housed in distinct traps remains a significant hurdle in scaling ion quantum computing. This theoretical investigation examines coupling the motional quantum states of ions in separate planar traps via a conducting wire, offering an alternative to laser-based coupling for distant qubits. Incorporating $1/f^{\tilde{\alpha}}$ (anomalous) surface heating noise, our analytical model relies on both aggregate and recent experimental data to determine the motional state decoherence time ($t_{\mathrm{deco.}}$). Our optimized coupling design enables quantum information exchange within a time ($t_{\mathrm{ex.}}$) less than one-tenth of the decoherence time. We introduce a correction coefficient $\zeta$, which relates the capacitances of the coupling system components and rectifies a common oversight in prior studies. Where feasible, we calculate classical signal and noise strengths, applying a classical signal-to-noise ratio criterion of $\ge 10$ to refine design parameters. We discuss ranges for all parameters and plot the ratio $t_{\mathrm{deco.}}/t_{\mathrm{ex.}}$ alongside the thermal noise signal-to-noise ratio to identify viable conditions for quantum information transfer. Despite the constraining influence of $1/f^{\tilde{\alpha}}$ surface noise, we find no obstacles to exchanging quantum information between ion qubits in separate surface traps using a conducting wire. Furthermore, this approach is achievable with current technologies, materials, and singly-charged ions.

This study introduces a novel approach to reconstruct the interparticle interaction potential from statistically averaged structural data, specifically the radial distribution function within many-particle systems. Utilizing a machine learning framework based on the differential evolution algorithm, we demonstrate, using the Lennard-Jones liquid as a case study, that the structure and interparticle potential of a disordered many-particle system at a specific thermodynamic state do not exhibit a one-to-one correspondence. Instead, an entire family of two-parameter Mie potentials, constrained by a specific relationship between parameters $p_1$ and $p_2$, can accurately reproduce the unique structure of the Lennard-Jones liquid. Notably, this family of potentials also correctly predicts transport properties, such as the self-diffusion coefficient across various temperatures, and the dynamic structure factor, a critical indicator of collective particle dynamics.

We demonstrate that Thurston geometries provide solutions to a broad spectrum of 3D quadratic curvature theories, with New Massive Gravity (previously examined in arXiv:2104.00754) serving as a specific instance.

Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) and deep ensembles offer principled methods for estimating predictive uncertainty in deep learning, yet their high memory and inference costs hinder their use in real-time, industrial settings. This limitation drives our investigation into principled uncertainty estimation techniques that rely on a single deep neural network (DNN). By framing uncertainty quantification as a minimax learning problem, we establish that a DNN must possess input distance awareness—the capacity to measure how far a test example lies from the training data in input space—to achieve high-quality, minimax optimal uncertainty estimates. We then introduce Spectral-normalized Neural Gaussian Process (SNGP), a straightforward approach that enhances the distance-awareness of modern DNNs by incorporating a weight normalization step during training and substituting the output layer with a Gaussian process. Evaluated across various vision and language tasks using architectures like Wide-ResNet and BERT, SNGP matches deep ensembles in prediction accuracy, calibration, and out-of-domain detection, while surpassing other single-model methods.

This research applies supervised machine learning (SML) and explainable artificial intelligence (AI) to model, predict, and analyze human decision-making within skilled joint-action scenarios. Long short-term memory networks were trained to forecast target selection choices made by expert and novice participants in a dyadic herding task. Findings indicated that these models were specific to expertise levels, accurately predicting target choices for both groups at timescales preceding conscious intent. To discern the differences in decision-making between experts and novices, the study utilized the SHapley Additive exPlanation (SHAP) technique to determine the significance of various informational features. This analysis demonstrated that experts relied more heavily on information regarding the state of their co-herders than novices did. Finally, the paper discusses the effectiveness of using SML and explainable-AI methods to investigate human decision-making processes.

Interpreting reflectance spectra of airless planetary bodies is significantly complicated by space weathering, specifically surface alteration driven by solar wind irradiation and micrometeoroid impacts. This study aims to assess damage caused by hydrogen (H) ions and femtosecond (fs) laser pulses on samples and correlate these effects with spectral alterations. We irradiated olivine (OL) and pyroxene (OPX) pellets using 5 keV H ions and individual fs laser pulses, then measured their visible (VIS) and near-infrared (NIR) spectra. Additionally, we examined the pellets using scanning and transmission electron microscopy to analyze structural, mineralogical, and chemical modifications linked to reflectance changes. Our findings indicate that H irradiation creates partially amorphous sub-surface layers with small vesicles in both minerals; however, these vesicles are more densely packed in OL pellets than in OPX. Consequently, H irradiation primarily alters the VIS spectral slope. In contrast, laser irradiation effects largely depend on the material's melting temperature. Notably, only laser-irradiated OL contained nanophase iron particles, which caused detectable spectral slope changes across the entire measured range. These results suggest that VIS-NIR spectral variations are primarily governed by the thickness of (partially) amorphous sub-surface layers. Amorphisation smooths microroughness, thereby enhancing volume scattering and absorption relative to surface scattering. Exposure to the space environment quickly generates these amorphous layers, leading to rapid VIS spectral slope changes. In later stages, coinciding with micrometeoroid bombardment, the emergence of nanoparticles is expected to mildly influence the NIR spectral slope. Furthermore, an increase in the dimensions of amorphous layers and vesicles in more space-weathered materials will result in band-depth variations and darkening.

While most prior research on data flow optimizations for ML hardware accelerators focuses on high-level algorithmic refactorizations like loop reordering and tiling, these methods offer limited guidance for mapping onto hardware-executable instructions. This paper introduces "Dijkstra-Through-Time" (DTT), an ahead-of-time scheduling algorithm designed for deterministic workloads that simultaneously handles computation and memory mapping. Although the compilation process is lengthy, DTT offers a straightforward implementation capable of supporting accelerators with complex Network-on-Chip (NoC) configurations. This initial proof of concept demonstrates how integrating scheduling with data cache coherence mechanisms can yield more optimized data flows.

Monte Carlo simulations, utilizing a two-stream kinetic transport equation coupled with a reaction-diffusion equation for bacterial-produced chemoattractants, examine how internal adaptation dynamics influence the self-organized aggregation of chemotactic bacteria. A key discovery is the nonmonotonic relationship between peak aggregation density and adaptation time, where aggregation is maximized when the adaptation time is similar to or moderately exceeds the mean bacterial run time. Additionally, a trapezoidal aggregation profile emerges at very large adaptation times; in this plateau regime, individual cell motion is significantly constrained because the tumbling frequency modulation becomes bounded. The study also performs asymptotic analysis on the kinetic transport system, deriving a new asymptotic equation for the large adaptation-time regime, whereas Keller-Segel type equations apply under moderate adaptation times. Comparing these asymptotic equations with Monte Carlo results demonstrates that the novel equation accurately captures trapezoidal aggregation, while the nonmonotonic peak density behavior is explained as a transient transition of asymptotic solutions across different adaptation time regimes.

Large language models exhibit an emergent capacity to acquire new tasks from limited input-output examples, known as in-context few-shot learning. However, recent studies indicate that in these scenarios, models primarily imitate the task distribution rather than understanding the underlying mechanics. We contend that standard evaluation methods for few-shot models, which randomly select in-context demonstrations, fail to separate a model's ability to learn new skills from the mere exposure of task distributions, as most randomly chosen examples lack information useful for prediction beyond revealing input-output patterns. Consequently, we propose an evaluation framework that distinguishes the gains from in-context learning by selecting demonstrations that share specific, informative concepts with the target samples, alongside those using mostly non-informative examples. Our findings reveal that, irrespective of model size, current few-shot learners cannot leverage such informative concepts in demonstrations. Furthermore, we observe that simply exposing these informative examples during training does not trivially yield this capability, leaving the challenge of training genuine in-context learners unresolved.

We perform a direct, iterative Foldy-Wouthuysen transformation on a general Dirac Hamiltonian interacting with an electromagnetic field, accounting for the anomalous magnetic moment. This process involves iteratively separating the particle and antiparticle Hamiltonians within an expansion for higher momentum orders. We find that the time-derivative term arising from the unitary transformation is essential for supplementing the transverse electric field component at higher orders. Closed-form expressions are derived for combined electric and magnetic fields, covering scenarios with strong magnetic fields. When executed in the standard manner, the time-derivative of the electric field appears only at the seventh order of the fine-structure constant. Particular attention is given to strong-field regimes, which are significant for various applications, including electrons confined in Penning traps.

As demonstrated in \cite{YZ}, global existence for the two-dimensional anisotropic quasi-geostrophic equations in Sobolev spaces $H^s(\R^2)$ with $s\geq 2$ was established under specific constraints on the parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$. This paper extends that result by proving the existence of global solutions within the same Sobolev spaces for the range $\max\{2-2\alpha,2-2\beta\}< s<2$, subject to additional conditions on $\alpha$ and $\beta$. The proof relies on the Gevrey-class regularity of the solution near zero.

The detection of the first confirmed neutron star-black hole (NS-BH) binary mergers by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA collaboration enables an in-depth analysis of the early confirmed and candidate event sample. This study primarily examines the black hole's spin tilt angle relative to the binary's orbital angular momentum and the physical mechanisms governing this orientation. Posterior tilt distributions for GW200115 and candidate events GW190426_152155 and GW190917_114630 peak at significantly anti-aligned configurations, albeit with broad distributions. Achieving such tilts via isolated binary evolution would necessitate stronger natal kicks than typically assumed (and would exclude preferentially-polar kicks) or require an additional tilt source like stable mass transfer. The early NS-BH sample exhibits lower masses than expected for classical formation channels, potentially indicating efficient mass transfer that causes more massive NS-BH binaries to merge before reaching the compact phase. If this interpretation holds, future gravitational-wave detections of NS-BH events are predicted to show total binary masses of approximately 7 M$_{\odot}$ and mass ratios of $q \sim 3$. Conversely, the high mass of candidate GW191219_163120 points toward a dynamical capture origin. Furthermore, large tilts in a substantial fraction of merging NS-BH systems would reduce the likelihood of electromagnetic detection; however, electromagnetic observations, including non-detections, can significantly refine constraints on spin and mass ratio.

Consider the difficulty of monitoring a single fruitfly within a swarm of hundreds. Advanced biological visual systems have developed the ability to track moving entities by leveraging both motion and appearance cues. We examine whether leading deep neural networks for visual tracking possess similar capabilities. To do so, we present PathTracker, a synthetic benchmark requiring both humans and machines to follow a target object among visually identical distractors. While humans quickly master PathTracker and adapt to systematic changes in task design, current state-of-the-art deep networks fail to do so. To overcome this gap, we identify and model circuit mechanisms in biological brains responsible for tracking objects via motion cues. When implemented as a recurrent network, our model learns to solve PathTracker using a robust strategy that matches human performance and accounts for a substantial portion of their decision-making processes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this circuit model's success generalizes to object tracking in natural video sequences. Integrating it into a transformer-based tracking architecture enhances resilience against visual distractions affecting object appearance, yielding new state-of-the-art results on the large-scale TrackingNet benchmark. Our research underscores the value of developing artificial vision models that not only advance computer vision but also deepen our understanding of human vision.

Galaxies experience mass loss due to their luminosity or gaseous outflows. I have computed the consequent outward radial migration of stars, demonstrating that it may be detectable using high-resolution spectrographs on upcoming large telescopes. Conversely, significant matter accretion within dense cosmic regions could induce inward stellar migration, a phenomenon that would be even more readily observable.

A recent publication in *Nature Physics* achieved a synthesis of thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, and information theory through a universal equation governing the temporal evolution of a system's information content. This equation quantifies the variation in the moments of an observable quantity across a probability distribution, comprising two distinct components: one representing shifts in the distribution itself and the other reflecting changes in the observable values for specific states. The authors demonstrate that this general framework for moment dynamics is mathematically equivalent to the Price equation from evolutionary biology, originally formulated by George Price. The discussion traces the equation's origins in biological contexts, examines its abstract mathematical formulation, and explores its capacity to unify disparate theoretical frameworks across various disciplines. Furthermore, the findings in *Nature Physics*, alongside applications in biology, indicate that this equation serves as a foundational tool for deriving new theoretical insights within each respective field.

Wu & Peek (2020) utilize machine learning to forecast SDSS-grade spectra from Pan-STARRS \textit{grizy} imaging. This study evaluates their method on UGC 2885, an isolated, massive disk galaxy ("Rubin's galaxy") within 100 Mpc. We compared the machine-learned spectrum against comparable existing spectroscopic data for the galaxy's center, including two archival datasets (one from VIRUS-P) and a new targeted MMT/Binospec observation. While the results show qualitative agreement, the ML prediction leans slightly toward active galactic nucleus (AGN) line ratios compared to the observed values. The new MMT/Binospec nuclear spectrum confirms strong emission lines (excluding H$\beta$) with ratios indicative of AGN activity. Consequently, the ML approach could serve as a viable complement to NIR colors for identifying AGN. However, the mechanism by which this massive, non-interacting disk galaxy ($M^* = 10^{11}$ M$_\odot$) powers its central AGN remains an open question requiring further investigation.

We utilize a kinetic-rate equation to assess the transport dynamics of $J/\psi$, $\psi(2S)$, $B_c$, and X(3872) within ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, subsequently comparing their production yields against experimental results from the Large Hadron Collider. This equation is governed by two primary transport parameters: the equilibrium limit and the reaction rate for each state. The temperature-dependent equilibrium limits are determined by charm- and bottom-quark fugacities derived from their initial production. Reaction rates for charmonia, bottomonia, and $B_c$ depend on charm- and bottom-quark masses and binding energies calculated using a thermodynamic $T$-matrix approach. Regarding the X(3872) particle, its internal structure is represented in the reaction rates and initial conditions of the hadronic phase through two distinct scenarios: a loosely bound hadronic molecule or a compact diquark-antidiquark tetraquark.

Although neural abstractive summarization models are widely recognized, there remains a significant gap in understanding their internal decision-making processes and how they construct summaries. We introduce a two-step interpretability framework designed to elucidate these decisions. Initially, we analyze the model's behavior by ablating the complete architecture to classify each decoder step into specific generation modes—ranging from language-model-like behavior to heavy reliance on the input or intermediate states. Once we isolate decisions that genuinely depend on the input, we evaluate various attribution techniques to interpret them. We assess these methods by their capacity to select relevant content and reconstruct the model's predicted tokens following input perturbations, thereby verifying the true importance of the highlighted attributions for token generation. While this approach holds broad utility beyond summarization, we specifically apply it to pinpoint phrases that the model has memorized and trace the location of this memorization within the training pipeline. Additionally, we utilize this framework to examine complex generation phenomena, such as sentence fusion, on an individual instance basis.

We introduce a multi-class point optimization framework grounded in continuous Wasserstein barycenters. This approach is engineered to manage hundreds to thousands of optimization goals and includes a practical optimization strategy. We validate our framework's efficacy across diverse sampling tasks, such as stippling, object placement, and Monte-Carlo integration. Additionally, we derive a multi-class error bound for perceptual rendering error that can be minimized through our proposed optimization. The source code is available at https://github.com/iribis/filtered-sliced-optimal-transport.

Ly-$\alpha$ tomography surveys are now generating three-dimensional maps of intergalactic medium (IGM) opacity at $z \sim 2.5$ with Mpc-scale resolution, offering a promising avenue to identify and study high-redshift overdensities such as protogroups and protoclusters—the ancestors of modern massive galaxy clusters and groups. Leveraging the IllustrisTNG-$300$ hydrodynamical simulation, we construct mock maps that faithfully replicate observations from the Ly-$\alpha$ Tomographic IMACS Survey (LATIS). We present a new technique for defining the boundaries of structures within 3D Ly-$\alpha$ flux maps by utilizing the watershed algorithm. Furthermore, we develop estimators for the dark matter masses of these structures at $z\sim2.5$, their descendant halo masses at $z=0$, and the associated uncertainties, while also evaluating the method's completeness for detecting protogroups and protoclusters. Unlike previous studies, our approach characterizes structures across a broader mass range, extending to massive protogroups. Additionally, we assess the fluctuating Gunn-Peterson approximation (FGPA) commonly used in dark-matter-only simulations; although adequate for estimating Ly-$\alpha$ absorption from moderate-to-massive protoclusters ($ \gtrsim 10^{14.2} M_{\odot}$), we find it erroneously merges a subset of lower-mass structures with more massive neighbors. Our methodology will be deployed on current and upcoming Ly-$\alpha$ tomography surveys to compile overdensity catalogs and investigate environment-dependent galaxy evolution during the Cosmic Noon era.

Subhalo Abundance Matching (SHAM) has significantly advanced our comprehension of how galaxies occupy their host dark matter halos. Fundamentally, the SHAM method seeks to identify a dark matter halo characteristic that most strongly correlates with a specific galaxy property, such as stellar mass. While the peak maximum circular velocity ($V_{\rm peak}$) achieved over a halo's lifetime has traditionally been a preferred metric, Tonnesen & Ostriker (2021) recently proposed that a combined quantity, $\phi$ (integrating current $V_{\rm max}$ and peak dark matter mass), offers superior predictions for stellar mass compared to $V_{\rm peak}$. Building on this insight, the current study demonstrates that performance can be further enhanced by a new metric, $\psi_5$, which merges the 90th percentile of a halo's historical $V_{\rm max}$ with the 60th percentile of its dark matter mass variation rate. Validation using the IllustrisTNG300 simulation reveals that this updated SHAM framework, requiring only three free parameters, boosts stellar mass prediction accuracy and mass-dependent clustering by 15% and 16%, respectively, relative to the $\phi$ method across the redshift interval $z=0-2$.

This research investigates the classic challenge of fairly distributing a heterogeneous, divisible resource—modeled as a cake $[0,1]$—among $n$ agents, focusing on a novel variant where agents are positioned within a graph. In this setting, an agent's envy-freeness is determined solely by comparing their allocated share to those of their immediate neighbors. The objective is to efficiently compute a locally envy-free allocation, ensuring every agent values their portion at least as highly as any of their neighbors'. While the best existing algorithm for general envy-free cake divisions by Aziz and Mackenzie suffers from hyper-exponential query complexity, this work introduces a significant contribution by identifying a specific non-trivial graph structure: tree graphs with a depth of at most two (Depth2Tree) for $n$ agents that supports a query-efficient protocol under the Robertson-Webb model. Specifically, we present a discrete algorithm that achieves a locally envy-free allocation for Depth2Tree graphs using no more than $O(n^3 \log(n))$ cuts. Furthermore, for the specialized case of a 2-Star graph (a Depth2Tree where every non-root node connects to at most two others), we demonstrate that $O(n^2)$ queries are sufficient. Finally, we complement these algorithmic findings with a lower bound of $\Omega(n^2)$ evaluation queries required to find a locally envy-free allocation for a 1-Star graph, assuming the root agent partitions the cake into $n$ connected segments.

This paper presents direct ATLAS detector searches at the LHC for lepton flavor violation in $Z$ boson decays, specifically examining channels where the $Z$ boson decays into an electron or muon paired with a hadronically decaying $\tau$ lepton. The analysis utilizes a dataset of proton-proton collisions recorded by ATLAS during 2015 and 2016, totaling an integrated luminosity of 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. No significant excess over the predicted background was found, leading to 95% confidence level upper limits on the branching ratios of $\mathcal{B} (Z\to e\tau) < 5.8 \times 10^{-5}$ and $\mathcal{B} (Z\to \mu\tau) < 2.4 \times 10^{-5}$. Notably, this represents the first ATLAS-based constraint on $\mathcal{B} (Z\to e\tau)$. For the $\mu\tau$ channel, the new limit is combined with a prior ATLAS result from 20.3 fb$^{-1}$ of data at $\sqrt{s} = 8$ TeV, yielding a combined 95% confidence level upper limit of $\mathcal{B} (Z\to \mu\tau) < 1.3 \times 10^{-5}$.

The Heidelberg MCTDH package was employed to simulate the intramolecular vibrational relaxation dynamics of formic acid and its deuterated variants using the full-dimensional potential energy surface developed by Richter and Carbonniere [J. Chem. Phys., 148, 064303 (2018)]. Analysis of artificially excited vibrational mode overtones reveals significant mode couplings involving the torsion coordinate, which primarily governs trans-cis isomerisation. Specifically, in HCOOH, the C-O stretch bright mode couples with the out-of-plane torsion mode, a relationship that could facilitate laser-induced trans-to-cis isomerisation. Distinct isotopic effects are evident: deuteration of the hydroxyl group (as seen in HCOOD and DCOOD) eliminates the coupling between the C-O stretch and torsion modes, whereas deuteration of the carbonyl group (in DCOOH) results in little to no change.

Modern high-performance computing (HPC) resources and optimized applications are essential for large-scale electronic structure calculations. Real-space grid-based Density Functional Theory (DFT) implementations utilizing the Projector Augmented Wave (PAW) method offer accuracy comparable to plane-wave basis set codes while demonstrating superior scalability on distributed memory systems. However, the performance of PAW Hamiltonian projection operations is often constrained by memory bandwidth limitations. This study explores the effectiveness of employing a 3D factorizable Hermite function basis for localized PAW projector functions, a strategy designed to minimize bandwidth demands during grid-based projection. By implementing additional on-the-fly sampling of 1D basis functions, the need for memory transfers is nearly eliminated. To quantitatively evaluate anticipated bandwidth reductions, we present performance data from an initial GPU implementation. Furthermore, we propose a PAW generation scheme tailored to the analytically defined projector functions.

We develop a complementary short-range correlation relativistic local-density-approximation functional designed for relativistic range-separated density-functional theory, utilizing a Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonian under the no-pair approximation. This process involves conducting relativistic random-phase-approximation calculations to determine the correlation energy of the relativistic homogeneous electron gas with an adjusted electron-electron interaction, analyzing high-density behavior, and fitting the findings to a parametrized formula. The resulting functional is anticipated to prove valuable for electronic-structure computations of strongly correlated systems involving heavy elements.

Local moments are a common feature in disordered semiconductors like Si:P, appearing in both metallic and insulating states. This study examines local moment dynamics specifically within disordered insulators, driven by short-range repulsive electron-electron interactions. We investigate paradigmatic models of interacting insulators—namely, one-dimensional Hubbard chains with quenched randomness—using density matrix renormalization group and strong-disorder renormalization group techniques. Our analysis of chains featuring random fermion hoppings or random chemical potentials, across both half-filling and away-from-half-filling regimes, reveals exponential decay in charge and fermion two-point correlations, alongside power-law decay in spin correlations characteristic of the random singlet phase. These numerical findings can be qualitatively explained by considering the large-interaction limit of the Hubbard chain, where a remarkably simple conceptual framework emerges.

Acquiring detailed annotations represents a major hurdle in training deep networks for part segmentation. We introduce a framework designed to leverage readily available coarse labels, such as figure-ground masks and keypoint locations, to enhance part segmentation performance for specific categories. A primary obstacle is the misalignment in labeling styles and collection tasks between these coarse annotations and standard part labels, making direct mapping difficult. To address this, we propose jointly learning the relationships between varying labeling styles and the segmentation model, thereby enabling the use of supervision from diverse data sources. To validate our method, we established a benchmark using the Caltech-UCSD Birds and OID Aircraft datasets. Our results demonstrate superior performance compared to baselines utilizing multi-task learning, semi-supervised learning, as well as competitive approaches that rely on manually crafted loss functions for sparse supervision.

This study introduces a rapid decorrelated neuro-ensemble leveraging heterogeneous features for large-scale data analytics. It utilizes Stochastic Configuration Networks (SCNs) as base learners and applies the established Negative Correlation Learning (NCL) strategy to determine output weights. Processing a vast number of samples through the SCN base models generates a massive linear system that is challenging to solve using the pseudo-inverse method typical of least squares approaches. Instead, the paper employs block Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel methods to iteratively compute output weights based on the heterogeneous feature set, providing a convergence analysis that demonstrates the uniqueness of these iterative solutions. Experiments conducted on two large-scale datasets compare the proposed method's robustness regarding the regularizing factor in NCL. The results suggest that these ensemble learning techniques hold significant promise for addressing large-scale data modeling challenges.

While convection zones in most stars transport heat via fluid motion, the dynamics at their boundaries remain poorly understood. This study introduces 3D numerical simulations that reveal "penetration zones": areas where the temperature gradient is nearly adiabatic and convection occurs, despite the potential for the entire luminosity to be radiatively transported. To quantify this phenomenon, we define a "penetration parameter" ($\mathcal{P}$), which measures the deviation of the radiative gradient from the adiabatic gradient across the Schwarzschild convective boundary. Building on the energy-based frameworks of Roxburgh (1989) and Zahn (1991), we develop a theoretical model where $\mathcal{P}$ dictates the depth of penetration. We validate this theory using 3D simulations based on a simplified Boussinesq model of stellar convection, driven by internal heating with height-dependent radiative conductivity. This setup allows for independent control of $\mathcal{P}$ and the boundary stiffness ($\mathcal{S}$). Our results show significant convective penetration across all simulations, which the proposed theory accurately predicts. Because developing these zones requires thousands of overturn times, long-duration runs or accelerated evolutionary methods are necessary. In stellar environments, we anticipate $\mathcal{P} \approx 1$; under these conditions, our findings indicate that convection zones may extend beyond the Schwarzschild boundary by approximately 20–30% of a mixing length. We demonstrate the viability of our parameterization with a MESA model of the Sun and discuss potential applications to more realistic stellar scenarios.

This paper introduces a novel multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communication framework utilizing movable antennas (MAs) to leverage position optimization for capacity enhancement. Unlike conventional MIMO systems that rely on fixed-position antennas (FPAs), the proposed architecture allows for the flexible adjustment of transmit and receive MA locations, thereby reconfiguring the MIMO channel to achieve superior capacity. Our primary objective is to characterize the capacity of point-to-point MIMO systems enabled by MAs through the joint optimization of transmit and receive MA positions and the transmit signal covariance. First, we present an efficient alternating optimization algorithm that iteratively refines the transmit covariance matrix and individual MA positions to find a locally optimal solution while holding other variables constant. Subsequently, we introduce lower-complexity alternative algorithms tailored for capacity maximization in low-SNR scenarios and for multiple-input single-output (MISO) and single-input multiple-output (SIMO) configurations. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed MA systems significantly outperform traditional FPA systems and various benchmark schemes in terms of MIMO channel capacity, yielding valuable insights into the capacity advantages of MA-based systems.

A critical reevaluation of the high-temperature effective potential in Yang-Mills theory, originally derived by Gross, Pisarski, Yaffe, and Weiss, concludes that the ground state at <A0>=0 is invalid because of infrared divergences arising from the Matsubara zero mode. This implies that the thermal ground state is primarily governed by infrared non-perturbative effects. Supporting this, lattice simulations conducted in the static gauge reveal that the field A0 acquires nonzero, non-perturbative expectation values at high temperatures. Consequently, thermal perturbation theory is deemed inconsistent with this non-perturbative ground state and is incapable of accounting for all contributions to thermodynamic quantities across any temperature. The discussion further addresses related topics such as dimensional reduction and confinement.

AT2019wey is a Galactic low-mass X-ray binary featuring a potential black hole accretor, initially detected as an optical transient by ATLAS in December 2019 and later linked to an X-ray source identified by SRG in March 2020. Following an X-ray brightening in August 2020, VLA observations showed the source's spectrum evolving from optically thin to optically thick as radio emissions intensified. This prompted VLBA observations, which revealed a resolved structure interpreted as a steady compact jet—a characteristic of black hole X-ray binaries in the hard spectral state. The jet's power is comparable to the X-ray luminosity of the accretion disk. This paper summarizes the findings from these observations.

A realistic extension of the minimal $SU(5)$ model, achieved by adding an adjoint fermion, is predicted to yield light real scalar and fermion weak triplets that could be detected at the LHC. Beyond their crucial role in gauge coupling unification, these particles carry significant phenomenological consequences. The fermion triplet, which provides a testable source of neutrino mass via the seesaw mechanism, has been widely studied. In contrast, the scalar triplet acquires a vacuum expectation value that alters the $W$-boson mass. We demonstrate that its low-energy effective theory is highly predictive: in the leading approximation, all relevant physical processes involving the scalar triplet are determined solely by its mass and the deviation of the $W$-mass from the Standard Model prediction.

Nonadiabatic holonomic quantum transformations (NHQTs) have garnered significant attention for their applications in quantum computing, though prior studies have largely remained within quantum physics. This work introduces the application of NHQTs to construct a unidirectional acoustic metamaterial (UDAM) for shaping classical beams. The UDAM consists of an array of three-waveguide couplers, in which acoustic wave propagation simulates the evolution of NHQTs. The strong consistency between analytical predictions, numerical simulations, and experimental results validates the potential of NHQTs in acoustic metamaterial engineering. By extending NHQT research from quantum physics to classical wave systems, this study enables the design of metamaterials with simple structures and offers a novel pathway for developing UDAMs with applications in acoustic isolation, communication, and stealth.

Depth data is valuable across numerous image processing tasks, yet because capturing an image involves projecting a three-dimensional scene onto a two-dimensional sensor, this depth information is inherently encoded within the image itself. Extracting it poses a significant challenge. A fundamental principle suggests that the degree of defocus blur correlates with the distance between an object and the focal plane. Leveraging this principle and the common assumption that Gaussian blur effectively models defocus, we frame the estimation of spatially varying defocus as a Gaussian blur classification problem. This was addressed by training a deep neural network to categorize image patches into one of twenty distinct blur levels. To facilitate this, we constructed a dataset comprising over 500,000 $32\times32$ image patches for training and evaluating various established network architectures. Our findings indicate that MobileNetV2 is particularly well-suited for this task due to its combination of low memory consumption and high accuracy. The trained model first estimates patch blurriness, which is subsequently refined using an iterative weighted guided filter to produce a defocus map representing the blur degree for every pixel. When compared to state-of-the-art methods, our approach demonstrates success in applications such as adaptive image enhancement, defocus magnification, and multi-focus image fusion.

Active Malware Analysis entails simulating malware behavior by performing actions to elicit responses and investigate various execution trajectories. A primary objective is to optimize the efficiency of action selection. This study models Active Malware Analysis as a Bayes-Active Markov Decision Process and employs a Bayesian Model Combination technique to train an analyzer agent. The results demonstrate enhanced performance compared to other Bayesian and stochastic methods used in Active Malware Analysis.

Driven by the need to enhance diversity within social networks, we examine pattern formation challenges on ring topologies. In this setup, $n$ mobile agents, each assigned a unique colour from the set $\{c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_q\}$, are distributed across the nodes of an $n$-node ring. The ring is segmented into $k$ contiguous blocks, each of length $p$. The objective is for agents to autonomously rearrange themselves to meet specific diversity constraints: every block $j$ must contain exactly $n_i(j) > 0$ agents of each colour $c_i$. Agents possess visibility of adjacent blocks and can transition to any node within those blocks in a single time step. For the case of two colours ($q=2$), we present an algorithm that concludes in $N_1/n^*_1 + k + 4$ steps, where $N_1$ represents the total count of agents with colour $c_1$ and $n^*_1$ denotes the minimum required number of such agents in any block. If diversity requirements are uniform across all blocks, our method achieves the goal in $3k+4$ steps, which is asymptotically optimal. Furthermore, the algorithm extends to handle an arbitrary number of colours, terminating within $O(nk)$ steps. We also demonstrate how to adapt this approach to realize any specific final pattern, assuming at least one agent of every colour exists within each target pattern.

Early detection is regarded as a critical component of cerebral palsy (CP) management. We introduce an affordable and interpretable classification framework to aid CP prediction using General Movement Assessment (GMA). This system employs a PyTorch-based attention-enhanced graph convolutional network to identify infants at risk of CP from skeletal data derived from RGB videos. Additionally, we incorporate a frequency-binning module to capture CP-related movements in the frequency domain while suppressing noise. By utilizing only consumer-grade RGB videos for training, our approach enables interactive-time CP prediction and delivers interpretable classification outcomes.

Organized into three sections, the first addresses significant geometric challenges associated with the concept of quasi-freeness for an algebra and proposes substituting formal smoothness with the smoothness of a minimal unital commutative algebra as an approximation. The second section focuses on approximating the properties of non-commutative (nc) schemes by utilizing two uniquely determined classical schemes: one that bounds the nc scheme from within maximally and another that approximates it from the outside via a minimal scheme. The concise final section aims to philosophically analyze and extract the principles underlying the construction of any "scheme-like" object over a suitable category.

Grasping the physics of turbulent transport in the tokamak edge and scrape-off layer (SOL) is essential for the success of fusion reactors. The dynamics within these regions are pivotal for achieving high performance, as they govern the formation of the H-mode pedestal that suppresses turbulence. Furthermore, a reactor's viability depends on the heat load imposed on vessel walls, highlighting the need to comprehend how turbulent heat spreads along open magnetic field lines in the SOL. Simulating turbulence in the edge and SOL is more complex than in the core due to large-amplitude fluctuations, magnetic X-point geometries, and plasma-wall interactions, which necessitate specialized gyrokinetic codes. Moreover, incorporating electromagnetic effects into gyrokinetic simulations capable of addressing boundary plasma challenges is crucial for understanding phenomena like the pedestal and Edge Localized Modes (ELMs), where electromagnetic dynamics play a significant role.

This thesis establishes the first capability for simulating electromagnetic gyrokinetic turbulence on open magnetic field lines, a vital advancement toward comprehensive simulations of the coupled edge/SOL system. By employing a continuum full-f approach through an energy-conserving discontinuous Galerkin (DG) discretization scheme that circumvents the Ampere cancellation issue, we demonstrate that electromagnetic fluctuations can be managed robustly, stably, and efficiently within the Gkeyll code's gyrokinetic module. Subsequently, we present results approximating the scrape-off layer of the National Spherical Torus Experiment (NSTX), illustrating that electromagnetic effects influence blob dynamics and transport. Finally, we formulate the gyrokinetic system in field-aligned coordinates to model realistic edge and scrape-off layer geometries found in experiments.

We report the discovery of four new fast radio bursts (FRBs) identified by analyzing the Parkes 70-cm pulsar survey archive for dispersed single pulses. Using the HEIMDALL and FETCH algorithms, we searched across dispersion measures (DMs) from 0 to 5000 pc cm$^{-3}$. All four newly found FRBs exhibit significantly broader widths ($> 50$ ms) compared to nearly all previously cataloged FRBs, with these large widths not primarily caused by interstellar scattering or channel dispersive smearing. One of these bursts possesses a DM of 3338 pc cm$^{-3}$, the highest recorded to date. Furthermore, these detections predate the Lorimer Burst by nearly ten years, marking them as the first FRBs ever observed by any radio telescope. Our findings indicate that pulsar survey archives continue to be valuable for uncovering undetected FRBs and suggest that extending search durations beyond approximately 100 ms could reveal a larger population of wide-pulse FRBs.

The analysis presents results from beyond the Standard Model Higgs boson searches utilizing up to 8.2 inverse femtobarns of data from the Tevatron's Run II. Since no significant excess was detected in any channel, 95% confidence level limits are provided.

Bounds for the quantum Fisher information and signal-to-noise ratio regarding the estimation of moments for general partially coherent objects have been established. Within an asymptotic framework applicable to the sub-Rayleigh regime, these bounds prove to be less stringent than those applicable to incoherent cases. Consequently, this suggests that the moments of object distributions may be estimated with greater precision when the object exhibits partial coherence.

Non-standard interactions (NSI) between neutrinos and electrons can substantially alter the process by which neutrinos decouple from the plasma. These interactions influence the broader physical picture in two ways: (i) they change neutrino oscillations via matter effects, and (ii) they affect scattering and annihilation events involving neutrinos, electrons, and positrons. This study investigates the impact of non-universal and flavour-changing NSI on neutrino decoupling and their consequences for determining the effective number of neutrinos, $N_{eff}$. We analyze degeneracies among NSI parameters and contrast the anticipated sensitivity of future cosmological surveys with existing constraints from terrestrial experiments, highlighting the complementary nature of these two methodologies.
